en: Preface to the *Lengyan jianglu*:
The teachings of all Buddhas comprise the provisional and the real, the universal and the particular, the partial and the complete, and the small, the initial, the final, the sudden, and the perfect.
In their skillful accommodation of capacities and their expounding of the Dharma, they may be esoteric or manifest, extensive or concise, and may employ both bestowal and withdrawal.
Sometimes they reverse the order to accord with the sequence; sometimes they roar like lions or thunder, sweeping away all traces and cutting off all vestiges.

Furthermore, as this teaching was transmitted to our land of Zhendan (China), the capacities of those who received it were diverse, and the karmic conditions that reached them were likewise different.
Among the successive masters who ascended the Dharma King’s throne and proclaimed the Dharma from their lips, who did not recognize this *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as the foremost among all [scriptures]?
The twelve divisions of the teachings are all subsumed within this sūtra, yet its underlying reasons have never been explained in detail.
How, then, can those among the ranks of beginners believe and accept it? Is this not tantamount to a hazy and confused understanding of True Suchness (tathatā)?

Having searched through this sūtra for many years, I possess a reliable lineage of transmission. I pray that you will not be sparing with your speech, but will investigate this thoroughly for the sake of the fourfold assembly. (Chengshi)
May those who have previously expounded this know that there are those who believe and accept it, yet for whom it is not easily seen or heard.
For this sutra represents the World-Honored One’s final and ultimate discourse; it emerges after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and precedes the *Nirvāṇa*.
According to the text itself, Ānanda states that the World-Honored One was conversing with Mañjuśrī and other Dharma-princes regarding reality.

Regarding the timing: since Yaśodharā received her prediction after the World-Honored One had already spoken [the *Yaśodharā-dhāraṇī*], we know it must have been composed after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
When the World-Honored One was about to preach the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, Ānanda was absent. Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "Ānanda has been disturbed by Māra.
The World-Honored One then spoke a dhāraṇī and commanded Mañjuśrī to go and restrain him; how could one know that this was not intended to rescue and bring back Ānanda?
If the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* were taught first and the *Nirvāṇa* afterward, one would know that it must precede the *Nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the World-Honored One spoke of two meanings for *nirvāṇa*:

First, for those whose capacities had not yet matured through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he subsequently taught the four vehicles (*catur-yāna*), fully expounding the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) so that they might realize the true permanence and enter Great *Nirvāṇa*;
this is therefore called the "Teaching for Gathering the Remnants of Latent Capacities" (*kunsik can-gi kyō*). Second, for...

Monks of the final age will possess impure things and delight in reciting non-Buddhist scriptures; having lost both their precepts and their vehicle, they will give rise to the view of annihilationism and forfeit the Dharma-body.
Therefore, [the Buddha] further presents the Tripiṭaka to extensively expound the doctrine of the eternal, establishing three kinds of provisional means to support the one perfect reality.

Thus, this is called the teaching that "supports the Vinaya and discusses the Eternal. From the point where Ānanda requests [the teaching on] the single mind and the three contemplations, the world...

The World-Honored One revealed the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama and elucidated the nature of the three Tathāgata-garbhas, leading from the stage of Dry Wisdom directly into the ocean of the fruit of Sublime Enlightenment—this is precisely the primary meaning of Nirvāṇa.

When Ānanda requested instruction on the skillful means for delivering sentient beings, the Buddha taught the four kinds of restraint and further extensively explained the seven destinies, all of which are summoned and experienced through deluded karma. Thus...
The demonic signs of *dhyāna* and the root of the five aggregates constitute the second meaning of *nirvāṇa*.
In the *Āgama* assemblies, the World-Honored One spoke only of the causes and effects for humans and devas to guide beginners.

This sutra, however, explains the three types of continuity, the ten habitual causes, and the sixfold mutual retribution, extensively clarifying the causes and effects of the seven realms of existence; thus, the teachings of the *Āgamas* are already fully contained herein.

At the assembly on the Prajñāpāramitā, the World-Honored One taught that the four noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings are fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning, and that the causes and effects of the primary and secondary realms are like illusions and dreams;

this was intended solely for those of superior faculties. This sutra explains the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and the seven great elements, all of which are like flowers in the sky or a whirling firebrand, and even states that they are not the five aggregates or the four great elements, nor the Four Noble Truths or the Six Perfections, nor Bodhi or Nirvana.

The *Bannihuan jing* (Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) is likewise complete in its teaching of Prajñā. At the assembly of the Vaipulya sūtras, the World-Honored One taught that which is neither empty nor existent, yet is both empty and existent, desiring to universally benefit those of the three faculties.
This sūtra also teaches that the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are themselves [the Buddha-nature], as are the seven great elements.
This refers to the Four Noble Truths and the Six Perfections; it is Bodhi and Nirvana, and even that which is neither identical to nor separate from them.

Thus, the Vaipulya teachings are fully complete. At the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, the World-Honored One preached the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge and the Perfect and Sudden One Vehicle for those of the highest capacity.

Yet this sutra also states: "The nature of madness ceases of its own accord; when it ceases, that is Bodhi. This is precisely that which is neither identical to nor separate from [the aforementioned]. It transcends both identity and separation.
It is free from the non-existent; it revolves within a single atom and manifests lands upon the tip of a hair. Its great nature is inherently pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm;
its wondrous enlightenment is profoundly still, yet it encompasses and breathes forth the ten voids. How does this differ from the four kinds of unimpededness?

At the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, the World-Honored One bestowed predictions that those of the three vehicles would all attain Buddhahood. This sūtra proceeds from the stage of Dry Wisdom through fifty [stages].

Having traversed the five stages of the path to Bodhi, one subsequently enters the two types of perfect enlightenment, Samyaksaṃbodhi and Pratyekabuddhabodhi. Furthermore, how does this differ from the Lotus Sūtra?
Therefore, this sūtra not only encompasses the five teachings in their entirety, but also perfectly subsumes the three schools. Indeed, sūtras such as the Lotus and the Avataṃsaka...

It is that which penetrates the inner sanctum of all the sutras. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* is that which simultaneously threads together the veins and arteries of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other scriptures.
Were it not for one who has read all the sutras extensively, how could they recognize the subtlety of this scripture?
And were it not for one who is thoroughly conversant with this scripture, how could they know it to be the guiding principle of all the sutras? After the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa, the devas...

The Venerable Daizhi had silently noted that this sūtra existed in the Western Regions. For eighteen years, he gazed toward it from afar and paid homage morning and evening, yet his wish remained unfulfilled.
Later, he was moved by the Venerable Prajñāmitra, who desired to disseminate it in this land;
though the King summoned him back three times, the Venerable secretly transcribed it upon fine white cotton cloth, concealed it within his broken arm, and personally delivered it.
This text was translated and presented for imperial review. At that time, however, the court was preoccupied with many affairs and had no leisure to promulgate it.
An edict was issued for National Preceptor Xiu to enter the palace and provide an exposition. The Master took this scripture with him when he subsequently departed for Tiangong Monastery in Luoyang.

Later, when the Master passed away, the Emperor accorded him the rites due to a prince and escorted his remains to Dumen Monastery in Dangyang; the scripture was also taken along with him. At that time, its circulation had not yet spread widely.
It was on the verge of being lost to oblivion when Dharma Master Huizheng visited Du-men and obtained it, whereupon he first began to proclaim it.

Thus, while it is certainly fortunate that this sutra has now reached this land and is clearly manifest and evident, when we reflect back upon its origins, how circuitous and winding was its path, and how arduous and obstructed were its transitions! Could this not be due to the Buddha’s compassion?

He compassionately bestowed expedient means; yet, as the faculties, capacities, and dispositions of sentient beings, as well as the temporal conditions and circumstances of this land, vary and differ, there are those to whom he did not lightly transmit [the teachings], nor were they easily able to believe or hear them.
(At that time,) I served my original teacher, the Venerable Monk Dumenji, for many years. My resolve was keen toward the Two Peaks (Ryōzen), and even a single word or half a verse was not...

When my mind was at ease, it felt as though I were ill or delirious; I would have sacrificed my head, eyes, brain, and marrow without a moment’s regret, determined solely to directly realize the Heart-Essence and ascend to the supreme life of wisdom.
Fortunate to have been encouraged by my original teacher, I occasionally discerned the intent through the words and met the mind apart from the text.

Through winter and summer I polished and refined myself, day and night I forged and tempered my spirit; shedding blood and vomiting out my heart, everything was nothing other than a sincere recognition of the Buddha’s intent.
The profound reach [of this work] thoroughly sweeps away the entanglements of various schools. A single commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* has recently been published;

however, regarding the lecture records of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, whenever I was at the lecture hall, I would seek the essence of the teachings and follow the oral instructions, never easily committing to pen those accounts that directly describe the fundamental source.
Recently, during the beginning of the Tianqi era, while resting at the Dashishan Hermitage on Mount Yu, I was fortunate enough to meet with the Layman Zhi...
The masters Fang Sun, Hong Su Zhang, Kongru Cheng, and Kuiyang Shen, on behalf of the various dhyāna practitioners, earnestly requested that you preside over the Dharma at the East Pagoda Hermitage.
You have graciously consented to expound it before the assembly; at that time, both the monastics and the laity will rejoice and long to hear it.
This shall be nothing more than following the natural intent of the scriptures, acting as the oral flame of the Awakened King, which we dare not [alter].

A single word that contradicts the ancestral teachings was, at one time, accepted and believed by the great assembly, all of whom considered it clear, manifest, and easy to understand—like traveling along a broad thoroughfare while abandoning the mountain paths.
Thereupon, the layman of constant virtue, Master Wang, firmly resolved to request its publication.
At that time, he firmly declined, saying: "I have long dared not engage in flowery speech or ornate rhetoric.
How could I dare to follow in the footsteps of the masters of Wenzhou and Changshui? The layman said: "Not so. What you have spoken is as it truly is; what you have heard is as it truly is.
This is truly what is called not being hindered by verbal designations, not treading upon established tracks, and not engaging in mere embellishment. This...

The *sūtras* thread together all scriptures, yet this discourse threads together all teachings. By means of the pen and tongue of a single moment, it serves as a ladder and a vessel for ten thousand ages.
To repay the Buddha’s grace above and to benefit all beings below—is this not truly great? (At that time) Weiwei said: "I have heard it said:

'To explain the meaning by relying solely on the literal text is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three periods; to depart from a single word of the *sūtra* is equivalent to the teaching of Māra.'"

Between neither relying upon nor departing from [the text], there exists something most subtle. (At that time) it was said: "Those who merely explain the meaning by relying on the words do not go beyond them;
I only wish that you would listen to the words so as to penetrate what lies beyond both the text and its meaning. Would it not be a grievance for one who might thus come to understand?
If one were to involve even a single word of forced interpretation, thereby deviating from and contradicting the original scripture, how could I dare to allow myself to become a demon?"
This is indeed a demonic act. Now, if one were to unify all sutras through a single scripture, then one might venture to clarify and deduce the profound purport of this sutra.
However, to attempt to erroneously unify various doctrines based on the words of a single corner [of a text] is something you, Layman, must investigate in secret.
Otherwise, I shall ultimately not dare to believe it to be so. I request that you examine this with me.
Preface to the *Lengyan jianglu* (Record of Lectures on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra), written by Zhuyi Mingyan on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment in the Renxu year, as revealed by Heaven,
at the Dashi Mountain Hermitage.
If we discuss this matter, it reaches the point where the Buddhas of the three periods of time have their mouths hanging on the wall.

Even if one can realize it beyond the side of Bhīṣmagarjitasvaras and even further beyond that, such a person is still but a dull-witted fellow. Furthermore, why labor to establish a great, firm samādhi? Why do you take golden dust into your eyes?
It is simply because in this defiled Sahā world, all beings take sexual desire as the very basis for their life and nature; therefore, there is the toil of purifying and adorning [the land].
Ānanda, you have merely acted as a bystander on the scene. Since this venerable one has already carved away the flesh to create a wound, he has "proven the tortoise to be a turtle.

Yet our Master, Preceptor Chaizi, because he had a secret entrustment, provided the final strokes for him, so that all who see or hear may use a wedge to extract a wedge, thereby attaining the wondrously pure and bright mind-nature and the wondrously pure and bright essence of the body. You should know that this was the Lankavatara Assembly.
Above, not a single word was ever spoken; it is no different from the horizontal and vertical explanations of Chai Zifeng.

(Yuan) I, the unwise one, have attended [the Master] for many years and have already carved the *Lengqie* lecture records. Now I again print the *Shoulengyan*, making it a satchel for crossing the sea.
If there are those who wish to penetrate this tangle of vines, please examine it within the vines themselves; do not—by any means—[seek it elsewhere].
A mere waste of straw sandals to wander about striking [the air].
Written in the winter of the Renxu year of the Tianqi era by the layman Yuanyi, Wang Yiyuan, while burning incense.
The Great Buddha-Crown Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning of All Bodhi...
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, the foremost of all practices, explained by Ming Chai Zishan. Recorded by Chengshi.
Regarding the titles of sutras, there are those personally bestowed by the World-Honored One, and those established by the compilers according to their meaning. This...

The Sūtra was personally titled by the World-Honored One himself. After the Buddha had spoken of the fifty-five stages of Bodhi, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "What should this sūtra be named?
How should I and all sentient beings uphold it? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "This sūtra shall be named 'The Great Buddha... [The text here is incomplete].
The Uṣṇīṣa. Sitatapatrā. The Unsurpassed Jewel Seal. The Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions.
It is also named the "Savior and Protector of Kinsmen," by which Ānanda and the bhikṣuṇī of this assembly were delivered and attained the bodhicitta, entering the ocean of universal knowledge.
It is also named the "Tathāgata’s Secret Cause: The Definitive Meaning of Cultivation and Realization. It is also named the "Mahāvaipulya."

The *Dhāraṇī-mantra of the King of the Sublime Lotus, Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions* is also known as the *Consecration Verses*, the *Śūraṅgama of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*, and so forth;
it possesses five titles in total. Later translators, however, maintained that although the phrasing differs, [the meaning remains the same].
The meanings may be presented interchangeably; therefore, retaining three [aspects] while concealing two, they are combined into a single title:

*The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas: The Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Now, as for "the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa": *The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa* refers to... [text continues]
This refers to the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*), the most honored and supreme among the thirty-two marks of a Buddha.
This mark is not only invisible to ordinary, ignorant beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); even Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) are unable to perceive its limits or surface.
Only a Buddha can see it with another Buddha. Why is this? Because those who possess vision cannot see it. Because...

One who holds no view likewise cannot see. Because one who views through neither existence nor non-existence cannot see, and because one who views through both existence and non-existence likewise cannot see—only one who is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and has departed from the paths of both ordinary beings and sages, can neither see nor be seen;
only such a person may be said to have personally beheld the mark of the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*). Yet, by relying upon this most honored and supreme crown, the most [exalted state] is revealed.
The Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle uses the existence of marks to manifest the absence of marks; it merely relies upon illusory marks to point toward the true mark.
For the true mark is precisely the fundamental, ever-present, true mind and the inherently pure, luminous essence with which all Buddhas are endowed from birth.

It is simply that ordinary, ignorant beings cling to existence, while those of the Two Vehicles fall into emptiness, such that they cannot know it. Even Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) have yet to glimpse it.
Regarding its ultimate limit: only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses the perfect penetration of the three virtues and the fulfillment of the ten thousand practices.

Relying upon the wondrous wisdom of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), he realizes the inconceivable realm and personally attests to the eternally abiding true mind. His entire being is the great function, and he also possesses the Great Uṣṇīṣa mark on his crown.
Furthermore, he is able to expound the teachings of the most supreme vehicle. Therefore, when the Venerable One was seized by Māra, the Buddha [acted] from his own crown.

Light radiated from the gate, and the emanation-buddhas recited the mantra. Thereupon, the Venerable Jīvaka earnestly requested the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the primary expedient means by which they attained Bodhi: the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*.
The Buddha immediately raised the full standard of the True Dharma and pointed directly to the human mind, saying: "There is a *samādhi* called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King."
Fully endowed with the ten thousand practices, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions traverse the path of wondrous adornment by emerging through a single gate.
When it came to Mañjuśrī’s request to establish the title of the sutra, he further prefixed its beginning with the three characters "Great Buddha-Crown" (Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa).

It is evident that those who have not entered the Great *Śūraṅgama* Samādhi do not realize the fruit of the Supreme Vehicle; and those who have not realized the fruit of the Supreme Vehicle do not perceive the Great [Buddha-Crown].
The Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa. One who beholds the Great Uṣṇīṣa of the Buddha is called a Tathāgata. Now, "Tathā" (Thus) points to his true essence; "Āgata" (Come) signifies his great function.
His essence is fully present beyond the limit of Vipaśyin; his function unfolds at the gateway of the present age.
Yet, while he is precisely beyond the limit of Vipaśyin, he does not hinder the gateway of the present age; while he is within the gateway of the present age, he does not hinder [the realm beyond].
"Yin" (sound) and "na-p'an" (the other shore). If one says it is quiescent and unmoving, then it responds and thereby penetrates all;
if one says it responds and thereby penetrates all, then it is quiescent and unmoving. It comes from nowhere, nor does it go anywhere; therefore, it is named Tathāgata.
Now, the Tathāgata is a title for the fruition-virtue. Without a secret cause, one cannot realize the fruition. Yet people know only that this is "secret," but do not know its meaning.

This reveals that while causes are not themselves the fruit, one must not fail to realize that the Tathāgata’s cultivation of the cause never departed from the sphere of seeing forms and hearing sounds;
these very six faculties, six objects, and six consciousnesses are the root of attaining Buddhahood, all of which are already fully present.

There is nothing that is not clearly understood. It is only because sentient beings pursue objects and delude their minds, gathering conditions so that they waver within and rush outward, remaining unaware throughout their daily lives, that it is called "esoteric" (*mi*).
This "esoteric" is spoken in relation to sentient beings; how could there be anything esoteric regarding the causes of the Tathāgata?
Thus we know that whether one is submerged in birth and death or realizes wondrous permanence, neither occurs outside of these dharmas of sense organs, objects, and consciousness.
Apart from this one dharma, there is no other dharma; apart from understanding this one meaning, there is no other meaning.

This is the cultivation of all through the cultivation of one, the realization of all through the realization of one, and the complete understanding of all through the understanding of one—a state where there is neither understanding nor non-understanding.

How could this apply only to the Tathāgata? All the myriad practices cultivated by all Bodhisattvas are likewise contained herein. "Bodhisattva" is a term from the language of India (Brahmī); it is fully [explained as follows]: [Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "菩薩半梵語。具". As the source text is incomplete, the translation reflects the available portion.]

"Bodhisattva" is translated here as "a sentient being who has resolved upon the Great Vehicle. This refers to the initial arousal of the mind, which must culminate in the attainment of Buddhahood and the deliverance of sentient beings before it is complete.
To benefit oneself and others, one must necessarily rely upon the six perfections and the four immeasurable minds.
These constitute the ten fundamental great practices. Furthermore, ten are used to support a hundred; a hundred are used to support a thousand;

and a thousand are used to support ten thousand. Now, ten thousand is the ultimate number according to worldly convention; how could these practices have a fixed number? If expanded, they may comprise many varieties;
yet if summarized, they do not go beyond the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama. In Sanskrit, this is called Śūraṅgama; in Chinese, it means...
It is said that "all phenomena are ultimately firm and solid. What are called "all phenomena" do not depart from the sixfold dharmas of sense organs, objects, and consciousness.
When their essential nature is investigated, they are found to be nothing other than the eternally abiding true mind. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "This Dharma abides in its own place;
the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. And as the *Zhao Lun* says: "How distant is the Sage? If one reaches out toward him, he is immediately divine. The Way..."
How far-reaching it is! To encounter phenomena is to encounter the Real. Furthermore, it is called the "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" and the "Śūraṅgama King.
This distinguishes it from the withered dhyāna and the extinction-samādhi of the Two Vehicles; it is as the Great Sūtra says: "Entering right concentration within a male body."

The female body arises from meditative concentration; even as the eye faculty enters right concentration, the ear faculty arises from concentration, the tongue faculty enters right concentration, and the body faculty arises from concentration. It is also as the ancestral house says: "Walking is Chan; sitting is also Chan."

Whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, the essence remains serene. Whoever attains this samādhi naturally causes the six sense faculties to return to their source and all phenomena to become quiescent, thereby restoring original enlightenment.
This restoration of original enlightenment is identical to the Tathāgata.
Now, the Tathāgata is the person who realizes, while the Śūraṅgama King is the dharma that is realized. Furthermore, the Great Uṣṇīṣa mark is both the person and the dharma.
This is the standard. These nineteen characters have their structural threads interpenetrating and their meanings encompassing all other titles.
For instance, "Siddhārtha-pāṇḍarā, the Unsurpassed Jewel Seal, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions" elucidates the fundamental truth inherent in the Buddha's birth.
In the Sanskrit language it is *Siddhārtha-pāṇḍarā*; here it is translated as "Great White."

The Parasol. This refers to the essence of this principle, which encompasses the ten voids and whose function pervades the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*, universally covering all things without being stained by even a speck of dust.
Within both the mundane and supramundane realms, there is nothing as precious as this, nor anything as exalted as this.
Using this to seal the mind, there is nothing that is not the true mind; using this to seal objects, there is nothing that is not the true object. It is like a seal pressing its mark.

It is exactly so, without the slightest discrepancy. However, because ordinary, ignorant people falsely recognize the conditioned shadows at the moment of seeing forms and hearing sounds, they are called "fleshly-eyed commoners.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions have personally realized this, and throughout the entire realm of the ten directions, it is a pure and wondrous state.
This meaning can be subsumed within the three characters of "Great Buddha-Topknot" (Mahā-uṣṇīṣa). As it is said: "To rescue and protect one's own causal kin, and to deliver..."

"Delivered Ānanda, as well as the bhikṣuṇī Nature (Prakṛti) in this assembly, who attained the bodhicitta and entered the ocean of universal knowledge"—this refers to those who were suited to the teaching and realized the fruit upon hearing the Dharma within this single assembly.

In meaning, this can be subsumed within the five characters of the "Ten Thousand Practices of the Bodhisattvas. As for "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Vaipulya), it signifies that while the principle is one, it fully embodies specific characteristics and functions.

The "King of the Wondrous Lotus" is a metaphor for this principle: it is identical with the myriad phenomena yet remains unstained by a single thing, just as a lotus dwelling in the mud is, in its very essence, fragrant and pure.
This meaning can be subsumed within the three characters of *Mahā-buddha-uṣṇīṣa*, and it can also be subsumed within the three characters of *Śūraṃgama*.
As for the phrase "the dhāraṇī-mantra that is the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions," *dhāraṇī* is a Sanskrit term.

*Ni* means "dhāraṇī" (total retention) in this language. Mantras possess the meaning of transforming the mundane into the sacred; they are called the wondrous gateway from which all Buddhas of the three periods of time are born.

Furthermore, they can encompass all dharmas and maintain immeasurable meanings. If one’s single thought accords with this, one enters the womb of the sages. This meaning can be subsumed within the four characters of the Tathāgata’s secret cause (*tathāgataguhyahetu*), and it may also be subsumed within [the following]: [The text continues: ... *ni*. This is translated as "total retention. Mantras have the significance of transforming the ordinary into the holy. It is said that these constitute the sublime gateway from which all Buddhas of the three times are born.

They are also able to encompass all phenomena and uphold immeasurable meanings. If one’s single thought accords with this, one enters the womb of the sages. This meaning can be subsumed within the four characters of the Tathāgata’s secret cause. It may also be subsumed within...
Regarding the three characters "Śūraṅgama" within the phrase "like the consecration chapter":
this indicates that this sutra is also subsumed within the Consecration Section (Abhiṣeka-varga), and these are indeed the chapter-words of that section.

Therefore, these nineteen characters not only encompass the meaning of the other titles, but can also encompass the textual content of the ten fascicles. For example, from the first fascicle, [it begins] because Ānanda mistakenly fell...

In the chamber of lust, the World-Honored One emitted light from the aperture at the crown of his head. From within the light, lotus flowers emerged; upon these flowers, transformation-buddhas appeared and recited mantras.
They commanded Mañjuśrī to take [the teachings] away and led Ānanda back to the Buddha’s presence. Ānanda requested instruction on the threefold contemplation of one mind.

The Buddha then examined the initial arousal of the bodhicitta. As soon as Ānanda replied that he had aroused the mind upon seeing the marks [of the Buddha], the Buddha already knew the nest of arising and ceasing.

[The Buddha] immediately established the true and the deluded, instructing him with direct words and a direct mind, further distinguishing between internal and external realms, and determining his prior and subsequent views.
When he sought the mind through the seven locations, not a single fixed view was found. Ānanda again requested the destination of the ultimate reality;
the Buddha once more emitted precious light from the gateway of his face, causing the worlds of the ten directions to merge into a single realm. Furthermore, within that—
Within body and mind, two kinds of roots are pointed out; one must know that the gates of truth and delusion do not depart from the single path of the sage and the ordinary person.
All of this is a singular extraction of the ultimate, establishing no stages or ranks.

To abandon the ordinary and follow the holy is, in its entirety, but a single deluded vision. To love the pure and loathe the defiled is likewise [a delusion].
One mind-consciousness: if one did not formerly love the marks of the Buddha, one likewise does not now hate the marks of Māra.
Since even the Buddha does not cling to them, how much less so Māra? One can see that before Ānanda had even finished his reply, the Buddha already knew the root of this ailment;
he simply caused it to be vomited out, so that there might be nothing hidden. Yet this root of the ailment is none other than the great earth and all sentient beings.

This is a universal affliction of sentient beings. Therefore, the Buddha and Ānanda mutually establish these four characters—seeing, hearing, thinking, and reflecting—as the structural thread of this sutra.
Throughout the subsequent text, they repeatedly apply "needles and moxibustion" to this point;

for instance, when it says, "This is not your mind," or "It is a mere reflection of discrimination based on sensory objects," all such passages refute this mode of thinking in order to reveal the Truth.

This refers to the mind. Passages such as "detached from objects and detached from views," and "even views are to be detached from views," all serve to demolish this view of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in order to reveal true seeing.
This is like striking a bell to test its permanence, as expressed in such passages as "turning the hearing back to hear the nature of hearing itself."
All of these [approaches] shatter the "hearing" of mere erudition in order to reveal true hearing. Nevertheless, how far apart are they?
It is merely that the ripples of the waves have subsided, yet the substance of the water remains. To seek the water apart from the waves would be the view of the non-Buddhists or the other vehicles.
This is the very core of this single sutra; it must be cherished and studied.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, Ānanda! You all should know that from [this point] until 'because this perception is not true, there is transmigration.
'All sentient beings' refers to those within the twenty-five realms of existence in the triple world. 'Without beginning' means that they have no prior beginning and no final end;
it refers to the swirling eddies of vast kalpas that never cease or extinguish. 'The eternally abiding true mind'—in terms of..."
Regarding the words: "The essence is pure and luminous. To speak in terms of this essence, saying "first function, then essence" refers to the gateway of Buddha-activity.
"Constant" does not mean a constant that is fixed and dead; rather, it means that while manifesting forms through things, there has never been any transition or change.
"Abiding" is not an abiding characterized by attachment; it is like the [four phases of] arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, yet fundamentally unmoving.
It is quivering. "True" means being without artifice even within illusion and transformation. That which illuminates objects is called the mind; it is the function of the nature (*prakṛti*).

"Nature" refers to the principle of ceaseless generation. "Pure" means remaining eternally clean while dwelling in defilement. "The luminous essence" means not becoming obscured even while dwelling in the long night [of ignorance].
All of these are inherently possessed by the Buddha from the beginning, lacking nothing and having no excess. They are... [not]... [incomplete].

It moves within the perfect, all-pervading *tathatā*. Because sentient beings do not awaken to this, they harbor feelings of acceptance and rejection and give rise to notions of purity and defilement.
If even a single thought is purely true, then the holy and the ordinary are equal, and defilement and purity are non-dual.
Thus, the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata are merely manifestations of reflected images; from where could craving arise?
Commentary: This establishes the coexistence of the true and the false, thereby enabling all sentient beings to abandon this and ascend to that.
The Buddha’s words, “Excellent! were spoken because Ānanda had responded with the actual truth; thus, He rejoiced and comforted him. His intention was:

“What you have related is indeed entirely in accordance with your original intent; however, from the very moment you first gave rise to the thought of enlightenment, you were already mistaken. You all—
To resolve the mind, one should seek the true mind that is neither born nor extinguished.
If one perceives superior signs and constantly dwells upon them, this is the deluded mind of birth and extinction belonging to all sentient beings.
Because this perception is not true, there is cyclic existence. Therefore, he exhorts them, saying: "You should know [and so forth]."
"You now wish to investigate Unsurpassed Bodhi... (until)... in the interim there shall forever be no signs of crookedness.

[Commentary: This directly points to the path of Bodhi. Since Ānanda has already formed the resolve to turn away from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle, he further presents his account of his original aspiration for enlightenment. The Buddha has thus established for him both the True and the False.
[The Master] struck him again, thereby making him understand the gateway. At this point, the aim was to ensure he could proceed directly without hesitation.
That which you now wish to investigate is what Ānanda seeks to exhaustively examine in its subtle details. The World-Honored One’s intention was this:
if one wishes to investigate Bodhi, it is not separate from the present moment. Unsurpassed Bodhi—how could it be anything other than that which is shared by all people? It is precisely this.
This is the true mind, yet it has not been revealed. If you can develop and clarify it, that is itself Bodhi.
As for the method of development, you need only maintain directness of mind and directness of speech; whenever there is a question, respond immediately without engaging in discursive thought.
Cut off all deliberation and conjecture, and you will be close to it. This is precisely what you asked regarding the manifestation of the ten directions of Tathāgatas.
Those who attain Bodhi through death likewise follow this same path; it is attained solely through a direct mind and direct speech. Such is the nature of cause and effect:
one proceeds directly out of birth-and-death and directly realizes Bodhi. From beginning to end, throughout all the stages traversed in the interim, there is forever no sign of detour or hindrance.
From this point onward, this is the single-pointed instruction directed toward the ultimate.

No hierarchical stages are enumerated, in order to manifest the Supreme Vehicle (Agryayāna). It requires that Ānanda attain Buddhahood in this very life, without depending on the awakening of another.
As for "directness beyond words and thought," it admits no deliberation and does not fall within the realm of consciousness.

This is achieved by employing the Immovable Wisdom (Acalajñāna) to eliminate the conceptualizing mind. It is as the Patriarchal School says: "To speak of 'Direct Pointing' is already to have become circuitous. Therefore...
As soon as there was any attempt at deliberation, [the Buddha] immediately administered blows and shouts.
However, Ānanda was unable to bear this burden, so the World-Honored One again opened another expedient means from a second perspective; this refers to the subsequent passage which states:
"All those with wisdom must rely on parables to attain awakening. The following text serves to truly elucidate the nature—that is, it elucidates the True.
This is merely a reversal of the characters; "direct mind" is precisely the "true mind. True nature is the essence (*tǐ*), and the true mind is its function (*yòng*).
Since both essence and function are true, what else could they be but *bodhi*?
"Ānanda, I now ask you: from the moment you first resolved your mind [to seek enlightenment] until this point, for what reason did you resolve your mind to abandon birth and death?

The character "yuan" (緣, *ālambana*) carries the meaning of both object and subject; "xiang" (相, *nimitta*) belongs to the object of perception, while "jian" (見, *darśana*) belongs to the perceiving subject.

That which lies between them—the sense of fondness—is the consciousness of deliberation (*manovijñāna*). Since the Buddha had already instructed him to respond with a straightforward mind, how could Ānanda not have followed this instruction? However—

Not knowing the directness of what the Buddha taught is called "immovable wisdom. It responds to all objects like a mirror reflecting forms, clearly distinguishing beauty from ugliness without the perception of subject and object;
amidst the chaotic coming and going, it is devoid of the marks of arising and ceasing.
Because it involves no deliberation whatsoever, it is called "direct. Ānanda, however, used the thought that arises from seeing appearances to initiate his resolve for enlightenment.
"O Venerable One, I speak according to the facts; please consider my words straightforward. Otherwise, it would be like turning medicine into poison.
[Commentary on the Title: These are the words of a question and answer.

Since the Master has already instructed him to respond with a straightforward mind, this serves both to test his honesty and to extract the root of his affliction, so that he may recognize its true location. Thereupon—
He swept away [the dust]. Therefore, he inquired about his initial resolve and that momentous occasion.
Had Ānanda attained a sudden, great awakening, the characteristics of the past mind would have been like a phantom dream. Not only the past, but even the present mind would be unattainable;
thus, the lacquer bucket would be shattered and the Great Matter would be clear. Alas, how regrettable that he still fell back into his former state.
"What is this cave?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "As you have said [up to] 'only the mind and the eyes,' where are they located now? (Commentary:
This investigates the location of the mind and the eyes. Following the previous statement, it asks: "You claim that the eyes see, yet the mind... )
Reflect thus: "I vow to abandon birth and death. Yet you do not know that the very thing which abandons birth and death is itself the cause of birth and death.
Why is this? What you describe as seeing superior forms with the eyes and the mind giving rise to attachment and delight is precisely the thief that robs the true mind.
For example, when a king is invaded by external enemies, he dispatches troops to suppress them.
These troops must first know the location where the enemies dwell before they can destroy their nests and exterminate their clans.
Since beginningless time, you have wandered through birth and death, revolving without ceasing; you have no other fault but that your own mind and eyes are the cause.
The thief acts as his own mediator; he plunders the treasures of his own house. If you now wish to realize the true mind, it is like protecting a king.

If you wish to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is like employing excellent troops. If you wish to eliminate the mind and the eyes, it is like exterminating a powerful bandit. Where are your mind and eyes located now?
Although this passage mentions both the mind and the eyes together, the emphasis lies primarily on the mind; thus, in the subsequent text, [the Master] refutes them repeatedly.

[The Buddha] said: "I see it. However, because the mind has no handle [to grasp it], I fear that those who are deluded will be at a loss for what to do; therefore, I have relied upon the perception of seeing to investigate and refute [this notion].
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [up to] ...in this way, the consciousness-mind truly resides within the body."

The character "dwelling" (*zhu*) in the subsequent passage is identical to the character "residing" (*ju*) in this context. Although seven points are raised for investigation and refutation, they refute only the single character "dwelling.
Whether it be internal, external, or intermediate, there is no place where it cannot exist. Though the consciousness-mind is analyzed, the Truth (*zhen*) is likewise present therein.
For the mind is like the great void, and the body is like a house. If one were to say that the void dwells within the house, would it not also dwell outside the house?
Is it not empty? It is likewise within, without, and in between. Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere.
Some may say that since the mind is non-existent in all seven locations, then [the same applies to] the five aggregates up to the seven elements.
Both are not the *tathāgatagarbha*. Please contemplate this deeply. The ten types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are as listed among the twelve classes of beings below;
those who are scattered in emptiness, submerged, or composed of earth, wood, stone, or metal are excluded, as they do not belong to the category of the mental eye (*cittacakṣus*).

As for the blue lotus (*utpala*), the petals of this flower in the Western Regions are extremely slender and long; the Buddha’s eyes resemble them. [The eyes] consist of the four sensory objects (*viṣaya*) of the floating roots.
Originally, these were the four "dusty" sense organs (*bu chén gēn*). It was likely the translators who, finding them archaic and clumsy, refined the phrasing for stylistic elegance.
Furthermore, this is merely Ānanda’s way of speaking in a single breath; it is as if he were saying, "Is it only the eye-organ?

Together with the ear and the other three dusty organs, they all reside upon my face. By observing the single character "only" (*zhǐ*), the meaning becomes self-evident. Because of this, various masters... [text continues]
Later in the text, there is a discussion of the eight factors consisting of subject and object, which refers to visible form, odor, flavor, and tangibility.

How could Ānanda have been speaking with such ambiguity? Moreover, the Buddha merely asked where the eye is located, yet Ānanda further stated that the eye is composed of four factors; why so much elaboration?
Commentary: This [passage] concerns Ānanda’s adherence to the view that the mind resides within. Ānanda sets forth the locations of both the eyes and the mind;
while this appears similar to the views of the deluded, his speech and expressions are nonetheless clear. Why is this?
Since he refers to "the ten kinds of ordinary beings," it is evident that those who have not yet transcended birth and death all share this same conception. Furthermore, he says, "consciousness..."

The mind itself is not the true mind. That all sentient beings are imprisoned within the six realms and submerged in the three miserable paths is entirely due to this [misconception], which serves as the deep root of the obstacle of ego-clinging (*ātma-grāha*).

It is said that even though the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes are upon the Buddha’s face, to point definitively to the four sensory objects of the physical sense-roots is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This refers to the sense organ (indriya). Although Ānanda’s words were carefully considered, they nonetheless suffered from occasional lapses.

Even regarding what he called the "conscious mind," there was no necessity to insist that it actually resides within the body. As for the one capable of seeing the thirty-two marks, how could this be merely the physical sense organ?
The Buddha was fully aware of this error, yet he did not explicitly point it out to him.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You are now sitting here [until] 'therefore I am able to see from afar within the hall.
(Commentary: These are the words of three questions and three answers. Since Ānanda has stated that the consciousness-mind truly resides within the body, the Buddha should then ask:
"If the mind truly resides within, can it see the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach? It is also...
Setting this aside without further inquiry, he first asked: "The lecture hall you were just sitting in to observe the Jeta Grove—where is it now?
Ānanda replied, "The pure lecture hall is within the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden; the Jeta Grove is actually outside the hall. These are the boundaries of the interior and exterior.
This allowed Ānanda to establish for himself [the distinction]. He then asked: "Within the hall right now..."
"What did you see first? Ānanda replied, "First I saw the Tathāgata; only then did my gaze reach the grove and garden.
This sequence of perception also served to establish for Ānanda his own certainty. Next, [the Buddha] asked: "When you gaze at the grove and garden, by what means do you see them?
Ānanda replied, "Because the doors and windows are wide open, I am in the hall and can look far off."
This seeing is the cause of what is seen; it also serves to settle Ānanda himself. Now, the World-Honored One’s threefold verification was specifically for Ānanda’s sake.

Having long possessed the habit of extensive learning and being capable of skillful debate, if he had not been restrained in advance, he would likely have shifted his tactics at the critical moment and expended much superfluous speech.
Generally speaking, whenever a spiritual friend provides guidance, [they do so with such intent].
In the future, this expedient means cannot be absent.
At that time, the World-Honored One was amidst the great assembly... (until) Ānanda prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and humbly received his compassionate instructions.
In Sanskrit, it is called *samādhi*, also known as *samāpatti*. This is translated here as "equipoise" (*samāhita*) or "right reception" (*samyak-pratipatti*).

According to the older tradition, because one does not receive anything at all within it, it is termed "right reception. Generally, it refers to that state within meditative concentration where not even a single thought exists.
It is precisely that which is being experienced, yet cannot be spat out nor swallowed; therefore, it is called *samādhi*.
When "Great Buddha-Crown" (*Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa*) appears before one, the Sanskrit term is *Śūraṅgama*, which here means "the ultimate solidity of all phenomena.

"King" (*rāja*) signifies the meaning of noble dignity, and also the meaning of sovereign mastery. "Sublime Adornment" (*Pratimaṇḍita*) refers to the state of the fruit of Bodhi. According to the ancient explanation, *ma*...

"Touching the crown of the head" means to stroke it as a sign of affection. "Prostrating at the feet" means to bow down as a sign of reverence. Because the superior loves the inferior, he strokes the crown;
because the inferior reveres the superior, he prostrates at the feet.
Commentary: This establishes the fundamental framework of this single scripture, demonstrates the universal ford for all Buddhas, and cuts off the divergent paths of other vehicles.
Why is it that, having already verified Ānanda, the Buddha did not subject him to further interrogation, but instead specifically rubbed his crown and bestowed instruction?
It was because he had initially requested the skillful means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and the Buddha himself—

Examining his initial resolve, [the Buddha] guided him from the left and supported him from the right until he reached this point. To the Buddha, this was never anything other than a skillful means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);
yet for Ānanda, its name had not yet been designated, nor had it been directly revealed. Had the Buddha further interrogated him, it would have left him at a loss for words.
Therefore, the Buddha extended his golden arm, rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head, and comforted him as well as the great assembly.
[The Buddha] addressed the assembly, saying: "There is a samādhi... (and so forth). Now, this *samādhi* is a general term for meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);

it is not one of the three contemplations previously requested. The phrase "named the Great Buddha-Crown" indicates that the physical form of the Buddhas' crowns is used as a metaphorical designation for the essence of this *samādhi*. The phrase "endowed with the myriad practices" [indicates...]
I provisionally employ the Tathāgatas of the ten directions to manifest the function of samādhi.

This means that this samādhi cannot be entered by either ordinary sentiments or saintly understandings; it cannot be realized by either having a mind or being without a mind; and consciousness cannot perceive it.
It cannot be known by the intellect. It is empty yet not empty; existent yet not existent; the Middle Way yet not the Middle Way.
It is the supreme, peerless Dharma of both the mundane and supramundane realms; therefore, it is provisionally named after the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.
Nevertheless, it does not depart from the names and characteristics of conventional truth. Thus, all phenomena are fundamentally suchness (tathatā), perfectly pervasive and immovable.
Possessing this samādhi, then hundreds of thousands of samādhis are all contained within it; this is the most honored and supreme king among all samādhis.
Not only does one possess this, but the six pāramitās, the four immeasurable minds, and so forth, are all fully perfected in a single thought-moment.
Therefore, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all emerge from the river of birth and death by means of this.
By means of this, one ascends to the shore of Nirvana; by means of this, one achieves the adornment of myriad virtues.
The Buddha fully proclaims the true mandate, seeking to cause sudden realization of the True and Constant. In the space of a single snap of the fingers, the fruit of three great aeons is perfected.

Nevertheless, although the World-Honored One demonstrated this to Ānanda, there remains a vast difference—like that between heaven and an abyss—between this and the *śamatha* and other practices he had been requested to teach.
In the case of Ānanda, it appears that he attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) through skillful means, and realized *bodhi* through that meditative concentration;

thus, there was indeed a gradual process of cultivation and realization. Since the Buddha has stated that there is "samādhi" called the "Great Buddha-Crown" and so forth, then every single form and scent is none other than the Great Samādhi.
As the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra says: "One enters right concentration within a male body."
From the body of a woman, one arises from meditative concentration; even until a single faculty enters right concentration, all faculties arise from that concentration.
It is also as the Patriarchs said: "Do not be attached; do not engage in false conceptualization. Therefore, the various Patriarchs proclaimed the style of our school.
Each time the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama is raised, the Buddha subsequently pursues the matter from many angles, also causing one to see Bodhi at the point where the deluded mind is exhausted.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said... [up to] 'it is impossible for it to dwell within the body.'"

From this point downward, many difficult questions are posed. Those who employ such circuitous inquiry do so with the intent that those who are deluded may attain awakening and those who are stalled may achieve penetration.
Furthermore, when encountering difficult terminology, one should not interrogate it by means of literal reality.

Because literal reality is not yet clearly understood, one uses what is not a difficulty as a difficulty; once difficulties reach the state of being no longer difficult, the literal reality reveals itself naturally. If one sees...
They employ tortuous and clever sophistry, yet demand that one be held accountable to actual principles;

they fabricate conjectures at will, claiming it is not that one cannot enter into the truth through words, but rather that the reasons for the words are profoundly obscure. Those who read the Buddhist scriptures must possess this eye for discerning the Dharma.
Commentary: This restates the preceding argument to refute the attachment that the mind resides within.
The four propositions beginning with "As you [have said]" cite the grounds for the aforementioned views to specifically define Ānanda. The four propositions beginning with "There is also...

represent the World-Honored One’s further employment of a logical device to examine and determine the matter. The four propositions following "Ānanda replied" indicate the point at which Ānanda fell into error.
"You have fallen into such a calculation. That you are likewise so is the Buddha’s definitive pronouncement. It is like saying that your calculating mind is within your body;
it is no different from being inside a hall and failing to see the Tathāgata while instead seeing only the forests and springs.
For nothing is more supremely sentient than your mind; wherever it may be, there is nothing it does not clearly and fully perceive.
If this mind that you clearly perceive before you truly resided within your body, then you should first see your own internal organs, and only thereafter could you see external objects;
this would accord with your earlier statement that you first saw the Tathāgata and only then cast your gaze upon the forests and springs.
Not only this, but according to what you have said, it stands to reason that there would be many such [internal organs] in the world.
Sentient beings first perceive the internal organs and subsequently observe external objects; yet, is there now [ultimately] existence or non-existence?
Indeed, within the body there are things that cannot be seen, and there are also things that cannot not be seen. Why is this?
If one claims that the mind cannot see the mind—just as the eye cannot see the eye—then the liver, spleen, and stomach, which are closest to the heart, would likewise [be invisible].

The eye cannot see its own eyebrows or eyelashes. Even if you cannot see these, the places where your nails grow and your hair lengthens, and the places where your tendons turn and your veins pulse—all these are within you and distinct from the mind;
logically, they should be clearly perceived. Why is it that both these separated parts and their points of connection are invisible? If this most spiritual mind of yours...
Being within, one must necessarily not know internal things; how then could one conversely know external things?
Thus, what difference is there between this and being in a hall and failing to see the Tathāgata while instead seeing forests and springs? Your calculation is erroneous.

Therefore, he concludes the refutation of the [doctrine that the] mind is within the body: "It is impossible for one who says, 'I am in the hall,' yet does not see the Tathāgata, to be able to gaze outwardly at the groves and springs. It can be known that your reckoning places the mind within the body;
that one does not see the internal but instead sees the external is likewise impossible. This concludes the refutation of the mind being inside the body. Even if one cannot...
To explain these traditional doctrines using profound [theories] and superficial [interpretations] is like moving from the outside toward the inside;
thus, it would imply that the mind exists externally, which is unacceptable. "Pō" (頗) means "mostly" or "frequently."
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying... [up to] "...would it not be as false as the Buddha’s definitive teaching?

*Guānzhù (Crown Commentary): This is the attachment that the mind is external. Upon hearing the Buddha say that the mind certainly does not know internally, Ānanda suddenly gave rise to a mistaken interpretation.
He thought that the Buddha was stating that the mind resides outside, and thus he grasped at the literal meaning of the words.*
[The monk] replied: "Therefore, I say that when I heard the Tathāgata’s Dharma-sound, I realized that my mind truly resides outside the body.
Why is this? My mind is like a lamp, and my body is like a room. The Buddha said that if the mind were inside, one should first see what is within before perceiving what is without.
For example, if a lamp is lit inside a room, it must first illuminate the interior of the room. From... [text continues].
Regarding the door of that room and the courtyard beyond, all sentient beings do not see within their own bodies, but see only what is outside the body.
This is just like a lamp situated outside a room, which cannot illuminate the interior. This principle is ultimately clear and free from any doubt;
it is in no way different from the definitive teachings (nītārtha) previously expounded by the Buddha. How could this possibly be the same as what was stated before?
"Is it the delusion within?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "As for these bhikṣus... (up to) "...how can one person cause the multitude to be satiated?
[Commentary: This first establishes a metaphor to clarify that the mind does not reside externally. Now, since the mind...
Externally, body and mind are divided into two, appearing like two separate people who do not interfere with one another.
Therefore, he questioned Ānanda, saying: "When these bhikṣus eat, does one person's eating satisfy all of them?
Ānanda replied: "No. Furthermore, he sought to clarify this by asking: "Even though these bhikṣus are arhats..."
Bodies and lives are distinct; how could the food of one person cause a multitude to be satiated?

This very point shows that the mind is situated outside, such that one is unaware of one's own body, and thus Ānanda’s calculation will surely fail. "Appropriately" (yadṛcchayā) means "fittingly" (yuktam).

As for "lump-food" (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra), it is also called "segmented food" (dharma-āhāra); it refers to that which has physical segments and can be grasped as a lump. Among the four types of nutriment...
This excludes contact, volition, and consciousness. "Sod" means to dwell; it is like saying, "I shall not eat today.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you were to perceive [the mind] as dwelling outside the body... such a thing is impossible."

Commentary: This refutes the notion that the mind does not reside within. If you could truly perceive and know that the mind which is capable of cognition and vision actually exists outside the body, then the body would be external to the mind and the mind would likewise be external to the body;
each would be independent of the other. In that case, what the mind knows, the body could not perceive, and what the body perceives, the mind could not know.
"It would be no different from when one person eats and the multitude cannot be satiated. Now I show you my 'tūla-cotton hand.
When you see it with your eyes, does your mind discern it? Ānanda replied, "When I see the hand with my eyes..."
A conceptualization arose in his mind. The Buddha said, "If that were so, then body and mind would fundamentally know one another and would not be external to each other.
Why then do you grasp at the mind as being outside? Therefore, the following concludes with words of refutation. *Touluo* (兜羅) means "fine fragrance";
this cotton is white and soft, and the Buddha’s hand resembles it.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has stated [up to] 'because there are no obstructions,' it is because the faculties are hidden within.

*Commentary:* This refers to the attachment that the mind is hidden within the faculties. Regarding the phrase "as the Buddha has stated" and below, this restates the preceding words to introduce the subsequent text.
The phrase "I now reflect and know it is located in one place" distinguishes this from the previous "one place" consisting of both the internal and external.
As for the question "Where does it reside now?", the Buddha is inquiring about the locus of that which was spoken.

Since [the opponent] does not understand the meaning of the phrase "internal equality," he implies that because the sense organ does not see the internal, if the organ were able to see the mind, it would necessarily follow its own conceptualizations.
This can be understood by examining the following text. It is like someone arriving and immediately distinguishing a single section; this is the analogy.

It serves to elucidate the meaning of the phrase "latent within the faculties. Thus, the *vaidūrya* (lapis lazuli) that is able to join with [the eyes] is used as a metaphor for the physical eye-organ (*cakṣur-indriya*).
The two eyes that are joined with it are used as a metaphor for the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*). Just as the *vaidūrya* does not obstruct the seeing of the eye, so too...

The faculty of the eye does not obstruct the mind’s seeing. Ānanda already possessed the notion that the eye sees and the mind knows at this point, yet he did not state it explicitly, and the World-Honored One likewise did not address it; how wondrous and ineffable!
However, regarding Ānanda’s subsequent failure, the emphasis lies on the two phrases: "that faculty follows seeing" and "immediately making discriminations. This is the analogy for the Dharma.
