This was because they did not understand the existence of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, and thus failed to realize that the transformation of the ālayavijñāna is itself the Tathāgata.

Concealing [the truth], they instead cling to the view of annihilation as being eternal. Now, having encountered the Buddha, although he has heard of the two kinds of fundamental [nature] and seen that the nature is indestructible, he still harbors doubts;
thus he requests of the Buddha: "How may you instruct and guide me so that I may realize and know this ground where the mind is neither born nor extinguished?
Thereby, his long-standing doubts will be dissolved like ice. Indeed, this true permanence is not merely hidden.
"O King, if you wish to know, there is no one among those subject to outflows (*āsrava*) who does not desire to hear this.
However, Great King, this question of yours is precisely intended to clarify that within the arising and ceasing of every thought-moment, there exists a nature that neither arises nor ceases.
Kātyāyana—here translated as 'Shearer of Hair'—and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa—here translated as 'Non-doing'—both established the doctrine of annihilation. *Nirvāṇa* has many translated meanings."
He still took non-arising and non-ceasing as his essential doctrine. The fox is a doubtful beast; those among ordinary people who harbor many doubts are like it.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "Your body exists now... (up to) "...it shall follow toward total extinction. The Buddha spoke thus.

Commentary: This is intended to demonstrate that within the midst of arising and ceasing, there exists that which neither arises nor ceases; yet first, it interrogates this arising and ceasing. The intent is:
"You claim that after the death of this body, there is annihilation. For now, let us set aside the question of what happens after death; I ask you concerning your present physical body:
is it identical to the adamantine and eternally abiding, or will it ultimately undergo transformation and decay? Ānanda.
The King then replied, "This body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and perish. The Buddha further questioned him, saying, "Your body has not yet perished;
how can you know of its perishing? The World-Honored One spoke these words, earnestly and repeatedly reminding him:

"If King Bimbisāra can, while [the body] has not yet perished, know the place of its perishing, he will immediately realize and realize the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Although sudden awakening..."
It is not so; yet there is naturally a distinction even in the gradual refinement of one's practice. As King Bimbisāra replied:
"Although this impermanent body of mine has not yet perished, as I observe it before me, every thought-moment shifts and passes away; it is ever-new and never remains still."
Regarding such phrases as "until death and ruin cease not," one realizes that impermanence is swift and takes it to heart with trepidation.
Thus, because one perceives that what is presently manifest does not abide, one knows that it must eventually reach extinction; why wait until death to realize this extinction?

Therefore, the Buddha said: "Such is the seal upon his answer; it is not erroneous. That things arise anew and do not abide is like saying that those who have passed one's arm in greeting are no longer the same as before.
"Great King, your present age has already succumbed to decay; how can you compare it to the time when you were in the full vigor of youth?"
Commentary: This passage cites both the old and the young to examine the matter, so that one may verify it for oneself and describe it in detail.

Therefore, the Buddha asked only about the appearance of the aged; however, King Bimbisāra further answered regarding the appearances of the three stages of youth, maturity, and old age, noting that they differ vastly from one another.
He stated that when he was a mere infant, his skin and its texture were [so smooth].
It was moist, fresh, and lustrous. By the time it reached full maturity, its spirit was complete and firm, and its blood and qi were fully abundant.
Now, in these declining years, constrained by decay, its form and complexion have withered; constrained by senility, its spirit has grown dim.
Its hair is white and its skin is wrinkled, bearing the unmistakable appearance of decrepitude. Since this state will not last much longer, how can it be compared to its former vigor?
How much more so now, let alone when I was a youth; there is no need to speak further.
The Buddha said, "Great King, from your physical appearance [it is clear that]... therefore, know that my body will ultimately undergo transformation and perish."

Commentary: This is a detailed and careful examination. The intention is to lead King Ajātaśatru from the coarse to the subtle, tracing the subtle delusions of arising and ceasing back to a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), and only thereafter pointing out that which is neither-arising-nor-ceasing.
Following the previous passage, it says: "According to what Your Majesty has said, your physical form should not have decayed all at once; rather, it is due to gradual [change]..."
It has come to this. The King said: "The transformations and subtle shifts I truly do not perceive;
I only see the passage of cold and heat gradually leading to this state. It is fitting that there should be gradual decay rather than sudden ruin.
How do I know this? When I was twenty years old, I was more vigorous than at ten; when I was thirty, I was again more vigorous than at twenty."
It has now reached sixty-two years. Looking back at the time when I was fifty, I appear as if I were still in the prime of my strength.
However, this estimation is based on a calculation using ten-year intervals; it merely serves to verify the general outline.

If I were to examine it with subtle scrutiny, it would not be a matter of change occurring only over one or two decades; rather, it is truly a transformation by year and a metamorphosis by month, even by day.
Xie Shiqian: If you further contemplate with deep reflection and observe with discerning clarity, you will see that every moment (*kṣaṇa*) and every thought-moment (*nāman*) ceaselessly passes.
Thus, one knows that this body ultimately undergoes transformation and extinction. This is the practice of observing the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
Even Ānanda, who previously took the six consciousnesses to be truly permanent, was still unable to reach this realization; how much less could ordinary people with their coarse minds perceive it?
As the Book says: "To fall and decline" means that when the *hun* ascends to heaven, it is called "falling" (*cu*); when the *po* descends to earth, it is called "declining" (*luo*).
This sutra, however, simply uses the daily rising of the signs of old age as "falling" (*cu*), and the daily descent of the vigor of youth as "declining" (*luo*).
It falls away. This is also as the former masters have said: "When I was first born as an infant, I died moment by moment, thought after thought.
How could I now, on the contrary, fear death? This is correct. A *kṣaṇa* is an extremely brief duration of time;
ninety-nine *kṣaṇas* constitute one *nimeṣa* (thought-moment), and within a single *kṣaṇa*, there are ninety-nine cycles of arising and ceasing. [This is] like using a sharp blade...
The severing of a single thread constitutes one *kṣaṇa*. Twelve years constitute one *yuga*. This is a restatement of the preceding ten years, with only the phrasing altered.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "You have witnessed these transformations... (until) I now show you the nature of non-arising and non-extinction."

Commentary: This refers to the non-arising and non-ceasing within arising and ceasing. Because the World-Honored One saw that King Ajātaśatru had described the process of arising and ceasing with such subtle detail, he was able to demonstrate the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing to him. [The King] asked:
"Since you know that moments do not remain and ultimately end in extinction, can you point out that which does not perish within those moments?"
Upon hearing these words, the King was involuntarily struck with awe; he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha: "I truly did not know this.
For so long I have been in ignorance regarding the nature of kingship. Had I known this earlier, I would never have allowed myself to be deluded by the heterodox teachers.
The Buddha said: "Since you do not yet know it, I shall now point out to you, with my middle finger, the nature that is neither born nor extinguished, in order to sweep away your [delusions]."
This is the attachment to annihilation.
Great King, at what age did you see the Ganges River? [From the age of twenty-five] until the age of sixty-two, it has remained without change.
(Commentary: This demonstrates the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing within the realm of arising and ceasing. The Buddha first restates the hidden premise.)
The King’s words were thus. Thereafter, he examined the water he had seen three years prior and compared it with the water he had seen thirteen times.
The King replied, "It is exactly as it was when I was three years old; there has been no difference whatsoever, even up to this year at sixty-two.
This very fact demonstrates that while the realm of arising and ceasing exists, the central essence is non-arising.
As for "extinction": the flow of water continues without ceasing day or night. Yet, is the water seen in the sixth year not the same as the water seen in the third year?
What is called "not different" is the nature (*dhātu*) of the water; what migrates and flows is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the water.
By means of the characteristic, one reaches the nature; therefore it is said: "The rivers compete to pour forth, yet..."
[The previous section] flowed on. Now, in order to cause the realm to be reached and the mind to be clarified, the realm is first distinguished and the seeing is subsequently distinguished.
*Jīva* here means "long life"; he visited this celestial deity to seek long life.
The Buddha said: "You now lament for yourself that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled... [until] you leap for joy, having attained what you never had before.
*Annotation:* This is a re-examination of the perception of the river, intended to demonstrate that the nature of seeing is indestructible. It restates the previous point, saying:
"You now lament for yourself that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled; you are certainly different from when you were a youth. Thus, your perception of the river..."
"Does this vision of seeing change as one grows from childhood to old age? The King replied, "No. The Buddha then pointed and said:

"Though your face may be wrinkled, the essence of the faculty of seeing that observes the river within it has never been wrinkled. That which is wrinkled changes, but that which is not wrinkled does not change.
That which changes undergoes extinction; that which does not change is fundamentally without birth or extinction. How could this be affected by you?"

While within this body of arising and ceasing, you shared in its birth and death; yet now, while manifestly not undergoing arising and ceasing, you claim that after death there is annihilation—this is already an error.

Furthermore, to cite Makkhali Gosāla and others who assert that the total extinction of this body after death is called *nirvāṇa* is the height of error. When the King heard these words, he believed them.
The statement that one "knows the passing away from this life and the proceeding to the next" may be used to eliminate the nihilistic views of ordinary, ignorant people;

however, it is not appropriate for one who takes joy in the unprecedented experience of passing away from this life and proceeding to the next to claim to have realized non-arising (*anutpāda*). Why is this so?
Even if one perceives this, it is merely the domain of the eighth consciousness; how could the true nature involve taking or rejecting?
This is precisely the single spirit—where does it go when the physical shell still remains? Yet one does not realize that the single spirit is the shell, and the shell is the single spirit.
It is just as the World-Honored One said: "The nature of this seeing-essence has never once wrinkled. He simply emphasizes this one point.
Regarding the character "nature" (*xing*): if one refers to the essence of seeing, it is precisely the consciousness-essence within the aforementioned fundamental [consciousness].

Although it is true, it is also accompanied by delusion, like a second moon. However, the World-Honored One likewise adapts to the capacity of the interlocutor rather than forcing the Dharma upon others.
King Bimbisāra had merely ceased [seeing] and attained the *saṃskāra-skandha*, yet he had not yet perceived the eighth consciousness; how could this be based on the True Suchness (*tathatā*)?
Is it that their natures are so strong? It cannot be that they do not know; yet one must not cling to this [view]. This is the discussion regarding the merits and faults of King Nigaṇṭha.
Makkhali Gosāla said, "The Way is not seen. He was the same as the two previous individuals; all were non-Buddhist teachers who held views of annihilationism.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha, and joined his palms (until: "I pray that you will arouse compassion and wash away my defilements.
[Commentary: This follows upon the preceding text, as he gives rise to doubt. Ānanda had previously requested an elucidation of the two natures.
The World-Honored One, for the sake of King Prasenajit, pointed out the nature of seeing that remains unchanged as one observes a river;
he had already clarified that within the momentary arising and ceasing of every thought there exists an originally non-arising, non-ceasing nature.

Yet Ānanda, conversely, gave rise to doubt and stagnation, thinking that seeing and hearing are entirely subject to arising and ceasing, and thus suggesting that by clinging to seeing and hearing, one loses the true nature. If this seeing and hearing...
"It must be neither arising nor ceasing. Why, then, has the World-Honored One just now stated that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of delusion?
Therefore, I pray for an explanation. Ānanda did not realize that what was just described as "neither arising nor ceasing" refers to the seeing-nature (*jianxing*) rather than the false seeing.
The seeing-nature is like the true moon; the essence of seeing (*jing*) is like... [the second moon].
In the second month, seeing and hearing are like the reflection of the moon in water; this is precisely where Ānanda has made an error and where he is inverted.
Therefore, in the following text, the inversion is explained first, followed by the explanation of the error.
Immediately, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm (until) [the beings] no longer knew where their own bodies and minds were inverted.
Now, as for this inversion and its rectification, there is no distinction greater than that; it is simply that with respect to a single thing, one does not follow the principles of physical reality.
To take the head as the tail and the tail as the head is called "inversion. To do the opposite is called "correctness.
Yet, correctness and inversion have never been separate from phenomena. Therefore, sentient beings and Buddhas share the same essential nature.
If one regards the mind and its objects as truly existent, one transforms the *dharmakāya* into the five aggregates and the four great elements. If one realizes...
The mind and its objects are fundamentally non-existent; thus, one transforms the four great elements and the five aggregates into the Dharma-body.

Therefore, to encompass the vast void with the mind and to harmonize the nature with the Dharma-realm constitutes "Right Universal Knowledge. To hold that the mind resides within the body and that phenomena arise outside of it is an inverted view.
Whether one speaks of "right" or "inverted," these are both merely names and marks. Ānanda, you should be able to, in this world...
When the Venerable One asks about the nature of names and designations, one realizes they are empty;

thus, deluded thoughts and attachments are exhausted, and even the pursuit of perfect universal knowledge (samyak-saṃbodhi) cannot be found. How could that which is the locus of inversion truly exist? *Mudrā*—this is translated as "seal."
This refers to the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*). The Dharma-body is "without body"; it takes the myriad dharmas as its body, yet no bodily form can be apprehended therein;
hence it is called the "Pure Dharma-body. "The eyes do not blink" explains the meaning of the two characters *dengmeng* (staring fixedly) mentioned above.
Commentary: This clarifies the nature of perversion (*viparyāsa*). Buddhas and sentient beings share the same single essence;
it has never been lost, yet it is merely a matter of perverted views. Now, the perversions within the mind are difficult to express in words and difficult to comprehend.
Therefore, the World-Honored One had no choice but to point to models and draw likenesses, manifesting them through the realm of existence (*sattvabhava*), so that [sentient beings] might...
Ānanda was easy to instruct. Therefore, [the Buddha] lowered his hand and pointed downward to question him about "stillness. Ānanda said, "Do you see my hand as upright or inverted?
Ānanda’s skillful means were exhausted; he did not dare to decide for himself, yet he could not remain silent.
He then said, "The sentient beings of the world consider this to be inverted. He proceeded to push the dry grass aside and said, "As for me, I do not know who is upright and who is inverted.
The World-Honored One, following his words, pursued him with a counter-question: "If the people of the world consider this to be inverted, then by what standard will they determine what is upright?
Ānanda was caught by the World-Honored One’s single word; he was hooked and could not escape.
As they departed, they said, "If the Tathāgata points upward toward the sky with his hand, that is called 'correct.
The World-Honored One then raised his arm and told them, "If you insist that pointing upward is correct, then you should take your head for your tail and your tail for your head.
You gaze at things in the same manner as the people of the world; how can you say that the people of the world [are wrong]?"
This is an inversion. Yet you do not know who is correct and who is inverted. However, in all things there is fundamentally no such thing as correct or inverted;
it is only by following the norm that something is considered correct, and by deviating from the norm that something is considered inverted.
If the hand is considered correct when pointing upward, why does it sometimes hang downward? If the hand is considered inverted when hanging downward, why does it not sometimes point upward?
Consider this: when one perceives all objects as they truly are (yathābhūta), in accordance with their true nature (dharmatā), this constitutes correct cognition;
when one pursues objects with agitation and forcibly gives rise to conceptual discrimination, this constitutes perversion.

Since you and your like have produced many such views and interpretations, whereas the Tathāgata has no such intentional mental activity, you should know that your own bodies and those of all Tathāgatas are the pure Dharma.
By means of analogy, it is revealed that the body of the Tathāgata should be called "Right Universal Knowledge" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*), whereas your bodies should be designated as "Inverted by Nature.

Since you point upward with your hands and consider that to be upright, while considering your own hands hanging downward to be inverted, the Tathāgata regards your bodies as inverted and the Dharma-body as upright. You...
"You consider your own dharma-body to be inverted and my body to be correct. Now, setting aside this 'correct knowledge' for a moment, observe closely according to your own understanding:
if both your body and the Buddha’s body are each called 'inverted,' then where, right now, do these two characters 'inversion' reside?
This is the World-Honored One further prodding with a needle, requiring Ānanda to point them out within these two bodies."
The delusions have been dispelled; names and reality now coincide. Where was Ānanda when he was pressed by the World-Honored One?
Together with the great assembly, he was as if dazed or mute, not knowing where the inversion of body and mind lay.
"The Buddha gives rise to compassion and pities Ānanda" (up to) "the jewel-bright, wondrous nature recognizes awakening within delusion.

This passage serves as the foundation for the three categories and seven elements in the subsequent text. Here, the *tathāgatagarbha* is pointed out as manifesting as the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world.
In the following text, these sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world are then integrated back into the *tathāgatagarbha*. Its...

The words and their meanings correspond to one another like two halves of a tally. Even though the subsequent text is extensive, it serves only to explain this single term "one thing" (*yiwu*) found here.
[Commentary: This clarifies the loss of the true mind. The previous reproach stated: "This is not your mind."

[The Buddha] taught these things primarily to make [Ānanda] realize that delusions have no substantial essence. Furthermore, he stated that "all phenomena are manifested solely by the mind," primarily to cause the extinction of delusion and the return to the True.
When Ānanda reached this point, he still recognized delusion and lost the Truth. Out of compassion for his dazed lack of awakening, the World-Honored One [spoke].

Therefore, he utters the sound of the ocean tide (and so forth). When the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma, it is neither before nor after its time; it never misses the proper moment, being comparable to the ocean tide.
"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the physical body as the foremost of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); "mind" (*citta*) refers to the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*).
It serves as the master of the single body. "Various conditions" refers to the five preceding faculties, which act as the faculties that perceive;
"the mind that is driven by mental factors" refers to the sixth and eighth consciousnesses, both of which can be what is driven. "The mind that drives" refers to the five preceding consciousnesses.
If the sixth consciousness is taken as the principal agent, it serves as the basis for discrimination and is thus driven by the sixth. If [the body] arises based on the eighth consciousness...

It arises; it is precisely that which is driven by the eighth consciousness. Regarding all objects of cognition (*ālambana-dharma*), these are explained in contrast to the aforementioned perceiving faculties (*indriya*).

They broadly refer to the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), encompassing all phenomena such as mountains, rivers, and the great earth, all of which are manifestations of the mind alone. This refers to the eighth consciousness.

It is able to manifest the two divisions of the perceived (nimitta-bhāga) and the perceiving (darśana-bhāga); yet these two divisions of the perceived and the perceiving encompass all that is sentient and insentient.
However, this eighth consciousness-mind is, moreover, the True Mind in a single thought-moment, arising in accordance with conditions. Therefore, to explain the preceding passage, it says:
"Viewed from this perspective, your physical body, as well as the sixth mental consciousness that presides over your person,"
All these are merely objects manifested within the true mind. It reflects upon encountering objects yet is not obscured by them; this is called "wondrous clarity.
It penetrates all phenomena universally yet is not mixed with even a speck of dust; this is called "true essence. It possesses all meanings;
this is called the "wondrous mind. Therefore, he rebuked and exhorted Ānanda, saying: "How is it that you have lost this wondrous mind and wondrous nature?"
Is this not rather recognizing delusion within enlightenment? To be wondrous of itself without relying on cultivation is called "primordial wondrousness" (*honmyō*).
To be all-pervasive with respect to the myriad dharmas while fundamentally never fluctuating is called "perfect wondrousness" (*enmyō*); this is the wondrousness of its function (*yō*).

To be luminously pure, firm, and solid, and to be of incomparable value, is the wondrousness of its essence (*tai*); this is the wondrousness of its substance. According to the traditional explanation, "mind" (*shin*) and "nature" (*sei*) are used interchangeably for essence and function; mind, then, follows from...
The wondrous arising of luminosity is perfectly interfused and clearly illuminating, like the luminous nature of a mirror; thus, luminosity itself is wondrous.
It is quiescent and profoundly still, like the substance of the mirror. Those who recognize delusion within awakening are unable to awaken to the fundamental wondrousness within illusory falsehood;
instead, they discard the fundamental wondrousness and cling to illusory falsehood. This refers to taking movement as the body and its environment, and further clinging to it...

"Things being for oneself" and so forth—all of these apply. However, if we discuss this according to principle, then those of the Two Vehicles are all those who are deluded within awakening, whereas ordinary beings are, conversely, those who are awakened within delusion. For this reason, the ancients [regarded] those of the Two Vehicles...
It is like ash from which the moisture has been removed; ordinary beings are likened to whole, unprocessed ash.

This means that although those of the Two Vehicles are within awakening, they will never have the opportunity to achieve Buddhahood; whereas although ordinary beings remain in delusion, they still possess the time when they shall attain Buddhahood.
"Obscuration and darkness constitute emptiness; within this dark and obscure void... (up to) all are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind.
This section of the sutra clearly demonstrates the arising of delusion from the truth, serving as the foundation for the three kinds of continuity that follow.
According to the fundamental purport of this sutra, it reveals that all phenomena do not transcend a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).

When a single thought arises, the myriad phenomena are simultaneously present; when a single thought ceases, the myriad phenomena are simultaneously non-existent. It is not that phenomena themselves possess existence or non-existence;
rather, existence and non-existence arise from the mind. As the ancients said: "The wise eliminate the mind, not the objects; the ignorant eliminate the objects, not the mind."
"Eliminating the mind. It is also said: "In delusion one does not recognize nature; in awakening one does not recognize emptiness. Both of these accord with this principle.
Within the text, the character "six" (六) should also be examined in its essential meaning. It is as if saying: emptiness is not empty of itself, but becomes empty because of ignorance;
form is not form of itself, but becomes form because of emptiness; the body is fundamentally not a body, yet it is taken as a body due to false attachment. Obscuration...

This state of restless agitation is fundamentally not the nature of the mind; yet you falsely identify it as the nature of the mind. Furthermore, the nature of the mind does not reside within the body.
Since you identify this state of murky agitation as the mind, you are certainly deluded into thinking it exists within the physical form.

Commentary: This clarifies the reason why the myriad dharmas manifest from the mind. Continuing from the above, it is said that although dharmas such as form and mind are indeed manifestations of the sole mind, by what cause do they first arise?
It is what is called the sudden arising of a single thought, wherein the myriad objects are fully revealed.
If one were in the fundamentally wondrous and luminous mind, the precious, luminous, and wondrous nature, before this single thought had arisen, then—
The phenomena of this world—body, mind, form, emptiness, and so forth—are all non-existent; they are nothing but the singular nature of the mind.
If this wondrously luminous mind-nature moves in accordance with conditions, it becomes deluded regarding its own luminous nature and turns into ignorance.

Thus, within a single thought-moment, one becomes attached to emptiness and consequently regards emptiness as a dull void. Having thus contrasted emptiness with ignorance, [one fails to realize their original unity].

It is a state of total obscurity and darkness; furthermore, within this darkness, they remain bound together and refuse to let go. Thus, by clinging to form through emptiness, and having already divided emptiness from form, ignorance gradually gives rise to deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).

These deluded thoughts then become entangled with the objects of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), leading one to further falsely identify the characteristics and appearances of the four great elements as one's own body.
In this way, confusion is accumulated upon confusion through delusion. By means of this delusion—
Inheriting delusion, one distinguishes between the internal and the external; yet, gathering external conditions, one stirs internal false thoughts.

By means of these internal false thoughts, one rushes outward in flight, becoming darkly ignorant and restless without ceasing. One then clings to this very darkness and restlessness, taking the appearance of agitation to be the nature of the mind.
Since you have once fallen into delusion and taken this darkness and restlessness to be your true mind, then...
You have determined that these delusions exist solely within this physical body; yet you fail to realize that the physical body within,
extending outward to the mountains, rivers, and even unto empty space and the great earth, are all merely objects manifested within the wondrously luminous true mind.
It is like discarding a hundred thousand vast oceans of clear, pure water (up to) what the Tathāgata calls "those who are to be pitied.
[Crown Commentary: This metaphor summarizes the abandonment of the true and the recognition of the false, as well as acting in a state of inversion.
It is like discarding a hundred thousand vast oceans of clear, pure water and instead recognizing only the substance of a single floating bubble, designating it as the entirety of the tide.

It is like Ānanda, who abandoned the vast and wondrously luminous nature of the mind, yet instead falsely identified the four elements as the characteristics of the body and took this confused and agitated state to be the wondrously luminous nature of the mind.

He did not realize that this body and this mind arise within the wondrously luminous mind, like a single bubble floating upon the great ocean. Even if you were to exhaust the entire expanse of the sea...
These are precisely those who are doubly deluded among the deluded. This analogy, interwoven with the Dharma, is the most urgent and essential point.
Within the analogy, to mistake a bubble for the ocean is not merely to mistake the substance of a single bubble and remain deluded by abandoning the great sea;

rather, it is to exhaustively search through and identify every bubble throughout the entire sea, seeing only floating bubbles until the end, never seeing the sea. To abandon the sea and recognize only the bubbles—furthermore...
To mistake a bubble for the ocean is to be deluded and yet further deluded. It is like Ānanda mistaking this illusory body and illusory mind for the wondrously luminous nature of the mind.
Not only does he mistake this single body and mind, but he is lost to the wondrously luminous nature of the mind.

Even if one recognizes [the self] through thousands or tens of thousands of lifetimes, knowing only that it is a conditioned shadow of the four elements, one will ultimately be unable to know the wondrously luminous nature of the mind.
Thus, deluded regarding the truth and pursuing the false, one further mistakes the false for the true; this is to be deluded yet again.
Yet, the bubble does not leave the sea; it sits within the great ocean and yet cannot see the sea. This is a metaphor for how delusion does not leave the truth:
one dwells within the wondrously luminous mind, yet fails to know that wondrously luminous nature of the mind. How could there truly be any loss? It is merely a matter of inverted perception.
It is like when I point my hand downward, yet you mistakenly think it is turned upside down. If I were to point my hand upward, [you would again perceive it as inverted].
To mistake the arm for the finger and yet consider it correct is no different from [mistaking] equality for non-differentiation.
Now, one who dwells beyond the sea and does not know the sea is hardly worthy of pity; how much less so one who dwells within the sea and does not know the sea?
It is like Ānanda: if he had truly lost the Way, it might still not be considered deeply lamentable; but now, the original has not been lost at all.
Yet in the end, he could not obtain it; like one who carries a jewel while begging for alms and thus undergoes needless suffering, such is why the Tathāgata describes him as pitiable.
"The entire tide" refers to the tide of the whole ocean, indicating the great sea.
"Yingbo" (瀛渤) is a synonym for the sea, also referring to the great ocean.
Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction, [has reached the point where] the roots of my doubts have been uprooted and I have returned to the Unsurpassed Way.

According to ancient exegesis, there are three inconceivable aspects of the Perfect Sound (*pariṣphuṭa-svara*): first, that beings from different regions and diverse species all hear it as their own fundamental language;

second, that whether their capacities are great or small, shallow or deep, they all benefit according to their understanding; third, that even those who are separated by distance and have a karmic connection [to the teaching] all hear it simultaneously.
At present, that which uproots my root of doubt is this very doubt itself; it is so profound that I am unable to uproot it by my own power.

Therefore, I rely on the Buddha’s power to extract it. Only now, upon reaching this point, does Ānanda realize that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of his extensive learning are so deep-seated as to be difficult to eliminate.
Commentary: This describes the expression of doubt and the request for a definitive resolution.

While the World-Honored One has elucidated the True Mind that transcends all dualistic oppositions of subject and object, Ānanda still clings to the mind that perceives objects; he thus continues to take this攀緣心 (mind of grasping and conditioning) as his own self-nature.
His intention is that, having long been inverted and submerged in delusion, he has now received compassionate rescue, yet he has remained consistently lost.
"O Wondrous Mind! Having now received these profound instructions, I am moved by the Buddha’s great compassion; thus, with tears falling and palms joined, I ask again:

although I have received such wondrous sounds from the Buddha and realized that this wondrously luminous mind-nature is originally my own fundamental perfection—encompassing the ten voids and pervading the entire Dharma-realm, never having been lost nor ever having arisen—"
This eternally abiding mind-ground has been utterly lost by us; we have mistakenly identified this mind with the deluded, conditioned mind (*pratyaya-citta*).
Therefore, the Buddha instructed me using the wondrous mind while censuring me for using the conditioned mind.
Yet, as I now hear the sound of the Dharma and realize the true mind, I am still employing the conditioned mind; that which I take to be the true mind is, in fact, the conditioned mind.
Beholding the Tathāgata is likewise a mind conditioned by objects. That which the World-Honored One has caused me to awaken to is the perfect true mind;
although it is called "ever-abiding," its function is not yet manifest at present. If one were to abandon this mind conditioned by objects, with what would one receive the Dharma?
Therefore, though I have obtained this mind in vain, I do not yet dare to recognize it as my original fundamental mind-ground, and thus I am left in doubt.

It seems so; I cannot yet determine what to accept or reject. I pray that the Buddha will take pity on me and proclaim his perfect voice, uprooting the foundation of my doubts, so that I may sever them and return to the One Vehicle, attaining the Unsurpassed Way.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You and the others [still] regard [the means of expression]... because there is nothing to be realized; you are also like this. (Annotation:
This rebukes him for recognizing the signifier while neglecting the signified. Ānanda recognizes the subjective faculty of cognition.)
The Buddha first causes the object of focus to be relinquished; if the objective realm is forgotten, then the subjectively cognizing mind will gradually subside.
This means that I have expended much verbal prolixity specifically to eliminate your mind of objective focus, so that you may accord with true nature.
Yet even now, you still listen to the Dharma with a mind conditioned by objects.
Since you use this deluded, objectifying mind to hear my teaching on the perfect and wondrous mind-dharma, that very perfect and wondrous mind-dharma becomes, in turn, a deluded object of perception.
How, then, can you realize this nature of phenomena? This nature of phenomena is none other than your own wondrously luminous ground of mind.
This is not my own voice. You must understand that I who preach the Dharma am like one pointing toward the moon, while you who listen to the Dharma are like those looking at the moon.

If you can, by means of my voice of the Dharma, bring forth the wondrous mind within yourself, this is like recognizing the moon because of the finger, and then forgetting the finger. If you merely pursue words and phrases, you will be caught by the sound.
Driven by sensory dust, this is like using a finger to point at the moon while, conversely, forgetting the very substance of the moon.

Is it not that one fails to recognize the moon? One also fails to recognize the finger. Is it not merely that one fails to recognize the finger? One likewise does not understand light and darkness. Why is this?
Because the substance of the finger is dark while the substance of the moon is bright; yet, regarding these two natures of light and darkness, there is no comprehension whatsoever.
It is for this reason. Now, you take the sound of the Dharma as an object of perception and give rise to a mind that perceives it;
thus, you lose sight of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and it is exactly like this.
If one discriminates that the sounds of my Dharma-teachings each have their own point of return, how can [the mind] be the master?
(Commentary: This rebukes the recognition of the conditioned mind and exposes the delusion regarding the wondrous mind. The preceding section eliminated the objects of perception.)
Now, I shall dispatch the mind that is capable of cognition. As it was said above: "You say that you currently employ the cognizing mind to faithfully attend to what you behold.

If this mind that discriminates the sounds of the Dharma were your true mind, then this mind should naturally possess the nature of discrimination even when separated from the sounds of the Dharma that are its objects of discrimination. Now, that which lacks such a nature is like a guest; that which possesses such a nature..."
It is like a host and guests: the guests come and go, while the host remains ever-present. The true and the false aspects of the mind are just like this.
If you take that which discriminates the sounds of the Dharma as your true mind, then this mind should remain eternally constant in its essential nature even apart from sound.
Why is it that, when separated from the sound of my preaching the Dharma, your discriminating nature no longer exists? How could this be?
It is merely your discrimination of the sound "I. Apart from the sound, there is no inherent nature.
Likewise, your discrimination of my form—apart from my physical appearance and the marks and signs—is likewise devoid of a discriminative mind-nature.

Not only do the six consciousnesses that arise and cease dependent on objects fail to be your true nature, but even if one were to take the six consciousnesses along with the six faculties and six objects—namely, the subject...

The discriminating mind and the objects discriminated by it are utterly quiescent and non-existent; they do not belong to the form of the sense organs and their objects, nor do they belong to the emptiness of consciousness and the mind.
Such illusory appearances of states are still within the limits of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Yet, heterodox teachers such as Kuśarī and others are muddled and fail to realize this, falsely designating them as the "Dark Principle" (*tamas-tattva*). As for this Dark Principle, it is a state of profound obscurity.

They cannot distinguish [the true from the false], yet they falsely establish a "True Truth. They claim that the Primordial Darkness gives rise to Awareness (*buddhi*), which is the original source of all phenomena, and they falsely revere this as the ultimate principle.
Since even this is not the True Mind, how much less so for a deluded mind that lacks an essence apart from sensory objects—how could such a mind be considered the True Nature?
If your auditory consciousness exists when it conditions sound, [it does not exist when there is no sound].
Apart from sound, it does not exist; when the eye-consciousness conditions form, it exists, and apart from form, it does not exist.
This continues up to the mental consciousness: when it conditions dharmas, it exists, and apart from dharmas, it does not exist. Thus, the nature of your mind has its respective places of return;
all are like temporary guests who stay briefly and then depart. How can this be your true mind? Is it like the permanent resident of the inn-keeper?
This passage corresponds to the two characters "seeing" and "hearing" first mentioned by Ānanda, as well as his earlier remarks regarding "listening to the Dharma" and "gazing up in reverence.
Ānanda said: "If my mind-nature has each its own place to which it returns... (up to) "...I shall now show you the ground where there is no returning."
Commentary: This seeks to demonstrate that there is nothing to be returned. First, a metaphor is employed to illustrate this.

Ānanda, having heard that the nature of the mind has something that can be returned, asks the Tathāgata: "How is it that the wondrously luminous original mind spoken of by the Buddha has nothing to be returned?
The Buddha tells him: "That which has nothing to be returned exists precisely within that which has something to be returned. How could one seek water apart from the waves?"
Furthermore, at the very moment you see me, within this faculty of vision itself there is an intrinsic function of clarity and brilliance that is not mixed with form;
this emerges from its own source and is called the "originally luminous essence" (*ming-yuan*).

Now, although this essence of vision flows forth from the originally luminous essence of consciousness, its substance has been permeated by delusion, causing it to divide into six locations and fail to turn back [toward its source].
Six have been lost and one remains; thus it is merely the essence of seeing, not yet the wondrous essence. It is merely the source of clarity, not yet the luminous mind.

Yet this does not prevent its being intimately close to the fundamentally wondrous and luminous mind, the precious, luminous, and wondrous nature. It is like a second moon: although produced by pressing upon the eyes, it is intimately close to the true moon.
It is not as if there were a gap as vast as heaven and abyss between it and the reflection of the moon in water. Now...
I shall now show you the ground where the essence of seeing has no place to return. This is because the wondrously luminous nature of the mind is vast, boundless, perfect, and without form;
it is ultimately difficult to point to with certainty. Therefore, we rely upon this essence of seeing as a skillful means for instruction.
If one awakens and enters through this essence of seeing, the entire body and its great function are likewise found herein. This should be understood by means of the true moon.

The excellent brightness of the mind-nature is illustrated by the analogy of the first moon; the visual essence is illustrated by the analogy of the second moon; and the deluded perception conditioned by sense objects is illustrated by the analogy of the moon's reflection in water.
This visual essence is precisely the aforementioned consciousness-essence and that which remains unchanging when observing the river.
This exists within Ānanda’s perception of the thirty-two marks, and it has never been deficient; it merely turns or does not turn.
"Ānanda, this great lecture hall is opened wide... [up to] "...therefore the Tathāgata is named 'the Compassionate One.
*Annotation:* This intends to demonstrate the vision that cannot be returned. First, it identifies the characteristics that *can* be returned.
The meaning is that without the characteristics that can be returned, the vision that cannot be returned is not revealed. When you see this lecture hall opened wide—
When the rising sun appears in the east, one perceives the appearance of light; when it is midnight, under a dark moon, or shrouded in clouds and mist, one perceives the appearance of darkness;
through the gaps of doors and windows, one perceives the appearance of openness; within the spaces between walls and buildings, one perceives the appearance of obstruction.
When one discriminates these various appearances, there arises a deluded perception that acts as the perceiving subject, which pervades throughout the midst of the stubborn void.
This is precisely emptiness (*śūnyatā*). That which meanders within the appearance of turbidity is the dust of obscuration;
when it clears and the mists subside, one further contemplates the appearance of purity. Now, these eight appearances also possess the distinction between subject and object;

the deluded perception of discrimination belongs to the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*), while the remaining seven types do not transcend brightness and darkness, as both color-form and emptiness are equally bound to them.
The objects of the eye faculty naturally belong to the realm of the perceived; yet the characteristics of both the perceiver and the perceived each have their own causes.
Since these characteristics are established in dependence upon causes, they are identical to transformations. You all observe these various transformed phenomena;
I shall now return each of them to its original causal source. What is this original cause? Each of these transformed phenomena has its own source from which it arises, which I shall now clarify.
The characteristic of light returns to the solar orb. Why is this? There is nothing that is not illuminated by the sun; the fundamental cause of illumination belongs inherently to the sun.

Therefore, the characteristic of darkness returns to the sun. The characteristic of the dark moon returns to its source. The characteristic of pervasion returns to the windows and doors. The characteristic of obstruction returns to the walls and buildings.
The seeing that acts as the perceiving subject returns to the fundamental faculty of discrimination. The characteristic of the stubborn void returns to its source.

This is the nature of original emptiness. When the signs of turbidity return to their original state as murky dust, and the signs of clarity and brightness return to their original state as a clear, cloudless sky, then all phenomena in the world do not transcend these categories.
You have perceived eight kinds of phenomenal signs; yet, while facing these objects, you did not become confused by them.
Within these eight signs, with which sign does the luminous nature of your seeing-perception necessarily correspond?
Do they both return together? Why is this? If, when returning from the appearance of light, one returns to the state of ignorance, the appearance of darkness manifests before you;
then, by what will you see again? Although the various distinctions between appearances such as light and darkness arise and cease without ceasing, your essence of seeing perceives them all at once.
Thus, it is sufficient to know that these various appearances exist within your own essence of seeing.
The characteristics undergo transformation, yet your essence of vision remains clearly manifest and unclouded, steadfast and immutable.
How could it possibly be the same as the deluded perception that acts as the subject of cognition, which returns along with light, darkness, form, and space?

If both the subjective and objective characteristics were all capable of returning, then naturally they would not be your essence of vision. You ought to relinquish this essence of vision and not [identify it] with these various phenomena.
As for those who return together after observing these signs: since they do not belong to any illusory appearances, they are simply your own visual essence (*darśana-viśuddhi*).

What else could they be but your visual essence? If you understand this visual essence, then you will know that your true mind is fundamentally wondrous without requiring cultivation, fundamentally luminous without requiring polishing, and fundamentally pure without requiring washing; though it is brilliantly radiant...
You perceive the various marks of sensory objects, yet you forget all subject and object. You transcend all obstacles and sever all defilement and purity;

yet now you cling and begrudge, maintaining deluded perceptions through the faculty of cognition. Confused and distressed, you do not relinquish them, thereby losing your original wondrous clarity and purity.
You suffer in vain as you wander through the cycle of birth and death, drifting and drowning within it with no hope of escape—all of this is of your own making. This is so.

Therefore, the Tathāgata said that you are truly worthy of compassion. Among these eight kinds of characteristics, the act of discrimination belongs to the subject that perceives (*ālambaka*), while light, darkness, form, and space belong to the objects perceived (*ālambana*). When the objects of perception undergo change, the perception of the subject naturally ceases;
thus, the deluded mind—which was previously shown to have no essence apart from its objects—arrives at this point. Within this:
It points out that the essence of seeing has no place of return; this refers to the method of "probing and examining" previously demonstrated.

By probing and examining within that which has no substance, that which possesses substance emerges. The reason for singling out the essence of seeing as having no place of return here is that the essence of seeing cannot be separated from the true nature;
therefore, it is presented while simultaneously clarifying that nature. This continues until the section on the two types of sameness and difference.
By eliminating these various false perceptions of the ten directions, this essence of seeing is made alone manifest as true nature, just as one removes the second moon to behold the true moon.
Ānanda said: "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has nothing to return to, how can I know it is my true nature?"
Commentary: This presents a doubt to seek a definitive resolution. Ānanda, following the Buddha’s previous instruction, says:
"Although the essence of seeing is not the wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind—it is like a second moon—it is nevertheless not the same as deluded vision, which returns along with all phenomena.
Yet, since it is like a second moon, it is still not the true moon; how then can one know that this essence of seeing is pure and bright?"
"Is this nature my true nature?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I shall now question you... [up to] "...sentient beings can see through objects no more than a few inches.
Anuruddha—this means "Unextinguished"—in the past, because of his offerings, he received merit that was never extinguished. This is from the Buddha...

Brother, you were rebuked for sleeping during the day; through your diligent practice, you lost your physical eyes but subsequently realized the four fruits of arhatship and attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

With this, you see the great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*)—here referred to as Jambudvīpa, or sometimes specifically indicating the Sahā world—as clearly as looking at an *āmra* fruit in the palm of one's hand.

(The term *āmra* here means "difficult to distinguish," as it is easily confused with a peach. One such great trichiliocosm constitutes a single world-system (*dhātu*). Although a bodhisattva may see hundreds or thousands of such systems, [the Buddha sees them all].

All are finite. To say they are "exhaustively as minute as atoms" is a general way of stating that they have no measure or number. What is observed by the Buddha-eye is that purity and defilement are equal;
it does not exceed a mere fraction of an inch. To speak of the inferior in contrast to the superior means that when compared with Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, [the world] is thus characterized.
Even at its maximum extent, the scope of seeing does not exceed a mere fraction of an inch. Furthermore, whenever one speaks of "sentient beings," it encompasses all that wriggles and crawls.
Below this are four sections of scripture: the first clarifies that objects are not seeing;
the second clarifies that seeing is not objects; the third clarifies that there is no seeing apart from objects; and the fourth clarifies...
To be free from seeing is to have no objects. One must view these four sections in conjunction to perceive the profound intent.

If one says that seeing is not an object, it does not preclude being free from seeing and having no objects. If one says that an object is not seeing, it does not preclude being free from objects and having no seeing.
If there were no objects apart from seeing, then objects could not be found upon seeking them. If there were no seeing apart from objects, then seeing itself could not be found upon seeking it.

Thus, both the subject (the capacity) and the object (the content) are simultaneously extinguished; right and wrong are both forgotten. In every dharma and at every point, there is the wondrous existence of true emptiness;
in every mote of dust and every world-system, there is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Yet, this is not something that can be grasped by those who lack the fundamental [wisdom].
Even those of great wisdom cannot penetrate it; therefore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva took it upon his own person to serve as a great banner for Ānanda and others.
Commentary: This intends to demonstrate the true nature (*tathatā*). First, it reveals the differences among the various modes of perception (*darśana-mātra*).

Above, the false perceptions that are devoid of objects and lack substantiality were eliminated, thereby revealing the essence of perception (*darśana-śuddhi*) which possesses substantiality while being free from objects.
Hereafter, the true nature is further elucidated by means of the myriad phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, it is said later: "To be free from all marks is to be one."
This marks the beginning of the examination of all phenomena. The meaning is this: if you wish to know true nature, you must first recognize the scope of your vision.
Ānanda has only realized the first fruit of the path; he has not yet attained untainted purity, nor does he possess the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

He must rely upon the Buddha’s power before he can see even the First Dhyāna realm. Aniruddha, however, has already attained the divine eye and sees the Jambudvīpa continent as clearly as looking at the palm of his hand.
As for the fruit: the Bodhisattva has already perfected the Dharma-eye, whereby they can see the five eyes of the Tathāgatas throughout hundreds of thousands of worlds with complete clarity;
yet their physical eye (māṃsa-cakṣus) can see sentient beings within lands as small as motes of dust, seeing through them without obstruction even down to the width of a hair’s breadth.

True nature is one; the holy and the ordinary are equal, fundamentally lacking nothing and in need of nothing. Nevertheless, this does not preclude the capacity for vision, wherein distinctions between the holy and the ordinary still appear.

This lack of uniformity is likely because their essence is the same while their applications differ. One must ensure that cultivation and realization proceed together, becoming increasingly clear and far-reaching;
otherwise, how could one ever neglect the essential work of cultivating the truth and severing delusions?
"Ānanda, let me and you observe the Four Heavenly Kings... (up to)... this exquisite, wondrous, and luminous clarity is your seeing-nature.
*Commentary:* This intends to clarify that objects are not the seeing. First, it causes Ānanda to personally examine and discern for himself.
The meaning is that while others may perceive all things far and near, you yourself do not know them, nor can you discern them.
Regarding that view: furthermore, let us together with you now observe the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings dwell.
They are situated upon the midsection of Mount Sumeru, reaching upward to the sun and moon and downward to the great earth.

From there, we shall survey everything in between, including all things moving on water, land, and through the air; wherever the various characteristics of phenomena may exist, despite their manifold states of darkness and light.
Forms and images are nothing other than objective phenomena before one's eyes; they serve as objects that obstruct or allow the passage of your faculty of discerning vision.
You should, regarding these perceived objects, exercise discrimination and selection: "What is my own essence of seeing? What is an external thing?
You must distinguish them clearly without confusion. Since you are unable to do so, I shall select them for you. Now—
"I shall lead you to perceive the essence of seeing. Within the realm of what is seen, I will cause you to clearly understand: what is the essence of your seeing?
This is the substance of the Tathāgata’s seeing. What are the objects and images? These three things are distinct and entirely unmixed.
You shall know for yourself that the essence of your seeing and the substance of my seeing are equally pervasive throughout all things. Ānanda.
"Difficult indeed it is to reach the source of your vision; it emerges from your own eyes and extends upward as far as the celestial palaces of the sun and moon.

Whatever you perceive therein consists entirely of objective forms and is not your essential faculty of seeing. Observe with thorough and precise scrutiny everything in between, reaching as far as the seven golden mountains."
Although there are various kinds of light, they are all material objects; they are not your seeing-essence gradually observing and gradually approaching them.
Furthermore, observe the rising clouds, the flying birds, and even down to the grasses, weeds, humans, and animals—all are merely phenomenal forms of matter, not your seeing-essence.
Since you have already understood that all objects are not your faculty of vision, then your faculty of vision itself ought to be discerned and extracted.
Therefore, he points it out again, saying: "Ānanda, whatever objects you see now—whether near or far, large or small—all these various natures of things stand arrayed before your sight.
Yet your faculty of vision pervades all these myriad forms; although the objects themselves are of many kinds,"
They are different, yet they do not obstruct your seeing-essence as it gazes with clarity; nor do they become confused or intermingled.
You should know that while the categories of objects naturally possess distinctions, there is no distinction within your nature of seeing.
This very essence of seeing, which does not mix with objects, is your wondrous, pure, and luminous mind. Thus, you should know that this wondrous, pure, and luminous mind is truly without...
Apart from the nature of seeing within your eyes, why are you unable to discern it among these various objects?
The palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings reside on the mid-slopes of Mount Sumeru, which is surrounded by the seven golden mountains on its exterior.
Look at this scriptural passage and the subsequent text; you must necessarily keep the preceding context in mind. Now, let me speak with you.
By observing the passage concerning the Four Heavenly Kings, one comes to understand why the World-Honored One observed the same object as Ānanda:
it was to rely upon the Buddha’s faculty of vision in order to discern Ānanda’s true nature of seeing.
"If you see this object, then you [must] also [be it]; since it is naturally not an object, how could it not be you?
(Commentary: This clarifies that seeing is not an object. Continuing from the above, it says: "Is it not only the case that objects are not seeing?")
Seeing is also not an object. If your seeing were an object, then my seeing would also be an object; in that case, you should also be able to see my seeing.

Fearing that he might mistakenly cling to the notion that when he views the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings together with all other objects, the World-Honored One’s seeing is likewise present upon all those objects, [the Buddha] asks: "How is it that I do not see it? Therefore...

The text states: "If you claim that when you and I see an object together, it is called 'seeing,' then when my seeing ceases and I withdraw my gaze so that I no longer see the object, why do you not see my lack of vision of the object and point out its location?
If you cannot see me when I am not seeing the object, then [you should likewise be unable to see] when we see the object together."

Furthermore, I have never seen it. If you insist on claiming that you can see even the place where I do not see, then my seeing would naturally not be that which is invisible to you; rather, it would become a visible phenomenon.
If my seeing is visible, then your seeing should likewise be visible; why then is it not seen? Since I do not [see it]...
[The Buddha said: "I see. How can you see? If you cannot see, then my seeing of things is not seeing; yet you are confused as to where that seeing resides.
Thus, my seeing is naturally not a thing with form. My seeing is not a thing, and your seeing is also not a thing.
Since it is not a thing, how could your seeing-nature not be your own seeing-nature?"
Furthermore, at this very moment when you see an object... (until) "the nature [of seeing] is not truly grasped by you; seek the reality from me. [Commentary:
This further clarifies that whether sentient or insentient, whether sage or ordinary person, there is not the slightest need to stir or disturb anything;
it is, of itself, the single true Dharma-realm. Continuing from above: if your seeing were an object, then...
Objects are also your seeing. Now, when you see objects, since you have already seen them, if the objects also possessed seeing, they would likewise be able to see you;

consequently, the nature of seeing in sentient beings of the world and the nature of insentient objects would become hopelessly entangled and indistinguishable. Thus, your seeing and my seeing would likewise be indistinguishable.
They are divided. Furthermore, all things in the world would be indistinguishable, lacking any discernment, and could not be established as such.
Now, when you perceive objects and perceive yourself, if that perception were fixed as yours alone and not mine, then you and I would be clearly established as distinct entities.
Consequently, the sentient and the insentient would be sharply distinguished without confusion; thus one knows that the nature of seeing is detached [from the self].

Regarding the characteristics of all things: even if you were to observe before you the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings, down to the smallest blades of grass, the people, and all objects, they are all the pervasive nature of your own seeing.
None of them belong to external objects, nor do they belong to a self. If it is not your own nature of seeing, then what could it be?
Why do you not have confidence in yourself, but instead harbor doubts? This is because it is your true nature.
You already possess it, yet you do not believe it to be real; instead, you take my words to seek its reality, asking, "How can one know that this is my true nature?
This is a profound delusion. The *dharmatā* of *tathatā* has two meanings: the established (*prajñapti*) and the non-established (*aprajñapti*).
This passage reveals the established *tathatā*, while the subsequent text reveals the non-established.
"It is *tathatā* (Suchness).
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing... [up to] "...I pray that you will bestow your great compassion and expound it for me.
**Annotation:** This follows upon the preceding text, as he harbors doubts regarding the nature of seeing. Continuing from above, he says: "If this nature of seeing..."
The essence of seeing is fundamentally all-pervasive; it is inherent within one's own mind and self, not something separate from oneself. Why is this so?

When you looked together with the Tathāgata upon the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings, your vision encompassed the entire Sahā world-system. Yet when you returned to the vihāra, you saw only the monastery grounds;
and as you entered further into the halls and chambers, you beheld only the eaves and corridors. Thus, the substance of this seeing is fundamentally all-pervasive throughout the one [Dharmadhātu].
"Worldly Realm, it is now inside this room, filling the room entirely.
Regarding such uncertainty as to its size—does the essence of seeing contract from large to small according to the dimensions of the room?
Or does the essence of seeing remain uncontracted, merely severed by the walls and unable to continue? I do not yet know whether this nature of seeing contracts in size."
As for the meaning of "severing," what is its definitive locus? I pray that you will expound upon this.

Now, the dialogue between teacher and disciple merely aims to clarify that the five kinds of views and measures are not uniform; this is simply due to the exhaustion or non-exhaustion of each individual's own delusions and karma.
It is not that the nature of seeing itself is anything other than one. As for the passage below regarding "removing the vessel to contemplate emptiness," you shall understand it for yourself.
It is perfectly clear.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All worlds... (up to) ...furthermore, excluding even the location of the spatial characteristics. [Commentary:
This demonstrates that while the dimensions of objects reside within sensory phenomena, the nature of seeing is fundamentally without expansion or contraction. This is the intended meaning.
It is as you have said: within all worlds, one perceives the large and the small, the internal and the external;

all phenomena, characteristics, and functional activities each belong to the objective realms before one's eyes. One should not say that the nature of seeing undergoes expansion or contraction, or interruption or continuity.
Your nature of seeing is like empty space, while all objective phenomena are like vessels. As for these phenomena...
Phenomena have dimensions—large or small, internal or external—but the nature of seeing has no expansion or contraction, nor does it have interruption or continuity.

It is like vessels that may be square or round, while the space within them has no fixed characteristics. You do not now understand the relationship between the nature of seeing and objective phenomena; you merely observe the empty vessel.
This can be understood. Within a square vessel, you perceive the space as square. Is the space you perceive fixedly square, or is it not fixedly square?
If it were fixedly square, then when placed within a round vessel, the space should not become round.
If it were not fixed, then when there is a square vessel in the present moment, there would be no square space; your seeing-nature is likewise so.
If it were fixed as large and pervaded the entire realm, then upon entering a room, it would not become small again.
If it were not fixed, then outside the room it should not be all-pervasive. You say that you do not know where this principle lies.
The meanings of its magnitude, contraction, interruption, and so forth are likewise like space. Yet, how could it be fixed in a specific location?
Indeed, one who can perceive the indeterminate within a fixed place and perceive the determinate within an indeterminate place has a mind identical to the great void.
Therefore it is said: "Ānanda, if you wish to cause the nature of space to enter into a state without squareness or roundness, you need only remove the squareness and roundness of the vessel;

the essence of space itself fundamentally lacks the characteristics of squareness and roundness. One should not say that after removing the vessel, one must further remove the location of the spatial characteristics themselves.
This means that if you wish to cause the seeing-nature to enter into a state without largeness or smallness, [the principle is the same].
Setting aside the objects of the senses, the nature of seeing is fundamentally neither large nor small.

One should not say that after removing the objects of the senses, one must further remove the location of the largeness or smallness of the nature of seeing. Therefore, the ancient masters said: "There is no need to seek the Truth;
one need only cease [discursive] views."
As for your question regarding whether there would not be a continuous trail when entering a room, this argument is incorrect.
[Commentary: This citation of the objection serves to refute it as being erroneous.

The meaning is that if you observe that when entering a room he causes his large body to contract and become small, then when looking up at the sun, he should likewise be able to stretch himself out to reach the sun’s edge.
If, at the place where a wall or house is being built, one can both block the view so that it is severed and then pierce a small hole to draw the view back so that it is restored—
yet now we observe that the sun cannot be drawn inward to expand its entry into the room, how could it possibly be contracted?
If one were to make small perforations, since there would be no continuous traces remaining, it would be possible to build a wall; furthermore, how could one possibly clamp them to cause a break?
This argument is certainly not tenable.

All sentient beings, from time immemorial [until] being able to universally contain the lands of the ten directions within themselves—such as a single hair-tip containing a world-system—is what the world calls a teaching difficult to believe. Please allow me to illustrate the profound by means of the shallow;
it may then be understood. For instance, when a person experiences pain or itching within a single pore of their body, they are without exception aware of it. That which is thus known...
This is the entire substance and great function of my mind-nature. When this mind-nature functions within a single pore, its substance and function do not diminish by so much as a hair’s breadth.

When it functions throughout the entire body, extending to bowing and rising before heaven and earth and pervading all things, its substance and function do not increase by so much as a hair’s breadth.
This very mind-nature is identical to that of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The Buddha is of one essence, perfectly complete, and equal without distinction. Formerly, Li Bo, the Regional Inspector of Jiangzhou, asked Guizong:
"Regarding what is said in the teachings—that Mount Sumeru can contain a mustard seed—I have no doubt; however, that a mustard seed can contain Mount Sumeru—"
“Is this not idle talk? Zong said, “It is said that you, Prefect, have read ten thousand scrolls of books; is this true? He replied, “Indeed.
Zong said, “From the crown of your head to the soles of your feet, you are no larger than a coconut. Where, then, do those ten thousand scrolls reside?”

Bo bowed his head and remained silent. Inferring from this, there is no reason why the mental capacity of sentient beings could not be equal to that of the Buddhas, such that the pores of their bodies might contain all world-realms—what would be impossible about this?
Commentary: This concluding section summarizes the meaning of the preceding passage on the five kinds of cognitive objects (*viṣaya-pramāṇa*).

The previous statement, "recognizing things as oneself," used the term "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*) to encompass both ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). This current statement, "deluding oneself into taking oneself to be things," uses the term "those of the Two Vehicles" to encompass ordinary beings.
This is because the seer and the seen are but the single True Nature (*tathatā*), which fundamentally lacks any obstruction and possesses neither magnitude nor minuteness.

This is fundamentally because the Tathāgatagarbha-nature has evolved from its original state to become the ālayavijñāna, manifesting as the two divisions of appearance and perception—the sense organs, the physical body, and the external world.
Ordinary beings, failing to penetrate the true nature of all phenomena, mistake these bubble-like reflections within the True Mind for substantial realities.
Even those of the Two Vehicles do not understand the ālayavijñāna; therefore, they are unable to realize that the myriad things are one with themselves.

Turning back from delusion: one regards oneself as being among external objects. Having already lost the originally possessed, vast, perfect, wondrous, and luminous mind, one is personally unaware that both the sentient and the insentient are of one's own single substance.

Being unable to transcend the sense organs and their objects, not only is one unable to turn the myriad things back toward oneself, but one instead turns oneself back toward the myriad things. Thus, regarding this one...

Within all things, movement is obstructed and hindered, such that one perceives the great as small. If one realizes that all phenomena are but mind, one is able to transform the myriad things back into oneself.

According to the principle that all phenomena are *tathatā* (suchness), this is identical to the Tathāgata’s transformation of the physical body (*rūpakāya*) into the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and the transformation of the conscious mind into true wisdom (*samyagjñāna*). Thus, the body fills the ten voids and the mind is like a thousand suns, encompassing all that is great.
The realms of the sands of a thousand worlds enter into the midst of body and mind, yet they possess no characteristics of coming, going, shifting, or moving.
This very body and mind is also the site where all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attain the Way. Within this body, take even a single hair-tip.

It is universally able to contain the lands of the ten directions; by means of the small encompassing the large, the small never increases, yet when the large is brought into the small, the large never diminishes.
Because the small does not increase, the large manifests within it; because the large does not diminish, the small manifests within it.

Thus, the environment and its inhabitants are perfectly interfused, phenomena and principle are unimpeded, and the wondrous perfection of the nature of reality is fully realized. This reaches the ultimate point.
How could there be any limitation of size or magnitude here? It is identical to the Tathāgata’s Buddha-eye that illuminates all before him.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this essence of vision [is as you have described], I pray that you will deign to bestow great compassion and reveal what I have not yet understood."
Commentary: This introduces the preceding meaning in order to raise a doubt and difficulty. The intention is this:

the World-Honored One said, "This subtle, wondrous, and luminous [clarity] is truly your seeing-nature," and he also said, "The seeing-nature is all-pervasive; if it were not you, who else could it be?
If that is so, then everything currently present is my essence of seeing. If this essence of seeing is necessarily my wondrous nature, then as for this wondrous nature...

Now appearing before me, he then raised an objection, saying: "If this pervasive seeing-essence were necessarily my true nature, then my true nature would, conversely, be outside my body. Yet it is now manifest within my body;
what, then, is that which currently discriminates external objects? He further presented a challenge, saying: "The mind within the body right now is truly capable of..."
One discriminates external objects; yet that nature of seeing which pervades those externals has never itself been subject to discrimination.
It is able to discern my own body, and thus this nature of seeing seems to reside within me rather than pervading all things.
If it were truly pervasive throughout the external, it would actually be my own mind. Now, let my body become the object seen by it.
If you can see that my body is all-pervasive, yet recognize that it is the nature of seeing that is "me" while the body is not "me," then you should not say, "I am able to see objects.
In that case, what difference would there be from the Tathāgata’s previous refutation: "Objects are able to see me"?
Furthermore, if you identify with the nature of seeing, you abandon both body and mind; if you identify with body and mind, [you miss the nature].
If that were so, the nature of seeing would not be all-pervasive. I pray that you will bestow great compassion and enlighten those who have not yet awakened.

Generally speaking, the nature of seeing shown by the World-Honored One is a seeing that is without subject and without object; whereas the state of mind and its environment grasped by Ānanda is one with a subject and an object.
If one realizes that subject and object are non-dual, then one's doubts will naturally be resolved. That which allows me to see now is...
The phrasing is inverted; it should rather say, "it causes me to see now.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Regarding what you have just said [up to] 'there is a separate self-nature,' the Buddha said: 'So it is, so it is.'"
Commentary: This demonstrates that there is no seeing apart from objects, thereby refuting this [notion of] seeing. Continuing from above:
"That which you now call the essence of seeing, which appears before you, is in all cases not a true reality; it is entirely false and deceptive.
