If your essence of seeing were truly present before you, and you truly saw it, then it would possess a specific form. If it possessed a specific form, it would certainly..."
If it has a location, then since it has a location, you should naturally point it out and show it to me. For now, we are sitting together in the Jeta Grove;
look all around at the grove and its streams, down to the grasses, trees, and even the finest details.

Though they differ in size, whatever possesses form can all be observed by the eye and pointed out with a finger to others. If this essence of seeing were necessarily in front of you, [it would be visible].
Furthermore, you should point it out clearly with your hand. Why? Which of these is the seeing that you show me? You should know this:
that which has form before us belongs entirely to material objects; that which is formless is space.
Apart from these two kinds, there is nothing else to point out. If space were seeing, then since space has already become seeing, what could be pointed out as being space?
If objects are the seeing, then since objects have already become seeing, what do you point to as being the object?

You should immediately take all the myriad phenomena and minutely peel them apart and analyze them until you extract that which is brilliant, pure, subtle, and wondrous—the original source of seeing—which is not mixed with objects, is not obscured by objects, and is not defiled by objects.
Deliver me this, pointing it out clearly from beyond all objects, just as you would clearly distinguish each of those objects.

"It is not delusion; it is possible. Ānanda replied, "In this regard, whether far or near, above or below, whatever can be observed by the eye and pointed out with the finger—all of these are objects. There is no such thing as 'seeing.
As the World-Honored One has said, how much less could I—a defiled beginner śrāvaka, or even a bodhisattva—perceive it within the myriad [phenomena]?"

The elephant then split open its forehead and manifested its consciousness (*vijñāna*), pointing it out to the World-Honored One as something possessing a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that exists separately from all material objects.
When the Buddha granted his approval, he was sealing the fact that this consciousness is devoid of material objects, thereby transcending such views.

This passage should be read in conjunction with the preceding section stating that "matter is not consciousness. However, the World-Honored One asked: "Is it not so? (i.e., is it not the case that it is not [consciousness]?)
As for the location, Ānanda replied: "It is in the place of non-separation. This is the subtle art of the master and disciple’s mutual proclamation.
To "open" means to reveal; to "peel" and "analyze" means to dissect and discern.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda: "As you have said... [up to] there is nothing that is not seeing. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
*Annotation:* This demonstrates that apart from seeing there is no object, thereby dispelling the notion of what is not seeing.
First, he recounts Ānanda’s words to confirm his meaning, as if saying: "According to what you have said, one knows that among the myriad phenomena..."

In the end, no such vision exists. Now I tell you again: when the Tathāgata and you were sitting in the Jeta Grove, as we further observed the groves and gardens, even down to the various distinct phenomena of the sun and moon, there was certainly no "vision-essence" that could be pointed out.
Now, within these myriad phenomena, you should likewise point it out: which among them is not your own vision-essence?
Ānanda replied, "In truth, as I survey all phenomena, I do not know what thing is not my seeing.
Why is this? Although the categories of things are many, if I were to cite one or two, they could be fully understood.
If the tree is not my seeing, how could I see the tree? If the tree were my seeing, then since the tree..."
It becomes a view. Furthermore, what can be pointed out as the tree? If the view that emptiness is not the self, how could I perceive emptiness?
If the view that emptiness is the self, since emptiness has already become a view, what then can be pointed out as emptiness?
I further reflected: within these myriad phenomena, even the subtlest manifestations of clarity are none other than the essence of my own seeing.
The World-Honored One’s approval signifies that he has certified [Ananda] as being free from the view that things are real entities, thereby transcending the view of non-existence.
This passage should be read in conjunction with the preceding section on "the view that things are not real entities.

However, while the World-Honored One’s question concerned the state of being "separate," Ananda’s response concerned the state of "not being separate"; this too is a marvelous instance of the mutual exhortation between teacher and disciple. Ananda—

The response appears to incorporate both the meanings of "neither non-view" and "not having a view. However, it primarily emphasizes the side of "non-existence," as this is frequently the basis [of error].

Thus, it merely includes [the other] by following the precedent of the World-Honored One’s previous statement. This should be considered when reflecting upon the two characters "contemplation" (guan) and "reflection" (siwei).
"It is certainly not an outflow consistent with the nature of reality.
At this, the assembly were not yet those beyond training (until: "You must contemplate this carefully so as not to disgrace my compassionate longing").
[Crown Note: Although both parties heard this and gave their assent, the integrity of the single session was lost; therefore, he comforted them with a heart of compassion.
This is because those of small capacity and beginners are obscured and their minds have not yet been opened;

they do not realize that both the physical body and the external world are but laborious manifestations of true nature, yet they regard them as truly existent. Consequently, they distinguish between right and wrong.

Now, having received the Buddha’s revelation of the wondrous nature that is neither right nor wrong, they have no place to which they can cling, and they no longer know where right and wrong have gone.

They still seek to grasp the meaning within the realm of right and wrong; thus, upon hearing the Buddha’s two successive endorsements, they remain utterly bewildered and ignorant, having no resolution whatsoever regarding the fundamental and derivative aspects, or the direction and cessation, of the two principles of "no view of right" and "no view of wrong."
The thought is this: if one were certain that something was right or wrong, one could remain steadfastly committed to it.
Now, however, both possibilities are denied and nothing has been definitively established; thus, people are struck with alarm and doubt, causing them to lose their firm resolve.
Out of compassion for such individuals, the Tathāgata consoles them, saying: "I am the Unsurpassed Dharma King; everything I have spoken is the truth."
These words of reality refer to the True Suchness (*tathatā*) and ultimate principle as realized by me; they are spoken without error or deception and are free from the fault of falsehood.

They are not like the claims of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who say that existence is non-existence, non-existence is existence, or that there is both existence and non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence—such confused and incoherent arguments. You all should examine this with careful discernment.
I reflect that I have not failed you in your heart of sorrowful longing. "To change and tremble" means to feel awe and alarm. "True reality" (zhenshi) refers to that which is certainly without error.
"As" (ru) is used here as a particle of comparison. "That which is as" (suoru) refers to the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā) that has been realized.
"To be disgraced" (tiantan) means to be solitary and to fail one's duty.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Prince of the Dharma... [omitted] ...in the interval between these points, there was neither "is" nor "is not.

[Commentary: These are words used to represent the inquiry. Although the great assembly had received the World-Honored One’s consolation and was urged to contemplate with careful attention, none among them had yet realized the emptiness of dharmas;
thus, they were at a loss and remained silent, having no questions to ask. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī—[the text continues].
The wise person should naturally take it upon themselves to inquire on behalf of others; thus it is said:
"The Tathāgata has already, for the sake of the great assembly, clarified that within the two categories of form and emptiness, there is fundamentally neither the meaning of 'seeing' nor 'not seeing.

Observing this assembly, one wonders how they have not only failed to awaken, but have instead fallen back into doubt, thinking: 'If these phenomena such as form and emptiness were indeed what is seen, then [they should...']"
Among the myriad phenomena, you were able to point out the essence of seeing; why can you not do so now?
If these phenomena such as form and emptiness were truly not that which sees, then among the myriad phenomena, there would be nothing at all to behold. Why, then, can you now gaze upon them?
Therefore, you do not understand where the two meanings—that there is no seeing and that there is not non-seeing—ultimately converge. Hence, you are struck with alarm, doubt, and fear.
Although this great assembly may still be subject to outflows, their past roots of goodness are not meager or slight such that they cannot be urged forward.
I only pray that the Tathāgata, in his great compassion, will illuminate these various objects and this essence of seeing.
"What is this original substance?"—within this very inquiry, there is neither the view of "it is" nor the view of "it is not.
These three words, "What is this original substance? could not have been uttered by anyone who was not possessed of great wisdom.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly... [up to] "...how could there be 'is' or 'is not' therein? (Commentary:
This assembly’s faculties, objects, and consciousnesses return to the one true fundamental substance; this serves as the answer to Mañjuśrī’s question.
Great Bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī and others, having relinquished the *ālayavijñāna*, attain the illusory-like third [liberation].)
The "obscured" refers to one's own abiding state, which is the wisdom of self-awakening and the samādhi of the Great Samādhi of the Lion’s Roar (Śūraṅgama).

By means of this wisdom of self-awakening, one dwells eternally in the Great Samādhi of the Lion’s Roar; there is no time of entering or emerging from it. To see the pointing finger is to see the essence of seeing.

This encompasses the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). "Seeing conditions" refers to the six sense objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*). "The characteristics of ideation" refers to the preceding six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*).

False conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is fundamentally without characteristics; it takes the objects that are being conceptualized as its characteristics. These two subsequent lines are employed to resolve the doubts of the assembly.

In response to the above, Mañjuśrī said: "If these characteristics such as form and emptiness involve the two meanings of 'seeing' and 'not seeing,' it is still like saying that since these characteristics such as form and emptiness are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent, upon what basis can one point to their being or not being so?"
This "seeing" and its "objects" are the same as in the preceding passage and likewise encompass the six consciousnesses; however, the text is abbreviated while the meaning remains complete.
From this point downward, it serves as a response to Mañjuśrī’s question, which still asks: "Regarding the essence of seeing and empty form, what are they originally?
Within them, there is neither 'is' nor 'is not. If this essence of seeing and empty form were to possess two distinct entities..."

Within this, one may speak of "seeing" and "non-seeing. Yet this essence of seeing, whether in relation to form or emptiness, is fundamentally a single, wondrously pure, and luminous substance of Bodhi. How could there be "seeing" or "non-seeing" within it?
This, moreover, serves as the foundation for the subsequent three categories and the seven elements.
Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: as for you, Mañjuśrī... [as it says] "it is therefore able to cause you to transcend 'pointing' and 'not pointing.
These two characters, "pointing" (zhǐ), correspond precisely to the previous "pointing is seeing" and "pointing is not seeing.

Previously, when one had not yet awakened to the one true dharma-realm, "pointing" was "pointing" or "not pointing"; now that one has attained awakening, one transcends both "seeing" and "not seeing."
Beyond this, one is able to extend the finger; yet that which is extended is not the finger itself. Within this there are two metaphors, explained through the application of two dharmas.
First, Mañjuśrī is used as a metaphor for the single true nature (*ekasatya-svabhāva*), which is devoid of the dualistic marks of "is" and "is not.

The passage beginning with "The Buddha said" applies the dharma to clarify this, thereby establishing the principle of subsuming the delusory back into the true. The section beginning with "Delusion manifests as form and emptiness" further introduces another [metaphor].
The analogy clarifies two meanings: the arising of delusion from the true, and the realization that delusion is itself the true.
Therefore, the section beginning with "Below this" uses the phenomenon to correspond to the second moon above, clarifying the meaning of the arising of delusion from the true.

The section beginning with "By this" uses the phenomenon to correspond to the single true moon above, clarifying the meaning that delusion is itself the true. Thus, through successive elucidations, it reveals only the one true dharma-realm.

Fundamentally, there are no two characteristics of right and wrong. Previously, the second moon was used as a singular metaphor for the seeing-essence (*darśana-vijñāna*), merely encompassing the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) to lead it back to the true nature.

Here, the second moon is used as a comprehensive metaphor for the sense organs, the body, and the physical world (*bhājana-loka*), fully encompassing both the subjective and objective aspects (*darśana* and *nimitta*) to lead them back to the true nature.
Therefore, the true moon is used as a metaphor for the vast and great true mind. Thus, toward...
Within the latter two types of false views, specifically regarding individual karma, the second moon is replaced by a red cataract;
using only this single red cataract as a metaphor for the two divisions of the seeing and the seen, one merely perceives the cataract itself, which is not the illness.
It can be seen that truth and falsehood are no other than this; they depend solely upon a single thought.

If for a moment a thought moves falsely, then mind and objects become chaotic and disputes arise like sharp blades. If for a moment a thought is purely true, then there is only the wondrous awakening, serene and all-pervading.
Yet, one is able to remain in all places without giving rise to deluded thoughts; nor does one extinguish those deluded thoughts.
Dwelling amidst the realms of delusive objects, one does not apply further cognitive discernment; and in the absence of such discernment, one does not discriminate between the real and the unreal.

Thus, the sudden awakening of the fundamental nature pervades the entire Dharma-realm; how could there be any room for "this is seeing" or "this is not seeing" within it? It is just as the ancient masters have said:
It is said: "This principle is inherently possessed by all people. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas call it 'the person who points out the pearl.
From the beginning, it has never been a thing. There is no need to know it or understand it; there is no need to say it is this or that it is not this.

Simply cut off the dualistic phrases—cut off the phrase of existence and the phrase of non-existence, the phrase of non-existence and the phrase of not non-existence. When the traces of these two ends do not appear, [the pearl is revealed]."
The head cannot grasp you; numbers cannot encompass you. You are neither deficient nor complete;
neither ordinary nor holy; neither light nor dark. You are not possessing knowledge, nor are you lacking it;
you are neither bound nor liberated. You are none of these names or categories. You are incomparable and beyond all metaphor. If one can...
It is thus. Even this wondrous, pure, and luminous mind cannot be perceived as existing; how, then, could there be such things as "seeing" and "not seeing"?

*Commentary:* This passage uses Mañjuśrī as a metaphor for a dialogue between teacher and disciple to reveal that the single true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is fundamentally devoid of the two characteristics of right and wrong. Therefore, it asks: "As for you, Mañjuśrī, [you are] simply and directly one..."
Regarding the essence: within your very own fundamental essence, is there further Mañjuśrī that can be pointed out and identified as "this is Mañjuśrī"?
Or, is it that together with the fundamental essence, there is absolutely no Mañjuśrī that can be pointed out and identified as "not Mañjuśrī"?
There are three meanings to this: first, the meaning of reality; second, the meaning of duality; and third, the meaning of non-duality. Within Mañjuśrī’s response, these are also...
There are three meanings. First: "The World-Honored One and Mañjuśrī are likewise so. This is because Mañjuśrī is merely the single true essence. Second:
Within that single essence, there is no further such thing as Mañjuśrī. Why? If one says there is a "is," there must necessarily be a "is not";
only with two Mañjuśrīs could one speak of "is" in contrast to "is not. Now, there is only...
First, because it is true, there is no such thing [as "is"]. Third, although it is indeed impossible to say "it is," yet truth (zhen) likewise cannot be obliterated;
thus, on this day, I am not entirely devoid of the true essence itself—how then could I further say that it is "not"?
However, within the single true essence, there are in reality no two characteristics of "is" and "is not" to be pointed out. This is just as the Patriarchal School says:
"If the mind has something it affirms, it must have something it negates. If you prize one thing, you will be deluded by that one thing.
Therefore, the World-Honored One, using the Dharma to provide clarification, said: "This essence of seeing is wondrously luminous; its relation to all empty phenomena is just like yours..."
Mañjuśrī, the single true essence is entirely devoid of the dual characteristics of "is" and "is not. This very seeing and the empty dust are fundamentally one and the same:
the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi, the pure, perfect, and true mind. Therefore, there is no such thing as "seeing that is correct," nor is there "seeing that is incorrect.
As for why "is" and "is not" arise, it is truly because of the fundamentally awakened true mind.

In a single thought-moment, following conditions, the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is formed and transforms into the two divisions of the seeing and the seen, giving rise to form and emptiness, as well as seeing and hearing.
Now, these forms, emptiness, seeing, and hearing arise based upon the True Reality (*tathatā*), like the second moon seen when one presses on the eye;
though it is not truly existent, two disks are clearly perceived. The deluded do not realize this and vainly attempt to conjecture about it. Its...
Who is this moon? And who is not the moon? If you claim it is the true moon, then it is not precluded that there are two.

If you claim it is not the true moon, then apart from the true moon, it has no substance. Thus, despite your来回 (back-and-forth) arguments regarding what is and is not, you cannot escape [this conclusion].
If you, Mañjuśrī, yourself knew that the original moon is but a single true entity, then even if two discs appeared, they would merely be a result of pressing on the eyes.
In the true moon that is perceived, there is inherently nothing of right or wrong to be distinguished. To further clarify this through analogy with the Dharma:
it is because of deluded fabrication that you now observe this essence of vision and distinguish between its internal and external aspects in relation to the various sensory objects.
Thus, that which is internal—the root-body; external—the vessel-world; and intermediate—the consciousness-mind—are all termed false and deluded thoughts.
They obscure the fundamental wondrous clarity and prevent one from transcending these views and non-views. This is like the second moon seen when pressing on the eyes:
though one may recklessly attempt to conjecture about it, one can never escape the dilemma of whether it is this moon or not.

This is a mistaken view. If, through this, one thought-moment becomes purely true and the boundaries of past and future are severed, then throughout the entire Dharma-realm there is only the great function of the singular, refined, and wondrous awakening, which does not depart from the total substance of the precious, luminous, and wondrous nature.
Thus, substance and function are as one, and mind and object are non-dual; even this very body, sense organs, and the vessel-world are nothing but the original self.
Therefore, you are able to transcend the realm of right and wrong.
How could you, amidst the myriad phenomena, point to anything as being "seeing" or designate anything as "not seeing"?
It is just like seeing the true moon: once that is seen, false conceptualizations have no place to arise, and right and wrong naturally vanish.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is truly as the Dharma King has taught... [until] one obtains the wondrously enlightened nature of the true mind.
This is entirely different from the previous discriminations; it is neither form nor emptiness. [It is not like] that which Kauśṛti and others mistakenly take for the obscure principle (tattva)."
These correspond to one another. The intent is to shatter the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) and thereby reveal true permanence.

Although it is said that both mundane and supramundane phenomena are solely the one True Reality (*tathatā*), non-dual, lacking nothing and leaving nothing behind, a mere, indistinct True Suchness is not yet the wondrous enlightenment (*samyag-bodhi*).
Therefore, one does not fall into the views and understandings of ordinary people; one distinguishes oneself from the nihilism and eternalism of external paths;
and one does not confuse this with the partial emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle. Yet, even this essence of seeing is like a second moon—it is still not the true vision of the wondrous mind.
As for the One True Dharma-realm, how easy is it to speak of? From here down to the section on the two kinds of false views, all clarify this very principle.
It is most worthy of being cherished and admired. "Brahmin" (梵志) here means "Pure Lineage," signifying that one is a descendant of Brahmā.

"The Ancients" (先者) refers to people of former times. "Sāṃkhyakāra" (娑毗迦羅) means "Golden Head. "The View of the Ultimate Principle" (冥諦見) appears before us; "Throwing Ashes" refers to the ascetic non-Buddhists.
"True Self" (真我) is the notion of a self-clinging (我相) maintained by these non-Buddhists, which does not exceed three types: first, large; second, minute...
"Subtle. "Three vastnesses" refers to the mark of self (*ātman*). In the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, this is translated as "unapproachable. Regarding "natural": it is inherently so by its own nature.
They [the opponents] reckon that all internal and external phenomena have no cause from beginning to end, and thus there is neither cultivation nor realization.

This is because they do not know that within the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) there exist seeds of defilement and purity that give rise to karma and moisten rebirth; consequently, they abandon one life and migrate to another birth.

This is the root [of delusion]. Consequently, they falsely calculate that within the body there exists a true self, which is constantly born in various realms of existence, pervading the ten directions, and that this nature is indestructible.

Commentary: This deludes heterodox schools so as to confound the True Dharma. Its intention is to claim that the World-Honored One is the Unsurpassed Dharma King, and that whatever he has taught must be free from deception or falsehood;
yet it asserts that this "seeing" and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi.
It claims that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive, that it is perfect and eternally abiding, and that it is the unmoving Way.
[Ananda] said: "That the nature of your seeing-essence is neither born nor extinguished—these are all the World-Honored One’s truthful words.
If both the seeing and its conditions were indeed able to pervade the ten directions of the world, and if they were truly eternally abiding and their nature were neither born nor extinguished,"

In that case, what difference is there between this and the "Ultimate Darkness" (*tamas-tattva*) discussed by the former brahmin Śāṃkara, as well as the various non-Buddhist schools such as the ash-smearing ascetics who claim there is a true self (*ātman*) pervading the ten directions? If so, it would contradict your own school’s tenets.
I have heard that on Mount Laṅkā, the World-Honored One expounded this meaning for the sake of Mahāmati and others, saying:

Those non-Buddhists cling to the view that all internal and external phenomena are without cause from beginning to end, arising spontaneously (*svabhāva*) without depending on causal cultivation or being attained through results.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that both the internal—the faculties and the body—and the external—the physical world—possess the seeds of the true cause;
it is only when aided by various external conditions that they can produce results from those causes. Thus, this...
This is the meaning of causes and conditions; it is not the meaning of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). This is the realm of cultivation and realization; it is not a realm that is negated as non-existent.
I now observe that this awakened nature is spontaneous, never having been lost or abandoned. It is neither born nor extinguished;

it is the single essence, fundamentally true, pervading the entire dharma-realm, and is named "Right Universal Knowledge" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). If so, does this not seem to contradict what was previously taught?
If this principle of causal conditions thus accords with the "spontaneity" (svabhāva) taught by the non-Buddhists,
then if there is indeed a difference between the spontaneity spoken of by the World-Honored One and that spoken of by the non-Buddhists,
by what further skillful means could you instruct me so that I do not fall into heterodox views, but may realize the wondrously enlightened nature of the true mind?
This is the complete essence and great function [of the nature].
The Buddha told Ānanda: "I now [do this] in such a way... how can you say that the seeing-nature is severed and extinguished?
How do you see light? (Crown Commentary): This refutes and breaks the notion of spontaneity (*ziran*). The intent is that I have now first opened up a skillful means for you.
I have subsequently explained the ultimate truth, yet you still have not awakened to it; instead, you are confused, wondering if it is something "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*).

Generally speaking, that which is called "spontaneous" must be inherently so by its own nature, not changing in accordance with conditions; only such a thing can be called spontaneous. If it manifests in accordance with conditions, it cannot be called spontaneous.
If you insist that the awareness which is all-pervasive, profound, and whose nature is neither arising nor ceasing is [spontaneous], and that conditions are...

Regarding "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*): you must discern it with clarity. Within your own body, there is a substance that does not manifest in accordance with external objects, one that is solid, real, and unchanging;
only this can be called spontaneous. Furthermore, observe this wondrously luminous seeing—this is what you call "awakening.
Brightness, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction—these are what you call "conditions. Among these, by means of what...

It is the body of spontaneity. If one takes the conditions of light as the self-substance of seeing, then because seeing the light is its fundamentally natural body, it would be fixed and immovable; in that case, this nature of seeing should only ever see light.
When darkness arrives, this seeing perishes together with the light; one would then see nothing at all of the darkness.

If you take the perception of emptiness to be the very essence of seeing, and thus regard the seeing of emptiness as your original, natural, and eternally unchanging body, then this nature of seeing should only ever perceive emptiness.
When it encounters an obstruction where there is no emptiness, it ought to perish along with that emptiness.
There is nothing; not even a trace of obstruction is seen, and this applies even to the various characteristics of darkness and so forth.
Now, when light comes, you see light, and eventually you see both emptiness and obstruction. Thus, you know that your faculty of seeing manifests according to conditions.

Why, then, do you deludedly regard it as being self-existent? From the section beginning with "guest-dust" down to the end of the "eight returns," all is a skillful means of instruction and revelation. From here on...
"Seeing is not an object. "From seeing itself to the conditions for seeing, they are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi"—all such statements are words of truth.
The two characters "awakening" (jue) and "conditions" (yuan) above correspond to the preceding "this seeing" (ci jian) and "conditions" (yuan).

The three characters "wondrous, luminous seeing" (miao ming jian) above correspond to the character "awakening" (jue). These "brightness, darkness, space, and obstruction" correspond to the character "conditions" (yuan) within the phrase "conditions for awakening" (jue-yuan) above.
This was largely because Ānanda had conflated the seeing-nature with form and emptiness, treating them as a single, spontaneous entity.
Therefore, the World-Honored One questioned him regarding the characteristics of light, darkness, and so forth, asking what constitutes the self-substance of seeing.

If one realizes that the ten dharma-realms are nothing other than this single, wondrously luminous, essential seeing, what further phenomenon could there be within it to serve as a spontaneous substance?
Ānanda said: "This wondrous nature of seeing must not be spontaneous; [it must] depend on light and depend on darkness, being the same as empty space or obstruction.
(Commentary: This abandons spontaneity and clings to causes and conditions. The intention is that since it is not spontaneous, it must rely on causes and conditions;
furthermore, causes and conditions are the True Dharma previously taught, not the doctrine of those non-Buddhists.)

However, phenomena born of causes and conditions are not necessarily eternally abiding and indestructible. Now, you claim that the wondrously luminous nature of seeing is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing, but is eternally abiding and all-pervasive; yet this meaning seems inconsistent with the nature of causes and conditions.
I do not know how it could possibly accord with the nature of causes and conditions. Since my mind is still not clear, I inquire of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, the Buddha followed up with a question to refute this, saying: "Now, your seeing of the sacrificial animal occurs only after you have perceived the characteristics of light, darkness, and so forth;
thus, this nature of seeing exists only within the midst of light, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction."
By what cause does it exist? If it exists because of light, then light is the cause for the arising of this vision. When darkness arrives, the light is extinguished.
Since it exists because of light, it must likewise be extinguished because of light—just as a flame exists because of wood, yet the flame ceases when the wood is exhausted.

In that case, one should not perceive darkness; for darkness is merely the void where light has been obstructed. This can be understood by analogy. Now, since [vision arises] through both light and darkness...
Since you can see both emptiness and obstruction, it is clear that this nature of seeing is not produced by those conditions; this should be self-evident.

Furthermore, within the midst of light, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction, upon what does your nature of seeing depend? If it depends on emptiness for its existence, then emptiness must be the condition that gives rise to seeing.
Yet, when one encounters an obstructed space, no emptiness appears. Since [you claim] it exists by depending on emptiness, [how can it exist where there is none?]
It still depends on emptiness for its cessation. It is like a vine that exists depending on a tree; when the tree falls, the vine withers. Thus, one should not see it as being obstructed.

The dependence of light and darkness upon obstruction is likewise so. Now, since you perceive each of these characteristics—light, darkness, and so forth—one by one, this nature of seeing does not exist dependently through false conditions;

this should be clear. "Condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to what is proximate, while "cause" (*hetu*) refers to what is remote. "Cause" carries the meaning of fundamental reliance, whereas "condition" [refers to the immediate support].
This is a metaphorical usage. In this context, the two characters "yīn" (cause) and "yuán" (condition) should be understood in a flexible sense;

they cannot be definitively identified as internal seeds and external auxiliary conditions respectively. If one maintains that light, darkness, and so forth are not the seeds of vision, then it follows that vision possesses its own seeds—what harm is there in asserting this?
If one maintains that light, darkness, and so forth serve as auxiliary conditions, then in reality...
As for the auxiliary conditions (*pratyaya*), what is the harm in speaking of them? Have you not heard that the Buddha-seed arises from conditions?
You should know that such subtle and wondrous clarity of refined awareness—[extending through] how could empty space possibly follow your grasping?
Commentary: This conclusion clarifies that the wondrous luminosity of essential awareness is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous.

It cannot be realized by anyone who sinks into emptiness or clings to traces. Therefore, it is said: "One should know that this wondrous luminosity of essential awareness is such that its essence and function are one and the same;
it remains unchanging while following conditions. Since the essence of purity is unchanging, it does not belong to the realm of causes and conditions. As for its wondrous function...
Because it follows conditions, it does not belong to spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Nevertheless, what is called "spontaneity through causes and conditions" is like mistaking a bubble for the ocean;
it has never been separate from this wondrous luminosity. Therefore, it is said: "It is not that it is not spontaneous, nor is it not due to causes and conditions.
Yet, the wondrous essence is fundamentally without any trace of words or signs; thus, its fundamental non-existence is neither "not due to causes and conditions" nor "not spontaneous. Furthermore—

There is nothing that is not non-cause-and-condition and not non-spontaneous. Fundamentally, there is no "this is cause-and-condition" or "this is spontaneous," nor is there "this is not cause-and-condition" or "this is not spontaneous.
This is because it is detached from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, it is identical with all phenomena (*dharma*).

Although it is said that the myriad marks are all empty, this does not preclude the fact that within the one true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there exists that which cannot be known by thought, mind, or speech.
As for this, how can you now, within this wondrous clarity, apply your mind to deliberate upon it?
Furthermore, how can you use worldly causes and conditions, spontaneity, oppositions, or any conceptual proliferations of names and marks to differentiate this subtle, awakened, and wondrous clarity?
It is just like grasping at empty space with one's hand; it only results in exhausting oneself. How can empty space be seized according to your grasp?
One cannot place a hand upon empty space; how could the wondrous brightness allow for the placement of a mind?

The phrase "it is not that it is not natural" [from the original text] must be supplemented by the sentence "it is not without causes and conditions," for only then will the meaning be complete. From the section beginning "the eight returns" below, all marks are transcended. (5)
From "the various kinds of views and measurements" onwards refers to all phenomena (*dharmas*).

This continues until the point where there is neither the view of existence nor the view of non-existence, and following the chapter on Mañjuśrī, it is neither identical to nor separate from them. This section below serves as a foundation for the subsequent text.

Hereafter, the three categories will repeatedly refute cause-and-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*), while the seven elements (*mahābhūta*) will repeatedly refute combination and non-combination. This is the beginning.
This concludes this case. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, regarding the nature of wondrous enlightenment—[from 'is it because of the mind' to] 'is it because of the eyes'—what is the meaning of this?"
Commentary: This Ānanda clings to his former words and is thus confused by the present instruction. His intention is this:

"While it may be acceptable to say that the nature of wondrous enlightenment does not belong to the 'spontaneity' (svabhāva) taught by non-Buddhist schools, to claim it is certainly not produced by causes and conditions contradicts our own teachings.
How is it, World-Honored One, that you constantly tell the bhikṣus that the seeing-nature possesses four kinds of conditions?"—thus spoke Ānanda.

It was not known that what was previously described was the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Rather, the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) serves as the fundamental condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), while emptiness, light, and the eye-organ serve as the dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Now, by relying upon the essence of seeing (*darśana-sāra*), one reveals the nature of seeing (*darśana-dharmatā*), intending to lead one to realize the wondrously enlightened luminous nature through this very nature of seeing.
Yet, you have mistakenly identified the nature of seeing as the eye-consciousness; you have utterly failed to understand.
In the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school, it is taught that visual consciousness alone arises from four conditions. How could it be said that the nature of awakening arises from four conditions?
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "I say that in the world... (up to)... both are called 'seeing. Why do you not see?"

This and the following passage should be considered two separate conclusions. Because Ānanda initially perceived the marks [of objects] and gave rise to the thought of enlightenment, he mistakenly identified seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving as the true nature; he did not realize they were like the reflection of the moon.

Therefore, from the "Seven Investigations" up to the "Eight Returns," the World-Honored One specifically refuted this deluded vision and pointed out the essence of seeing (*jijing*), which is like a second moon, relying upon this [essence].

The "seeing-essence" (jìng) reveals the true nature (zhēn-xìng). Having reached this point where one is about to directly point to the true nature, this preceding section of text first concludes the previous intent regarding the "eight returns. From the following passage beginning with "Therefore, below...
down to "...the seeing cannot reach it," another section of text further eliminates the seeing-essence and directly points to the wondrous enlightenment that is like the true moon.

Clarifying the nature [of the mind]: from the conclusion of the "eight returns" up to the point where it is "detached from all marks," this is the intent of the passage concerning all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
Although the text is repetitive, its meaning does not exceed these three layers. If one follows the text to discern the underlying principle, the matter will become clear of itself;
I have set this forth here so that those who understand may examine it in detail.
Commentary: This concludes the refutation of false views in order to reveal the essence of seeing.

Because Ānanda mistakenly identified the nature of seeing as the eye-consciousness, the World-Honored One did not immediately engage in a detailed analysis; instead, he spoke of what he had previously taught regarding causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

This was specifically to refute heterodox schools and, by expedient means, to guide those of lesser capacity, leading them to understand that all myriad phenomena in the world rely upon causes and depend upon conditions.
Conditions are not substantially existent; this is not the purport of the first definitive meaning (nītārtha) as explained here. How can you take that [provisional teaching] to challenge this?
Nevertheless, without the false, the true cannot be revealed. If you wish to clarify the first definitive meaning, [you must proceed accordingly].
First, one must understand the deluded views of worldly people. If worldly people say, "I am able to see," on what basis is this called "seeing"?
And when they say they cannot see, on what basis is this called "not seeing"? Ānanda replied:
"Worldly people rely upon the light of the sun, moon, and lamps to perceive various forms and appearances; therefore, they call it 'being able to see. Furthermore...
Because one does not see various forms due to the absence of the light of the sun, moon, or lamps, it is not called "seeing.
Thus, both seeing and not seeing belong to external conditions. Therefore, the World-Honored One, taking up these words, refuted them by asking:
"If you claim that because these three kinds of light are absent it is not called 'seeing,' then it should follow that in darkness as well, one likewise cannot see. If this were not so..."
When one sees light, one must necessarily see darkness as well. Since darkness is already seen, it is merely the absence of light;
how can this be called "not seeing"? Furthermore, he refutes their error by providing a counter-example, saying:

"If you claim that when dwelling in darkness one does not see the appearance of light, and therefore it is called 'not seeing,' then now, while the three types of light are manifest before you, you likewise do not see the appearance of darkness."
One might then say that [the nature of seeing] does not see. If this were so, then when one sees darkness, there would be no characteristic of light;
when one sees light, there would be no characteristic of darkness. To call both instances "not seeing" is surely erroneous. For these two characteristics cannot coexist;

yet within them, the nature of seeing has never been absent. If one further understands this—that when light comes, darkness departs, and when darkness arrives, light dissolves—then [one realizes its constancy]. From oneself...
