Regarding perception, hearing, cognition, and vision: how could one know that above deluded vision there is true essence, and above true essence there is true nature?
For this true vision is itself true nature, and true nature is fundamentally not a cataract; therefore, it cannot be termed perception, hearing, cognition, or vision.
If it were termed perception, hearing, cognition, or vision, then it would be the cataract of true vision. Furthermore—
It is like a person with diseased eyes seeing circular halos; consequently, true vision becomes obscured and darkened. This point is the ultimate conclusion of these three layers.

"Cognition and vision" (zhìjiàn) refers to deluded vision, like the reflection of the moon in water. "True essence" (zhēnjīng) refers to the essence of vision, like a second moon [seen by one with cataracts].
"Nature" (xìng) refers to true vision, like the real moon in the sky.
Ānanda, it is like the deluded vision shared by those sentient beings (up to): "The pure fundamental mind and fundamental awakening are eternally abiding.
When they are in combination, this is the meaning of causes and conditions; when they are not in combination, this is the meaning of spontaneity.

What was previously called the "essence of seeing" is said to fall short of the true seeing because it has not yet extinguished the cause of birth and death; therefore, in the preceding passage, it was said that "awakened seeing is itself a cataract," which leads us to this point.
"Truly seeing with seeing" refers, in the case of Ānanda alone, to returning to original enlightenment through subtle and secret contemplation.

"Furthermore, returning to original enlightenment" refers, in the case of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm, to returning to original enlightenment through subtle and secret contemplation.

"Perfecting bodhi" points to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). "The nature of non-arising and non-ceasing" points to the principle of *tathatā*. When object and wisdom are as one, the beginning and the source are identical.

Non-dual is the pure fundamental mind. In terms of its function, it is called "fundamental enlightenment" (mūla-bodhi) which is eternally abiding; in terms of its essence, it is likewise not outside the two designations of the "twofold conversion of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
Commentary: This is a combined clarification. Using one person as an analogy for one country, and one country as an analogy for the great trichiliocosm, it does not go beyond a single delusive error.
The meaning is that all the people of a previous country will collectively perceive various kinds of calamities and auspicious signs.

For example, consider a person with a diseased eye who sees circular shadows. Taking another person with a diseased eye as an analogy for the inhabitants of a single country, we can clarify this through mutual comparison.
That one individual alone sees circular shadows arises from the delusive affliction (*taimira*) within his own eyes.
That these many people together see inauspicious signs arises from the noxious miasma (*dhatu-dosa*) within their collective karma. (2)
These various views, though not uniform, are all produced by the delusive perceptions of beginningless inverted discrimination.
This "delusive perception" refers to the aforementioned delusive perception, which points to the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).

How could it be that only these two are produced by the same delusive perception? Extending this principle as a universal rule, it applies to all within the three thousand continents of Jambudvīpa in the southern continent.
All lands are likewise produced from this deluded vision. Since the lands of the various continents within Jambudvīpa are identical, so too are the lands of the other three continents.
Since the four great continents are identical, then the realms of Śākyamuni’s transformation are likewise identical.
Since the ten billion suns and moons are identical, then all the contaminated lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as their...
Sentient beings all share the same deluded view. This deluded view arises based upon the true nature; it is a state of outflows that results from being deluded regarding the outflow-free.
Therefore, it is said that they are equally the nature of awakened, profound clarity—the wondrous mind free of outflows.

Initially, due to a single thought following conditions and adhering to this profound clarity, delusion is produced. Thus, from that one refined spirit, the six combined faculties are divided, and consequently, [the world of phenomena] comes into being.
Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing constitute the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*). They are like the red film over the eye;
there are also the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), which are the conditions for illusory affliction, like the floating hairs seen before a lamp.

When the organs and their objects encounter conditions, deluded consciousness arises, whereby one falsely identifies the four elements and five aggregates as the characteristics of the body, and the shadows of the six objects as the characteristics of the mind. Thus, karma is produced in that very place.
As karma revolves, one falsely perceives birth when causes and conditions conjoin, and falsely perceives death when causes and conditions disperse.

If one can turn the light back upon itself to reflect, exhaust the coarse delusions within the first six consciousnesses, and no longer fall into the cycle of birth and death with distinct segments, then one will distance oneself from all conjunctive conditions. Furthermore, one must sever the innate [delusions].
When subtle afflictions no longer lead to the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*), one is then far removed from disharmony.

Furthermore, if one eradicates the seeds of the two types of birth-and-death within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), one is able to transform the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms.
Thus, bodhi is perfected; one attains fundamental wisdom, accords with the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, and realizes the principle of suchness (*tathatā*). Then, forever...
The cycle of rebirth is severed; the originally pure fundamental mind and fundamental enlightenment are restored and abide eternally.
Ānanda, although you have previously awakened to the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment, [it extends] even to all sentient beings and the obstructed realms, which are likewise so.

Commentary: This refutes the notion of conjunction (*saṃghāta*). Previously, Ānanda had said, "Please explain for me the conditions of conjunction and non-conjunction, whether caused by external factors or arising spontaneously.
His mind was still not yet enlightened, and upon further hearing that "seeing is not seeing," his confusion and delusion increased even more.
The World-Honored One has now completed the clarification that seeing is not [the faculty of] seeing. If [it were] caused by external factors or...
However, this has already been refuted previously. It remains only to clarify that it is neither a combination nor a non-combination, which has not yet been explained.

Therefore, without waiting for further questioning, he reveals it, saying: "Although you have previously realized that the wondrously luminous nature of original enlightenment is neither a causal-nature nor a spontaneous-nature, you have still not clarified that awakening itself is fundamentally neither a combination nor a non-combination. If you were to say..."
If the nature of awakening were definitively a composite, it could not be separated from all phenomena; thus, it would be identical to illusory phenomena, eternally subject to arising and ceasing.

If one claims that the nature of awakening is definitively not a composite and cannot be identical to all phenomena, then one would discard all illusory phenomena as being outside of the nature of awakening;
therefore, it is neither a composite nor a non-composite. Furthermore, based on the preceding...
Vimalakīrti examined Ānanda and said: "You have merely awakened to the nature of awareness as being neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously;

yet you still harbor doubts based on the various compounded natures of worldly delusions, thinking that the wondrous mind of fundamental enlightenment which realizes Bodhi is likewise a worldly delusion that arises in dependence upon the compounding of external objects. Thus it was said.
This wondrously pure essence of seeing of yours now confronts light and darkness, penetration and obstruction; with what, then, could it possibly blend?

If you claim that the essence of seeing blends with light, consider this: when you lift your eyes and see light, at the very moment the appearance of light manifests before you, from where does it intermingle and blend with your essence of seeing? If the essence of seeing [blends] with the appearance of light...
Before they were mixed together, although they could not be pointed out individually, they were still distinguishable. What is called "mixing" is like this:

seeing is like water, and clarity is like earth. Once the water and earth have mixed, the water loses its clarity and the earth loses its solidity, and their blending forms the appearance of mud. Now, seeing and clarity are likewise mixed; seeing comes first...
Seeing it, one knows that this is clarity. Yet, what is the form of the state in which they harmonize and complete one another? Some say:

at the time of seeing clarity, the appearance of clarity manifests before one; within the clarity itself there is the essence of seeing, and within the seeing itself there is also the appearance of clarity.
This is precisely the image of their mingled fusion. Even if one were to grant that there is seeing within the light, it would simply be called "light," and the "seeing" would be lost.
Therefore, he refutes this, saying: "If it is not seeing, how can one see the light? Thus, if the essence of seeing does not even exist, what form could its mixture take?
Even if one were to grant that there is light within the seeing, it would simply be called "seeing," and the "light" [would be lost].
This is an error. Therefore, I refute it, saying: If it is identical to the seer, how can there be both the seeing and the seeing-of-seeing?
In that case, since the characteristic of light would not even exist, with what form could it be mixed? Or, they may further argue:

Although the seeing enters into the light, the seeing has never been lost, and it remains as perfectly complete as the characteristic of light; likewise, although the light enters into the seeing, the light has never been lost.
Yet it is equally pervasive as the essence of seeing. Therefore, he refutes this by saying: "If the nature of seeing were truly pervasive, there would be no place that is not seeing;
where then could there be room for 'brightness' to exist, such that one could speak of its blending with brightness?

If the characteristic of brightness were truly pervasive, there would be no place that is not brightness; where then could there be room for 'seeing' to exist, such that one could speak of its blending with seeing? Thus...
The preceding text concludes with a double-knot: "Since seeing and light are each individually complete, seeing cannot contain light, and light cannot contain seeing;
thus, seeing must be distinct from light, and light must be distinct from seeing. Therefore, it is said that their blending is not logical.
If seeing were mixed within light, the nature of seeing would be lost; and if light were mixed within seeing..."
In the middle [of the text], the character "clear" (ming) is missing. This would result in a mutual confusion, such that one would merely lose the clear characteristic of seeing the nature.
Therefore, it is said: "To harmonize with clarity is also not the meaning. The cases of darkness, penetration, and obstruction can be understood by analogy with this.
Furthermore, if your faculty of vision were to adhere to or combine with clarity, darkness, penetration, or obstruction, it would necessarily be like a lid fitting a box; the two would not...

They are mutually opposed, yet they are not separate from one another. If this essence of vision were necessarily conjoined with light, then when darkness arrives and the characteristic of light has already ceased, this vision would likewise perish along with the light and certainly could no longer be conjoined with darkness. If it were not conjoined with darkness, [it would not perceive it].

It must be impossible to see darkness. How, then, could it also see darkness? If you claim that although it sees darkness, it does not actually conjoin with darkness—just as it conjoins with light—then since that which sees does not conjoin [with its object], that which conjoins must not see.
Consequently, when conjoining with light, it should not see light. Since it does not see light, how can it conjoin with light?
When in conjunction, do you clearly know it is light and not darkness? Now, this essence of vision can see both light and darkness;
one must certainly know that its conjunction with light is illogical. By analogy, the same applies to darkness, penetration, and obstruction.
Although the term "nature of awareness" is not used here, the use of "essence of vision" precisely reveals that although the text is currently [discussing]...
This meaning remains as it was before; it originally concerns two kinds of deluded views regarding a case that has not yet been resolved.
This is merely intended to quickly clarify that "seeing" is not "seeing," and so forth. Therefore, with this intention, I have paused here for now; the same applies to the subsequent text.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, as I contemplate this... [and so on] ...it is the same for all sentient beings.
*Commentary:* This refutes the notion of non-conjunction. The nature of awakening pervades both the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.

If one refers to the principle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a speck of dust can be established; therefore, it is not a conjunction. If one refers to the gateway of the present world, [it is likewise].
There is not a single dharma that is abandoned; therefore, it is not a lack of harmony. Thus the *Prajñāpāramitā* says:
"If one sees all marks as non-marks, one sees the Tathāgata. An ancient worthy also said: "If one sees all marks as non-marks, one does not see the Tathāgata."
It is further said: "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, one sees them immediately above the eyebrows and eyes. Ānanda did not comprehend this principle;

therefore, when he heard the World-Honored One rebuke him for using the various compounded natures of worldly delusion to doubt the mind that realizes Bodhi as being produced through compounding, he again attempted to refute that compounding by means of conceptual thought.

"It is mind-only. Because [Ananda] held that the wondrous fundamental enlightenment does not enter into combination with the faculties, objects, or consciousnesses, the World-Honored One again examined and confirmed it for Ananda, saying:

"If this wondrous essence of your seeing does not enter into combination with the various objects, then now, amidst brightness and darkness, penetration and obstruction, with which of these would it not be in combination? If this wondrous, pure essence of seeing does not..."
When there is light, the essence of seeing and the appearance of light each have their own boundaries and limits. You should carefully observe the demarcation between these two:
where does the light cease, and where does the seeing cease? Since seeing is not connected to the light, from what does it derive its boundary?
Since the light is not connected to the seeing, from what does it derive its boundary? If you claim that where the light ends, seeing must necessarily be absent—
This means that seeing and light each have their own boundaries and do not reach one another.

If seeing does not extend to the edge of the light, it cannot know where the characteristics of that light reside. Since it does not know where the characteristics of the light reside, how can it be said to be "with" the light?
By demarcating their boundaries, how can one say that they do not harmonize with light? The cases of darkness, penetration, and obstruction may be understood by this analogy.
Furthermore, if the wondrous seeing-essence does not harmonize with the various sensory objects, then consider it now in relation to light, darkness, penetration, and obstruction.

With what would it not be conjoined? If this essence of vision were not conjoined with light, then the nature of vision and the characteristic of light would be mutually antagonistic and unable to stand side by side, just as the faculty of hearing and the characteristic of light do not touch one another at all.
If the ear hears light, they are utterly unrelated; since the essence of vision is like the faculty of hearing, then this essence of vision would likewise [be disconnected].
One knows the location where the characteristic of light resides. How can one discern with clarity that they are not conjoined?
If one cannot discern this clearly, yet falsely claims that the essence of seeing is not conjoined with light, it is utterly unreasonable.
The examples of darkness, penetration, and obstruction may be understood by analogy with this. The "awakening" (jue) spoken of by Ānanda originally refers to the true nature;

"conditions" (yuan) refers to the six sense organs as the subjective perceivers; "objects" (chen) refers to the six sense objects and mental deliberations; and collectively, they refer to the minds of the first six consciousnesses.
Because the World-Honored One rebuked him for using the various compounded natures of worldly delusion to doubt the capacity for realization, [he clarified the distinction].
Since the bodhicitta arises through the convergence [of conditions], one might again doubt that this awakened nature must exist separately apart from these [conditions],
which would be like seeking water apart from the waves.
"Ānanda, you have not yet clearly understood that all floating dust [of phenomena]... (up to)... delusion and enlightenment, birth and death, are utterly unattainable.
*Commentary:* This is a general clarification of the overall intent of the three categories [of phenomena].
What was previously referred to as "the great dhāraṇī, the various samādhis, and the sublime path of practice" begins from this point. Following the previous statement: "Although you..."

If one awakens to the fact that the nature of wondrous, enlightened clarity is neither caused nor conditioned, neither spontaneous nor produced by combination, nor yet non-combined, then one will know only that the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world belong to causes and conditions and their combinations, and thus are empty, false, and unreal.

Yet, one would not know why the body and the vessel-world are called illusory and transformative manifestations—that they arise in dependence upon the *tathāgatagarbha* nature. Therefore, it is said: "You..."

Furthermore, you have not yet clearly understood that all phenomena—such as the various sensory organs, material forms, and objects—are like mirages, empty flowers, or the illusory vision of floating hairs;
they arise precisely where they are and perish in that very place. That which is born at the outset is simultaneously subject to extinction—a truth difficult to explain to the ignorant.
However, when we speak of "illusory falsehood," we are merely using names to point toward appearances; their true nature is...
The essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity can perceive the sense organs, the physical body, and the world of vessels, yet these fundamentally lack any substantial reality;
only the sentient beings' mind of wondrous, enlightened clarity constitutes substantial reality.

If you can understand it in this way, then even the aggregates, bases, elements, and sense-fields are fundamentally without birth. This is merely because of the conjunction of causes and conditions between parents and one's own karmic consciousness.
They falsely perceive arising; because they are separated according to the limits of their own karma’s duration, whether long or short, they falsely perceive extinction.
They are utterly unable to know from where arising comes or where extinction goes.
Furthermore, how could they know that arising, extinction, going, and coming are all illusory and false designations, lacking any inherent nature, yet capable of manifesting in this way?
This is originally the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Its nature conforms to all phenomena yet remains unchanging and immutable;
therefore, it is called "eternally abiding. Its function dwells within the path of delusion yet is neither obstructed nor obscured; therefore, it is called "wondrously luminous."
The essential substance is unmoving, yet its wondrous function is all-pervasive. When substance and function are one as such, it wondrously transcends all things and reaches the state of the Divine;
it pervades all phenomena without distinction. Therefore, it is called the "Unmoving, All-Pervasive, Wondrous Nature of True Suchness.
If one can personally realize this realm, then within the eternally true nature, one will thoroughly understand the seeking of coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death.
There is nothing to be attained; even awakening does not exist. How, then, could there be the arising and ceasing, or coming and going, of causes and conditions within it?
What are called nirvana and birth-and-death are equal to flowers in the sky.
Ānanda, how are the five aggregates fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha? (Up to: "As for the aggregate of form, you should know it is likewise.

[The section] beginning with "Suppose there is a person" below marks the true reality as the established substance. The passage "That person, for no reason" below shows the arising of delusion from the truth.
The passage "If it comes from emptiness" below discriminates that delusion is unreal. Therefore, the passage below clarifies that delusion is itself the truth. [This applies to] the subsequent text.

Follow this pattern. However, in this context, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) refers exclusively to a single body, unlike other instances where all that possesses material obstruction—whether the sensory faculties, the physical body, or the objective world—is considered the aggregate of form.
Thus, all these things are not themselves the characteristic of form; they are merely referred to as such by way of association.

Nor is it necessary to emphasize this point. If one were confined to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiangzong), which generally enumerates eleven categories of material phenomena (rūpa-dharma), then the subsequent mention of the five faculties and six objects would all become redundant.
Furthermore, if one were to claim that matter and mind are combined or that mind and matter are separated, [it would likewise be untenable].
These are all the fabrications of those who seek to embellish the text; they do not represent the original, correct intent of the scripture. One should speak in a general sense;
if one were to refer specifically and exclusively to "sentient beings," then the preceding word "one person" (一人) would be incoherent.
Commentary: This is a general inquiry that establishes that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all illusory and false designations, while their nature is fundamentally true.

The five aggregates are form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). "Aggregate" (*skandha*) is also called "heap" (*skandha*); it carries the two meanings of accumulation and concealment.
That is to say, they accumulate conditioned phenomena and conceal the true nature. The meaning is that the five aggregates are all...
Belonging to the conditioned, these are the phenomena of worldly arising and ceasing. How, then, can they be called the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
Therefore, a metaphor is established to clarify this. First, regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), it says: "Suppose there is a person."
This person speaks in general terms: the pure eye is a metaphor for correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*); the clarity of the pupil within the void is a metaphor for ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

That it is utterly devoid of anything else is a metaphor for the non-duality of principle and wisdom (*li-zhi yi-ru*). That this person, for no reason, does not move his eyes is a metaphor for the true mind (*tathatā-citta*) following conditions and moving delusively to form the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
His staring until he becomes fatigued is a metaphor for the deluded mind of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). Thus, regarding the void...
The "separate vision of mad flowers" is a metaphor for the illusory forms of the *bhāga* (objective aspect); it refers specifically to the physical body.
Furthermore, "all other mad and chaotic non-forms" collectively refers to the external sensory objects (*viṣaya*) of form outside the body.
Ānanda, these various illusory flowers do not come from space (up to: they are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature). [Commentary:
This uses illusory flowers in the void as a metaphor to clarify the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); it is precisely the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
The meaning is that these illusory flowers seen by the fatigued eyes do not come from space, nor do they issue from the eyes; for this is the aggregate of form.
It is not according to suchness, nor is it the wisdom of immovability; rather, it is seen only after false movement has occurred. Therefore it is said:
"If these delusory flowers come from space, since they come from space, they must return to space.
If these flower-forms have both coming and going, then this empty space must also have interior and exterior. If there is interior and exterior, then it is not empty space."
If it were not empty space, it would possess substantial reality. That which possesses substantial reality cannot, by its very nature, allow for the arising and ceasing of illusory flowers within it.
It is just as Ānanda, having a substantial body, cannot further accommodate another Ānanda coming and going within him;
how then can one say that mad flowers arise from empty space? If they do not arise from empty space, could they possibly arise from the eyes? If this madness...
Regarding the flowers emerging from the eyes: since they emerge from the eyes, they ought likewise to enter back through the eyes.
If they emerge from the eyes, then these delusive flowers must belong to that which produces them—the person—and thus there should be seeing.
If there is seeing, then since they have emerged as flowers in mid-air, one should instead see the eye capable of producing them. If there is no seeing, then once they have emerged...

If it can obscure the sky when rotated, it should likewise be able to obscure the eyes. Since the canopy emerges and obscures the sky, yet you still see the flowers, your eyes should be free of obstruction;
one ought to say that clear and bright eyes see the flowers in the sky. Why, then, do you conversely claim that obscured eyes see flowers in the sky?
If rotating it were to obscure the eyes, one ought to say that obscured eyes see the clear sky; how then could they see the clear sky?
Is this not, on the contrary, called the Eye of Clear Purity? If you know that these two—the madness and the flowers—are both non-existent, then delusion fundamentally has no cause.
You should then know that the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; it is merely a false designation of appearance.
Its nature is neither caused by conditions nor is it spontaneous; it is the wondrous true suchness-nature (tathatā-svabhāva) of the original Tathāgatagarbha.
Ānanda, it is like a person whose hands and feet are at ease... [down to] ...it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature. (Commentary):
This is a provisional metaphor used to clarify the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*);

it is, in fact, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. To receive and experience is called "sensation. If analyzed individually, these constitute the first five consciousnesses; if considered collectively, they are subsumed as the aggregate of sensation. However—
It must be that the first five faculties encounter the first five objects to give rise to the first five consciousnesses;
only when they are able to receive and grasp objects that are disagreeable, agreeable, or neutral can this be termed the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Therefore it is said:

"For example, suppose there is a person whose hands and feet are at ease and whose hundred limbs are in harmony, such that he suddenly forgets his very life and his nature is free from both the disagreeable and the agreeable"—this refers to the moment before a single thought has moved.
They do not yet know that there is a body; how could they know that there are faculties and objects? Since there are no faculties or objects, from what could sensation arise?
That person, for no reason, rubs his two palms together in the air; within his hands, various illusory sensations of roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat arise.
This is just like when a single thought-moment moves, the faculties and objects encounter one another, resulting in opposition or accord, separation or union.
These differences give rise to various consciousnesses within it; thus it is said that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is like this.

The subsequent passage distinguishes the illusory sensations of roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat, which do not arise from space nor emerge from the palm, in order to reveal the emptiness and falsity of the aggregate of sensation.
If one were to claim that these illusory sensations come from space, [one must consider that] space is devoid of discrimination and certainly lacks...
If it can touch the palm upon being selected, it must also touch the body; how could there be such selection that it touches only the palm?
Since it does not come from space, how could it emerge from the palm? If you claim that this illusory touch emerges from the palm, [it would follow that it arises from nowhere else].
A single palm can also produce it. When the palms have not yet joined, why are the various characteristics of roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat absent?
Why must they necessarily wait for the palms to join before they emerge? It does not end there.

If it were definitively produced from the palms, then since one knows it emerges when the palms join, one should also know it enters when the palms separate. If there were truly such coming and going, then its...
Within the palms, arms, wrists, marrow, and bones, one should likewise perceive the traces of its entry; why then is it not perceived?

If there were indeed a conscious mind within the arms, wrists, marrow, and bones that perceives its coming and going, then it would be a distinct entity moving within the body, never failing to make contact [with the senses]. Why, then, must it wait for...?

Only after the palms have joined does one know that they have emerged; can this first be called "contact"? If one realizes that both this illusory contact and its locus are non-existent, then delusion is fundamentally without cause.
One should then know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, being merely a false designation of appearance.
Its nature is neither caused by conditions nor is it spontaneous; it is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous True Suchness.
This is their nature. Roughness and smoothness, cold and heat, contain the two meanings of opposition and conformity; the palm contains the two meanings of separation and union.

These collectively reveal that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) arises based on these. However, the fundamental intent is simply to rely upon illusory contact to demonstrate the emptiness and falsity of the aggregate of sensation.
To cite the Dharma-characteristics school (*Faxiang-zong*) and forcibly assign it a different meaning would be a grave error.
Ānanda, it is like a person speaking of a sour plum... (up to) "it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature. [Commentary:
This metaphor is used to clarify that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is itself the *tathāgatagarbha*.

To discern and contemplate objects is called perception; this refers to the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which is also termed the "pervasive deluded thought. Therefore, it says: "It is like a person..."
When a person speaks of pickled plums, water flows from their mouth; when they think of treading upon a precipice, their feet tingle with acid pain.
This is precisely like the movement of a single thought of delusion, whereby the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) arises.

In the following passage, it is through the mere metaphor of water and acid pain that the emptiness and falsity of the aggregate of perception are discerned. That is to say, because of the mention of vinegar, the water that appears does not actually arise from the plum.
It does not enter through the mouth. If you claim that this water arises from the plum, the plum should speak of it itself;
why wait for a person to say "sour" before water flows from the mouth? Since the plum does not speak of its sourness, this water certainly does not arise from the plum.
If this water were to arise from what enters the mouth, then the one who hears the word "sour" should be the mouth itself. Why [is it the person]?
One must further wait for the ears to hear the mention of vinegar before water is produced in the mouth.
If the mouth has not yet heard the mention of vinegar, this water certainly does not enter through the mouth.
If this water arises solely because the ears hear the mention of vinegar, why does it not emerge from the ears instead of emerging from the mouth? Furthermore, as for this sourness and astringency...
It does not arise from the cliff, nor does it enter through the feet. If it arose from the cliff, the cliff itself should have thought; why wait for the person to think?
If it entered because of the feet, the feet themselves should have thought; why wait for the mind to think?
If it were produced by the mind alone, why would this sour and bitter sensation not arise within the heart, but instead arise within the feet? If one understands this water...
If it were associated with both sourness and astringency, it would be absent in both locations; thus, this delusion would fundamentally have no cause.

One should therefore know that this aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; it is merely a phantom delusion designated as a "mark. Its nature is neither caused by conditions nor is it spontaneous;
it is the wondrous True Suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Ānanda, it is like a violent torrent where waves succeed one another... (up to)... fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor arising spontaneously. [Commentary:
This metaphor is used to clarify that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

That which migrates and flows is called "formations"; this refers to the seventh consciousness, the *manas*. It is what is known as the constant and discerning reflection on the mark of self, following along with it; it is also called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*).
The wind forms a violent torrent. Here, emptiness (*ākāśa*) is used as a metaphor for *tathatā* (suchness), and water as a metaphor for the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).

Without emptiness, water could not be contained; without water, a torrent could not be formed. Therefore it is said: "For example, like a violent torrent where waves succeed one another, the preceding limit and the succeeding limit do not overstep each other.
This means that just as the true mind, through a single moment of deluded movement, becomes the storehouse consciousness.
The ocean of the consciousness-mind is further stirred by the winds of objects, thereby forming the *manas*.
Within it, there arise subtle phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, which do not cease for even a single moment. Such is the nature of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

In the following text, the author uses only the metaphor of a violent torrent to demonstrate the falsity of the aggregate of formations; yet the very nature of this torrent does not arise from emptiness.
It does not exist because of water; nor is it the nature of water, yet it is not separate from empty space and water.
This means that empty space has tranquility as its nature, water has clarity and stillness as its nature, and turbulent currents have ceaseless flux as their nature.

It is just as the true mind has non-arising and non-ceasing as its nature, while the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) has profound stillness and immovability as its nature, yet [it manifests] activity...

The *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has momentary arising and ceasing as its nature. However, apart from the True Mind and the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), no such *saṃskāra-skandha* can be found.
If you claim that this nature of a violent torrent exists because of space, then [consider] the empty space of the ten directions.
It forms an inexhaustible current, and the worlds are all submerged and drowned within it. Now, while this space is inexhaustible, this violent torrent is finite;

thus we know that its existence does not depend on space. It is just as True Suchness (tathatā) is quiescent and inexhaustible, whereas the shifting flow of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is finite.
If the nature of this violent torrent were to exist because of water, then the nature of this flow should not be water itself.
Nature. Why is this? The nature of water belongs to that which possesses (the capacity), while the nature of flowing belongs to that which is possessed (the manifestation).
It is just as when there are fruits because of a tree; one clearly distinguishes the tree as that which possesses them and the fruit as that which is possessed.
If the nature of this torrent were identical to the nature of water, then this water would necessarily have turbidity as its nature, [and not clarity]. At the clear...
If it were the nature of water, then it would not be the nature of water. Thus, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses arise in mutual manifestation;
they do not definitively possess a single nature, nor do they definitively possess two natures.

If this flowing nature were separate from space and water, then space would not exist externally [to it], and there would be no water external to the flow. Furthermore, it is not separate from space and water. That is to say:
Just as apart from the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), which is the treasury of the true mind, no aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) can be found on its own.
If one knows that this torrent does not arise from empty space, yet is not separate from empty space and water, then delusion is fundamentally without cause;

one should then know that this aggregate of formations is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, being merely a phantom and a false designation of appearance. Its nature is neither caused by conditions (*paratantra*) nor self-arisen (*svabhāva*).

However, this is precisely the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. The first, second, and fourth instances of the character "nature" (xìng) are distinguished according to movement and stillness;
the third instance of the character "nature" should not be taken as the nature of water itself, but rather is distinguished according to subject and object.
Ānanda, it is like a person taking a *piṅgala* jar [and so forth, until: originally neither through causes and conditions nor by spontaneous nature.

The above collectively refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Fundamentally, they are without arising or ceasing; they are merely illusory and false designations. Their nature is fundamentally true.
Thus, having used the metaphor of flowers in the sky to clarify the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), he immediately relies on the appearance of those flowers to analyze and deconstruct it.

Having used the illusory sensations of roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat as metaphors to clarify the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), he immediately relies on those illusory sensations to analyze and deconstruct it.

Having used the characteristic of water in the mouth and the characteristic of numbness in the soles of the feet to clarify the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), he then relies upon the characteristics of turbidity and astringency to analyze and refute it.
Having used the characteristic of a violent torrent to clarify the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), he then relies upon the characteristic of flowing to analyze and refute it.
This is because the preceding four aggregates do not differ significantly; it is only this aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) that— [is distinct].
Take a *piṅgala* jar, plug its two openings, and fill it with emptiness. Traveling a thousand li to a distant land, one uses it to bring provisions to another country;
thus the meaning is initially complete. When it comes to the refutation, however, the jar and the person are equal, and both are set aside;
one then distinguishes only the emptiness within the jar, which has no place from which it departs or to which it arrives, no trace of entering or exiting, and no deficiency or excess.
This clearly demonstrates that although the first four aggregates (*skandhas*) are not devoid of true nature (*tathatā*), delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*) blaze forth within them;
whereas in the final aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), although delusion is not absent, the true nature remains unchanging.

Therefore, regarding the first four aggregates, one specifically distinguishes the characteristics of delusion as being without cause, so that one may know the essence of delusion is fundamentally empty, and thus the true nature may be realized. Regarding the final aggregate of consciousness, one distinguishes only...
The true nature comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; yet it traverses the realms of delusion and enlightenment without ever entering or exiting.
Its essence pervades the substance of both the holy and the ordinary, fundamentally lacking nothing and possessing no excess. This causes one to know that true emptiness is unchanging.

Then delusive habits will naturally perish. This is the distinction between extinguishing delusion to return to the True, and using the True to eliminate delusion; it is something one must not fail to understand.
[Commentary on the Preface:
This metaphor is used to clarify that the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. This is precisely "reception" (*vedanā*).
The *ālayavijñāna*, perfumed and sustained by seeds, is that which all sentient beings abandon at death and enter into rebirth; it is the "lord" who precedes the departure and follows the arrival.

This is because *tathatā* (Suchness) possesses two aspects—following conditions and remaining unchanging—and *avidyā* (Ignorance) possesses two aspects—the manifestation of phenomena and the emptiness of essence.
When *tathatā* follows conditions, it becomes the *avidyā* that manifests phenomena; yet, the essence of *avidyā*...
Emptiness is precisely the unchanging *tathatā* (suchness). It is neither definitively a single entity nor definitively two entities.
Thus, that which is formed by the union of the real and the false to constitute the *ālayavijñāna* does not transcend these two aspects. Therefore it is said:
"It is like a person who takes a *piṅgala* jar, plugs its two openings, fills it with space, and carries it a thousand miles away to offer it to another."
The "country" is a metaphor for the power of human good and evil karma; the "jar" is a metaphor for the ignorance that brings about phenomena;

and the "space within the jar" is a metaphor for the unchanging *tathatā* (suchness) within ignorance. These together metaphorically represent the union of the true and the false, which constitutes the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).

"Plugging the two apertures" means that when True Suchness (*tathatā*) has not yet followed conditions, it possesses both the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Once it follows conditions to form consciousness (*vijñāna*), these two wisdoms are blocked and instead become the two obstacles (*dvividhāvaraṇa*).
"A long journey of a thousand *li* to provide provisions for another country" means that consciousness is dragged by karma, transmigrating through the three realms (*tridhātu*) without end.
It does not go to its location. Such is the nature of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
In the following passage, it does not speak of the person or the jar, but speaks only of the emptiness within the jar as having no characteristics of coming or going;

therefore, it says that the emptiness within the jar does not come from that direction nor enter from this direction. If the emptiness within the jar were brought from that direction, then since the jar was originally filled...
If space were to depart, then at the site of the original jar, there should be a deficiency of the space occupied by that one jar;
yet that site has never lacked the space of that one jar. Therefore, it is certain that the space was not brought from that other direction.

If the space within the jar must necessarily enter from this direction, then wherever there is entry, there must be exit; thus, when the jar is opened and overturned, one should see the space exiting.
Now, even if one were to open a hole and turn the bottle upside down, no emptiness would be seen coming out; thus, it is certainly not that which entered this [bottle] from elsewhere.

This is because the emptiness within the bottle lacks the characteristics of going or coming; it is unchanging True Suchness (*tathatā*). Although it exists within the karmic consciousness of sentient beings, it remains as such.
It has never possessed the characteristics of arising and ceasing, or of going and coming.
When a person carries a vase for a journey of a thousand li to another country, it serves as a metaphor for those who go first and later return, wandering through the various realms of rebirth;
this is nothing other than the power of ignorance and karma. Nevertheless, the space within this vase and the vast, inexhaustible space outside are fundamentally not two different things.
It has never been obstructed, nor is there any deficiency or excess. If this bottle were released from one's hands and shattered, it would become entirely one vast and inexhaustible emptiness.

Just so, when all sentient beings sever the power of karma and overturn ignorance, they are identical in essence, without distinction, to the wondrous principle of true emptiness realized by the Buddhas of the ten directions.

How could there be any distinction between the arising of a Buddha? If one knows that the space within a jar has never come or gone, and that the space outside the jar has never been deficient or in excess, then one will know that the true nature is fundamentally without birth, death, coming, or going;
rather, it is karma and ignorance that give rise to what are called birth, death, coming, and going—what are termed "delusory birth through conjunction" and "delusory death through conjunction."
Listen. You should know that this aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; it is merely a phantom and delusion designated as a characteristic.
Its nature is neither caused by conditions nor is it spontaneous; it is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true suchness (tathatā).

Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)? [From here until] they are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.

This essence of vision should be identified as the *paramārtha-indriya* (the ultimate sense organ). If it were identified as the *ābhāsa-indriya* (the physical sense organ), then it would not be an organ that emerges from an organ;

there would necessarily be no basis for its existence. Furthermore, the physical organ is already subsumed within the deluded body. To say it "dwells therein" means it dwells within the physical organ.
If one were to say it dwells between the organ and its object, then it is called consciousness (*vijñāna*) and not an organ. This essence of vision—

Furthermore, this is not the same as the "seeing-essence" mentioned previously. The former belongs to the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving division), while this belongs to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objectified division).

If one is restricted to and immersed in the nature of seeing itself, it must belong to the *darśana-bhāga*; it is then called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and is not called the "eye-faculty" (*cakṣurindriya*).

This is precisely where the foolish find it difficult to distinguish between consciousness and the faculty. If you claim that the previous passage granted the seeing-essence a substantial existence apart from objects, yet now speaks of seeing...
If consciousness were to be separated from its objects, it would lack a substantial nature; this would seem to contradict one's own words.

Yet you fail to realize that what was previously indicated as the "seeing-portion" (darśana-bhāga) is not yet mixed with form, and thus remains closely proximate to the ultimate reality. This refers exclusively to the pure material sense-faculty (rūpa-indriya) as the "image-portion" (nimitta-bhāga).

Furthermore, since the previous analogy compared it to a second moon, and it was stated that "when seeing the seeing, the seeing is not seeing," it is sufficient to know that—though [it appears otherwise]—[the true nature remains].
When it says "it has a substance," this too relies upon the essence of seeing to point toward the true nature;
it does not mean that the essence of seeing alone possesses a substance apart from objects. You should investigate this deeply; do not treat it with superficiality.
Commentary and Annotation: This section investigates and explains that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are themselves the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

First, there is a general inquiry; subsequently, there is a detailed explanation. "Bases" (*āyatana*) refers here to the faculties (*indriya*). This means that each of the six faculties is able to draw in (*āhara*) the objective phenomena (*viṣaya*) they encounter;

therefore, the faculties are designated as the "places where the objects enter. The Tathāgatagarbha is the true mind of ultimate reality (*dharmatā-citta*). "Tathā" (*tathā*) signifies the unmoving essence.
"Coming" refers to its all-pervading function. "Treasury" means that this mind is able to contain immeasurable meritorious qualities and the wealth of the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "the wondrous nature of True Suchness is like a treasury of jewels": it means that this Tathāgata-garbha naturally reflects and manifests throughout every sense organ and every sensory object, just as a pearl reflects various colors. Its fundamental substance is unchanging; all phenomena are suchness, arising again and again without end.
This is the principle of cessation. The following clarifies that the faculty of sight (*cakṣur-indriya*) is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

That which is the exhaustion produced by staring with the pupils—along with the eyes themselves—is identical to Bodhi. "The appearance of exhaustion produced by staring" means to gaze fixedly and straight ahead.
This exhaustion arises because the pupils have stared for a long time; therefore, it is called "the appearance of exhaustion produced by staring. As in the preceding passage: "For example..."
When one with clear eyes gazes at the empty sky, the fixed stare causes fatigue, leading to the perception of illusory flowers.

Thus, the illusory flowers seen by the deluded vision are the signs produced by the fatigue of the eyes from being fixed in a stare. This means that it is not only the seeing of illusory flowers that constitutes the sign of ocular fatigue.

Furthermore, this is compounded by the exhaustion of the eyes; both are likewise manifestations of fatigue arising from the gaze upon the true mind of Bodhi—what is called the "seer" and the "object of seeing," which are like flowers in the sky. Why look at those eyes? They are but the signs of fatigue of the true mind.
For this nature of seeing is fundamentally without self-nature; it merely arises falsely due to the floating roots [the eyes] in relation to the two conditions of light and darkness.

When the sense-objects and their counterparts interact, they adhere to the profound stillness and give rise to seeing. Residing within the floating root (the eye), it absorbs the images of the objects;
this is called the "nature of seeing. If this nature were not these two types of objects, it would not be called the "nature of seeing.

Indeed, that which is named the "nature of seeing" is established because of these two kinds of deluded objects. If one were separated from these two objects, even the name itself would not be formed.

How could it have a substance? Why do you see that it has no substance? Is this seeing-substance something that does not come from light or darkness, nor emerge from the physical sense-organ, nor arise from empty space? If this seeing-substance came from light, then in the presence of darkness there would be no light;

Empty space itself can perceive forms; it has no connection whatsoever with your faculty of sight.

If you know that the substance of seeing is absent in all three locations [the eye, the object, and space], then you should know that your visual faculty (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. It is merely a false designation of form;
its nature is neither caused by conditions nor is it spontaneous. It is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true suchness-nature.
Ānanda, it is like a person who uses two fingers [to plug his ears]... (up to)... fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor arising spontaneously.
*Commentary:* This clarifies that the ear-base (*śrotra-āyatana*) is itself the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha.

Previously, by staring fixedly for a long time, he falsely perceived illusory flowers in the sky; this was merely a symptom of the eyes' fatigue. Now, by suddenly blocking his ears, he falsely hears [a sound].
The sound produced within the head is a sign of the ear’s exhaustion. One might wonder: is it only the sound that is a sign of the ear’s exhaustion?
Furthermore, both the ear-organ and its exhaustion are likewise signs of exhaustion produced by staring at the true mind of Bodhi.
How can one see the ear itself as a sign of exhaustion upon the mind? For this nature of hearing is fundamentally without self-nature; it exists only because of...

The floating organ corresponds with the two kinds of delusive objects: movement and stillness. Adhering to the profound clarity, it gives rise to hearing and resides within the floating organ, absorbing the characteristics of these two kinds of objects;
therefore, it is called the "nature of hearing. If this nature were not in relation to these two objects, it would not be called the nature of hearing.
Indeed, the reason it is named the nature of hearing is precisely because of the characteristics of these two kinds of objects.
Established. If one is separated from those two objects of movement and stillness, even the name "hearing" cannot be formed; how could there be a substance? How do we see that it has no substance?
For this nature of hearing is absent in all three places: within delusive objects, the floating sense organs, and empty space.

If one were to claim that the nature of seeing and hearing arises from the state of stillness, then when there is movement, there is no stillness, and this nature of hearing would consequently [cease to exist].

It ceases when the environment is still. Once it has ceased, one should not hear movement; yet if there is sound, one hears it. Therefore, this hearing certainly does not arise during the state of stillness.
If you claim that this nature of hearing arises from the time of movement, then since there is no movement during stillness, this nature of hearing would necessarily cease along with that movement.
Once it has ceased, one should not hear stillness; yet if there is no sound, [one still hears].

Awakening is certainly not produced when there is movement. If you claim that this nature of hearing arises from the floating sense-organ, then when the floating organ exists alone, the two objects—movement and stillness—would necessarily be absent; yet this essence of hearing lacks any inherent self-nature apart from those two objects.
If you claim that this nature of hearing emerges from space, then it would follow that space itself possesses the faculty of hearing, which is a contradiction.

If it possesses a nature, it is not an empty void devoid of cognition. Furthermore, if emptiness possessed a nature, it would be able to hear sound on its own, without any connection to your auditory faculty (*śrotra-āyatana*).

If you realize that this nature of hearing is absent in all three locations [the ear, the sound, and the space between], then you should know that this auditory faculty is fundamentally without arising or ceasing;
it is merely a false designation of appearance. Its nature is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous.
This is the wondrous true nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Ānanda, it is like a person who forcefully pinches their nose [until they experience a sensation]—this is fundamentally neither a nature produced by causes and conditions nor a spontaneous nature.
Commentary: This clarifies that the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇa-āyatana*) is itself the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. "Accumulating" refers to the breath.

This means that by long retaining the breath in the nose, one falsely perceives cold sensations within the nostrils, as well as their openness or obstruction; these are all merely signs of exhaustion within the nose.
The intent is to suggest that it is not only cold sensations and the like that are signs of exhaustion within the nose, but that this also includes the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) itself.
It is associated with toil. Furthermore, it is likewise a mark of toil upon the true mind of bodhi;
how can you see this faculty of the nose as a mark of toil upon the mind? This is because the nature of hearing fundamentally lacks self-nature;

it merely arises from the interaction between the floating organ and the two kinds of delusory objects—openness and obstruction—which, by adhering to the profound stillness, gives rise to hearing and dwells within the floating organ, drawing in the two [objects].
Dust. This is what is called the nature of smelling and hearing. If this nature were not these two kinds of dust, it would not be called the nature of hearing.
Indeed, that which is named the nature of hearing is established in dependence upon these two kinds of dust. If one were separated from those two kinds of dust, even the name would not be formed;
how could there be a substance? How can you see that it has no substance? Now, as for this nature of hearing, regarding the delusive dust and the floating faculties—
In the three states of space, [this hearing-nature] is entirely absent. Why is this? If one claims that this nature of hearing comes from openness, then when there is obstruction, openness is absent;
consequently, this nature of hearing should likewise perish along with the characteristic of openness. If it perished, one should not perceive obstruction.
Since one can perceive obstruction, it must not come from openness. If, on the other hand, one claims that this nature of hearing exists because of obstruction...

If that were so, when there is unobstructed passage, this nature of hearing should likewise perish along with the obstructing object. Once it has perished, one would not perceive the unobstructed state;
how then could it discern fragrances, stenches, and so forth? Furthermore, if the sense of touch can perceive fragrance, it must not originate from within the obstruction itself.

If you claim that this nature of hearing arises from the floating sense-organ, then when there is only the floating organ alone, the two objects—penetration and obstruction—must necessarily be absent.
Yet this nature of hearing lacks any inherent substance apart from those two objects.

If you claim that this nature of hearing emerges from space, then this nature of hearing should naturally reside within space; try then to turn back and smell your own nose, for space itself has its own [nature].
The nature of hearing is entirely unrelated to your faculty of hearing; is there any such principle?

If you know that this nature of hearing is absent in all three places, then you should know that this nose-faculty is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, and its characteristics are merely false designations.
Its nature is neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous; it is fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha.
The term "penetration" refers to the presence of fragrance and stench, while "obstruction" refers to the absence of fragrance and stench. It does not refer to the obstruction of being closed off.
By using the two characteristics of movement and stillness as an analogy for this penetration and obstruction, the intended meaning becomes self-evident.
Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who uses their tongue to lick their lips... [up to] "it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature. (Commentary:
This clarifies that the tongue-faculty is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Here, the person uses the tongue to lick the lips;
if they lick incessantly and then fall ill, it is because of that licking that a false sensation of bitter taste arises. If the person is not ill...)
There is a slight sensation of sweetness. From repeatedly licking it, there arises the false perception of sweet and bitter flavors.

Furthermore, through these sweet and bitter sensations, the constant presence of the neutral (bland) nature prior to licking is revealed. All of this is merely because the tongue’s experience of sweetness does not cease, causing the appearance of fatigue to manifest.
One might wonder: is it only the sensations of sweet, bitter, and bland that constitute the fatigue of the tongue-organ? Indeed, this very tongue-organ and its fatigue [are likewise illusory].
This is likewise upon the true mind of bodhi; it is a state of exhaustion produced by staring. Why is this? Know that the nature of tasting has no inherent self-nature of its own.

It arises because the floating sense-organ (the tongue) encounters two kinds of delusive objects. This clinging to stillness gives rise to cognition, which dwells within the floating organ and inhales these two objects;
therefore, it is called the "nature of knowing taste. If this nature were not dependent on these two, it would not exist.

If it were merely the dust, it would not be called the nature that knows taste. Indeed, the reason it is named the "nature that knows taste" is established based on the characteristics of two kinds of dust.
If one were separated from those two kinds of false dust—sweet, bitter, and bland—even the name would not be formed;
how could there be a substance? How do we see that it has no substance? Because this nature that knows taste exists within false dust, the floating sense-organ, and empty space.

It is absent in all three instances. Why is this? If one claims that the nature of this cognition arises from sweet or bitter tastes, then when encountering a bland taste, since the sweet and bitter have already ceased to exist, this cognitive nature should likewise perish along with them, and thus it should not perceive the bland.
If it can perceive the bland, then it originally does not arise from the sweet or bitter. If one claims that this cognitive nature arises from the bland taste...
Upon emerging [from meditation], when encountering sweetness or bitterness, the neutral taste has already vanished;

yet this cognitive nature should have perished along with that neutral taste, and it would likewise not be aware of the two characteristics of sweet and bitter. If it still perceives the sweet and the bitter, then it does not arise from the neutral taste.
If this nature of cognition arose from the physical sense organ, then when the tongue-organ alone exists, there would necessarily be no sweet, bland, or bitter objects.
Yet this organ that perceives taste has no inherent self-nature. If this nature of cognition emerged from space, then that empty space itself would be able to know taste;
it would not necessarily be your mouth that knows it, and space itself would be the one knowing it.
Then what connection is there between this and your tongue-faculty (*jihvā-āyatana*)?

If you realize that the nature of this cognition of taste is absent in all three locations [the tongue, the object, and the consciousness], then you should know that this tongue-faculty is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; it is merely a false designation of appearance.
Its nature is neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous; it is fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Ānanda, it is like a person who has one hand that is cold [and another that is warm]... [it is] fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature. (Commentary:
This clarifies that the body-faculty (*kāyāyatana*) is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Touch is the object-field (*viṣaya*) corresponding to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).

When the faculty and its object-field encounter one another, they must necessarily undergo conjunction and separation, as well as opposition and compliance; only then do the two dharmas—the faculty and the object-field—begin [to function].
It is evident that this [notion] takes only the two hands as the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
Merely through the mutual contesting of cold and heat within the two hands, one falsely establishes contact (*spraṣṭavya*) based on their separation, union, opposition, or conformity.
In truth, it is revealed to be nothing more than a mark of empty, deluded toil. Therefore it is said: "For example, suppose there is a person who touches a hot hand with a cold hand. If...
The cold force is predominant. That which is hot follows the cold; this is because the cold force prevails and the hot force fails.
If the efficacy of the heat were predominant, the cold would become hot; this is because the hot force prevails and the cold force fails. To conclude briefly:
thus, by means of this contact that is perceived through conjunction, the cognition of separation is manifested. If the engagement of forces is established, it is due to the contact of exertion.
Thus, by means of these four characters, the two characters "awareness" (覺知) from the preceding text are specified, as well as the faculty of the body (身根).
This refers to the contact-object (觸塵) conjoined with the faculty of the body; it precisely coincides with the temporal object (時塵). Yet, this temporal object cannot manifest itself independently;
it must await the cognition that is separated from time before the characteristics of the temporal object conjoined [with the faculty] can be manifested. Two lines should be added below:

The knowledge of separation manifests when union and contact are present, for only then is the intention complete. Indeed, separation is not manifested without union, nor is union manifested without separation;
it is only through their mutual manifestation that separation and union first become visible. It is not without cold that heat is encountered, nor without heat that cold is encountered;
they must necessarily interact through their respective forces. If victory and defeat are mutually established, then opposition and compliance first become visible. This is essential.
The first two lines establish the two characteristics of union and separation; the latter two lines establish the two characteristics of opposition and conformity.
Although union, separation, opposition, and conformity are indeed the characteristics of the body-faculty’s exhaustion resulting from fixed gazing, the body-faculty and this exhaustion—
Furthermore, within this same true mind of bodhi, when one stares fixedly, the signs of fatigue arise. Why then do you see its physical organ?
This is merely a sign of fatigue upon the mind. Therefore, know that this perception originally has no self-nature;

it arises only because the floating organ meets with the delusive objects—whether through their union or separation, their opposition or accord—and by clinging to the profound stillness, it gives rise to awareness. Abiding within the floating organ, it inhales these objects.

Because it possesses these characteristics, it is called the nature of cognition. If this nature were not characterized by union and separation, or by opposition and compliance, it would not be called the nature of cognition.

Indeed, the designation "nature of cognition" is established based upon these four characteristics. If one were to depart from union and separation, or from opposition and compliance, even the name itself could not be formed;
how then could there be an essence? How do we see that it has no essence? It is for this reason that it is known as such.
This awareness is entirely absent in the three locations: the point of contact, the point of separation, and empty space. Why is this so?
If this cognition were to arise because of contact, then at the time of separation—when there is no longer contact—this cognition should likewise perish along with that contact.
How does one know separation? Since one can know separation, it is certainly not because of conjunction that there exist the two aspects of opposition and compliance.

By analogy with this, one may understand that if this cognition arose from the floating sense-organ alone, then where there is only the floating sense-organ, there would necessarily be no four kinds of delusive objects—conjunction, separation, opposition, and compliance.
Thus, your bodily cognition, when separated from these four aspects, is fundamentally devoid of self-nature.
If this perception must arise from emptiness, then emptiness itself would possess perception; what connection, then, could there be between it and your body’s sense-faculties?

If you understand that this perception is absent in all three locations, then you should know that these sense-faculties are fundamentally without arising or ceasing, being merely false designations of appearances.
Their nature is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously; it is fundamentally the Tathāgata.
This conceals the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Ānanda, it is like a person who falls asleep when weary... (up to) "it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
[Commentary: This clarifies that the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) is itself the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. For the sense-base of mind has no form; it is merely—

The manas-vijñāna serves as the characteristic of the faculty (indriya), while the two phenomena of arising and ceasing serve as the characteristic of the objects (viṣaya). This faculty is precisely the grasping at self;

the seventh mental object is the past. When the first five objects are dormant—such as during sleep—the sixth consciousness does not arise, nor is there any perception of a faculty that cognizes objects.
The World-Honored One previously established [this] by means of states such as sleeping and waking, remembering and forgetting.

The faculty of mental cognition (*manovijñānendriya*) is intended to make it easy for people to understand. Therefore, it is said: "For example, when a person’s mind is weary and exhausted, they fall asleep.
While in the midst of sleep, the faculty of mental cognition has not yet become manifest; however, upon reaching deep sleep and then awakening," [it becomes manifest].
When a false thought first arises, it does not arise in isolation; it must necessarily arise in dependence upon the past five sense-objects that have been perceived.
Furthermore, these perceived objects are not necessarily arranged in a systematic order. Thus, when one grasps them, it is called "recollection," and when one loses them, it is called "forgetting.
Within this cycle of recollection and forgetting, one cannot avoid falling into inversion and confusion—this occurs in a single kṣaṇa.

Gradually, one awakens to this realization. Thus, within a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), one perceives that initial recollection is like arising, the sustained recollection is like abiding, the near-forgetting is like change, and the complete forgetting is like cessation.
One draws in the sensory marks (*nimitta*) of the past and brings them all back into this process of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing;
in every moment, these four characteristics follow one another without ever overstepping their sequence.

This is the characteristic manifestation of the faculty of mental cognition (*manas-indriya*). "Mind" refers to sleeping, waking, remembering, and forgetting; these are certainly the manifestations of fatigue resulting from the fixed gazing of the mental sense-base (*mana-āyatana*).
However, both the mind and its fatigue are likewise manifestations of fatigue resulting from the fixed gazing of the true mind of Bodhi.
Why then do you see only the mental sense-base as a manifestation of fatigue within the true mind? It is for this reason that it is called "awareness."

Nature is fundamentally without nature. It merely arises because the faculty of mental cognition (*manas*) relies upon the two kinds of delusive objects—those that arise and perish—and thereby adheres to and gathers consciousness within the faculty of the mind. It attracts and extracts the five sense-objects of the past, which are termed "internal objects.
Although it extracts these internal objects, it does not share the same objective domain as the preceding five faculties; for the former...

The five sense faculties take present objects as their conditions; this is called "flowing with the stream. If they instead take internal objects as their conditions, this is called "flowing against the stream";

however, even if they were to flow against the stream, they would still not reach those internal objects. Thus, it is only by way of the first five faculties that there is "flowing against the stream."

That which does not reach [the objects] is called the nature of awareness and cognition. If this nature were not dependent upon the two kinds of false objects—the states of waking and sleeping, and arising and ceasing—it would not be called the nature of awareness and cognition.
Indeed, the reason it is named the nature of awareness and cognition is that it is established based on the characteristics of these two kinds of objects.
If one were separated from those two objects of waking and sleeping, and arising and ceasing, even the name would not be formed; how then could its substance exist?
How can one see that this nature of awareness lacks substantiality? It is absent in all three locations: during waking, sleeping, and the arising and ceasing of the mental faculty within space.
Why is this so? If one were to claim that this nature of awareness comes from the state of waking, then since one is not awake during sleep, it should cease along with the waking state.
Yet, as for that which remains in a state of dark oblivion while asleep—who is it that experiences this? Since...
As for this nature of awareness that persists whether one is awake or asleep, it does not originate from the states of waking or sleeping.
If you claim that this nature of awareness must exist at the moment of birth, yet at the moment of death it is no longer born, then it would follow that it perishes along with its birth.
And as for that which undergoes cessation, who is it? If you say it exists from the time of cessation, then at the very moment of arising, there is no cessation;
thus, it would follow that once it has ceased, it is non-existent, so who then is it that knows the arising?

If you say this nature of cognition arises from the faculty of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), you fail to realize that this faculty of mental consciousness itself lacks intrinsic substance, being merely dependent upon the two states of waking and sleeping.

Characteristics manifest and arise; yet, both waking and sleeping are themselves without characteristics. It is merely that, according to the expansion of the physical form, one calls it "waking," and according to the contraction of the physical form, one calls it "sleeping.
Now, apart from these two entities of waking and sleeping, even the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) does not exist;
how much less so the nature of cognition that issues forth from the mental faculty? This is like flowers in the sky—ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature.
If you claim that this nature of cognition arises from emptiness, then it is simply the awareness of emptiness itself;
what connection does it have with your "mind-faculty" (manas-āyatana)? Therefore, the conclusion below is the same as before. The term "fatigue" refers to the mind;
it does not refer to physical fatigue. When it says "the mind-cognition faculty is like one seeing in a dark chamber," it is contrasted with the five "floating faculties" (mukha-indriya).
In this parallel enumeration, that which does not arise from the faculties (*indriya*), as well as the faculty from which it arises, both refer to the aforementioned mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
The nature of cognition (*vijñapti*) is likewise enumerated alongside the natures of seeing, hearing, and so forth.

While the first five are all described as "arousing seeing" and so on, this one alone is described as "collecting cognition" (*saṃjñāna*). This is because the first five faculties pertain to the manifestation of their respective objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*).

Regarding the statement "within the stage": although these are identical to the *bhāga* (aspect) of the object (*nimitta-bhāga*), there is still a distinction between the coarse and the subtle within the stage of the seeds (*bīja*).
