The above concludes the explanation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). Below, the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) are explained; these are precisely the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Twelve. Six.

The "roots" (indriya) are the six sense organs; the "locations" (āyatana) are the sites where the roots and objects reside. Here, [the text] specifically refutes the six roots but does not mention the roots themselves;

it speaks only of the locations where the objects enter. Although below there is a mutual analysis of roots and objects, the primary refutation lies in the objects, yet it still does not mention the roots or objects directly, but speaks only of the locations of the roots and objects.
This is just as in the subsequent text, where although the triad of root, object, and consciousness is present...

They distinguish them from one another. In the true refutation, even when discussing consciousness (*vijñāna*), he does not speak of consciousness itself; he speaks only of the boundaries of consciousness.

This is because the dharmas of sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), though designated as eighteen, are fundamentally the single, perfect, wondrous, jewel-like nature of enlightened awareness.

It is only due to the deluded攀緣心 (*pānluánxīn*,攀缘心) of ordinary fools that they falsely give rise to discrimination, dogmatically insisting that the organs are internal and the objects are external, [and thus establishing] consciousness...

The sense organs (*indriya*) arise within the midst of the objects (*viṣaya*). Therefore, we now merely refute their directions, locations, and boundaries, so that the objects have no place to enter, the organs have no basis for perception, and consciousness has no realm of division.
By knocking down the walls and moats and forging them into a single expanse, the dharmas of organ, object, and consciousness will no longer be separated; they will naturally attain integration.
They return to the single true dharma-nature. Therefore, it is not the dharma itself that is negated; rather, only the locus and boundaries of that dharma are negated.
Furthermore, Ānanda, as for what are the twelve bases (āyatana), they are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.

Commentary: The following clarifies that the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are themselves the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. First, there is a general inquiry; subsequently, there is a detailed explanation.
Although both faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are mutually deconstructed, the primary intent lies in the deconstruction of the objects.

However, because they stand supported by one another like bundles of reeds leaning against each other, it is necessary to analyze and deconstruct them reciprocally. Therefore, the World-Honored One first cites the two bases of faculty and object to investigate thoroughly the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
The objection states: "Consider for a moment the Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds. That which is capable of observing is the locus of seeing;
that which is observed is the locus of form (*rūpa*). How do you explain this?
Does the observation arise within your eye from external forms, such that there is first a locus of seeing? Or does the observation within your eye likewise give rise to the external?"
Is it that only when there is a form-characteristic does one begin to have a place of seeing?
If you claim that it is your eye-organ that produces external form-characteristics and only then has a place of seeing, then the nature of form would belong to the eye;
in that case, when your eye-organ sees only empty space—where no form-characteristic exists—that nature of form should naturally perish along with its counterpart. Since the nature of form...
It is dissolved. Even the marks of form do not exist. Even if your seeing were present, there would be nothing to manifest it.
If you claim that emptiness can manifest seeing, you fail to realize that emptiness depends upon form. Since the marks of form do not exist, what could possibly manifest the substance of emptiness?
That which is not empty cannot manifest either form or emptiness; since both form and emptiness are absent, the faculty of the eye has no basis to rest upon. Thus, all...
There is none at all. Indeed, it is an error to calculate that the eye arises from the appearance of form.

If you claim that the capacity for seeing first exists only when external forms arise within your visual field, then the nature of seeing would belong to form; in that case, when you contemplate emptiness—
One sees only empty space; there are no forms or characteristics of color. If this nature of seeing were identical to form, it would perish along with it.
Once the nature of seeing has perished, even if empty space and forms still exist, if the eye-faculty is absent, who else could possibly see them? Who would be there to perceive them?
Indeed, to calculate that the production of form gives rise to visual perception is likewise erroneous. The text concludes by returning to the true nature, saying:
"Therefore, one should know that both seeing and form-emptiness have no location. Since they have no location, then form and seeing are fundamentally without arising or ceasing.
Yet these two locations are false designations; their nature is neither caused by conditions nor is it spontaneous. It is fundamental..."
The Tathāgatagarbha is the wondrous nature of True Suchness.
Ānanda, listen further to how this Jeta Grove (up to) is fundamentally neither of the nature of causes and conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
Commentary: This clarifies that the sense-object of sound is itself the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha.
For although the locus of sound is refuted, the locus of the ear is likewise addressed; they are refuted through mutual analysis. Therefore, Ānanda is examined with the words:
"Listen again to the sound of the gongs and bells in this Jeta Grove as the assembly gathers for the meal—continuous from beginning to end. What do you think?"
[The opponent] explains: "This sound comes to the vicinity of the ear, while the ear goes to the place where the sound is.

If one were to say that this sound of the drum or bell comes to the vicinity of the ear, it would be like my own body: having already gone to Śrāvastī to beg for food, I am no longer present in the Jeta Grove.
Since a single person cannot simultaneously attend to two places, one knows that [the sound does not come]."
A single sound cannot possibly reach the ears of all listeners simultaneously. This sound must come to the location of Ānanda’s ears;
thus, Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa would not hear it together. How much less could twelve hundred people hear that sound at once and all arrive at the place of the meal?
It is evident, therefore, that the calculation that the sound travels to the side of the ear is false. If you claim that your own faculty of hearing travels to that [place], [then...]
The sound has gone away. Furthermore, taking my own body as an analogy for your faculty of hearing:
when I went to the place where the drum was being struck, just as I returned and stayed within the Jeta Grove, the sounds of the bells would not have been heard simultaneously.
If there were no "I" within the city of Śrāvastī, how much less could one hear all the various sounds of elephants, horses, and so forth all at once? Is this not so?
To reckon that the ear goes to the place of sound is false. If both the ear-faculty and the sound-object each lacked coming and going, then there should be no hearing;
yet how is it that all sounds are heard? Thus, to reckon that there is no coming and going is likewise false.
The concluding summary returning to the true nature states: "Therefore, you should know that hearing and sound both have no location.
Since they have no location, hearing and sound fundamentally have no arising or ceasing, nor coming or going. Yet these two are merely false designations of appearances;
their nature is neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous. It is fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha."
"Ānanda, you should again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner... (up to) "...it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature. [Commentary:
This clarifies that the object of fragrance (*gandha-viṣaya*) is itself the *tathāgatagarbha*. Now, wishing to discern the object of fragrance, there is no place from which it emerges;
first, he points to a distinct fragrance to examine the reality of it. Ānanda said: "You should again smell this in the incense burner..."
Sandalwood: if this incense is burned, its fragrance can be smelled simultaneously within a radius of forty *li* even from a single *zhu*.
What do you think? Do you understand this fragrance to be produced from the wood, or produced from the nose, or produced from space?

If you claim that this fragrance is produced in your nose, and thus is designated as "produced by the nose," it should then emerge from the nose. Yet your olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) is not the sandalwood tree. Why?

How can there be this fragrance within the nose? To say merely that the nose smells the fragrance is insufficient; it must be said that the fragrance enters the nose before it can be called "smelling.
If one were to claim that the fragrance issues forth from within the nose and yet call it "smelling," it would be utterly inconsistent with reason.
Thus, it is evident that the calculation that fragrance arises from the nose is erroneous. If one were to claim that this fragrance arises from space, [it could] produce...
If emptiness were eternal, then the fragrance produced from it should also exist eternally.
Why, then, would it depend upon burning this withered wood in an incense burner for the fragrance to arise? Thus, it is evident that the calculation that fragrance arises from emptiness is erroneous.
If one claims that this fragrance must necessarily arise from the wood, then the substance of this fragrance is produced as smoke by burning, which allows the nose to perceive it.
If this nose perceives the fragrance, it should logically be covered by that; thus, one could say the fragrance arises from the wood.
However, once the smoke rises into the air, it has not yet traveled even forty *li*. How then can it already be smelled? This should be considered.
It is also erroneous to claim that fragrance arises from wood. The text concludes by returning to the true nature, saying:

"Therefore, one should know that fragrance, the nose, and the act of smelling all lack a fixed location. Since they have no fixed location, smelling and fragrance are fundamentally without arising or ceasing."
These two locations are merely false designations; their nature is neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous, but is fundamentally the wondrous true suchness of the Tathāgatagarbha.
According to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school, however, the nose perceives its object through contact.
Now, it is said that while they have not yet been reached by the smoke, they have already been able to perceive the fragrance. Furthermore, this constitutes knowledge within separation.

Examining this, it is evident that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas’ preaching of the Dharma has never possessed a fixed form; rather, they specifically established teachings according to the times, administering medicine in response to specific ailments.
If one were to conflate that with this and forcibly align this with that, not only would the source of the teaching be thrown into disorder, but also—

Furthermore, those who are ignorant of the essential principles of the times—those who study the Inner Canon (Buddhist scriptures)—are they not merely dazzled by the splendor of the rhetoric, failing to investigate the ultimate reality?

Ānanda, you have often, during the two periods of the day amidst the assembly, held the alms bowl [and so forth, until]: "It is fundamentally neither a nature caused by conditions nor a nature that is spontaneous."
Commentary: This clarifies that the object of taste is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
It is because one wishes to discern that the object of taste has no fixed location that [the Buddha] examines Ānanda specifically at the moment he holds his bowl to receive food; thus it is said:
"You regularly hold your bowl among the assembly twice a day. Your tongue may encounter ghee, curd, or clarified butter, which are called superior flavors."
What do you think: does this taste arise from space, from the tongue, or from the food?
If you say that this taste arises from your tongue, then since you have only one tongue in your mouth, it should produce only a single taste.
Once that tongue has become the flavor of ghee, it should likewise remain as ghee without undergoing any change. If it were to encounter [another substance] again...
Regarding black stone honey: it should not undergo transformation, yet one would not know it as honey.
If, without undergoing transformation, one were to perceive only the taste of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), then that too would not be called "knowing the taste.

How could there be a tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) that is not called "knowing the taste"? If you claim that the tongue-faculty can transform and thereby perceive many tastes, then those tastes must likewise proceed from the tongue.
If [the taste] were produced [independently], the tongue would have to possess multiple bodies; how then could multiple tastes give rise to the cognition of a single tongue?
Thus, it can be seen that the calculation that taste is produced in the tongue is incorrect. If one claims that this taste is produced solely within the food, then taste itself cannot be established.
Why? Because the nature of taste is only established by depending upon a cognizer. If there were no tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*), the food...
It is not consciousness. How could it be known whether [the taste] is sweet or bitter? Even if food were able to know its own flavor, that would be equivalent to someone else knowing the flavor;
it would have no concern with you. How, then, could your tongue-faculty be called the knower that tastes the flavor?
Thus, the calculation that the perception of flavor arises from the food is also incorrect. If you claim that this flavor arises...
Regarding the void: if you were to consume empty space, what flavor would it have? That void must necessarily have a salty taste;
once your tongue is salty and your face is also salty, then all people in this world would be equally salty.

Since the fish in the ocean constantly experience saltiness, they certainly do not know what fresh water is like. If they do not recognize the fresh, they likewise cannot perceive the salty. Regarding these two—
Such a person would necessarily have no cognition. How, then, can one be called a knower of taste?

If there is no one capable of knowing taste, nor even the arising of the lower fetters, it returns to the true nature. Therefore, one should know that taste, the tongue, and the act of tasting are all without location.
Since it has no location, it is simply tasted along with the flavor; fundamentally, it is without arising or ceasing.

It is merely that these two aspects are falsely designated as characteristics, yet its nature is neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous; it is fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
○ Regarding "black stone honey" (*kṛṣṇa-śarkarā*), the ancient explanation states that it is granulated sugar.
"Ānanda, you have often in the early morning rubbed your head with your hand... [up to] 'it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

To explain this passage, one must first clearly distinguish between the two terms 'subject' (the agent) and 'object' (the recipient), as well as between 'ignorance' and 'cognition,' so that they are judged with absolute clarity and free from doubt;
only then will you understand its meaning. If one speaks from the perspective of the single aspect of contact..."

If one takes the object (*viṣaya*) as the "tactile agent" (*spraṣṭṛ*) and the sense organ (*indriya*) as the "object of touch" (*spraṣṭavya*), speaking from the perspective of a single aspect of cognition:

one must take the sense organ as the "cognizer" (*jñātṛ*) and the object as the "known" (*jñeya*). Thus, that which is called the "tactile agent" necessarily belongs to the category of the non-cognitive, while that which is called the "object of touch" necessarily belongs to the category of the cognitive.
However, that which is the "object of touch" is precisely the cognizer, and that which is the "tactile agent" is precisely...
Because it is that which is known, it is called "this" (the object) as that which is known. Who is the one that acts as the agent of contact?
If either one is missing, both are not established; that is to say, a single sense organ does not stand alone, and a solitary object does not arise.

Therefore, above the phrase "each having its own," if there were only an object capable of being contacted, contact would certainly not be established. Below the phrase "each having its own," if there were only a single sense organ that performs the contacting...

Furthermore, since contact is not established, it is said that space should not enter into contact with you. "That which is produced by a single contact" refers to the opposite of the two aforementioned types of contact.
It is like saying, "My hand and my head"—it simply requires the establishment of a single contact. Its substance is precisely awareness (*jñāna*). It exists; it is present; it is not non-existent.
It exists as the subject (*grāhaka*), not as the object (*grāhya*); it points to the knower, not the known. It exists as the locus, not as... [the object].
"Capable. This refers to that which is touched and that which touches.
[Commentary: This clarifies that the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

Generally, touch necessarily arises through the union of the sense organ and its object, the subject and the object, the sentient and the insentient, and through their mutual resonance—whether through contact or separation, opposition or conformity. Yet here, it is treated as a singular entity.
The clarity of the body and its contact [with objects] truly reveal that the myriad phenomena are of one essence, fundamentally devoid of subject and object;

their union and separation are merely matters of circumstance, yet through the obstruction of sensory dust, they are falsely perceived as existing. Therefore, the World-Honored One confirmed for Ānanda, saying:
"I have constantly instructed my disciples to rub their heads three times a day. Since you practice according to this dharma, you should regularly do so at dawn."
He rubs his head with his hand. At the moment of this rubbing, that which knows [the sensation] should be called the "capable toucher.
Whom do you take to be the capable toucher? Does this capable toucher reside in the hand, or does it reside in the head?
If you say the capable toucher resides in the hand, then the hand is a sense-object devoid of cognition. Yet, the hand and the head belong to only one person—yourself.
Since the hand is already considered an insentient object, the head should likewise be insentient.
In that case, there would only be the "object" (dust) that touches, while the "organ" (root) that is touched would not exist; how, then, could contact be established?

If you claim that the one who touches resides in the head, then the head too is an insentient object. Furthermore, since both the head and the hand belong to your single body, [how can they be distinct]...?

If the head were to be considered the insentient [object], then the hand would likewise be useless. Furthermore, there would only be the object that can be touched, and necessarily no faculty that touches it;
thus, these would all be solitary objects that do not arise. How, then, could contact be established? Or perhaps you argue:
"When the hand touches the head, the hand can be the subject that touches and the head can be the object that is touched. But how could this be?
It is not that the hand lacks consciousness while the head possesses it. When the head touches the hand, the head can be considered the agent of touching and the hand the object touched.
Is it not then the case that the head lacks consciousness while the hand possesses it? What would fail to be established here?
Therefore, he refutes this, saying: "If your head and hand each possessed consciousness, and yet each also lacked consciousness..."
If there is one consciousness, it constitutes a single body; if there is one insentient part, it becomes a single particle.
In that case, Ānanda, you should have two bodies, and you should experience two sensations of touch. Alternatively, he might attempt to defend against this previous fault by saying:
"Although each has its own head and hand, they constitute only a single sensation of touch. Therefore, he again rebuts him, saying: "If the head and the hand were a single sensation of touch..."
If [the hand and head] were produced as one, then the hand and the head would have to be a single entity. If they were a single entity, there would be only a single cognition;
thus, where there is necessarily only the sense organ that is touched, there could not possibly be the object that touches.

Alternatively, if one attempts to rescue this position from its error by claiming they are indeed two entities, one further refutes it by saying: "If they are two entities, even if there were two cognitions, who would be the agent?"

As for the object of touch, where does it currently reside? It is simply that these two types of cognition exist only in the location of the faculty that knows, not in the location of the object known;
they exist only in the location of the faculty that is touched, not in the location of the object that touches.
Since neither of them can be established as a single independent entity, how could contact be formed? One should not take empty space to be the agent of contact.
The object of touch, together with your body-faculty, constitutes the emptiness of touch; furthermore, it is not an object belonging to the body.
One can see that, ultimately, there is no place where the object of touch exists. Since the object is non-existent, the faculty likewise does not exist.
Therefore, the conclusion below returns to the true nature as previously described.
"Ānanda, that which you constantly take as the objects of your mental consciousness—whether good or evil—is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
[Commentary: This clarifies that the dharma-object (dharmāyatana) is precisely the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. The dharma-object refers to the five preceding sensory objects.
Setting aside the reflected image, it is divided into the objective marks that serve as the objects of the mental faculty (*manas*).

These faculties and their objects must necessarily arise in dependence upon causes and conditions. Therefore, Ānanda was questioned: "The objects you habitually perceive within the mental faculty—must they not be either wholesome, or certainly unwholesome?
If they are neither distinguished as wholesome nor unwholesome, they must certainly be of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Thus he spoke.
Good, evil, and pure-defiled are dharmas; the indeterminate is a dharma of dull stagnation. These constitute the track for the generation and completion [of phenomena].
Apart from these three natures, no objective dharma-dust (*dharmaraja*) can be found. As for such dharma-dust:
does it arise from your own mental faculty (*manas*), or does it exist separately outside the mental faculty in some other direction or location? If you say that this dharma...
If the sense-object (*viṣaya*) were identical to the mental faculty (*manas*), then this phenomenon would not belong to the sense-objects.
Since it does not belong to the sense-objects, it certainly cannot be an object of cognition for the mental faculty. How, then, can it be called a locus for the mind’s engagement?

If one were to claim that this phenomenon as a sense-object exists apart from the mental faculty in a specific direction or location, then does the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that phenomenon-object actually possess cognition? Indeed...
Is it devoid of cognition? If it truly possesses cognition, it ought to be called the mind (*citta*) rather than an object (*viṣaya*).
How could it be anything less than not being called an object? If it were to exist apart from the mind in a distinct location, then this object would be different from you;

furthermore, since it possesses cognition, it would not be a dharma-object (*dharmaviṣaya*), but would resemble the faculty of the mental organ (*manas-indriya*), which is also not your dharma-object.
This would then be the same as the mental capacity (*citta-pramāṇa*) of another person; what business is that of yours?

If you must insist that although it has a separate location and is not an external object (*viṣaya*), it certainly does not enter the mental capacity of another, but is instead yours—your very own mind—then why does your mind not unite with you, but instead acts in opposition and further separates from you?
Is this so? Is there such a principle? It is a delusion to claim that one can perceive the mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) as having cognition apart from the faculty of mind (*manas*).
If you say that these mental objects exist apart from the mind and lack cognition, then they would be like insentient things in the world.
All these belong to the first five sense objects (*viṣaya*). Now, each of the first five sense objects corresponds to one of the first five sense organs (*indriya*).
Since this [sixth] object is apart from the five sense objects and external space, where could it possibly reside? It is not indicated anywhere within form or emptiness. It cannot be among humans;
nor can there be another place outside of emptiness where the mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*) dwells. Since the mental object...
If there is no locus, then the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) likewise has no object of perception (*ālambana*).
Since the faculty has no locus for its object, from what could the name "faculty" be established? Therefore, the conclusion below returns to the true nature, following the previous principle.
The term "mind" (*citta*) here refers exclusively to the mental faculty; these two are not one. One must not follow those who speak of two minds.
The following clarifies that the eighteen realms (*dhātus*) are the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

"Eighteen" refers to the six sense organs (*indriyas*), the six objects (*viṣayas*), and the six consciousnesses (*vijñānas*), which together constitute the number eighteen. "Realm" (*dhātu*) means a boundary or limit; it signifies that the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses—
There is only the single true nature; however, because false discrimination arises, boundaries are established.
That which acts as the perceiver is called the "element of the sense faculty" (indriya-dhātu); that which is the perceived object is called the "element of the sense field" (viṣaya-dhātu);

and that which is able to discern between the faculty and the field is called the "element of consciousness" (vijñāna-dhātu). Since the actual refutation below targets consciousness, the eighteen elements are mentioned for this reason.

When the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) is established, the faculties and their objects manifest in mutual dependence; when the element of consciousness is not established, the faculties and their objects are mutually quiescent.

For this reason, one does not destroy the consciousness itself, but rather destroys its "element. This is because once the boundaries of the elements are dissolved, consciousness, the faculties, and the objects do not require further conjunction to become one with the true nature.
Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the eighteen *dhātus*? [This continues] until: "they are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
**Commentary:** This clarifies that the six consciousnesses are themselves the *tathāgatagarbha*. First, there is a general inquiry; subsequently, there is a detailed explanation.
Wishing to break down Ānanda’s conception of the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*), [the Buddha] first challenged him with a dialectical inquiry regarding what he himself understood:
"According to your ordinary understanding, the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) serves as a condition for form (*rūpa*), and consciousness arises therein.
Does this consciousness arise because of the eye? Is the eye the element of that consciousness? Or does it arise because of form? Is form..."
Is it the element of consciousness? If you claim that this consciousness is produced by the eye, then the single sense organ would be able to produce its own consciousness.
However, consciousness has discernment as its nature; since there is neither form nor space, and only the eye-organ exists, even if your consciousness were produced, what would you use it for?
Therefore, your calculation that the eye can produce consciousness is false. If you claim that it is through seeing...
The sense faculties serve as the boundaries for consciousness. Your seeing is not a color such as blue or yellow; it is fundamentally invisible.
Since there is no formal characteristic of color by which it can be represented, even if your consciousness exists, from what object would the boundary of that consciousness be established?
Thus, the calculation that the consciousness-element (vijñānadhātu) is established based on the eye is false. If you claim that this consciousness arises because of color...

Regarding that which is produced by dust (sensory objects): it is the unique object alone that can produce its corresponding consciousness. Now, consciousness has the nature of discernment (*vijñapti*).
If this consciousness discerns emptiness and the absence of form, then since the form that could have produced it has already ceased, the consciousness produced by it should likewise cease.
Since it would have ceased along with the form, how could the consciousness know that this is the nature of emptiness rather than the nature of form?
Since one has already realized that emptiness is not the nature of form, then even when form ceases, consciousness has never ceased.

Thus, it is evident that the calculation that form can produce consciousness is false. If one were to claim that form serves as the boundary for consciousness, then consciousness and form—[must necessarily be...]

It would be appropriate for them to be eternally inseparable. If, when matter changes, your consciousness also perceives that the characteristics of matter are undergoing transition, then matter would be transitioning while consciousness remains non-transient.

Even if consciousness were to exist in isolation, since there would no longer be a counterpart to define the boundaries of your consciousness, from what phenomenon could it be established? Or perhaps you might attempt to rescue your previous position by saying: "If, when matter changes, consciousness..."
Furthermore, since [the object] departs by changing its form, one might as well establish the realm (*dhātu*) based on that form itself. Therefore, he refutes this, saying:
"If it depends on change, then the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the realm of consciousness would naturally not exist; who then could establish the realm based on form?

If one were to argue that both form and consciousness remain unchanged, then the realm of consciousness could indeed be established based on form. Yet, one fails to realize that even if both remain unchanged—
Then the two entities would exist eternally. Since this consciousness arises from form, it would likewise be devoid of cognition;

it should not be able to discern the location of empty space. If it does not know the location of space, it would also not know the location of form. Under such circumstances, upon what basis could the "element of consciousness" (vijñānadhātu) be established?
To calculate that the element of consciousness is established from form is therefore erroneous. If one were to claim that [consciousness] arises from the single sense organ alone...
If you claim that an object cannot produce consciousness alone, but must do so in conjunction with both the eye and the form,

does this arise from the eye and form being joined together, or from them being separated? If you say that the eye and form are joined as one place such that there is no intervening space between them,
then even if a consciousness were produced, it would have to perceive by remaining outside of that middle position.

The characteristics of the elements (*dhātu*) do not exist in themselves. If one were to claim that the eye and form exist separately in two locations, then even the consciousness produced from them would necessarily be divided between the two sides:
half would be conjoined with the eye and half would be conjoined with form. Thus, the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of consciousness would be disordered;
how could it constitute the element of consciousness? If the two are conjoined, there is disorder; if they are separated in the middle, there is no locus.
If the element of consciousness were originally non-existent, then the eye and form would likewise have no locus. Therefore, it is concluded:
"For this reason, you should know that regarding what you claim—the eye and form as conditions giving rise to eye-consciousness—there is no boundary whatsoever among these three locations.
Thus, since there is no boundary among the three locations of the eye, form, and the consciousness that cognizes form, one knows them to be illusory."
Regarding their characteristics: their nature is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous; it is the wondrous True Suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Ānanda, as you have understood, the ear and sound serve as conditions [and so forth, until] their nature is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous.
Commentary: This clarifies that the auditory consciousness is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

However, addressing Ānanda based on what he already understands, [the Buddha] interrogates and examines him, saying: "Furthermore, regarding the faculty of hearing which you habitually understand—that which serves as the condition for the sense-object of sound—"
And consciousness arises within it. Is this consciousness produced by the ear-faculty, with the ear-faculty serving as its boundary?
Or is it produced by the auditory object, with the auditory object serving as its boundary?
If it is claimed that this consciousness arises because of the ear, then this would mean that the sense organ alone acts as the producer.
This, however, fails to realize that when the two objects—motion and stillness—are not present before it, the ultimate sense organ cannot constitute cognition.
Thus, if there is necessarily no object to be known, the organ capable of knowing it likewise does not exist; how much less can one claim that the organ produces consciousness?

From what, then, does the form and appearance of consciousness arise? If both the faculty (*indriya*) and the consciousness were non-existent, then the calculation that consciousness arises from the hearing-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), taking the hearing-faculty as its boundary (*dhātu*), would all be false.

If you must insist on saying: "The ultimate faculty (*paramārtha-indriya*) has no form, and therefore it cannot serve as the boundary for consciousness; however, the physical faculty (*ābhāsa-indriya*) does have form—why should it not be so? then [the text] restates the previous argument, saying: [The passage continues: "If the ultimate faculty has no form, it cannot be the boundary for consciousness. But the physical faculty has form; why should it not be so? Thus, the preceding text is cited: "Furthermore, if the ultimate faculty has no form, it cannot be the boundary for consciousness. How much less so for the physical faculty! If one says, 'The ultimate faculty has no form, and thus it cannot be the boundary for consciousness; the physical faculty has form, so why should it not be so? then this is refuted by the following: If the ultimate faculty has no form, it cannot be the boundary for consciousness. How much less so for the physical faculty! Thus, the text reiterates the prior point to demonstrate the error in such an argument.
If one takes the nature of hearing within the ear, since there are no two objects [of sound], then this very nature of hearing is likewise not established.

How then could one further take the physical ear-organ as the boundary for consciousness? For although the physical ear has the form of an ear, it is a color-form (rūpa-lakṣaṇa) belonging to the body-organ (kāya-indriya).
Since the organ belongs to the body, its object must be the tangible (spraṣṭavya), and certainly not the audible (śabda). This is certain.
This establishes the sphere; it is called the body-consciousness sphere (*kāyavijñānadhātu*). Then, from what is the ear-consciousness sphere established?

It is incorrect to reckon that the physical sense organ (*mūlindriya*) constitutes the consciousness sphere. If you claim that this consciousness arises from the object of sound (*śabdaviṣaya*), [then...]

If this [consciousness] arises solely because of sound, then it has no connection with the faculty of hearing. How could one know that if the faculty of hearing were absent, the characteristic of sound would also perish?
Since the sound capable of producing [consciousness] does not exist, the calculation that consciousness is produced from sound is incorrect.

If you claim that consciousness takes sound as its objective field (*viṣaya*), then even if you grant that consciousness arises from sound, you must further grant that it depends upon the faculty of hearing.
If there were a characteristic of sound, then when the sense organ hears a sound, it should hear it together with consciousness.
If consciousness is not heard, then consciousness and sound have not yet been differentiated; they would still be nothing more than a single auditory object—how then could there be "consciousness"?

If one claims that at the time of hearing sound, one actually hears its consciousness, then consciousness, like the sound, would become an external object. Since consciousness [would thus be externalized]...
Externally, it has already been heard by the ear; yet, who is it that knows this hearing? Could there be two knowers within a single body?
If you claim that there is no further knower who knows, hears, and perceives, then [who is] your own self?
In the end, it is like grass and trees. Why? Because there is only a single cognition, which has already become an external object.
For if there were knowing, hearing, and consciousness, there ought to be two cognitions; yet "not-knowing" and "hearing-consciousness" constitute a single cognition—is this not illogical?

Thus, the calculation that the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*) is established based on sound is false. Since neither the sense organ alone can produce [cognition] nor the object alone can emerge, [consciousness cannot arise].
The auditory faculty and the sound-objects should not intermingle to form a middle realm.
For if they are already intermingled, then a middle position does not exist. It is only when there is a middle position that one can distinguish between "inner" and "outer.
Now, if there is no middle realm, from what realm could the two characteristics of inner and outer arise? Concluding the argument, it says: "Therefore, one should know that..."
If you claim that the ear and sound serve as conditions to produce auditory consciousness, there is no boundary whatsoever among these three locations.

From this it can be known that the organ, the object, and the consciousness are all illusory and false manifestations; their nature is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous, but is fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified—that the nose and fragrance serve as conditions (up to the point that they are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature)—the marginal note states:
"This clarifies that the nose-consciousness is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. The meaning is that the sense organ and the object serve as conditions.
Yet consciousness arises within them; this, Ānanda, you have long understood. Therefore, I question you:
does this nose-consciousness arise because of the nose-faculty, taking the nose as the realm of consciousness?
Or does it arise because of the fragrance-object, taking the fragrance-object as the realm of consciousness? If you say that this consciousness arises because of the nose-faculty...
Then, by what do you define the nose-faculty? Do you take the physical form of the fleshly organ—the appearance like two melons—to be the nose?
Or do you take the supreme faculty (paramārtha-indriya), which is the nature of vibration that perceives through smelling, to be the nose? If you take the physical form of the flesh, [then...]

Thus, the substance of the flesh belongs to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), not the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*). Since the faculty that produces [consciousness] does not exist, how could the consciousness produced by it exist?
Therefore, the calculation that consciousness is produced from the "floating root" (the physical organ) is incorrect.

If one were to claim that the floating root constitutes the boundary of consciousness such that it is the knower, then that which knows would be touch (*spraṣṭavya*) rather than odor (*gandha*), and the body would be the knower rather than the nose.

Since the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are already designated as "bodies" (*kāya*), they cannot possibly be the nose-faculty. Since the objects (*viṣaya*) are already designated as "touch," they are the object-field of the body.

When even the nose itself lacks a name [in this context], how can the nose be the constituent element (*dhātu*) of consciousness? It is incorrect to reckon the floating root (*tūla-kośa*) as the constituent element of consciousness.
If you take the nature of that which knows by smelling to be the nose-faculty, then by what means do you know it? If you say...

If the physical form of the flesh constitutes cognition, then that which is known by the flesh must fundamentally be what is known by the sense-object of touch; it belongs to touch and not to fragrance.

Consequently, the cognizer must belong to the body and not to the nose. If you claim that the space within the nose constitutes cognition, then space would be cognizing itself, and the flesh would be devoid of sensation.
In that case, space would be your cognition, and your body would not be your cognition.
Today Ānanda should not exist anywhere. If that were so, even the knowledge through smelling would not exist;

from what object, then, would consciousness arise? Or perhaps he might further argue: "Setting aside the knowledge of the flesh and the knowledge of space, there is currently the ability to know fragrance—is this not knowledge?
Thus, one takes fragrance as the knowledge, and since knowledge belongs to the fragrance itself, what concern is it of yours? Or...

To rectify the previous error, he said: "It is not that fragrance constitutes cognition; rather, fragrance is manifested through cognition. If it were not for the act of smelling and cognizing, what would fragrance even be?

Furthermore, if fragrance arises because of cognition, then if the two gases of fragrance and stench were necessarily produced within your nose, they would not have to arise from the *eranda* (Ilan) and sandalwood trees respectively. If those two objects did not come [to you], [the scents would not be perceived]."
Do you yourself smell the fragrance of your own nose? Is it foul? If the nose itself were foul, it could not perceive its own foulness;
if the nose itself were fragrant, it could not perceive its own fragrance. How could there be a faculty of the nose that does not know fragrance and foulness?
If the nose can perceive fragrance and foulness, yet these two qualities are...
Regarding the consciousness that discerns [taste]: when the five flavors, such as those of sugarcane and so forth, are entirely absent, do you yourself taste your own tongue as sweet or as bitter?
If you claim that the nature of the tongue is bitter, then your tongue-organ itself has already become the flavor of bitterness;
who then comes to taste the tongue? If the tongue cannot taste itself, then what is it that perceives? And yet, you claim that the tongue is bitter.
As for taste: since there is no cognition, the tongue-faculty itself does not yet exist. To calculate that the faculty can produce consciousness—is this not an error?
If you claim that the nature of the tongue is not bitter, then flavor will not arise on the tongue of its own accord; and if there is no object of flavor, [how can there be cognition?]

In that case, the tongue-faculty (jihvendriya) would also not exist. How then could the elements (dhātu) be established based on the faculty? It is a delusion to reckon that the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) is established from the tongue-faculty.
If one were to claim that this consciousness arises solely because of flavor (rasa), then it would follow that flavor exists independently of the tongue-faculty.
Within the sensory dust, a consciousness that discriminates arises spontaneously. However, since this consciousness is produced by taste and thus constitutes taste itself, it cannot experience taste;
it is just like the tongue-faculty, which cannot taste itself. Since it cannot experience it, how can it recognize whether something is a flavor or not?
Not only this: since the tastes capable of producing it are manifold, that which is produced...

This consciousness should likewise consist of multiple entities. If one were to claim that the essence of consciousness is a single entity yet must arise in dependence upon multiple flavors, then it would mean that many flavors collectively produce a single consciousness.
In that case, when the five flavors are blended together to become a single flavor, this tongue-consciousness should have no discrimination.
Why? Because the essence of consciousness originally possesses all the flavors—salty... [and so forth].
Consciousness does not know the taste of salt; likewise, up to the consciousness of pungency, it does not know the taste of pungency.
Therefore, since such discrimination is absent, it cannot be called "consciousness. Since consciousness has no name, what kind of thing could it be that arises from taste?

Not only can the object of taste (rasa-āyatana) not produce consciousness, but since consciousness lacks even the name "consciousness," how can it further be called the tongue-faculty (jihvendriya) or the object of taste?
Since there are neither faculties nor objects, from what substance could the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) possibly be established?
It cannot be that empty space gives rise to your conscious mind and then demarcates its boundaries from that consciousness.

Not only do the individual faculties and solitary objects fail to produce it and fail to constitute the element, but even the union of the tongue and flavors cannot produce it. Why is this? Because the faculty...
Although the objects are two, since they have merged into one, their dual nature is fundamentally non-existent. How could there be any space for consciousness to arise within them?
Furthermore, why establish "realms" (*dhātu*) based on sense organs and objects? The conclusion below summarizes this, saying: "Therefore, you should know."

If you claim that the tongue and flavors serve as conditions to produce tongue-consciousness, then since there are no boundaries among these three locations, you must know that the tongue, the flavors, and the tongue-consciousness are all illusory and false manifestations. Their nature is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous;
it is fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. Regarding the old explanation of "conjunction," it refers to the collective formation of various flavors.
That which is innate is its unchanging fundamental nature. That which is transformed is the altered flavor produced by roasting or boiling.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified—that the body and touch serve as conditions [for tactile consciousness]—it is fundamentally neither a causal condition nor a spontaneous nature.
Commentary: This clarifies that bodily consciousness is precisely the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. The meaning is as follows: bodily consciousness arises with bodily contact as its condition;
this is something Ānanda already understands well. Therefore, [the Buddha] interrogates him regarding that which he clearly knows, asking:
"Does this consciousness arise from the faculty of the body? Or does it take the faculty of the body as its boundary?"
Is it produced because of the sense-object of touch? Or does it take the sense-object of touch as the boundary of consciousness?
If you claim that this consciousness is produced because of the body, then as long as there is only your body, there can certainly be no two kinds of tactile objects—namely, contact and separation.

In that case, although the body-faculty exists which is capable of sensation and observation, there would be no objective conditions for such sensation and observation; thus, even if bodily consciousness were to arise, it would be without an object.
What is it that is cognized? To reckon that the sense organs can produce consciousness is incorrect.

If you claim that this consciousness arises because of contact, then there would be only the object of contact and necessarily no "you" as a body. Even though there are two kinds of contact-objects—union and separation—who would be there to know them?
How could one who lacks a body be able to know union and separation? You reckon that contact can produce consciousness.

This is incorrect. If one claims that this consciousness is delimited by the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), one fails to realize that the organs and objects themselves have no inherent delimitation.
Why is this? A mere object does not know contact; it must await the cognition of the body before contact is established. A mere body cannot cognize;
it must await the presence of contact before cognition is established. Thus, that which possesses the knowledge of the body is...
One knows through contact; it is not that the body knows by itself. That there is contact is because contact occurs in dependence upon the body;
it is not that contact touches itself. Since one knows that the body is precisely contact, then the body has no independent existence.
Since one knows that contact is identical to the body, then contact has no location. For the two characteristics of body and contact are fundamentally without a place of abode;

from what object could the boundaries of consciousness be established? Not only can a single faculty or a solitary object not produce consciousness, nor can they serve as its boundary, but even when the faculty and object are joined, it is likewise so. If it is contact...
When conjoined with the body, it constitutes the very self-nature of the body, and no further object is perceived; thus, external objects are not established.
If the body were separated from touch, it would be like the nature of empty space, and no further cognition would be perceived; thus, the internal sense-faculty is not established.
Since both the internal and external are not established, how could a middle [consciousness] be posited? This is the absence of sense-faculties and objects, along with consciousness.

Nor does it exist within; it is not established therein. Since internal and external natures are empty, there is no substance to consciousness. When the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are both dissolved, all three lack substance.
How then can the elements (*dhātu*) be differentiated? It is a delusion to reckon that consciousness arises from the conjunction of the faculty and the object.

The conclusion summarizes this, saying: "Therefore, you should know that regarding what you claim—consciousness of the body arising with the contact of the body as a condition—the three [factors] do not [exist]."
By defining these boundaries, one knows that both bodily contact and the consciousness of the body are all illusory and false manifestations.
Their nature is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously; it is fundamentally the wondrous True Suchness of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified—that the mind and dharmas serve as conditions (up to:

they are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature)—the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma does not depart from the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional. This extends fully from the five aggregates to the eighteen realms.

The emphasis lies in refuting both causes-and-conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*), thereby clarifying that all worldly phenomena are like flowers in the sky or bubbles and reflections;

it solely reveals the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the *tathāgatagarbha*. The latter seven sections are complete, their emphasis lying in refuting both conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and non-conjunction, thereby clarifying that all worldly phenomena do not move even a hair’s breadth, each and every one being as they are; this solely reveals the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Contemplate the Tathāgatagarbha. Even in the later passages, which speak of being "neither identical nor different," and "both identical and non-identical," it further reveals that the ultimate and the conventional are both identical and non-identical, leading ultimately to the unimpeded interpenetration of all phenomena (*śaśva-vastu-asangata*).

This is because the ultimate truth is subsumed within the single nature, while the conventional truth pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Due to this single nature, all phenomena are gathered back into principle; due to its pervasive nature, [all phenomena] are universally present.

When principle is integrated with phenomena, and principle and phenomena are perfectly interfused such that the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual, then there are no objects apart from the mind, and no mind apart from objects.
When the mind arises in contact with objects, there is nothing that is not the wondrous nature. How could there be a Tathāgatagarbha existing separately from the sense organs and their objects?
This is the great purport of the thorough integration of the ultimate and the conventional within the three categories and seven elements.
Commentary: This clarifies that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
However, taking what Ānanda has explained as the basis for inquiry, [the Buddha] questions him: "As for this mental consciousness, is it produced by the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*)?
Is the faculty of mind the boundary of this consciousness? Or is it produced by mental objects (*dharmadhātu*)? Is the mental object the boundary of this consciousness?"

Yes. If you claim that this consciousness arises because of the mental faculty (*manas*), then within that mental faculty there must necessarily be an object of thought (*dharma-viṣaya*) before the thinking mental faculty can manifest its activity.

Without the previously thought object of thought, the mental faculty would likewise have nothing from which to arise. Once separated from the object of thought upon which it depends, the mental faculty—

Furthermore, no form or appearance can be apprehended. Even if consciousness were to exist, what use would it be? Is it not also erroneous to calculate that consciousness arises from the mental faculty (*manas*)?
If you take the mental faculty to be the boundary of consciousness, then as for what you call the "conscious mind," it is merely capable of discernment;
and as for what is called the "mental faculty," it takes the *manas* as its root. Therefore...

It is capable of both deliberation and discernment. If you claim that consciousness (vijñāna) and the mind (citta), together with the faculty of intellect (manas), take discernment as their intrinsic nature, yet further distinguish between that which produces and that which is produced, are these then identical or are they different?
If consciousness were identical to the faculty of intellect, then consciousness would simply be the faculty of intellect; how then could one say that the intellect is the producer?
Consciousness is that which is produced. If consciousness were distinct from the mind-faculty (manas), then consciousness would be devoid of cognition and would have nothing to perceive.
If there were nothing to perceive, it would not be of the same category [as the mind]; how then could it be said to be produced by the mind-faculty?
If there is something perceived, yet no mental objects (dharmas) exist, what is it that is perceived? It would simply be a matter of consciousness turning back to perceive the mind-faculty itself.
Consider this: does such a principle exist? It cannot be established if [consciousness] is identical [to the mind], nor can it be established if it is different.
That consciousness is not produced from the mind is certainly beyond doubt. To claim that the mind serves as the "boundary" (dhātu) for consciousness is likewise incorrect.

If you claim that this consciousness arises because of mental objects (*dharmas*), then all phenomena in the world are not apart from the five sensory objects; beyond these, there is not a single phenomenon that exists.
It can be known. At present, the five sense objects each have their own distinct characteristics, clearly manifest and perceived by their respective five sense organs;

none of them are subsumed under the mental faculty (*manas*). If you claim that your consciousness arises solely and determinately based upon the dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*), [you must explain this].
This does not interfere with the sense faculties. Now, observe closely the characteristics of the dharma-object (dharmāyatana). What is its form?

If its form resembles that of visible matter (rūpa), it is called the object of visible matter and is not called the dharma-object. This continues until: if it resembles that of tangibility (spraṣṭavya), it is called the object of tangibility.

It is not called a mental object (*dharmāyatana*). If none of these resemble [the external], then apart from these characteristics of form and emptiness, up to and including arising and ceasing, no external shape can be apprehended.
Or perhaps one might insist that this arising and ceasing is itself the mental object; is it not indeed a shape?
Yet you fail to realize that arising is the production of the shadow-aspect of all phenomena such as form and emptiness, while ceasing is...
This emptiness of form is the cessation of the reflected images of all phenomena; apart from the five sense objects, there is nothing else that can be found as subject to arising and ceasing.
Since the dharma-objects (dharma-viṣaya) which serve as their cause have no substantial form of their own, what form could the consciousness produced by those dharma-objects possibly have?
Since the characteristics of consciousness themselves do not exist, how can it be said that it is produced by dharma-objects, or that it is established by means of dharmas?

[The text asks: "Is it the realm? The conclusion below returns to this point, saying: "Therefore, you should know that as for your claim that mental objects serve as conditions to give rise to mental consciousness, these three have no boundaries.
Thus, one knows that the mental faculty, the mental objects, and mental consciousness are fundamentally without arising or ceasing;
they are merely illusory and false designations. Their nature is neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous; it is fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha."
Furthermore, the two lines beginning with "But merely by means of appearances" refute the boundaries [of the sense organs]. There is also no textual passage for reconciling or distinguishing them;

this precisely reveals that the illusory falsity of the mental faculty (*manas*) and its objects (*dharmas*) is extreme. Moreover, this cannot be analogized to the five preceding faculties and their objects, whose essential natures consist of real *bhāga* (parts) and *viṣaya* (objects).
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often spoken of the Middle Way, the definitive meaning, and the dharma free from conceptual proliferation.

This was Ānanda grasping at the illusory appearances of the world; he took them to be produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions, whereas they are in fact only the wondrous nature of awakening, not produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions.
He perceived these as two extremes and failed to realize the principle that nature and appearance are non-dual. Therefore, World-Honored One...
To clarify the seven great elements, we first demonstrate their nature and characteristics: they are neither conjoined nor non-conjoined. The meaning is this:
if they were conjoined, their nature would be identical to birth and death; if they were not conjoined, then nature and characteristics would be two separate things.
Thus, both conjunction and non-conjunction are denied because their nature is like water and their characteristics are like ice—just as when water forms [ice].
Ice merely returns to being water again.
(Commentary) This takes the provisional and conflates it with the ultimate, raising once more the question of the causes and conditions of harmonious integration.
Ānanda’s intention was to say: "The World-Honored One previously stated that the wondrous clarity of essential awareness is neither caused nor uncaused, neither integrated nor non-integrated."

[The interlocutor] agrees. Furthermore, it is taught that [all things] are called "phantasms" because they are false and illusory, and that they are born falsely through combination and die falsely through combination.
This refers to the true nature of the subtle, wondrous, and luminous awareness, which fundamentally is neither a combination of causes and conditions nor something spontaneous;
yet the illusory appearances of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are certainly subject to the combination of causes and conditions. Moreover, all that the Tathāgata has commonly taught...

Regarding the meaning of the conjunction of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*): as it is said, "The various transformative appearances of all worlds are all manifested through the conjunction of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Is this not to say that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) likewise appear in the world through the conjunction of causes and conditions?
If one were to claim they arise spontaneously (*svabhāva*), one may dismiss such a view by saying, "It is not the true teaching. This is the principle of causes and conditions.
“Harmony (*saṃghāta*) is precisely the True Dharma spoken of in the past.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata now cast aside both ‘causality’ (*hetu-pratyaya*) and ‘spontaneity’ (*svabhāva*)? I truly do not understand the underlying intent behind this rejection.
Previously, we were instructed by the Tathāgata that what we call ‘causal harmony’ is merely a conventional designation born of worldly conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).”
This is not the true nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Thus, worldly names and characteristics and the ultimate truth appear to belong to two separate sides;
this is certainly not the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) and does not transcend conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), ultimately failing to provide a definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
We pray that you will compassionately grant instruction to sentient beings regarding the Middle Way, the definitive meaning, and the dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda... (until) Ānanda remained silent, accepting the Buddha’s holy command. *Commentary*:
This reproaches Ānanda for his delusion and parsimony while granting him instruction. It says:

"Previously, because you were constrained by the power of Māra, you felt weary of and detached from the various Hinayana teachings you had heard; thus, you resolved to diligently seek the [Mahayana]."
To attain supreme enlightenment. Therefore, I now reveal the ultimate truth for your sake.

The reason I reject the conjunction of causes and conditions is precisely to cause you all to abandon the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of the Lesser Vehicle and to grasp the definitive meaning of the Middle Way.
Why, then, do you again rely upon worldly conceptual proliferations and deluded thoughts regarding causes and conditions?
Entangled. Now I observe you: though you claim to be learned, you are merely able to feel weary detachment yet unable to let go;
you are merely able to strive in pursuit yet unable to recognize and grasp [the truth]. You are like worldly people who can merely speak of medicines but do not actually know their natures;
even when presented with the genuine medicine before them, they are not only unable to distinguish the real from the false.
Moreover, you have instead produced a state of stagnation and rejection; is this not deeply pitiable?

For the Middle Way of definitive meaning that you inquire about—the dharma free from conceptual proliferation—is precisely the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Mahāyāna, and not the provisional teaching of the Hīnayāna.
Yet, this true reality does not depart from the various transformed phenomena such as the four great elements; it is only through delusion regarding them that one ultimately undergoes transformation.
An illusion. To awaken to it is the initial realization of reality; therefore, it is not something that can be reached by verbal explanations, nor is it a domain of discursive knowledge.

It is accessible only through the correspondence of direct realization. It is specifically because you all cling to and begrudge the provisional teachings that I shall provide you with skillful means to guide and instruct you.
However, this is not only for your sake, but also so that those who will practice the Mahāyāna in the future may likewise attain it.
He thoroughly penetrates the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Ānanda remains silent, receiving the holy command.

○ "True reality" is the general designation for the three *tathāgatagarbhas*. Therefore, while it was previously called the "pure true reality," it is here called "thoroughly penetrating true reality" because it universally penetrates the three truths.

Ānanda, as you have said, from the "conjunction of the four great elements" up to "just as water becomes ice and ice returns to water," this should be clarified by using the analogy of empty space to illustrate the nature (*dhātu*) of the great elements, and the analogy of a whirling firebrand to illustrate their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the statement that "water and ice are of one essence and nature, like space, which does not mix with various forms" is a counter-statement used as an analogy for the preceding text.
It means: if one speaks of the essential substance of those great elements (*mahābhūta*), it does not intermingle with the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the various great elements;
this is similar to saying that space does not intermingle with various forms. This is so.
Is this not so? One should know that the nature of emptiness and the characteristics of form possess two meanings:

neither conjunction nor non-conjunction. "Neither conjunction" means the sense of immutability; "neither non-conjunction" means the sense of following conditions. This applies not only to empty space.
It is able to possess these two meanings. From the mountains, rivers, and great earth down to a single form or a single fragrance, all possess these two meanings.
If there were even one thing that did not possess these two meanings, then there would be some residual phenomenon outside of the mind, and true nature would not be all-pervasive.
If one uses empty space alone as a metaphor for the meaning of non-aggregation, then the nature of emptiness would conversely become...

Obstruction. If one does not understand that the nature of emptiness is omnipresent, please observe how the World-Honored One, in clarifying the general principle of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), first cites space as an analogy.
Thereafter, within each of the great sections, he repeatedly takes up this space to provide mutual illustration by way of comparison.
Furthermore, he places the element of space after earth, water, fire, and wind, [and then treats] the two great elements of sight and consciousness.

Previously, we also used the metaphor of digging a well to demonstrate that within the solid and firm appearance, the nature of emptiness is fully pervasive; how could this not be a state of integration?
Yet, one sees only the earth being excavated, while no emptiness is seen emerging—how, then, can this be called integration? Such is the nature of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*);
there is no need to speak further of the others. Furthermore, it is said: "If you do not awaken to the fact that those six elements are fundamentally the *tathāgatagarbha* nature..."
It is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unshakable; one should know it to be like the boundless, immovable void.
By observing this, one can clearly understand that the World-Honored One has used the analogy of space to clarify the nature of the great elements.

Furthermore, just as water forms ice and ice returns to water, so too is the nature of form true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness true form; even unto the nature of awareness being true emptiness. The nature...
The "True Awakening of Emptiness" (*kō-shingaku*) and other such terms all share the same essential intent as the passage in the *Prajñāpāramitā* stating, "Form is emptiness; emptiness is form";

they merely differ in their phrasing. This is not all. Even when it says, "like a whirling firebrand," although this is a metaphor for illusory appearances, the reality (*shin*) is also present therein.
Within the metaphor, there is only the single spark at the end of the staff, which has never wavered. It is also...

There is no characteristic of a circular wheel; rather, it is the turning force of a child’s hand that causes the false perception of a wheel. As soon as the hand ceases its motion, the wheel disappears.
Within the Dharma, there is only the single true nature, which has never undergone saṃsāra and possesses no characteristics of the various realms of existence.
It is through the provocation of delusion and karma that one falsely perceives these realms. Once delusion and karma are exhausted, the various realms vanish of their own accord.
There is none.
[Commentary on the Preface: This is a general clarification of the framework of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*). First, it restates what Ānanda previously said:
"You claim that the various phenomena of transformation in the world definitely belong to the four great elements, which combine and manifest. Only...
As for this wondrous enlightened nature, how could one fail to know that its essence and its characteristics are non-dual?

For this wondrous enlightened nature has never been separate from the natures of those great elements; it is simply that the essence is like the vast void, while the characteristics are like a whirling firebrand.
Ānanda, if you were to claim that the substance of those great elements is not a combination, then it would be unable to interact with the various great elements.
Their mutual intermingling is like what people say: that empty space does not mix with various forms.
Yet they do not realize that the nature of emptiness and the characteristics of form are fundamentally neither combined nor uncombined.

If one were to say that emptiness and form are not combined, it would be as if two objects were set against each other, each excluding the other; yet currently, there is emptiness within form, and there is form within emptiness.
Is this not a case of conjunction? If you say that space and form are conjoined, then when the characteristics of form perish, the nature of space should perish along with them;
yet now, while only form perishes, space has never perished—is this then conjunction? You should know that the same applies to the Great Nature (Mahābhūta).
If you claim it is not a conjunction, then it certainly does not manifest its characteristics in accordance with conditions. If you claim it is a conjunction...

As for "conjunction," it is also not the unchanging true nature; rather, it would be identical to all transformed phenomena, beginning from the start and ending at the conclusion, and proceeding from the end back to the start.

Where there is a beginning and an end, one proceeds from birth to death, and from death one continues again into birth, such that there are traces of continuity in birth, extending from birth to death, and from death continuing into birth. And...
Born again and again, dying again and again—like a whirling firebrand, how could there ever be a time of rest?
As for those great elements (*mahābhūta*), they originally had no beginning; how could they have an end? Having never been born from the start, how could they now undergo extinction?
Being fundamentally without movement, from what could they rest? All things that possess a beginning and an end, even down to birth and death, are all...
Illusory delusions are designated as "characteristics. Thus, they are like a whirling firebrand. Yet this essence and these characteristics are fundamentally not two distinct entities.

Essence is like water; characteristics are like ice. True nature, following the conditions of ignorance, illusorily manifests as the myriad phenomena, just as water freezes into ice due to cold vapors.
Illusory phenomena, following fundamental wisdom, melt back into the single essence, just as ice dissolves when encountering warm air.
It returns to becoming water; yet water and ice are fundamentally not two separate things. At the time of freezing, one falsely conceives of them as a composite;

at the time of melting, one falsely conceives of them as non-composite. To thus give rise to false discrimination regarding this single substance is to fail to realize that form is itself emptiness and emptiness is itself form.
"Observe the nature of earth: from being coarse as the great earth (up to) there being only words and no real meaning.
[Commentary: This clarifies that the earth-element is the *tathāgatagarbha* nature.

The intent is that you do not yet realize that the nature of earth is neither a composite nor a non-composite; you should therefore rely on what you previously heard regarding the analysis of form to clarify emptiness.
Reflect upon this repeatedly, and you will know it for yourself. Observe the nature of the earth element: in its coarse form it is the great earth; in its subtle form it is minute dust.
If one were to gradually break down and refine minute dust until reaching the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal), this would involve analyzing minute dust until reaching the ultimate atom.
Although it is called the ultimate atom, it still possesses the characteristics of spatial boundaries. If one were to further analyze these characteristics...
If it were divided into seven parts, the subtle atom would be almost exhausted; therefore, it is called the "proximate void" (paramāṇu).
If one were to further analyze this proximate void, it would be the nature of actual emptiness rather than the nature of earth. Ānanda, as for what you call "conjunction," if these proximate voids—
Once it has been analyzed into emptiness, you should know that empty space can still give rise to the appearance of form; only then can it be called a true characteristic of conjunction.

As for your current question—asking how the various transformative appearances of the world arise through conjunction—you should first observe this single *paramāṇu* (subtle atom): by the conjunction of how many instances of empty space does it exist?
Regarding that which exists: it should not be that atoms are reassembled from atoms; rather, they must necessarily be assembled from empty space.
Only then can it be called the "conjunction of empty space forming material characteristics.

If one cannot form matter by conjoining space, then it is clear that it is not through the conjunction of the four great elements that the characteristics of the four great elements are formed. Thus, the nature [of matter] is clarified.
Someone said: "Although emptiness cannot be synthesized to form a *paramāṇu*, a *paramāṇu* can be analyzed and dissolved into emptiness.
Is this not the case where color-form (*rūpa*) is combined to produce emptiness? Therefore, [the Master] refutes it, saying:

Furthermore, as for the analysis of a *paramāṇu* into emptiness, this is merely called "analyzing color-form to produce emptiness," not "combining color-form to produce emptiness. This must necessarily involve several instances of color-form.
Only by synthesizing them into a single void can it be called "combined form" that constitutes the void.

If one cannot combine form to produce the void, then it is clear that this is not the characteristic of the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), but rather the nature of the four great elements themselves.
Therefore, to clarify the correct principle, it is said: "If at the time of the union of form, it were originally just the union of form, how [could it be otherwise]?"
One might be able to combine form to produce emptiness; yet, when emptiness is combined, it is fundamentally the combining of emptiness—how then could it combine emptiness to produce form?
If form can still be analyzed and dissolved into empty space, how could emptiness be combined to form the characteristics of matter?
However, you merely know that one cannot combine emptiness to produce form, nor combine form to produce emptiness; you do not realize that these are produced through the nature of combination itself.

Characteristics do not constitute their nature through combination. You fundamentally do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Now, as for "the nature of form," it means that nature and characteristics are non-dual.
If one realizes that the characteristic of form is itself the true nature, then this is "form being identical to emptiness"; therefore, it is called "true emptiness. And...
