I only pray that the Tathāgata will proclaim the secret intent and disseminate his great compassion, so that the clouds of my delusion may suddenly part and the sun of wisdom alone shine brightly, enabling me to awaken to the continuous arising of all phenomena.
This is because their respective natures are mutually interfused; thus, one may ultimately reach the stage free from doubt and confusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa [until] he reverently listened to the Buddha’s voice, remaining silent and attentive.
Commentary: This is the Great Compassionate One’s permission for the discourse. The intention is as follows:

although previously, from the five aggregates up to the seven elements, all were shown to return to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha—thereby collectively refuting the false and returning to the true, which is the ultimate among ultimates—I now further address you and all those in this assembly who have exhausted all outflows and attained the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa).
This proclaims and clarifies how delusion arises from the True, so that one may know that the myriad dharmas arise from the single nature, and all the great elements return to the One Mind.
It reaches the point where delusion is itself the True, neither identical nor separate; where the one and the many are unimpeded, and the small and the large mutually contain one another.
Furthermore, it is the true ultimate nature within the ultimate meaning. Now, there are three kinds of ultimate meaning: first, the ultimate meaning of the object (*arthaparamārtha*).
This refers to *tathatā* (suchness). For *tathatā* possesses the meaning of remaining unchanging while following conditions; it is so called because it can surpass all other meanings.
Second is the "meaning of supreme attainment," which refers to *nirvāṇa*. This is the ultimate fruit attained by the noble ones (*ārya*), and it is so called because it is the most excellent of all.
The third is the ultimate truth of practice (*pratipatti-paramārtha*), which refers to the Noble Path. This is the Dharma of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) traversed by the Noble Ones;
this Dharma is most preeminent, for neither mundane nor supramundane dharmas can equal it. One who possesses these three [qualities] perfectly accords with the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama*.
As for those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*), it means that they have not yet turned their minds toward the Mahāyāna. They have not yet attained...
"Two kinds of emptiness" means that while they have attained only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), they have not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
"Turning toward the Mahāyāna" means that they have already turned their minds to aspire toward the Great Vehicle.

The meaning is that although the faculties of these three types of people are not equal, upon hearing this Dharma, they all obtain the supreme One Vehicle and collectively return to the ground of great quiescent extinction (*mahā-nirvāṇa*). [In] Sanskrit: [mahā-śūnyatā].
*Āraṇya* is also called *āraṇya*; this is translated as "leaving behind clamor and strife," and also as "a place of leisure and tranquility.
All *arhats* receive this title. However, being free from clamor and strife and abiding in quiescence is not yet the ultimate truth.

This is because they remain attached to empty stillness, having not yet realized that all phenomena are inherently quiescent from the very beginning. Therefore, what they practice are merely byways and minor paths.

This is the direct path. Only by attaining the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama does one find that the faculties have no distinction of great or small, the mind has no distinction of clamor or stillness, and objects have no distinction of movement or tranquility;

thus one enters equally into the Buddha-vehicle and returns to the ultimate. When contact with objects is harmoniously integrated and the mind attains mastery, only then can one be called a true *āraṇyaka* in the proper place of practice. It is said: "Only this one matter is real; the other two are..."
This is not the truth. Therefore, I shall cause Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra and the others to listen with careful discernment; I will now explain it for them.
Then, out of reverence for the Buddha’s Dharma-voice, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra and the others listened in silence.
The Buddha said to Pūrṇa... [up to] "...therein there is neither identity nor difference;
truly, conditioned phenomena do not exist. A monk asked Chan Master Changsha Jingcen:
"How can one turn mountains, rivers, and the lands back into oneself? The Master said: "How can one turn oneself into mountains, rivers, and the lands? [The monk] said: "No."
Hui said, "Under the city walls of Hunan, it is good for nourishing the people; rice is cheap and firewood is plentiful, sufficient for all four neighbors.
The monk remained silent. The Master presented him with this verse: "Who turns the mountains and rivers? The mountains and rivers turn toward whom?
Perfect penetration has no two sides; The Dharma-nature originally has no place of return. Lecturer Zixuan of Changshui, from the time he first shaved his head, recited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*...
He ceased [his studies] and followed Dharma Master Hongmin. When the lecture reached the passage, "The two aspects of motion and stillness are clearly seen as non-arising," he had an awakening.

He said to Min, "Even 'beating the void' or 'striking wood' still falls within the realm of the trap and the snare; even 'raising the eyes' or 'lifting the eyebrows' has already become a matter of deliberation.

Only by departing from these two paths can one accord with this principle. Min patted him on the back and certified his realization. However, though he wished to explore the source of Chan, he knew nothing of it.

Yiowang heard that the Way of Langya was highly esteemed in his time, so he immediately went to attend his lectures. He arrived just as the master was ascending the hall to teach. Yiowang stepped forward and asked:
"If it is fundamentally pure and still, how did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Langya replied with a commanding presence: "It is fundamentally pure and still;
how did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Upon hearing this, Yiowang attained realization. Later, he resided at Changshui. One day—

One day, he looked at the assembly and said: "The Way is not attained through words or images; Chan is not known through conjecture or deliberation. To realize the meaning and penetrate the source, there is never any other method.
In this regard, all may participate as fellow practitioners."
Commentary: This clarifies the source and development of how [the mind] manifests according to karma.
From "As you have said" onwards, this restates and confirms the words of Pūrṇa’s doubt. He then interrogates him, saying:

"In your ordinary course, have you not heard the Tathāgata proclaim that the nature of awakening is wondrously luminous, and that fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous? Pūrṇa replied: "I have constantly heard the Buddha proclaim..."

To explain this meaning: the "awakening of nature" (*xing-jue*) is the true substance that arises and arises without ceasing; the wondrousness of this substantial nature is eternally self-luminous and precise.
"Original awakening" (*ben-jue*) is primordially complete and does not depend upon cultivation or effort;
the luminosity of this original substance is eternally self-silent and wondrous. Yet, when Pūrṇa asked: "If it is pure and fundamentally so, how did the mountains and rivers suddenly arise?"

Regarding the World-Honored One’s interrogation using these two phrases—"the great earth and all conditioned phenomena" and so forth—it is said that "purity and original suchness" refers to the fundamental nature of awareness (*xing-jue*) and original awakening (*ben-jue*), which is termed the "substance" (*ti*). "The appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth" refers to the wondrous clarity and the clarity of the wondrous, which is termed the "function" (*yong*).
However, in the former phrase, one should emphasize the arising of function from substance; in the latter phrase, one should emphasize... [text fragment ends].
Subsuming function back into essence, there is thus the distinction between the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) and its manifestations, and the inversion between clarity and subtlety.

If the nature-awakening (*prakṛti-bodha*) is like the wisdom of differentiation, it illuminates and perceives the appearances of mountains, rivers, the great earth, and so forth, such that its wondrous function is brilliant and precise.

If the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodha*) is like the wisdom of non-movement, it penetrates and reflects the appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth, such that its luminous essence is still and subtle. However, these are not the ultimate reality.
If the essence does not manifest wondrous function, the wondrous function cannot reveal the true essence.

However, when essence and function are inseparable and both subject and object are simultaneously extinguished, the principle that nature and characteristics are non-dual is realized. Therefore, two further points of inquiry are established to investigate Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra’s statement:
"You call your nature-awareness wondrously luminous, and your fundamental awakening luminously wondrous; by what principle is this so?"

[The interlocutor] asks: Is it that which is the essence of "awakened nature" (xingjue), inherently and originally luminous—that which is manifest, numinous, and never obscured—and is thus directly named "awakened nature"?

Or is it the essence of "original awakening" (benjue), which was originally obscure and possessed moments of non-illumination, such that one must apply specific effort to clarify it, and is therefore called "luminous awakening" (mingjue)?
In the former case, one falls into the extreme of luminosity; in the latter case, one falls into...

Regarding the point of "not being clear": although Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra had realized the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and was foremost in preaching the Dharma, how could it be that one who is not clear is called the essence of awakening?
Therefore, it is said: if this essence that is not clear were also called awakening, then since there would be nothing capable of clarifying, there would be nothing to be clarified.
Only when the fundamental nature itself is capable of clarifying can it be called awakening. This is by no means...
[The Buddha] knew that because [Ananda] possessed a certain capacity for conceptualization, his understanding of the wondrous clarity of intrinsic nature was far removed from it.

Therefore, the Buddha reiterated his words, saying: "If you insist that there must be something perceived in order to be called 'clear awareness,' then if there is nothing perceived, there would be no clear awareness.
Thus, this awareness takes the presence of an object and the absence of an object as its arising and ceasing. How could you know that true awareness is steadfast?"

However, fundamentally there is neither subject nor object. He then told him: "If you say that the clarity and subtlety have an object, they are no longer the true essence, and thus cannot be called original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
If you say that the nature-enlightenment has no object, it is no longer the function of illumination, and thus cannot be called wondrous clarity (*prabhāsvara*).
Since it lacks the wondrous function of illuminating awareness, it is also not the true clarity of profound stillness."
This is the essence of the nature. For the nature is awakening within ignorance, yet there is nothing that is not illuminated; this is precisely what constitutes wondrous illumination.

However, if one says that the awakening of the nature must necessarily be wondrously illuminated, then deluded conceptual attachments arise. To cling to the non-existence of ignorance is to fall entirely into nihilism;
to cling to the necessity of its being illuminated is to fall entirely into substantialism. As the former masters said: "It is just this very thing."
This is like placing one's head upon one's own head; yet if you say it is not so, it is like cutting off one's head and seeking to remain alive.

Thus, within the wondrous clarity of the awakened nature and the luminous subtlety of original awakening, the slightest thought of attachment immediately transforms into the ignorance of karmic consciousness.
Therefore, the World-Honored One pointed directly to it, saying: "The fundamental substance of the nature of awareness originally has nothing that is illumined.

It is because you recognize the deluded vision of the 'capable of illumining' that you establish the deluded realm of the 'illumined. Once the deluded object is established, the deluded subject arises in turn;
thus, these two divisions of seeing and appearance arise mutually. From this, there naturally emerge the faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing."
Are not these perceived phenomena of mountains, rivers, and so forth, instances of manifesting diversity within that which is neither identical nor different?
Yet you fail to realize they arise from deluded thought; instead, you doubt that which is pure and fundamental, wondering how such phenomena as mountains and rivers could suddenly appear.
You further question how the natures of the great elements, which are supposedly mutually exclusive, can all simultaneously pervade the Dharma-realm. This must surely be...
Only when their natures are made identical can one then allow them to be co-extensive. Thus, if one loathes their difference, one establishes identity to dispel that difference.

Is this not a case of wishing to differentiate from what is already differentiated, yet establishing identity by means of that very differentiation? Once identity and difference have been brought forth, one again grows weary of both identity and difference;
the intention must surely be to wait until these appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth are exhausted without remainder, and then to transform [them].
It becomes empty space and begins to return to its original state of pure essence. Is this not, therefore, the re-establishment of "neither identical nor different"?
Your intention is that only by proceeding in this way can one ultimately reach a state free from doubt.

But how could you know that the more you investigate, the further away you go, and the more your doubts multiply? Thus, he cites the preceding text to point out: "It is simply because you recognize the subject..."
Recognizing objects, one establishes identity based on difference; based on identity and difference, one further establishes neither-identity-nor-difference.
Thus, through such turmoil, they alternate in mutual dependence, falsely giving rise to the appearance of weariness. This is the True Mind becoming weary and producing false views;
the weary, false views giving rise to false objects. Yet, all of this does not transcend the mind taking its own mind as an object, thereby returning to a state of total confusion.
Thus, the inherently pure nature is turbidified, and the wondrously luminous fundamental awakening becomes "luminous-wondrous. Therefore, the conclusion summarizes and rebukes it, saying:

"Because of this single thought that recognizes luminosity and falls into the realm of objects, the karmic consciousness is incited, transforming into the two divisions of subject and object, and further giving rise to the ten afflictions (*kleśas*).
Once one has become a vessel for worldly toil and affliction, if one stirs the mind and moves..."
Contemplate this: since time immemorial, the three periods have flowed on and the four directions have been demarcated.

If one is in a state of dullness or neutral ignorance (*avyākṛta*), one naturally becomes a stubborn void, like stagnant water. This is what is meant by the principle that good, evil, and the neutral give rise to phenomena.

Since these dust-like shadows exist within the mental consciousness, they are likewise present in external objects; thus, one perceives the void as undifferentiated and consequently reckons it to be uniform.
Regarding "characteristics": one perceives the world as having the three periods of time and the four directions, and consequently calculates them to be distinct characteristics.
This is fundamentally due to the deluded movement of a single thought-moment. Because of the manifestation of clarity, an objective realm is established;

thus, that which is originally pure, being neither identical nor different, is inverted into the truly conditioned phenomena of the world and empty space. "Exertion" refers to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*); "dust" refers to the characteristic-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*).
The clarity of awareness and the dullness of emptiness interact to produce agitation... (up to) ...therefore there is a water-wheel containing the worlds of the ten directions.
A separate sutra states that regarding the establishment of the world: beneath the earth-wheel rests the gold-wheel; beneath the gold-wheel rests the water-wheel.
"The water mandala rests upon the wind mandala; the wind mandala rests upon the space mandala; the space mandala has no support.
This [statement] is not in slight agreement with this sutra. That [sutra] concerns the establishment [of the world], proceeding from below upward to form its sequence.

This [sutra], however, concerns the cause for the arising of the four great elements as they appear before one's eyes. Therefore, "wind mandala" here refers to the wind within space, which is capable of stirring and supporting [the elements].
The world. Thus, although the golden wheel belongs to the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*), it also refers to the precious gold that circulates within the present world;

therefore, it is said to "sustain the land. As for the fire element (*tejo-mahābhūta*), it speaks only of its transformative nature; as for the water element (*apo-mahābhūta*), it speaks only of its containment of the ten directions.
These do not require further analysis to be self-evident. These four great elements are formed solely through deluded thought (*vikalpa*).
This constitutes the correct intent. If one were to subsume earth under metal and wood under wind, then the five elements' cycle of production and overcoming would likewise be complete;

however, it is not necessary to insert them [into this context]. Although it is said that wind and metal rub against each other to produce fire, the "shaking clarity" mentioned in the preceding line is itself ignorance (*avidyā*).
Although it is said that metal and fire vaporize to produce water, the "precious clarity" refers to the clarity of the jewel.
The original text refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). Within this passage, the meaning of the "hooked chain" (*gō-sō ren-gen*) must also be understood. An ancient transcription states:

"Because of the movement of deluded views, the external wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) is manifested; because of the hardness of the grasping mind, the external gold-circle (*kāñcana-maṇḍala*) is manifested;

because of the dryness of seeking and investigation, the external fire-circle (*tejo-maṇḍala*) is manifested; because of the depth of the loving mind, the external water-circle (*ap-maṇḍala*) is manifested."

[End of previous section]. Commentary on the Preface: The preceding section clarified how true nature transforms into deluded awareness; this section clarifies how deluded awareness, in turn, constitutes the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The intent is as follows: the Tathāgatagarbha is intrinsically pure, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, fundamentally unmoving, and likewise...
There is no fixed characteristic; it merely manifests according to the karmic power of sentient beings.
Thus, there are characteristics such as movement and agitation, which constitute truly conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). The karmic power of sentient beings begins with ignorance (*avidyā*).

From the essence of fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*), a deluded clarity suddenly arises, whereby the dark and obscure true emptiness becomes a dull, insentient void. Furthermore, one reckons this ignorance to be clarity, and reckons this dull...
Space is characterized by obscurity. When clarity and obscurity confront one another, they mutually agitate each other, thereby forming the wind of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Consequently, this evokes the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), which arises within the voids of space to support the world-systems. These great elements of wind originate from ignorance.
Since the awakening of clarity perceives the obscurity of space and gives rise to the agitation of ignorance, wherever there is movement, there must also be stillness; thus, deluded thought arises.

It is through stubborn attachment that solidity and obstruction are established. Thus, when there are gold and jewels in the world, they arise because of the stubborn obstruction of ignorance within deluded cognition;
consequently, one experiences the golden wheel that sustains the realm. Even the earth-element (mahābhūta) therein originates from ignorance.
Since the stubborn cognition of ignorance has already formed the gold and jewels, once the shaking of ignorance produces wind, then—[one...]
The solid and the mobile rub and wash against one another; thus, they evoke the presence of fire in the world. By steaming gold, water emerges; by congealing water, earth is formed.
Fire can further melt, disperse, and mature all things, serving as the nature of transformation.
This element of fire (tejo-mahābhūta) likewise arises from ignorance. Once there is luminous awareness, the solid gold and jewels are established, and it is able to manifest them.
Regarding the characteristic of moisture: there is the fiery light produced when the golden wind rubs against it, which gives rise to vaporous and steaming mists.
Thus, as the metal and fire combine, they evoke the water-wheel in the world, which possesses the nature of moisture and encompasses the realms of the ten directions.
The great elements of that water also arise from ignorance.
Fire ascends and water descends, interacting to produce solidity; through these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession.
The *Yījīng* says: "Heaven produces Water as the first; Water produces the Wood of the Eastern trigrams Zhèn and Xùn;
Wood produces the Fire of the Southern Li; Fire produces the Earth of the southwestern Kūn; Earth produces the Metal of the Western Duì;

and the Metal of the northwestern Qián again produces the Water of the Northern Kǎn. Thus it revolves like a ring without end. Indeed, the Five Elements take mutual overcoming as their marital relationship.
They give rise to one another as father and son. The son is born from the wife; it must be that the husband is subordinate to the wife before Yin and Yang harmonize to produce the child.
Thus, Zhen is wood and Dui is metal. Wood looks toward metal as its wife who overcomes it.
Metal’s relation to wood is that of the "husband who overcomes me. Facing each other east and west as husband and wife, Zhen is the husband and Dui is the wife.
Metal and wood produce fire; thus, the husband is inferior to the wife as they together produce a child.
Li is fire and Kan is water. Water’s relation to fire is that of the "wife whom I overcome," while fire’s relation to water is that of the "overcomer."
My husband and I face each other, north and south, as husband and wife. Thus, Kan represents the husband and Li represents the wife. Water and Fire produce Earth;
this is also a case where the husband is inferior to the wife in producing offspring. Kun represents the Earth and Gen represents the Mountain; both belong to Earth.
This is where all things begin their formation and reach their completion. Therefore, in spring and summer, all things flourish and emerge.
It is always visible above the earth in spring and summer; when the myriad things are gathered and stored away in autumn and winter, it is always hidden beneath the earth and invisible.
This is why the *Hetu Tu* (River Chart) accomplishes transformations and carries out the workings of ghosts and spirits through its pervasive and circulating function.

This provides the source for the arising of this [world]. Although the phrasing is complex and interwoven, the underlying meaning is consistent; therefore, I have recorded them together. Preface to the Commentary:
This clarifies how the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) is formed from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The intent is that once ignorance has...
When the four great elements are formed, the nature of these four elements is such that they are mutually contradictory yet complementary.

For example, the nature of fire is inherently to blaze upward, while the nature of water is inherently to flow downward; one ascends and the other descends, interacting and complementing each other, and together they establish solidity.
They form the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). Furthermore, the moist element becomes the great oceans; thus, there are watery realms in the world such as the four great oceans.
The dry element becomes the continents and sandbanks; thus, there are terrestrial lands in the world such as the four great continents.
Since these are formed by the combination of water and fire, it might seem that within those great oceans—which are originally deep pools containing moisture—fire should not exist; yet, fire...

That light constantly arises is due to the existence of the pneumatic channels (*nāḍī*) of fire. Within the sandbars and shoals, where there is originally solid and dry ground, it would seem that water should not exist;
yet, that rivers and streams constantly flow there is due to the existence of the pneumatic channels of water.
Now, water is able to overcome fire; if the force of the water prevails, it must extinguish the fire—how then could they be said to produce one another? Yet now, [the fire] descends...
The superior overcomes the inferior; thus, water follows fire and coagulates to form high mountains.

Therefore, when mountain rock is struck and produces flames, it is because the vital energy (*qi-mai*) of fire has not yet perished. When it melts and becomes water, it is because the vital energy of water has not yet perished.
Furthermore, earth can overcome water; if the power of earth prevails, it will surely dry up the water—how then could it produce living things?
Now, the superior descends to become the inferior; thus, earth follows water and is drawn forth as grasses and trees.
Therefore, when forests and thickets encounter fire and become earth, the seed-nature of earth still persists; when they are compressed and become water, the seed-nature of water still persists.
Goodness first arises from a single thought of deluded movement, which constitutes the agitation of ignorance.
The wind-element becomes great; through the obstruction of solidity, the earth-element is formed.
Subsequently, as solidity and agitation rub against one another, the fire-element is formed. Thereafter, as the substantial clarity and the fire-light steam together, the water-element is formed.
Thus, the four elements arise from mutual delusion; furthermore, through the interaction of water and fire, they become the seeds of continents and oceans.
Furthermore, the water-element descends, following the fire-element, to become the seeds of mountains and stones;
then the earth-element descends, following the water-element, to become the seeds of grasses and trees. Thus, by acting as seeds for one another, they form the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
For these reasons, the world undergoes formation, subsistence, destruction, and emptiness; it ends and begins again, continuing in an uninterrupted succession.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa, [you have explained] that delusion is not caused by another... (up to) ...for these reasons, sentient beings continue in succession.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "That which is called the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) refers to the body of sentient beings belonging to the five destinies that exists in the interval between the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*) and the existence of death (*maraṇabhava*);
it is termed the intermediate state. It likewise has the five aggregates of maturation (*vipākapañcaskandha*) as its substance, because it is summoned by karma.

The intermediate state bodies of those born from a womb or an egg possess a physical form identical to their future 'existence at birth' (*pratisandhibhava*); for instance, the intermediate state body of a human resembles [a human]."
It is the same for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of other realms. Its body is the size of a child of five or six years;
although its physical dimensions are small, its sense faculties are as sharp and keen as those of a fully formed being (*pūrvakālabhava*).
It is capable of performing various karmic actions and gives rise to perverted perceptions toward its parents—seeing either only a male or only a female—and thus gradually approaches their location.
Gradually, the intermediate being no longer sees his parents or other surroundings; he sees only the sexual organs.
If he is a male intermediate being, he conceives desire for the mother; if he is a female intermediate being, he conceives desire for the father. Thus, desire arises.
Having given rise to these two kinds of craving, it unites with the object of craving; the impurity thus discharged flows into the womb, where it is perceived as one's own body, and joy arises.
Once this mind has arisen, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) ceases and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*) is assumed;
therefore, it is said that "those of similar karma entwine. As for those of moisture-born and transformation-born births, by the power of prior karma, [the process is] not...
[The intermediate state being] examines the near and the far; if there is an object of attachment that accords with its disposition, it will take rebirth at the very place where the fragrance is.
The *Abhidharmakośa* clarifies that within the womb there are five stages: the first seven days are called *kalala*, translated as "congealed mucus";

the second seven days are called *arbuda*, translated as "blister," resembling a sore or blister; the third seven days are called *peśī*, translated as "soft flesh"; the fourth seven days are called... [the text continues].
*Ghana* means "solid flesh. *Pañca-saptāha* is named *peśī*, meaning "the stage of shape.
Here, I have briefly cited the first two [stages] to include the remaining three by implication.
Commentary: This clarifies the cause for the continuity of sentient beings. As stated previously, that which is "delusively taken as luminous awareness" does not arise from anything else;
rather, it is simply the deluded arising of a subject capable of illumination upon the substance of true awareness itself, which constitutes the fault.

When there is a subject capable of illuminating, that which is illuminated is established. Once the object of delusion is established, then the truth of the wondrous luminosity of the nature-awareness and the sublime luminosity of fundamental awareness cannot transcend the realm of subject and object. As it is said: "Originally one is a single refined spirit;
it divides into the six harmonious combinations. For this reason, hearing does not go beyond sound, and seeing does not transcend form. Thus...

The six deluded faculties of cognition and the six deluded objects mutually interact and achieve [their existence]. This refers to the past state of already being deluded, wherein one inherits delusion and enters further into delusion;
thus, in the present, things continue as before, and the principles of clarity are not transcended.

One distinguishes the six deluded faculties of cognition—seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and knowing—and grasps the six kinds of deluded objects—form, sound, fragrance, flavor, texture, and dharmas—thereby giving rise to attachment for self and others.
Deluded by hatred, they create karma through the union and separation of emotional thoughts. Those who share such karma mostly do so because their passions are profound;
in the future, they will necessarily be born when the parents and themselves—these three—have their shared karma entwine them, belonging to the categories of womb-born or egg-born beings.
Regarding their union and separation, these are mostly due to the power of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). In the future, they do not depend on parents;

rather, it is solely through their own karma that they either coalesce with moisture to form a body—such as insects and crawling creatures—or undergo transformation through detachment from a different source, such as in the heavens or the hells.

This refers to how, based on the fundamental physical body (*mūla-skandha-kāya*), one gives rise to delusions and performs actions, thereby inducing the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) at the time of rebirth in the future.

Regarding the state of entering the womb through the reception of thought: what is that state like? It is said that when the retribution of the previous existence has ended, the active manifestations of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) also cease;
only the seeds remain, which collectively merge into the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*), and thereby manifest the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
When the intermediate state bodies of those born from wombs or eggs are about to enter the womb, they see a place devoid of conditions, appearing entirely like the pitch-black night. Only at...
In a place where there is a karmic affinity with one's parents, one perceives a single point of subtle light.

However, before this light is seen, there is only the *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness), which is dark and devoid of cognition. Upon seeing the light for the first time, the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) is activated, giving rise to craving and desire.
One then rushes directly toward the source of the light; either seeing the father as a male object of desire or the mother as a female object of desire, it appears clearly before them.
Thus, with perverted perceptions and thoughts, [the consciousness] achieves its formation. If it is a male entering the womb, he feels aversion for the father and love for the mother;
if it is a female taking up residence in the womb, she feels aversion for the mother and love for the father.

Once these objects of affection are established, the stream of consciousness flows into the already-loved two drops of red and white from the parents, taking them as its seed-nature. Thus, within the two drops of red and white from the parents, it is received.

Having already conceived craving, which serves as the embryo’s seed, once the three conditions have converged and given rise to birth, it further draws in past karma of a similar kind to enter the womb.
Thus, through the causal conditions of shared karma, the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and subsequent stages come into being.

Furthermore, among the four modes of birth—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—each has its own fixed karma; therefore, they manifest in accordance with what is evoked by that karma.

This is categorized according to the retributions of the four modes of birth. According to ancient exegesis: unsettled and disordered thought is called *saṃjñā* (perception); the entanglement of craving and deluded attachment is called *vedanā* (feeling); the firm and unwavering clinging is called *saṃyoga* (union);
and the abandonment of this state to move toward that is called *viyoga* (separation). It is through the invocation of these four mental states that [rebirth is induced].

Thus, the various categories of the four modes of birth correspond to these states. Yet it does not stop here. From this point forward, they will change their heads and alter their faces, undergoing endless cycles of birth and death.
Sometimes emotion transforms into perception, and perception transforms into emotion; union changes into separation, and separation changes into union, for there is no fixed cause.
Sometimes the egg-born transforms into the womb-born, and the womb-born transforms into the egg-born; the moisture-born transforms into...
The transformed may further transform into the moist; there is no fixed destination. Sometimes the flying changes into the submerged, and the submerged changes into the flying;
there is no fixed retribution. By these causes and conditions, sentient beings undergo saṃsāra, beginning again after it ends, in an uninterrupted succession.
Pūrṇa’s conceptualization and craving are bound together as one (up to: "by these causes and conditions, karma and its fruit continue in succession").
*Commentary*: This clarifies the reason for the continuity of karma and its fruit. The meaning is that the world belongs to the dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
Originally, insentient things do not form karma because they lack consciousness. Sentient beings belong to the category of primary retribution; being inherently sentient, they possess karma.
Among all karmas, none is greater than the three of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. Yet the root begins with sexuality:

taking the flow of craving as the seed and the reception of thought as the womb constitutes the very source from which karma arises. If thought and craving do not coalesce, then [karma] may still be avoided.
Separation. Since both parties are bound together as if by glue or lacquer, they cannot separate from one another life after life.
Parents and children are born in succession without end; all of this has desire and greed as its root.
For all who possess body and life must seek nourishment: they crave the grain-fed delicacies of the other, while the other craves their flesh and blood. Greed...
Affection grows together with it; as its flavor becomes increasingly pervasive, killing arises therein.
When greed for flavor does not cease, beings within the four modes of birth, according to the strength or weakness of their power, devour one another in succession, and thus theft arises therein.
All of these have their root in the craving for killing. Consequently, humans eat sheep, and when the sheep dies, it becomes a human;
when the human dies, they become a sheep. Thus, among the ten classes of sentient beings, birth and death continue without end as they prey upon one another in turn.
Furthermore, those who commit such evils will be born together life after life, meeting in the same place to repay their debts until the very end of the future.

There is no end to this; it all has its root in the greed for theft. Because of these two forms of greed—killing and theft—there arise such claims as "You owe me my life" and "You must repay my debt," or "I owe you my life" and "I must repay your debt.

Due to these causes and conditions of life-debts, one remains constantly within the cycle of birth and death, repaying them without end. Furthermore, because of the greed for desire, there now exists...
"You love my mind; I cherish your form. I love your mind; you cherish my form.

Because of these causes and conditions of mutual love and cherishing, we remain constantly within the cycle of birth and death, bound and fettered without end. Now, these three [actions] truly arise from craving and attachment.
When craving and attachment are not fulfilled, one forcibly seizes another's life through killing, or takes what is not given through theft; these are all the reasons for such actions."

This brings about their craving and attachment. Thus, when one karma arises, all three karmas are simultaneously present. Whenever craving and attachment are fulfilled, they inevitably lead to a heart of affection that covets form and color;
whenever craving and attachment are not fulfilled, they inevitably lead to the taking of life and the repayment of debts.
Therefore, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are the fundamental causes of karma, while the entanglements of birth and death are the revolving fruits of karma.
It is a continuous succession without interruption.
Pūrṇa, these three kinds of inverted successions continue (until) because of this delusion they end and then begin again. [Commentary:
This refers back to the aforementioned three kinds of succession to conclude the answer to Mañjuśrī’s question regarding the sudden arising of beginning and end.
Regarding this inquiry, the meaning is as follows: These three kinds of continuity all arise from turning one's back on the Truth and uniting with delusion, born of madness and inverted confusion.
Why is this? For these three are, in their very essence, the wondrous clarity of intrinsic awareness and the luminous subtlety of fundamental awareness.

The fundamental essence and true nature are always clearly known. Because you first gave rise to the perceiving faculty capable of cognition, which simultaneously produced the perceived objects, the karmic consciousness was formed, resulting in the division of subject and object. From this deluded seeing, the appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth suddenly arose;
thus there came to be successive fluxes that continue without end. You ask: "How did it suddenly come to be?"
One should know that the arising of appearances such as mountains and rivers occurs solely because of this delusory continuity of inversion;

thus they flow on in succession, ending and beginning again. These perceivable false phenomena have never existed from the outset; there is only the single, fundamentally enlightened, luminous, and wondrous nature.
Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous awakening [is thus], how could the outflows of conditioned habituation ever arise again?

*Commentary:* This [objection] takes the essence of awakening while it is still enmeshed in the bonds as the basis for the difficulty regarding the essence of awakening once it has emerged from those bonds. He says:

"According to what the World-Honored One has taught, when these sentient beings have not yet given rise to the appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth, the nature of their awakening is wondrous."
Luminosity. This fundamental awakening is luminous and wondrous; from the beginning, it is unstained and unimpeded.

When compared with the minds of all Tathāgatas, the Buddha-mind does not increase, and the minds of sentient beings do not decrease. Those sentient beings merely cause this essence of wondrous awakening-luminosity to transform into deluded luminosity.
Because they perceive the luminosity of awakening as empty and obscure, the appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth suddenly arise without cause. Thus says the Tathāgata.
Now that you have attained this wondrous, empty, luminous awareness, it stands in contrast to all common experience.

As for these mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as all conditioned phenomena and the deluded habitual tendencies of outflows—when will they ever arise again? These mountains, rivers, and the great earth constitute the world-system.
The conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) contains sentient beings; the outflows (*āsrava*) contain karma and its fruits.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "For example, as with a person who is lost... (up to)... Awakening (*bodhi*) and Nirvāṇa are also like this."

The first two metaphors reveal that the essence of pure awakening is originally perfect and complete, requiring no cultivation or realization. The latter two metaphors likewise do not preclude cultivation and realization.
If one were to cite only the first two metaphors, there is a fear that practitioners might fall into the error of nihilism and develop a view of annihilationism.
If one were to cite only the latter two metaphors, there is a fear that practitioners might falsely identify with the essence of awakening.
Fundamentally not pure, originally possessing birth and cessation, it forms defiled views; therefore, four metaphors are presented together to let one know that delusion is fundamentally unborn.
Yet, without realizing the True, one cannot extinguish delusion. The True is fundamentally unchanging, yet without removing delusion, one cannot realize the True.
Thus, one knows that all sentient beings have never experienced birth and death, and yet—
Samsara does not cease; the Buddhas and Tathāgatas have never entered nirvana, yet they abide eternally and immutably.
Thus, birth is itself non-birth, and non-birth is itself birth. In this state, from where could the appearance of a continuous succession of beginning and end possibly arise?

Commentary: The following presents four metaphors to clarify the essence of awakening. The first metaphor illustrates that delusion has no cause; the second illustrates that false phenomena have no substance;
the third illustrates that once the true is realized, it does not revert to the false; and the fourth illustrates that once the false is severed, it does not arise again.
These collectively reveal that the true and the false fundamentally have neither beginning nor end. Therefore, the metaphors are first presented to examine the cause of delusion, saying:
Suppose there is a person who has lost their way in a village and suddenly becomes confused, taking south for north.
Do you think this person's confusion exists because of a prior state of confusion, or because of a prior state of awakening?
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra replied: "This confusion neither arises because of confusion nor because of awakening. Why is that?"
Before delusion arose, there was originally no root from which delusion could be produced; how, then, could it exist because of delusion?
Awakening and delusion are opposites; since awakening is fundamentally not the root from which delusion arises, how could it exist because of awakening?

If one knows that awakening does not give rise to delusion, then one knows that the false arises in dependence upon the true, yet the true has never been false. Therefore, he again employs the previous analogy to illustrate this point.

He questioned Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, saying: "Since you know that delusion fundamentally has no root, suppose there is a person who is lost in a village and, while they are currently taking south for north, a person who has attained awakening suddenly points it out to them so that they awaken.
Even though this person was long lost, now that they have attained awakening, would they become deluded again regarding this village? Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra replied: "Once awakened, they would not."
Once severed, one will never again be deluded. The subsequent passage should read: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions are likewise. Having awakened, they will never again be deluded;
however, while they have not yet realized the ultimate fruit, although ignorance exists, its essence is ultimately empty—just like this present delusion, which originally has no root or foundation.
Therefore, the true substance of enlightened clarity is fundamentally pure. Previously, while in a state of delusion...

At that time, there is fundamentally no deluded nature to be found. It is like one who has lost their sense of direction: even while they are in a state of confusion, the directions themselves have not actually shifted.
How much more so is it that not only is delusion unfindable, but awakening is likewise unfindable; it is merely a matter of comparing the time of delusion with the time of awakening.

It seems as though there is delusion and awakening. For example, when one mistakes south for north, from the perspective of one who knows the south is not the north, it seems as though there has been a movement and a fixed state.
If a single instance of awakening dispels delusion, then delusion is instantly extinguished;
once extinguished, even awakening cannot be found. How could delusion ever arise again? Again, he provides a further analogy to refute Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, saying: "It is also like this..."
When there is a film in the human eye, one sees flowers in the sky; when the disease of the film is removed, the appearance of the flowers ceases.
Suppose there were a foolish person who, in that empty space where the flowers had vanished, waited for the flowers to be born again. Do you consider this person to be foolish or wise?
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, being thus questioned, answered according to the facts: "In emptiness, there were originally no flowers; how could there be arising or ceasing?"
To see the flower perish in mid-air is already a perverted and deluded vision;
yet to expect the flower to be reborn is the height of foolishness and madness. How can you even distinguish between such folly and wisdom?
The Buddha addressed him according to his words, saying: "This person who awaits the flower is indeed as you say—utterly foolish and mad. However, you..."
Since you already know this, why do you ask me about the Tathāgata’s wondrous enlightened clarity and empty space? And when will the mountains, rivers, and great earth ever arise again?
From this day forward, you should know that the Buddha is like the person who removes the cataract, while you are like the person waiting for the flowers [to reappear].

Once you realize that the void was originally flowerless and that the arising and ceasing were but false perceptions, you will immediately know that all dharmas are fundamentally quiescent from the beginning.

Extinction. The essence of awakening is fundamentally devoid of delusion or enlightenment. To grasp at the Buddha as truly existent, extinguishing the false to realize the true, is already a perversion;
how much more so to wait for the Buddha to arise from the true and produce the false—what difference is there between this and waiting for a flower to be born again?
Again, he offers a metaphor: "It is like when gold ore is mixed with refined gold; at that time, the gold exists within the ore, blended together."
There is no distinction. If one uses a furnace and fire to smelt [the ore] into refined gold, once that gold is pure, it will never again be mixed with dross.
Furthermore, just as wood, having been consumed by fire, becomes ash and can no longer be wood, so it is said in accordance with the Dharma:
"The Buddhas and Tathāgatas who have attained *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* have already perfected the essence of unsurpassed wisdom and realized the nature of *tathatā*."

Thus, having already emerged from afflictions and the cycle of birth and death through true cultivation and authentic practice, one attains a realization that is final and eternal, never again subject to regression or fall.
It is like gold extracted from ore: once it is pure, it remains eternally pure and will never again be mixed with dross.
These afflictions and the cycle of birth and death, having already passed through the wisdom of the dual emptiness contemplation, are transformed into bodhi and nirvana;
they are severed once and for all, never to arise again. This is just as wood that has been reduced to ash can never become wood again.
Pūrṇa, as for what you asked [up to] "why do you further ask about those that are not mutually compatible"?
[Commentary: This clarifies that the nature and characteristics of the seven great elements all depend upon the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, manifesting according to karma.

This is used to answer the question regarding how the seven elements, being all-pervasive, could not possibly coexist. Furthermore, from the words "Moreover, you... onwards, [the text] restates the doubts held by Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
The phrase "For example, the substance of empty space is not composed of manifold characteristics" serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgatagarbha, which is pure and fundamental by nature.
Pervading the entire dharma-realm, it is fundamentally not the various great elements; thus, it does not fall into the extreme of existence.

Yet, it does not reject the manifestation of those various signs; this is illustrated by the seven greatnesses (mahābhūtas) appearing according to karma, such that they do not fall into the extreme of non-existence.
The following section provides a further inquiry and explanation, asking: "Why is this so? When that great void is illuminated by the sun, it manifests..."

When the manifestation of light gathers like clouds in the sky, it brings forth the manifestation of darkness; even when earth accumulates in the sky, it brings forth the manifestation of dust and mist;
and when water clarifies in the sky, it brings forth the manifestation of translucent clarity. What do you think?
Thus, in different directions simultaneously, there exist various conditioned manifestations such as light and darkness. Regarding these manifestations—
Does this arise because of the sun, clouds, and so forth, or does it exist because of empty space?

If you claim that this appearance of light arises from the solar disk, then when the sun shines upon the sky, since it is the light of the sun, all places throughout the ten directions where there is light would likewise be the color of the sun; thus, the entire world would immediately become one.
Regarding the substance of the sun: how could one see the circular body of the sun again within empty space?

If one sees the circular sun, then there must be a further luminous appearance outside the substance of the sun that does not belong to the sun itself; how, then, can it be said that this light arises because of the sun?
If you claim that this appearance of light is not produced by the sun but belongs to space itself, and since space is ever-present, the light should always illuminate.
Why is it that during the middle of the night, when there are clouds and mist and no sun, one perceives only the appearance of darkness and no radiant glow?
You should know that this light is neither identical to space and the sun, nor is it different from space and the sun. If this appearance of light...
The sun is originally not separate from space, nor does it depart from space; it cannot be pointed out or described. Thus it is with all phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*).

Now, that empty space does not obstruct the manifestation of various phenomena; this is analogous to the *tathāgatagarbha*, which does not obstruct the seven great elements (*mahābhūta*) from manifesting according to their respective karma.
The seven factors, from the sun and clouds down to water and earth, are metaphors for the individual natures (*gotra*) of the seven great elements; they likewise belong to [the *tathāgatagarbha*].
Delusion. The seven characteristics, from light and darkness up to mist and reflection, serve as metaphors for the seven great illusory manifestations.
By examining the characteristic of light, one finds it is neither identical to nor different from the sun and space, neither the same as nor separate from them;

this serves as a metaphor for how the seven great illusory manifestations are neither identical to nor different from their respective natures, nor the same as nor separate from the *tathāgatagarbha* nature. Yet, these seven are [as follows]:
One should merely correspond to their number; one must not forcibly construct seven great elements.

Furthermore, the text below contains passages that harmonize with this, which reveal only that this emptiness-nature is pervasive and eternal. However, the nature and characteristics of these seven have no fixed essence;

they are neither pervasive nor eternal. Therefore, it is said: "Observing their characteristics, they are fundamentally false and cannot be pointed out. Because these seven characteristics are fundamentally false, [they do not exist].
It can be pointed out and described. You should know that the characteristics of the seven great elements are likewise fundamentally false and cannot be pointed out or described.

Since their characteristics are fundamentally false, so too are their various differentiated natures. If one were to falsely claim they exist and can be pointed out, it would already be a state of delusion, like grasping at the flowers of the sky as being real;
how much more so when one interrogates them regarding the meaning of their mutual subversion and extinction? This is yet again...
To invite empty flowers and yet expect them to bear the fruit of emptiness is truly delusion within delusion, and falsehood within falsehood.

If one knows that space is pervasive and eternal, and that the various seed-natures such as the sun and so forth are neither identical to nor separate from space, one should contemplate that the nature of the seven elements is, in its entirety, the single true nature; it is solely the wondrous intrinsic awareness of this nature.
It is luminous. Innate awakening is luminously wondrous and inherently pure, pervading the entire dharma-realm; it is not a separate phenomenon.

One who can contemplate in this way will know for themselves that the nature of awakening is wondrously luminous—that the true mind of innate awakening was originally not of the nature of water, fire, or other elements.

Since the natures of water, fire, and so forth are currently absent, one might ask: what, then, is it that is mutually incompatible? According to the ancient explanation, "qi" (air/vapor) coagulates like a gathering of smoke and mist.
The character *mái* (haze/dust-storm) is derived from *lí* (a wildcat); it originates from the leaping and trampling of mountain beasts, causing the earth to obscure the sky.
Alternatively, when wind and rain fall together in a chaotic swirl, it is called *mái*. As for "water being clear and reflective," it is like the ocean when it is calm and deep on a clear day. And...
Empty forms reflect one another; they are luminously clear and transparent.
True wondrous awakening and clarity are also like this—[up to:]—they are merely winding illusions with nothing upon which to rely.
Commentary: This uses the dharma to correspond with the metaphor, clarifying how the seven elements manifest according to karma.
The meaning is that the wondrous clarity of the nature-awakening and the luminous subtlety of the fundamental awakening are like the great void: when the sun shines upon it, it becomes bright;
even so, when water is clear, it reflects. Therefore, following the karma that manifests the void, the appearance of the void immediately appears—just as when one digs a well, the void [appears].
Manifesting: as one follows the activity of the four great elements, the characteristics of those four great elements immediately manifest.
Just as when water is sought in one place, water arises there; and when fire is sought in another place, fire arises there;

so too, if the activities of all the great elements are followed simultaneously throughout the entire dharma-realm, the characteristics of all the great elements will simultaneously manifest throughout the entire dharma-realm, just as [the manifestations] pervade the dharma-realm.
[The Master] said: "They arise filling the world. Below, he again provides a metaphor to clarify that which manifests as a collective illusion through the common karma of all beings;
this too is a simultaneous presentation of the real and the false, further demonstrating that [the world] is utterly illusory and lacks any objective basis.

Furthermore, while manifesting individually, one has not yet seen their mutual interdependence and mutual falsity; however, when they manifest together, this can be fully expressed. For the body of the sun serves as the primary metaphor.

Wisdom. Water is a metaphor for ultimate truth (*tattva*). Wisdom and truth are of one suchness; fundamentally, they possess no marks of coming or going. This is the totality of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature.
The reflection of the sun is a metaphor for the various great illusory appearances. The two people viewing it together is a metaphor for the deluded perception of shared karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*).
Each walking toward the east and west, each having a sun-reflection that follows their respective person, is a metaphor for following along with what arises simultaneously.
Through deluded karma, the illusory manifestations of the great elements appear simultaneously, one to the east and one to the west, with no prior fixed point of reference.
This is analogous to how the single true nature manifests the illusory appearances of the great elements, yet it is determined which manifestation serves as the actual, substantial essence.
Therefore, the precept for cessation states: one should not raise the objection, "If this sun is but one, how can it travel both east and west?"
Since each realm is already dual, why is it that we perceive only one sun? This is precisely the cessation of the deluded perceptions and conceptualizations of sentient beings regarding the precepts.
One should not raise the objection: "If these various great marks do not depart from the locus of the single truth, how can they manifest as various marks in accordance with collective karma?
And since they manifest as various marks, how can you say they do not depart from the single truth?"
A locus where there is a determinate essence can indeed be subject to debate and refutation. However, the present case is exactly like that of the dawn-light and the sun, or space:
they are neither identical nor different, neither the same nor separate, and fundamentally lack a determinate essence.
To engage in circuitous debate and refutation regarding that which lacks a determinate essence is to become more and more entangled in falsehood the more one debates; it can truly be said that—
Within the absence of identity and difference, they vigorously establish difference, proceeding until identity and difference are fully elucidated;
they then further posit neither identity nor difference—what basis can there possibly be for such a claim?
"Pūrṇa, because form is empty... [and so forth]... you have thereby brought forth the wondrous, enlightened nature of true thusness.
*Annotation:* From this point downward, the text contrasts delusion and enlightenment to summarize the meaning of the preceding questions and answers. The intent is as follows:

it means that one does not realize that the natures and characteristics of the great elements are merely manifestations arising from the Tathāgatagarbha in accordance with karma; rather, one conversely interrogates [the Buddha on this matter].
Regarding that which is characterized by mutual sublation and extinction: it is like two people seeing the sun and walking in opposite directions, east and west;

their movements are illusory and appear similar. Someone might ask: "According to the nature of the various great elements as they exist now, they blaze forth differently and clearly undergo sublation and extinction.

What is the reason for this? Therefore, he clarifies it for them, saying: "It arises from you establishing an object based on illumination. Once the subject and object are established, then karma [arises]."
Habitual tendencies become even more firm. While the perceptions of characteristics have not yet been eliminated, you cling to emptiness and cling to existence;
thus, you follow the karmic habits of form and emptiness, causing them to contend with and supplant one another within the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Consequently, the *tathāgatagarbha* follows your karmic habits, manifesting as either emptiness or form, pervading the entire dharma-realm. For this reason, I say it is like space: when wind arises within it, then...
When wind stirs, the appearance of movement is manifested; when the wind ceases, there is only the appearance of the clarity of empty space.
When the sun shines, the appearance of brightness is manifested; when clouds gather, the appearance of darkness is manifested.

Thus, sentient beings turn their backs on the wondrous luminosity of the nature-awakening and the luminous wondrousness of fundamental awakening, instead conforming to and uniting with delusive conditions and sensory objects, whereby their own characteristics become turbid.

The true essence is fundamentally pure and serene; therefore, it gives rise to worldly toil and afflictions, causing one to perceive the world as consisting solely of such phenomena as mountains and rivers.
Consequently, one clings to these mountains, rivers, and other forms as dharmas existing outside the mind.

I, however, regard these mountains, rivers, and other phenomena entirely as the wondrous luminosity of the nature-awakening—the luminous wonder of original awakening—which has been fundamentally non-existent [as separate entities].
Arising and ceasing encompass this wondrous function and accord with the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Yet, when the wondrous function is initiated from the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is solely the wondrously enlightened clarity that perfectly illumines the *dharmadhātu*; not a single dharma can be apprehended therein.
Therefore, within the totality of the great function, one attains non-obstruction regarding phenomena. For a single atom is many atoms, and many atoms are a single atom;
thus it is said that "the one becomes the immeasurable, and the immeasurable becomes the one. Within the tip of a hair, the ocean of lands manifests.
The oceans of lands appear upon the tip of a hair; thus it is said that the large appears within the small, and the small appears within the large.

Without moving from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one pervades the worlds of the ten directions; this is the manifestation of the infinite within the one. The body contains the inexhaustible voids of the ten directions;

this is the manifestation of the one within the infinite. Upon the tip of a single hair, one manifests a jewel-king land; within the center, the support [the world] appears. Furthermore, as for these jewel lands...
Small. The tip of a hair is not large, yet one sits within a mote of dust and turns the Great Dharma Wheel. Based on the middle, the correct is manifested;
thus, the bodily marks are not small, and the mote of dust is not large—both the small manifests the large, and the large manifests the small.

All of this is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom manifesting the wondrous realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Yet the Tathāgata is solely wondrous enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating all phenomena.

The "Dhātu" (element) is that which the Buddha possesses innately and completely, without any deficiency. It is only because sentient beings turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of the senses that they give rise to worldly appearances through the toil of defilement.
When the Tathāgata extinguishes the dust and unites with awakening, he gives rise to the wondrous realm of True Suchness;
this wondrous awakening is clear wisdom. Nature is the very essence of wisdom.
"The Tathāgatagarbha is, from the beginning, the wondrous, perfect, and complete mind" (up to) "detached from both identity and difference, being neither identical nor non-identical.
*Commentary:* This relies upon the essence and function of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*) to conclude by revealing the three aspects of the Tathāgatagarbha.

First, it clarifies its detachment from all phenomena to conclude by revealing the *Tathāgatagarbha* of True Reality (*tattva*), which is empty. Continuing from above, it says: "The nature of enlightenment is wondrous..."

Luminosity. The luminous wondrousness of original enlightenment, though it manifests the two aspects of defilement and purity according to delusion and awakening, the Tathāgatagarbha—the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and circular mind—is primordially pure and inherently so.
Originally, it is not the seven elements (*dhātu*), nor the six sense organs (*indriya*), nor the six sense objects (*viṣaya*), nor the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
This is not a mundane phenomenon. It is neither luminosity nor ignorance, and so on, up to neither old age and death nor their cessation. Thus...
It is neither the two dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas—transmigration nor cessation; it is neither suffering nor its origin;
and so on, up to neither wisdom nor attainment. Thus, it is neither the cause and effect of the mundane or supramundane realms, nor the wisdom that can empty, nor the principle that is emptied.
If it were not dāna, nor even up to pāramitā, then it would not be the practice by which a bodhisattva can advance, nor would it be the principle toward which one advances;
in short, it would not be a supramundane dharma. Thus, it would likewise not be the Tathāgata.
If it were not the Arhat Samyak-saṃbuddha, it would not be the three titles of the Tathāgata;
if it were not Great Nirvāṇa, nor permanence, bliss, self, and purity, it would not be the four virtues of Nirvāṇa, up to and including the supreme dharma of the supramundane.
*Dāna* is translated here as "giving" (*boshī*). *Śīla* is translated as "precepts" (*jiè*). *Vīrya* is translated as "diligence" (*jīngjìn*). *Kṣānti* is translated as "patience" (*rěn*).
*Dhyāna* is translated as "meditative concentration" (*dìng*). *Prajñā* is translated as "wisdom" (*zhì*). *Pāramitā* is translated as "reaching the other shore" (*dàobītàn*).

*Tathāgata* is translated as "Thus-Come One" (*rúlái*). *Arhat* is translated as "Worthy of Offerings" (*yìnggòng*). *Samyaksaṃbodhi* is translated as "Right and Universal [Enlightenment]" (*zhèngbiàn*).
"Knowledge. Nirvāṇa—here translated as "non-arising and non-ceasing"—is the collective name for the four virtues. Regarding "Permanence":

it is not only that the two deaths are forever forgotten and all arising and ceasing are absent, but also that the characteristics of the world abide eternally, being ultimately firm and solid. Regarding "Bliss":
it is not only that one is free from the sufferings of birth and death, but also that one attains inconceivable liberation and enjoys [the Dharma] without end.
This is the measure of the joy of the Dharma. As for "I," it is not only that I have realized the true Dharmakāya, which is like empty space;
it is also that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, and even the finest motes of dust are all fully revealed as the Dharma King.

As for "purity," it is not only that the wondrously pure essence of principle is free from all defilement and attachment; it is also that this purity is omnipresent, such that there is nothing stained that is not pure. This is Nirvana.

This refers to their distinct characteristics. Next, it clarifies that they are identical with all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), thereby concluding the demonstration that the conventional truth is the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Because the *tathāgatagarbha* is immovable and all-pervasive, yet manifests in accordance with karma, it is said to be "identical with the *tathāgatagarbha*."
The original, luminous, and wondrous mind is precisely the seven elements (mahābhūtas), the six sense organs (indriyas), the six sense objects (viṣayas), and the six consciousnesses (vijñānas);
this is the mundane dharma. It is precisely the dharma of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharma of the śrāvakas, and the dharma of the bodhisattvas;
this is the supramundane dharma. It is precisely the three titles of the Tathāgata and the four virtues of nirvāṇa; this is the supreme-supreme supramundane dharma.
Furthermore, it clarifies the *tathāgatagarbha* by means of both negation and illumination, thereby establishing the emptiness and non-emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Since the *tathāgatagarbha* cannot be apprehended through thought, mind, speech, or deliberation, it is said:

"The wondrously luminous fundamental mind of the *tathāgatagarbha* is fundamentally not fixed as being identical [to phenomena], nor is it fixed as being non-identical. Therefore, it is described as "transcending identity" (*li ji*).
It is "separate from non-identity. This pair negates both extremes. Furthermore, it is not definitively restricted to being separate from identity; hence it is said to be "identical.
Nor is it definitively restricted to being separate from non-identity; hence it is said to be "not identical. The character "is" (shi) runs through the following.
"Like clouds, 'not separate' is itself 'not not-separate. This also illuminates both extremes simultaneously.

If one were to clarify the *tathāgatagarbha* solely by means of its being "not all phenomena," one would stagnate in emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If one were to clarify the *tathāgatagarbha* solely by means of its being "identical to all phenomena," one would stagnate in existence (*bhava*).
If one were to clarify the *tathāgatagarbha* by means of "neither separate nor identical," one would [fall into] abandonment.

If one clings to the Middle Way while remaining stuck in the two extremes, or if one regards "being identical" as "not being identical," one merely clarifies the *tathāgatagarbha* while abandoning the Middle Way and remaining stuck in the two extremes.

Therefore, when one is entirely non-identical yet identical, entirely identical yet non-identical, separate yet not separate, and not separate yet separate, then the three truths are harmoniously integrated.
Beyond names and transcending marks, this is the inconceivable essence, perfectly wondrous and ultimate.
...Indeed.
How is it that sentient beings within the three realms of existence (up to: cherish the Lesser Vehicle and consider a small attainment sufficient?
This sutra takes the three Tathāgatagarbhas as its primary theme. Although it speaks of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it does not [separate them] from the Dharma.
Huā agreed. He [the Buddha] revealed it for the sake of the assembly, so as to cause them to awaken to and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This was specifically because Pūrṇa did not understand that the nature and characteristics of all dharmas are non-dual, and that they all manifest according to karma based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Therefore, he asked why the appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth suddenly arise, and further spoke of their mutual submergence and extinction; this would then accord with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Seeing things as contrary, you instead give rise to erroneous challenges; therefore it is said: "Using worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Yet, the Tathāgatagarbha has never not been the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it is simply that one need not "place a head upon a head.

Furthermore, the World-Honored One, relying on a single truth, designates names according to circumstances and expounds them for the sake of others, just as a mani jewel [reflects various colors] according to [the objects it encounters].
Regarding the reflection of colors: if the pearl is a single entity, can it be said that blue, yellow, red, and white are merely a single color?
The lute and zither serve as metaphors for the essence of the jewel-like awakened nature; the exquisite sound serves as a metaphor for the wondrous function of the true mind;
and the skillful fingers serve as a metaphor for wondrous wisdom. Just as skillful fingers can produce exquisite sounds, so too can wondrous wisdom give rise to wondrous functions.
Regarding "treasure" (ratna), the traditional explanation briefly outlines three meanings: first, being free from defilement; second, possessing radiance; and third, abounding in wealth and utility.

The essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-avikāra*), which is immutable, corresponds to the meaning of being free from defilement. Its aspect of perfect illumination corresponds to the meaning of radiance.

The function of responding to conditions is the meaning of "wealth. Consider the two characters "pressing the finger" (àn zhǐ) in contrast with the two characters "raising the mind" (jǔ xīn) that follow;
this specifically reveals its wondrous function. View them simply as a method of expression; do not be restricted by the metaphorical text.

It is merely a case of using the pressing of a finger to illustrate that the raising of the mind is not [ordinary] wisdom. As for the "Ocean Seal" (Hǎiyìn): it is like, for example, in Jambudvīpa, one...
The bodies of all sentient beings, as well as external forms within the great ocean, all bear their reflections; therefore, it is called the "Ocean Seal" (Sāgarāmudrā).

It is the same for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: having attained the Samādhi of the Great Ocean Seal, they are able to discern the mental activities of all sentient beings and attain the illumination of wisdom regarding all dharma-gates.
Commentary: This passage universally rebukes those of the mundane and the Hinayana, urging them forward toward the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). The intended meaning is as follows:

the wondrously luminous, primordial mind of the *tathāgatagarbha* is the perfect fusion of the three truths (*triratna*), wherein not a single dharma is established. It is a realm that cannot be reached by thought, mind, speech, or deliberation.

How then can the sentient beings of the three realms of existence in the world, as well as the practitioners of the two vehicles who have transcended the world, each rely upon their respective [limited understandings]?
One takes the object of knowledge and the knowing mind and reflects upon and measures them, claiming that the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed bodhi is likewise realized by oneself.
How could one know that unsurpassed bodhi is the Tathāgata, who has personally realized the inconceivable realm of liberation through unobstructed wisdom?
How can it be grasped through the discrimination of the conscious mind? Moreover, how much less can it be attained by employing worldly [means]?
In the midst of such talk, when questions are posed, various conceptual signs suddenly arise; they overwhelm and exclude one another, yet you wish to enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?
You do not realize that no matter how much you employ thought and measure with it, you cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom. Below, a metaphor is set forth to urge him forward:
"It is like the lute, the harp, the *konghou*, and the *pipa*; though they possess exquisite sounds, if there is no..."

Even with exquisite fingers, one can never produce a sound. You and all sentient beings are just like this: the essence of the precious awakening and the wondrous function of the true mind are each perfectly complete within you.
If you attain unimpeded, wondrous wisdom, you will immediately be able to manifest its immeasurable, wondrous functions.
If you lack this wondrous wisdom, then although you possess the essence of the precious awakening, you cannot manifest its wondrous functions. Thus it is said:
Just as lutes, zithers, and other instruments all possess exquisite sounds, whether they can produce them or not depends solely on the presence or absence of skillful fingers.
Likewise, within the essence of the precious nature of awakening, a single press of the finger constitutes the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*), which radiates great light;
thus, the mental activities of all sentient beings and all dharma-gates [are revealed].

All have attained the brilliance of wisdom. Within the essential substance of the precious nature of awakening, if you momentarily raise your mind, you will immediately perceive the deluded mind and the deluded objects perceived by it;
