thus, the dust and toil of the world fill your eyes and arise before you first. This is what is meant by:
"I take this wondrous, bright, unarisen, and undying [nature] to be conjoined with the Tathāgata-garbha," yet the Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened brightness, perfect and complete.
It illuminates the dharma-realm. You take form and emptiness to mutually negate and supplant one another within the Tathāgatagarbha;
yet the Tathāgatagarbha, in turn, conforms to form and emptiness, pervading the entire dharma-realm.

Now, the reason why its essence is perfect while its function remains deficient and unrefined is truly because your faculties are dull and your will is weak, such that you are unwilling to diligently seek the unsurpassed path of enlightenment, and instead cherish only the small [vehicle].
They merely attain the *śeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder), clinging to the illusory city and losing sight of the true treasure. This is because they consider a small attainment to be sufficient.
Pūrṇa said: "I and the Tathāgata... [up to] ...self-obscuring our wondrous clarity and undergoing this drowning."
Commentary: This section consists of one summary and one question, intended to exhaustively investigate the cause of delusion.

From the words "I and the Tathāgata" onwards, it summarizes the meaning of the preceding passage regarding the treasure-like true mind (*tathatā-citta*) being perfectly complete in each and every instance. However, in the past, I encountered beginningless false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Having long remained in saṃsāra, you accepted the prior argument that establishes the object; once the object was falsely established, your false subjectivity arose.
This leads to the meaning of the "threefold continuity," which concludes with the two phrases regarding the attainment of the fruit of sainthood.
The passage beginning with "The World-Honored One [says] all delusions... accepts the previous four metaphors, as well as the bodhi of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
The meaning of "expounding Nirvana" is likewise thus. [The passage] beginning with "I venture to ask" is the formal inquiry into the cause of the arising of delusion.
The intent is this: I have only attained a minor fruit and have not yet reached the ultimate; therefore, I do not know what causes delusion to arise.

The World-Honored One has exhausted the five abodes and forever forgotten the two deaths; that which is called the total and perfect cessation, the solitary, wondrous, true, and eternal, transcends the world.

There is no worldly phenomenon that he does not fully comprehend. I venture to ask: for what reason do all sentient beings give rise to delusion, thereby obscuring the wondrously luminous function upon the essence of their precious awakening, and thus undergo this drowning in samsara? My previous question was: "How did the appearances of mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?

You replied: "Because of clarity, the objective world is established. Once the objective world has been falsely established, within the state where there is neither sameness nor difference, [the world] blazes forth..."
Yet, they have established a distinction. Now, let us further inquire: since that which was falsely established is itself false, from what does it arise?

This dialogue is intended precisely to clarify the principle of perfect awakening and perfect realization—transcending all stages and attaining right enlightenment at the very moment of first resolving to attain the Way—thereby serving as the fundamental basis for the "Section on Cultivating the Path."
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "Although you have removed your doubts... [the nature of delusion is thus; for what reason does it exist?
*Commentary:* This clarifies that delusion fundamentally has no cause, thereby refuting Pūrṇa’s doubt regarding the extinction of delusion to seek the truth.

The meaning is: although you heard that "based on illumination, the object is established," and since the object is already falsely established, you have already removed the doubt that mountains suddenly arise.
The doubts regarding the river and the delusions concerning the extinction of what cannot be contained do not yet realize that these are false and without cause;
thus, you forcibly seek their causes and attempt to extinguish them. This is precisely because residual delusions have not been exhausted.
If you do not realize that the root of the false is fundamentally without cause and likewise without extinction, I shall now question you based on a single present matter. Examine this thoroughly.

From this, it can be understood. Have you not heard of the story of Yaśoda in the city of Śrāvastī, who one morning suddenly looked at his face in a mirror, mistook his own head for a reflection, and—believing it to be a goblin—ran about wildly and uncontrollably?
What do you think? How would you explain this? For what reason did he run about so frantically without cause?
"Yes, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. Because the World-Honored One first demonstrated this to him without cause, he then investigated it by asking why there was no cause;
thus, upon these words, he attained realization. He replied, 'This person has merely gone mad and run away due to the arousal of his own mind;
there is no other cause. The Buddha then raised the Dharma to clarify this, saying: 'The wondrously enlightened and luminous mind is the source from which Buddhas are born.'"
It is equally perfect. Its essence is fundamentally complete; its function is fundamentally luminous and wondrous. It has never lacked anything, nor has it ever experienced delusion or awakening.
Within the midst of sentient beings, delusion has never actually arisen. Furthermore, since it is called "delusion," how could it have a cause?
If it had a cause, it would be substantially existent; how then could it be delusion? If one investigates its cause, from the very beginning—
These are one's own deluded thoughts, arising through a continuous succession of mutual causes; from the beginning, they possess no substantial reality.

Yet these deluded thoughts rely solely upon a single moment of mental confusion, whereby confusion begets further confusion, passing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust until they have accumulated to a profound depth. Therefore:
Although the Buddha has explained this to you in various ways, you are still unable to turn back from delusion to return to the truth, and instead merely seek the cause of delusion.
How could you know that such a cause for delusion exists solely because one has become deluded regarding one's own wondrously enlightened and luminous perfection?
It exists because of this fundamental, perfectly luminous wonder; there is no other cause. You further said: "World-Honored One, all delusions are completely extinguished."
If one can simply recognize that this delusion is fundamentally without cause, then your own discursive thought will have nothing upon which to rely.

If this is so, then since all sentient beings currently transmigrating do not yet perceive even the existence of such delusory arising, how can you say that the World-Honored One has completely extinguished all delusions and seeks to eliminate them by searching for their causal source? From the very beginning, [this has never been the case].

If it has already arisen, why does it now cease? As for one who has attained Bodhi, although they have achieved great awakening, how could they definitively point to past delusive causes to show them to others?
To now explain delusion in detail is like a person upon waking recounting the events of a dream;
however brilliant their mind may be, by what means or cause could they directly seize the objects perceived within that dream?
This is to demonstrate it to others. Yet, even the objects perceived therein, though belonging to a dream, are not entirely non-existent in the world;
they ought to be graspable, yet one cannot grasp them. How much less so for groundless delusions, which fundamentally lack any cause?
Now you wish for me to point out its cause and extinguish it; how could this be possible?
That you harbor such deluded thoughts is just like that Dāmadhara who possessed a nature of madness; how could one become mad only after there has been a cause and condition?
Originally, it was because one was deluded about one's own head and mistook it for a reflection, running about in terror.

If that head were truly subject to gain or loss, it would not be called madness. Suddenly, when the nature of madness ceases, the head is not obtained from without; even if the madness has not yet ceased.
The head is fundamentally sovereign; what loss could there be? If the essence of the wondrous enlightened nature truly possessed gain or loss, it would not be called delusion.
Awakening is not obtained from without, and delusion is not a true loss; therefore, it is called delusion. Such is the nature of your delusion.
Since the deluded nature of Yajñadatta has no location, its cause cannot be found; how then could it be extinguished?
○ *Yajñadatta* means "receiving from a shrine," as he obtained [his name] by requesting it from a deity.
This [story] of running mad after looking into a mirror serves as a metaphor for the two types of retribution—the primary and secondary—within the nine realms of existence. All...
The images within the great round mirror are by nature fundamentally empty;
yet, because all sentient beings mistake their heads for these reflections, they give rise to false notions of grasping and rejecting, and thus run about wildly without ceasing.
"You need only not follow after the discrimination of the world (up to) will suddenly realize that the divine pearl was not obtained from without.
[Commentary: This demonstrates the dharma-gate of perfect awakening and perfect realization. The meaning is: you have been seeking the cause of delusion.

It was as if you had sought this cause and exhausted your sinews and pained your bones in order to sever it. Now that you have realized that delusion is without cause, why must you still act in such a manner?
You need only awaken to the fact that the world, karma, and its fruits, as well as the threefold continuity of sentient beings, are like reflections in a mirror—fundamentally not truly existent.
One falsely perceives them as existing, yet even this delusion is without cause; it does not exist of itself.
To accord with these three is to give rise to the deluded mind of discrimination.

Once this mind ceases for a moment, the three conditions are suddenly severed, and the habitual tendencies of the threefold flow can no longer arise. This is what is called the "cessation of active manifestation."
Then the seeds will not sprout. Again, he brings up the previous analogy and points it out directly, saying:

"For you to recognize these three kinds as truly existent and thereby give rise to grasping and attachment is exactly like Datta recognizing the reflection of a head in a mirror and running about in a frenzy.
If you truly understand that the delusion is without cause and your discrimination suddenly ceases, this is precisely the Datta within your own mind."

Much. At the moment when the nature of madness naturally subsides—since this single instance of madness ceases, it is immediately *bodhi* itself, requiring no further effort—it is just as when Upāli’s madness suddenly ceased;
his head was not obtained from without. Even if the madness has not yet subsided, [it is already so].

What, then, has been lost? Therefore it is said that the supreme, pure, and luminous mind is fundamentally coextensive with the Dharma-realm; it is not obtained from others. What is meant is simply this:
when one is free from deluded thoughts, one is immediately the Tathāgata. Why rely on investigating the truth, severing afflictions, or undergoing arduous cultivation and realization?
Alas, all sentient beings are currently shrouded by the five aggregates, and thus their supreme, pure, and luminous mind is likewise obscured.
It is as if a person has tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within their own garment, yet remains deluded regarding this mind and is unable to realize its ultimate potential;
they merely pursue the minor fruits of the human and celestial realms, like one who carries a jewel while wandering abroad to beg for food.
Although they remain on a path of delusion, they have never fundamentally lost the truth; it is just as one may be truly impoverished, yet the jewel has never been lost. One day, upon seeing it—
The Buddha heard the Dharma and realized this supreme, pure, and luminous mind, which has always been coextensive with the Dharma-realm and was not obtained from another.
Only then did he know that it does not depend on arduous labor or painstaking cultivation and realization; it is like a wise person suddenly pointing out a pearl to someone.
One’s wishes will follow the heart, leading to great abundance; only then will one realize that the divine pearl is not obtained from without.

Nevertheless, to say that the cessation of madness is itself *bodhi*—how easy is that to talk about? *Bodhi* is the designation for the wisdom of the fruit; it is the essence of the supreme, pure, and luminous mind.
It is the simultaneous elevation of both the essence and the wisdom. "Ken" refers to the meat between the bones; it is the binding of the muscles and sinews.
The term *qi* (綮) refers specifically to the subtle meaning of severing delusions. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"Nothing arises from conditions; nothing ceases from conditions. Arising is merely the arising of conditions; ceasing is merely the ceasing of conditions."
At that moment, Ānanda was among the great assembly... (until) "I only pray that you will, out of great compassion, enlighten me who am bewildered and distressed.
[Commentary: This is the third instance of the disciple seizing upon the teaching according to his capacity. Following the Buddha’s words, he clings to the idea that causes and conditions are real.
Initially, he clung to the seeing-essence as belonging to causes and conditions; next, he clung to all phenomena as belonging to causes and conditions; this is the proof of his clinging.

The fruit must indeed belong to causes and conditions. My intention is this: previously you utterly rejected causes and conditions, yet now you speak of severing the three kinds of discriminative conditions so that the three causes—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—do not arise. This makes it perfectly clear that causes and conditions exist.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata, having already taught causes and conditions, subsequently and abruptly discard them? Furthermore, as for people like us...
By means of these causal dharmas, the mind attains awakening. Furthermore, how could it be that only we junior śrāvakas in training have attained realization through this?

Even those in this assembly such as Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who initially followed an old brahmin to practice heterodox paths, encountered Uruvilvākāśyapa and others along the way and heard his teaching on [the arising of suffering].
Having extinguished the causes and conditions of the Four Noble Truths and attained awakening through faith and compliance, one then beholds the Buddha and achieves the fruit of sainthood.
Now it is said that the nature of madness ceasing of itself is *bodhi*; it does not rely upon causes and conditions. This is like what Kuśarī and others previously taught:
that after eighty thousand kalpas, one spontaneously attains the Way, just as a ball of thread comes to rest when its end is reached, without requiring further effort.

"Practitioner and Realizer" (xiūzhèng zhě) is a translation for the *paramārtha-satya* (the ultimate truth). If the World-Honored One does not fall into [the realm of] causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), he would then fall into spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
This is another point where we are bewildered and unable to resolve it; we pray that you will grant us great compassion and elucidate it.
Regarding "killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct," the traditional explanation briefly cites the causes of karmic results, yet its intent encompasses all beings in the world.
It is born. Yet the seed of Buddhahood arises from conditions; causes and conditions fundamentally do not obstruct Bodhi—it is merely the grasping at them that constitutes an obstruction.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is just like [the people] in the city... (up to)... as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, who only increase their frivolous proliferation."

According to this sutra: "In principle, there is sudden enlightenment; through this enlightenment, all is simultaneously extinguished. In phenomena, there is no sudden elimination; they are exhausted through gradual stages.
Thus, the two gates of understanding (*jie*) and practice (*xing*) must not be neglected in isolation from one another. However, practice arises from understanding;

when practice arises, understanding is transcended—this is how one draws near [to the goal]. Furthermore, if one knows that the cessation of madness is itself Bodhi, yet fails to realize that the ground of the cause is not...

The mind of arising and ceasing; its fruition-ground awareness is non-arising and non-ceasing. It is not through practice that it is realized, nor does one fall into the obstacle of principle while abandoning actual practice.
[Crown Commentary: This simultaneously brushes away both causes-and-conditions and spontaneity, thereby clarifying that the nature of madness subsides of itself. When it subsides, it is...
This is the correct purport of Bodhi. Desiring to sweep away such calculations, one must first examine the underlying disposition.
The intention is this: that which you cling to and begrudge does not exceed two possibilities. Now, let us examine one of these through the case of Madhyantika.
You must surely maintain that if the causal conditions for Madhyantika’s madness were to be extinguished, then the state of non-madness would naturally emerge; therefore, you hold to this.
One must scrutinize the principles of arising-and-ceasing versus non-arising-and-non-ceasing. If it is not through causes and conditions, it must be spontaneous;
if it is not spontaneous, it must be through causes and conditions. Once these two paths are exhausted, reasoning reaches its limit and all calculations are spent.

Examining this closely and determining it with certainty, [the text] says: "Suppose that the head of Devadatta is fundamentally spontaneous; since it is spontaneous, it is also fundamentally natural."

Thus, whether one is insane or not insane is nothing other than spontaneous (*svabhāva*). For what reason, due to the act of looking into a mirror, does one suddenly become terrified of having no head and run about in madness?

If one calculates both possibilities together, saying that there is a head by way of spontaneity, yet one becomes terrified of having no head due to the causal conditions of looking into the mirror, and thus runs about in madness—then [the text] immediately refutes this calculation of causal conditions, stating: "This is..."
Causes and conditions are not real. Why is this? If causes and conditions were truly existent, why would that which is naturally present not remain as it is?
How could one’s original head be actually lost simply because of looking into a mirror? Although he fears being headless, his original head has not been lost;
yet, he is pointlessly and madly terrified, falsely claiming only that he is headless. Furthermore, while he is in the midst of such frantic terror, he perceives nothing at all.
When one has a head, there is nothing lost; when the madness subsides and one awakens to the fact that one has a head, there is nothing gained.

Yet, the arising of madness and the subsiding of madness have never undergone any change. Thus, it is clear that the original head certainly does not cease to exist depending on the conditions of looking into a mirror.
Below, he refutes the notion of "naturalness" by saying: "If you claim that both madness and sanity belong to..."

If [madness] were natural—that is, not dependent upon causes and conditions—then madness would originally arise from nature itself. Consequently, one ought to have been constantly possessed by madness and fear from the very beginning;
yet one does not know where this nature of madness was hidden during the time before one was mad, such that it did not arise.
Since there is no place for it to be hidden, it is clear that madness does not belong to nature. If you claim that non-madness arises...
Within the realm of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), the head is fundamentally without loss; one ought to always remain free from delusion and madness.
Why then do you fear your head and run about in a frenzy? If you know that the head is subject to no change, it does not exist by depending on causes and conditions, nor does it exist spontaneously.

It is evident that [the notion of] madness has been recklessly produced out of delusion and fear. Since one knows that the head and madness are thus related, one then knows that the true nature of Bodhi is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor is it spontaneous;
those who calculate it as being either caused by conditions or spontaneous are all merely producing delusions.

Therefore, directly expressing the correct intention, it is said: "If one awakens to the fact that the original head has never been gained or lost, one will naturally be able to recognize and know it."

"Frantic running is merely the manifestation of delusion. If one were to truly and personally perceive the true nature of Bodhi—neither lost through delusion nor attained through awakening—then the nature of madness would suddenly cease.
Thus, both causes and conditions are naturally but idle discourse, entirely devoid of real meaning. He further elaborates his own view, stating: "For this reason, both are equally idle discourse."
Therefore, I say that when the three kinds of discriminative conditions are severed, this very moment is the true mind of Bodhi.
However, those who calculate that the mind of Bodhi arises only after the conditions have been severed likewise fall into conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Why is this?
Because they claim that the mind of Bodhi arises while the mind of birth-and-death ceases; this is merely a mind of birth-and-death and is still not Bodhi.

This is the true mind. Now, to permit the arising of bodhicitta only when conditions are severed, while not permitting the arising of bodhicitta through the mere severing of conditions, precisely reveals that not only must the mind of arising and ceasing be exhausted, but that which exhausts arising and ceasing must also be exhausted.
One must relinquish the *ālayavijñāna* and reach the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*) before one is close to Bodhi. Upon reaching this stage, Bodhi—

The arising of the mind is likewise not permitted. How could it be permitted that [arising] occurs spontaneously? If there were such spontaneity, then the spontaneous nature of the mind’s arising would be a mind of arising-and-ceasing;
this very spontaneity would itself be arising-and-ceasing. This is merely frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Why is this so?
You define "spontaneous" as that which is without arising or ceasing according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); yet this is merely a relative designation.
That which arises and ceases according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is established by means of causes and conditions; it is not truly characterized by arising and ceasing.
To clarify this through an analogy: just as in the world, when various elements combine and blend to form a single entity, this is called "the nature of combination" (*saṃghāta-svabhāva*).
Regarding this nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), one then points to that which is not conjoined and calls it the "original nature" (*prakṛti*).
Thus, this original nature and that conjunction both belong to the realm of duality; how could they be anything other than conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)?

Only when the original nature is no longer the original nature, and conjunction is no longer conjunction—when both non-being-as-such and non-conjunction are transcended, and both transcendence and non-transcendence are likewise transcended—is there liberation.

No. Only at this point can it be called the "phrase beyond words and transcending negation," the final phrase that stands forth in solitary excellence; only then is it the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*).

However, while the principle must be realized suddenly, its realization depends on the gradual exhaustion of phenomena. Even if one’s realization reaches this level, it still belongs to the mind of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*);
the *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* of the fruition stage remain far distant. How much more so for one who does not abandon the dharma of conceptual proliferation?

And yet you wish to realize Bodhi—how could that possibly be achieved? Therefore, know this: Bodhi and Nirvana are not something that can be cultivated or realized by one who has labored diligently through kalpas in mere learning and memorization.
It is not only because you have failed to realize Bodhi despite memorizing the Dharma I have taught;
even if you were to recall and uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, [you would still not attain it].
Even knowing the subtle principle of purity as many times as the sands of the Ganges is itself an obstruction to the principle;
furthermore, if the habitual tendencies of names and words are not eliminated, it merely serves to increase frivolous proliferation.
"Although you speak of causes and conditions and spontaneity (up to the point of asking), how can you still deceive yourself by lingering in mere observation and listening?
This was the World-Honored One’s most earnest reprimand and exhortation, intended to urge him toward further cultivation.

He stated that cultivation for a single day cannot be compared to [cultivation over] kalpas, and cultivation for a single thought-moment cannot be compared to [cultivation over] a single day. Is it not so, Ānanda Bhikṣu?
Even Yaśodharā’s female body cannot be compared to her; how much less so could the courtesan Āmrapālī? Furthermore, she was inferior even to Yaśodharā.
In a previous life, Āmrapālī was a Brahmin woman named Prakṛti; she now bears that former name, and is thus called Bhikṣuṇī Prakṛti.
The above concludes the section on the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga); the following text elucidates the section on the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Commentary: This passage is an extreme rebuke of the hindrance of mere erudition (*bahuśruta*), intended to spur the cultivation of the out-flow-free (*anāsrava*) wisdom. It says:

"Although you are able to discourse upon the conditions-dependent (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the spontaneous (*svabhāva*), being decisively clear and without the slightest error, such that you are ranked as the foremost among those of great learning;
yet, despite this erudition accumulated through熏習 (*vāsanā*, habitual perfuming) over many kalpas, you cannot escape or abandon evil."
The difficulty of subduing through incantations is such that, had he possessed this much learning, he could have been liberated from the arts of lust.

Why wait for me to emit light from my great crown and proclaim a divine incantation before Daṅga’s heart-fire of lust could suddenly be extinguished, his coarse delusions severed, and he realized the third fruit, thereby attaining the status of a Non-returner who dwells in retribution and is no longer born in the desire realm? Even if Daṅga were in the river of craving—
It will not wither. How could it enable you to escape the calamity of lust?

Therefore, although you have labored diligently through kalpas to memorize and uphold the secret verses of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and their wondrous, adorned, and pure realms, your habitual outflows of seeing and hearing remain.
In the end, none can eliminate it. It is better to enter non-discrimination for a single day and suddenly sever the three conditions;
thus, one will not fall into the discrimination of defilement and purity. Even upon seeing the coarse and turbid appearance of a courtesan, one does not give rise to a mind of aversion;

even upon seeing the pure and wondrous appearance of a Tathāgata, one likewise does not give rise to a mind of attachment. One is then naturally able to distance oneself from the many births of the mundane world.
These are the two sufferings of hatred and attachment. Furthermore, he cites those of inferior capacity who have received benefit, yet rebukes them sternly, saying:
"Consider Mātaṅgī, who was formerly a courtesan; how profound and heavy were her karmic obstructions!

Yet, through the power of the divine mantra, her lustful desires were dissolved, and she now dwells within the Dharma under the name and surname of Bhikṣuṇī. Moreover, consider Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula."
Together they realized their past causes; only then did they know that throughout successive lifetimes they had been reborn in female bodies entirely due to the depth of their sensual desires.
Now, by virtue of the opening of their past destinies, they clearly perceived many kalpas and repented with utmost sincerity.

Because they cultivated untainted goodness based on this single thought-moment, Trijaṭā was immediately released from her entanglements, and Yaśodharā already received her prediction of enlightenment. Indeed, Yaśo...

To have been born as a woman is already a state of inferiority and weakness; yet even the courtesan Sundarī, being even more base than that, has now attained great benefit through the cultivation of a single thought-moment.
How much more so for you, who possess the faculties and wisdom of a man and have received the Buddha-dharma!
On the contrary, some are attached to mere erudition and do not cultivate the outflow-free (anāsrava) states.

Although they clearly understand that conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is fruitless while cultivation is beneficial, they still retain the discrimination of what has been seen and heard, remaining addicted to conceptual proliferation; how can this be anything other than self-deception?

Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, remained with single-minded attention in the assembly, awaiting the Tathāgata’s compassionate teaching on *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, the awakening of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), and the path of the original arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), which is the mind of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).

This was specifically to seek instruction on the mind of the causal stage in order to attain the awakening of the stage of fruition. As for the two attachments of objective grasping and discursive discrimination, these have already been [discussed] previously.
"Having been revealed, shown, awakened to, and realized. This is again a request for the path of entry. Revelation and showing depend on others; awakening and entry depend on oneself. [Commentary:
This first describes the assembly’s realization, followed by their request for the gateway to practice. Having heard from the Buddha...

This instruction serves to eliminate doubts and confusion, comprehensively pointing back to the numerous previous refutations regarding the conditions of causality, spontaneity, and the union or non-union of phenomena.

For those who awaken to the true reality (*dharmatā*), it refers distantly to that which is neither identical to nor different from [phenomena], being both identical and non-identical—the *Tathāgatagarbha* mind;
and it refers proximately to the natural subsiding of the nature of madness, wherein such subsiding is itself *bodhi*, the supremely pure and luminous mind.
This week’s Dharma realm is not obtained from others; for the three conditions have been simultaneously severed.

This is precisely the bodhicitta, the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*), and all such states as being neither joined nor separated. As for the lightness and ease (*praśrabdhi*) of body and mind, it consists in relinquishing conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

He attained the perception of right concentration; his mind was like the empty ocean. "Attaining what he had never before" means that he was profoundly rejoiced at hearing what he had not heard before.
Ānanda’s realization deepened further upon reaching this point, and his sorrowful emotion became even more acute;
thus it is said that he wept again and again, all of which is recorded by the author of the sutra. This unsurpassed great compassion surpasses all other compassionate minds.
Furthermore, "purity" refers to stainless wisdom (*vimalajñāna*). When compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem, benefit and bliss become inexhaustible.
Like a *maṇi* jewel, one attains mastery in rescuing and uplifting others according to their needs; therefore, it is called the "King of Jewels. Regarding the phrase "skillfully opening my mind":
it means that we were shrouded by delusion and ignorance, remaining unenlightened for a long time, until now we have received manifold instructions that enable us to attain awakening.

"Penetrating. The following clarifies the meaning of "skillfully opening up. "Thus" refers to the preceding words. "Various causes and conditions" refers to the intent beginning with the account of Yantradatta.
"Skillful means of uplifting and encouraging" means being able to rouse [the mind] to awaken it from deluded attachments, and to exhort and encourage it to shake off weariness and indolence.
"Lead" means to guide and assist. "Sinking" means to be mired in [suffering]. "Obscure" means to be obstructed.
"Obscured. "The ocean of suffering" refers specifically to the two oceans of suffering: hatred and attachment.

From the words "World-Honored One" onwards, [the text] conveys the realization of the aforementioned wondrous enlightened clarity of the Tathāgata-garbha-nature, which perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm, even to the point of turning the Great Wheel of Dharma while sitting within a mote of dust.
"Containing" means encompassing; "nurturing" means giving birth and raising. "Tathāgata" refers to the primary retribution; "land" (kṣetra) refers to the secondary retribution.

This means that we inherently possess such a vast Tathāgatagarbha-mind, adorned with pure jewels and nurturing the ten directions, yet we do not recognize this ourselves and merely sink into the sea of suffering.
The World-Honored One, giving rise to great compassion, uses various causes and conditions to uplift and encourage us.
I am deeply grateful that you have guided me to attain awakening; it is a source of unsurpassed joy.

Yet, the World-Honored One further rebuked my extensive learning as being without merit, stating it does not equal a single day’s cultivation of the outflow-free karma (*anāsrava-karman*). However, wishing to cultivate this karma, I find no door through which to enter.
I am now like a traveler who has suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King, yet fails to find its entrance. Ultimately...
None are able to enter. We pray that the Tathāgata will show us the place where the entrance lies.

Although the assembly here is obscured by obstructions and cannot see the path ahead, we have long lingered at the City of Transformation; now we shall ultimately renounce the Lesser Vehicle and proceed directly toward the Tathāgata’s Nirvana without remainder.
Therefore, we seek the ancient route of the Guide. If we may receive your instruction, we would be most grateful.
Furthermore, it causes those practitioners who have not yet entered the illusory city to, through this Dharma-gate, subdue their past攀緣 (pān-yuán) and deluded conceptualizations;
thereafter, they shall attain single-minded dhāraṇī, realize the perfect fusion of the Tripiṭaka, and deeply penetrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those in the assembly—[from "to" (至) through] "the two definitive meanings for awakening the initial resolve"—proceeded below to demonstrate these two definitive meanings.

This was because Ānanda had asked about the Tathāgata’s path of the original resolve for *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, as well as the subduing of objective conditions (*ālambana*) and the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, the World-Honored One [taught] by means of the two definitive meanings.

I shall explain this to you. If you wish to know the path by which the original aspiration was first generated, you must select the mind that is free from arising and ceasing to serve as the causal-ground mind;
only then can you perfectly accomplish the fruit-virtue of Nirvana, which is neither born nor extinguished. This is the foremost definitive principle regarding the initial aspiration.
If you wish to subdue and control discursive attachments, you must carefully examine where the root of these attachments lies.
Having understood the locus, one knows the root. Thereafter, one simply selects a single door among those of perfect faculties and enters deeply;

then, all six faculties of cognition will simultaneously become pure. This is the second definitive meaning for the beginner. To realize non-arising, one must select that which is subject to arising and ceasing.
To select that which is subject to arising and ceasing, one must know the fundamental afflictions. To sever these afflictions, one cannot be apart from the six [faculties].
The faculties (*indriya*). They merely know how to sink into birth and death and realize wondrous permanence, yet they have not yet transcended the six faculties;

therefore, these two meanings have never failed to complement one another. [Commentary on the Preface: This is a general indication of the two definitive meanings. One has not yet attained mastery over the bodhicitta.

"Those who abandon the small and aspire to the great, yet fail to find the gate through which to enter," refers to sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age, as well as ordinary practitioners of the Small Vehicle.
"The Unsurpassed Vehicle" refers to the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), indicating the awakening of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*).

"The Path of Sublime Cultivation" refers to entering directly into the Buddha Vehicle by means of this path; this indicates the causal practice. "Resolutely generating the Bodhicitta" [refers to] regarding the Buddha...

"The Tathāgata’s wondrous samādhi does not give rise to weariness" corresponds to the preceding passage, "having fully attained the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa without remainder. "Wondrous samādhi" refers to the path of wondrous cultivation.
"Does not give rise to weariness" means that one has now abandoned the illusory city and will proceed resolutely and directly to the place of treasure, no longer experiencing fatigue.

Furthermore, regarding "awakening the beginner": "Awakening" refers to *shijue* (initial awakening), meaning that one initially gives rise to this right mindfulness, remaining resolute without regressing and free from hesitation.
How are the two meanings of the initial mind determined? (Up to: From the beginning until the end, there are five layers of turbidity. *Commentary*:
This intends to clarify the first determined meaning of the initial mind; it first demonstrates the distinction between arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing.
The phrase "How... is a general inquiry. "Ānanda," and so forth, is the definitive determination, stating: "You all must be determined..."

Having renounced the Hīnayāna and cultivated the Bodhisattvayāna with the desire to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully and minutely examine whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is identical to or different from the awakening at the stage of the resultant fruit. If, within the causal ground...

To take a mind of birth and extinction—characterized by discrimination between causes and conditions and spontaneity—as the fundamental cause for cultivation, while seeking the fruit of the Buddha-vehicle’s nirvana of non-birth and non-extinction, is like wishing to go north while heading south; how could such a thing ever succeed?
Because the mind possesses both birth and extinction as well as non-birth and non-extinction, the root-body and the vessel-world are likewise so. You...
Since you have not yet recognized the meaning of arising and ceasing versus non-arising and non-ceasing within the realm of the body, you should illuminate all things in the world:
whatever phenomena are subject to action, they all undergo transition, change, decay, and destruction. You should further examine with subtle discernment:
among all conditioned phenomena, what is indestructible? Yet, one never hears of empty space decaying or being destroyed. Why is this? Because it is empty.

There is no fabrication, because there is neither beginning nor end. Yet, the phenomena that possess a beginning and an end—characterized by formation and destruction—are from the very outset never separate from the emptiness that is without beginning, end, formation, or destruction. Taking this vessel-world as an analogy for the realm of your own body:
the solid aspect of bone and flesh constitutes the earth element; the moistening fluids constitute the water element; the warmth...
The breath that touches is the fire element; the pulsating tendons and vessels are the wind element.
All of these are phenomena subject to arising and perishing. Because you grasp at these four great elements as the characteristics of the body, you bind yourself.
Thus, your original essence—naturally limpid, pervasive, and perfect—the wondrous functioning of the intrinsically awakened luminous mind, becomes like the vast void.

That which is without beginning or end, birth or cessation, instead becomes turbid rather than limpid and tranquil; it instead becomes fragmented and obstructed rather than all-pervasive and complete.
Thus, it is divided into the six faculties of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing. Once these six faculties have been formed, [the state of unity is lost].

Thus, the five sense faculties and the six sense objects are collectively termed the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). From the interaction of the first five faculties with their respective five objects, the five consciousnesses are initiated;

this is termed the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*). From the mental images conditioned by the preceding objects, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is induced; this is termed the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).
The first six consciousnesses, having already become defiled conditions, arise and perish moment by moment within them while firmly grasping at the mark of a self;

this is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Since there are the prior seven kinds of manifest perfuming, that Tathāgata-garbha transforms into the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*);

this is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Thus, with the aggregate of form as the beginning and the aggregate of consciousness as the end, there are consequently five layers of turbid confusion.
Furthermore, that which has a beginning and an end corresponds with the aforementioned absence of beginning and end.
Why is this called turbidity? Ānanda, it is like clear water... (up to)... this fifth layer is named the turbidity of life (*āyuṣkaṣāya*).

Regarding these five turbidities: from the moment a single thought causes the luminous true mind to become a deluded mind, and one becomes confused about true emptiness as being a dull void, one immediately undergoes the suffering of saṃsāra for hundreds and thousands of kalpas—all of which is entirely turbid and incapable of clarity.
Therefore, the method for clarifying this turbidity is bestowed; first, the cause of the arising of turbidity is shown. This uses the essence of clear, still water as a metaphor.
The profound, perfect, and wondrous awakening uses obstructed earth and sand as a metaphor for the four great elements and the six sense organs.
The image of two substances churning together to form a state of turbidity is a metaphor for grasping the four great elements as a self;

thus, through the faculties, objects, and consciousness, the true nature becomes turbid and forms the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Regarding the arising of the five aggregates, it initially originates from the true nature.

Following conditions, it transforms into the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*). Driven by the winds of objects, the karma-consciousness evolves into the two divisions of the perceiving subject and the perceived object (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*), which subsequently arise through mutual interaction in an uninterrupted succession.

This sutra begins with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and concludes with the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) to ensure that the practitioner cuts away from the outside, like clearing turbid water, proceeding from the coarse to the subtle.
It is for this reason. Furthermore, as in the preceding section on the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it was illuminated by the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

therefore, the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world were none other than the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. In this present section on the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one still relies upon the knowledge and vision of sentient beings.
As contact with objects gives rise to mental states, the two realms of the body and the environment are nothing other than illusory objects.
Therefore, one must resolutely understand from where these illusory objects before one arise and from where they cease. Thus, the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) should be realized everywhere;
the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) should be undertaken within one's own body and mind. As the ancient masters said: "The mind is like a wall."
Only when one is like a wall can one enter the Way. It is also said: "From time to time, gather [the mind] within the cavity.
The holy teachings likewise state: "Seek only the lost mind. All of these convey this same meaning.
Commentary: This first presents the analogy followed by the application to the Dharma, together clarifying the turbidity of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

In the analogy, only the two substances of water and earth are borrowed; their mutual inseparability serves merely to describe the single characteristic of turbidity. *Lunlei* (倫類) means "category" or "analogy. *Liuai* (留礙) means "obstruction" or "impediment."
This refers to a solid mass with form. "The nature of things" (*dharmatā*) means the innate, fixed nature bestowed by Heaven.
"Not following one another" means not being in accord; it is like earth not following water to become clear, or water not following earth to become obstructed.
*Gul* means turbid and agitated. This precisely reveals the profoundly still, perfect, wondrously enlightened, and luminous mind, [in contrast] to the four great elements and the six...
The faculties and the fundamental [elements] do not originally correspond to one another. Due to the deluded attachment of a single thought, the four great elements constitute a body;
thus, the essence of awareness becomes turbid, giving rise to seeing, hearing, feeling, and cognizing. Consequently, there are five layers of turbidity.

Therefore it is said: "Your fivefold turbidity is likewise so. To accord with the Dharma, it is said: "Your profoundly still, perfect, and fundamentally awakened true vision and the great empty space are, from the beginning..."

It originally comes from a single essence that pervades the realms of the ten directions. Due to the movement of a single thought of delusion, it is divided into the six sense organs, whereby the subject and object become separated.
Thus, when one raises the eyes to see space, clarity and turbidity cannot be distinguished; there is space, yet there is no essence capable of seeing.
It is like water losing its clarity; there is a state of seeing where there is no awareness of emptiness. It is like earth losing its solidity;
when these two interweave, they falsely form the appearance of turbidity. As it is with the perception of emptiness, so it is with the perception of form.

As it is with the faculty of the eye, so it is with the other faculties. This is because, by grasping the four great elements as the characteristics of a body, the first five faculties naturally arise.
Confronting external objects, it robs the true mind and turbidizes its pure subtlety, collectively forming the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*);

this is the first layer, called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Once the aforementioned five sense organs confront their respective objects, the five consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) immediately arise.
By apprehending external objects, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is formed; therefore it is said:

"You currently grasp the four great elements as your substance, yet seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition are fundamentally one profound, pervasive, and wondrous awakening, originally free from obstruction. It is only because they are congested by the four great elements that this is so."
Thus, obstructiveness is established, just as water loses its clarity. The four characteristics of water and the other elements originally belong to material objects and possess no awareness;
yet, being whirled by the four natures of seeing and so forth, they come to possess awareness, just as earth loses its obstructiveness.
As these two interweave, they falsely create turbidity, which muddies the true mind. This is the second layer, called [the layer of] turbidity.
This constitutes the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*). "View" here carries the meaning of apprehension and reception.

Furthermore, by means of the images reflected from the external objects (*viṣaya*), the sixth consciousness is induced to form the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Therefore it is said: "Moreover, within your mind, you recollect and maintain past objects."
It discriminates present objects, recites and studies future objects; yet these three are originally without intrinsic nature.

Because they are produced by the cognition and vision of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they acquire the quality of existence. The mental consciousness itself has no original form, yet because it is manifested by the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), it also acquires form.
Thus, apart from these three kinds of dharmas as objects, there is no characteristic of the mental consciousness, just like water.
Purity is lost. Detached from the consciousness that perceives and cognizes, the nature of the three kinds of objects vanishes, like earth losing its solidity.
As the two interweave, they falsely produce turbid appearances that disturb the true nature; this is the third layer, called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*).
Once the first six consciousnesses have become defiled conditions, the seventh consciousness then engages in deliberation and clings to a self.

Within the profound, perfect, and wondrous awakening, the phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing arise; these moment-to-moment transitions constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Therefore it is said: "Arising and ceasing ceaselessly from morning until evening. Thus, the cognition and views that involve deliberation and grasping at a self desire, in every thought-moment, to remain eternally in the world;
yet the karmic movements of one's good and evil deeds secretly and constantly seek to migrate to another realm.

Earth: Thus, that which desires to remain cannot abide permanently, just as water loses its clarity; that which desires to shift does not necessarily depart all at once, just as earth loses its obstructive stability.
When these two interweave, they falsely produce the appearance of turbidity, thereby overturning the seed of Bodhi and forming the root of birth and death.
This is the fourth layer, called the *sattva-kaṣāya* (the turbidity of sentient beings). As for "sentient beings":

The mind arises through the conjunction of various conditions; it exists through the phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. The body exists through earth, water, fire, and wind—all of which share the meaning of being conjunctive.
Furthermore, due to the three factors of the preceding sense organs, objects, and consciousness, each possesses specific seeds and activities that permeate the *tathāgatagarbha*.
It transforms into the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), which contains and sustains [all seeds] as the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Therefore, it is said:
"Your six faculties—seeing, hearing, and so forth—are originally the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), yet their nature has never been different.

It is solely because you grasp the four great elements as a body that they are divided into the six faculties; these then confront the six sense objects and give rise to the six consciousnesses. Thus, there is the duality of subject and object."

The two parts are clearly separated and distinct, appearing as unrelated and different beings; yet their essential nature is fundamentally one, and their cognitive awareness is mutually pervasive, such that they seem identical rather than different—like earth losing its solidity. Their functions and activities are each distinct, diverging according to their respective objects.
Furthermore, it is as if they were different yet not the same, like water that has lost its clarity. Whether identical or distinct, these two cannot be fixed;
they interweave with one another, falsely forming the appearance of turbidity. Thus, the *tathāgatagarbha* is transformed into the cause of both defilement and purity.

This is the fifth layer, called the turbidity of life (*āyuṣkaṣāya*). "Life" (*āyu*) here refers to the act of commanding or impelling; it means that the *tathāgatagarbha* originally possesses no [defilements].
Arising and ceasing, going and coming, it is perfumed by the preceding seven consciousnesses and becomes the ālayavijñāna.

Since this [ālayavijñāna] contains both defiled and pure karmic seeds, it is driven by those karmic seeds to transmigrate through the various realms of existence; hence it is called the turbidity of life.
"Ānanda, you now wish to cause seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition (up to: all of these) to accord with the pure and wondrous virtue of nirvāṇa.
[Commentary: This explains through the union of dharma and metaphor; it is the subtle method for clarifying turbidity and returning to purity. It says:
"Your six faculties now—initially due to identifying the four great elements as the self—cause the profound, perfect, and wondrous awakening to be divided into seeing..."
Although hearing, knowing, perceiving, and cognizing are separated from one another, their nature has never been different.

If you wish to cause these four natures to harmonize distantly with the Tathāgata’s four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, you should first select and eliminate the root of birth and death.

In your daily routine, do not allow the consciousness-mind to arise following the sense organs and their objects; rather, rely solely on the Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) to respond to things according to circumstances. Thus, you will transform your grasping.

Taking the mind as the object, one perfects the nature of the perfectly clear and profound essence. Thereupon, by means of this clarified and profound correct wisdom, one turns back the illusory realm of false delusion and the cycle of birth and extinction;

thus, names and marks are transformed into the true realm of suchness. When the realm and wisdom are of one suchness, subject and object are both forgotten, leaving only the single, perfectly accomplished reality-nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This is the subduing and restoration of primordial awakening. Primordial awakening is none other than fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*).

Thus, once one has attained the luminous essence of original enlightenment, which possesses the nature of being beyond birth and death, and takes this as the mind of the causal stage—thereby having already acquired the true, eternal, and wondrous nature within that causal state—then what difficulty could there be in subsequently perfecting the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage?

Everything prior to Equal Enlightenment (samyagjñāna) constitutes cultivation; only Subtle Enlightenment (miao-jue) constitutes realization. To illustrate the process of revolving back from delusion toward perfect stillness, an analogy is provided:

The Master said: "It is like settling turbid water by storing it in a still vessel; when it is deep and motionless, the sand and silt settle of their own accord, and the clear water appears before one.

This is a metaphor for the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*), which are the two delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya*) and the two types of conceptual grasping (*parikalpita-upādāna*).
When these do not arise, the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are deeply subdued. As for the removal of the mud so that only pure water remains, this is a metaphor for..."
The fundamental ignorance is eternally severed and transformed into fundamental wisdom. This essence of ignorance is empty; it is precisely the unchanging *tathatā*.
Thus, the illusory appearances of ignorance are entirely the wondrously luminous true reality (*dharmatā*). It is refined and not mixed; pure and non-dual.

As it is said, it is replete with myriad virtues and utterly devoid of even the slightest speck of dust. Therefore, in accordance with the conditions of sentient beings' responses, it manifests its response.
When phenomena manifest their forms, they are free and unimpeded in both vertical and horizontal dimensions; furthermore, there is no further affliction.
Thus, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure are all in perfect accord with the four virtues of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa. This is the foremost path of wondrous cultivation.
Regarding the second meaning: you all will certainly be unable to transcend the receptacle world (bhājana-loka).
[Commentary] This explains the second definitive meaning mentioned above, clarifying the fundamental locus of arising and ceasing.
"From you all, down to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)," is a statement that establishes the premise.

"To give rise to great valor" means to subdue and overcome former objects of attachment (*ālambana*). "All conditioned phenomena" refers to the four great elements, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and so forth;
these are what are called "conditioned dharmas. The intended meaning is that former objects of attachment and conditioned dharmas fundamentally belong to birth.
It must certainly be eliminated. However, without knowing its root, how can one decisively discern it? Therefore, it is said that one should carefully examine the root of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
For the afflictions are precisely the ignorance (*avidyā*) that initiates karma; that is to say, they manifest as the activity of karma.
Such things as grasping, rejecting, and attachment belong to the sixth consciousness. The fundamental [ignorance] is the ignorance that moistens birth;
this refers to the innate moisture that, like entering a house upon conception, gives rise to hatred and love, and belongs to the eighth consciousness.
Regarding those who grasp at objects and perform actions, it is solely these six consciousnesses that are the masters of action, for they are able to create the causes of defiled and pure karma.

Regarding those who receive retributive fruits, it is solely these eight consciousnesses that are the masters of the total retribution, for they are able to contain and store the seeds of the defiled and the pure, maintaining them so they do not disperse.
However, upon subtle investigation, the first seven are all manifestations of the eighth.
It arises as if one were acting upon oneself and receiving the retribution for it oneself. Therefore, one who cultivates bodhi is like one clarifying turbid water:

proceeding from the coarse to the subtle, they first subdue the six consciousnesses so that they do not engage in攀緣 (pān-yuán, objective clinging). Thus, active manifestations do not arise, and there is nothing further to be created.
Gradually, the various seeds within the eight consciousnesses are eliminated, until both seeds and manifestations are exhausted, resulting in a pure white state.

Consciousness is called the empty Tathāgatagarbha. However, if one wishes to subdue the six consciousnesses, one must know where the root of the sense organs, objects, and seeds of consciousness currently resides.
Therefore, it is revealed by way of contrast: "One who practices cultivation must certainly know the root of the afflictions.
If one does not carefully examine the root of the afflictions, one will be unable to know the false root."

Objects. Wherein lies the inversion? It is because the seeds of the faculties, objects, and consciousness—what are called the causes of subtle arising and ceasing—all reside within the eight consciousnesses.

Since one does not know this, one cannot naturally understand the phenomena of the faculties, objects, and consciousness. Although they manifest in active operation (*pravṛtti*), they are fundamentally illusory.
It is merely due to the failure to awaken at the initial moment that one falsely distinguishes between subject and object, pursuing delusion and losing sight of the truth.
Thus, one falls into perversion. Yet, the very locus where perversion arises is fundamentally within the eight consciousnesses;
if one cannot even know the place where delusive inversion originates, from what means can one subdue the habitual攀緣 (pān-yuan, objective clinging) of the past?

Since one cannot subdue it, by what cause could one hope to attain the fruit-stage of the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding? Therefore, if one wishes to eliminate delusive inversion, one must certainly prepare in advance.
Knowing that delusion arises from perversion, he again uses a metaphor to clarify it, saying: "Observe those in the world who untie knots;
if they do not see the place where the knot was tied, how could they know how to untie it? Yet, there must be a place of tying and untying before one can select and remove [the knot].
Without a place of tying and untying, how could one possibly select and remove it? This is why you have never heard of empty space being destroyed by you."
As for "breaking and splitting," it is because there are no knots to be untied;
this is a metaphor for your profound, perfect, and wondrous enlightenment, which likewise has no knots to be untied. What constitutes having knots to be untied?
It is your present six sense-faculties and the six consciousnesses within your body, which inhale and grasp external objects, thereby turbidifying the Truth.
Nature. Within the world of True Suchness (tathatā), people instead act as intermediaries for seductive thieves; they invite external bandits to plunder their own family treasures.
Thus, the three dharmas of sense-faculties, objects, and consciousness originally arise from the false recognition of the four elements as a body, thereby creating self-imposed fetters.
This divides your profoundly still, perfect, and wondrous enlightenment into the functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing. Consequently, seeing does not transcend form, and hearing...
Without transcending sound and the other objects, they subsequently interweave with one another to form a knot;
thus it is said that because sentient beings in the world have produced entanglements from beginningless time, they are unable to transcend the vessel-world.

Viewed in this light, the three dharmas of sense-faculties, objects, and consciousness originally arise as a single, profound, perfect, and wondrous awakening, yet [beings] instead diminish and extinguish it.
The merits and dharma-treasures within the Tathāgatagarbha—could these not be plundered by internal thieves?
Yet, when the fetters are once untied and resolved, the faculties and their objects no longer meet; thus, even these internal thieves are transformed into excellent weapons.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "sentient-being world" (sattva-loka)? [This continues until: each possesses twelve hundred merits. *Commentary*:
This clarifies that sentient beings are bound within the world of phenomena (bhājana-loka) and are unable to transcend it;
therefore, there is a fixed number and limitation. True nature (*tathatā*) is fundamentally without flux and has no boundaries; it is only due to delusion...
Establishing subject and object, the fabrications of delusion mutually reinforce one another, resulting in the two types of retribution: the environment and its inhabitants.

Once there are internal and external realms, there is consequently temporal flux and spatial orientation. With these, there arise quantity and measure; with quantity and measure, there arise degrees of excellence and inferiority;
and with degrees of excellence and inferiority, one cannot help but engage in selection and rejection. All of this is presented by way of the laws of arising and ceasing.

This refers to humanity. To say that "the world" consists of temporal flux and "the realm" consists of spatial directions means that within the bodies of sentient beings themselves, there exists the flux of the three periods of time as well as the positions of above, below, left, and right.
You should now understand that [the text] first borrows the vessel-world (the physical environment) to clarify the three periods and the ten directions of space.
This is because [the practitioner] still does not know the flux and the spatial orientations within their own body.
One should know that the realm of the vessel-world and the realm of the body are not different. How is their non-difference perceived?

It is because all sentient beings originally possess no marks of a body; it is only through the interweaving of the four great elements and the five aggregates that they falsely form the marks of a body. Thus, there are the marks of a body.
Since there are physical forms, there are spatial directions and boundaries;
and since within these bodies there is also change and flux, there are worlds that intersect and interpenetrate without separation.

Although there are ten directions, only the four cardinal points are taken and not the four intermediate corners, because the latter are not primary. Neither the zenith nor the nadir are taken, because they lack fixed positions.
The central positions are excluded because they lack fixed orientation; only the four cardinal directions are taken, as they intersect with the three periods of time.

When the periods intersect with the directions, the number becomes twelve; when the directions intersect with the periods, it likewise becomes twelve. This constitutes the "threefold cycle of flux and transformation."

From one, it becomes three layers (*tri-koṭi*). Regarding "one, ten, hundred, thousand," the traditional explanation is that increasing one makes ten, increasing ten makes a hundred, and increasing a hundred makes a thousand. Now, in order to engage with the world, I shall clarify the three layers:
first, regarding each of the four directions, we discuss the three times, which together constitute twelve; second, within the three times of the eastern direction, we transform the one.
The ten become thirty. The same applies to the south, west, and north. Together, the four directions total one hundred and twenty.
Thirdly, the thirty of the east transform the ten into a hundred, becoming three hundred; the other three directions are likewise.
The four directions together constitute one thousand two hundred. This can be understood by analogy with the world’s engagement with the directions;
this is the fixed number for the mutual interpenetration of worlds. "Total inclusion" means being entirely contained within a single body. As for "beginning and end":
This refers to the beginning and end of the three-fold repetition. Regarding the statement that each of the six sense organs possesses one thousand two hundred functional capacities and virtues:
although within the body there are generally the three periods of time and the four directions, within each of the six organs there are likewise the four directions and the three periods of time.
Thus, even from a small number they can transform into many, thereby perfecting the total count. However, this is merely based on the perspective of sentient beings.
The term "endowed" (*ju*) refers simply to possession. As for the merit of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) of a sage, their number would indeed be immeasurable.

"Exchanging" (*mao*) means the trade between having and not having. "Transferring" (*qian*) means mutual arrival between this and that. Here, we take only the meaning of transformation, change, and flux.
"Ānanda, you must further determine the relative superiority and inferiority among them... up to one thousand two hundred merits.
(Commentary): This determination of the superiority and inferiority of the six faculties is intended to enable their selection.

Above, it was based on the mutual correspondence within their intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*), where there is fundamentally no superiority or inferiority; here, it is based on the mutual divergence within their functions, and thus superiority and inferiority exist.
Regarding the two-thirds of the visual faculty: this refers to two hundred [yojanas] in each of the four cardinal directions and one hundred in each of the four intermediate corners.

What is currently seen by the eye consists of the front and the three sides—left, right, and rear—which together total six hundred; when combined with the two hundred from the two preceding corners, they form eight hundred.
Together they form eight hundred [parts], yet only the final two hundred and the two corners of two hundred are not seen.
As for the faculty of hearing, it listens all-pervasively without omission; if drums are struck in the ten directions, one hears them simultaneously in all ten places.

Thus, when hearing a sound, it seems as though there is near and far, but when not hearing a sound, there is in reality no near or far. Therefore, it is called a "perfect" faculty (*vibhu-indriya*). The faculty of smell lacks its center.

Regarding "intersection" (*jiao*): according to the ancient explanation, the points of entry and exit intersect within [the field of speech], together forming three parts. One part consists of four hundred;

because the central intersection is missing, there are only eight hundred. As for the tongue faculty not perceiving tastes but only taking up speech—wherein speech has spatial divisions while principle is inexhaustible—it is said that while the words (*ci*) are limited, their meaning (*yi*) is universally pervasive throughout the mundane and supramundane.
Worldly wisdom can all be proclaimed; therefore, it possesses complete and perfect merit. Regarding the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) being "separated from both unity and duality":

this means that when separated, one does not know [objects], which constitutes a deficiency of one part; when in contact, there is sensation, involving both opposition and compliance, and thus it possesses two parts.
Regarding the mind-faculty (*manendriya*) being "silently receptive": this means that this mind-faculty is well able to contemplate the ten directions.
The three periods of time, as well as all mundane and supramundane phenomena, and the intentions of both ordinary beings and sages—there is nothing that is not encompassed by it.
Reaching the very limits of all things, it thus attains perfect and complete merit.
Ānanda, if you now wish to turn back the current of the flow of birth and death (up to) those six organs of cognition so that they are simultaneously purified:

as for what is called "the interwoven flow of deluded karma," it means that because the four great elements and the six organs are interwoven and falsely formed, one flows out and rushes toward objects, thereby creating the karma of birth and death. Therefore, if you wish to reverse this flow, you must turn it back from the six organs.

The World-Honored One secretly selected the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) to suit the immediate needs of the practitioner, enabling them to enter through a familiar path—what is known as "passing beyond right and wrong" and "realizing it within right and wrong.
Yet, alas, the practitioner had long been immersed in the drowning waters of extensive learning and did not dare to accept this responsibility.
Although this teaching uniquely reveals the ear-faculty as being profound and perfect, [it was not immediately grasped].

It is for the sake of detachment. Furthermore, it is not necessary to speak of "penetrating" [the truth]. Later, when Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva distinguishes between the three kinds of reality—perfect, penetrating, and constant—it is precisely this meaning.
That which is "penetrating" is this meaning of detachment; that which is "constant" is this meaning of profundity.
As for the meaning of "perfection," it requires no further explanation.
Commentary: This instructs Ānanda to select the "perfect faculty" (*yuan-gen*) from among the six faculties.

The intention is that since he now understands the root of delusion and has also discerned which of the six faculties is perfect and which is deficient, it is precisely at this time that he should select the perfect faculty to subdue and control his former habits of objective clinging (*pān-yuan*). Now, what you call "objective clinging" refers to the six [faculties].
The faculties (indriya) rush forth toward external objects; they sink deeply and fail to return. This is called following the current of desire toward birth and death.

To subdue them means to turn the six faculties inward, detach from the six objects outward, and extinguish the six consciousnesses within. This is called reversing the current of desire toward birth and death.
However, this merely reverses the birth and death of limited segments (paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa); one must necessarily proceed from the shallow to the deep.
Trace back to the root of the stream of birth and death, so that the seeds of arising and ceasing within the *karmic consciousness* are exhausted without remainder;
only then will you reach the point where the roots of the two deaths are severed and quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*) manifests before you.
Therefore, if you wish to attain this stage, you must first examine these six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), which experience sensory objects and manifest functional capacities.
Who is the consciousness that functions through contact? Who is the consciousness that functions without contact? Who is profound and subtle? Who is shallow and superficial?

Which is the perfect penetration? Which is not complete? If you can, within these six faculties of sensory reception, examine and verify for yourself who constitutes the root of perfect penetration, then from this very faculty, you shall reverse that weaving of delusive appearances into their mutual formation.

If one follows the flow into the nature that is neither born nor extinguished—the very root of karma that otherwise flows and scatters toward external objects—then when compared with the efficacy of the incomplete faculties, it is as if a day and an eon were multiplied against one another.

Now, within the first definitive meaning previously established, I have revealed that your six faculties are, in essence, a single, profound, perfect, and wondrously enlightened mind; herein, I shall further clarify these six faculties.
The merits originally possessed [by all beings] involve distinctions of separation and union, depth and shallowness, and completeness or deficiency;

they are all clearly manifest and fully revealed. Yet, according to your own inclinations, you must carefully select from among them those that can lead you into the state of non-arising and non-ceasing.
I shall then elucidate these for you with clarity, enabling you to proceed directly and swiftly, never again to fall back. However, let...

"Regarding your choice for yourself, it was according to your own root-nature (*gotra*). If one were to observe with the Dharma-eye of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, then regarding the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is nothing they do not penetrate.
Whether acting in opposition or in accord, they all employ skillful means (*upāya*) in their practice and all attain the perfection of Bodhi;
among them, there has never been any distinction of superior or inferior. It is simply that your own root-nature is still inferior."

Because you have not yet attained pervasive penetration and sovereign wisdom regarding all phenomena, and because among the six sense faculties you have not yet escaped the barrier of separation, I shall proclaim their relative strengths and weaknesses so that you may select one faculty from among them.

If you can enter deeply through a single gateway, causing the false to be exhausted and the true to manifest, then the remaining five faculties will simultaneously achieve complete liberation. Thus it is equalized.
One enters the state of non-arising without depending on any other power.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...ultimately, your faculties are not one root or six roots.
*Commentary:* This section, through a series of questions and answers, briefly demonstrates how by entering deeply into a single gate, all six sense-faculties become purified.

This is the culmination. Ānanda’s thought was: "To flow against the current of birth and death and reach the state of non-arising and non-extinction, one must have all six sense-faculties enter [the path] together;
how can one deeply enter through a single gate and cause all six faculties to become pure simultaneously?
The World-Honored One’s intention was: "The profound, perfect, and wondrous enlightenment is neither one nor six; it is only because of delusion that it is falsely [differentiated]."
Divide this into sixteen. What are these delusions? They are precisely what you, as a *srotāpanna*, call the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).

This is because, by not entering the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), you have turned against the flow of the desire-stream of birth and death and entered the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

That which is severed therein is solely the discriminative self-clinging within the [desire] realm; it is also called the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*). As for that which exists within the sixth faculty...
