The accumulation of seeds that can produce manifest activity consists of beginningless, empty habitual tendencies; these are the eighty-one afflictions of thought (*vitarka*), also known as innate self-clinging (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*).
Their root still resides within the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) and must necessarily be severed through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Only by severing this can one eliminate the greed, pride, and ignorance pertaining to the two upper realms, thereby attaining the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
One may be called an Arhat only after first realizing the four fruits by means of the outflows of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the outflows of ignorance (*avidyā*).

How much more so regarding this *ālayavijñāna*, wherein the ignorance that is identical in essence to arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing is also termed the two innate attachments (*sahaja-grāha*);
these consist of forty-two categories, which cannot be severed until the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Such is their extent.
"Number! How could you possibly know this? Because you do not understand this, you are unable to enter deeply through a single gate to achieve the purity of the six sense faculties.
If you do not believe that understanding one leads to the purification of all six, then observe the six sense faculties before you:
are they truly one, or are they truly six? If you say they are definitely one, then the ear should also be able to see, and the eye should also be able to hear."
"The head can also tread, and the feet can also speak; yet now it is not so. How can you determine that there is only one?
If you say they are fixed as six, then the body, the mouth, and the ears do not function for one another.
As I now preach the Dharma to you, which of your six faculties comes to receive it? Ānanda replied, "I hear with my ears. The Buddha said, "Since they are fixed as six..."
Your ears hear for themselves; what business have they with your body or mouth? Why must you, at the very moment of hearing, ask with your mouth and nod with your body?
It is evident that [the sense organs] are not fixed as six. Therefore, you should know: if they are not one, they must ultimately be six;
if they are not six, they must ultimately be one. How could your faculties be fundamentally fixed as one? Furthermore, fundamentally...
Is it fixed as six? Since it is neither one nor six, it is evident that "one" is established in relation to "six," and "six" is established in relation to "one.
Originally, there are no fixed names such as "one" or "six. Below, the reason for the arising of one and six is shown.
Ānanda, you should know that these faculties are neither one nor six (up to: the six faculties of experience are likewise so). [Commentary:
This is intended to demonstrate the arising of the meaning of "one" and "six. First, a metaphor is raised to clarify this. Following the previous statement:
since they are neither fixed as one nor fixed as six, for what reason do sentient beings perceive them as either six or one?

Alas! It is because of a single moment of inverted thought since beginningless time that you have falsely established sense organs and objects, following the stream of birth and death and sinking into decay.
Thus, regarding this one perfectly湛 (zhan) and profound essence, you have clung to either one or six. Now that you have attained the first fruit, you do not enter the six dusts;
although the six functions no longer operate, you have merely eliminated the manifest activities. As for those seeds of empty habituation—

It still resides within the *ālayavijñāna*; therefore, not even one [of its aspects] has perished. Because both the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), along with their seeds, persist, one does not realize that the six [consciousnesses] are pure.

Nevertheless, although the meanings of "one" and "six" arise based on the essence of perfect clarity (*paripūrṇa-vimala-tattva*), this fundamental essence of perfect clarity has never been different from the beginning.
It is just like the great void accommodating various vessels; by virtue of the vessels...
There are squares, circles, long, and short, yet space is called "different" [from them]. In truth, space has never been different.

It is because one observes space by removing the differences of the vessels that space is said to be "one. This is merely saying "one" in contrast to "difference"; how could there be any "oneness" in the essence of space itself?
However, because of the inclusion of the vessel, one speaks of emptiness as being different; because of the exclusion of the vessel, one speaks of emptiness as being the same.
This is merely a matter of words. Furthermore, when the vessel has not yet been joined, by what means could that great empty space be established by you as either the same or different?
Its sameness or difference cannot be expressed at all; how much less can it be called "this"?
One is not one. If you say that this emptiness is one, where else could there be a second?
Your understanding of the six sense organs is likewise so. This perfectly湛 (zhan—tranquil and profound) essence is divided into the six sense organs;

because of the six organs, the essence is spoken of as six, yet the essence has never been six from the start. When the six organs are turned back and subdued, the essence is spoken of as one. This is in response to...

The six [senses] are one; how can their substance be six? One may observe that based on the differentiation of the faculties, the substance is said to be six, but based on the dissolution of the faculties, the substance is said to be one. This is merely a matter of verbal expression.
Furthermore, when the faculties have not yet been separated, by what basis do you speak of this perfectly湛 (zhàn) substance as being "one" or "six"? If you say this substance is...
First: Where else could there be a second?
Because of the mutual conditioning of two aspects such as light and darkness, [the mind] loses its essential clarity and, adhering to delusion, emits light.
Commentary: This applies the Dharma to the analogy to clarify that the meanings of "one" and "six" arise.

Now, the profound, perfect, and wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally devoid of "one" and "six," just as the great void is fundamentally devoid of identity or difference. Due to the mutual entanglement of the sense organs and their objects, one falsely distinguishes between "one" and "six.
This is also like various vessels occupying space; one speaks of the space within them as having identity or difference. As previously stated regarding the world...
"One who unties the knots does not perceive the knots themselves; how then could they know 'untying'? This demonstrates the origin of what was knotted.
Following the instruction that 'after the sixth knot is untied, all are gone,' he further imparts the method for the removal.

This refers to the profound, perfect, and wondrous awakening, which—like a pearl reflecting colors—is fundamentally free from defilement. It was only at the very beginning that the two objects of light and darkness appeared in mutual contrast."

Within the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened nature, there exists a profound, perfect, and wondrous essence. Through a single moment of non-awakening, it becomes defiled by attachment to sensory objects, thereby triggering the visual essence (*darśana-vijñāna*).
This essence reflects upon the two types of objects; subsequently, it grasps the object of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) and coalesces to form the "supreme sense-faculty" (*indriya*).

Although this faculty belongs to the category of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), it remains pure and white in nature. Therefore, it is said that the fundamental source of the faculties is termed the "pure four great elements. Its...
The characteristics [of these] are subtle and most difficult to distinguish; that is to say, it is difficult for the ignorant to differentiate between consciousness and the sense faculties.

Because they possess ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and serve as the source of the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*), they are designated by this name. Thus, there exists the substance of the eye, which is like a cluster of grapes.

Since there are already the floating faculties, which externally depend on form, fragrance, flavor, and touch, and internally depend on earth, water, fire, and wind, they combine to form the two faculties.
Thus, the essence of vision relies upon these faculties and flows outward, rushing toward forms; as it follows the flow of forms, there is no time for it to return to its source.
Due to the mutual impact of the two objects—movement and stillness—within the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened nature, that which is tranquil, perfect, and subtle [is obscured].
By nature, a single thought-moment fails to awaken and becomes adhered to by sensory dust (*rajas*). This triggers the essence of hearing (*śrotra-śukra*), which reflects upon the object of sound.

Consequently, it rolls up the object of sound and binds it into the faculty of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-indriya*). Although this faculty belongs to the category of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*), it is nonetheless a pure white color;
therefore, its fundamental source is termed the "pure four great elements" (*mahābhūta*). Its characteristics are subtle and difficult for the ignorant to discern. Because of this...

The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the source of the floating sense-organ; it is based upon this that the name is established. Thus, there exists the substance of the ear, which is like a newly unfurled leaf.
Once it has become a floating sense-organ, it relies externally on form, odor, taste, and touch, and internally on earth, water, fire, and wind.

Through these eight factors—four objects and four faculties—it forms two organs. Consequently, the auditory essence rests upon the organ and flows outward, rushing toward sounds; thus, it follows the flow of sound.
"Transforming" means there is no time when it ceases. "Mutually striking" means they do not tolerate one another. "Rolling up and encompassing" means gathering and grasping.

From "due to penetration and obstruction" below, the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) is clarified. "Mutually eliciting" means they trigger one another. "Ingesting and absorbing" means taking in and assimilating.

The rest is to be understood according to the above. From "due to tranquility and change" below, the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) is clarified. "Tranquility" refers to the taste of flavorlessness. "Change" is...
The totality of the five flavors is the flavor of flavors. By contrasting "having flavor" with "being without flavor," two types are formed.
*Can* (參) means to mix; *jiao* (絞) means to take up by turning. From "separation and union" (*li-he*) downwards, the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) is clarified.

The meeting of these two is called *mo* (摩). *Tuan* (摶) means to grasp. The "waist drum" (*yaogu*) is what is commonly called the *zhanggu*; its head is the *sang* (顙), which refers to the resonant cavity.
From "By arising and ceasing... below, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is clarified. "Knowing the essence" refers to the ultimate sense-faculty (*paramārtha-indriya*).
As for "mental intention," it means that the mind has deliberation and discernment as its nature. Regarding "seeing within a dark chamber":

it is like a person in a bright place who cannot see someone inside a dark room, yet the person inside the dark room can see the person in the bright place; this is because the mental faculty abides here.

Within the body, they serve as the five sense organs for the purpose of contemplation and deliberation. However, since one perceives them within a dark chamber, this describes the essence of the thinking mind;
it seems unnecessary to be dogmatically attached to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* and insist that it refers specifically to the physical "flesh-ball" heart.
The conclusion below clarifies this by stating: "Thus, these six faculties all arise from the perfectly湛 (zhàn) and luminously aware consciousness."

Substance: Through a single moment of non-awakening, there arises a "luminous awareness" that can perceive. This awareness, being a single instance of delusion, consequently loses its original essence as true awareness—pure and lucid.

From this, it becomes attached to light and darkness, thereby giving rise to the light of vision; it becomes attached to motion and stillness, thereby giving rise to the light of hearing, and so forth.
The emergence of the meanings of "one" and "six," as well as the causes by which they are bound, all do not transcend this.
This refers to the "seeing-essence" and so forth.
Therefore, as you now depart from darkness and depart from light... (up to)... by this, the six faculties function interchangeably for one another.
[Commentary: This demonstrates that the substance of the root-knots is empty, thereby clarifying that when one is liberated, the six are extinguished. From this, the six...
The faculties originally consist of the knots of sensory objects. Therefore, if you now depart from the objects of light, darkness, and form, there is no essence of seeing;

if you depart from the objects of motion, stillness, and sound, there is no substance of hearing; and so on, until if you depart from the objects of dharmas involving birth and extinction, the mental faculty that cognizes has nowhere to rest.
You ask how one can enter deeply through a single gate and cause the six [faculties]— [...to function as one.]

The faculties are, at once, pure. You need only turn back the six faculties so that they do not follow after movement and stillness, nor after the various marks of arising and ceasing such as light and darkness.
This is to go against the current of birth and death and to follow the current of nirvana.
This is the method of practice for the simple, direct, and sudden [teaching]. However, it is not necessary for all six sense faculties to be reversed simultaneously.

Choose one of your most acute faculties according to your preference and apply yourself with single-minded effort to revolve and extract it. By doing so, this single faculty will externally shed the appearances of objects and internally subdue the nature of the faculty itself.
When the faculty and its object no longer meet, the conscious mind will not arise, and you shall return once more to the original, luminous true body.
Never clinging to delusions, it radiates light; its primordial luminosity shines forth in solitary clarity.

Since true light is thus initiated from the fundamental nature, the other five sense faculties are simultaneously uprooted and liberated. Reaching this state, one no longer depends on external objects.
Internally, it does not follow the sense organs; its constant radiance is quiescently illuminating, pervasive and unimpeded.
Although it relies upon those organs to manifest this function of illumination, in reality it does not follow them. Thus, the ear could see forms and the eye could hear sounds;
a single organ could perform the functions of all the organs. This is precisely "entering the one without delusion," whereby those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously [unified].
It is pure. Ānanda, do you not know that within this assembly... [up to] "the perfect, clear, and lucid knowledge does not depend on mental thought"?
(Commentary: This cites six individuals to prove the mutual functioning of the six sense organs. Aniruddha...)
The eye-faculty can see by means of the mind; Vāḍananda—here called "Worthy Joy"—is a nāga who can hear with his horns;
Gaṅgā—here called "Constant River" or "Coming from Heaven"—is the deity presiding over the river who can smell with her body.

Gavāmpati received the retribution of being a cowherd; hence he is called "the one with a distinct tongue. Śūnyatā (Śunyata) means "emptiness" in this context; he is the deity who presides over emptiness.
His substance is like wind, yet he is capable of perceiving touch. According to ancient accounts, for many kalpas this deity suffered from having no physical form.
When the Buddha emitted the "Light that Extracts Suffering," it illuminated him, causing him to manifest a temporary body; upon touching it, he experienced bliss.

It may be said that the same applies to the devas and humans of the formless realm. Kāśyapa—here translated as "Drinking Light"—is one who has cultivated the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
In him, both the discriminative and innate forms of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) associated with the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are entirely severed; therefore, he is without mental activity.

These six individuals cited here are either ordinary beings experiencing karmic retribution or practitioners of the Lesser Vehicle who have attained this through cultivation; all such states are merely the power of delusion.
If they do not yet follow their respective sense-faculties, how much less so when they are perfectly liberated? Is it not that they function interchangeably?
Ānanda, if your various faculties were now to be completely uprooted, they would—upon being contemplated—transform into supreme awareness.
Commentary: This concludes the clarification that [the state] is accomplished based on the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing perfect stillness (*cīn-zhàn*).

By means of this stillness, one turns back the false notions of extinction and birth, thereby restoring original enlightenment. Thus, within the body and the world, one is no longer entangled by birth;

one is then able to transcend the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). As for "the various faculties being perfectly uprooted and the inner clarity emitting light," this signifies that the light of the mind has become fused and penetrating.

The "inner" is suchness (*tathatā*). "Floating dust" refers to the six sense faculties. The "various changing phenomena of the vessel-world" collectively refers to the appearances of mountains, rivers, the myriad things, and the states of defilement and purity, suffering and joy, and so forth.

The phrase "like hot water dissolving ice, it transforms in accordance with thought into supreme enlightened awareness" means that through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one directly realizes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); thus, heaven and earth are identical with oneself.
Root: All things are my single body; even to the point where the one and the many are without obstruction, and the small and the large mutually merge—there is nothing that cannot be so.
Ānanda, it is like those worldly people who gather their vision in the eye (up to: why would the enlightened clarity not be perfect and wondrous?
Commentary: This clarifies the fundamental substance from which the luminosity of the sense organs emerges. Within the physical eyes of ordinary beings, it has never been lacking.

The intent is this: if you do not believe that luminosity does not follow the sense organs and is fundamentally all-pervasive, simply observe how people in the world perceive without relying on external light, and you will understand. It is like those worldly people who have not yet awakened to true luminosity.

One does not realize that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive and unobstructed; it is only because the nature of seeing is concentrated within the faculty of the eye that one cannot see when separated from both the faculty and light.
Suppose that person were suddenly to close their eyes tightly: the appearance of darkness would manifest before them.
Although the faculty of the eye exists, they would be as dark as if it were no different from their head or feet. Furthermore, suppose there were another person who, in that situation...
Standing before [the object], this person with closed eyes uses their hands to trace the body of that outsider, feeling it out and examining it.
Although they do not rely on the eyes, they distinguish head from foot clearly and without confusion; this is awareness in the dark that has never been different from awareness in the light.
If seeing were dependent on conditions, it would necessarily require light to begin seeing; [if it did,] darkness would become [an obstacle].

There is no seeing. If the nature of seeing were to manifest spontaneously without depending on the condition of light, then true illumination would be uniquely revealed, and one would possess constant, clear awareness.
In that case, light itself could not cause it to be bright, and darkness itself could not cause it to be dark.

Thus, if even the worldly person’s perception of the nature does not depend on a gateway to see it, how much less so for the inner luminosity that radiates light, once the sense organs and their objects have ceased?
"If they can be dissolved, how could they not achieve the wondrous function of perfect penetration?
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...I only pray that you will bestow your great compassion and dispel my ignorance and hesitation."

Commentary: This Ānanda has misinterpreted the Buddha’s words. He erroneously identifies the "adhesive clarity" that gives rise to the visual essence (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and so forth as the fundamental, perfectly round essence (*tattva*).
Consequently, he gives rise to doubts regarding annihilationism. First, let us establish the intent of the teaching according to what the Tathāgata has said:
"If, at the stage of the causal ground, one takes a mind subject to birth and death as the fundamental cause for cultivation while seeking Buddhahood..."
To ride upon that which is neither born nor extinguished is impossible. It must be that the two stages of cause and fruit are identical within the eternally abiding true mind;
only then can it be so. Furthermore, we have frequently heard the World-Honored One speak of the awakening of the stage of fruition, calling it bodhi.
That which is attained by severing and exhausting all afflictions is called *nirvāṇa*. That which is realized by completely purifying the root of the two deaths is called *tathatā* (Suchness).
It is the ultimate *dharmakāya*, unchanging and immovable, called *buddhatva* (Buddha-nature).
It is the true nature of original enlightenment, called the *amala-vijñāna* (Amala-consciousness), the pure white consciousness that is free from all defilements.
It is called the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. This is that which is empty of all adventitious phenomena. It is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*);
it is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) accomplished by the transformation of the *ālayavijñāna*.

Although these seven types differ in name, they are all within the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), where ignorance has been completely severed and innate virtues are fully perfected; their essential nature cannot be diminished or disturbed, just like gold.
The adamantine king-jewel can destroy all things, yet nothing can destroy it; it is ultimately firm and solid, eternally abiding and indestructible.

Once formed, it is forever formed, never again subject to change. Previously, I was graced by the World-Honored One’s full exposition of the six profound, perfect luminosities, and commanded me to choose one perfect faculty for him to clarify and reveal, so that I might advance. Now...
It is said: "The six faculties, such as seeing and the rest, have no inherent nature apart from their objects.

If these six faculties—seeing, hearing, and so forth—are separated from their six objects, such as light and darkness or motion and stillness, they ultimately possess no substance. This is identical to what the World-Honored One previously refuted:
that the discerning consciousness-mind, which arises and ceases in accordance with its objects, has nothing at all that exists inherently apart from those external objects."
How can one who intends to bring about this ultimate cessation take it as the mind of the causal stage,
while desiring to obtain the seven fruits of the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding? If you mean that seeing and so forth are ultimately empty of self-nature when separated from light,
darkness, and other conditions— just as you have refuted— I now observe that my own thoughts recur repeatedly, beginning again and again in a subtle cycle.
Upon investigation, the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are ultimately empty; thus, fundamentally, there is no self-mind. If one is separated from objects (*viṣaya*), then the mind has no locus.
Since it would then result in annihilationism (*uccheda*), by what could one establish a causal mind to seek and attain unsurpassed enlightenment?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata previously stated that the six [faculties] are profoundly clear and perfect; now you say they have no nature when separated from objects. This is a contradiction.
To transgress truthful speech ultimately results in frivolous discourse. How can the Tathāgata be called one who speaks with truth?
To "be deluded" means to be dull-witted and fail to awaken to the Buddha’s words; to "be parsimonious" means to be stagnant and fail to advance oneself through resolute effort.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for your study of much learning... [regarding] worldly matters, you should eliminate your doubts.
*Commentary:* This rebukes him for clinging to permanence as being annihilation. It says: You merely study much learning, yet have no leisure to exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*).
Therefore, you err at every turn. Previously, I pointed out for you the place where inversion arises; this is essential.
"You have eliminated its manifest seeds and habits, yet within your mind you merely know the causes of delusion while those seeds and habits still remain;
thus, you can only retain names and phrases, but when true delusion actually manifests before you, you truly fail to recognize it.
Now, as I wish to directly reveal that the fundamental nature is eternally true and constant, I fear your sincere heart is too stingy and you have not yet submitted in faith. Therefore, I shall now—"
I shall now provide you with a skillful instruction by means of matters easily understood in the mundane world;
you should resolve your doubts by way of these examples. As for the cause of perversion, it refers to the locus of prior perversion; "cause" here signifies the seed.
"True perversion" consists in taking the permanent to be the impermanent. "Not yet having exhausted all outflows" means that the habitual tendencies of perversion have not yet been eliminated.
At that moment, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula [to strike the bell]... [until] closing off the openings and speaking of the lack of intrinsic nature in hearing. *Commentary*:
This uses the arising and ceasing of the provisional auditory object to verify the true permanence of the nature of hearing;

it serves as the definitive case for the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty. From the time Rāhula struck the bell until both sound and resonance had ceased, this was termed "no-hearing. It was then...
Investigate this a second time, commanding him to personally determine whether it exists or does not exist: both [the presence] and the absence are the faculty of hearing.
Later, when one refutes this with correct principle, one finds that it is merely the object of sound, which has no relation to the faculty of hearing.
This is precisely the point of inversion. Because of this inversion, one becomes deluded regarding the fundamental faculty of hearing and flows along with sounds. Below...
This is to reverse [the argument] by means of a correct inquiry. Suppose the Tathāgata again commands Rāhu to strike the bell;

when the sound has completely ceased, it is called "no-sound. This is a third time he has scrutinized and determined the matter before revealing the correct principle, so that one may know whether there is sound or no sound is not a matter concerning the faculty of hearing.
After a short while—where "a short while" refers to a brief moment or instant—from this point onward...
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "In such a case, why would this not be called evasive confusion (*vikṣepa*)? This is a rebuke for his lack of a fixed response, which results in self-induced confusion.
For although the question was posed using the term 'hearing' (*śruti*) in common with the Śrāvakas, the presence or absence of hearing belongs exclusively to the auditory faculty.
How could one, following the mere verbal wrangling of others, give a confused answer regarding the existence or non-existence of what is heard? Thus, one loses one's own settled view."

Thus, this constitutes evasive and confused speech. From the statement that when sound vanishes there is no resonance, up to the teaching that hearing has no inherent nature, [the Buddha] directly demonstrates the true permanence of the nature of hearing, saying:
"When the first stroke of the bell ceases, you replied that there was no hearing.

How could you know that this was merely the absence of sound, rather than the absence of hearing itself? If there were truly no hearing, then your faculty of hearing would have perished along with the sound."
Your body is like a senseless, withered tree. When the second round of the bell is struck again, you should not hear it;
yet, as you still hear it when struck once more, you know that your faculty of hearing does not cease along with the sound.

Since your faculty of hearing knows both the presence and the absence of sound, it is evident that its existence or non-existence depends on the sound-object itself. How could this [faculty] be that [sound]?
The nature of hearing exists or does not exist depending on the presence or absence of the sense-object of sound; it is by this that you establish its existence or non-existence.
If the nature of hearing were truly extinguished, then who would be the one who knows that sound is absent?
Therefore, know that the sense-object of sound arises and ceases within the nature of hearing itself; it is not that your nature of hearing arises from the sense-object of sound.
It would mean that your nature of hearing exists; yet it is not your nature of hearing that ceases within the sensory object of sound, thereby causing your nature of hearing to become non-existent.
Therefore, he concludes with a reprimand, saying: "Its essence would be subject to annihilation or permanence, or else it would be indeterminate."

The existence or non-existence of the sense organs and their objects should be easy to understand. Yet even now you remain inverted and confused, mistaking sound for hearing without realizing it yourself.
How can you not wonder at taking the true, eternal essence as the cause of annihilation? I shall now clarify this for you:
you must no longer claim that the six sense organs lack inherent nature when separated from their objects.
"Just as a person in deep sleep rests upon a comfortable bed and pillow... (up to) "...how could it not constitute unexcelled perfect enlightenment?
*Commentary:* This passage cites both dream-obscuration and the dissolution of the physical form to verify that the nature of hearing is uninterrupted.
It is also consistent with the previously mentioned seeing-nature which does not depend on light. "Deep sleep" refers to the time when one is in a state of profound slumber.

It is also like this. "Beating the silk" refers to the sound of the mortar and pestle. When one hears the sound of pounding and yet perceives it as the sound of drums and bells, it is because the consciousness of deep sleep is clouded and the sensory objects have become disordered.

That, during the dream itself, one marvels that the bells are merely the echoes of wood and stone, is precisely the realization that although one dwells in the obscurity of a dream, the fundamental nature of the faculties remains uninterrupted. Upon suddenly waking, one immediately recognizes the pestle.

Regarding sound: it is only after awakening that one realizes the dream-scene was an error. One then informs the family members, saying, "While I was dreaming, I was deluded by this sound of pounding grain and took it to be the sound of drums. This describes the circumstances within the dream upon waking.
To establish the definitive nature of the faculty as being permanent, [the Buddha] said to Ānanda: "This person is currently in the midst of a dream; how could there be any volitional thought?"

It is simply that you recall and maintain the two objects of stillness and motion, as well as the faculty of the body, along with the opening and closing, the penetration and obstruction [of the ears].
However, although its form is asleep, the nature of hearing does not become darkened. You suspect that when separated from the two objects, the nature of the faculty is severed and extinguished.
One should then observe this person in deep sleep: at the moment when both the sense faculties and their objects are forgotten, they are still able to distinguish the sound of a pestle or a mortar.
Thus, it is clearly proven that the nature of hearing is independent of external objects and does not perish. Furthermore, it is not only the case that it does not perish during sleep;
even when the physical form dissolves and the life-force passes away, how could it possibly be subject to your physical form?
[The objects] are extinguished; does the nature of hearing also perish along with them? Since it does not perish, why would it not be perfectly wondrous?

Because sentient beings pursue the delusive and are confused about the Real, from time immemorial they have followed after forms and sounds, flowing with every thought without ever attaining enlightenment;
thus they do not know that the essential nature within the sense-faculties is untainted and unbound, primordial [purity].

It is eternally abiding. Therefore, one cannot go against that which flows; rather, following this which is constant, one pursues the various delusive objects of arising and ceasing, creating all karma.
By means of this, birth after birth is defiled, and one transmigrates through the various realms of existence.

If one can abandon these delusive objects of arising and ceasing, detach from sensory clinging and settle within, guarding the true and eternal, then the original, ever-present radiance will truly manifest its illumination.

The radiance [of the mind], along with the sense organs, objects, consciousness, and the mind, shall at that moment dissolve away. That which is called the "radiant nature" will manifest its brilliance;

all other five types of adhesions shall be uprooted and liberated in their entirety. Furthermore, you can completely eliminate the two divisions of subject and object (the perceived and the perceiver) as well as the subtle seeds.
These conceptualizations constitute the dust, and the conscious emotions constitute the defilement. When both are distanced from, then throughout the entire Dharma-realm, this is your pure Dharma.
The eye—namely, when birth and death have ceased and quiescent extinction has manifested before one—how could it not constitute unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?
My meaning is this: you ask why one takes this ultimate annihilation as the cause for cultivation while desiring to obtain the Tathāgata’s seven fruits of eternal abiding;
do you not know that this very nature of the faculties is itself primordial enlightenment, devoid of the nature of birth and death?
By relying on this causal cultivation, one will spontaneously attain the realization and certification of the stage of fruition.
How could one fail to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment? *Lengyan jing jianglu*, Fascicle Four.

Lecture Record on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Five.
Ming Dynasty. Chaizi. Śramaṇa Chengshi. Lecture Record.
Annotated and published by the Dharma-disciple of Xin’an, Wang Yiyuan.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One... [omitted] ...awaiting the unsurpassed instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata.”

Commentary: This further seeks the root of the knot, hoping for its release. From "The Tathāgata" down to "in the end cannot untie it," this reiterates what was stated previously in the second section on definitive meaning: "One should carefully examine the root of the afflictions."
From time immemorial, this has given rise to karma and moistened rebirth;

even now, if one does not carefully examine the root of afflictions, one cannot know where the delusions regarding the false sense-bases and sense-objects arise. Observe those in the world who understand how to untie knots.
Regarding the phrases "not knowing what is bound" and "knowing and understanding," and so forth:

the statement that [the ālayavijñāna] has co-arisen and co-ceased with various forms of ignorance since beginningless time refers back to the previously mentioned accumulation of false habits within the sense-faculties, as well as their arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, along with their specific limits and enumerations.
As the subsequent text states: "The subtle *ādānavijñāna*—its habitual tendencies form a torrential stream."
It is precisely this innate ignorance that, within the stream of birth and death, accompanies one from exiting the womb to entering the womb, never for a single moment to be separated from it.
Those who attain the name of "one who has gone forth" by virtue of their roots of goodness refer to those who have attained the minor fruits of a learner (śaikṣa).
It is like a tertian malaria: when one attains the fruit [of the path], there is a temporary semblance of liberation;

yet upon entering the flow of birth and death and desire, one remains bound as before. It can be seen that the roots of the fetters have not been eliminated. As stated previously: "Though six have been dissolved, one has not yet perished.
This so-called "one" refers precisely to the root of the fetters. This is true not only for the lesser fruits, but even for Bodhi...

Even those who have attained the Way still experience the delusion of being separated by the intermediate state (antarābhava), much like one who desires purity yet remains stained, or one who loves what is correct yet turns toward the perverse;
all of this is caused by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) accumulated over many lifetimes. What is meant by "knots"?
It means that although one knows the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are knots, one does not know which among them is the root-source of these knots. What is meant by "liberation"? It means...
The root of the fetters does not lie outside of co-nascent ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*);
yet, one remains ignorant as to where to apply oneself and what method to employ to unravel them. "Craning the neck" refers to a bird spreading its wings and looking out for its food.
Ānanda looked to the Buddha for an exposition that would clarify this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda... [up to] "...is likewise none other than the six faculties of yours."

Commentary: These Buddhas collectively bestowed this supreme Dharma of the Crown upon Ānanda. Its essential meaning is identical to the aforementioned six states of profound stillness and perfect luminosity.
Out of compassion for those in training, he specifically pities them for their inability to eliminate even a single [delusion].
Sentient beings of the future will be increasingly distant from the Sages, and their faith and understanding will become ever more difficult.

To serve as a cause for transcending the world and to act as eyes for the future, this work provides a reliance for their cultivation and realization, so that their faith and understanding shall not be deluded. This is the Mahānirvāṇa-śīrṣa.
Desiring to bestow the supreme *mūrdha-dharma*, he preempts [the disciple's] fear and doubt by comforting him, lest his capacity be too small.

Regarding the six kinds of earth-tremors, the explanation may be found previously. Whenever a Great Sage appears in the world, such auspicious signs invariably occur; they do not represent specific doctrinal meanings.
The World-Honored One first emitted light from the crown of his head, and subsequently emitted light from the gate of his face, which drenched the crowns of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Even when he emitted light from the tips of his fingers, it all manifested the fundamental wisdom-light innate to the Buddha’s birth.
While it does not emerge from the six sense organs, it also transcends them; this is the supreme *ūrdhvamārga* (topmost) dharma, which Ānanda was unable to perceive.
Having received this entrustment and undergone repeated instructions until reaching this point, his root-nature was nearing maturity and he possessed the capacity for entry.
Consequently, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions were moved to emit light from their cranial protuberances (*uṣṇīṣa*), which together poured over the crown of Śākyamuni Buddha’s head.
They then conferred upon him the supreme *uṣṇīṣa*-dharma in unison. This clearly demonstrates that this dharma is the single gateway of all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
Transcending the Path of Sublime Adornment, when this light alone irrigates that [other realm], it is the arising of function from essence;
when that light irrigates this [realm], it is the returning of function to essence. Thus, this great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.

This is an error. Therefore, you should sincerely believe my words and choose a faculty with perfect roots.

If you enter deeply through one gate, the remaining five faculties will be uprooted and completely liberated. Once the knots of the faculties are removed, the seeds of the seeing-part (the subjective) will be exhausted;

once the characteristics of objects (the objective) naturally cease, the seeds of the phenomenal part will be exhausted. All deluded seeds and habitual tendencies will perish together. How could this not result in perfection?
This refers to the fulfillment of wondrous enlightenment. As for the twenty-four sages who followed, each attained entry into perfect penetration by focusing on a single faculty and a single object;
the fundamental cause in every case was that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions.
"Ānanda, I now ask you about this *karpāsa* cloth... (up to) attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) from *samādhi*.
[Commentary: This clarifies the sequence of unfolding and untying. First, he uses a counter-interrogation based on common understanding and common removal."
This causes them to realize for themselves that there is a sequence to the binding, and likewise a sequence to the untying. As for the sequence in the analogy:
it is like taking a single cloth and successively tying it into six knots. As for the sequence in the Dharma:

it is like the deluded agitation of the mind-nature, where false perceptions arise, and through the exhaustion of vision, the dust of phenomena is produced. However, this does not refer to the side of re-binding.
Regarding the sequence: we emphasize only the sequence of resolving the boundaries. Why is this? It is because one must cause the mind to be gathered into a single point.
If one attempts to apply effort simultaneously across all six sense faculties, it is unavoidable that the mind will be divided and distracted by objects, resulting in a mere waste of energy.
One must select a single "perfect faculty" (*yuan-gen*) and begin one's practice within that faculty. Even if one faculty returns to its source, the others...
The five faculties should be uprooted, perfected, and liberated. Therefore, Ānanda realized that while the six knots share the same substance, they are not tied at the same time;

thus, when untying them, one must proceed step by step and cannot remove them all at once. Yet the World-Honored One, seeing that there were those with the capacity for guidance, led him on by saying:
"The liberation of the six faculties is also like this. When this faculty is first untied..."

First, regarding those who have previously attained the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*): this refers to the time when the single faculty returns to its source and the six faculties are liberated.

At that moment, the sense organs and their objects do not encounter one another, and the six consciousnesses do not arise. Consequently, one attains the wisdom of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons, clearly understanding that the characteristics of the body fundamentally belong to the four great elements and the five aggregates (*skandha*), being formed through provisional combination.
By breaking down these common characteristics, one realizes that the grasping at a self is empty. This is known as "mere emptiness" (*buta-kū*).

Because of the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*), even emptiness remains limited. Furthermore, by means of the wisdom of the dual-emptiness contemplation, one realizes that the four great elements and the five aggregates each lack intrinsic nature, thereby destroying their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Once the luminous perfection of emptiness is attained, this empties the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
Although the two kinds of emptiness are attained, the conceptual marks of the dual-emptiness contemplation still remain; next, one must again empty those two kinds of emptiness. Thus...

Ignorance is suddenly shattered and afflictions are forever forgotten. One immediately realizes that the body, its faculties, and the objective world are nothing other than the single *tathāgatagarbha*-mind, which perfectly illumines the *dharmadhātu*.
One never perceives even a single phenomenon as having the characteristics of coming and going, birth and extinction; thus, one personally realizes the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.
This is what is meant by "the sequence of the binding and the untying," wherein the six are resolved and the one also vanishes.
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, [continued] until they withdrew to conceal their secret capacities, hoping for the Buddha’s hidden transmission.
*Commentary*: This is the request for the fundamental basis of perfect penetration. "Having received the Buddha’s instruction" refers to what was said previously:

"Once the faculties and objects have been extinguished, how could enlightened clarity not become perfectly wondrous? and "Far removed from dust and free from defilement, the Dharma-eye becomes clear and bright."
"How is it that they do not achieve supreme enlightenment? Even until all things are empty and non-arising, they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*);
all such cases are included herein. Because one awakens to the perfect and sovereign wisdom through this, it is called 'the perfect penetration of wisdom.
Although one has not yet realized it in actuality, it is clear within the mind and free from doubt. Regarding 'the body and mind being unobstructed,' it is because of the six [senses]."

Having understood that the one [self] is extinguished, one realizes the emptiness of persons; thus, the body is unimpeded. Having understood that all phenomena are likewise empty and non-arising, the mind is unimpeded.
Although this is so, one has not yet reached the faculty of discerning the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*) to enter the stream and achieve true awakening;
therefore, he specifically requests further instruction. Wandering aimlessly through the various realms of existence and not having entered the stream of the sages, he is called "lonely" (*gū*).

Having accumulated [merit] through kalpas outside the gate, yet not yet resting in the Precious Abode, it is therefore called "exposed" (*lu*). As for the phrase "with what heart and what concern," it expresses the self-congratulation of emerging beyond all expectations.

"Already present" means he was already there. "Heavenly brother" refers to his being the younger brother of the Buddha. It is like a child who has lost its mother’s milk suddenly encountering a compassionate mother;
having long been deprived of the Dharma-milk, one now fortunately obtains it. This is the convergence of opportunity where the Way is realized. This is the pointing [to the truth].
"First awakening to the law of dependent origination" refers to the time when one attains the first fruit of realization. "The secret mantra obtained" points back to the previous instruction.

Although one has received this instruction, if one has not yet seen progress toward the noble fruits of sainthood, it is said that "it remains the same as the original awakening," meaning there is no difference between this and having not heard it at all.
"Bestow upon me the secret adornment" means to request once more the secret instructions so that I may refine [my practice].
This refers to the solemnization of the holy fruit (*ārya-phala*). As for "the final revelation," this specifically points to the present sutra.
It means that without the secret key, one cannot solemnize the holy fruit; thus, one would ultimately be unable to accomplish what the Tathāgata has revealed here.
Would this not be to fail the Buddha’s grace? "Withdrawing to conceal the secret mechanism" means that once the worship of the Buddha is completed, one immediately remains silent.
He said: "Furthermore, since I have requested the secret and solemn [teaching], it certainly cannot be expressed through words;
I only hope that the World-Honored One will grant a single thread of insight from the side, so that I may attain intuitive realization. Therefore, it is called 'mysterious transmission' (ming-shou)."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the entire assembly... [up to] "...by what skillful means does one enter samādhi?
(Commentary: This causes the twenty-five sages to each present their *yuan-tong* [perfect penetration], thereby secretly transmitting the secret essentials to Ānanda.
"The initial arousal of the mind" refers to the question regarding the arousal of the *bodhicitta*. As for the "eighteen realms":)

The faculties subsume the great element of seeing; consciousness subsumes the great element of consciousness; and the objects subsume the five great elements. The three categories and seven great elements previously mentioned are all the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
It is further said: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions each cultivate practice within each of the eighteen realms."
All have attained the perfection of unsurpassed Bodhi. Furthermore, it is said that "to sink in birth-and-death and yet realize wondrous permanence" applies only to those of the six faculties;
as none of them had yet provided direct evidence, the various Sages were each asked to state what they had realized, so as to demonstrate that what was taught was not erroneous.
These twenty-five Sages—regardless of the greatness or smallness of their names and ranks, or whether their Dharma-gates were partial or complete—all entered [the state of realization].
In the Mahāyāna, perfect penetration is never subject to superiority or inferiority; one must not judge the depth of realization based on the size of the names [of the gateways].
Kātyāyanaputra and the other five bhikṣus rose from their seats... [up to] "...as I have realized, sound is supreme."
Commentary: This refers to awakening to and entering the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) through the sense-object of sound.

Among the twenty-five methods of perfect penetration, beginning with the sense-object of sound and ending with the faculty of the ear is because they were all established specifically for Ānanda and the spiritual capacities of those in this land.
The Deer Park and the Cock Garden were both sites where ancient emperors raised livestock.
Kauṇḍinya—translated here as "Fire-Apparatus"—was so named because in his previous life he was a fire-worshipping heretic. The five bhikṣus were those whom the Buddha first brought to liberation.
When the Buddha went forth from home, his father the King ordered three members of his paternal clan and two of his maternal clan to follow and protect him.
Later, they abandoned the Buddha and each practiced a different heterodox path. On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment, he first sought them out and ordained them;
therefore, it is said that he beheld the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of the Way. For these five men, the Buddha turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths three times, and thus Cunda...
He was the very first to realize and witness [the truth]. Therefore, it is said that regarding the Buddha’s voice, he awakened to and clarified the Four Noble Truths.
"Ajñāta" means "understood" (in Chinese, *jie*); because he was the first to understand, the Buddha certified him with the name "Understood. As for "wondrous sound, subtle and perfect":
By hearing the sound of the Dharma, one awakens to and enters perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). Thus, the sense faculties and their objects dissolve, and subject and object no longer exist;
hence it is called the "Wondrous Sound. All phenomenal sounds are the Dharma-sound of Vairocana; hence it is called the "Perfect Sound.

Those who awaken know this, while those who are deluded remain unaware; hence it is called the "Secret Sound. Yet, when a single object is awakened to and entered, every faculty and every object simultaneously enters perfect penetration.
However, because he first entered through sound, it was appropriate that he took sound as supreme; all subsequent cases should be understood according to this principle.
Upānanda then rose from his seat (until: "As I have realized it, form is the cause that is supreme."
Commentary: This refers to attaining entry into perfect penetration through the sense-object of form (*rūpa*).
Upānishaṭa means "the emptiness of the nature of form" or "the near-slight," referring to the fact that atoms are but a small portion of form.

Because he was excessively prone to lustful desires, the Buddha instructed him to practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to remedy it, thereby causing him to turn his greedy mind into one of revulsion.
Regarding "form is impure, etc.," this refers to the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*).

That is to say, one contemplates that within this body there are thirty-six substances, and externally there are nine orifices from which foul secretions constantly flow; from birth until death, it is ultimately without a single point of purity.
It is impure in its seed, impure in its dwelling place, impure in its place of birth, and impure in its ultimate nature.

The nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) are: first, the perception of bloating; second, the perception of bluish discoloration; third, the perception of decay; fourth, the perception of being smeared with blood; fifth, the perception of festering pus;
sixth, the perception of being devoured by worms; seventh, the perception of scattering; eighth, the perception of bones; ninth, the perception of burning.
From these nine perceptions, the white bones are transformed into dust and return to emptiness. Thus, one initially employs the nine perceptions to enter into emptiness.
To treat those forms and appearances: upon reaching this point, one is able to empty both the object and the emptiness itself, eliminating them both at once.
One suddenly awakens to perfect penetration and achieves the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). An ancient worthy said: "Know that when form arises, it is merely emptiness arising;
when form ceases, it is merely emptiness ceasing. It is like drawing patterns on water; there has never been any arising or ceasing. As for "wondrous form, subtle and perfect," it means:
All sensory objects of form are entirely the Dharma-body of Vairocana. Thus, one may take a single blade of grass and employ it as the sixteen-foot golden body;
likewise, one may take the sixteen-foot golden body and employ it as a single blade of grass. As for the causal aspect of form, it is as explained previously.
The youth Incense Purity immediately rose from his seat... [up to] "...as I have realized, the incense-purity is supreme. (Commentary:
This refers to the entry into perfect penetration through the sense-object of fragrance. "To observe with discernment" means to observe with thorough and authentic scrutiny.
"All conditioned phenomena" refers to the dharmas of the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses. "Tranquil and dark" means peaceful, secure, and profoundly still.
A pure room is called a "pure chamber" (*qingzhai*). Incense is a phenomenon within the realm of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).
That which is silent is devoid of the characteristic of sound. Contemplating this fragrance: it is not the wood itself, for without fire there is no fragrance; thus it is said to be "not the wood.

Yet it is not identical to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), for emptiness is eternal and unchanging; thus it is said to be "not emptiness. When fire burns other types of wood, they likewise lack fragrance. Therefore...
It is said: "This is not smoke or fire. That which departs has nowhere to which it is attached; thus the faculty has nowhere to go. That which comes has nowhere from which it proceeds;
thus the sensory object has nowhere from which it comes. Because the faculty and the object do not encounter one another, the mind attains dissolution and enters into non-discrimination.
To manifest the untainted (anāsrava) is to realize that the essence of this fragrance is not a phenomenon such as cause and condition, but is rather suchness."
This is the nature of the *ālayavijñāna*. "The dust-like vapors suddenly vanish" means that illusory appearances have melted away like ice.
"Sublime fragrance, subtle and perfect" means that all breaths are, in fact, the fragrant light of the *dharmakāya*. However, while the awakened realize this, the deluded do not recognize it;
hence it is called "subtle. As for Xiangyan being superior, it follows the previous explanation.
The two Dharma-Prince sons, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata... (up to) "...as I have realized, the cause of flavor is supreme. [Commentary:
This refers to the entry into perfect penetration through the sense-object of flavor. The five hundred Brahmā devas are their accompanying retinue.
"Tasting medicine and acting as physicians" describes their past causes. When various flavors combine to form a whole, it is called "harmonious blending" (*saṃskṛta*).
That which is used in its natural state is called "innate" (*sahaja*); that which has been refined through processing, such as by steaming or roasting, is called "transformed" (*vikṛta*).
Both terms refer to the *taste* (*rasa*). Whether it is cold or hot, and whether it is toxic or non-toxic, these all refer to the *nature* (*svabhāva*) [of the taste].

Having served the Tathāgata and fully understood taste and nature, one clearly realizes that past habitual tendencies are not forgotten; thus, one is able to observe from within the sensory object of taste. The tongue and taste are ablaze.
Therefore, it is said that it is not empty. Flavor has no form or substance; it is like the taste of salt in water. Therefore, it is said that it is not existent.

The body is the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*), and the mind is the tongue-consciousness (*jihvāvijñāna*). When flavors do not arrive, the tongue and consciousness are always naturally tranquil and indifferent.

Therefore, this nature of taste does not arise as being identical with the body and mind. If the gustatory consciousness does not experience it, then tastes such as sweet and bitter cannot manifest of themselves.
Thus, this nature of taste does not exist independently, apart from the gustatory consciousness.
When each factor is analyzed in terms of the causes of taste, they come from nowhere and go nowhere; yet the sense object and the faculty are neither identical nor separate.
Detached. Suddenly transcending the sense organs and their objects, the true and eternal is revealed alone. Thus it is said: "By discerning the causes of flavors, one attains awakening from this.
The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "Phenomena arise from discrimination; they likewise cease through discrimination."
To extinguish these various discriminations—this Dharma is not something that exists to be extinguished. "Awakened clarity" refers to the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment;
it is through the sensory object of flavor that one attains awakening.
Bhadrapāla and his companions... [up to] "...as I have realized, taking contact as the supreme cause.
(Commentary: This refers to the entry into perfect penetration through the sense-object of contact.
Bhadrapāla means "Worthy Head" or "Worthy Protector," signifying that he protects his own virtuous qualities and also protects sentient beings. *Kāyastha* [is translated here as] "Bodhisattva.")
This is an alternative name for a Bodhisattva: one who has awakened themselves and is further able to awaken sentient beings.

The passage beginning with "Formerly, under the Buddha King of Majestic Sound, he heard the Dharma... describes his past lives; it explains how he entered awakening through the cause of water. "Contact" refers to the sensory characteristic of the body;
that is, when the faculty of the body comes into conjunction with external objects, one perceives within that interval their qualities of cold, heat, roughness, or smoothness.

Smoothness is called the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*). Now, at the time of bathing, the body comes into contact with water, and qualities such as cold, warmth, roughness, and smoothness manifest therein.
Consequently, one must investigate from where the characteristic of touch itself ultimately arises.

If you claim that this characteristic of touch exists because of the water, then the water should manifest this characteristic of touch while washing itself; why then must it wait for the body to be washed in order to be known?
There is the characteristic of touch. Since water does not wash water, it is clear that touch does not exist because of water.
If you claim that this characteristic of touch exists because of the substance of cognition (*buddhi*), why does it not manifest when [the mirror] has not yet been washed?
Furthermore, at the time of washing, the washing does not apply to the substance of cognition; since it does not wash the substance, it is clear that touch does not exist because of the substance.
Thus, the sense objects have no place of arising, the faculties have no basis for reliance, and the conscious mind is suddenly extinguished.

Therefore it is said that in the interval one attains tranquility and reaches the state of non-existence. From this, one awakens to the fact that what is called "phenomena" is illusory and false, while their nature is fundamentally true.

Thus, during the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, one had already attained wondrous enlightenment; now, following the Buddha’s transformation, one further realizes the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). For this reason, upon a single touch—
When the nature of the treasury is revealed, every point of contact is none other than the true essence; hence it is said: "Sublime touch proclaims clarity.
From Mahākāśyapa and the Purple Golden Light [passage]... up to: "As I have realized, the Dharma-cause is supreme."
Commentary: This is the entry into perfect penetration through the dharma-object (dharmāyatana).
Mahākāśyapa—translated here as "Great Radiance"—is identified as one of the three Kāśyapas. The nuns and others are self-evident.

Because of two superior causes—kindling lamps and anointing the Buddha—he experienced a body of purple-gold radiance throughout kalpas. His patriarchal robe swallowed the sun. As for "observing the six objects" (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), this is precisely...

Contemplation focuses on the dharma-objects (*dharmāyatana*). This is because dharma-objects are the shadows cast by the cessation of the preceding five sense-objects; therefore, they are mentioned together.

As for "transformation and decay": this refers to how dharma-objects rely upon the mental faculty (*manas*), appearing momentarily and then vanishing, arising and ceasing in every thought-moment within a single *kṣaṇa*.

Out of weariness with this transformation and decay, one cultivates the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), whereby the perceptions and mind gradually subside, and one subsequently enters [the state of non-conceptualization].
The Samādhi of Cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). This samādhi can extinguish the mental faculty (*manas*), empty the objects of cognition (*dharmaviṣaya*), and cause deep conceptualization to cease;

therefore, it can pass hundreds of thousands of kalpas in the time it takes to snap one's fingers. He is now in the Cock’s Foot Mountain (*Kukkuṭapādagiri*) in meditative absorption, awaiting the appearance of Maitreya in the world.
It is so. When I speak of "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*), I mean that by emptying the objects of the dharmas (*dharmālambana*), one awakens to and enters the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
*Dhūta*—newly translated as *duṭuo*—is here rendered as "shaking off. This means being able to shake off the dust of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding "the wondrous Dharma illuminates and eliminates all outflows": this means that within the objects of the mind (dharmas) there is the true nature itself;

within the deluded mind there is the wondrous clarity itself. When this true and wondrous state is revealed, then every phenomenon is truly real. Thus, the ignorance of desire and existence is extinguished.
All were extinguished together. This concludes the section on the six sense objects entering perfect penetration.
Aniruddha then rose from his seat... [up to] "...turning the vision back to its source; this is the foremost."
Commentary: This is the entry into perfect penetration through the faculty of the eye. Aniruddha (Āniruddha) means "Free from Poverty" and is also translated as "As One Wishes.
He was the younger cousin of the Buddha and the son of King Śuklodana. In a past life, he offered a single meal to a Pratyekabuddha;
as a result, for ninety-one kalpas, he experienced the joy of having his every wish fulfilled. According to the old tradition, this is recorded in the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
The Āgama states: When the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park preaching the Dharma to the assembly, Rāhula fell asleep there.

The Buddha spoke a verse in reproach, saying: "Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like a snail, a clam, or an oyster; having slept for a thousand years, you shall sleep again for another thousand."
"Aniruddha, you did not hear the name of the Buddha; thus, having stayed awake until dawn, you have lost both eyes.
The World-Honored One then showed him the Vajra Samādhi of Joyful Vision and Illumination, instructing him to collect his mindfulness within the faculty of the eye.
With a single mind, one delights in seeing; with exclusive intent, one desires to illuminate.

With only this one thought and no other thoughts, even when facing spears before and blades behind, this thought shall not shift. Even if heaven collapses and earth cracks, this thought remains unmoved.
Like the Vajra King jewel, which can destroy all things while nothing can destroy it, if this thought is maintained for a long time, then—
Because one can observe the worlds of the ten directions by means of the eye-faculty, it is clearly known that this is not a deluded vision following the faculty;

rather, it is what is manifested by the wondrously luminous true mind. Being pure, true, and brilliantly radiant, it is thus able to penetrate through the ten directions as clearly as observing fruit in the palm of one's hand.
Because one does not perceive external forms, the seeing turns inward and does not run outward; because there is no eye-faculty, it follows [the source].

The "Original" does not mean following the roots. Because Ānanda possessed extensive learning, he was taught the practice of "reversing the hearing to hear one's own nature," whereby he attained the Vajra Samādhi and realized the fundamental source of perfect penetration.
Because Nālada had lost both his eyes, he was taught the practice of "delighting in seeing and illuminating," whereby he likewise attained the Vajra Samādhi.
Thus one realizes the fundamental root of perfect penetration. One method involves turning the hearing inward; the other involves following the vision outward.

Yet when success is achieved, they both converge in the nature of concealment (*tathatā*). As it is said: "The sagely nature has nothing it does not penetrate; whether moving against or with the flow, all are skillful means."
"How marvelous are these words!
Zhouli Pan-te-ka immediately rose from his seat... [until]... reversing his breath and following the void—this is the foremost.
*Annotation:* This refers to awakening through and entering the perfect penetration via the faculty of the nose. Pan-te-ka means "Snake Slave" (*Ajnata-Kaundinya*).
It is also called "continuing the Way," because it arises at the edge of the Path. This refers to the story of the Bhikṣu Sweeper, who in the past was a great Dharma Master;

because he was secretive and stingy regarding the Buddha-Dharma and did not constantly teach others, he received the retribution of being dull-witted. Nevertheless, due to his past roots of goodness, he encountered the Buddha and left the household life.
Although five hundred bhikṣus taught him a single verse together for ninety days, he could not master it. This is also recounted in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
If one recites "sticks" (*tiáo*), one grasps the sticks while forgetting the broom (*zhǒu*); if one grasps the broom, one forgets the sticks.

Because this serves to remedy distraction as well as dullness and stupidity, he was taught to practice counting the breaths (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) to collect the mind and prevent it from being distracted by other conditions.

As his practice gradually matures and the mind becomes increasingly subtle, he first practices the counting of the inhalation and exhalation in both forward and reverse order, and subsequently, within a single breath, he exhaustively investigates its...

Regarding arising, abiding, change, and cessation—extending even to this primary cessation—and applying it to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one sees that a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) possesses ninety-nine moments.
Within each moment, there are further ninety-nine instances of arising and ceasing.

After proceeding in this manner for a long time, suddenly, at the point where arising and ceasing are exhausted, one thoroughly realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*). Having reached the realization that arising is itself non-arising, [there is no]...
When arising is itself arising, then mind and breath are both forgotten; suddenly free from obstruction, one achieves the fruit of sainthood.

As for "reversing the breath to follow emptiness," it means that after contemplating the breath for a long time, no breath can be apprehended, and one thus follows true emptiness as wondrous existence.
Gavāmpati immediately rose from his seat... [until] ... returning to the flavors and revolving within the faculty of cognition;
this is the foremost. (Commentary and Annotation: This is the entry into perfect penetration through the faculty of the tongue.
Gavāmpati means "ox-chewer" in Chinese. Even when not eating, he would habitually engage in empty chewing. In the past, seeing an old monk who had no teeth yet was eating, he laughed at him.
Because he resembled an ox, he was reborn with an ox’s tongue in life after life and constantly chewed his cud like one.
To prevent slander against him, the Buddha granted him a rosary and instructed him to constantly recollect the Buddha.

Furthermore, he taught him to contemplate this single flavor upon the very root of his tongue, causing his mind to dwell on a single object, becoming purely unified and severing all discursive thoughts; this is the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground. After a long time...

The mind of craving ceases, and one enters right concentration. One further contemplates and knows that the cognition of taste is not produced from the substance of the tongue, nor does it belong to the taste itself;
thus, the nature of both sense organ and object is empty. When one sense organ is transcended, all sense organs are likewise so.

Consequently, by responding to this thought, one transcends all worldly outflows (*āsrava*) and awakens to and enters the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, one is internally liberated from the body.
The mind casts the external world behind it, like a bird escaping from a cage. As it is said: "Conceptual appearances are the dust; cognitive emotions are the defilement.
When both are left far behind, your Dharma-eye will become clear and bright at that very moment. "Returning to the flavor" means shedding attachment and losing the objective realm.
"Revolutionizing cognition" means subduing the internal mind and entering the stream.
Pilingavatsa immediately rose from his seat... [until] "Pure Awakening leaves the body behind; this is the foremost. (Commentary):
This is the entry into perfect penetration through the faculty of the body. Pilingavatsa means "Residual Habit," as he was a Brahmin in a previous life;
because of these residual habits, he possessed much pride, such as when he called the river deity a "slave-girl."
My son, all these are habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). "The initial arousal of the mind" refers to the time of leaving the household life.

"Frequently hearing of things that are not to be enjoyed" refers to hearing the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) among the Four Noble Truths, such as the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering.

Consequently, reflecting upon things that are not to be enjoyed and encountering circumstances that are not to be enjoyed is also an occasion for awakening to the Way. It is the cognition that knows pain.
The awareness that perceives pain is entirely the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*).

When one thinks, "I am currently cognizing this deep pain," and investigates this awareness, although it is able to perceive pain, it arises based on the contact between the physical sense-organ and its object;

it possesses no substantial reality. Upon realizing this, both the sense-faculty and its object are empty, and the discriminating mind ceases. Within my own originally enlightened, pure essence, [it has never existed].
There was no consciousness that could perceive it, nor was there any pain that could be perceived. I then examined the matter with subtle and thorough scrutiny:
at the very moment of experiencing pain, there is one who perceives the pain and there is the pain itself which cannot reach [the perceiver].
Since I am originally a single body, how could there be two distinct perceptions? Reflecting thus, I gathered my mental faculties and returned to the essence of pure awareness. Before long—
In this interval, body and mind are unimpeded, suddenly like empty space. When habitual outflows are completely exhausted, the nature-awareness manifests before one.
This is to be unstained by even a speck of dust; it is the pure, singular nature of precious awakening and luminosity, wherein no further bodily form can be perceived.
Subhūti immediately rose from his seat... [until] returning to the Dharma through its own revolution—this is the foremost. *Guānzhù* (Commentary):
This is the entry into perfect penetration by means of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). Subhūti is here translated as "One Who Understands Emptiness" (*Kṣāntika*).
He was also called Shanjie (Well-Understanding). He said: "Since the distant past of kalpas, my mind has attained non-obstruction.
I recall my births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet I have never experienced the delusion of the *ganyin* (the interval between lives) nor the darkness of emerging from the womb.

In this very life, from the moment I was first in my mother’s womb, I immediately knew emptiness and stillness. Although I follow the world in taking birth, the principle of emptiness remains unclouded. His...
The characteristics of the five-aggregate body are utterly unfindable; how could it be that only its primary retribution is empty?
From the mother’s body outward, even all the environmental retributions throughout the worlds of the ten directions all return to the principle of emptiness.

Upon emerging from the womb, one then extensively transforms sentient beings so that they together realize the nature of emptiness. This is the emptiness of both person and phenomena, wherein both self and others are benefited. Yet, there remains...

Having not yet realized the wondrous existence of true emptiness, one further receives the Tathāgata’s illumination regarding the true emptiness of the nature of awakening and the true awakening of the empty nature.

Thereupon, one attains fundamental right wisdom and realizes the principle of the emptiness of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Furthermore, there is neither the wisdom that realizes nor the principle that is realized;
thus, the nature of emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, and one suddenly enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of jewel-bright emptiness, becoming one with it.

The Buddha’s knowledge and vision thus fully realizes that the ten dharma realms, including both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as their causes and effects, are nothing more than reflections within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
This is the perfect fusion of the three truths, through which true liberation is attained.

Regarding my own realization—that all phenomena enter into non-existence—"non-existence" refers precisely to emptiness. This concludes the preceding section on "Since the beginningless kalpas... and expresses its intended meaning.
Initially, one attains the wisdom of the contemplation of dual emptiness, which empties the characteristics of the environment, the inhabitants, persons, dharmas, and so forth.

"Neither the subject nor the object is exhausted" means that both the negating and the negated are simultaneously empty. This concludes the preceding section on the meaning of the Tathāgata’s teaching.

It states that both the wisdom that negates and the emptiness that is negated are completely exhausted without remainder; this is precisely what is meant by being neither real nor unreal. Thus, one turns back from phenomena.
"Returning to non-existence" means that the phenomena of both emptiness and existence, as well as the physical body and its environment, all return to the jewel-bright ocean of space.
This is what is meant by "originally there was not a single thing. Because the faculty of the mind (*manas*) is able to encompass all things, it is not called "returning the faculties."

It is said that "revolving" refers to the method (*upāya*). "Nature-awakening" (*prakṛti-bodha*) points to wisdom (*jñāna*), and "true emptiness" (*bhūta-śūnyatā*) points to principle (*tattva*). That "emptiness-nature is perfectly luminous" means that wisdom and principle are of one suchness.
This concludes the section on the five sense organs entering through universal penetration.
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat... [until] "...this supreme knowledge and vision is foremost. (Commentary:
