This is the entry into perfect penetration through the awakening of eye-consciousness. Śāriputra is here translated as "Son of the Śāri.")
Since beginningless lifetimes, his visual consciousness has been clear and sharp. He said, "Throughout kalpas as vast as the void, whenever I have seen forms, not even a speck of dust has defiled me.
Although I rely upon the visual consciousness, it is actually the mind that sees. I have taken such births as many as the sands of the Ganges."

Life after life, regarding mundane and supramundane phenomena, as well as their various differentiated causes and effects and all manifestations of transformation, I have passed them with a single glance.
With both the exterior and interior thoroughly penetrated, I have attained unimpeded mastery without expending further effort.
Furthermore, in this present life, midway through my journey, I encountered the brothers Kāśyapa, who proclaimed the teaching on phenomena arising from causes and conditions. I...
To speak of it is itself emptiness; it is also called a provisional designation, and it is also called the meaning of the Middle Way.

Thereupon, one awakens to the fact that mundane and supramundane phenomena arise from the mind as their substance. Since phenomena have no boundaries, the mind likewise has no boundaries. For this reason, he left the household life to follow the Buddha.
When one attains the perfect clarity of awakened insight, then regarding both phenomena and principle, there is nothing that is not harmoniously integrated.
In all circumstances, one gives rise to no fear; moreover, among the assembly, one is foremost in wisdom and becomes the Buddha’s eldest son.

This is entirely for the sake of upholding the Buddha’s teachings, transforming the ordinary into the sacred, repeatedly ascending to the stage of fruition, and gradually manifesting the Dharma-body. Thus, the mind and vision emit radiance.

This refers to the radiance of the mind arising from one's own visual consciousness. "The light reaches the ultimate limit of knowing and seeing" means that this single light perfectly permeates all six sense faculties;
that is to say, when one faculty is purified, the remaining five faculties are simultaneously and completely liberated.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva then rose from his seat... [up to] ...this mastery of discernment is foremost. (Commentary:
This is the entry into perfect penetration through the auditory consciousness. According to the ancient explanation: "Pervading the Dharma-realm" is called *Samanta* (Universal);
"ranked as a neighbor to the ultimate Sage" is called *Bhadra* (Worthy). Because he succeeds to the family legacy of the Buddha, he is the son of the Dharma King; thus he is a Bodhisattva.
"Roots" refers to the roots of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching]. "The Practice of Samantabhadra" refers to the Ten Great Vows;

it is this wherein even a single color or a single fragrance universally pervades the entire Dharma-realm. All those throughout the ten directions and across the sands of Ganges who cultivate the practice of Samantabhadra derive their names from this;
it may be called the ultimate in establishing a model for emulation. Generally speaking, although hearing sounds is termed "ear-consciousness," in reality, it is the mind.
Having heard this, one is able to discern the various understandings and views of sentient beings; by selecting those with great roots, one accomplishes the conduct of Samantabhadra.

Furthermore, even if there were a single sentient being beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who were to resolve their mind [on enlightenment], I would immediately manifest a division of my body and go to that place.
Although they may not see me, I shall secretly bestow my protection and grace them by placing my hand upon their heads.
"Protect them so that they are not disturbed by Māras; comfort and bring them to fulfillment so that they do not fall back.
As for what I call the 'original cause,' although ancient Buddhas have long since realized it, there is nevertheless a primary original cause.
'The mind-hearing brings forth illumination' means that the tainted consciousnesses are transformed into untainted wisdom. 'Mastery in discernment' means the discernment of all sentient beings."
Regarding knowledge and vision, both subject and object are simultaneously transcended.
Sundarananda then rose from his seat... [until] ...this perfection of clarity and the extinction of outflows is the foremost.
Commentary: This refers to the entry into perfect penetration through the nose-consciousness. *Sundarī* means "Lovely"; *Nanda* means "Joyful Beauty.
By naming him together with his wife, his identity is clarified; he is not the cowherd Nanda, who was the Buddha’s maternal cousin.
At the beginning of his renunciation, Nanda’s worldly desires did not cease, so the Buddha sent him to stay with Kauṣṭhila.
Focus the mind on the tip of the nose and observe its whiteness to remedy mental distraction.
Seeing the inhalation and exhalation of the breath as smoke refers to the initial stage of practice, as one is observing at the level of gross phenomena.

That this sign arises when the visualization is perfected is also because the vital energy (*prāṇa*) of those with distracted minds is coarse and turbid. From this point onward, through gradual observation, the sense organs, the physical body, and the external environment will all become smoke.

The sign becomes universally perfected as empty and pure, like lapis lazuli. Upon reaching the stage where the pure contemplation is manifested, the sign of smoke gradually vanishes, and the tip of the nose becomes white.
When the true light finally breaks through, every inhalation and exhalation is nothing but radiance.
When the mind and its objects unite, there is perfect illumination without omission; this is the transformation of afflictions into bodhi.
Through my practice of cessation, as cessation deepens, clarity is revealed. This perfected clarity extinguishes the outflows: it transforms coarse turbidity and cessation into the fire of wisdom.
This is because it burns away the seeds of desire. According to the ancient teachings, this [sign] arises from wind and fire;
as it stirs up the turbidity of the afflictions, its appearance is like smoke. Those who are deluded do not perceive it; only those who observe with discernment can first see it.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra—[up to] "the foremost among those who have extinguished all outflows.
[Commentary: This is the entry into perfect penetration through the consciousness of the tongue. "Since the distant kalpas" refers to the narration of past causes.
"Unimpeded eloquence" refers to the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). "Suffering and emptiness" are the provisional meanings of the Two Vehicles. "True reality" is the One [Vehicle].
"Riding upon the ultimate meaning. "In this manner, up to and including" refers to proceeding from a single Buddha to immeasurable Buddhas.
"The secret dharma-gate" means exhausting all profound mysteries. "Subtle and wondrous revelation" means elucidating through the utmost skillful means.
"Attaining fearlessness" means attaining the four kinds of fearlessness. By means of the three wheels, the Buddha responds to sentient beings without hindrance.
He was adept at manifesting supernatural powers with his body, preaching the True Dharma with his mouth, and maintaining the profound mysteries of karmic conditions within his mind.
The Buddha, recognizing his talent, bestowed upon him the Wheel of Speech to assist in propagating the transformation of the Dharma.

To "assist the Buddha in turning the wheel" means to support the Buddha’s teachings from above by means of the Lion’s Roar, and to transform sentient beings from below; both serve to manifest the practice of benefiting others and thereby achieve the fruit of sainthood.
This is the dedication of transformative merit to oneself. Demons and enemies are subdued and all outflows (*āsrava*) are extinguished.
The demons of internal afflictions are eliminated through the preaching of the Dharma; the celestial Māras and non-Buddhists outside the body retreat and hide upon hearing the Dharma.
When neither the internal nor the external can cause intrusion, one will then peacefully realize and enter perfect penetration.
Upāli then rose from his seat... [until] ...he was foremost among all those who possess universal penetration and benefit.

Commentary: This refers to entering the perfect penetration through the body-consciousness. Upāli means "Foremost," because he maintained the Vinaya and served as the guiding principle for the assembly;
he is also called "The Close Attendant," because when the Buddha was a prince, he served as his close personal attendant.
"The outflows of greed" refers to the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Furthermore, "receiving the Buddha’s teachings and precepts" refers to receiving the two hundred and fifty rules of the Śrāvaka precepts.

Continuing in this manner down to the "inferior" level refers to the Bodhisattva precepts. According to the traditional explanation, for each of the four postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—there are two hundred and fifty rules of restraint (*saṃvara*).

These, when combined with the three clusters (*triskandha*), total three thousand. These three thousand are then further multiplied by the seven branches of body and speech, resulting in twenty thousand.
One thousand [types of afflictions] are further multiplied by four categories of affliction to become eighty-four thousand.

Regarding the "three aggregates" (triskandha), they refer to the aggregate of gathering wholesome dharmas (kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka), the aggregate of gathering ethical discipline (saṃvara-saṃgrāhaka), and the aggregate of gathering sentient beings (sattva-saṃgrāhaka).

The "four categories of affliction" refer to those with excessive greed, excessive hatred, excessive delusion, and those with equal proportions of these three. "Natural transgressions" (prakṛti-sāvadya) refers to those prohibited actions whose essential nature is inherently evil, such as killing.

Stealing and sexual misconduct are inherently evil by nature; they do not require external restraint, for the moment one commits them, karma is formed. "Prohibitive actions" (śīla) refer to the dharmas that serve as precepts;
their essential nature is not evil, yet they are able to open the gates to various evils and act as preliminary conditions (*purva-prayoga*).

Thus, one begins to treat the faults at their source in order to block all evils—examples include [the prohibition against] alcohol and so forth. Through maintaining the body, body and mind attain tranquility and extinction (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
Through the precepts, one attains tranquility of body; by upholding the precept of the mind, one attains tranquility of mind.

Thus, concentration arises from the precepts, and wisdom is developed through concentration, whereby one realizes the fruit of sainthood. As for being a leader among the multitude, it is because one’s name and actual realization are in accord.

This means to cause one to examine and oversee both the transgressions and the merits of upholding or violating the precepts. "Sealing the mind" means to seal and maintain the fundamental mind that cultivates the body through the precepts.
"The body attains mastery" means that once the practice of upholding them is pure, one not only avoids transgressions, but moreover reaches a state where there are no longer any precepts to uphold.
"The mind attains penetration" likewise means that one not only reaches the state of neither upholding nor violating, but furthermore [attains] meditative concentration and wisdom.

"Interpenetration" means profoundly penetrating the true reality (*dharmatā*). "The body and mind are entirely permeated and functional" refers to entering into perfect penetration through the consciousness of the body, thereby realizing that the two realms of the physical body and the objective world are, in their entirety, a single wondrous nature.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately rose from his seat... (omitted)... having long since attained clarity and purity, he is foremost in this regard.
*Annotation:* This refers to the entry into perfect penetration through the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Maudgalyāyana means "The Clan of the Mung Beans. Uruvilvā means "Papaya Tumor"; because there was a tumor on his chest that resembled a papaya fruit, [he was so named]. Gha... [text fragment]
"Ya" refers to the name of a mountain, namely Mount Elephant Head (*Gajapadaka*). "Nadi" refers to the name of a river.

The profound meaning of these causes and conditions reveals that [the reality] is neither a coarse phenomenon produced by worldly conjunction nor a dharma realized by the Śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle. "I suddenly resolved my mind" means that I immediately gave rise to the Bodhicitta.
"Attaining great penetration" means that the nature of wisdom was opened and developed, whereby I gradually beheld the realm of perfect penetration.
"Realm. "The Tathāgata bestowed upon me a kāṣāya robe, and as I donned it, my beard and hair fell away of their own accord," describes his renunciation by entering the Buddha's path.
"I traveled through the ten directions and eventually attained the state of an Arhat," describes that he was about to achieve the great function of perfect penetration.
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions praised my spiritual power" means that not only did Śākyamuni Buddha certify his spiritual power, [but all the Buddhas did so].

This is the foremost penetration, which all Buddhas have equally sealed and authorized. "Perfectly clear and pure" means that by entering the samādhi of perfect penetration through one's own mental consciousness, one attains universal knowledge free from all defilement and attachment.

"Sovereign and fearless" means that with mastery according to one's will, one is forever beyond being crushed or constrained. Thus, I have manifested this through the revolving, tranquil light of the mind.

This refers to turning back the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to return to the wondrously profound fundamental substance (*dharmatā*). From this profound substance, the wondrous functions of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are manifested.

The analogy of clearing a turbid stream illustrates the practice of turning back toward the profound stillness. "Long since perfected in clarity and transparency" illustrates the manifestation of luminous function from the profound substance.
This concludes the entry of the six consciousnesses into universal penetration (*pariṣuddha-vyūha*).
Ucchuṣma, before the Tathāgata... [until] he attained unsurpassed enlightenment; this is the foremost. *Commentary*:
This is the entry into perfect penetration through the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*). Ucchuṣma means "Fire-Head" (Kāpālika); he is the Vajra Fire-Head.
According to ancient exegesis, those who are excessively lustful are fundamentally impelled by the sensation of warmth (*uṣman*).
Life is the fire of desire; death is the fire of karma. Because the power of karma increases and blazes, it becomes a mass of fierce flames.

When [the Buddha] instructs me to observe throughout the hundred bones and four limbs all the "cold-warmth breaths," the character "cold" (lěng) is likely an error. According to the concluding text, it should read "all warm tactile breaths" (zhū nuǎn chù qì).
This is because in those who indulge excessively in lust, the element of fire (tejas) is particularly intense; therefore, he instructs me to observe them right where they are.
The Fire Element: Begin the practice by contemplating this karmic fire within the hundred limbs and four extremities;

observe from where it arises. Then, visualize it as a mass of blazing fire until fear arises in the mind, whereby lust will suddenly cease and the essence of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) can be established.
Once the essence of contemplation is established, one is able to transform the hot flames into divine light and transform mental distraction into [concentration].
This is the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus, I transformed my manifold lustful mind into the fire of wisdom; therefore, my entire being dwells within the *tejovatī-samādhi*.
By means of the fire of wisdom, I have utterly incinerated the seeds of lustful roots and fully realized the state of an Arhat.
The Buddhas have named me Fire-Head (Agnimukha). I, moreover, have made a great vow to serve forever as a powerful attendant to all Buddhas and to personally subdue demonic adversaries.

When I contemplate with clarity the warmth and tactile sensations within my body and mind, I mean that I observe throughout my hundred bones and four limbs how the fires of desire arise entirely from the blazing intensity of the lustful mind. This [realization] flows unimpededly through all...

"The outflows having been extinguished" means that the lustful mind has suddenly ceased and the fire of wisdom blazes forth—namely, the true emptiness of the nature-fire and the true fire of the nature-emptiness.
Being pure and fundamental, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm and gives rise to great jewel-flames;
this refers to one who ascends to unsurpassed enlightenment by means of the Fire-Light Samādhi, which is the Tathāgata-garbha-nature.
Bodhisattva Earth-Holder (Dharaṇīdhara) immediately rose from his seat... [omitted] ...to achieve the Unsurpassed Way; this is the foremost.
*Annotation:* This refers to the great awakening and entry into perfect penetration based on the ground. Because he leveled the external earth, he awakened to and clarified the mind-ground.
He subsequently maintained his fundamental practice and realized the fruit; thus, he was named Earth-Holder. From the passage "I recall in the past" onwards, the former lives are recounted.

The "passages for living" (*shēng zhī xíng*) refer to essential locations. "Land routes" refers to overland paths; "ferry crossings" (*jīnkǒu*) refers to waterways, namely riverheads—places where boats and carriages must necessarily pass.

If there were places that did not conform to the proper standard—whether they were perilous and steep, narrow and constricted, or neither spacious nor level—they would obstruct and damage carriages and horses. Therefore, one levels the high ground, fills in the low ground, and constructs bridges.

"Carrying earth" refers, in common parlance, to repairing bridges and roads. "Having served immeasurable Buddhas" describes how his practice of offering labor extended over an exceedingly long period.
*Huán* (闤) means the wall surrounding a marketplace; *yì* (詣) means to go toward. "Not taking its price" means not accepting wages.
*Vipaśyin* (毗舍浮) is translated here as "Pervasive Sovereignty over All. He accepted only a single coin because it was a time of famine.
This is because it briefly provides for one's physical life and sustenance. Or, there may be carts and oxen used to eliminate their suffering;
since their vows and practices are eternal, they invoke spiritual power to assist those practices.

"At that time, the great king of the country, and even all others, were at peace" refers to the Tathāgata Viśeṣa, who taught the gathering of phenomena to lead them back to principle. The mind is the source of the myriad dharmas.
It is that upon which all things rely; it impartially nurtures and brings all to maturity. Therefore, it is called the "Mind-Ground.

To awaken to and clarify this mind is to realize that the sentient and the insentient have fundamentally been one body, and that the two types of retribution—the environment and the inhabitants—are originally without self or other.

Regarding the causes and effects of the holy and the ordinary, everything is *tathatā* (suchness). All perceived differences arise solely through the transformations induced by the mind’s responses. This is what is meant by "according to its..."
When the mind is defiled, the land is defiled; as the mind becomes pure, the land becomes pure.

From the passage "My mind was then opened" (*wǒ jí xīn kāi*) onwards, he describes how, by receiving the Buddha’s instruction, he attained realization and entered into perfect penetration. Regarding the statement that the body and the particles of the world are without distinction:

this means that one realizes the characteristics of the element of earth are manifestations of one's own mind and have no substantial reality from the beginning; such is the intrinsic nature of the subtle particles.
There is no mutual touching or rubbing; even weapons do not touch anything. This is because the intrinsic nature of the earth element is empty and non-existent.
In its entirety, it is the single reality of the Tathāgatagarbha. How, then, could one distinguish between the subject that touches and the object that is touched?

Since one has realized that both the world and the self are but two types of dust, and that all phenomena—whether defiled or pure—are nothing other than the single *tathāgatagarbha* mind, one awakens to the nature of phenomena and realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because one cultivates the bodhisattva practices based on this awakening to non-arising, [it is said] at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Having heard the teaching on the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, his karmic conditions were in harmony with it; thus, he was the first to receive verification and become a leader.
In the section beginning with "The Buddha asked about perfect penetration," the preceding realization is fully recounted.

This means that through the contemplation of the internal and external earth-elements as fundamentally being the one nature of the Tathāgata-garbha, which manifests according to karma, he had previously falsely divided them into sense organs and objects; now, he has awakened to this.

When the fundamental nature is realized, the faculties and their objects naturally dissolve, and the mirror-like wisdom spontaneously becomes perfect. How could one then fail to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment?
The Youthful Moonlight then rose from his seat... [until] ...the fulfillment of Bodhi is the foremost of all.

Commentary: This is the entry into perfect penetration through awakening by means of the water element. "Boy" (*dāraka*) is an alternative name for a Bodhisattva, representing the virtue of youthful purity (*kumārabhūta*).
The passage beginning with "I recall in the past... recounts his past causes and conditions. As for the Buddha named Water-Heaven (*Varuṇa*): [the text continues].

This means that from the water-element (*āpas*), one awakens thoroughly to the natural, original state of one's own nature. As for the instruction to practice the contemplation of water, it is to demonstrate to others what one has realized oneself.

Regarding the passage "contemplating within the body" and below, it refers to hearing the Dharma and practicing contemplation: first, one contemplates how mucus, saliva, spittle, and other fluids exist within a single body;

although they swirl and flow without ceasing, being neither uniform nor consistent in their clarity or turbidity, their fundamental nature— [...is such that... (The text continues with the realization of the non-duality of these phenomena and the nature of the mind.)
Since their essence is identical, they do not compete or supplant one another. Once the internal visualization is perfected, it is extended outward;
expanding this perspective, one contemplates the Floating Banner King Lands and so forth. According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within the Flower Treasury Ocean there is a great lotus flower.

Within those lotus flowers, there are seas of fragrant water. Within each sea of fragrant water, there is a single flower that serves as the world-system seed for the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu).
Because this Flower Treasury World resides within the seas of fragrant water, it is called the Floating Banner King World-system (*Udānadhvaja-rāja-kṣetra*).
This is because the Flower Treasury World rises in twenty successive tiers, making it the most towering and magnificent, like a banner.
Therefore, he is called a King. Now, because his contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) has matured, he perceives that the water of his own body and the water of the ocean are non-different in nature.
Although his contemplative practice is matured, he has not yet attained selflessness (*anātman*);

thus, when entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he does not see a single object, but sees only profound, still water. Within that concentration, the observing mind still persists. As for the observed...

Because of this water, even when emerging from meditative absorption, the physical form remains present. Therefore, although the power of contemplation is relaxed, as it enters one’s own being with increased excellence, all that is seen is the same;

yet, because the meditative forms have not been eliminated and subject-object duality has not been forgotten, there occurs the incident where the sound of splashing water causes an immediate sensation of pain in the heart. When Śāriputra entered meditative absorption on the banks of the Ganges, two ghosts appeared.

"O King, he was actually an old enemy from a past life who struck him with his palm while he was emerging from meditative absorption. Because of this, the monk suffered a headache upon leaving samādhi and reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

'If he had not been in meditative absorption when he encountered that blow, he would certainly have been reduced to fine dust. It is only by relying on the power of concentration that he has been able to recover. Now, as he emerges from absorption, his heart aches;
thus one says he is 'the same' as that [headache]. Furthermore, reflect for yourself: you have long since been free from the afflictions of view and thought.'"
He does not fall into the stage of birth-and-death (pariccheda). Now his heart again pains him; could it be that he has regressed from the four fruits?

His physical constitution is as it was before, and his heart no longer pains him. He encounters immeasurable Buddhas—which refers to the many kalpas that have passed—and only then does he attain the extinction of the self (mushin).

This means that when there is no mind capable of observing, and likewise no water to be observed, then the form produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) vanishes and the aggregate-body (*skandha-kāya*) is also empty.

To be one with the nature of the true void, inseparable and non-dual from the various seas of fragrant water throughout the worlds of the ten directions—this is what is called "the true void of the nature of water" and "the true water of the nature of emptiness. I [perceive this] through the single flavor of the essence of water.
"Penetration" refers to that which is fundamentally pure and pervades the entire Dharma-realm. "Attaining the patience of non-arising" refers to attaining the mind of the causal stage.
"Perfecting Bodhi" refers to harmonizing with the awakening of the resultant stage.
The Dharma Prince Vairocanaraśmiprabha rose from his seat... [omitted] ...transmitting this single wondrous mind; this is the foremost. *Commentary*:

This is the realization of the perfect penetration through the element of wind (*vāyu-mahābhūta*). By observing that both body and mind are driven by the power of wind, he attained perfect enlightenment through this contemplation.
It was transparently unobstructed; therefore, he was named Vairocanaraśmiprabha (Lapis Lazuli Light). The object of his practice—
The Buddha is named Immeasurable Sound (*Amitaghoṣa*), for he likewise realized this Dharma-gate.
He revealed the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) and instructed those who contemplate the great element of wind: "Original enlightenment is the unmoving essence;
wondrous clarity is its all-pervading function. The worlds and sentient beings are all driven by the power of the wind of delusive conditions. This means that, first of all, by...

Because fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) follows conditions for a single thought-moment and thereby gives rise to the wind of ignorance (avidyā), it evokes the wind-circle that sustains the world-system.
Now, when one contemplates that the nature of wind is fundamentally empty and its moving aspect is quiescent, one turns back from delusion to the real and returns to fundamental awakening.
However, this is still merely the gateway of contemplation shown by the Buddha. From the phrase "At that time, I... onwards, the entry into contemplation is described.
"Contemplating the establishment of the realms" means contemplating the establishment of spatial directions, as they are sustained by the power of wind.
"Contemplating the movement of the world" means contemplating the flux of the three periods of time, as they are driven by the power of wind. "Contemplating the body's..."

That which possesses motion and stillness is driven by the power of wind. To observe that the mind undergoes arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing is to see how the ocean of the mind is stirred by the winds of objects, thereby forming waves of consciousness. Thus, the world and the body-and-mind are not uniform in their movement and stillness;
yet when one observes their origin, they all arise from the single thought of deluded movement within fundamental enlightenment, as the wind of clarity emerges.
Birth—how could there be a nature of differentiation? When my contemplative practice reached maturity, I realized that the nature of these manifold movements is fundamentally illusory;

it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. By inferring from this, I see that all subtle and minute sentient beings are driven by the power of the winds of false conditions—from the sentient beings of a single world-system, even unto...
The sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm are also like this.
Each dwells within a single world, comparable to a hundred mosquitoes and gnats contained within a single vessel, chirping and clamoring in disorder.
These sentient beings, truly due to a single thought of non-awakening, merely stir up madness and turmoil within their own square-inch minds. Apart from the mind—
Externally, how could such a mark of movement exist? Because one realizes that there are no phenomena outside the mind, one swiftly awakens to non-arising amidst birth and death;
thus, the originally enlightened mind opens, and one beholds the Buddha Acala within the trembling land.
Thereupon, one becomes a Dharma Prince under the Tathāgata Acala, and eventually serves all Buddhas everywhere, succeeding them.

This flourishes the transformation of the Dharma. That body and mind emit light and penetrate all things without obstruction is due to observing that both body and mind are driven by the false conditions of the power of wind;
having realized that these delusions have no cause, one clearly perceives original enlightenment as being like pure lapis lazuli.
That the power of wind has no basis means realizing that the characteristics of wind are fundamentally empty, with nothing coming or going.
Awakening to the bodhicitta means transforming consciousness into wisdom. Entering samādhi means realizing the truth of perfect penetration.
Unifying with the Buddhas of the ten directions means ascending to accord with the fruit of Buddhahood. Transmitting the one wondrous mind means descending to transform sentient beings.
What is called the true nature of the wind of intrinsic emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is the wind of the void, which is truly the single wondrous mind.
Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha then rose from his seat... [up to] "...this perfect clarity of wondrous power is the foremost."
Commentary: This is the entry into perfect penetration through awakening to the great element of space.

"Boundless Body" refers to the Dharma-body. The true emptiness of the Dharma-body pervades all places; furthermore, the Dharma-body has no body, for it takes the myriad dharmas as its body, and is thus called "boundless.
This is because, by contemplating that the four great elements are without self, one realizes this boundless Dharma-body. Consequently—
The eight consciousnesses are transformed to form the four wisdoms. By maintaining these wisdoms and illuminating the lands of the sensory realms, one realizes that every form is empty.
Thus, the Dharma-body and the four wisdoms universally permeate and harmonize both the environment and its inhabitants.

Furthermore, within one's own mind, the Great Perfect Mirror manifests, radiating ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-light that flows and irrigates the ten directions, reaching to the very limits of empty space.

This is because, by means of a single wisdom, ten wisdoms are manifested, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions and exhausting the ultimate reality of wondrous existence within true emptiness;

this is the arising of function from essence. That all the various banner-kings of lands enter within the mirror and penetrate my body, such that the body is identical to empty space and there is no mutual obstruction, is because it accords with the essence of the Dharma-body wisdom, which encompasses all oceans of lands. All...

To enter therein is to withdraw function back into the essence. That the body is able to skillfully enter lands as numerous as motes of dust and extensively perform Buddha-activities, thereby attaining great accordance (*anuloma*), means that with a single body one enters everywhere, manifesting forms within all things and responding universally according to the capacities of beings.
As the *Avataṃsaka* says: "The pure and wondrous Dharma-body is serene and responds to all."

It is so. This "great supernatural power" (mahā-ṛddhi-bala) generally refers to the aforementioned ability to fuse with all things, to enter into all things, and the mutual inclusion of essence and function.
"By my earnest contemplation that the four great elements have no basis" means emptying the characteristics of the body.
"Delusive thoughts arise and perish" means emptying the characteristics of the mind. "Space is non-dual; the Buddha-lands are fundamentally the same" refers to the nature (*dharmatā*).
"Emptiness is the true form; the nature of form is true emptiness. Regarding "attaining the patience of non-arising through illumination within sameness":
this means realizing that form is itself emptiness and emptiness is itself form, thereby realizing the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

"Contemplating the boundlessness of emptiness to enter *samādhi*" means that by contemplating the great expanse of emptiness, one awakens to and enters perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna-avabheda*). "Sublime power, perfectly luminous" refers to...
This speaks to the ultimate truth that form and emptiness are non-dual, and that the environment and its inhabitants interpenetrate with sovereign freedom and without obstruction.
Maitreya Bodhisattva then rose from his seat... [up to] ...attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; this is the foremost.
**Commentary:** This refers to entering through perfect penetration by means of the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*). Maitreya’s proper name is *Maitreyīna*.

According to ancient exegesis, this is translated as "Kindness-Bequeather" (*Cizhong*); that is, his kindness flourishes in the present age, while his compassion reaches the future kalpa, for he takes pity on sentient beings who are deluded regarding consciousness and thus manifests his traces to bring illumination.
"I recall the past" describes the ancient account of how one enters the state of a sage from the level of an ordinary being.

This refers to the causal practice. One whose mind prizes worldly fame and delights in associating with noble clans is said to have left the household life in body but not yet entered the Way in mind;
such a person prizes empty worldly reputation and takes pleasure in befriending the aristocracy. By practicing the concentration on the nature of mind-only, they enter *samādhi*.
This means that those who prize worldly fame and clans, and whose distracted minds wander in pursuit, perceive phenomena as existing outside the mind and grasp at them.

Because they are attached to the characteristics of names and forms, he grants them the samādhi of Mind-Only Consciousness. This "Mind-Only" serves to negate the existence of external objects while distinguishing consciousness from a void mind.

Upon entering this gate of contemplation, one realizes that there are no phenomena outside the mind; all internal bodies and external environments are merely the manifestations of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of one's own consciousness, appearing like dreams or illusions—arising and ceasing without substantial reality. If one can contemplate in this way, then the outward wandering [of the mind] will cease.

The mind comes to rest, and the practice of contemplation is perfected. As for the phrase "from kalpas past until the present of immeasurable Tathāgatas," it means that because cultivation has been long sustained and the concentration on consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) has become profound, one personally realizes that all phenomena are like lightning; thus, one contemplates within the single mind.
There is no further seeking externally; delusive conditions are completely stilled, and the so-called mind is entirely empty.

Progressing gradually in this manner, one attains the supreme, wondrous perfection and awakens to the realization of the Tathāgata-garbha nature. Thus, one understands that the triple world is nothing but mind and that all phenomena are nothing but consciousness.

Thus one attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), because one realizes the principle of suchness (*tathatā*). One clearly perceives that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the body-and-mind are fundamentally without dual characteristics.
All Buddhas and Tathāgatas flow forth from their own nature; they do not manifest through anything else.

That one now receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) to succeed to the Buddha’s position immediately thereafter precisely demonstrates that, by cultivating the samādhi of mind-only consciousness (*citta-vijñapti-mātra*), one attains the perfection of the cause and the fulfillment of the fruit. Therefore...
This supplements the Buddha’s position. Regarding the passage from "The Buddha asked about perfect penetration" up to "attaining the patience of non-arising":

it means that because they had not previously cultivated the samādhi of mind-only consciousness, they did not know that the two divisions of appearance (*nimitta*) and seeing (*darśana*) are merely transformations arising from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Because they grasped these as being truly existent, they established the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Furthermore, based on those two, they engaged in pervasive conceptualization, giving rise to the notions of self and phenomena (*ātman* and *dharma*).

Because of these two attachments, the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is established. Now, through the cultivation of meditative concentration, one attains awakening to the nature of consciousness.
One clearly understands that the luminosity of awareness is the true consciousness; its wondrous enlightenment is profound and still, pervading the entire dharma-realm.

Thus, one realizes that pervasive conceptualization is fundamentally empty and dependent origination is illusory existence, such that there is only the single perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Consequently, one is able to distance oneself from both dependent and pervasive conceptualization, and thereby realize [the ultimate truth].
This is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Verses on Representation-only) states:
"When the cognition and its objects are both entirely unapprehendable, at that time one abides in representation-only, because one is free from the characteristics of the two graspings.

This is because, through the initial contemplation that the phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants, as well as defilement and purity, are merely transformations arising from consciousness and lack inherent self-nature, one does not give rise to deluded conceptualizations or pervasive attachments, such as calculating a self or... [calculating phenomena].

The Dharma is thus free from parikalpita (imagined nature). Furthermore, one realizes that both the transforming subject and the transformed object are nothing other than the single, wondrously enlightened, luminous nature, with no separate dharmas existing apart from it;
this is freedom from paratantra (dependent nature), and is the perfectly accomplished pure jewel-like awakening. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says:
The first is the absence of nature in terms of characteristics; the second is the absence of self-nature; and the last is the absence of the nature of the self and phenomena as previously grasped.
Among those of his same class, the Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta attained samādhi; he is the foremost.
Commentary: This refers to attaining great awakening and entering the perfect penetration through vision. According to the traditional explanation based on the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Guānjīng):
"Using the light of wisdom to universally illumine all beings, causing them to leave the three miserable realms and attain supreme power; thus he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta."
Furthermore, it is said that whenever this Bodhisattva lifts his foot or sets it down, all worlds tremble, causing those in the three miserable realms to attain liberation;
thus he receives this name because he invariably causes such vibrations whenever he enters the assemblies of the Buddhas.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that in the past, during the causal stage, when Amitābha was a universal monarch (cakravartin), Avalokiteśvara was his eldest son, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta...
He was the second son [of Amitābha] and now resides in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, dwelling at the left and right sides of Amitābha. "Lun" means class or category.
As for the twelve Tathāgatas, they are: Immeasurable Light, Boundless Light, Unattached Light, Majestic Light, Loving Light, and Joyful Light.

He is the One Worthy to Behold, the One of Inconceivable Light, the One of Peerless Light, the One of Unmeasurable Light, the One who Outshines the Sunlight, the One who Outshines the Moonlight, and the One who Transcends the Light of the Sun and Moon. Possessing these great titles, Amitābha has these thirteen names.
As for the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation (*nien-fo san-mei*), it consists of fully gathering the six sense faculties so that pure mindfulness continues without interruption.

If one recollects Amitābha as the self-nature, the subject who recollects belongs to correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and the object recollected belongs to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); when wisdom and truth are of one suchness, the Buddha of the original nature manifests.

If one recollects Amitābha of the Land of Bliss, the subject who recollects belongs to oneself and the object recollected belongs to the Buddha; it is simply that one’s own mind becomes darkly harmonized [with the Buddha].

To "record without forgetting" means that the Buddha himself emits light to welcome and guide them. "One person is single-mindedly mindful" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s mindfulness of sentient beings.
"One person is single-mindedly forgetful" is a metaphor for sentient beings who do not mindfully recite the Buddha's name.
As for "meeting those one has not met, or seeing those one has not seen," it is because the Buddha has no other concerns; he thinks only of sentient beings, never for even a moment parting from them.

Therefore, it is said: "If one encounters or sees [the Buddha]. Sentient beings may lack the mind to recite the Buddha’s name, yet even if the Buddha occasionally appears before them, they remain in darkness and do not know it; hence it is said: "Not encountering and not seeing.

That "the two people remember each other and do not become estranged" is a metaphor for the Buddha and sentient beings sharing the same thought, just as a form and its shadow are never separated. How could this be otherwise?
It is merely a matter of encountering and seeing [the Buddha]. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish and pity sentient beings as a mother remembers her child.
This corresponds to the previous metaphor of one person who remembers exclusively. "If the child has fled and gone away, though the mother remembers, what can she do?

This corresponds to the previous metaphor of one person who forgets exclusively. "If the child remembers the mother, just as the mother remembers the child, then throughout successive lives, mother and child will not..."
Regarding "being far removed": this corresponds to the preceding analogy of two people remembering one another, even to the point where form and shadow are never separated.

As for the passage from "if the mind of sentient beings" up to "even attaining the opening of their own minds," this explains the meaning of the above: it means that if the fruit-mind is single-mindedly mindful of the Buddha and recollects the Buddha, one will spontaneously see the Buddha before one's eyes;
this sufficiently demonstrates that the Buddha is not separate from the mind. It is only due to delusion or awakening [that they appear distant or near].

This merely concerns the manifestation and concealment [of the Buddha]. Since one has already attained the state where he is present before one's eyes, how could there be any failure to see him in the future?
Moreover, being not far from the Buddha, one attains the opening of the mind and sees the Buddha by oneself, without even relying on the expedient means of the Buddha.
Just as the body of one who has been perfumed with incense carries a fragrance, this is a metaphor for the mind being close to the Buddha; it possesses the inherent potential to attain Buddhahood.

Regarding "adorned by fragrant light," this means that by relying on the adornment of the Buddha’s fragrant light through mindfulness of the Buddha (*nien-fo*), one realizes one's own primordial *dharmakāya* Buddha.
"In my original stage [of practice], I realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) through mindfulness of the Buddha" refers to the causal practice. Now, at this [present]...
"This realm" refers to those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and are brought back to the Pure Land; this speaks of the fruition virtue, wherein cause and effect are one and the same.
"Completely gathering the six sense faculties" means that mindfulness is the mental faculty (*manas*), for the mind is the basis upon which all the other faculties rely.

When the mental faculty practices mindfulness of the Buddha, all the other faculties are thereby gathered into a single point. This is because, at the very beginning of practicing mindfulness of the Buddha...

At that time, using a mind characterized by arising and ceasing, one takes as objects the Buddha’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), as well as his secondary retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*), adornments, retinue, and so forth—each and every joyful phenomenon.

One dwells single-mindedly on a single object with an uninterrupted mind. One perceives the Buddha’s two types of retribution—the primary and secondary—as if looking into a clear mirror, surveying them all at once;
there is nothing that is not a wondrous realm. Thereafter, one contemplates the wondrousness of these perceived marks of the Buddha.

Both the object and the subject are equally false and illusory; they have no inherent nature from the beginning and are manifested solely by thought. Furthermore, one contemplates the mind that thinks:
from where does it arise? Thus, not a single dharma is perceived; it is ultimately empty and quiescent. Because the mind does not perceive the mind, no characteristic can be apprehended.
This means that both the subject and object are simultaneously stilled, being originally free from thought. Once the characteristics of thought are transcended—
Equal to the realm of empty space, there is nowhere it does not pervade; the Dharma-realm is of one suchness, and thus one realizes the equal Dharmakāya.
By recollecting the marks and signs [of the Buddha], one realizes the Buddha of the Dharmakāya; for birth is itself non-birth. Now that I have realized the Dharmakāya,
The *dharmakāya* of sentient beings is non-dual with mine; moreover, this nature of non-duality involves mutual interpenetration.

Therefore, those who practice *nienfo*, I gather and include them all. A practitioner who can understand these Dharma gates will not consider those who engage in *chan* meditation to be of superior benefit, nor will they regard those who practice *nienfo* as inferior or dull-witted.
Lecture Record on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Five.

Lecture Record on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra of the Great Buddha-Crown, the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Six.
Recorded by Shi Chengshi, Chaizi; edited and published by his dharma-disciple from Xin’an, Wang Yiyuan.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva... (until) "When birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests."
Entering the flow and reversing the flow are contrary to the nature of ordinary roots. To flow outward and rush toward objects is called "outflow" (*niṣyanda*);
to reverse the flow and unify with the One is called "inflow. As the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "Not entering form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas.
This refers to the extinction of both the subject and the object. The two instances of the character "object" (*suǒ*) here are the same as those established for Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.
Because that object is established, the three kinds of continuity are suddenly accomplished; because that object is extinguished, the two kinds of excellence are suddenly attained.
Indeed, "object" (suǒ) refers to the locus. When the mind clings to an object, it is the state of delusion;
when the mind is detached from an object, it is the state of awakening. Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. However...
In these cases of losing what is heard, what is perceived, what is empty, and what is the locus, each has its ailment and its remedy.
Because one initially uses a remedy to treat an ailment, although the ailment is removed, the remedy itself becomes an ailment;

therefore, one must apply further remedies to eliminate it until the root of the ailment is exhausted and the nature of the remedy becomes empty, leaving nothing at all, after which one spontaneously enters the stream and loses [the distinction between subject and object].

This is where one reaches full understanding. Yet, one does not give rise [to further conceptualization], as it says in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*: "One should remain far removed from all illusory and false realms.
In this way, as one gradually increases [in practice], that which hears and that which is heard both come to an end.

As it says, "The mind is like an illusion," one likewise remains far removed; the awakened and the awakened-to are empty. As it says, "Remaining far removed is itself an illusion," one likewise remains far removed until even the awakening to emptiness reaches its ultimate limit.
"Perfection, emptiness, that which is emptied, and cessation—just as one transcends clouds, one likewise transcends the transcending of illusions.
This passage extensively clarifies the meaning of the two preceding phrases: "entering samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The subsequent text, "the Vajra-samādhi of illusory hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation," restates the meaning of this very passage.
Commentary: This is the entry into perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) through the faculty of hearing. If followed in sequential order, it should follow the faculty of sight;

however, the perfect penetrations realized by the twenty-four sages mentioned previously were not the causes and conditions for Ānanda’s entry into the Way, nor were they the teaching-essence suited to the capacities of beings in this land.
Only this single door is perfectly thorough in both cause and fruit, and accords with the capacities of beings.
The teaching is appropriate to the occasion; its principles and phenomena are harmoniously integrated, and both the shallow and the profound are fully provided.

Therefore, it is presented separately at the very end. As for Avalokiteśvara, this is a title for one who possesses perfect enlightenment and perfect response. Regarding the sounds of the world, it is called "observing" (guān) rather than "hearing" (wén);

this means that one illuminates with the light of wisdom rather than hearing through the auditory consciousness. Furthermore, it was initially through the faculty of the ear that enlightenment was attained.

Having entered [the state of non-obstruction], one then uses contemplation to contemplate the auditory faculty; this clearly demonstrates that the six sense organs are fundamentally free from obstruction.
To employ the ear for contemplation likewise does not contradict principle. However, the interpretation of the name in this sutra differs from that in the *Lotus Sūtra*.

The latter explains it from the perspective of the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), revealing only the magnificent virtue of benefiting others (*parārtha*). This [sutra] explains it from the perspective of the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*), primarily manifesting the profound depth of self-benefit (*svārtha*).

Furthermore, as these two aspects mutually manifest and conceal one another, we perceive the perfect subtlety of name and reality. The Buddha whom he takes as his teacher is also called Avalokiteśvara;

this reveals that there is a realization to be attained and a transmission to be received, such that the capacity of the practitioner and the teaching harmonize, and cause and effect do not err—a connection that has existed for a long time.
To "arouse the bodhicitta" means to bring forth right knowledge and right awakening.
Above, it seeks the fruit of Buddhahood; below, it transforms sentient beings. If one does not give rise to this mind, all practices cultivated will be entirely seized by Māra.
Therefore, if you wish to cultivate the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, you must first give rise to this mind of the Great Way.
"Entering samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation" refers to the essence of the teaching of this direction. "Hearing" refers to the wisdom of hearing;
it reaches from the ear to the mind, not following the sensory object of sound to give rise to arising and ceasing, but rather returning to the single flavor of the nature of hearing itself.

This causes the remaining faculties to be completely uprooted. "Contemplation" (si) refers to the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā). Externally, one is liberated from the five sensory objects; internally, one transcends the three natures (trisvabhāva).

When no thoughts arise, one enters into dark resonance with the realm of gnosis (jñāna-viṣaya). "Cultivation" (xiu) refers to the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā). It grinds away and eliminates the habitual tendencies of falsehood.
It sweeps away the seeds of names and words, subduing delusion and following the truth.

Once the three types of wisdom have attained perfect clarity, then body and mind will both enter the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama. However, this practice of the three wisdoms must proceed from the coarse to the subtle.

The principle of the wisdom of the three contemplations likewise proceeds from the shallow to the deep. That is to say, this nature of hearing is fundamentally the profound, perfect, and wondrous awakening.

It is only because of the two objects—movement and stillness—that it adheres to the profound clarity to give rise to the faculty of hearing; as it flows outward and rushes toward external objects, it is called "outflow.
Now, for the initial application of the practice, one must first, within the faculty of hearing, turn back the hearing that hears sounds and instead hear [the source of] hearing itself.
As for its intrinsic nature, it is called "entering the stream. Thus, it does not become entangled with the auditory objects (śabda-viṣaya) that one has previously heard;

the characteristics of sound vanish of their own accord, and the discerning mind (vijñāna-citta) does not arise. This is because entering the stream causes the sense organ (indriya) to be stilled, and the disappearance of the object causes the sensory field (viṣaya) to be stilled.
When both of these are stilled, not only do active phenomena (spanda-lakṣaṇa) fail to arise, but even the state of stillness (sthiti-lakṣaṇa) does not arise. Although this—

The faculty of hearing and external objects do not merge as one; yet, when turning back to hear, the auditory mechanism that hears and the auditory nature that is heard still persist as subject and object due to long-standing habitual tendencies.
Therefore, one must further apply effort and practice to sever the grasping at a self.
Then one is able to hear that which is heard; both [the subject and object] are utterly extinguished. This is the ultimate perfection of the merit of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
It is what is called "this faculty first being liberated, whereby one first enters emptiness.

Nevertheless, because abiding in this state where both subject and object are exhausted is still an obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one must further apply contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to awaken to and shatter this obstacle, thereby penetrating through this state. Although it is thus—

This is so. If one is stingy with this contemplation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*) and cannot relinquish them, these too constitute subject and object; one would still fall into attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).

One must further apply the contemplation of the dual emptiness, wherein wisdom precedes the object of wisdom, thereby exhausting all attachments to phenomena. Thus, the merit of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) reaches its culmination.
This is what is meant by "the perfection of the luminosity of emptiness resulting in liberation through the Dharma. Nevertheless, even if subject and object are empty, [one must proceed further].

This emptiness, because its characteristic has not yet been extinguished, also constitutes the "sickness of emptiness. Therefore, one must further cultivate the perfect practice to the utmost degree, causing both the wisdom that can empty and the emptiness that is emptied to vanish together.
This is the culmination of the merit of cultivating wisdom, reaching the stage of effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*).
As it is said: "When the dharmas of liberation have already ceased, both are empty and do not arise; thus one attains the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."

Indeed, from the initial entry into the stream where objects cease to exist, right up until the state where emptiness itself is extinguished, all the stages and positions traversed in between belong to the realm of subtle arising and ceasing.
Once one arrives at this point, the two types of grasping are forever forgotten, and both [subject and object] are simultaneously emptied and discarded.
All arising and ceasing are likewise extinguished together; this very mark of extinction is quiescent and invisible, whereby one enters the great ocean of nirvana.
There remains only the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, pure and fundamental from the beginning, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
This is precisely the sign of a single faculty returning to its source, whereby all faculties become pure, one enters samādhi, and perfects Bodhi.
This is the heading.
Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds... [down to] "sharing the same sorrow and aspiration with all sentient beings.
*Commentary:* This is a general indication of two kinds of excellence, used to manifest the fruit-virtue of the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty.
"Suddenly" means in an instant. "Transcending" means attaining true liberation. This refers to the sudden severance of afflictions and the sudden realization of the true and eternal;
thus, all mundane and supramundane phenomena, as well as those of the ordinary and the small, are liberated in an instant. One is no longer bound by anything within or without the three realms.
Dividing one's body throughout the *dharmadhātu*, one illuminates the ten directions perfectly and attains the two kinds [of knowledge].
This is the sublime merit. The fundamental wondrous enlightened mind is the essence; compassionate power is the function.

First, "harmonizing upward with the Buddhas of the ten directions" means that this Bodhisattva, having perfected the cause and fulfilled the fruit, unites initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) with original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), thereby becoming entirely in accord with the true essence and wondrous function realized by the Buddhas of the ten directions. Second, [harmonizing downward with all sentient beings...]

Regarding "harmonizing with the sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions below": this means that the Buddha and sentient beings share the same true essence and wondrous function.
That which the Bodhisattva realizes is precisely the Buddha-nature, for it is the entire body and great function equally possessed by all.
At the moment of realizing the Truth, one is immediately able to harmonize with both the upper and lower realms without omission.

This is what is meant by the statement that "the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. Because one is able to transcend worldly dharmas, one attains harmony with the Buddhas above, sharing in their identical power of compassion.
Because one is able to transcend supramundane dharmas, one attains harmony with the multitude below.
They gave rise to a shared sense of sorrow and longing.
Because I made offerings to Avalokiteśvara, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
(Commentary: This refers to entering extinction through the cultivation of the Path.
If there are sentient beings whose minds of desire seek clear awakening... [he] preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve it.
(Commentary on the Preface: This refers to manifesting in the form of a celestial being to preach the Dharma according to the capacity of the audience.

The two instances of the character "yù" (desire) in "yùxīn" (mind of desire) and "yùshēn" (body of desire) both refer to the desire of longing. "The mind of desire seeks clear awakening" means to profoundly realize that carnal desire is what invites suffering.
This is the foundation. If the mind is enlightened, the body is naturally pure; if the mind’s awakening does not open up, the body likewise remains defiled and turbid.
Therefore, one delights in not transgressing the dust of desire. However, this "dust of desire" does not refer solely to the coarse desires of the lower realms;

even the pleasures of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) are included therein. As for the Brahma King, he is the Lord of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), specifically the zenith heaven of the First Dhyāna.

Regarding the "preacher of the Dharma," the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "The Great Brahmā King expounds the Discourse on Transcending Desire for those seeking liberation, causing them to abandon the dust of desire and be reborn in the Brahma Heaven. As for Śakra, he is the second lord of the Desire Realm.
Those heavens have thirty-two tiers in total, and Śakra rules over them and preaches the Dharma, namely the ten wholesome dharmas.
As the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Śakradevendra expounds various excellent discourses. This refers to that. The Heaven of Mastery (*Īśvara-deva*) is the zenith of the desire realm;
it is also called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*). This means that [the beings there] rely upon the creations of others.
"Attaining one's own bliss. Some say that on the sixth heaven there is a separate dwelling place for the Māra King, which is also subsumed under the category of the Īśvara Heaven.
"Wandering through the ten directions" refers to the ten directions of the six desire heavens and the four continents.

"Mahā-Īśvara" refers to Maheśvara, the deity at the summit of the form realm (rūpāvacara). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "He has three eyes and eight arms; he rides a white ox and holds a white fly-whisk."
They are able to fly through the void and reach other realms. The Great Heavenly Generals (*Mahārājika*) are generals under the jurisdiction of Śakra;
they reside separately in the thirty-two heavens, each leading spirits and deities to guard and protect the four directions.

They belong to the category of the Eight Divisions (*aṣṭanikāya*) and are capable of subduing Māras and protecting living beings within the lands of the lower realm. As for the Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*), they ascend...
They are the leaders of the lower realms and the first heaven among them. Each resides upon one terrace of Mount Sumeru and serves Śakra Devānām Indra, governing the four continents.
The spirits and deities under their command are divided into two groups per king, totaling eight classes of gods who protect the boundaries of the realm.
The princes of these Four Kings are of the same class as Nātsi (Nārāyaṇa). According to the *Tongji* (Comprehensive Records), these are the Four Heavenly Kings.
O King, there are each nine thousand one hundred and ten [beings] who are able to subdue and grasp spirits and objects, protecting the world and benefiting humanity.
The Four Heavenly Kings rank below Śakra-devānām-indra; these Great Generals are those commanded by the Four Kings.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being human kings (up to [the point where they desire such status]), he preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve it.
*Annotation:* This refers to manifesting in the human realm and preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of those beings.

According to the traditional explanation, all [kings] from the Golden Wheel-turning King down to the "scattered" (*xiūsuàn*) rulers are subsumed under the category of human kings. The "scattered" rulers refer to minor kings of small states scattered throughout the world.

As numerous as grains of millet, the Great Being manifested himself before them and preached the Dharma, causing them to cultivate the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions as the causes for becoming lords and nobles, and to honor their virtuous deeds so as to perfume the seeds of their future lives.
A householder possesses ten virtues, namely: noble lineage, high status, great wealth, majestic power, profound wisdom, advanced age, pure conduct, and complete etiquette.
The superior sighs in admiration and the inferior submit in reverence; because both virtue and rank flourish together, the world offers them its respect and deference.
As for the *jushi* (lay practitioner): they do not seek official office nor delight in fame. Possessing broad learning and extensive knowledge, they find joy in the Way themselves.

Whether discussing the Way and debating virtue to serve as a model for others, or composing books and establishing doctrines to leave instruction for future generations—all such individuals are [the *jushi*]. They cherish...
Those who govern a kingdom or territory are like those who establish the guiding principles and rectify the regulations, such as those who transform customs and leave behind a noble legacy.

Those who adjudicate within a state or district are like those who promote benefit and eliminate harm, ensure administration is clear and peaceful, resolve legal cases and untangle disputes, and are trusted and loved by officials and citizens;

these include the Three Dukes, the Chancellor, the Provincial Governors, and the Prefectural Magistrates. Although their respective jurisdictions differ, they are all collectively termed "officials" (*zhai-guan*). [Their] love...

As for various arts and techniques—such as astronomy and geography, the synthesis of divination and physiognomy, and the calculation of celestial cycles of waxing and waning—as well as those who cultivate *brahmacarya* (purity of conduct) for the sake of self-protection, such as the regulation and guarding of body and mind to prolong life and increase longevity:
the *brāhmaṇa*, translated here as "Pure Conduct," is one of the four castes. As for the various codes of discipline (*vinaya*), beginning with the ten precepts...
Up to full ordination (*upasampadā*), there are two hundred and fifty precepts. As for the various precepts, they likewise proceed from the five precepts up to five hundred.
*Upāsaka* is translated here as "male attendant" (*jinshi nan*); *upāsikā* is translated as "female attendant" (*jinshi nu*).
Both are so named because, by maintaining themselves through the five precepts, they are capable of attending upon the ordained monks (*bhikṣu*) and nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*). [End of] Inner Section.
"Governance" refers generally to all the duties of a wife; that is to say, she maintains cultivation within the inner chambers while harboring no ambitions beyond them.

"Establishing one's character" means being diligent, frugal, secluded, and tranquil. This applies to the household for those from the rank of Great Officer (*daifu*) downward, and to the state for those from the rank of Feudal Lord (*zhuhou*) upward.
As for female rulers, these include the Empress (*tianzi zhi hou*), the State Lady (*guofu*), the Wife of a Feudal Lord (*bangjun zhi qi*), and the Ennobled Lady (*mingfu*).
Regarding those whose wives attained glory through their husbands: there was the Lady of the Great Family, daughter of Ban Biao of the same commandery, named Zhao, styled Huaiji.
She was the wife of Cao Shetou of Fufeng during the Later Han. Emperor He summoned her to the palace several times; she was received by the Empress and the Noble Ladies.
He served him as a teacher and was called "The Great Master" (*Dajia*). Regarding the phrase "not damaging the male organ":
this refers to those who have the resolve to refrain from sexual desire for their entire lives. "Virgin" (*chǔnǚ*) is also termed "maiden" (*chǔzǐ*);

it refers to an unmarried woman who delights in remaining in her state, wishing always to remain a virgin and never to marry. "One who does not seek to be violated" means one who does not wish [to be so].
To follow [others] while remaining steadfast and self-possessed; even if there is forceful imposition or violent aggression, one vows never to comply. "Jia" (家) is pronounced as "Gu" (姑).
If there are various devas who wish to leave their celestial status (天倫), one preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve perfection.
Commentary: This manifests bodies in the various realms of existence to preach the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings.

For those in the higher heavens who delight in desire and wish to enter the celestial realms, he causes them to achieve their aim. For those in the heavens who weary of pleasure and wish to leave the celestial ranks, he causes them to achieve their aim.
As for manifesting the body of a nāga, it means that although the nāga class possesses supernatural powers, merit, and authority, they still belong to the realm of evil.
[Beings] undergo various sufferings and afflictions. Desiring to escape [these realms] and become human beings, they cultivate spiritual progress with aspiration;
therefore, I preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve success. The lower realms follow this pattern. Yakṣas—this is translated as "light and swift"—are of three types:
first, those on the earth; second, those in the void; and third, those in the heavens. They are included within the [six] destinies (*gati*). Gandharvas—this is translated as "fragrance-body."
They are also called Gandharvas, meaning "those who travel by scent. They are the musical deities of Śakra.

Because when Śakra desires to perform music and burns aloeswood incense, these deities follow the fragrance to arrive, they are so named. Asuras means "the uncomely," as their women are beautiful while their men are ugly;
they are named after the men. They are also called "Non-Gods" (Asura), because they are deceitful and lack the conduct of gods. Kinnaras—
Its form resembles that of a human, yet it has horns on its head; for this reason, it is called the "Doubtful Deity" (Yishen Tian).

It is a deity of the celestial string and wind instruments (*sishuzhu*), slightly inferior to the *gandharva*. It is also called the "Deity of Song. The *mahoraga* is called the "Earth Dragon" and is also known as the "Great Python.
Because of excessive anger and the violation of precepts, it receives this retribution. Regarding those who practice music and those who cultivate themselves, these refer to the present [state].
Among humans, after seeking the relinquishment of the body, one may again obtain a human body. This is because only in the human realm is it easy to hear the Dharma and easy to practice;

this is not the case for the various heavens that receive pleasure, nor for the other realms submerged in suffering. Therefore, one seeks not to lose the human body from lifetime to lifetime, practicing and progressing without slackening.
As for those with form, they are like the *Xiujiao Jingming Temple*; as for those without form, they are like...

Those who are scattered, dissolved, or submerged possess perception, such as gods, ghosts, and spirits; those who are without perception have their spirits transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone, and are none of them human beings.

Mahāsattva, you manifest forms according to the various classes of beings and preach the Dharma to bring them to accomplishment—just as Nāgārjuna transformed five hundred dragon hosts so that they all received full ordination, and as [the Buddha did for] Kapi... [and so forth].
"Venerable One, for the sake of the great python, he received the Three Refuges; having finished listening, he manifested as an old man and departed in plain clothes.
All such instances are of this kind.
This is called the "Miraculous Purity of the Thirty-two Manifestations," up to the "Accomplishment of Sovereign Mastery in Unconditioned Miraculous Power."

Commentary: This is a summary of the names. It means that manifesting bodies according to types and preaching the Dharma in response to capacities all appear when conditions assemble and vanish when conditions are exhausted.
They come from nowhere and leave no trace of going anywhere; because their essence is utterly quiescent, they are called "wondrously pure.
"Hearing-perfuming" and "hearing-cultivation" refer to the perfect clarity of the three aforementioned wisdoms. This is based on non-active wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*).
He manifests great spiritual transformations, universally responding to the capacities of all beings. Like the interreflecting jewels of Indra’s net, they encompass one another without obstruction;

he exerts no mental deliberation and relies on no physical effort. Therefore, it is called the "wondrous power of non-action. It appears immediately upon meeting with conditions, such that there is nothing it cannot appropriately respond to.
Therefore, it is called "sovereign accomplishment."
“World-Honored One, by further practicing this cultivation through hearing and refining what is heard, I have attained fourteen kinds of fearless merits.
[Annotation: This clarifies the second excellence: being one in sorrow and aspiration with sentient beings.
It is because the Bodhisattva has turned the hearing back toward the self-nature that he attains the perfect penetration of the three wisdoms and realizes the body of the Dharma-realm.

Mind is of a single essence and function; thus, the mind of sentient beings’ compassionate longing is subsumed within the Bodhisattva’s mind of great compassion, and the Bodhisattva’s mind of great compassion pervades the minds of sentient beings’ compassionate longing. The essence of ordinary beings and sages is identical.
Through mutual resonance and response, it is said that all sentient beings shall obtain fourteen kinds of fearless merits within my body and mind.
Indeed, when sentient beings encounter suffering and calamity, they are delivered from their state of terror at this very moment.
Thus, one is immediately free from fear and attains merit. This is as when the World-Honored One attained enlightenment;
he surveyed the sentient beings throughout the great earth and saw that they were all already identical to his own perfected realization.

It was simply because the Bodhisattva had realized that the Buddhas and sentient beings are of one essence and equally perfected, being entirely devoid of the marks of "self" and "other. Therefore, when the Bodhisattva leaves behind fear and attains merit, [it is for this reason].
All sentient beings in the great earth are like this; it is not necessary to speak of his bestowing of grace. The subsequent passages follow this pattern. First:
"Because of me, Avalokiteśvara, [they] do not look upon themselves... passing through dangerous roads, they cannot be plundered by bandits."
Commentary: This enables sentient beings to attain within my body and mind the merit of fearlessness regarding the eight difficulties.

The Bodhisattva’s faculties do not follow after objects; thus, the dust of sound is naturally stilled and the nature of hearing is unborn. When objective conditions do not encounter [the faculty], [the sense-field] is empty.

One immediately attains liberation and achieves contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). Realizing that this contemplative wisdom is fundamentally identical in essence with the minds of all sentient beings, it is said:

"Because I do not observe my own voice, but observe it solely through contemplative wisdom, those throughout the ten directions who suffer and contemplate my name shall all be gathered and brought into the midst of this contemplative wisdom."
Therefore, my observation of sentient beings and the observation of sentient beings of me are identical in essence and function;
suffering and joy are non-dual; the holy and the ordinary are equal; and emotion and wisdom are interfused.

Thus, I have attained the return of a single faculty to its source, no longer following the deluded karma arising from the six faculties, and thereby cause all sentient beings to immediately return to true stillness and liberation from suffering and affliction.
