As for the second [section], "Below," it reveals the liberation of the sense faculties and collectively subsumes the seven elements.

For although seeing and cognition belong to the element of fire, they originally arise from the external objects adhering to the profound stillness (*zhan*) to emit light. Now, by again reversing the faculty of sight back to that profound stillness, the activity of seeing no longer intersects with its objects, and the fire of the external dust naturally subsides.
The nature of this fire is empty and quiescent; it is the *tathāgatagarbha*, pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm. Therefore, it causes...

Sentient beings cannot be burned by fire. Although the nature of hearing belongs to water, it originally arose from delusion due to being adhered to by external objects within the profound stillness (*zhan*).
Now, as hearing is turned back and returns to that stillness, the activity of hearing no longer interacts with objects; thus, the water naturally dries up.
The nature of water is empty and quiescent, for it is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, sentient beings cannot be drowned by water.
Deluded thought (*vikalpa*) is precisely the dark ghost. Ghosts take the obscure and hidden as the cause of their perception, and they take killing and harming as the condition for their descent.

Thus, deluded thought arises and ceases, killing the Dharma-body and destroying the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*). If deluded thought is severed, then internally the dark ghost is extinguished and externally the karma of killing is eliminated.
Because one returns to the single *tathāgatagarbha*-mind, sentient beings are enabled to escape from becoming ghosts.
This is harmful. Fifth, "the lower" reveals that the function of the ear-faculty is superior as it subsumes the six faculties. Regarding "perfuming hearing to become hearing":
this means that when one turns back the hearing, through the internal perfuming of the true hearing of original enlightenment, false hearing becomes the nature of true hearing;

thus the six faculties dissolve and all return to being identical with the ear-faculty—what is called "one turning back and the six becoming pure. Once the faculties and their objects have dissolved, [the text continues:]
Then the mirror of the mind is empty and luminous, and the light of wisdom is unmoving. Who could distinguish self and other, such that one would be on the verge of being harmed?
Weapons are shattered into fragments; the nature of dust is empty. Cutting water or blowing upon light—the nature of the sense faculties is quiescent.
Thus, although the body exists, it is like light: visible yet ungraspable; like water: divisible yet indestructible. This is because...
This means bringing one's head close to the white blade; it is the wisdom-sword that cuts through the spring breeze.

"The brilliance of the permeation of hearing" means that by using true hearing to permeate false hearing until the practice reaches its ultimate limit, one returns to the fundamental essence of brilliant clarity, wherein inner luminosity radiates light.

It universally illuminates the dharma-realm. As for the nature of the darkness of ignorance and perversion, it cannot be fully [perceived]. *Yakṣa* refers to a spirit that understands what is seen before one;
*rākṣasa* means a terrifying ghost; *kumbhāṇḍa* means a ghost that causes loathing or bewitchment; *piśāca* means a ghost that devours vital essence.

Pūtana—translated as a "fever-demon"—is one of the various classes of ghosts. Since all ghostly beings are formed by receiving and sustaining a subtle, obscured energy (*yūqi*), they cannot manifest themselves here, for light can destroy darkness.
Seventh, the passage below reveals that when the sense-object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*) is dissolved, all other sense-objects are likewise dissolved;
this refers to the withdrawal of the six objects. When the nature of sound is completely dissolved, there is nothing within to bind one. When hearing is turned back and enters within, then...

Externally, there is nothing to which one is bound. Because the mind is burdened by sensory dust (*viṣaya-rajas*), there are prohibitions; because the faculties and their objects are obstructive in substance, there are shackles and fetters.

If internally there is nothing to which one is bound and externally there is nothing with which one is coupled, then even while situated in bonds and imprisonment, the mind and its objects are empty and tranquil.

Sensory sounds afflict the mind and harm its nature, just like thieves; therefore, when sounds are extinguished and hearing becomes perfect, then sound— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The above translation reflects the available portion.*
Dust is extinguished, yet the nature of the faculties is perfected; being without adversaries within or without, good and evil are fundamentally the same.

Reaching every place, one universally generates the power of compassion, so that no one again harbors an evil intent toward another. Thus, even though sentient beings pass through perilous places, bandits are likewise transformed into compassionate forces.
Ninth, the perfuming of hearing leaves the sense-objects behind so that one is not plundered by forms (up to: all *icchantikas* forever leave behind the darkness of ignorance).
[Commentary: This causes sentient beings to attain the merit of fearlessness regarding the three poisons within my own body and mind.
Ninth is "The Lower. This raises the issue of greed, anger, and delusion, thereby exhausting the fundamental ignorance at their root.
When the cultivation of hearing becomes perfected, one is utterly detached from form; yet one can still reflect forms according to their direction, like a mirror manifesting images.
How then could form ever plunder the true mind? Once the faculties and their objects are disengaged, from what source could the thought of greedy desire arise? As for anger—

They arise from opposition and manifest through conflict and resistance. Once one has realized the single, perfect sound, then whether it be slander or praise, there is nothing that is not a wondrous sound;
all returns to the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*). When the sensory object of sound is thus purified, the faculty of hearing has no partner with which to pair;
then all things are perfectly interfused, devoid of subject and object. Thus, the mind of right and wrong is fundamentally quiescent, as are the conditions of opposition and compliance.
Since it is itself empty, how can there be any anger? As for delusion: because the false objects of perception obscure it, the true mind’s ignorance covers its essence of wisdom.

Now, being able to eliminate the darkness of these objects and restore its brilliant clarity, both the internal body and mind and the external dharma-realm are transparently and thoroughly illuminated, like pure lapis lazuli. There is only this single essence of wisdom; who, then, could be the deluded darkness?
*Ātyantika* (阿顛迦) means "one who lacks a virtuous mind"; this refers to the ultimate state of dullness and delusion.
These afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion are not possessed by ordinary beings alone. Even those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) who rejoice in *nirvāṇa* possess greed;

their aversion toward *saṃsāra* is hatred; and their confusion regarding the Middle Way is delusion. Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas extensively seek the Buddha-dharma, this is greed; [their] disparaging of the Two Vehicles...
"Mounting" refers to anger. "Not yet having realized the Buddha-nature" refers to ignorance.
Twelfth: "The merging of forms and returning to hear the Immovable Bodhimanda... [until] the multitude lovingly reveres a woman with physical marks."
Commentary: This causes sentient beings to attain the merit of the two kinds of fearlessness within my own body and mind.

"Fusing the form and returning to hearing" means that by dissolving the illusory body and reversing false hearing, one returns solely to the pure and wondrous precious awakening, thereby realizing the single truth that is boundless.
Thus, the myriad functions are fully manifested; because the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual, one is able to... [not fear].

He moves through the site of enlightenment and traverses all dharma-realms. With infinite bodies, he serves countless Buddhas, until finally, by making offerings to the Buddhas, he attains sufficiency in merit;
by receiving the Dharma, he attains sufficiency in wisdom. Thus, he is able to perpetuate and glorify the Buddha’s transformation, ensuring it is never interrupted.
Possessing the way of a true son of the Buddha, he also enables sentient beings to have their petitions fulfilled within his own body and mind.
Thus, a son endowed with merit and wisdom is born. His six sense faculties function interchangeably, perfectly penetrating and unimpeded.
Because it is the single, wondrously luminous true mind and the precious, brilliant, wondrous nature, it is both able to illuminate and able to contain.

Since illumination and containment are non-dual, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is established to signify that all reflections appear without error. Because it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm, the Space Tathāgata is established.
The "Treasury" (Zàng) signifies that it contains and nurtures all things without exception. Because it solely contains and nurtures, it is able to receive and accord with the secret dharma-gates;

because it solely illuminates the present, it is able to accept and grasp them without error. Thus, "receiving and acceding" corresponds to the meaning of the Earth (*Kūn*) and its quality of flexibility;
"accepting and grasping" corresponds to the duties within the inner chambers. Since she possesses the virtues of a woman, she also causes sentient beings to [attain] my body and mind.
In accordance with their requests, he brought forth a daughter endowed with auspicious marks.
Fourteenth: throughout this trichiliocosm, he bestows the power of fearlessness and brings blessings to all sentient beings.
Commentary: This indicates that sentient beings shall attain the merit of fearlessness through the recitation of my name within their own bodies and minds.
"The three thousand great thousand worlds with hundreds of billions of suns and moons" refers to the sphere of transformation of Śākyamuni Buddha.

"Sixty-two *asaṃkhyeya* oceans of *gangesāṇikā* bodhisattvas" refers to those capable of being transformed and delivered within that sphere of influence. "Expedient means" (*upāya*) refers to provisional wisdom. "Wisdom" (*prajñā*)...

This is true wisdom. It is said that although this Bodhisattva possesses both types of wisdom—those for self-benefit and those for benefiting others—and their respective Dharma gates are diverse and different, the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have realized is solely the gateway of the ear.
It opens up the perfect and subtle, perfectly accords with the capacities of beings, and is able to follow the essence of the teaching; only then can one take all body and mind as one.
Because it is both body and mind, it is called "subtle and wondrously all-encompassing. Because one can, with a single body-mind, be all body-minds, it is called "pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Indeed, this perfect faculty (root) is the foundation of the myriad practices and the basis of the three virtues.
When realization is attained herein, all things are equal. Therefore, the merit of upholding my single name is equal to that of upholding [the names of] the multitude.

It is called "Merit. It is equal and without difference from the World-Honored One. Regarding the reason why one attains true perfect penetration by descending [from the state of the World-Honored One], it means that the faculty of hearing possesses three kinds of reality; by attaining this perfect penetration, one realizes the equal Dharma-body.
This is called "Below," which summarizes the preceding text. "Blessings are complete for all sentient beings" means that it is not only to cause them to be without...

It is out of fear, and furthermore, to preserve their merit and virtue. According to ancient teachings, because the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) is sharp among the sentient beings of this land, those who receive the Way are numerous;
thus, Avalokiteśvara’s transformation is superior. Because the other faculties are dull, those who receive the Way are few; thus, the transformations of the other sages are inferior.
From this we know that although their stages and positions may be equal, the capacities they encounter differ. [This applies] generally to those bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...
Śākyamuni. Because he alone can subdue adversaries, the merit of holding his name is equal to that of Avalokiteśvara.

Based on this teaching, the essential point for attaining perfect penetration has already been subtly discerned; however, for those who have not yet understood, I await further detailed discernment by Mañjuśrī.
“World-Honored One, I have further attained this perfect penetration and realized [the path] up to the four inconceivable, effortless, and wondrous virtues.

(Commentary: This is a general heading indicating the four inconceivables. “I have further attained this perfect penetration” refers to the aforementioned perfect penetration of the non-differentiation among mind, Buddha, and sentient beings. “To cultivate and realize the unsurpassed path” means...
It appears to be the realm realized by a Samyaksambuddha. Regarding the four inconceivables:
while the former two kinds of excellence can still be contemplated and deliberated upon, these are even more perfectly complete and sublime, allowing no room for thought or verbal discussion.
All manifestations of form and all preaching of the Dharma are not produced through volitional effort; rather, they are spontaneously and effortlessly accomplished.
Therefore, they are called "the wondrous virtue of non-action."
First, by virtue of my initial attainment of the wondrously wondrous mind of hearing [the Dharma], I have attained great mastery in rescuing and protecting sentient beings.
(Capitulation Note: This clarifies that a single embodiment manifests many capacities; it is the inconceivable power of a single voice expounding many mantras.
It is said that the faculty of hearing fundamentally possesses three kinds of reality (*tattva*), which are far more exquisite than those of the other faculties.

Because I first turned my hearing back toward its own nature within the process of listening, I attained perfect penetration in a single realization, whereby all the faculties function interchangeably. This is the most exquisite among the exquisite;

therefore, it is called "exquisite-exquisite" (*miaomiao*). Below the phrase "the mind of hearing," the text further explains this by stating: "This mind of exquisite-exquisite hearing arises from that turning back..."
Having heard this for a long time, one concentrates the mind with singular purity until the faculties and their objects are completely liberated.

Thus, the six sense organs are simultaneously and perfectly uprooted, so that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing can no longer be partitioned. They return to the single True Dharma-realm, where Bodhi is perfected and the myriad existents are harmoniously integrated.
Being neither defiled nor pure, it encompasses all things; therefore, within a single body, it manifests the multitudes.
It extensively contains and expounds boundless secret mantras (*vidyā*). For their principle issues from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and their divine efficacy is unfathomable;
truly, they are inconceivable. *Śakara* means "firm" or "solid"; *mudrā* means "seal.
The "Pure Jewel Eye" refers to the five eyes being perfectly clear and bright, illuminating all phenomena. It is the head, serving as the totality of the six faculties.

The arms possess the power of lifting and receiving; the eyes possess the function of illuminating and discerning. By overturning the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), one achieves the eighty-four thousand hands and eyes;
by transforming the eight consciousnesses, one realizes the four wisdoms; by transforming the five aggregates (*skandha*), one realizes the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Thus, every pore of the body becomes a sublime function, sometimes manifesting a compassionate countenance to protect the roots of goodness.
Sometimes he manifests majestic spiritual power to subdue those of evil nature; sometimes he employs the marks of meditative concentration to arrest their distraction;

and sometimes he utilizes the marks of wisdom to dispel their delusion. Thus, while he gathers and transforms all capacities and responds universally to all beings, he never initiates any deliberate mental effort.
Without relying on deliberate effort, one responds in accordance with conditions, never encountering obstruction; therefore, it is said that one attains great mastery (*mahāvaśitā*).
This arises because the nature of hearing has been perfumed by the *vajra-samādhi*, thereby perfecting the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa-citta*);
thus, one is able to rescue and protect sentient beings, attaining great mastery.
Second, by means of my hearing and contemplation, I have emerged from the six sense objects... (up to) all name me as the one who bestows fearlessness.
[Commentary: This clarifies that he manifests various forms and speaks each respective mantra, which are inconceivable. Hearing and contemplation.

That is to say, the aforementioned wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) cannot be obstructed by the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), as they have transcended them.
Furthermore, because the faculties and capacities (*indriya*) of sentient beings differ, the manifestations of form (*rūpa*) that appear according to those capacities also differ.

Because the inclinations and preferences of sentient beings differ, the spells (*dhāraṇī*) taught according to those capacities also differ. Nevertheless, each individual form is manifested and each [spell] is taught.

Through these mantras, I am able to cause all sentient beings to be free from every fear. For this reason, the sentient beings in lands as numerous as motes of dust all call me "the Bestower of Fearlessness.
This is because, by being permeated with the Vajra Samādhi, my faculty of hearing has developed the immeasurable mind of compassion;
thus, I am able to cause all sentient beings to call me "the Bestower of Fearlessness."
Third, because I have cultivated the fundamentally wondrous and perfect penetration (up to the point where they) offered their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassion.
[Commentary: This clarifies the inconceivable transformation of those who have passed through [the stages]. "Fundamentally wondrous and perfect penetration" refers to the faculty of the ear.
By means of this, one realizes the pure fundamental root; thus, the *ālayavijñāna* is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Regarding all...
Because there is no grasping whatsoever toward sensory objects, the worlds in which they roam all transform stinginess into joy;
they also sacrifice their own bodies and treasures, seeking my compassionate acceptance. This arises from the Vajra-samādhi permeating the nature of hearing.
Because one accomplishes the immeasurable mind of joy (*muditā*), one is able to cause all sentient beings to rejoice without begrudging their own bodies or wealth.
Fourth, I have attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate; having sought great *nirvāṇa*, I have attained great *nirvāṇa*.
Commentary: This clarifies that making offerings to the Buddha gives rise to inconceivable results.

"Attaining the Buddha-mind" means that one has cultivated the mind of the causal stage until it wondrously accords with the awakening of the resultant stage. "Realizing the ultimate" means finally entering the ocean of the fruit of Sublime Awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);
thus, immeasurable dharma-treasures of merit manifest before one, enabling the production of all manner of precious jewels.
They extensively perform Buddha-works; having already made offerings to all Buddhas with various kinds of rare jewels, they further provide for sentient beings with various kinds of Dharma-wealth.

This means that because Bodhisattvas, with a mind of equanimity throughout the entire Dharma-realm, perceive that there is no one who is not a Buddha, they conceive the thought that all are Buddhas and thus extensively bestow offerings. [The result is] long life for wife and children, and the worldly wealth of the Dharma.
Wife and children belong to the external; life span belongs to the internal. Samādhi and nirvāṇa are the supramundane wealth of the Dharma.

The phrase "and so forth" (*naiti*) is a term used for abbreviation. Among the two types of giving—the mundane and supramundane wealth of the Dharma—whatever cannot be fully enumerated is all included herein.
This is because, by reversing the hearing toward the faculty [of hearing], one attains the Buddha-mind and thereby accomplishes the mind of immeasurable relinquishment.
May all ordinary beings and sages, both mundane and supramundane, have their aspirations fulfilled as they wish.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I [responded] from the gateway of the ears... (up to)... therefore, the name Avalokiteśvara pervades the worlds of the ten directions.

Commentary: This concludes the response regarding the perfect penetration (*yuantong*). It means that I have entered deeply through the single gateway of the ear-faculty into those six faculties of cognition;
thus, they were uprooted and liberated in their totality. Consequently, I attained the perfect illumination of the three types of wisdom, which is a single essence of pure truth.

Thus, I accord with all Buddhas above and harmonize with all sentient beings below, responding and manifesting according to conditions, while my mind attains sovereign mastery. Now, if one traces back its cause:
Beginning from the entry into the stream and the forgetting of objects, one attains samādhi and ultimately achieves bodhi, in perfect accord with original enlightenment.

This means that one takes the mind of non-arising and non-extinction as the fundamental cause of cultivation, and subsequently realizes the complete fruition of the stage of fruition through practice and realization.
Furthermore, that Buddha’s bestowing of my prediction and my attainment of this name were entirely due to my skillfully attaining this root of perfect penetration.
Once a single faculty returns to its source, the functions of the six senses cease; then the ten directions are perfectly luminous, being nothing other than the single Tathāgata-garbha mind.
Therefore, when I observe or listen, my capacity pervades the entire Dharma-realm, and throughout the Dharma-realms of the ten directions, all hear my name.
At that time, the World-Honored One [sat] upon the lion throne... (up to)... where Brahma-songs and hymns were spontaneously performed. [Commentary:
This clarifies that the holy and the mundane, the dust-motes and the lands, are all one—the fundamental root of perfect penetration.
The five limbs simultaneously radiate precious light to manifest the entire body; from top to bottom, all is the fundamental root of perfect penetration. The Buddhas radiate [light].

Light. Regarding those who receive the empowerment through its coming and going: this reveals that the true awakening of self and others is fundamentally interfused and devoid of superiority or inferiority;
this is the actual substance of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*).
Empowering the crown of the head alone manifests this dharma-gate of perfect realization as the most sublime and unsurpassed. From the Buddhas down to the Arhats, it is thus empowered.

This reveals that the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit penetrates to the source of the cause. Furthermore, for those who have already realized perfect penetration, the fruit allows both self and others to be fully expressed;
for those who have not yet realized perfect penetration, they cannot avoid the arising of internal obstructions.

When the sounds from the forest and the pond are played and the lights intermingle, it reveals that once the sense organs and their objects have dissolved, sound and light interact; thus, the two types of retribution—the primary (the physical body) and the secondary (the environment)—[are transformed].
Because the nature [is thus]... true wisdom manifests before one; then all sounds are the voice of the Buddha, and all forms are wondrous forms.
There is nothing that is not a point of awakening and entry, and nothing that is not the principle of perfect penetration. Therefore, the entire great assembly—
Upon seeing this form once, or hearing this sound once, one is able to shatter the obstacles of delusion and attain samādhi—namely, the "Ultimate Solidity of All Phenomena.
Nothing lies outside of this. Furthermore, it encompasses the twenty-four sages, bringing them all back to the fundamental source of Guanyin’s perfect penetration;
all may be termed the "Vajra Samādhi. At that moment, flowers rained down from the sky.
"Reaching the state where [the faculties] naturally unfold and present themselves" reveals that when a single faculty returns to its source, the five turbidities are all purified;
the nature of the faculties dissolves away, and the sensory realms merge into one. Only the wondrous mind of one's own precious awakening manifests wherever it may be;
effortless, wondrous conduct is spontaneously accomplished, and the pure, wondrous sound resonates perfectly everywhere. These two lines regarding *brahma*-chanting are in profound accord with this.
Regarding the "Roots' Perfect Penetration":
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī (up to the point where he asks), "By which door of skillful means can [enlightenment] be easily accomplished?
[Commentary: This was an order to Mañjuśrī to select the perfect penetration. Although it may follow either the sense-faculties (*indriya*) or the sense-objects (*viṣaya*), there is no...
They are not the ultimate truth; all may enter into realization through them. However, when first beginning one's practice, one must choose a single gateway.

Furthermore, while the essence of the teaching has its various methods and capacities for the Dharma are not uniform, the realization of the nature ultimately converges upon perfect penetration. To accommodate the faculties of sentient beings, one must select the appropriate expedient means.

However, one who is not a person of great wisdom cannot discern and select [the true path]; therefore, Mañjuśrī was commissioned. "Initial skillful means" refers to the time before realizing perfect penetration;
"true perfect penetration" refers to the time after realization. This is what is meant by "opening the door of skillful means and revealing the mark of reality.
In truth, there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or posteriority; it all returns to the One.

The Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally without differentiation. As for who is suited to its root—that is, the state realized by the various sages—although it is equal for all, how could the gateway for initial entry be restricted solely to the capacity of Ānanda?
Nevertheless, in responding to capacities, one takes up only a single door; therefore, one must exercise discernment so that Ānanda may focus exclusively upon it. Which direction is this?
Regarding "attaining easy accomplishment through an expedient gate": this refers not only to the present occasion of Ānanda alone,

but also to those who, after my parinirvāṇa, cultivate the causes of a bodhisattva within this realm seeking the unsurpassed fruit— by what gate must they necessarily proceed to easily attain accomplishment?
Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha:
“The nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect; ... (omitted) ... The initial mind enters samādhi; its slowness or speed differs from one person to another.”

Commentary: This clarifies that because the true nature follows conditions (*pratyaya*), delusion and falsehood arise; yet, by reversing falsehood to follow the truth, there are skillful means (*upāya*).
Entering these skillful means for the first time also involves varying degrees of slowness or speed, and one must necessarily exercise discernment to accord with the individual's capacity (*yogya*).
From the passage beginning "Mañjuśrī," the scribe records the text, stating that the essence of the fundamental awakened nature (*mūla-bodhi-citta*) is like a great ocean. Fundamentally...

It comes forth as clear, tranquil, and perfectly complete. This awakened nature inherently possesses perfect, penetrating, and wondrous function; it requires no contrived effort and is utterly free from subject and object.
This is truly because, upon the fundamental essence of original luminosity, delusion gives rise to the capacity to illuminate, which in turn generates that which is illuminated.
Once the distinction between subject and object is established, the capacity to illuminate the true nature is lost. When the original nature is obscured, emptiness and awareness become separated;
this is precisely how one becomes deluded regarding the *tathāgatagarbha* and forms the *ālayavijñāna*. Being deluded regarding true emptiness, one falls into a state of inert emptiness.

From this, relying on that obscure emptiness, material forms (*rūpa*) are bound together, and further, the divisions of delusive thought arise, establishing the two kinds of worlds: the body and the vessel-world.
When deluded thoughts coalesce, they form the realm of the insentient; when deluded thoughts differentiate, they form sentient beings with cognition.
This is precisely how the two divisions of "seeing" and "appearance" arise from the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*).

How could one know that empty space arises within the substance of Great Enlightenment, no different from a single bubble emerging from the great ocean? When compared with empty space, [the world] is but a tiny fraction.
If even the Great Awakening is thus limited by its inferiority, how much more so must the minute, conditioned lands of dust be, for they are all established upon emptiness?
If one knows that waves upon the sea quickly perish, then the essence of emptiness itself is fundamentally non-existent;
how much more so the three realms of existence produced in dependence upon that emptiness? Therefore, know that when all delusive objects are extinguished, one returns to the source.
The primordial awakening is by nature fundamentally non-dual. Yet, in the desire to restore this non-dual awakened nature, there are many gates of skillful means, not merely a single path.
Once one has ascended to the ground of the sages, the original nature is fully realized, and entry may be achieved from any place.
All dharmas are perfectly penetrating. This means that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are all able to realize this within the eighteen realms; why, then, should one make distinctions?

However, for a person who has first resolved their mind and wishes to enter samādhi, there is a difference between those with perfect faculties and those with imperfect faculties, such that a single day for the former is equivalent to an eon for the latter.
Because of these differences in speed—whether slow or fast—one selects those with perfect faculties. This distinction of speed corresponds to the concepts of "favorable" and "adverse."
It is because the ear-faculty is compliant that its accomplishment is swift; because the other faculties are contrary, their accomplishment is slow. In other realms, it is the opposite.
Since the perception of forms binds one to sensory objects, and the subject and object do not pervade all things, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Commentary: This clarifies that the six sense objects do not correspond [to reality]. For those of this region who are retrograde and slow-witted, these must be carefully distinguished.
That is to say, although Śāṇavāsa attained awakening through the sense object of form, the nature of this form is actually formed by the binding of deluded thoughts;
it is a defiling object that creates obstruction. Since it is produced by thought, the essence of the discerning mind does not [correspond to it].
It is capable of clear penetration. How could there be any defilement of darkness that it cannot penetrate? Yet, how can a beginner rely upon this to attain perfect penetration?
Although Cunda entered through awakening to the sound of the Dharma, this sound is merely a mixture of speech;
it is nothing more than names, phrases, and syllables. A single character directly constitutes a "name" (nāman), which designates its own essential nature. Many...
The "character" (word) serves both to express and to distinguish the meaning within a phrase. "Flavor" refers to the underlying principle or meaning.
Now, a name cannot contain a phrase and its meaning, nor can a phrase universally encompass all principles and meanings.
How then could a beginner understand how a single word universally contains all meanings, wishing to rely upon it to attain perfect penetration? It is exactly so, Incense-Venerable, although...
One enters through awakening to the object of fragrance. However, fragrance is known to exist only when it meets the nose; apart from the faculty of the nose, fragrance fundamentally does not exist.
Furthermore, the knowing that can perceive it cannot be eternally identical with the fragrance that is perceived.
But how could fragrance be eternally abiding? As for beginners, how can they rely upon it to attain perfect penetration?
Although the Medicine King attained entry through the sense-object of taste, this nature of taste is likewise not an inherently eternal essence.
The nature of the tongue-sense faculty exists only when it encounters flavor; apart from the sense organ, it does not exist at all.
Furthermore, the faculty that perceives it does not actually join with the object of flavor to become a single entity, for the sense organ is not constant and flavor is not constantly present.
How, then, can you seek perfect penetration through this? That which is the tasting of flavor is simply the act of tasting itself. Although [this was said], Subhūti...
One enters into awakening through the sense-object of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*). However, this object of tangibility can only be manifested by means of the body that is touched;
if there were no body to be touched, the touching agent would likewise not be manifest. Thus, the subject and object must be conjoined.
If the sense-object of touch has a nature, then when subject and object are both separated, the sense-object of touch would lack a nature.
Thus, it exists when combined and lacks existence when separated; its nature is not fixed. How can you rely upon this and seek to attain perfect penetration?

Kāśyapa, although one may enter through awakening by means of the dharma-object, the dharma-object is merely the shadow of the five preceding objects that have passed away; therefore, it is called an "internal object. Furthermore—

The internal sense-object (*viṣaya*), which is that which depends [upon a support], can only manifest when there is necessarily a supporting mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). Apart from the faculty, it does not exist at all.

Although they depend upon one another for their establishment, within that which depends there is fundamentally no nature of the support, and within the support there is likewise no nature of that which depends.
Since the dependent and the supported do not mutually pervade one another, how can a beginner, based on this, desire to attain [realization]?
"Perfect penetration? No. It relies [upon conditions].
Although the seeing-nature is transparently clear... (up to)... thoughts and perceptions cannot be shed; how then can perfect penetration be attained? Commentary:
This clarifies that the five sense organs are not the direct path for those of this region who are regressive and slow-witted; therefore [it is not the means for them].

One must examine this carefully. Although Luṭa once attained entry through awakening to the nature of seeing, and although this nature of seeing was indeed transparently clear, when it came to the four directions, he could only clarify three directions and could not clarify the direction behind him.
When it came to the four intermediate points, he was further deficient regarding the two points behind. How can a beginner rely upon such a [realization]?
How can one achieve perfect penetration through a faculty that is circular? "Wei" (維) means a corner; "kui" (虧) means deficient. To be deficient by half means to perceive only the first two corners.

Although Pāṇṭhaka attained entry through the faculty of the nose, this faculty of the nose— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. This translation reflects the partial nature of the source.)
When the exhalation has ended, one cannot immediately inhale; when the inhalation has ended, one likewise cannot immediately exhale.
Between the exhalation and inhalation, there is a gap in their intersection. This constitutes a state of fragmentation and interruption, where they do not flow into one another.
How, then, can one attain perfect penetration based on such fragmented faculties? "Fragmented" (zhīlí) means not being continuous. It is not [the case that...].
"No, Śāriputra. 'Jiao' (涉) means 'to intersect. Although Pāṭirātri attained entry through the faculty of the tongue, this tongue-entry was not without cause;
its manifestation must depend upon the object of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*) before sensory awareness can arise.
If taste were to vanish entirely, then this cognitive discernment could no longer be found. How, then, O beginner, could you rely upon this to attain perfect penetration? Piṅgala.
Ga. Although one gains entry through the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), this body-faculty shares the same significance as the aforementioned tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*).

It is only by means of the tangible object that acts as the agent of contact that the body, which is the object of contact, is manifested; thus, the dependent is revealed by the supporting factor, and the supported is made manifest by the supporting factor.
Each of these is not Perfect Enlightenment. Furthermore, the body-faculty and the object of touch each have their own boundaries and limitations;
they cannot meet in profound union. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration by relying upon them? Well said.

Although one may enter through awakening by means of the mind-faculty, this faculty of mental cognition is intermingled with the consciousness of distracted thoughts. Even if that consciousness were made limpid, tranquil, and clear—

At that time, one ultimately does not perceive the existence of a faculty of mental cognition (*manovijñānendriya*). If there were such a faculty of mental cognition, there would necessarily be conceptualization (*saṃjñā*);

yet, as the faculties and consciousnesses are mutually dependent, they cannot be separated. Therefore, even those who have long cultivated the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) are still unable to discard conceptualization and perceive the mental faculty (*manas*) alone.
How then can you, with your initial resolve, wish to rely upon this to attain perfect penetration?
"Disturbed thoughts and recollections" both refer to the sixth consciousness. However, since the sixth takes the seventh as its root, it is called the "mental faculty" (manas-indriya).

When consciousness, seeing, and the three harmonious conditions [of sense organ, object, and consciousness] are mixed together—[extending from] "recollection depends on objects" to "how can one attain perfect penetration apart from things?"—[it is impossible].
Commentary: This distinguishes that the six consciousnesses are not the perfect penetration suited for the capacity of the practitioner.

Although Qiuzi attained awakening through the visual consciousness, this consciousness arises from the conjunction of the sense organ and its object. If one investigates its source, it has never possessed an intrinsic substance or characteristic.
When the organ and the object meet, there is the organ and the object; when they separate, it has no self-nature. It is indeterminate.

"On what do you rely to seek to attain perfect penetration? Samantabhadra, although you entered through the faculty of auditory consciousness, this 'hearing of the mind' that penetrates the ten directions arises solely from the power of great vows cultivated over a long period of causal practice;
it is not something that can be attained through the inferior practices of a beginner. How then can you seek to attain perfect penetration through this?"

Yes, Sunda. Although one enters through awakening by means of nose-consciousness, this perception of the nose is fundamentally a provisional device intended only to gather and collect the scattered mind so that it may dwell for a time.
Once the mind has achieved the ability to dwell, then the white sign at the tip of the nose—
It also establishes that which is dwelt upon. How can one, relying on a mind that dwells within existence, seek to attain perfect penetration?

As for the contemplation of the nose, it refers to forming the visualization of white at the tip of the nose. "Adaptive means" (upāya) refers to establishing expedients to respond to the capacities of beings.

Pūrṇa attained awakening through the consciousness of the tongue; yet, although the preaching of the Dharma involves the modulation of sounds by the tongue-consciousness, [it is not the tongue itself that constitutes the essence].
Sounds and written characters can only awaken others, enabling them to first achieve fruition; however, as for one's own fruition, it may not necessarily be achieved immediately.

Furthermore, names and phrases are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and are not subsumed within the untainted (*anāsrava*). How, then, can one rely upon them and hope to attain perfect penetration?
As for awakening others so they may first achieve fruition, it is like teaching the Mahāyāna to those who are already Bodhisattvas.

The Dharma, yet one does not personally realize it for oneself—this is so. Upāli, although one may gain entry through the consciousness of the body, the observance of precepts can only restrain a single body.
If there is no [mind], even if that consciousness exists, there is nothing to be restrained.
Furthermore, the consciousness of the body is limited solely to the body and cannot pervade all things. How can one rely upon this which is not pervasive?

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, do you wish to attain perfect penetration through consciousness? Although you have entered realization by means of the mental consciousness, this supernatural power was originally accomplished through the causes and conditions of vast eons past;
what connection, then, does it have with the discrimination of hearing the Dharma?
Or if one says that you attained entry into realization because you heard the Three Kāśyapas proclaim the Buddha’s teachings on causes and conditions, how could that not be relevant?"
This is the Buddha-dharma. Therefore it is said: "Even though one contemplates the dharma of causes and conditions, it is not separate from phenomena.
How can one, by relying on this consciousness that grasps at objects, hope to attain perfect penetration?
"If one contemplates through the nature of earth... (up to) 'cause and effect now differ; how can one attain perfect penetration?
[Commentary: This selection of the seven elements indicates that they are not the perfect penetration suited to the capacities of those here in this land.

Although Sthavira Mahāsthāmaprāpta attained awakening by means of the element of earth, if one contemplates through the element of earth, it is fundamentally a nature of solidity, stagnation, and obstructive resistance."
They cannot attain thorough penetration. Furthermore, leveling and filling major roads involves conditioned effort (*saṃskṛta*) and is fundamentally not the nature of the Sage.

Only upon encountering the Buddha’s instruction can one finally achieve awakening and entry. Yet, how can those at the initial stage of practice hope to attain perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna*) by means of this?
Candraprabha, although you attained awakening through the element of water, if you contemplate it from the perspective of the nature of water, it is characterized by conceptualization (*sa-saṃjñā*).
One contemplates and subsequently accomplishes these meditative practices; however, these are not the principle of true suchness (*tathatā*).
To accord with the principle of unmoving suchness, one must possess the wisdom of unmoving suchness, which cannot be realized by a mind of discursive thought, observation, or reflection.
How, then, can one hope to attain perfect penetration by relying on this? Oṣadhipati, it is because of the fire element...
To enter into awakening: although he universally contemplates the nature of fire, he still loathes existence and seeks liberation from it;

this is not the true liberation that is neither the capacity to liberate nor the object to be liberated. Furthermore, because he practices this contemplation due to excessive desire, it is not a universal expedient means.
How can one rely upon it and hope to attain perfect penetration? Vairocanaprabha, it is like the wind.
He entered through Great Awakening. Although he observed everywhere that both the internal and external are driven by the power of wind, this is a duality of movement and stillness.
Since there is duality, it is not the Unsurpassed Awakening. How can one rely on this and hope to attain perfect penetration?
Ākāśagarbha entered through the Great Element of Space. However, this nature of space arises from ignorance.
It is grasped and established. Its nature is dull and obtuse, lacking any conscious awareness. Since it lacks conscious awareness, it is diametrically opposed to the wisdom of the fruit of Bodhi.
How can one rely upon this and hope to attain perfect penetration? Maitreya attained great awakening through the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).
However, the nature of this consciousness arises and perishes from moment to moment; it is not a permanent, abiding nature. Furthermore, consider this by observing the mind: it is...
It belongs to the realm of delusion. How can one, relying on a deluded mind, hope to attain perfect penetration?
Śrī-Ābhāsvara, you attained entry through the contemplation of the Buddha by gathering the six sense faculties. However, all that involves mental calculation belongs to the impermanent;

since the nature of mindfulness is fundamentally a succession of before and after, with arising and ceasing never ceasing, that which serves as the cause for arising and ceasing must necessarily not [be permanent].
It is capable of producing fruits that are neither born nor extinguished. How can one, relying on these dharmas of distinct causes and effects, hope to attain perfect penetration?
I now address the World-Honored One: [until] "Excellent, Avalokiteśvara, who leaves suffering behind and attains liberation."
The ancient teachings state that when the Sages establish their instructions, they differ according to the circumstances;

there may be buddha-fields where the Buddha’s radiance constitutes the Buddha-work, or there may be buddha-fields where the Buddha’s bodhi tree constitutes the Buddha-work, and so on, even including gardens.

The forest terraces and pavilions are sometimes composed of empty space, and sometimes they demonstrate through silent non-existence, as in the land of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa, where there are no written words for teaching;
rather, it causes all devas and humans to enter into the practice of discipline solely by means of various fragrances. Such is the teaching of this region.
The substance [of sound] is merely a provisional phoneme; all that is heard occurs according to individual capacities due to the conditions [of the faculties].
(Commentary on the Preface) This selection of the ear-faculty alone is because it is the perfect penetration suited to the capacities of those in this region.
The two phrases "in this region" emphasize only the aspect of the teaching, meaning that among the sentient beings of the Sahā world, the ear-faculty is uniquely predominant.
All are able to realize the true and eternal through the nature of hearing. Thus, the Buddha, responding appropriately to the capacities of sentient beings, performs buddha-work by means of sound.
To accommodate these sharp faculties, the union of sound and hearing constitutes the true teaching-essence for this region and serves as a gateway to pure practice.
If one were to select two phrases from this, one would emphasize only the "faculty" (the capacity of the listener).

The boundary: while the substance of the teaching certainly resides in sound and hearing, if one wishes to attain right concentration, it is actually within the nature of hearing of the ear-faculty that one establishes the foundation for entering meditative absorption.
For while the sound of the teaching can only express and represent, the nature of hearing can truly and wondrously accord with reality.
Therefore, although the Path of Seeing relies upon auditory learning, its cultivation and realization depend solely upon the nature of hearing.

This phrase definitively identifies the faculty of the ear as the fundamental root of perfect penetration and the most wondrous Dharma-gate. Regarding the two lines on "leaving suffering," the emphasis lies solely on the person;
it means that among those who have awakened to and entered perfect penetration, although there are twenty-five sages, they are all able to leave behind the two types of death.
To be liberated from the suffering of birth and death, to cast off the attachments to self and phenomena, and thereby to achieve the virtue of benefiting both oneself and others— truly,
this is possible through Avalokiteśvara alone.
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges... [until] the Savior brings all to peace and security, and one transcends the world to attain the eternal abode.
(Annotation: This explains the meaning of the two preceding phrases regarding "freedom from suffering. As for "the number of kalpas being like the sands of the Ganges":
"Shining back through incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" demonstrates that time is infinitely long.

"The number of lands is like motes of dust" refers to entering all those lands previously mentioned, demonstrating that space is infinitely vast. "Attaining the power of great mastery" means illuminating the aforementioned [realms] through the wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), manifesting the thirty-two transformations to preach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, and bestowing fearlessness upon the multitudes.
Birth. By manifesting as before, he causes all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of meritorious qualities of fearlessness within their own bodies and minds.
Universally responding to the various capacities of beings, there is nothing that does not accord with what is appropriate; thus he is called "Wondrous Sound" (妙音).

Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, observing and rescuing all those in suffering and affliction across the six realms and the three miserable paths, he is called "Avalokiteśvara" (觀世音). He preaches the Dharma with purity, remaining free from attachment.
The four voices are: the Brahma-voice; the ocean-tide voice, which responds to conditions and reaches sentient beings without missing the proper time;
and because he possesses these four voices, he is able to bring peace and security to all those who suffer in the world, and likewise to those who have transcended the world.
All shall attain the ultimate fruit of eternal abiding.
I now address the Tathāgata: [this state] transcends discursive thought and observation, and cannot be reached by the body or mind.
(Annotation: This explains the meaning of the two preceding phrases, "desiring to take," in order to manifest the merit of the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*).
It is excellent. My present two lines serve to conclude the preceding and introduce what follows;
they are equivalent to saying, "I now speak these eight lines of verse concerning kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

That I address the Tathāgata in this way is not from my own imagination, but merely recounts the merits of the ear-faculty as taught by Avalokiteśvara. If one infers from his words, then one will know:
The faculty of hearing is not only all-pervasive and interfused, but moreover is eternally abiding and indestructible.
Yet, because the minds of sentient beings are mostly clouded and disturbed, they do not realize this in their daily lives.

Those within this [discussion] belong to three categories, which are subsumed under the many categories; therefore it is said: "Even if one possesses much wisdom in meditation..."
It is evident that one must possess both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) while harboring a murderous intent to fall into this class of beings.

If one merely kills without such intent, the retribution lies in the hells. As for these deities—such as worldly blood-and-flesh gods, powerful spirits, or *rākṣasas* who roam the heavens and are now venerated by humans, whom they address as "Emperor" or "Heaven"—most of them are [of this nature].
This is of that same category. Those who each claim to have attained the Unsurpassed Way falsely exalt themselves and delude people with demonic paths.
Those who say that eating meat provides the path to Bodhi proclaim that eating meat does not obstruct the fruit of Buddhahood.
Regarding the five kinds of pure meat: they are meat not seen to have been killed for one's sake, not heard to have been killed for one's sake, and not suspected to have been killed for one's sake.
"I killed it" refers to birds that have died naturally or been left over by others; what is merely designated as "meat" is a transformation produced by supernatural power, not a true living being.
How can those who eat the flesh of sentient beings after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa yet claim to be disciples of the Śākya be seen otherwise?
Indeed, all instances where the Buddha granted permission were expedient adaptations during his lifetime, intended to gradually lead others toward compassionate transformation.
Nowadays, people are merely encouraged to observe "day-long fasts" or "month-long fasts," which is like this.
If there are those who aspire to the Supreme Vehicle (Agrayāna), they must apply themselves to actual practice; they must not deceive themselves by resorting to expedient means.

Even if one attains a state where the mind opens up as if it were *samādhi*—meaning that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) have gained power and one experiences the blissful realm of correct reception (*samyaksamāpatti*)—if one still consumes meat, the obstruction is heavy; such a state is a semblance rather than the reality.

This is indeed so. That they are all great rākṣasas is the manifest retribution of their current flowers; that they will surely sink into the sea of suffering is the ultimate fruit of retribution to come.
Their mutual killing and devouring means that evil karma arises together with them as they settle their karmic debts against one another;
liberation is beyond hope, so by what means could they transcend the world? Therefore, one should believe this and resolutely renounce killing; this is purity.
This is the pure and clear instruction.
Therefore, Ānanda, if you do not cease killing—[and so forth]—if it is not spoken thus, it is the speech of Pāpīyān.
[Corresponding Note: This clarifies that only by decisively ceasing killing can one hope for true liberation. [Regarding] the cultivation of dhyāna...

To emerge from birth and death, one instead commits acts of killing and falls back into the cycle of birth and death. It is like someone who plugs their ears to avoid others, yet instead raises their voice;

this is to try to hide something while making it even more manifest. To neither trample upon nor pluck [plants] is the height of benevolence and compassion, extending even to grasses and trees—how much more so regarding the eating of the flesh of sentient beings?
According to ancient accounts, furs and woolen garments are not unknown in the East, nor are they absent in the Western lands.
"Silk and cotton" refers to these by way of their predominance. Fur, skin, milk, curds, and so forth are all things that constitute a portion of those beings' bodies;
therefore, whether one wears their fur and skin or consumes their milk and curds, these all serve as conditions for rebirth there.

As for "feet not leaving the ground," the people at the beginning of the eon possessed a radiant light on their bodies, such that their feet seemed to tread upon clouds; this was due to their consumption of the "earth-fat" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*).
Because it is fragrant rice, its substance is firm and heavy, such that the feet do not leave the ground. "Body" refers to the flesh, blood, bones, and marrow.

"Body-parts" refers to milk, curd, skins, and wool. Regarding the two applications of body and mind—those which are neither worn nor consumed—it means that not only is the body not to wear or consume them, but the mind likewise must not harbor even the slightest attachment or thought of wearing or consuming them; therefore, both [body and mind] must [be restrained].

Only when [the defilements] are wiped away and severed can one attain true liberation. The passage beginning with "As I... serves as the standard for distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox cords of binding.
This is because Ānanda, fearing that heterodox teachings would flourish in the final age, requested the rules for assisting the orthodox and crushing the heterodox;
therefore, the World-Honored One preached these four root precepts to definitively distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox, so that in the final age...
Those who hear the Dharma should know only this: that what I have spoken is precisely the Buddha’s true teaching.
If it were not as I have said, and someone claimed that eating meat does not obstruct the path to Bodhi, that would indeed be the teaching of Māra.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding the sentient beings of the six realms in the world... [up to] the third definitive, pure, and clear instruction.
*Commentary*: This demonstrates the benefits of observing and the perils of violating the precept against stealing. This act of theft does not merely consist of pilfering another's wealth;
it includes all instances of deceitful speech and conduct, such as using fraud to delude or intimidate others, even down to a single thought of seeking gain through such means.
To be respectful while still coveting gain and offerings is to violate the precepts. One whose mind does not steal is said to have forgotten the desire for profit;
only when the thought of greed does not sprout for even a single moment can one sever the root of birth and death.
If the thieving mind is not eliminated, one will certainly be unable to escape from birth and death. To "inevitably fall into the heterodox paths" means that one harbors such a mind.
Those who turn toward the heterodox, pursue profit through devious means, and whose words and deeds are improper, will be reborn among the heterodox classes.

As for "refined spirits" (*jingling*), they include mountain sprites and water monsters; they resemble immortals but are not immortals, and resemble deities but are not deities, yet they possess heterodox supernormal powers.
As for "goblins and specters" (*yaomei*), they appear and disappear within the world, using their demonic energy to bewitch people; they may seize one's vital essence or steal one's wealth.
As for those who are heterodox, they are possessed by malevolent spirits; their words and deeds are strange and demonic, and they delude and confuse the multitude.

However, all of these cases refer to those whose power of concentration and wisdom is superior, yet whose thieving mind has not been eliminated. If one merely practices such thievery, the retribution incurred will not stop at this alone.
Therefore it is said: "Each person claims for themselves that they have realized the Unsurpassed Way, yet they do not realize they are but demons and devils."
Furthermore, those who harbor treachery and deceit conceal their own evils and falsely claim to be realized masters (*jñānin*).

They may utter demonic words or manifest demonic powers, fearing that the ignorant and deluded might change their hearts and alter their wills, thereby causing them to disregard their own bodies and wealth.

They devote their hearts to serving them; therefore, wherever they go, the households they pass through suffer depletion and dissipation. Within my teaching, to openly violate the precepts and harm the multitude is a transgression of profound depth.
For those who wander for alms according to the "directions" (*fang*), "direction" (*fang*) refers to the Dharma (*dharma*).
This means distributing gifts to sentient beings, protecting the power of the Path, not hoarding anything, and having no lingering attachments—these are all methods of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the mendicant who begs for food eliminates arrogance and abandons greedy thoughts, thereby accomplishing the Unsurpassed Way.
By not cooking for oneself, one removes attachment. Moreover, one should know that this body is but a temporary lodging and that the world is a transient sojourn.
This body, once departed, shall never return; how then can one remain attached to the mundane world and accumulate the causes of karma?
Indeed. My intention is this: only by practicing in such a manner can one truly be a child of the Buddha. How is it that these thieves destroy the Buddha’s legacy?

Internally harboring secret ambitions while externally feigning the deportment of a monk, they instead treat the Buddha-Dharma as a tool for profit, engaging extensively in trade and commerce to create various karmic causes—can this truly be called the Buddha-Dharma? They consider themselves right and others wrong.

If one instead points to those who possess the full set of precepts as followers of the Hīnayāna, while falsely claiming that what they themselves practice is Mahāyāna, then these are like the blind leading the blind;
they will surely fall into the Avīci Hell—how could there ever be a time of escape?
Furthermore, I instruct those among the people of the world who, after my parinirvāṇa, wish to cultivate *samādhi*:
even if they have not committed the act of stealing in their present life, I fear they may have transgressed in previous existences; therefore, they must also perform repentance.

Thus, I require them to create minor causes—such as lighting lamps or burning off a finger—before an image of the Tathāgata to repay the debts incurred in past lives, only then permitting them to [enter] the long [path].

One bows to the world and is forever liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*). If one is truly able to practice this, although one has not yet suddenly awakened to the path of unsurpassed enlightenment, such a person is certain to be able to believe in the True Dharma.

If one does not perform repentance, even if one attains the fruit of Buddhahood, one will still return to the human realm to repay past debts. As when I once ate in King Piḷindavatsa’s horse stable at the city of Vairaṇyā.
Regarding the three months of eating barley: this was because in a previous life I reviled a bhikṣu, saying he should eat horse-barley;

thus I am now repaying this karmic retribution. If even for a casual, ill-spoken word I must still undergo such compensation, how much more so for the debts incurred in past lives—how could those ever be avoided?
Therefore, all who cultivate the causes for transcending the world should believe that this third precept against stealing is definitive.

This is a pure and clear instruction. Regarding the relinquishing of the body as a minor cause to repay karmic debts from the past: this refers to having previously stolen the external wealth of others to support one's own person;
by now further relinquishing one's own body to provide for the Supreme Sages, one is finally able to overturn and destroy the karma of theft committed since beginningless time.
According to ancient teachings, there is nothing more difficult to relinquish than the body; that which is most difficult to relinquish can [only be given away]...
If one abandons [the self], then all other forms of craving can certainly be relinquished; hence it is said that such a person has attained a mind of certainty regarding the Dharma.
However, if the craving manifest before one remains unaltered, then to merely long for the abandonment of the body and to wound or mutilate the physical frame is in vain.
This would only increase the suffering of karma; how could it clarify the path of awakening and resolve the True Dharma? "Bì" (裨) means to supplement;
"fàn" (販) means to sell.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever theft... [and so forth] ...if it is not spoken thus, it is the speech of Pāpīyān.
Commentary: This clarifies that only by decisively severing theft can one be permitted to aspire toward true samādhi. First a metaphor, then the Dharma. The meaning is this:

if the fundamental precepts are broken, even if one cultivates concentration and wisdom for a thousand or ten thousand kalpas, one will still be unable to nourish the nature of wisdom or bring bodhi to fulfillment.
It is like pouring water into a leaking cup; it will be difficult to fill it even over aeons of dust.
Furthermore, not accumulating even a fraction beyond one's robes and alms bowl is to sever the mind of greed.

Giving away the remnants of one’s begged food to hungry sentient beings is to sever the mind of stinginess. Joining one’s palms in reverence toward the assembly during a great gathering is to sever pride and conceit.
Treating those who strike or revile one as if they were praising one is to sever anger and resentment. Thus, both body and mind are completely relinquished.

This means severing the two attachments to self and dharmas. As for sharing one’s body, flesh, bones, and blood with sentient beings, it refers to transforming greed, anger, and egoism into the great compassion of the single essence (*samatā-mahākaruṇā*).
Regarding the teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), as stated in the *Āgama* Sūtras, one may keep animals to provide for one's own needs and advance on the Path;
furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* permits keeping one of each of the hundred types of items, provided that—

He prohibits the other two [types of giving]. Furthermore, he claims that giving does not equal [the gift of] one's own body or life, and that dedicating [merit] for one's own liberation is intended to mislead beginners.
He asserts that he himself is unable to practice the Mahāyāna and instead distorts and draws upon the provisional vehicles (Hīnayāna), thereby deceiving both himself and others.

If, however, one can maintain the purity of the roots of precepts and permanently sever the mind of self-interest, the Buddha seals such a person as having attained true *tri-yāna* (the threefold vehicle).
It is obscure. As for "As I [have taught] below," it follows the preceding.
Ānanda, thus [it concerns] the sentient beings of the six realms in this world... up to the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction.
Commentary: This clarifies the benefits and harms of observing or violating the precept against false speech.

The passage beginning with "In this way" reveals that even those who have maintained the purity of the preceding three precepts still fear this transgression; how much more so for those who have not yet observed them?

Generally, speaking or acting without regard for the truth constitutes minor false speech; to falsely exalt oneself and claim to have realized the fruits of the path constitutes major false speech. If one commits [this offense]...

Regarding this precept: even if the preceding three precepts are fully perfected, if one fails to attain purity in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) due to craving for gain and honor, and considers oneself superior to others, this is called the "demon of attachment" (*tṛṣṇā-māra*).
To falsely give rise to wrong views, claiming that one is equal to the sages, constitutes the "demon of views" (*dṛṣṭi-māra*).

Both of these result from the failure to sever the two delusions of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). This explains, as stated below, how it constitutes a great falsehood (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*). Thus it is obtained.

"Attainment" (*prāpti*) refers to the principle; "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*) refers to the stage of fruition. The stages of *srotāpanna* and so forth are called "fruition," while the *arhat* is called the "path.
This refers to the fruition stage of the Hīnayāna, which reaches its culmination at the *arhat*; therefore, it is termed the "path. As for the "vehicle stage": [text continues].
It is the fruit of the Way. To seek the excellence of the World-Honored One requires reverence; to seek his ritual repentance is to hope for offerings.

*Ekantika* is the same as *icchantika*. Just as a *tāla* tree severed by a blade will never revive, this serves as a metaphor for great falsehood, which forever cuts off the wholesome seeds of the Tathāgata.
The "three seas of suffering" refers to the three miserable realms. I shall enter extinction.
[The phrase] "After my parinirvāṇa" [at the beginning of the next section] clearly demonstrates that the Son of the Buddha is absolutely free from false speech. It says:

after my parinirvāṇa, I shall enjoin all bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest either pure appearances or defiled appearances during the age of the Dharma’s decay (mofa), in order to gather others through the practice of "acting in concert" (samānārthatā).
He praised the Buddha Vehicle, causing their bodies and minds to cultivate dhyāna and attain samādhi.

He never permitted them to claim for themselves the status of true sages or to divulge the Buddha’s secret mechanisms. Even when encountering beginners, he did not speak lightly of his own seeking of reverence;

rather, he waited until the end of life to leave behind a subtle and profound testament to entrust the Dharma, so that they might believe, accept, and practice it. This was because he remained in the world...
Thus, one must not reveal secret mechanisms; were they revealed even once, one would certainly not remain in the world.
This is the true method for establishing transformation; it is a fixed rule. This is exemplified by such figures as the Monk of the Cloth Bag and Chan Master Yongming.

If one continues to remain while leaking [secret] words, then that person is a wicked individual seeking gain and offerings—how could anyone believe them? I command the sons of the Buddha to act accordingly.
Practicing the Path: How could such a person delude sentient beings and commit a great falsehood?
Therefore, those who cultivate the causes for transcending the world should have faith in this fourth precept against lying as a definitive, pure, and clear instruction.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever this great falsehood... (until) if one does not speak thus, it is the speech of Pāpīyān.
[Commentary: This clarifies that only by decisively severing false speech may one be permitted to aspire for Perfect Enlightenment.
"Carving dung to seek fragrance" is a metaphor for adorning one's physical appearance while losing the integrity of one's mental conduct, yet desiring to share the same essence as the Holy and True.

"Penetration—this shall certainly not be attained. In my teaching, I am severely rebuking those who previously had not attained but claimed to have attained, and who had not realized but claimed to have realized.
A 'direct mind' is the site of the Way; this means the mind is free from falsehood, which is itself the field where the Way is accomplished.
I say that for a bhikṣu in my teaching, even within the midst of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, not even a single thought of falsehood is permitted."

How can one claim to have attained the state of a superior person? What difference is there between such a person and a destitute pauper who falsely styles himself an emperor, only to bring about his own execution and the extinction of his lineage?

Furthermore, if even a king of a single nation cannot tolerate the false assumption of a sovereign title, how could one possibly wish to fraudulently usurp the name and station of the Unsurpassed Dharma King of both the mundane and supramundane realms? Is this not permissible?
If one seeks the fruit of Buddhahood by taking such great falsehood as a cause, then seeking progress will result in regression; seeking the correct will result in the perverse;
and seeking elevation will result in a fall. It is like attempting to bite one's own navel with one's own mouth—how could it ever be reached?
If one truly desires to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment, one must take a straightforward mind and straightforward speech as the practice for the causal ground; only then...

This enables one to perfectly realize the awakening of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*). The passage beginning with "As I... follows the previous [explanation]. Although it initially designates the Threefold Training (*tri-śikṣā*), it concludes by mentioning only the four precepts;

this is because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are already contained therein. That is to say, concentration arises from the precepts, and wisdom is developed through concentration;

therefore, they are not explained separately here. "Superior person" (*śreṣṭha-pudgala*) refers to one who has attained the stage of fruition. Liu Youqiu, the District Magistrate of Tang, said to Huan...
Xu Jinghui said to Yanfan, "As long as Wu Sansi remains, you gentlemen will ultimately have no place for burial.
If you do not plan for this now, it will be too late to regret it when you bite your own heels."
