Ānanda, as to your question regarding the gathering of the mind (up to): how do all demonic activities arise?
Commentary: This concludes the response to the question. "The Sublime Gate" refers to the four *dharmas* mentioned above.

By taking these four *dharmas* as the foundation, one is naturally able to give rise to concentration (*samādhi*) and develop wisdom (*prajñā*), whereby the remaining secondary precepts are spontaneously accomplished.

When the root is pure, the branches do not sprout; when one does not encounter sensory objects (*viṣaya*), demonic activities (*mārakarma*) are subtly extinguished. Thus, one enters right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
Therefore, it is called the "Sublime Gate. Regarding the three [transgressions] of the mind, they are greed, anger, and delusion.
Regarding the four [transgressions] of the mouth, they are false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech. By severing these, the three causes do not arise.

In contrast to the aforementioned great falsehood, one views these four oral transgressions as secondary branches; "not losing them" means to keep the root precepts in constant mindfulness, whereby one will naturally be free from them.
Even the slightest transgression against the autumn hair [of the scale] constitutes an offense. All demonic activities arise based on the sensory objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) and enter by relying upon them.
If the mind is entirely free from craving for the six sensory objects, then the root of the precepts is pure, and demonic activities will depart.
When present karma no longer intermingles with the senses, concentration and wisdom will spontaneously manifest.
"If there are past habitual tendencies that cannot be extinguished... (up to)... what difficulty would there be in blowing [them] away with a following wind? [Commentary:
This instructs one to maintain the recitation of mantras in order to eliminate past karma. The three trainings mentioned above can destroy the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
the divine mantras below can eliminate the obstacles of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) and retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). "Past habitual tendencies" refers to the delusions of the past.

This is the seed of karma. According to the ancient teachings, present actions are easy to restrain; one may personally deviate from them. However, long-standing habits are difficult to eliminate and must rely upon spiritual power.

Now, when a practitioner desires what is correct yet remains firmly attached to the perverse, or wishes for purity yet is biased toward defilement—when there is something hidden that seems to urge and drive them so they cannot stop—all of these are the instigators of past habits. Furthermore, there are the afflictions of demonic diseases.
Intrusion and disturbance; worldly surnames and entanglements. Whenever one encounters favorable conditions (*kuśala-pratyaya*), various demons (*māra*) arise in competition.
These are none other than the delusive karma of past lives acting as enemies to the Path. For a beginner, the power of practice is weak and cannot dispel them;
one must rely upon divine mantras (*vidyā-mantra*) before they can be eliminated. *Mahā-sattva-bhadra*, which is translated here as "Great White."
The *chattra* (parasol): Its substance pervades the ten voids, and its function encompasses the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*. It is called "Great" (*mahat*) because it is free from all delusive defilements;

it is called "White" (*śukla*) because it covers and protects all beings; it is called a "parasol" because it provides shelter. This refers to these secret syllables, which flow forth entirely from within the *tathāgatagarbha*;

therefore, their power and majesty are immeasurable, capable of eliminating past karma. Regarding the "Unseen Crown Mark" (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*), the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, fascicle nine... [text continues].
The Earth-Knowledge (Dharaṇī) was the Buddha’s wet nurse; at his birth, she personally cradled him and gazed intently at him, yet could not see the crown of his head.
This demonstrates that the Dharma of the Crown cannot be seen by the eye. Because it is manifested within the light, it is called the "Unconditioned Mind-Buddha.
Because the ultimate truth is beyond words, it is said to be "unfolded from the crown. Seated upon a precious lotus flower, he preached the Heart Mantra to reveal this mind.

This demonstrates that both the cause and the effect of the mantra are clearly manifested. The mention of Dhanakṣema (Dengjia) serves to show the profound depth of his past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

"The heart of craving was forever liberated" refers to his attainment of the third fruit (*srotāpanna*) upon first hearing the mantra. "He attained the fourth fruit" refers to the period following Mañjuśrī’s selection of the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
This was truly because he first relied on the power of the mantra to eliminate his past habitual tendencies, and subsequently relied upon the sound of the Dharma.
To awaken to and realize the fruit of sainthood, were it not for the power of mantras to eliminate these latent habitual tendencies, how could one possibly accord with the Dharma?
Therefore, the merit is still attributed to the mantra. A bhikṣu is not the same as a courtesan; seeking the Supreme Vehicle is not the same as practicing without a focused mind.
For it is observed that if any practitioner applies the power of mantras, they will certainly attain Buddhahood.

Past habitual tendencies are like dust; the power of mantras is like the wind. Reciting mantras to eliminate these tendencies is like blowing dust away with a favorable wind—what difficulty or peril could there be?

If there are those in the final age who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment (up to the point where [the Buddha] places his hand upon their heads to comfort them and cause them to attain awakening).
Commentary: This clarifies that those who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment must first select a teacher.
"Pure and clean prohibitory precepts" refers to the aforementioned four fundamental great precepts. A teacher is the model for a student; if the model is crooked and deviant...
Yet those who are able to become a perfected vessel are rare. Therefore, one who wishes to cultivate pure precepts should select a preceptor. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states:

"If within a thousand li there is no preceptor to confer the precepts, one should receive them through a self-vow before the Buddha. First, repent for the seven heinous offenses; afterwards, seek the dharma of the precepts.
Only when one clearly perceives the [Buddha’s] marks and signs does one know that the offenses have been extinguished and the precepts obtained. Otherwise, it is not so."
One attains the precepts. Once the precepts are established, wearing pure garments signifies that the inner and outer are as one, and both the exterior and interior are cleansed.

Reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times serves to eliminate the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*). When the internal precepts are thus established, they can also give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
however, fearing that past obstructions have not yet been removed and wisdom (*prajñā*) cannot yet be generated, one must therefore seek the present Buddhas.
The empowerment through the emission of light assists in perfecting great wisdom. As for the white-robed [lay practitioners], they include both male and female attendants;
although the fourfold assembly shares the same altar, monastics and laity, as well as men and women, each follow their own kind and must not be intermingled.
One who seeks to arouse the bodhisattva vow only after the fourfold precepts are pure does so because the precepts serve as the foundation for the power of that vow. Regarding coming and going...
"Bathing" means externally purifying one's body. "Practicing the Way during the six periods of the day without sleeping" means internally collecting the mind by dispelling dullness and distraction.
"The Buddha manifests his own body to stroke the crown of the head and offer comfort" is what is evoked by pure conduct;
it is like the moon appearing when the water is clear. "Causing them to attain awakening" means relying on the Buddha’s majestic power to assist in the arousal of the Great [Vehicle].
This is wisdom.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [up to] "...in accordance with the pure rules of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
*Commentary*: This is the request for the rules regarding the consecration of the maṇḍala. These unsurpassed compassionate instructions refer to the four kinds of purity mentioned above.

This is the instruction on Pure Clarity. "Knowing for oneself that the path of no-more-learning has been realized" means that having already attained self-awakening through perfect penetration, one further relies on the secret assistance of the mantra's power;
thus, one knows that the holy fruit will certainly be realized. "Establishing the *dōjō*" refers back to the previously mentioned "establishing the site of practice," meaning:
if one wishes to establish a *dōjō*, how should one perform the ritual boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*)? How should it be done?
This accords with the World-Honored One’s pure ritual rules.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people of the final age [should practice], they must burn only aloeswood incense and not allow the fire to be seen.
[Commentary: This demonstrates the pure ritual rules for the altar site. [It refers to] the great-power white ox of Mount Yunshan.
This is not an ordinary ox. Although this ox emerges alone from the Snowy Mountains, it does not appear constantly; it is, in fact, an auspicious omen.
Furthermore, as it feeds only upon the fragrant herbs of the Snowy Mountains and drinks only the clear waters of the Snowy Mountains, its dung is fine and subtle.
It may be mixed with incense and smeared upon the ground. If it were not the ox of the Snowy Mountains, that ox would be foul-smelling;
how much more so its dung? Therefore, it is unfit for smearing the ground. "High and level" refers to a plain (*yuan*).
To dig five feet into the earth is to take soil that has not been trampled and is thus pure. "Yellow" refers to taking the color of the center.
Using ten kinds of incense, grind them finely into powder and mix with the aforementioned ingredients to form a paste, which is then applied to the ground to ensure its purity and fragrance.
A square altar of sixteen feet (one *zhang* and six *chi*) is made with eight corners. Formerly it was said that a "tan" (*tán*) refers to a leveled clearing of the earth;
this seems to suggest it was constructed by piling up soil. The scripture should clearly describe tiered levels, yet none are present today, leading to doubt.
This refers to leveling the ground and coating it to form an octagonal shape. Placing a single lotus flower in the center of the altar constitutes the first type of adornment.

The *pātra* is a vessel of proper measure; filling the *pātra* with dew collected on the eighth day of the month and placing lotus petals within the water serves to enhance the fragrance and purity of the lotus.
Mirrors are placed at the eight directions surrounding the flower and the *pātra*.
This is to capture the reflection of their circular halos shining upon one another.

As for the sixteen lotus flowers and incense burners placed outside the mirrors, arranged at intervals, it is to achieve a layered and magnificent adornment, desiring that the assembly of devas, humans, and others may deeply revere and faithfully believe in these supreme matters.
When burning aloeswood incense, do not allow the flames to be seen; this is the constant rule for offering incense. This...
As for the sequence of the altar rituals, they are merely worldly arrangements of conditioned dharmas.

Their dignity and solemnity serve no purpose other than to cause those who behold them for a moment to withdraw their minds and bodies from distraction, so that they may practice walking meditation and advance upon the Path.
In both ancient and modern times, the *biao* (offering-table) method has been widely used; it seems unnecessary to insist on forcibly correlating [the ritual] with [specific symbolic assignments].
Take the milk of a white cow and place it in sixteen vessels (until) burning it so that the smoke is exhausted, then offer it to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Commentary: This demonstrates the ritual procedure for making pure offerings. Previously, the ground was smeared with the dung of a white ox;
here, the thick milk of a white ox is offered to the Buddha. This clearly shows that these are distinct types of substances.
Regarding milk, sugar, and so forth: it is said that by blending these with milk, curd, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one creates the supreme offerings.
As for the sixteen [deities] surrounding each [deity] outside the lotus: this is the offering set out in correspondence with the visualized image.
Whether at the time of eating or during the middle watch of the night, this accords with the ritual rules for receiving food at midday. Take half a measure of honey...
For the offering, use three *liǎng* (three *hé*) of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Burn it until the smoke is exhausted to make offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
this is because one takes its fragrant scent and hot flames, which are able to eliminate all impure odors.
"Have banners and flowers hung everywhere on the four outer sides" (up to) "so that their forms and shadows interpenetrate one another in layers.
[Commentary: This demonstrates the pure ritual rules for the installation of images. Regarding "having banners and flowers hung everywhere on the four outer sides":
this is to adorn the exterior of the altar. According to the old interpretation, it refers to Vairocana at the site of enlightenment (*Ji-chang*).
The Lord. Śākyamuni is the Teacher of the Sahā world. Maitreya is the Teacher of the future.
Akṣobhya and Amitābha are briefly cited as the Teachers of the four directions. The various great manifestations of Avalokiteśvara are the Teachers of universal penetration.
Vajragarbha is the Teacher who constantly leads the vajra-holders to protect those who recite mantras, subduing demons and severing obstacles.
On either side of the gate stand the assemblies of Śakra, Brahmā, and others, who provide powerful external protection.
In the practice of the Dharma during the Final Age, one relies entirely upon these; if even one is lacking, success will certainly not be achieved.
Ucchuṣma (Fire-Head Vajra), Nīladaṇḍa (Blue-Face Vajra), and Cundā are alternative names for Vajrapāṇi. Bhṛkuṭī is the Three-Eyed One who holds...
This refers to the *śikhā* (topknot). Piṇāyaka refers to the two messengers, the Boar-Headed and the Elephant-Nosed.

As for the mirrors in the air and the mirror on the altar facing each other across the four directions, causing their forms and shadows to interpenetrate one another repeatedly, the purpose is to ensure that the practitioner sees only the Buddha’s light everywhere, thereby eliciting the light of one's own mind within every phenomenon (*dharma*).
"Head-to-head" (tòutóu) means that perfect penetration is fully manifested.
During the first seven days, through sincere prostrations, the body and mind become clear and pure, like lapis lazuli.

Commentary: This demonstrates the ritual procedure for pure recitation according to the precepts. According to the ancient exegesis, whatever one aspires toward, taking refuge in the Triple Gem is the primary expedient means.
Therefore, during the first seven days, one should with utmost sincerity prostrate to the names of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats.
By thus relying upon their inconceivable power, one initiates the practice that aids the Path.

Furthermore, those who single-mindedly make vows during the second seven-day period do so by means of no more than four kinds of great vows, or perhaps the ten great vows as found in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
During the third seven-day period, one should practice without interruption and recite mantras without limit.
Through single-minded application of effort, one is uniquely able to move the divine through sincerity and integrity; thus, by advancing with diligence, one achieves success.

On the seventh day, at the point where the light of the mirror intersects, one receives the Buddha’s touch upon the crown of the head. This signifies that the water of the mind has become clear and the Buddha’s radiance is reflected therein;
as the causal mind and the resultant wisdom meet in a path of resonance, one is thereby able to cultivate right concentration within the very site of practice.
This causes the practitioner to attain great awakening; their body and mind become luminous and pure, like lapis lazuli, transparent both inside and out.

The sense faculties and their objects are unimpeded; this is the arising of wisdom from meditative concentration. Thus we know that the perfect penetration attained through the manifest cultivation of the Exoteric and the secret recitation of the Esoteric are equal and without distinction.
Ānanda, if this bhikṣu’s original preceptor... [down to] ...you ask about the establishment of the *bodhimaṇḍa*, it is thus.

*Guānzhù* (Annotated Note): This clarifies the accomplishment of the *bodhimaṇḍa*. Although one relies upon the sacred empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha, if one's teachers and friends are impure, it will be difficult to achieve success even if one so desires.
"Non-accomplishment" means being unable to realize the fruit within a fixed period. From...

The "thirty-seven" [days] below clarify the realization of the fruit. Regarding those of "keen faculties," the traditional explanation states that they are those whose afflictions and hindrances are both light and whose nature of wisdom is luminously awakened.
*Srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer): according to the stages, this corresponds to the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

If one follows the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it refers to the initial entry into the stages and dwellings of the Distinct (*bie*) and Perfect (*yuan*) teachings. Upon reaching this point, one gains faith that one's own mind is the Buddha and arrives at a state free from doubt.
"Once the ground [of realization] is attained, one will certainly not run outward in pursuit. The passage beginning with 'As for your question' is the concluding response.
Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to the Buddha: [up to] "...I await the hearing of the Tathāgata’s secret verses."
Commentary: This is a repeated request for the exposition of the mantra. Regarding the phrase "those who have not yet realized the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) and so forth:

it means that those at the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) possess weak power and are thus susceptible to being seized by Māras. Although they previously relied upon Mañjuśrī’s secret retention (*dhāraṇī*) to resolve their peril, they had not yet personally heard [this teaching].
The reason for requesting the World-Honored One to proclaim this teaching once again is the desire to ensure its circulation in the final age.

Regarding the phrase "one's power is not free," it means that because the power of the Way has not yet been fully realized, one cannot attain mastery. Previously, by secretly relying on the power of the mantra, he was able to escape the calamity of lust;
thus, it is said that he "secretly obtained what had not been heard. "Liberation of the body" refers to the dissolution of karma and the departure from suffering. This is the meaning.
"Deliverance" means to shatter delusions and realize the Truth. Since the power of the mantra is thus supreme and profound, one awaits the hearing of the Tathāgata’s secret verses and phrases.
At that time, the World-Honored One [from his *uṣṇīṣa*]... [until] the Tathāgata Emitting Light proclaimed the divine mantra.
Commentary: This is a reiteration of the divine mantra. When the World-Honored One spoke the mantra, he first employed it to expel heterodox arts and lead beings onto the Right Path.
Furthermore, worldly incantations and curses are nothing more than illusory arts;

the World-Honored One, conforming to worldly conventions and responding to the capacities of sentient beings, used illusion to eliminate illusion. Thus, from within the Tathāgatagarbha, he manifested through the wondrous function of non-action.
Various manifestations of transformation serve to awaken and stimulate the diverse capacities of sentient beings; only then does one proclaim the mantra.
"Hundred-jewel radiance" signifies a color formed from a hundred jewels, manifesting as that which flows forth from the fundamental wisdom while encompassing all phenomena.
"Lotus flowers surging forth from within the light" signifies the arousal of causal practices from the essence of wisdom. There is...
The manifestation of the Tathāgata seated within a precious lotus flower reveals that the fruit is realized from the cause, such that cause and fruit are of one essence.
The emanated Buddha emits precious light from his crown, and within that light, Guhyapada appears again, pervading the realm of empty space;
this reveals that he is the illusion within illusions, the most honored among the honored, the greatest among the great, the secret within secrets, and the most wondrous among the wondrous.
Exquisite! Therefore, the essence of wisdom is unmoving, while its divine function is unfathomable; there is no good it does not assist, and no evil it does not destroy.
To "embrace both awe and love" means to stand in awe of its majesty while loving its compassion; thus, one finds it difficult to abandon either.
To "listen with a single mind as the Buddha proclaims the divine mantra" means that sentient beings, harboring both awe and love, receive [the teaching].
In accordance with this, the Tathāgata proclaims and disseminates [this teaching] solely through his spiritual transformations. *Namo satvatha sugataye* (up to) *hūṃ dhuḥ phaṭ svāhā*. (Guanzhu:
According to the ancient explanation, "mantra" (*zhòu*) means "to pray for blessings. The World-Honored One uses this mantra to bless sentient beings, causing them...)

In transforming the ordinary to become the sage, one does so without being self-aware, much like the *gonglo* (a parasitic wasp) that incants over the *miling* (a caterpillar), saying, "Become like me! Become like me!
After a long time, it will resemble it. It is also said that the divine mantras (*dhāraṇīs*) of the various sūtras are generally not translated.
Since ancient times, masters of men have had many differing interpretations, but Tiantai synthesized them as nothing other than the four *siddhāntas*. One says: "As for 'mantra' (*zhòu*):"

The name of the King of Ghosts is invoked by calling upon the name of its leader; the tribes respect their leader and do not dare to commit transgressions—this is the *loka-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of worldly convention).
Second, it is said that a mantra is like a secret password within an army: when the passwords correspond, there is no need for questioning or interrogation;
those whose passwords do not correspond are immediately seized and punished—this is the *pudgala-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of the individual). Third, it is said that a mantra is...
One should secretly and silently restrain evil. Others who lack discernment are like a lowly man fleeing to a foreign land who falsely claims to be a prince;
the king then gives him his daughter as a wife, yet he is prone to anger and difficult to deal with.
A wise man came from that country, and the husband went to him to complain. That man said: "When he is about to become angry, you should say: 'Wander without kin.'"
"In another land, he deceives all people; coarse food is his constant sustenance. Why trouble yourself further by becoming angry? When this verse was spoken, his anger subsided in silence.
This is precisely the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the method of counteracting). Fourth, as for "mantra": these are the secret words of the Buddhas, known only to the sages.
It is like the Western King who requested *saindhava*; though it is a single name, it possesses four meanings.
"Objects" refers to salt, water, horses, and vessels; none of the subordinates can distinguish them, yet only a wise minister understands them according to the occasion.

Mantras are likewise: though consisting of only a single dharma-utterance, they universally encompass many meanings and possess great power, enabling those who maintain and recite them [to achieve their aims].
The arising of goodness accords with the Way; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, the original phonetics are preserved.
Among the "five reasons for not translating," this is the case of "not translating due to secrecy. Among the "four categories," it is a case of "translating the characters but not the phonetics.
It is also called a "secret mantra" (*mantra*); it is not merely a term from the Sanskrit language, but rather the secret speech of all the sages and worthies. Indeed...
The Sanskrit language is not understood here in this land, yet it is that which the people of India understand and employ in their daily lives.

As for secret mantras (vidyā-mantra), they are not only unknown to the ordinary people of India; logically, it follows that sages and worthies of lower stations do not comprehend the mantras of higher stations.
Generally, when sages propagate the Dharma, there are two types of teaching: the Exoteric and the Esoteric, just as in the case of medicine.

There are generally two approaches to treating illness. The first is to provide a prescription, which clearly explains the origin of the disease, the nature of the medicine, and the methods for its preparation and administration, much like the Buddha’s explicit teachings (*vyākṛta-dharma*).
The second is to provide the medicine itself, without any explanation whatsoever, merely giving the medicine to be taken so that the illness may be cured;
there is no necessity to know what medicine it is or how it was treated, much like the Buddha’s secret teachings (*guhya-dharma*).
Therefore, these secret mantras are exactly like administering medicine; there is no need to seek their meaning. If an intellectual understanding arises, the mantra’s power is lost.
Sentient beings should simply believe in and uphold them, and they will naturally receive all benefits.

Commentary: According to the traditional interpretation, the portion prior to the syllable *oṃ* consists of taking refuge in the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and various worthy sages, as well as the recitation of prayers for protection against all evil enemies and calamities.

Upon reaching *tadyathā* (which is translated here as "Now I shall speak the mantra"), the section from the syllable *oṃ* onwards constitutes the actual mantra. What was previously described as "practicing the path and reciting the mantra" refers to this point.

Regarding the "one hundred and eight recitations," this refers to the recitation of this mantra. However, throughout the preceding and following sections of the root sūtra, the praise of its merits consistently points to the *dhāraṇī-hṛdaya* (the heart-mantra).
Therefore, that which should be recited must be the *dhāraṇī-hṛdaya*; it certainly cannot be these few phrases.
Ānanda, it is impossible for [this] *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-raśmi-samcaya* (The Radiant Mass of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa) [to allow] the influence of various māras to reach it;
such a thing cannot exist. **Commentary:** This clarifies the efficacy of the mantra-heart (*dhāraṇī-hṛdaya*).

Generally, when one speaks of the "mantra-heart" or the "heart-mantra," it refers to this Great White Parasol (*Mahāsitātapatrā*), which flows solely from the *tathāgatagarbha-citta* (the heart-mind of the Tathāgata-store). Therefore, it is vast and expansive.

It is unstained and universally pervades all things; it is also the essential core within the Secret Treasury (Guhyagarbha), just as the four limbs and hundred bones of a human body are governed by the single mind.
"Subtle and wondrous" means hidden, profound, and marvelous, being inconceivable.
"Giving birth to all Buddhas" means that this mantra-heart is able to contain and nurture sublime virtues, and to foster their growth.
The "Noble Womb" (āryagarbha) is precisely the true samādhi that is the Mother of Buddhas. Regarding those who attain perfect enlightenment by means of this mantra-heart:
it is said that this mantra-heart is the true seed from which the Tathāgatas are born; therefore, all Buddhas must necessarily rely upon it.
And thus one attains the correct fruit. Regarding "grasping this mantra-heart to subdue demons and restrain outsiders": it means that this mantra-heart is like the precious sword of the Vajra King;
by grasping it, its majestic power is fierce and courageous, enabling one to sever all delusions and errors.
Regarding "riding upon this mantra-heart to respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust": it means that this mantra-heart is a great vessel of compassion, capable of...
It carries sentient beings across, leading them out of the river of birth and death to ascend the shore of nirvana.
Regarding those who "contain this mantra-heart and turn the Great Dharma Wheel": it means that this mantra-heart can encompass all virtues and store up eloquence;

thus, in responding to things on its left and right, there is nothing it does not possess. Regarding those who "hold this mantra-heart and receive the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment": it means this...
The Mantra Heart. It encompasses all dharmas and upholds immeasurable meanings; it is the heart-seal of every Buddha and the secret instruction of every Patriarch.
Those who rely on this Mantra Heart to rescue and deliver the masses from suffering do so because this Mantra Heart is like a sovereign victory banner, capable of removing all fears and hardships.
Therefore, hell becomes empty by relying upon it, and the realm of hungry ghosts [becomes empty] by relying upon it.
Through this, those who are hungry are satiated; through this, animals are liberated from their state; through this, the blind and deaf become clear-sighted and hearing;
through this, the mute and speech-impaired gain the power of speech; through this, those who harbor enmity and hatred find joyful reunion; through this, those who are separated find harmony;

through this, one becomes fully endowed with wealth and virtue. Therefore, there is nothing to seek. Because suffering cannot be found, and because both "self" and "dharmas" are empty by means of this, there is no [suffering].
The five aggregates are ablaze with suffering; by relying on this [dhāraṇī], all shall submit and obey, and thus there will be no untimely calamities.
As for other bandits, difficulties, or even poverty, there are none that do not dissolve upon being brought to mind through reliance on this.
Therefore, by relying on this dhāraṇī-heart, there is no hardship that cannot be resolved. Those who follow this dhāraṇī-heart as a Dharma Prince refer to this very dhāraṇī.
The mind then accords with the nature of awakening; from this mind, all wishes are fulfilled. It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), for which there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
As for those who practice this mantra-heart without giving rise to fear or alarm, it is because this mantra-heart penetrates all things without obstruction;

it is the great thoroughfare for entering the holy from the mundane. Therefore, regarding all that is encompassed by it, although there may be inherent affinities and causes, and although faculties may be great...
[Those with] small [roots of virtue], upon hearing this mantra for the first time, would experience alarm, doubt, fear, and dread that could never arise again. Take Ānanda and Daṅgā as examples:

both had small roots due to their immediate causes, yet upon hearing this secret treasury, not only did they fail to feel alarm or dread, but they also permanently severed their lustful attachments and immediately ascended to the stage of sainthood.
As for those who recite this mantra-heart and enter Great Nirvāṇa, it means:
This mantra-heart is the ultimate, perfect treasury of the three virtues; therefore, by reciting and practicing it without interruption, one immediately realizes the supreme fruit of perfection.
It is said that all who transmit this mantra-heart and attain purity do so because this mantra-heart has been transmitted from Buddha to Buddha in an unbroken succession.
Thus, it is regarded as the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye; it is regarded as the ultimate...
The ultimate stage of awakening. By this, the Dharma is made to abide for a long time; by this, the Great Way is sustained;
by this, the precepts are adorned and purified, attaining complete purity. Even if one were to speak for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one could not exhaustively describe it.
It is like the *Avataṃsaka*’s Dharma-gate of a Single Syllable, which could not be fully recorded even with ink as vast as the ocean.
Furthermore, this mantra is called the "Crown of the Tathāgata" because it is the heart-mantra, the unsurpassed crest-dharma transmitted by all Buddhas.

You who are still at or below the stage of the three fruits and have not yet exhausted the cycle of birth and death within the realm of conditioned existence (*saṃvṛti-jarāmaraṇa*), should resolve to become true Arhats.
If one does not maintain this dhāraṇī while sitting in the place of enlightenment, how could one possibly remain far removed from the works of Māra?
Ānanda, in whatever world or in whatever land [this is maintained], it shall reach the point where all poisons cannot cause harm.

Commentary: This clarifies the merit of writing mantras and wearing them as amulets. Birch bark and palm leaves are materials that can be used for writing, each according to what is produced in their respective lands.
White cotton cloth (*pata*) is a product of India; it is a type of paper, some of which is of such value that its price is immeasurable—such as does not exist in this land.
One may store [the manuscript] in a pouch and wear it on the body, or write it within one's home; [these benefits apply to] all.
That which cannot be harmed by any poisons demonstrates that the merit of this mantra-heart is inconceivable.
Ānanda, I shall now further explain this mantra for you, [extending] until its accomplishment of the supramundane wisdom of all sentient beings.
Commentary: This provides a general indication of two meanings to clarify the inconceivable, wondrous function of the mantra-heart.

That is to say, this mantra-heart can protect living beings in the mundane world and assist the Path in the supramundane realm; what is called "bringing peace and security to all who are saved in the world" and "attaining eternal abiding upon transcending the world."
"If, after my parinirvāṇa, sentient beings in the final age [until] all receive my profound grace, I shall constantly provide them with protection.
(Commentary: This precisely clarifies that by rescuing and protecting the world, one attains great fearlessness. For those sentient beings who recite and uphold [this teaching].)
Fire cannot burn it; water cannot drown it; and neither great nor small poisons can harm it.

This means that once one has attained this mantra-heart, the objective realm becomes empty and the mind becomes tranquil; wisdom arises and delusions are extinguished. When encountering various evil conditions, they are transformed by a mere thought, and thus cannot cause harm.
As for the fact that worldly evil spells cannot take hold, it means that [this mantra] is truly capable of crushing them.
"Evil! Just as Mañjuśrī’s secret retention can immediately destroy the evil spells of Ḍaṅga, so it is here.
'The mind attains right reception' means that one attains samādhi through the power of the mantra. Once right reception is achieved, one then does not receive anything at all;
thus, even if there are many evils, they are like fire burning the void—without the slightest impairment. Yet, by the power of samādhi, [the evils] are dissolved."

It eliminates all poisons, like a single grain of an elixir of immortality that transforms iron and stone into gold; therefore it is said that once it enters one's mouth, it becomes the flavor of ambrosia (amṛta).
As for the statement that no poisonous substance can give rise to evil, this means that by means of this mantra-heart, one realizes the Samādhi of Compassion;
thus, all cruel poisons are transformed by the breeze of compassion, such that they are not only unable to [harm].
It shall guard against further harm; not only will it prevent calamities, but it will instead bestow auspicious blessings.
Ānanda, you should know that this mantra is ever-present (up to: ...), pervasively understood, and free from doubt.
Commentary: This clearly elucidates the accomplishment of supramundane wisdom for the benefit of sentient beings. Regarding the "Vajra Attendant":
this refers to the heart-mantra of the spell, which is the unsurpassed crest-ornament (uṣṇīṣa) dharma transmitted by all Buddhas; it is the Vajra Bodhisattva.
Because they ride upon their vows to protect the Dharma, they attend [the practitioner] day and night. Even those who recite mantras with a distracted mind are constantly followed;
this means that although such a practitioner has not yet attained stable abiding in samādhi, because they constantly maintain the mantra, [the deity] likewise follows them.
Since it is said that they "mindfully remember and orally maintain" [the mantra], and are called "sons of good family," they are certainly not negligent.

Regarding those who are defiled and evil, yet have resolved upon the bodhicitta and claim to abide within the samādhi of permanence while also reciting mantras in their longing for the swift attainment of perfect enlightenment— for such Bodhisattvas, not only will [the deity] constantly follow and protect them,
but shall also provide assistance through spiritual power from the hidden realm, causing them to swiftly awaken their divine consciousness.
Having attained awakening, even regarding all subtle principles beyond kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one is able to comprehend them thoroughly and universally,
thereby entering a state free from doubt.
From the first kalpa until the final body—in states that are impoverished, lowly, and undesirable.
(Marginal Note: This clarifies the mind of mantra-holding; it is to be forever separated from the evil destinies and not born into lowly births.
"The first kalpa" refers to the time of first generating the bodhicitta. "The final body" refers to the time of attaining Buddhahood at the end. [This is based on] the path of seeing and cultivation.
This practice brings about eternal freedom from hindrances and afflictions. To face the text is called "reading" (*pāṭha*); to recite it from memory is called "chanting" (*svādhyāya*);

to transcribe the diagrams and seals is called "copying" (*likhana*); to wear it secretly is called "concealing" (*gopana*). Poverty leads to the suffering of hardship; low status leads to the suffering of servitude—both are obstacles to those who practice the Way.
By departing from such unpleasant conditions, one will certainly be born in a pleasant realm. This *dhāraṇī*-heart is the supreme vehicle of pure, white Dharma. Because...
Because they uphold the supreme and pure Dharma, they experience supreme and pure retribution.
These sentient beings, even though their own bodies [do not formally observe the precepts], naturally fulfill the observance of the fast and the precepts.
Commentary: This clarifies that one obtains merit immediately upon maintaining the mantra.
"The Tathāgata’s merits are all bestowed upon this person" means that this *dhāraṇī-heart* is the secret treasury of all Buddhas; all meritorious dharmas and treasures are fully contained within it.
If one maintains it single-mindedly for a long time, they will naturally manifest. "All Buddhas are born in the same place" refers to this *dhāraṇī*.
The mind originally flows forth from the Buddha of the unconditioned mind. By holding it for a long time, one becomes "the mind itself is the Buddha.
This is what is meant by: "Morning after morning, rising together with the Buddha; night after night, sleeping while embracing the Buddha," like the *akṣa* fruit cluster that never disperses.
This refers to holding this mantra-heart, whereby the seeds of Buddhahood are perfumed by the three types of outflow-free karma and become eternal.

There is no loss or dispersal. Regarding "the person who has broken the precepts attains purity of the root of the precepts": this means they are able to transform defilement into purity. Regarding "one who has not yet attained the precepts attains the precepts":

this means they are able to establish the root of the precepts. Regarding "one who has not yet attained progress attains progress": this means they are able to give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) from the precepts.
Regarding "one who lacks wisdom attains wisdom": this means they are able to generate wisdom from their own meditative concentration. Regarding "that which is impure becomes pure": [this means...]

Regarding "purifying those who have not yet achieved the purity of fasting and precepts": this refers to individuals who possess past obstructions such that they repeatedly desire to observe the purity of fasting and precepts but are unable to do so.
By holding this mantra-heart, their past obstructions will naturally dissolve, and they will certainly achieve success.
Ānanda, when these sons of good family maintain this dhāraṇī (until) all [faults] are completely eliminated, leaving not even a hair’s breadth behind.
*Commentary*: This clarifies that maintaining the dhāraṇī can extinguish defiled karma of the present.

"Those who have violated the precepts before receiving them" refers to the time prior to receiving the precepts while maintaining the dhāraṇī. "Maintaining the dhāraṇī" means recollecting this dhāraṇī in the mind, as if with one's own hands.

"Maintain the object; it must not be abandoned. "To extinguish at once" means that the offense was committed prior to holding the mantra, while the extinction of the offense occurs after one has already held the mantra.

Even the statement that "drinking alcohol or eating pungent foods shall not be considered a transgression" refers specifically to events that occurred before holding the mantra; once the mantra has been held, all such things [are purified].
This explains that it is not a matter of indulging in unrestrained excess after reciting mantras. It is rather like saying: "Although such things occurred in the past, they no longer exist now;
therefore, one should naturally be granted leniency. This applies equally to wearing tattered, worn-out clothes and wearing new, clean garments.

"Those who do not enter the altar and those who do enter it are equal" means that when one holds the mantra with single-minded concentration and forgets all else, then this very body becomes the pure Dharma-body and this ground becomes the site of quiescent extinction. What distinction, then, can there be between purity and defilement?

According to the ancient explanation, the "four abandonments" (*catur-pārājika*) for a bhikṣu refer to the four root offenses: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. In the Sanskrit language, they are called *pārājika*.

*Pārājika*. This is translated as "abandonment. It means that one who commits any of these four offenses is forever abandoned by the Buddha-dharma and cast beyond the seas, just as the great ocean will not accept a corpse.
For *bhikṣuṇīs*, there are four additional *pārājikas*: namely, touching, the eighth [offense], concealing, and following.
Specifically, the fifth is that one must not touch a man with a defiled mind; the sixth is that one must not grasp a man with a defiled mind.
