Having already passed through the forty-one minds, one then awakens to the principle of the three truths: they are neither three nor one, yet they are precisely one and precisely three. As for "augmenting practice" (*prāyoga*):

it is only upon reaching this stage that one augments one's effort and application to enter the ground of the sages. Regarding "Buddha-awakening," this refers to the fundamental mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of the fruition stage.
Regarding "one's own mind," this refers to the mind of one's own causal stage. Although previously one’s awakening was equal to the Buddha’s awakening, one had not yet [reached the fruition].
It is employed as one's own mind. Although it is now used as one's own mind, its perfection has not yet been fully realized.

Were the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) to be completely transformed, then the deluded habitual tendencies of ignorance would vanish like ashes in smoke. This occurs only at the eighth stage; at this present stage, one merely anticipates such a vision.
Thus, whether it has emerged or not, it is likened to drilling wood for fire: the wood is about to ignite, yet it has not yet caught fire.

Because it possesses only the sign of warmth (*uṣmagata*), it is called the "Stage of Warmth" (*uṣmaga-bhūmi*). Previously, one took the wisdom of the Buddha’s fruition-stage as the mind of one's own causal stage;
now, one takes this mind of one's own causal stage to become the wisdom of the Buddha’s fruition-stage.

Since the characteristics of the mind have not yet been fully purified, although it can serve as a basis for reliance, it is not yet a state that can be relied upon. It is like a person climbing a high mountain; their body—
If one enters emptiness, yet the feet have not left the ground and there remains a subtle obstruction below, it is therefore called the "Stage of the Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

Previously, what was termed "function" and "accomplishment" still retained the two marks [of cause and effect]. Reaching this stage, however, cause and effect interpenetrate and the Buddha-mind is no longer divided.

Nevertheless, because the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) has not yet been forgotten, although one has skillfully attained the Middle Way, one has not yet truly attained it. This is illustrated by the metaphor of a person who endures an injury and wishes to harbor...
Within the mind, there is nothing to be cherished; when one wishes to express it with the mouth, there is likewise nothing to be uttered.

Regarding the matters already endured, they are at the point of being forgotten yet not yet forgotten—just as if one had attained something well but has not yet truly attained it. Therefore, it is called the Stage of Patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
Previously, there were the provisional emptiness and the middle way, all of which were quantitative. Previously, the mind had not yet forgotten its own causes, which constituted delusion.
The Middle Way. When one has not yet forgotten the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit, it is taken as the awakening to the Middle Way; these two are still objects of perception.
When one reaches this point where the three contemplations are integrated, then numbers and quantities are extinguished, and both cause and effect are forgotten.

Below, there is no self-mind; above, there is no Buddha-wisdom. Thus, the two are no longer objects of perception. Having attained the extinction of numbers and quantities, when both delusion and awakening are exhausted, one transcends loftily.
Because it transcends the world, it is called the "First Ground of the World. The superior practice is now complete.
Ānanda, when this son of good family reaches the limit of great bodhi and enters the intersection [of the stages], he is named "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksaṃbodhi).
Commentary: This clarifies the stages of the ten bhūmis and the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*). "Great Bodhi" refers to the three Tathāgata-garbhas.

Through the preceding preparatory practices (*prayoga*), both mind and Buddha are forgotten, and the Middle Way is not established; thus, one is able to transcend the worldly stages and skillfully reach the realm of the Buddhas.
However, this is not yet the ultimate realization; it merely constitutes the initial penetration into the true realm and the first ascent to the rank of the Sages.
As the two attachments are about to be exhausted, one brings universal benefit to oneself and others; because this accords with one's original vows, it is called "Joyful.

Previously, the nine realms of distinct natures were made to enter the single realm of the Buddha, which is termed "Entering the Same from Distinct Natures. However, even within the joyful mind of the Buddha-realm, there remains subtle defilement;
this must also be extinguished through the same nature. Only when the pure awakened mind is free from even these subtle defilements is it termed "Detachment."
Regarding "defilement": previously one was already free from defilement; now, by further departing from that very freedom, the essence of awakening becomes supremely pure and its radiance manifests.
Therefore, it is called "Emission of Light. While the previous stage was the initial arising of light, this stage is its blazing intensity.

With the vajra-flame wisdom, which is like a great mass of fire, all shadows of objective conditions are completely incinerated. When luminosity reaches its ultimate limit, it is the Tathāgata; hence it is called the "Flame of Full Awakening."

The Stage of Wisdom (*prajñā-bhūmi*) is the ultimate attainment of wisdom. That which possesses discrimination is called "differentiated wisdom" (*vibhinna-jñāna*); that which is without discrimination is called "identical wisdom" (*sama-jñāna*). When there is difference, the sentiments of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may be surpassed;
when there is identity, the understanding of the sages (*ārya*) may be surpassed. Now, since neither identity nor difference can be reached, both the ordinary and the sage are forgotten.

Prior to this, the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) were still divided, and identity and difference were still in opposition; here, however, the ultimate and the conventional are both transcended.
Fusion. The two wisdoms shine simultaneously; what were previously contradictory become harmonious, and thus it is called "Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjaya*).

Because the afflictions of both the holy and the ordinary have been exhausted as described above, the two wisdoms are in correspondence, whereby the various supreme *prajñās* manifest before one, illuminating the unconditioned true nature.

It is naturally revealed and manifest; hence it is called "manifest before one" (*pratyakṣa*). Because the preceding prajñā illuminates fundamental *tathatā* (suchness) to its very limits, it transcends both mundane and supramundane dharmas;
therefore, it is named "Far-Reaching" (*dūramgama*). Having reached the ultimate limit of reality, everything returns to the single essence.

Right gnosis functions spontaneously without relying on effortful practice, and one directly attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), whereby all mental states cease to arise.
Therefore, it is called "Immovable. Previously, one attained the entire substance of True Suchness (*tathatā*); here, one brings forth the great function of True Suchness.
In the former case, every speck of dust and every hair returns to the true essence; in this case, they mutually encompass and mutually enter, all becoming wondrous functions.

One is fully endowed with the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge—of phenomena, meaning, language, and eloquence. Whatever is illuminated or responded to is none other than the wondrous function of True Suchness.
Therefore, he is named "Excellent Wisdom" (*Sādhumatī*). From "Ānanda, below... onwards, this serves as a general conclusion for the preceding stage.

This means that from the four stages of application (*prayoga*) up to this point, this bodhisattva has repeatedly undergone cultivation and abandonment; thus, both the essence and function of *tathatā* (suchness) manifest before him, and there is no cultivation of supramundane merit that is not fully perfected.
Hence, it is called "Perfected. Furthermore, within this stage, it is precisely the time when one should extensively bestow [benefits].
The Buddha-dharma extensively delivers sentient beings; therefore, it is also termed "cultivation.
Once the essence and function of True Suchness (Tathatā) are realized as perfected, then compassion is like the mist and great wisdom is like the clouds—these are the causal virtues of a Bodhisattva.
Nirvana is like the ocean—this is the resultant virtue of a Tathāgata. Because these cause and effect are contiguous, the Bodhisattva, by means of...

Based on compassion, it universally responds to the capacities of all beings; whatever it nurtures and moistens is unconditioned and non-active, perfectly accordant with the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescent extinction.

Therefore, it is named the Dharma-Cloud Ground (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). As for the Tathāgata “flowing against the current,” this means that the Tathāgata has long since realized the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment and has nothing further to advance toward or attain;
yet, out of a desire not to abandon sentient beings, he turns his back on the flow and steers the vessel of compassion upstream.
And he emerges. Yet this Bodhisattva has not yet completed his forward progress; he is still hastening toward the ocean of fruition, entering it by following the current.

Regarding "the boundary of awakening and the limit of entry intersecting": the Bodhisattva’s initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) and the Buddha’s wondrous awakening (*prakarṣa-bodhi*) are precisely equal in their measure; they differ only in being "with-flow" versus "against-flow.
Because there is no interval between him and the Buddha, he is named Equal Awakening (*samyak-sambodhi*).
Ānanda, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one gradually penetrates deeper through pure cultivation and realization.
[Capitulation Note: This generally reveals the practice of all stages and concludes by returning to the ultimate fruit of the Tathāgata.
"From Dry Wisdom up to Equal Enlightenment" comprehensively encompasses the preceding stages in order to show the beginning and end of the various positions. This is so.

"Awakening" refers to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). "Vajra-mind" takes its name from the fact that the power of this mind is uninterrupted, reaching the ultimate and most sharp state, capable of severing even subtle ignorance—just as a vajra-kings jewel can destroy all things while its own substance cannot be destroyed by anything else. "The initial stage of Dry Wisdom" refers to the stage prior to the [first] ground of faith. A single stage is called "simple" (*dan*); ten stages combined are called "complex" (*fu*). The seven stages—dry wisdom (*ganhui*), the four stages of preparatory application (*jiexing*), and the [first] three of the marvelous [stages] (*miaojue*)—are simple.
The five stages—faith (*xin*), abiding (*zhu*), practice (*xing*), orientation (*xiang*), and ground (*di*)—are complex. Together they constitute twelve.

Taking dry wisdom as the beginning of attainment and marvelous enlightenment (*miaojue*) as the point of ultimate completion, eleven belong to the cause and the final one belongs to the fruit. "Attainment" refers to the initial acquisition of something gained.

When these are exhausted, there is ultimately nothing to be attained. This clearly demonstrates that even if one enters the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), if there is even the slightest trace of attachment remaining, one has not yet perfected the Unsurpassed Way (*anuttara-mārga*).
These points collectively explain the reasons for the progression from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) up to the Equal and Wondrous [Enlightenment].
One might still ask: "From where does this Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) arise? It is said:

from the initial attainment of the Vajra-mind, through the stage of Initial Dry Wisdom (ādi-śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi), and by thus traversing these successive stages of faith, abiding, practice, direction, and preparatory application (prayoga), one finally reaches Equal Enlightenment.
From this Equal Enlightenment, one then exhausts [all traces] to reach Sublime Enlightenment (miao-jue), thereby accomplishing the Unsurpassed Way. This concludes the section clarifying the Sublime.
The nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks. To "see the various stages" refers to the twelve positions, both single and combined.

"Vajra-observation" is the prajñā of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Having already accomplished the unsurpassed Way, one further employs the prajñā of the true mark to look back upon the stages previously traversed;
not a single one possesses substantial reality. This is what is called the "illusion-like samādhi."
Mati, it is said that one does not merely contemplate conditioned phenomena as being like dreams or illusions; one likewise contemplates unconditioned phenomena as being like flowers in the sky.
Therefore, they are called "profound metaphors. As for the ten types: a phantom person, a mirage, the moon in water, flowers in the sky, an echo in a valley, and so forth.
It is like a city of *gandharvas*, a dream, a shadow, an image, or a transformation. *Śamatha* is the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama*;

*vipaśyanā* is right contemplation. This is the reverse of what was stated above: having reached this point, one turns back to contemplate; although it is like an illusion, one practices through gradual stages.

Realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) likewise must not be neglected at the expense of cultivation. At the outset, one must enter right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) and employ the correct contemplation (*samyagdarśana*) of all Tathāgatas to bring the five abodes (*pañcāvasthā*) to their ultimate end and cause the two deaths (*dvimaraṇa*) to be forever forgotten. Furthermore, one must not cling to the marks of concentration or contemplation;
it is only by practicing without practice and realizing without realization that one can achieve the unsurpassed, wondrous Way. Therefore, it is said: "Pure Cultivation."
Realization proceeds through gradual and deepening stages.
Ānanda, it is by means of these three progressive advancements that [realization occurs]; otherwise, to view it differently is called "erroneous observation.
The section on the realization of the Way (the *pramāṇa-mārga*) concludes here. From the beginning of the first fascicle up to this point, the previously mentioned *samādhi* is finally completed.

It is named the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King, because it fully embodies the myriad practices and constitutes the path of wondrous adornment through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend by a single gate.
The following section clarifies the conclusion of the scripture. Mañjuśrī requests its name, and the World-Honored One again places "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" at the beginning;
this precisely reveals the meaning of the cause in order to establish the title, manifesting it through that name.
Meaning. Name and meaning are always mutually dependent. [Commentary:
This encourages those at the initial stage of practice to abandon the heterodox and incline toward the orthodox. This is because perfect cultivation leads to perfect realization.
Although cause and effect mutually penetrate one another, when setting out to advance toward the goal, one must revere the initial resolve.

Therefore, following the previous passage, it says, "Thus gradually entering deeper," meaning that from the very beginning, one uses the three gradual stages as the means for furthering one's cultivation.

As for the fifty-five stages and so forth—namely, the stages of faith, abiding, practice, direction, application, equal-enlightenment, and so on—all are ultimately directed toward this [enlightenment].
The path to the house of Bodhi: prior to the stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi), one has not yet set out on the journey, and thus it is excluded;

subsequent to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (miao-jue), one has already returned to that house, and thus it is no longer called a path. Such contemplations as these mean that [liberation] is determined by śamatha.
Only that which is pure cultivation and realization is rightly termed "right contemplation" (samyag-darśana). All else is termed "erroneous contemplation" (mithyā-darśana).
This means that, apart from the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna), all practices of the Three Vehicles are termed erroneous contemplations; it does not refer to heterodox or external paths.
At that time, Mañjuśrī... [up to] "O all Bodhisattvas, you should uphold the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the foremost of the ten thousand practices.
(Corrigenda and Notes: This is the request to establish the title of the sutra.

Since this sutra takes the cultivation of the *Śūraṅgama* Great Samādhi and the realization of the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of purity and luminosity—as its essential purport, it first employs Ānanda to initiate the source of the teaching.)
Therefore, he causes those of great learning to cultivate the Great Samādhi. As for the fact that Mañjuśrī ultimately requested the name [of the scripture] so it might be upheld:
were it not for the fundamental Great Wisdom, one could not possibly maintain the entire sutra or realize the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature.
Thus, the World-Honored One bestowed a name upon it; the title begins with "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. Here, "Great" (Mahā) refers to—
These are words of praise. It is said that the Buddhas realize the ultimate truth through perfect wisdom;
thus, with mind realizing mind, they perceive no characteristics of subject or object. This is the unsurpassed, most venerable, and supreme *mūrdha* (crown) dharma.

As for the term "Great White Parasol" (*Mahāśvetachattra*), it signifies that which covers all, remaining unstained by even a speck of dust, nurturing the children of the Buddha, and providing shelter for sentient beings.
Furthermore, as for the term "Unsurpassed Treasure Seal," it means that all ten dharma realms are entirely sealed by a single dharma;
this is the mind-seal transmitted from Buddha to Buddha and from patriarch to patriarch. Because sentient beings are deluded regarding this, they encounter obstacles everywhere.

The Tathāgata, having awakened to this, realizes the perfect penetration of the dharma realm; therefore, it is called the "Pure Eye of the Ocean. This name is established based on the union of wisdom and principle.
It is also called "The Savior of One’s Kinsmen and Causes," and so forth. "Kinsman" refers to Ānanda; "Cause" refers to Caṇḍā; "Bodhicitta" refers to Correct Wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*);

and "Ocean of Universal Knowledge" refers to the True Realm. These terms indicate that the principles of these Exoteric and Esoteric teachings enable those individuals to escape the sufferings and difficulties of the causal stage and realize the blissful realm of the fruition stage;
this is a naming established in terms of persons and dharmas. It is also called "The Tathāgata," and so forth.

The Tathāgata is the resultant fruit; the secret cause is the causal practice. It is said that in this very day, in the common experiences of seeing forms and hearing sounds, these are themselves the true cause.
Yet ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle do not know this, and thus it is called the "secret cause. One should cultivate practice in reliance upon it.
Thus, one cultivates that which is without cultivation; relying upon this, one realizes that which is without realization. Therefore, it is called "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*).

This name is established in terms of cause and effect. It is also called "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Extensive), signifying that while the principle is one, it fully embodies essence, characteristics, and function.
It is like a wondrous king of lotuses: it abides within the myriad dharmas yet does not cling to a single thing, just as a lotus remains in the mud yet is pure and fragrant in its very essence.
The Mothers of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions and others say that this Dharma can give birth to all Buddhas and can encompass all dharmas, upholding immeasurable meanings.
To accord with this in a single thought-moment is to transform the ordinary into the sacred. This is based on...
This is the establishment of the name based on both principle (*dharma*) and metaphor (*upamā*).
It is also called the "Mantras of Consecration" (*abhiṣeka-pada*), meaning that this sutra emerges from the *Abhiṣeka* section and is the supreme dharma for the succession to the Buddha’s position.

For all Bodhisattvas and others, it is said that this Dharma-gate, when condensed, is the single mind; when expanded, it encompasses the myriad practices. It fully prepares and summarizes everything as nothing other than the one true samādhi. From...
It establishes meditative concentration and gives rise to practice, reaching ultimate firmness; this is the naming based upon its doctrinal practice.

Therefore, one should know that this sutra’s teaching encompasses both the Exoteric and Esoteric, and there is nothing—whether principle or wisdom, person or dharma, cause or effect, dharma or metaphor, teaching or practice—that it does not contain.
Since it fully possesses many essential and subtle aspects, it is established with various titles and categories, such as the Three Schools and Five Teachings, all of which it universally embraces.
"You should practice and maintain this; it must not be lost.
Having spoken these words, Ānanda immediately [attained] the six stages of mental cultivation regarding subtle afflictions.

According to the ancient explanation, regarding the afflictions abandoned through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*): in the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), within the nine stages (*bhūmi*) of the three realms, each stage consists of nine grades.
By abandoning the first six grades of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), one realizes the second fruit; by abandoning the final three grades, one realizes the third fruit;
and by abandoning the nine grades of each of the two upper realms, one realizes the fourth fruit. Ānanda, having heard the entire sūtra in its entirety, only then realized the second fruit.

The result [of this] manifests the inferiority of mere erudition; it is not equal to the excellence of advancing in the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*). The section on the "Concluding the Sūtra" is finished.

Below this, the "Aids to the Path" (*bodhipakṣa*) are clarified. From the first fascicle up to this point, although both the real and the false have been explained in alternation, the primary intent has been solely to cultivate the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama* in order to realize the eternally abiding true mind and the essence of pure luminosity, thereby attaining perfection.
From the initial fruit of bodhi and nirvāṇa, through the stages and positions from beginning to end, there is forever no trace of any circuitous or devious phenomena.
This will be explained extensively below in the section on the seven destinies and so forth. The first fascicle states:
"By means of various false imaginings, because these imaginings are not true, there is cyclic wandering. Thus, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been variously deluded.

The fruits of inverted karma arise naturally, like a cluster of akṣa fruits. Even through erroneous cultivation, one becomes a follower of the Lesser Vehicle, an externalist, a celestial Māra, or a member of Māra’s retinue;
all these are results produced because the causal ground was not true, thereby inviting a crookedness that perverts what is correct.
This refers to what are known as the various detailed aspects. Therefore, one should know that prior to the formalization of the sutras, it was called "gathering the remnants" (*kūṇśi tsan ki*);
after the formalization of the sutras, it was called "upholding the rules and discussing the eternal" (*fu lü tan chang*). Both are essential Dharma-gates for those at the initial stage of practice;

thus, they are explained in detail so that people may thoroughly understand their essential points, avoid falling into partiality or error, and subsequently be able to transcend the realm of existence.
[They] exhaust the outflows and proceed directly toward unsurpassed bodhi.
*Guānzhù* (Annotated Commentary): This describes the benefits obtained from hearing the sutra. "Mudrā" (mìyìn) refers to the secret heart-seal;

it is precisely what was previously transmitted as the three Tathāgata-garbhas and the fundamental source of universal penetration (*yuántōng*). The meaning of *paṇḍara* (bāntáluó) is... [text continues].
The divine spells and the merits of those spells previously mentioned are the designations for the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), namely the five types of names [of the Tathāgata].

"Sudden awakening to *dhyāna*," and so forth, refers to the sixth stage: the dissolution of the one through the understanding of the six. This is the sudden awakening to the true permanence and the perfect interfusion of the three truths (*triratna*).
From this point, one cultivates and advances through the fifty-five stages until reaching the ultimate state of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi*), thereby accomplishing the Unsurpassed Way.

Regarding the passage "The mind’s deliberations become empty and coalescent," once one reaches this point, the cultivation and realization of both the primary and auxiliary practices, the stages from beginning to end, and the essential meanings of both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings will be fully understood at once; there shall forever be no doubt.
Having severed the six grades of afflictions of thought cultivated within the three realms, one attains the realization of the second fruit (Sakṛdāgāmin).
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet... [up to] "...because of the arising of the delusive habitual tendencies of these sentient beings.
(Commentary: This expresses the desire to inquire about the causes of the seven destinies while pre-emptively expressing gratitude for the previous benefits.

The phrase "immediately rose from his seat" is recorded by the scribe of the sutra. "Great majestic virtue" refers to the World-Honored One possessing the majesty to subdue and the power to gather and sustain.)
Because of his virtue, he is able to reprove and instruct, encouraging others to look up to him with reverence and receive his teachings. His compassionate voice is without obstruction;

it does not weary in teaching nor withhold from others, nor does it exclude or discard those whose capacities are limited. "Skillfully opening" means demonstrating with artistry. As for subtle and deep-seated delusions:

I thank you for what you previously showed me regarding the refutation of delusion; my body and mind feel refreshed and joyful. I thank you for what you previously showed me regarding the manifestation of truth;
I have gained great benefit. By hearing your compassionate voice, I have been able to sever the six grades of afflictions of the realm of thought.

Regarding the subsequent inquiry concerning the seven realms of existence: because the preceding discourse on the wondrous nature’s perfect luminosity and its freedom from all names and marks might cause beginners to give rise to the view that negates all things, he requests a resolution of his doubts.
The essential point is that practitioners must not seek outwardly, nor must they negate cause and effect; only then does one possess correct wisdom and true cultivation. This is the intended meaning.
It refers to the wondrously luminous true substance and the pure, wondrous functioning of the mind, which are fundamentally all-pervasive and perfect.
Thus, the fundamental True Suchness (tathatā) of both insentient and sentient beings in all places is entirely non-dual and without distinction from the true substance of the Tathāgata’s Buddhahood.
Since this is the Buddha-body, it is truly without difference. How, then, can there again be the various forms of the seven destinies?

Are they each distinct? Furthermore, by what cause do these types arise? Do they exist inherently within the essence of True Suchness from the beginning, or are they produced by the habitual tendencies of the deluded thoughts of sentient beings?
This question is identical in intent to that of Pūrṇa.
“World-Honored One, just as the Bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā... [she] received it with joy upon her head, maintaining it with purity and without transgression.
During the time when the Buddha was in the world, King Prasenajit, having newly ascended the throne, sent an envoy to seek a marriage alliance from a Śākya family in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Mahānāman’s maidservant gave birth to a daughter of upright and beautiful countenance, who was then sent to King Prasenajit.
O King, later a son was born to him named Rāhula. When he reached the age of eight, he went with the son of a Brahmin, Bhadraka, to the house of Mahānāman.
At that time, a new lecture hall had been built in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, and they wished to invite the Tathāgata to offer him worship.
Then, Prince Rāhula arrived at the lecture hall and immediately ascended the lion throne. At that moment, all...
When the Śākyas saw him, they reviled him, saying, "This offspring of a slave dares to sit among us.
Vimalakīrti (Liu-li) spoke, and Bhadraka (Hao-ku) said, "These Śākyas have brought such humiliation upon me; when you succeed to the throne, you must inform me.
Later, when Vimalakīrti succeeded to the throne, Bhadraka informed him of these former events. Vimalakīrti then assembled his troops and went forth to wage war.
The Śākyas. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In times past, at this city of Rājagṛha, there was a fishing village.
At that time, the world suffered from famine. In that village there was a pond with many fish. Then the many people of the city went to the pond to catch and eat the fish."
In a pond there were two kinds of fish: one named *Kṣāra* (the Flour-fish) and the other named *Bahujihva* (the Many-tongued). Each harbored a grudge against the other.
At that time, a young boy on the bank saw the fish leaping and, being delighted, struck them on the head with a stick.
Those who were the people of Rājagṛha at that time are now the Śākyas; the *Kṣāra* fish was King Virūḍhaka; and the *Bahujihva* fish was the Brahmin.
"That one who was so fond of bitterness was none other than my own self. For this reason, King Virūḍhaka killed the Śākyas, harboring a grudge from former enmity."
Commentary: This is a detailed inquiry concerning the hells. In Sanskrit, they are called *niraya*; here they are translated as "hells" (*diyu*).
They are also called "lack of autonomy," meaning that those sinners are bound and restrained by the hell-wardens, such that they cannot attain freedom.
Regarding the Bhikṣuṇī Rāvaṇa (Bǎoliánxiāng), there were three causes for her offense: first, committing sexual misconduct; second, slandering the precepts; and third, an error.

Because people gradually reach the point of extreme gravity, they fall into Avīci. There are two types of retribution for this: first, retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*), meaning one's own body is consumed by fire;

second, retribution in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), meaning falling into the Uninterrupted Hell (*Avīci*). Virūḍhaka violated the precept against killing, while Sunakṣatra violated the precept against false speech;
both were those who fell due to experiencing retribution in their subsequent births. According to ancient accounts, Virūḍhaka was the son of King Mahānāman...
The son usurped his father’s throne and established himself as ruler. Driven by long-standing resentment, he slaughtered the Śākya clan and seized twelve thousand Śākya women.
He mutilated them by cutting off their ears and noses and severing their hands and feet, then cast them into pits and ditches. The Buddha prophesied that he would enter hell within seven days;
the king sailed out to sea to escape, but he was spontaneously consumed by flames upon the water. As for "long-standing resentment," it refers to ancient enmity.
Furthermore, Shanxing was the Buddha’s own younger cousin. He falsely taught that all phenomena are empty and denied the existence of cause and effect.

As for his being "born trapped," it means that due to the intensity of his karmic forces, he was cast into hell with his physical body still intact. Regarding these various hells, do they have fixed locations?
This means that there are inherently fixed locations [for retribution]. Question: Regarding "distinct karmas with shared retribution" (*bipakya-sabhāga-karman*):

sexual misconduct, killing, and lying are distinct karmas; yet all result in falling into hell, which is shared retribution. Is this automatic, or do those who initiate these various karmas each privately undergo their own retribution? Answer:
It is because they have each created their own karma that they each privately undergo their respective retributions. Question: What is meant by "distinct karmas"?
This is a separate retribution. Later, when the World-Honored One provides his definitive answer, these two meanings will be present; one shall see them for oneself in the text.

I only pray that you will deign to look down upon this request and grant instruction on how to protect the precepts to strictly restrain the initial mind, so that one may resolve to maintain them and not commit transgressions intentionally.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "How excellent is this question! [up to] "...thereby distinguishing between the internal division and the external division.
(Commentary: This generally clarifies the two divisions of internal and external, which serve as the causes for the seven destinies.

What was asked accords with the Buddha’s intention; therefore, it is said, "How excellent. The aforementioned instances of violating precepts, slandering [the Dharma], and so forth, are all false views.
None of these are the true cause. Therefore, I now clarify this in response to your question, so that all sentient beings may not fall into false views.
That which is truly and fundamentally pure refers to the essential nature possessed by sentient beings of the seven realms of existence;

it is the original source of True Suchness (*tathatā*), the pure and wondrous mind of intrinsic nature, free from all defilements. Due to a single moment of delusion regarding this truth, it subsequently gives rise to...
False view. Since false view exists, false habituation arises. What is called "false view" is the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*);

what is called "false habituation" is the seeds of affliction (*saṃkleśa-bīja*). With the seeds and habituation of ignorance as the cause, the notion of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*) arises spontaneously.

This continuity is uninterrupted; therefore, it is divided into two parts: internal and external. Nevertheless, as sentient beings fall or ascend according to their superior or inferior states, they are all in essence nothing but the habitual tendencies of delusion.
"Ānanda, the 'internal division' (*antarbhāga*) refers to the internal sphere of sentient beings... [down to] falling naturally of itself; this is called the internal division.

*Commentary:* This is a specific explanation of the internal division. Because all sentient beings follow their own emotional attachments and remain complacent in their original state, seeking no further progress, it is called "their internal sphere.
"Attachment and defilement" refers to the seeds within the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*), which serve as the cause.
There are seeds that, through attachment to objects, give rise to active manifestations; clinging to them firmly and refusing to let go is called "delusive sentiment.
As these sentiments accumulate without ceasing, they secretly nourish the karma of greed, becoming the "water of craving.
Consequently, there is nowhere one goes where the "stream of desire" is not formed. How can this be verified? Simply observe sentient beings: when their minds recall delicacies, even as their mouths—
Water emerges. Out of pity and resentment for those who came before, tears fill the eyes; out of attachment to wealth and treasures, the entire body becomes lustrous and moist;
out of lustful desire, the two organs flow with fluids—all of these are brought about by emotional craving.
Since craving is transformed into water, it must inevitably lead to downfall. Although the objects of one's affection differ from one another, they are all capable of [producing this effect].
The heart of craving is firmly bound and never loosened; it has never known change. Because emotional attachment serves as its water, it flows downward and does not ascend.
Thus, those who fall into the three miserable realms all have emotional attachment as their cause.
Ānanda, the external division (*bāhya-bhāga*) refers to that which is beyond the realm of sentient beings (up to: "naturally transcending this," which is called the external division).

[Commentary: This is a specific explanation of the external division. Because all sentient beings, riding upon that conceptual mind (*saṃjñā-citta*), do not abide in their original destination but resolve to seek liberation, it is called "beyond the realm. "Yearning with thirst" means to look up with admiration toward the supreme state, as if...
"Thirst" refers to the desire for drink; it is used here as a metaphor for the seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Because these habitual tendencies exist, one yearns for superior realms and gives rise to illusory conceptions. Consequently, the spirit races toward vast distances without rest.
As these conceptions persist and the will becomes concentrated, a superior energy is further generated, such that there is nowhere one does not ascend with lightness. How can this be verified?

Yet observe sentient beings: their minds maintain the prohibitive precepts, yet their entire bodies feel light and pure; their minds maintain mantras and mudrās, yet their gazes are bold and resolute;
their minds desire to be born in heaven, yet in dreams they soar aloft; their minds dwell upon the Buddha-lands, yet sacred realms manifest in the dark;
they serve spiritual friends, yet they disregard their own bodies and lives—all of these are driven by empty conceptions.
However, although the objects of thought differ, the mind that conceives them rises spontaneously and effortlessly, never having been otherwise from the beginning.
Because it takes empty conceptions as its superior vital energy (*prāṇa*), it ascends without falling.
Thus, those who fly up to the higher realms all take empty conceptions as their cause.
Ānanda, throughout all worlds, the cycle of birth and death continues (until) the two habits of "death-contrary" and "birth-favorable" intersect.

[Commentary: From this point downward, it clarifies the fruits summoned by emotional desire and conceptual thought. The meaning is that although the various realms of existence differ, [they are governed by these habits].
It does not arise from the two causes of emotion and thought; rather, it is because karma has degrees of lightness and heaviness that retribution varies accordingly.
"Birth follows habitual tendencies" means that the suffering and pleasure experienced in the present life all derive from the habitual tendencies of good and evil karma created in the past.
This follows from the manner of birth. Regarding "death proceeding from transformation and flow":

it means that once this body has died and the karmic retribution of one's previous life is exhausted, one undergoes a change of head and face; such migrations and transformations are manifold and cannot be known in advance.

Therefore, at the moment when the present *skandhas* (aggregates) are about to cease and the subsequent *skandhas* have not yet continued—though the warmth and tactile sensation have not yet been abandoned—the entirety of what was practiced throughout one’s life...
The cultivation of good and evil manifests simultaneously and all at once; it will then further transform into its respective categories based on these habitual tendencies of good and evil karma.
Furthermore, because all sentient beings love life and loathe death, at this time, if one is born, it accords with their habits, and if one dies, it opposes their habits.
Nevertheless, as these two tendencies intersect, they are experienced solely through the power of karmic retribution.
How could one possibly allow the mind to be attached to these transformations?
"Pure thought leads to flight and one will surely be born in the heavens" (up to) "when thought is clear, the faculties are sharp; when the emotions are obscure, they are dull."
Commentary: This clarifies those whose thoughts are predominant and whose emotions are slight; it is the place of transcendent ascent.
Regarding "those whose thoughts alone lead to birth in heaven," this refers to the various heavens within the three realms, all of which are induced by the wholesome karma of the thinking mind.

Among them, there are those who concurrently practice the Six Pāramitās and aspire to see the Buddhas; these also attain rebirth in accordance with their vows. For example, if one thinks of and vows for the Western [Pure Land], and...
Those who are born into the Pure Land are of this class. As for those with little emotion and much thought, their superior thoughts are not pure, as they are slightly tainted by deviant emotions.

Regarding "light elevation that is not far-reaching": vertically, they do not transcend the Four Heavenly Kings; horizontally, they do not go beyond the Cakravāḍa Mountains. With nine thoughts and one emotion, one becomes a Flying Immortal (*vidyādhara*);
with eight thoughts and two emotions, one becomes a Great Power Ghost King (*mahābala-guhyaka-rāja*); with seven thoughts and three emotions...
They are *khecarī-yakṣas* (flying yakṣas). Those with six perceptions and four feelings are *bhūmicara-rākṣasas* (earth-walking rākṣasas). "Wandering" means traveling for a temporary period;
it does not refer to those who, like the aforementioned [beings], dwell permanently in the heavens. "Go" means to depart. "Among them" refers to [the former category].

These are included among the four aforementioned categories. Regarding "wholesome vows and wholesome minds": this refers to those who, though possessing deviant sentiments, do not cease their aspirational resolve.

Regarding "protecting the Dharma, protecting the precepts, protecting mantras, and protecting meditative concentration": each follows one's own aspirations and possesses its respective seeds and habitual tendencies.

"Sui" means to pacify and bring peace. "Dharmakṣānti" (Dharma-patience) refers to such practices as the cultivation of forbearance (*kṣānti-caryā*) and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Those who dwell beneath the Buddha’s seat are those whose hearts vow to protect the Teaching, such as the eight classes of beings.

"Sentient feelings and thoughts are equal" refers to the five feelings and five thoughts. "Neither flying nor falling," etc., means that they do not exist above among the celestial immortals, nor below among the host of hair-like creatures;
they are mostly born as human beings. Although their sentient feelings and thoughts are equal, if within those thoughts they possess understanding—
If one is clear-sighted and discerning, then the principles of phenomena will be lucid and penetrating; such a person is one who is sharp and intelligent.
If, within the realm of emotions, one’s understanding is obscured and stifled, then the principles of phenomena will be clouded and confused; such a person is one who is dull and ignorant.

"Affection (qing) is much and thought (xiang) is little; one flows into the horizontal births (hengsheng), [extending] into the various homogeneous classes (zhong tongfen), while also possessing the original ground.
*Annotation:* This clarifies that "affection is much and thought is little" refers to sinking into the dark paths. The six affections and four thoughts constitute the horizontal births.
Among them, those whose karma is somewhat heavy become the hairy multitudes (maoqun); those whose karma is somewhat light become the feathered tribes (yuzhu).

Those with the seven afflictions and three delusions become hungry ghosts. An old commentary states that according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, at the very bottom of the great earth are the three wheels of gold, water, and wind;

above these wheels are the eight cold and eight hot hells. However, this present sutra says they "sink beneath the water wheel and are born at the limit of fire," which suggests there is a fire wheel beneath the water wheel. This refers to the first of the cold hells.
Eight: At the junction of water and fire, one receives a fierce vital energy. "Fire" refers to receiving fiery energy to form a body; therefore, one is constantly burned by fire.
Even when obtaining water to drink, it transforms into fire; thus it is said that water can harm oneself.

With eight passions and two thoughts, one is born in the *Antara* (Intermediate) Hell; with nine passions and one thought, one is born in the *Avīci* (Uninterrupted) Hell, where below one penetrates the wheel of flames.

These refer to the eight hot hells. Regarding "the body enters the place where wind and fire intersect": this is the location where wind and fire intermingle, and the suffering experienced by one whose body dwells therein can be imagined.
"With intervals" refers to the eighteen hells; "without interval" refers to the eight Avīci hells.
Regarding "pure emotion sinking into Avīci," the traditional explanation concerns the nature of the retribution, the instruments of torture, the dimensions of the body, and the duration of kalpas.

Regarding the five types of lifespan, because there is no interval between them, they are called the "five immediate" (*pañcānantarya*) offenses. These are committed by those whose mental karma is most grave;

they fall into this state and remain until the kalpa is destroyed, at which point they emerge. However, if one additionally slanders the Mahāyāna and so forth, then even when this kalpa is destroyed, one enters the Avīci hell of the ten directions, from which there is no time of emergence. This is because those who slander the Dharma cause countless people to fall into error.

Because it is seen. Following the section on "creation" (nirmāṇa), the conclusion is provided. Since the preceding question asked whether these various hells have fixed locations or are experienced individually, the answer states:

although they are summoned by one's own karma and experienced individually, they exist within a commonality of shared destiny (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and therein also possess an original ground (*mūla-bhūmi*).
This original ground is the fixed location; this is the direct answer to the point that individual karmas share a common retribution.
Ānanda, all these sentient beings (up to) create ten causes of habitual practice and undergo six types of intersecting retributions. [Commentary:

This is the text that concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one. Previously, it was explained that emotional thoughts (*qingxiang*) serve as the cause, and the seven realms of rebirth (*qiqu*) experienced thereby constitute the result.
From here on, it is explained that the ten habitual practices serve as the cause, and the three miserable paths (*santou*) experienced thereby constitute the result. [This is] one's own karma.
That which is experienced refers to the karma created by one's own mind and the fruits manifested by one's own mind; it is neither created by a celestial deity nor bestowed by another person.
As it is said: "One should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm: all things are manifested and experienced as created solely by the mind."
What are the ten causes? Ānanda, the first is the habit-energy of lust (*kāma-vāsanā*)... [up to] "the Bodhisattva views desire as avoiding a pit of fire. (Annotation:
This provides a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habit-energy of lust. According to the old interpretation, evil karma arises from emotional delusion.)
Since lust is the foremost among delusions of the passions, it is clarified at the beginning and end [of the section]. The opening sentence generally interrogates the ten causes.

First, "The first," etc., presents the characteristics of the causes created during one's lifetime. Next, "As with a person," etc., employs a metaphor to verify the reality of that cause-and-effect relationship.
Third, "The two habits," etc., clarifies the characteristics of the results experienced after death. Therefore...
Below: Fourth, citing the sages to demonstrate the precepts so that one may know to fear and avoid them; all subsequent sections are modeled after this. "To intersect" means to form a structure.
"To join" means to conjoin. "To initiate" means to move. "Mutually grinding" refers to the defiled mind contacting pleasure.
When the grinding continues without ceasing, the essence and blood are naturally depleted, and the fire-element blazes intensely; at the time of its arising, there is naturally a wasting thirst.
Internal fevers and other ailments are created by one's own mind; thus, the signs [of retribution] have already manifested within the hells.
Therefore it is said that "a great, fierce fire breaks out therein. This is established through metaphorical illustration to allow one to know the reality of cause and effect.

Regarding the two types of habituation: "habituation during life" refers to that which is manifested in the present and is produced by seeds; "habituation after death" refers to that which is perfumed by present activity.
Habituation during life belongs to the cause, while habituation after death belongs to the fruit; thus, they correspond as cause and effect.

As for "the manifestation of such [results]," this refers to the occurrence of burning events such as the iron bed, as stated in other sūtras when describing the transformation of the king’s daughter.

When the sinner embraces it, it immediately becomes a bed of fire and columns of flame. This clearly demonstrates that it is a manifestation produced by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the eye and mind.

The Tathāgata names this "the fire of desire" (*kāma-agni*); by showing the cause through its effect, he causes [beings] to know and feel alarm and dread. The Bodhisattva views desire as one would avoid a pit of fire;
by presenting the effect to reveal the cause, he causes them to know how to fear and avoid it. The intended meaning is that the effect is ultimately non-existent...
Others still feel weary even at the mere mention of its name; having ascended to the stage of a sage, they still avoid its harmful poison—namely, desire.
How much less, then, can a beginner draw near to it? The following cases are all to be understood in this manner.
Second, the habitual tendencies of greed interact through calculation, arising from mutual attraction... (up to) the Bodhisattva views greed as one would avoid a sea of miasma.
[Commentary: This provides a detailed clarification of the causes and effects of the habitual tendencies of greed. "Greed" refers to absorbing and taking; "calculation" refers to attachment.
Because one clings to the body and wealth as being "mine," greed arises. "Sucking" refers to grasping at all things; this greedy suction belongs to the element of water.
When one sucks incessantly, it becomes increasingly solidified and congeals like water turning to ice; this is created by one's own mind.
Thus, the signs of the hell have already appeared within it. Therefore it is said: "Accumulated cold and hard ice freeze and chill within. Suppose...
This is illustrated by analogy to allow one to know the reality of cause and effect. "Ling" means to encroach upon or seize.
In passages such as "the two habits encroach upon each other," because cause and effect correspond to one another, they give rise to the resultant characteristics of the *ṭaṭa* hell and so forth.
*Ṭaṭa*, *papa*, and *lala* are all sounds of enduring cold suffering. The blue, red, and white lotuses are all colors of solid ice. "Greed-water" refers to...
The "Thirsty Spring" (Tanquan) mentioned here is a spring that causes the mind of whoever drinks from it to be inflamed with greed. "Miasma" (zhang) refers to a pestilential vapor;
upon contact, one immediately falls ill, or even dies. Since the sea has already drowned people, how much more so this pestilential vapor?
This is said to emphasize the severity of its harm, causing people to be startled and avoid it. The remaining meaning follows the previous pattern.
Third, the habitual tendencies of pride intermingle and assail one another, arising from mutual reliance. (Up to: "The Bodhisattva views pride as he would avoid a great drowning. [Commentary:
This provides a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habitual tendencies of pride. To rely on oneself and suppress others is called pride (*māna*).

"Assail" (*líng*) means to deceive and oppress. "Rely" (*shì*) means to depend upon; for example, relying on wealth and power, as well as fame and status, and so forth. One assails others by imitating such things. Therefore—
It is said that this arises from mutual reliance. "Chiliu" (galloping flow) means rushing against the current. Arrogance and reliance belong to the nature of water;

when habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are loftily elevated, they are like water flowing upstream. Therefore, it is said that "the galloping flow is unceasing. This is precisely what is created by one's own mind.

Because the signs have already manifested within the prison, there is leaping, fleeing, and rushing about. The accumulation of waves constitutes water. This is established as a metaphor for verification.
This is to cause [them] to know the reality of cause and effect. "Savoring" means that the tongue repeatedly presses against the palate.
"Churning" (gǔ) is like the wind churning objects; it conveys the sense of everything surging upward.

"The two habits churning against each other" and so forth refers to the fruit-phase of experiencing the river of blood and even being drenched and swallowed by molten copper, arising because the causes and effects correspond to one another. "The waters of delusion" [is located in the] west.
The earth contains water; drinking it causes one to become deluded, much like the "Greedy Spring" (Tan-quan) of this region.

"Seeing arrogance" means that arrogance arises from seeing within one's own mind, not that one sees another person being arrogant toward oneself. All subsequent cases should be understood accordingly. "Drowning" refers to deep places in the mud and water.
It is easy to fall into and difficult to extricate; thus, it is called "giant" (gū), which makes it even more fearsome.
Fourth, the habit of anger (*krodha-vāsanā*) manifests as mutual conflict when encountering opposition; [this continues until] the Bodhisattva views anger as one would avoid execution.
Commentary: This passage provides a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habit-energy of anger (*dveṣa*). To have one’s spirit surging and rebellious is called "anger.

"Mutual collision" refers to mutual conflict and confrontation. "To oppose" means to欺陵 (to deceive and insult). Because of this mutual deception and insult, [the resentment] becomes firmly rooted and does not cease;
because the spirit moves the mind, the heat of the mind becomes fire. Because the mind drums upon the spirit, the spirit is cast as metal. It accumulates.
When these are practiced for a long time, the fire of the mind grows ever more intense and the metal of the vital energy (prāṇa) becomes increasingly rigid. This is created by one's own mind;
thus, the signs [of retribution] have already manifested within the hells. Therefore, there are the "Sword Mountains" and "Iron Stakes," up to the "Spears" and "Saws.

These are established as metaphors to verify that cause and effect do not err. "Striking" means contact. "The two practices strike each other," and so forth, because of the mutual relationship between cause and effect.
This is because [the karmic] signs correspond to their causes. The "palace" (*gong*) refers to the severing of one's roots; "cutting" (*ge*) refers to the excision of one's nose;

"beheading and hacking" (*zhanzhe*) refers to the decapitation or the amputation of arms; "crushing" (*cuo*) refers to the pulverizing of one's bones; "piercing" (*ci*) refers to the carving away of one's flesh;
"beating with clubs" (*chuiji*) refers to whipping and flogging; and "sharp swords and blades" refers to the immediate loss of life upon contact.
Fifth, regarding the practice of deception and mutual seduction:

when it arises through such mutual provocation, the Bodhisattva views deception as one would fear a jackal or a wolf, for those who commit such acts will have their heads severed if they violate [the precepts].

**Commentary:** This passage provides a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habit of deceit. To speak with flattery and falsehood is called "deceit" (*zhà*). "To entice" (*jiāoyòu*) means to mutually delude one another.
"To cajole" (*tiáo*) means to toy with others using flattering words. "To lure" (*yǐn*) means to draw others in through deceptive conduct.
Those who are "subjected to such cajoling and luring" are like those caught by ropes and snares; they are bound, constrained, and shackled, unable to escape.
One can escape [from this]. If one dwells therein for a long time without ceasing, then that which is created by one's own mind—the causal signs—will already have manifested within the prison.
Thus, there are ropes, wood, shackles, and collars; a "jiao" (校) is a yoke.

By using flattery and deception to entice people, one must gradually soak them in these conditions over a long period before causing them to willingly accept their bondage and be unwilling to cast it off. Therefore, it is likened to water.
When fields are flooded, grasses and trees grow; their causes flourish and their fruits spread like creeping vines—it is just the same with this. "Extending" (*yan*) means to draw out and lengthen.

The mutual extension of the two habits and so forth occurs because cause and effect are of one suchness (*yīrú*). Thus, one experiences the fruit of shackles, fetters, and even the blows of clubs and staves.
Because one uses slanderous words to injure upright persons, they are called "slanderous thieves. They are as cruel and fierce as jackals and wolves.
Such things are therefore to be feared and avoided.
Sixth, the habit of deception leads to mutual fraud arising from one another’s delusion; (until) when a Bodhisattva encounters deception, they view it as treading upon a venomous snake or viper.

Commentary and Sub-commentary: This passage provides a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habit-energy of deception (*māyā*). To dazzle others with words is called "deception" (*śāṭhya*);

it refers to mutual cheating where both parties remain in a state of ignorance and delusion. To "mislead" (*vañcana*) means to deceive someone by making them believe they do not know or see something, thereby mocking them. To "falsify" (*abhyākhyāna*) means...
To speak of the void as real is to point to non-existence while claiming it exists. When such habitual practice has persisted for a long time, the mind becomes flighty and its wisdom grows dim;
thus, one commits wicked and evil deeds, appearing and disappearing like a spirit or a ghost, causing others to fall into their schemes without even realizing it.
This is created by one's own mind, and because the signs have already manifested within the prison, there is dust and soil.
Excrement, urine, filth, and impurities deceive and delude people, just as a fierce wind stirs up dust so that others cannot see it.

Examining their causes and effects, it should be understood that they are likewise so. When the two habits reinforce one another, because cause and effect correspond, they result in the karmic manifestations of drowning and even drifting away. For through deception, one is able to bring harm and ruin upon others.
Therefore, because deception can incite and stir people, one receives the retribution of being submerged and drowned;

because deception can suppress and elevate people, one receives the retribution of being tossed upward and cast down; and because of it, one encounters the retribution of flying, falling, drifting, and sinking.
As for those who murder by robbery, they will inevitably harm the Dharma-body; as for snakes and vipers, they will inevitably injure both feet upon being stepped upon.
Seventh, the habit-energy of resentment manifests as mutual hatred arising from harbored bitterness. (Up to: "The Bodhisattva views an enemy as if drinking poisoned wine. [Crown Note:
This provides a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habit-energy of resentment. To harbor a hidden grudge is called "resentment" (*yuan*).

"Mutual hatred" means that both parties loathe one another. "Harboring" (*xian*) means to contain or store within. Because of containing this heart of bitterness, it immediately manifests its causal characteristics within the hells.
Therefore, there are accounts of flying stones, even down to the matter of the "sack-slaying" (*nang-pu*). To "throw" means that it falls immediately. *Lè* is also a stone.
To "store in a casket" refers to a casket-bier. A "carriage cage" is a prison cart. To "fill a jar" refers to things such as the *zhong-zhi* (bell-roasting) vessel.
"Sack-slaying" means to store someone in a sack and then strike them to death; this is like the First Emperor’s sack-slaying of his two younger brothers. These are established metaphors.
The verification of cause and effect is thus. "Swallowing" means devouring; it further reveals their resentment.

In the phrase "the two habits swallow one another," etc., because cause and effect correspond to one another, they evoke the resultant characteristics of being thrown, cast down, or even seized and tossed.
The *Vighāsa* ghost refers to one who violates correct principle and harms people in the darkness; it is the most evil among ghosts.
The *Candra-haṃsa* bird is the most venomous; its feathers and plumage drip with poison, causing the intestines to break into pieces.

Eighth, the mutual illumination of the habit-energies of views is like the *satkāya-dṛṣṭi* (view of a self-entity), [extending] to the pervasive grasping at what is false, as if facing a precipice of poison.

*Commentary:* This provides a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habit-energies of views. "View" refers to wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*). "Mutual illumination" refers to the mutual deluded discrimination between self and other.
There are five types of habit-energies of views: first, *satkāya*, here translated as the "view of a self-entity," which refers to the attachment to the body.
1. Various attachments to a self (*ātman*). 2. The two extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), which grasp at phenomena as either annihilated or eternal. 3.

Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which is erroneous speech and misunderstanding that denies cause and effect. 4. Adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which regards what is not a fruit as a fruit, such as taking the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) to be *nirvāṇa*.
5. Adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which regards what is not a cause as a cause, such as observing the precepts of cattle or dogs.
These categories, which serve as causes for rebirth in the heavens and so forth, are collectively termed "false views.

Because they accord with what is perverse and oppose what is correct, it is said that they "arise from rejection. Because they involve mutual right and wrong, it is said that they "give rise to opposites.

Since these are created by one's own mind, their causal characteristics manifest within the hells; thus, there are kings, messengers, and chief clerks who consult legal documents and registers to adjudicate them.

Regarding the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, I shall employ metaphors to test them, so that they may understand that cause and effect are substantively linked and there is no way to evade them.
"Interacting" means that the two habits interact with one another; because cause and effect correspond, there arise the resultant phenomena of interrogation, guile, documents, and verbal sophistry.
"Expedient transformation" refers to using clever techniques to elicit truthful testimony.
Furthermore, "interrogating" means to investigate and examine minutely in order to determine what is erroneous and what is correct.

"Inquiring and scrutinizing" means to investigate thoroughly and probe exhaustively to analyze the situation fully. "Illuminating" means to use the mirror of karma to illuminate everything, so that nothing may be concealed.
These five types of wrong views can undermine the Dharma-body; therefore, they are called "pits of views," for they lead people to suffering.
Because it is like the ocean; it is likened to a ravine of poison.
Ninth, the habit of injustice intermingles and gives rise to slander (up to): when a Bodhisattva encounters injustice, it is as if they were struck by a bolt of lightning.
Commentary: This explains in detail the causes and effects of the habit-energy of injustice.
"Injustice" means taking what is straight and making it crooked. "Mutual entanglement" means that both parties inflict offenses upon one another.
"Slander" means heaping baseless calamities upon others solely to satisfy one's own desires, regardless of the oppression inflicted upon the minds and bodies of others. Furthermore—
This is the characteristic of the cause. Because it manifests within the hells, there are such things as the "conjoining mountains" (*saṃghāta-parvata*) and so forth.

As for the "conjoining mountains," two mountains close together, leaving no place for people to escape. "Conjoining rocks" refers to being pinched between two stones. "Grinding mills" refers to the class of pestles and stone grinders.
By means of these, the wicked prisoner inevitably brings about evil retribution; this serves as a metaphor for slanderous and treacherous persons who are certain [to suffer such consequences].
To oppress and wrong the virtuous and good. "To push aside" (pai) means to crowd out or suppress. "The two habits push against each other," and so forth;

because cause and effect do not err, they result in the karmic manifestations of being pressed down, weighed, and measured. "Pressed down" (ya na) means to subdue by pressure. "Beaten and pressed" (chui an) means to strike and pummel.
"Cramped and squeezed" (cu lu) means to wring out until blood flows. "Weigh" (heng) refers to a scale; "measure" (du) refers to a balance.
It is a measure; that is to say, weighing their lightness or heaviness and measuring their length or shortness in order to administer punishment.
It is also called a "balance-measure" (*hengdu*) because one measures the body through a narrow aperture, like the manner of pulling out a thread.
Because slander can injure people, it is named the "slanderous tiger. Because it can cause terror, it is named "thunderbolt" (*pili*).
Tenth: The habit of litigation, arising from concealment, leads to mutual clamor; (extending) up to "like bearing a high mountain while treading upon a vast ocean.
[Crown and Annotation: This provides a detailed explanation of the causes and effects of the habit of litigation. One conceals one's own shortcomings and exposes the secrets of others.

This is called "litigation. To "speak with one another" means that both parties dispute with each other. Because they expose the hidden faults and private secrets of others, it is said that these emerge from what has been concealed.
Since such causal conduct exists within one's own mind, its manifestations appear within the prison; therefore, it is said there is a "mirror that reflects and illuminates.
This mirror and the like refer to the so-called "Mirror of Karma" (karmādarśa) before the throne, where all hidden and private matters are fully revealed. There is no... [omission].
It is like being covered by a veil. Just as when one attacks the faults of another, others will likewise attack one's own faults.
With such a cause, there must inevitably be such a result. It is comparable to standing in the midst of the sun; one can certainly not conceal one's shadow. "Chen" (陳) means to present or offer.
In phrases such as "the two habits are presented to each other," it is because the evil cause and the evil result correspond to one another.
This refers to being moved by the karma-mirror and fire-jewel of evil companions, leading even to the verification of the causal signs of various matters.
"Hidden thieves" (yin-zei) harm others in secret while concealing their own transgressions; once they are exposed, they only bring ruin upon themselves.
"Wearing mountains and treading upon the sea" is a metaphor for how the more one conceals, the deeper the concealment becomes, and thus the harm becomes increasingly grave.
"What are the six retributions? Ānanda, for all sentient beings (up to) the evil retributions they attract, these emerge from the six sense faculties.
*Annotation:* This section provides a general explanation of the "mutual retributions" (*jiaobao*). There are two types of mutual retribution: first, the intersection of cause and effect.
At the stage of the second fruit, the six sense organs mutually receive retribution; this is consistent with the previous twelve inversions, where citing one encompasses the whole.

It is also similar in principle to the previous "returning to the source through a single organ" and the "liberation of the six organs," though the phenomena appear contrary while the underlying principle remains the same.

Regarding the six consciousnesses performing karma: because consciousness possesses the capacity for discernment (*vijñapti*), it is able to produce karmic retribution. Regarding their emergence from the six sense organs (*indriya*):
although the organs themselves lack discernment, they can nonetheless give rise to consciousness; thus, retribution also emerges from the organs.

Nevertheless, the six consciousnesses are the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the karmic consciousness, while the six organs are the image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the karmic consciousness. In total, they are all the karmic consciousness itself acting upon itself.
This refers to self-retribution. It shares the same intent as the previous examination of the root of karma, which asks: "Who acts and who receives?
How is it that evil retribution issues from the six sense organs (up to: like sparks flying and scattering, fanning and stirring the realm of space)?
Commentary: This provides a detailed explanation of the retributive responses of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). "How so? below serves as a general inquiry into the six types of retribution.

"The first" below refers to the fact that because the karma created by the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) together with the concomitant mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) was predominantly excessive, it draws forth evil fruits that emerge from the eye-faculty and intersect with this visual karma.
Below, the vision of the evil realms encountered at the moment of death is shown.
Consciousness belongs to the element of fire. Because the power of karma is also predominant, it brings about a fierce fire that fills the worlds of the ten directions;

the spiritual consciousness then rides upon the smoke and falls into hell. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "For those of extreme goodness or extreme evil, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Therefore, they enter directly into the six retributions. All say they "enter directly"; this is merely a way of speaking based on their gravity. Hereafter, all cases shall follow this principle to clarify the two characteristics.

This refers to the initial vision encountered at the moment of entering hell. It is fundamentally no different from the visions of light and darkness experienced during one's previous life when the senses ran wild and pursued external forms.
Thus, when there is light, one sees various malevolent objects and gives rise to immeasurable dread;

when it is dark, all is silent and nothing is seen, and one gives rise to immeasurable terror. This is because dread arises from the objective realm, while terror arises from the mind. Thus it continues below.

To explain in detail the mutual correspondence of retribution: when karma is created within the causal stage, although the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) acts as the primary agent, all the other consciousnesses necessarily assist it.

For example, when the eye perceives a beautiful form, the ear grasps licentious sounds, and so on until the body experiences licentious touch, with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) presiding over craving and attachment—all these are present simultaneously in a single kṣaṇa.
Thus, it is entirely appropriate that there should be mutual retribution within the resultant stage.
However, regarding the characteristics of the fruits as clarified in the sūtras, they arise solely through the transformations of the fundamental natures.

If one were to forcibly correlate them with the preceding causes, it would ultimately be difficult to enumerate them exhaustively, serving only to increase unnecessary complexity. Hereafter, all cases shall follow this pattern. The nature of hearing belongs to water;

because it is scorched by the fire of seeing, it becomes the boiling cauldrons and molten copper. The nature of smelling, which primarily consists of air, also belongs to earth; because it is scorched by... [seeing].
Because it is burned by fire, it becomes black smoke and purple flames. The nature of the tongue belongs to metal; it also presides over the five flavors.
Because it is burned by the fire of [wrong] views, it becomes scorched balls and molten iron dross. The body possesses the five elements and also presides over touch; in terms of earth and wood—
Because it is being burned, it becomes hot ashes, stoves, and charcoal. The mind is the master of the five elements; its true nature belongs to fire.
Because it is burned and grows ever more intense, it becomes sparks that scatter and fly about, fanning and stirring the realm of space.
Second, hearing reports that summon and attract evil retributions (up to) being struck by lightning or hail that shatters one’s heart and soul.
[Commentary: This is a specific explanation of the mutual retribution of the ear faculty.

It means that because the karma created by the ear-consciousness and its associated mental consciousness is particularly abundant, it summons and attracts evil retributions that emerge from the ear faculty and intersect with this karmic activity of hearing.

The following shows the realm perceived at the time of death. Since the nature of hearing belongs to water and karmic force is likewise powerful, at the moment of death, one first sees waves and surges that submerge heaven and earth;
then the spiritual consciousness descends and flows along with the current, falling into hell.
The manifestation of these two signs refers to the realm heard at the very moment of first entering hell, which is fundamentally the same as [the experience] at birth.
Previously, as the flow rushed toward sounds, there was no difference between hearing movement and hearing stillness.

When the ears were opened, one heard movement—meaning that by nature one hears all manner of clamorous, noisy, and jarring sounds, which cause the spirit to become confused and disoriented, lacking a master. When the ears were closed...

"Hearing" refers to stillness; it means there is nothing at all to be heard, causing the dark spirits to sink into oblivion with no support. Below, the text details the mutual retribution of the faculties.

The nature of hearing belongs to water, hence it is called the "wave of hearing. Because the faculty can manifest sound, it serves as the locus for the indictment of offenses and the interrogation of circumstances.
When the fire of seeing and the water of hearing clash, it is like the mutual friction of yin and yang; therefore, it constitutes thunder.
It becomes roars and poisonous vapors. The nose belongs to earth; breath is qi (vital energy).
Because earth-qi transforms according to water, it becomes rain, mist, and various venomous insects that pervade the body. The nature of the tongue belongs to metal; dust possesses the five flavors.
Because the sense faculties and their objects change according to the water, they become pus, blood, and various impurities. The body is composed of the five elements;

since the element of touch possesses form and substance and changes according to the water, it becomes animals and ghosts. Since the earth element changes according to the water, it becomes feces and urine.

The mind is the master of the five elements; its true nature belongs to fire. Because water and fire interact and influence one another, it manifests as lightning and hail, which shatter the heart and soul.
Thirdly, through the retribution of smelling [noxious odors], it draws forth evil fruits, resulting in flying sand and gravel that strike and crush the body.
Commentary: This is a specific explanation of the retributive interaction involving the nose faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*).

It means that because the olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*) and the concomitant mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) have predominantly created karma, they attract and bring forth evil fruits that emerge from the nose faculty and interact with this karmic odor.
The following shows the foul objects encountered at the moment of death. The faculty of the nose belongs to the earth element and likewise possesses inhalation and exhalation;

when inhaling, it enters downward, and when exhaling, it issues upward. Because the power of karma is also predominant, at the time of death, one first sees poisonous vapors filling the near and far surroundings.
Then, the consciousness emerges from the earth and, having ascended, falls back down into hell. It arises.

To clarify the two characteristics: when first entering the prison, it is no different from the state of sensory wandering and flight experienced before birth—whether the sense of smell is open or obstructed.
"Open smelling" refers to the nose having something to scent; being permeated by foul and evil vapors, they intensely afflict the olfactory faculty, causing the mind to become agitated.
"Obstructed smelling" refers to the faculty having nothing to scent, such that the vapors merely press against it.
