It does not pass through; one faints upon the ground, knowing nothing at all. "Below" refers to the detailed account of the mutual retribution of the physical obstruction and the passage.

"Obstruction" (*zài*) means being blocked; "passage" (*tōng*) means moving freely. Because the nature of smelling is not separate from passage and obstruction, when the breath is stifled, it becomes an obstruction and cannot move;
when it is unobstructed, it can move. Because the vital energy (*qi*) transforms according to fire, it becomes a torch; because the vital energy transforms according to water... [it becomes mist].

Therefore, they become submerged or boiled in scalding water; as the objects of taste all change according to the air, they turn into putrid fish or spoiled soup, which is why it is said they become "starved" or "corrupted.

Since the body possesses the five elements, it is all steamed and ruined by the air, becoming things such as tattered, torn, and rotting objects, and thus encounters immeasurable devouring. The mind presides over the five elements, and its nature likewise belongs [to them].
Because fire interacts with wind, fire, earth, and dust, it becomes ash, dust, and miasmic vapors, as well as flying sand and gravel that strike and shatter the body.
Fourth, the retribution for the sense-object of taste invites evil fruits (extending to): flying red-hot iron raining down from the sky.
Commentary: This is a specific explanation of the retributive response involving the tongue faculty.

It means that because the tongue-consciousness and the concomitant mental consciousness have predominantly created karma, they attract and draw forth evil fruits. These emerge from the tongue faculty and intersect with this karma of flavors.
"Flavor" (rasa) means tasting. The following indicates the realm perceived at the moment of death. The nature of the tongue belongs to metal.
Furthermore, because one greedily craves flavors, one sets nets and burns the wilds to seize living beings for the sake of nourishing one's own mouth and belly;

therefore, at the time of death, one first sees iron nets with fierce, blazing flames covering the entire world, through which the consciousness passes downward, caught in the net and hanging upside down.
Their heads fall into hell. As for the manifestation of the two signs, this is the realm perceived at the moment of first entering hell;
it is no different from the objects experienced while one was previously flowing toward and rushing after flavors, swallowing and inhaling their essences. Thus, they inhale. From...
As for those who enter from the outside, because they are inevitably cold, they congeal into freezing ice that splits the flesh of the body and causes one to gasp as breath issues from within.
As for those who emerge from within, because they are inevitably hot, they fly forth as fierce fires that char and rot the marrow and bones. Furthermore, regarding the detailed mutual retribution:

those who have devoured living beings with their tongues or slandered the virtuous are all made to endure these sounds and accept them; by experiencing them through successive trials, one is able to become a vessel [of endurance].
Enduring suffering is also like this. Because one relies on the craving for the taste of sensory objects, it is as if gold and fire are ignited together;

thus, they can burn metal and stone. Because one relies on hearing to produce evil, the lips become spears and the tongue becomes swords; this is also because gold and water grind against each other, enabling them to form sharp weapons.
Because one relies on smelling to indulge in flavors, one ensnares the multitude of living beings; this is also because gold changes according to the air, just as [the senses follow their objects].
Fire smelts gold; thus it can form great iron cages that cover the entire land.

To crave flavors and thereby harm living beings is likewise gold obtaining wood to become bows, arrows, and crossbows for shooting. To contemplate flavors and thereby injure living beings is likewise gold being melted by fire.
Therefore, they become glowing red-hot iron, falling from the sky.
Fifth, as a retribution for their contact with others, they attract evil fruits: they are made to fall, to fly, to be boiled, and to be roasted.
Commentary: This is a specific explanation of the reciprocal retribution of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).

It states that because the karma created by the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) together was predominantly excessive, it draws forth an evil fruit that emerges from the body-faculty and intersects with this karma of touch (*spraṣṭavya-karma*).

The following shows the evil realms seen at the time of death. As for this particular faculty, the reason why its perceived signs are so exceptionally evil and numerous is that the body possesses the five elements;

furthermore, due to the defilement of craving for male and female touch, as well as matters such as the service of large households, guarding, driving, and being whipped or beaten, one commits every transgression—lust, killing, stealing, and lying—without exception. Thus, accumulated sins are as vast as a mountain. For this reason...
At the time of death, one sees a great mountain approaching from all four sides, closing in until there is no further way out.
Furthermore, the consciousness perceives an iron city with fire-snakes, and even the hell-wardens and rākṣasas holding spears and lances, who drive one into hell.
These two manifestations that appear are the initial sights encountered upon entering hell; they are also consistent with the [experiences] of one's previous life.

They rush forward in flight, colliding with one another; because there is no distinction between union and separation, or grasping and attachment, contact through union causes them to encounter mountains that press against their bodies, shattering their bones, flesh, and blood.
Contact through separation causes them to encounter swords and blades touching their bodies, carving and tearing their hearts and livers.

"Below" refers to the detailed explanation of mutual retribution; "path" refers to the road leading to hell; "gates" refers to the two towers at the gate of the King of Hell; and "hearing the cases" refers to the adjudication of crimes.
All these locations are the bases upon which the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) relies. Because two fires intersect and flare up, there is burning and scorching.

Because water and fire interact, there is clashing, striking, and piercing—“piercing” (*tsi*) meaning the insertion of a blade into the flesh. The “enclosing bag” (*kuāidài*) is that which collects the vital energies (*vāyu*).
When earth and water obstruct and block [the channels], they cause the energies to become impassable. As for “torture and binding,” it means not allowing the body-faculty any movement or shaking.
This is of one intent with the "bound sack" (guōdài). Because gold is cast by fire, it serves as an instrument for plowing, tongs, and cutting. One's thoughts thus become drifting and unsettled;
this is also because two fires blaze together, and thus one experiences the realm of flying and falling, and being seared and roasted.
Sixth, the contemplation of retribution that invites evil fruits (up to) all being created by the delusions and false conceptions of sentient beings.
These ten causes and six retributions discussed above are all treated within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) as the causality of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Thus, they have not yet transcended the mundane realm. As for physical principles, life is yang and death is yin; this is what is meant by "not yet having departed from the three [realms]."

That which exists outside the realms still remains within the five elements; therefore, the objects transformed by the faculties and natures are all explained according to yin-yang and the five elements.
Yet, when tracing back to the source and exhausting the root, nothing transcends one's own mind.

Not only the causes and effects of sentient beings, but even the transformation and retribution bodies of the Buddhas are all images manifested by one's own mind; how much more so, then, for yin-yang and the five...

These are still the two divisions of the perceived and perceiving aspects (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*) of the *karmic-consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*). Furthermore, how could they exist externally apart from one's own mind?

Moreover, although cause and effect and karmic retribution are said to be coarse and superficial teachings, they are nonetheless the inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation within the *karmic-consciousness*.
Neither the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) nor the perfection of the five eyes can fathom them.
Regarding the source and its course: it is said that the vast Three Piṭakas are inexhaustible; their depths are profound, with the seven waves stirred by the wind of objective conditions.
How could those of worldly wisdom and fleshly eyes dare to treat this with contempt?
Commentary: This is a separate explanation of the retribution associated with the mental faculty (*manas*).

It states that because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) serves as the basis for the first five consciousnesses and has predominantly created karma, it draws forth and invites evil fruits. These emerge from the mental faculty and intersect with this karma of volition (*cetanā*).
Below, the evil realms seen at the moment of death are shown; volition is the master of the five elements and is moreover volatile.
The *Dang* [Hell] is so named because it also involves the thought that what is fundamentally formless can destroy things that possess form.
At the time of death, one first sees an evil wind blowing away and destroying the land; the consciousness is then blown by the wind up into the air, only to fall back down from the sky.
Driven by the wind, they fall and enter hell. The manifestation of these two signs is the first scene encountered upon entering the prison;

it is no different from the state of drifting and rushing toward phenomena during one's life, characterized by distraction, dullness, and mental fog. Thus, they remain unaware until their delusion reaches its ultimate point.
Thus, one does not know the primary path; one merely runs about in frantic haste without rest.

If one does not lose awareness, one will undergo immeasurable, unbearable suffering of scorching heat. To explain the retribution in detail: although thought has no fixed location, it must have an object upon which it dwells.
When thought is bound to that object, it constitutes the commission of an offense; the fire seen in the place before one is able to cast this very thought.
Because of gold, it acts as a mirror to illuminate the deeds of sinful persons.
Because water and earth congeal together, it can become great rocks, ice, and frost, as well as upper mists capable of moving about.

Because it transforms according to fire, it can become fiery chariots, fiery ships, and fiery cages. Because it seeks to obtain a tongue and produces speech, it can manifest as wailing, lamentation, and weeping. The body...

They possess the five elements, all of which transform according to thought and likewise lack a fixed substance; thus they can manifest forms large and small, as well as the affairs of birth and death, reclining and rising.
Below, Ānanda, the conclusion provides the answer: these ten causes and six retributions are all manifestations of deluded karma arising from one’s own true mind;
fundamentally, they do not truly exist. If one can realize that these delusions have no cause, one will immediately abide [in the truth].
In the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), arising and ceasing are like illusions; how much more so, then, the hells?
If all sentient beings collectively create evil karma (up to the point that) deluded thoughts arise and do not exist from the beginning, [how could the hells exist?]

Commentary: This clarifies the relative gravity of causes and effects. The meaning is that although these are created through delusion and ignorance, they nonetheless vary in degree, being either heavy or light.
Regarding those who "jointly create evil karma," this refers to those who possess the six faculties and ten causes in their entirety, creating [karma] together at all times;
because what they induce is extremely grave, they enter the Great Avīci Hell to undergo suffering.

"Immeasurable" means that even throughout kalpas, they are likewise immeasurable. "Each of the six sense organs creates [its own karma]" means that although all ten causes are present, they are created at different times, one after another;

therefore, it is said they act "individually. As for "that which is produced by them, involving both objects and sense organs," it refers to the combined operation of the sense organs and their respective objects.
This refers to cases where one commits this offense by engaging both a single faculty and a single object, up to three faculties and three objects;

because these are more serious than the former, one enters the Eight Uninterrupted Hells (*aṣṭāv avīcayaḥ*). If one engages only in killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through the three doors of body, speech, and mind, without committing the other offenses, it is slightly lighter than the former and thus one enters the eighteen hells. The *Niraya Sūtra* states: "There are eight fire hells."

There are ten cold hells; these are they. Regarding those whose three types of karma are not complete: this refers to those who possess both bodily and verbal actions yet commit killing and stealing, but lack [the intent for] sexual misconduct;
or those who possess both bodily and mental actions yet commit killing and sexual misconduct, but lack [the action of] stealing.

Or, one may possess both speech and mind yet commit theft and sexual misconduct, lacking only physical [killing] and [harming]. This is again slightly lighter than the former, and thus one enters the thirty-six hells.
"Seeing each with a single faculty" means that among the six faculties, one commits an offense against only one faculty and its corresponding object, while the other five remain unoffended.
"Committing a single action" means that among the three types of karma, one commits only one type of karma.
The other two cases do not constitute an offense; this is because they are lighter than the preceding ones. Consequently, one enters the one hundred and eight hells.

From here below, the conclusion resolves the doubts and questions. Because Ānanda previously doubted whether there is a fixed location or whether each receives [the retribution] privately—this refers to acting and creating separately—the answer is that it is received privately.
This means entering a common ground (*sabhāga-bhūmi*). The answer is that there is indeed a fixed location.

This generally explains that individual karmic actions result in collective retribution. Regarding the previous doubt as to whether [these actions] exist inherently from the beginning or arise from deluded habituation, this response states that they are produced by false conceptualization and do not exist originally.
Furthermore, Ānanda, these sentient beings (up to) are then wondrously perfect and luminous, fundamentally having nothing at all. [Commentary:
This clarifies that only after the retribution for hellish offenses is exhausted does one enter the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). It is not that they do not exist.

Those who violate the *vinaya* discipline refer to those who transgress the precepts of the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, who do not believe in sin or merit, and who cause themselves and others to fall. Those who violate bodhi...
"Transgressing the bodhisattva precepts" refers to the subtle violation of the Mahāyāna precepts. "Destroying the Buddha’s nirvāṇa" refers to slandering the Buddha and slandering the Dharma.
Vinaya is the root from which sentient beings emerge from suffering; the bodhisattva precepts are the direct cause for sentient beings to attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha is the compassionate father of both the mundane and supramundane realms, and nirvāṇa is the unsurpassed, wondrous principle. If...
If these three are entirely absent, then the lineage of the Triple Gem is severed and extinguished;
this very land will be destroyed by hell, and one will further enter the hells of the ten directions with no time of escape for eternity. Therefore it is said:

if these three are lacking and one commits only miscellaneous karmas such as the ten causes, then even though one enters the hells and is scorched through kalpas, there will still come a time when the retribution for those sins is exhausted.

This refers to those who, having escaped the retribution of hell, receive the form of a hungry ghost (*preta*). The following provides a detailed explanation of the realm of ghosts. Regarding "craving objects":
this is the residual habituation resulting from the intensification of the habit of greed. Having completed their punishment in hell, they still remain attached to material things;

like spirits that rely upon gold and jade or cling to grasses and trees to become malevolent apparitions, it is said that they "become strange ghosts upon encountering objects. Regarding "craving form": this refers to lust.
Because of the residual habits from their former practice of sexual intercourse, when their punishments in hell have ended, their lustful passions still flow;

since the fire element remains thus, they take form by attaching to the wind and become the ghosts of drought-demons (*hánbié*). Their greed and delusion constitute the deceptive practices used for seduction.

It is solely because they use clever means to delude people and cause them to lose their natural vitality that, when their retribution for sins is exhausted, their residual habits cause them to take form by attaching themselves to animals, becoming *mei*-ghosts;
those such as solitary spirits (*gu-jing*) are examples of this. As for "greed and resentment," these refer to those who harbor hatred through the habit of enmity;

thus, when their retribution is exhausted, their residual habits cause them to attach themselves to venomous insects, using them to inflict harm upon humans. This is why there exist sorcery arts today that cause the manifestation of *gu*-diseases.

All these are presided over by this lord of ghosts. "Greed and remembrance" refers to those whose habitual tendencies of anger clash with one another; they do not forget past evils and wait for a moment of decline to inflict harm.
When their retribution is exhausted, residual habits attach themselves to a state of decay to take form as *māra* ghosts, such as those who currently spread epidemics or cause malarial fevers.
"Greed and arrogance" refers to those whose habitual tendencies of pride mutually assail one another; they are stingy and devoid of virtue, yet falsely conceited.

Relying on their own spirit, they insulted others and treated all things with arrogance; therefore, when their retribution was complete, residual habits attached to their vital breath (*prāṇa*) to form their bodies, and they became hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Because of their greed and delusion—specifically the habit of deception and the act of cheating—they harbored their minds in dark obscurity, casting a spell of suppression over all things; thus, when their retribution was complete...

The residual habit-energy clings to the obscure darkness and becomes a *yāma* ghost (a nightmare-demon). It still dwells in dark rooms and causes people to be bewildered by nightmares; thus it craves light.
This is what is meant by "the habitual tendency of views intersecting with clarity": originally, this was false view, wherein one falsely fashioned oneself as lofty and wise.

When the retribution for this crime is exhausted, the residual habit-energy secretly clings to spiritual essences and becomes a *vālmīka* ghost (a goblin or sprite). It constantly dwells in profound obscurity, appearing as if present yet as if non-existent; thus it craves completion.

Having habituated oneself to the practice of wrongful slander, one distorted others to serve one’s own ends; thus, when the retribution for the crime is exhausted, residual habits attach to the luminous spirit (*ming*) to take form, becoming a servant to ghosts.
"Luminous" (*ming*) refers to the numinous spirit (*shenming*). Because one previously distorted others to serve oneself, one now relies upon a spirit temple and is driven by the deity;

this is the reversal of having distorted others to serve oneself. As for "greedy factions," this refers to those who, through the habit of litigation, engage in clamorous disputes and form cliques and alliances to provide testimony.
Because they expose the private secrets of others, their offenses are all [retribution]. Residual habits attach themselves to people to form shapes, becoming "transmitting ghosts" (*chuan-song gui*).

This is truly because, during their causal lives, they pricked others at their hidden vulnerabilities and transmitted such matters; thus, now as ghosts, they likewise attach themselves to shamans and priests to transmit omens of good and ill fortune.
[The passage] beginning with "Ānanda" concludes that delusion has no cause. The term "pure emotion" (*chun-qing*) refers to the heavy case, which encompasses the light.

The nine types of afflictions (*kleśa*) and eight types of emotions mentioned in the preceding text are all contained herein. As for "the fires of karma burning them dry": since emotion belongs to the element of water, once the retribution for emotional offenses has been fully experienced, it is said they are "burned dry.
This refers collectively to the fact that because the causes of their imprisonment and the resulting retribution are exhausted, they are reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
All of these are summoned by one's own deluded karma; within the wondrous, perfect mind, such things fundamentally do not exist.
That which is called the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and characteristics.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the karmic retribution of the hungry ghosts has been exhausted—[down to] "all are merely the congealing of empty, false imaginings. (Commentary:
This clarifies that once the retribution for the karma of the hungry ghosts is finished, one is reborn in the realm of animals. Regarding "sentimental thoughts are both empty":
this refers to the sentimental thoughts of the realms of humans, hell-beings, and hungry ghosts. As previously stated, those of pure sentiment fall into the Great Avīci Hell. 9.
With one thought and nine emotions, one falls into the Avīci Hell; with eight emotions and two thoughts, one falls into the hells with intervals;
and with seven emotions and three thoughts, one is born among the hungry ghosts—all these are scorched by the fires of karma.

Even when six emotions and four thoughts remain, one is born among the fur-bearing and winged species to repay the karmic debts owed to those from whom one was previously indebted. Below, the animal realm is explained in detail. Formerly, because of...

Through the habituation of greed, one becomes a *guàiguǐ* (strange ghost). When the object it possesses is consumed, the retribution of the ghost also ends. Following this habituation, one is born into the human world; for the most part, one becomes a species of *xiāo* (owls).

Those who are excessively greedy for wealth and property, to the point of severing all sense of righteousness, mostly bring about rebirth as this class of being. "For the most part" refers to those whose karmic habits are heavy;
it does not necessarily apply to all cases. Hereafter, all cases shall be understood in this manner. Due to the habituation of lust, one becomes a *póguǐ* (drought-demon). When...
When the wind that carried them dissipates, the retribution for the ghosts also ends. To be born [as such] is an omen of calamity;

an omen of calamity is a precursor to misfortune, such as the flying squirrel calling out to people or the *shangyang* bird dancing upon the water—these are also remnants of the habitual behavior of the drought-demon *hanba*.

Due to the habitual practice of deception, one becomes a possessing ghost (*bhūta*). When the animal it possesses dies, the retribution of the ghost also ends, and one is reborn among the species of foxes;
these are all remnants of the habit of bewitching others with charms. Due to the habitual practice of resentment, one becomes a poisonous ghost.

When the insect it possesses perishes, the retribution of the ghost also ends, and one is reborn among poisonous species such as snakes, vipers, *vṛścika* scorpions, and the like; these are all remnants of the habit of secret malice. Due to anger...

Through habitual practice, one becomes a *lēi* ghost; that which it clings to decays and perishes, and the retribution of the ghost likewise ends. Such beings are mostly reborn as types of worms that dwell within humans and consume their food;
this is also the residual habit of clinging to others, as in the case of malaria. Due to the habitual practice of arrogance, one becomes a hungry ghost (*preta*);

that which it clings to withers away, and the retribution of the ghost likewise ends. Such beings are mostly reborn as types of food; those who were formerly haughty, stingy, and relied upon their own vital energy now serve as the sustenance for humans.
Hunger and emptiness—this is what is called retribution. Due to the habit of deception, one becomes a *yàn-guǐ* (suffocating ghost).

When the obsession ends and the karmic retribution of the ghost is exhausted, one becomes a type of soil creature; constantly emerging from the darkness to deceive and suffocate people, now one becomes a silkworm, a cow, or a horse, serving as clothing or a mount for humans—this too is retribution.
Due to the habit of false views, one becomes a *wǎngliǎng-guǐ* (phantom ghost).

When their refined merit is exhausted and their retribution comes to an end, they will become beings corresponding to their many past lives, arriving like swallows in spring or wild geese in autumn according to the seasons;
this is also the lingering habit of craving light. Clinging to light through the habit of servitude, they become ghosts employed for service.

When that light is extinguished and their retribution ends, they will become beings corresponding to the auspicious signs of many past lives, such as the magnificent phoenix or the auspicious qilin; these too were once dependent on the divine spirit to act as its attendants. Thus it is curved.
These are the residual habits remaining from having been human. Because of the habit of litigation, they become ghosts who transmit messages;

their reliance on shamans perishes, and the retribution of the ghosts is likewise exhausted. They are mostly reborn as animals of similar kind, such as cats and dogs, which are also residual habits of sycophancy and compliance with humans.
Below, Ānanda, the three miserable realms are summarized: all are summoned and drawn forth by one's own deluded karma. If one awakens to this clarity...
"Bodhi" means that there is nothing at all. "As you have said below" refers back to the previous question:
regarding those who fall into hell due to such evil karma—this uses the evil karma of three people as an illustration to encompass all evil karma.
"Originally self-manifested" means that the aforementioned evil causes and evil effects are all one's own *tathāgatagarbha*.
Within, they manifest according to karma. This is truly because the nature is luminous and perfect, and thus nothing is lacking;
it is simply that according to whatever kind of karma one follows, a corresponding retribution manifests. It does not descend from heaven nor emerge from the earth, nor is it bestowed by others;

it is fundamentally one's own created deluded karma and one's own received deluded retribution. If one observes this with mirror-like wisdom, all are seen to be floating and empty, originally [non-existent].
They have no substantial reality. Although there are the three miserable realms, they are all formed by the condensation of one's own deluded thoughts, just as water turns into ice.
Furthermore, Ānanda, from these animals [until] the appearance of a Buddha in the world, [suffering] cannot be brought to rest.
Commentary: This passage generally clarifies that when the retribution of the animal realm is exhausted, one returns again to the human realm.

Although those who were ghosts as animals possessed the six sense-faculties and four types of perception, it was fundamentally for the purpose of repaying past debts. Once the debt has been fully repaid...

Thus, the two are entirely unrelated. Should the compensation exceed what is rightfully due, or should they be driven with harsh whips and fed without moderation, then these animals will attain a state where their emotions and thoughts are balanced, and they will be reborn among humans.
Yet, one would instead demand the "excess" from them; "demanding the excess" means seeking back that which was taken beyond the proper measure. If they are thus over-exacted—
Such a person, whose power of pure karma is superior, is able to maintain a human body.
If they further possess the merit of giving and other virtues, they will settle their karmic retributions among humans by encountering such things as theft, robbery, or being cheated and deceived.
However, if they lack pure karma and are devoid of merit, they have no power to maintain a human body; consequently, they will again be reborn in the animal realm to undergo retribution.
This refers to the remaining debt owed by those animals. The following clarifies that debts for goods are easy to repay, whereas debts for life are difficult to repay.
As for the statement that "this person repays the surplus value," it means that if the original amount was over-collected, it is used to purchase items for their sale.
They still sell their money to repay it; they still employ their strength to carry heavy loads over long distances to repay it.
Once the repayment is complete, they stop of their own accord, and there is forever no further entanglement.

Suppose, however, that one not only uses up their money and strength, but furthermore kills them therein and eats their flesh—then life after life, age after age, they would devour one another in succession, like a well.
The cycle turns like a wheel, with one being high and the other low in endless succession.

Unless one rectifies oneself through right concentration, transforming the heavy into the light, or seeks the Buddhas' appearance in the world to cast oneself before them for repentance and purification, it will be eternally difficult to clear this karmic enmity.
Thus, the World-Honored One’s compassionate heart speaks with bitter urgency; one should take these words as a warning and must not indulge one's desires in killing and eating.
"You should now know that those of the owl species... (up to)... this class is called 'the pitiable. [Commentary:
This explains in detail how beings of the animal realm exhaust their retribution and are reborn as humans. Having the habit of greed as their nature, they are owls;
yet, while possessing human form, they remain stubborn and dull-witted, unable to discern the principles of human relations and refusing to receive instruction."
This is caused by residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). As for those who are "intermingled" (*saṃmiśra*), they are mixed among them;
they are not necessarily foolish or evil, nor are they all transformed from owls (*kāka*). Hereafter, all cases shall follow this pattern.

Those whose sexual habits result in *pūtanā* ghosts and manifest as portents of calamity, and who are subsequently reborn among humans with abnormal physical traits that do not harmonize with natural principles, are those who bring harm through their licentiousness.
These are residual habits (*vāsanā*). Those with the habit of deceit become *māra* spirits or foxes;

when reborn among humans, they are mixed with the base and mediocre, those who toil wearily at their livelihoods—this is the residual habit of flattery and seeking favor in the world. Those with the habit of resentment become *gū* (sorcery) spirits or poisonous creatures;
when reborn among humans, they are mixed with the wolf-like, utterly lacking in benevolence—this is the residual habit of harboring grievances and secret malice.
The habit-energy of anger results in being a leper or a parasite worm; yet, returning to human form, one is born into a lowly and mixed station.

Though one may associate closely with others, people pay no heed to them—this is the residual habit of clinging to decayed things. The habit-energy of pride results in being a hungry ghost or a scavenger;
yet, returning to birth among humans, one is of a mixed disposition of gentleness and timidity, unable to be courageous, and prone to dejection and incapacity.
To rely on one's own spirit and treat others with arrogance is the retribution for such conduct. The habit of deception becomes a nightmare or a domestic animal;
only upon returning to human form does one join the class of laborers, toiling incessantly in the world without rest—this is the retribution for being driven as a mount or a beast of burden.

The habit of false views becomes a *wangliang* (a type of malevolent spirit) or a responsive apparition; when reborn among humans, one joins the class of artists and craftsmen, gradually attaining proficiency.
Regarding the meaning of the text: those who can be called "of small wisdom" harbor the residual habits of falsely considering themselves eminent.
Their habit of misdirection serves as a servant to ghosts; though they possess human form, they are merely categorized among the enlightened class.

Those who largely rely on worldly cleverness and eloquence, imitating minor worldly functions, construct [their views] based on the residual habits of the divine spirit. Their habit of litigation serves as a messenger and follows [the cycle of rebirth].
[Beings] are reborn among humans as those who are integrated with the *da* class—those who are well-versed in worldly affairs and understand human nature.
This is because, having long followed humans while in the animal realm, they naturally possess residual habits that cause this to be so.

Of the ten types mentioned above, the first seven resemble those whose subtle sentiments are dull; the latter three resemble those whose thoughts are clear and thus acute. Nevertheless, their civilizing culture remains pervasive.
These individuals all possess cleverness in various arts and worldly wisdom with eloquent discernment; they are not those who are truly worthy, enlightened, or possessed of civil refinement.
The conclusion below summarizes the warning: "These ten types of people, while formerly in the human realm, created karma for the three miserable destinies."
They undergo retribution in the three miserable realms; once that retribution is exhausted, they again take form in the human realm.

All of this stems from the evil karma created since beginningless time, which remains hidden yet unforgotten. Thus they circle in transmigration, killing and being killed by one another, repaying their debts of life without rest.
Though they possess human forms, if they do not encounter the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world and do not hear the Tathāgata’s True Dharma...
The Dharma causes one to dissolve enmities and liberate oneself from adverse conditions.

Yet, if one continues within the midst of worldly toil, indulging the passions and following one's whims while disregarding the fundamental source, then in the space of a single breath, one will again enter the three miserable realms.
Indeed, this revolving according to karma is the natural law of things; how can it be avoided? Alas! Having obtained a human body, one must not fail to preserve it well.
[He] maintains [this]. Truly, he is one who deserves compassion.
Ānanda, furthermore, there are followers who do not rely on perfect enlightenment (until) their retribution is exhausted, at which point they return and disperse into the various realms of existence.

The first five characters are read with the level tone (*ping shēng*); the latter five characters are read with the departing tone (*qù shēng*). The explanation of the realm of immortals (*xiān qù*) is concluded above.
Below this, the realm of devas (*tiān qù*) is explained. There are three realms of devas: the desire realm (*yù jiè*), the form realm (*sè jiè*), and the formless realm (*wú sè jiè*).
In the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), from the two heavens at the waist and summit of Mount Sumeru up to the four heavens of the sky-dwellers (*antarīkṣa*), there are six tiers in total.
All possess food and drink, sexual desire, and sleep; because they are fully endowed with these three desires, they are collectively termed "Desire Heavens" (*kāmadeva*).
Their men and women marry and take wives and concubines just as humans do; however, these celestial beings have no flesh and bone, nor do they have [excrement].

They urinate little; their bodies possess radiance that makes no distinction between day and night; they have obtained the five supernormal powers as a karmic reward; and their forms encounter no obstruction.
For these reasons, the celestial realm is the most honored within the world-system.
Commentary: This clarifies the cultivation and entry into the realm of the immortals (*ṛṣi-gati*) from the human realm.

Now, this particular realm arises from sentient beings' thoughts of craving life and loathing death; thus, although there are many varieties, they all fundamentally involve a wearying fear of impermanence and a seeking for the body to abide eternally.
Little do they realize that this body is but a phantom within the eternally abiding true mind.

Therefore, they obscure the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and practice in a confused manner, such as the non-Buddhist schools of the Western Regions who take Maheśvara as their celestial lord, or the followers of Huang-Lao in this land who revere the Great Purity (*Taiching*) as the Primordial Beginning (*Yuanshi*). These are all the ultimate reaches of the realm of immortals.
"Following humans" means practicing and realizing [enlightenment] among human beings; it does not mean cultivating *samādhi* without relying on perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Ground" refers to not relying on the eternally abiding true mind to give rise to right wisdom and cultivate the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama, thereby realizing the ultimate, adamantine principle.

"Cultivating separately through deluded thoughts and the like" means that such people do not realize that the physical body is formed by the binding of solidified false conceptions and must ultimately undergo change and extinction;
thus, they mistakenly believe there is a life-essence (xing-ming) that can be cultivated.

He nurtures them so that they may attain longevity and immortality, preserving their mental conceptions and firmly maintaining the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) so that it neither disperses nor perishes.
"Places where people do not reach" refers to famous mountains, caves, and grottoes, such as Mount Kunlun and other similar locations.

It is a place where no human footprints reach; it is purely a dwelling for immortals. Although the ten types of practice below differ in their degree of excellence, "preserving one's thoughts to solidify the physical form" is their essential secret.
The following ten types—such as "firmly adhering to the ingestion of elixirs" and so forth—are explained in detail.
For instance, by refining sesame seeds or red lead as food, one solidifies and guards the physical form. Even if one succeeds in these practices, they can only...
One may strengthen the physical body and prolong life, yet be unable to fly or ascend; therefore, this is called "walking on the earth.
By fortifying plants such as *huangjing* and pine trees—much like consuming them raw—one solidifies the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Even if success is achieved, one merely attains lightness of body and swiftness of foot, walking as if flying; therefore, this is called "flying. By fortifying metals and stones—such as by smelting lead...
The smelting of cinnabar into elixir through nine cycles of great return involves steadfastly maintaining both body and spirit.

Even if one succeeds in this practice, it can only serve to transform white stone into gold and transmute ordinary bones into immortal bones, allowing one to travel everywhere without obstruction; hence it is called "wandering.

Regarding the steadfastness of movement and stillness, this means that whether moving or resting, one always maintains the vital breath and solidifies the physical form, just as one refines the essence (*jing*).

Returning the Qi; refining the Qi to return it to the Spirit; refining the Spirit to return it to the Void. After a long time, when the practice is perfected, one may undergo feather-transformation and ascend.
Hence it is called "empty travel. Regarding "solidifying the vital fluids" and so forth: this refers to stirring the Celestial Pond and swallowing the Jade Elixir.

This can cause the Water to rise and the Fire to descend, thereby forming the Inner Elixir to solidify the physical form. After a long time, when the practice is perfected, one becomes as firm as ice and snow.
Not engaging with worldly desires and elevating oneself toward the heavens is called "Heavenly Practice" (*devayāna*). Regarding "firmness," "purity of color," and so forth:

this refers to consuming rainbows and drinking mists, gathering the solar essence in the morning and the lunar radiance at night; when the practice is perfected over time, the vital energy (*prāṇa*) penetrates and unites with the principles of phenomena, hence it is called "Pervasive Practice" (*sarvayāna*).
Regarding "firmness," "incantations" (*mantra*), "prohibitions" (*vidyā*), and so forth: this refers to exclusively maintaining one's resolve through the power of incantations and esoteric arts.
Regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*): having practiced the recitation of mantras for a long time, one concentrates the spirit to prolong life and thereby attains the Way of Longevity.

Thus it is said: "The practice of the Way is firm, and the contemplation is equal. Initially, one binds the mind below the navel center (*nābhi-cakra*). It penetrates the coccygeal barrier (*pudgala-kapāṭa*), ascends the spine, and reaches the *nirvāṇa* [center].
It then strikes the crown of the head to emit the spirit, thereby firmly guarding the physical form. Through long-term contemplation, the merit is perfected; the form and spirit—

It is said to be "the practice of illumination" (*zhàoxíng*) because it illuminates and responds [to conditions]. Regarding "firmly joined," and so forth: internally, it means the union of the male of the *kan* trigram and the female of the *li* trigram as husband and wife;

externally, it means gathering the yin to assist the yang and sustaining the vital spirit (*shénjīng*). Through long-term practice, success is achieved; this internal resonance elicits an external response, whereby one inhales the essence and energy (*jīngqì*) of the other to consolidate one's own physical form.

Therefore, it is called "the practice of essence" (*jīngxíng*). Regarding "firmly transformed," and so forth: [it refers to the transformation of the body through the stabilization of the vital energies.]
This refers to observing that the myriad things of the world arise from the principle of transformation (*huàlǐ*).

By contemplating this principle of transformation for a long time until awakening occurs, one can move mountains and overturn waters, alter the four seasons, and likewise preserve one's physical form to remain in the world.

This is the ultimate technique of the Way of the Immortals; hence it is called "Ultimate Practice" (*juéxíng*). The following section concludes the discussion on delusion, stating that these ten types of cultivation are all—
Within the human realm, one refines the deluded mind but fails to realize the eternally abiding true mind;
one does not cultivate the adamantine right contemplation, but instead seeks the principle of longevity apart from within the deluded body.

Even if one were to achieve perfection in practice and attain a lifespan of a thousand million years, dwelling in deep mountains or on remote islands, cut off from the human world, such a state remains nonetheless within the delusions of saṃsāra.
They transmigrate within the middle stream, yet remain utterly ignorant of their own eternally abiding true mind,
the essence of pure and luminous nature. If they do not hear the True Dharma and cultivate Right Samādhi, but instead vainly practice deluded thoughts to preserve and solidify the physical form,
then when their karmic retribution as immortals is exhausted in a single day, their forms will once again dissolve, and they will flow back into the ranks of other species.
"Ānanda, those people in the world who do not seek the eternally abiding [state]... from this point downward, it is called the Desire Realm.

(Commentary: This clarifies the six heavens of the Desire Realm. It refers to those who, starting from the human realm, cultivate the causes of the ten wholesome deeds and thereby enter the heavenly realms;
yet they are unable to cultivate the true *samādhi* or seek to realize the eternally abiding true mind.)
Because they lack right contemplation and right concentration, they have not yet been able to relinquish their own attachment to wives and concubines;

however, regarding the wives and concubines of others, they do not merely refrain from physical transgression, but their minds likewise do not wander. Due to this rectitude in sexual conduct, although improper thoughts of lust may arise, they are stilled;
thus the waters of passion become clear and bright, and the ground of the mind is luminous. At the time of death, they abandon the human realm.
Possessing bodies yet receiving celestial forms, they are born at the waist of Mount Sumeru, dwelling in the first tier of the Desire Realm adjacent to the palaces of the sun and moon;

this is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*). If one were in the human world, not only would one refrain from dissolute conduct and illicit lust, but even toward one’s own wife and concubines, one would become distant and dispassionate, seldom indulging in them; when dwelling alone, there would occasionally be [moments of]...

When mindfulness arises, one cannot [be surpassed]. Because this person excels others by a factor of ten, after the end of life, they likewise surpass the brilliance of the sun and moon and are born upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, dwelling in the second tier of the Desire Realm, known as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The two heavens mentioned above are called the Earth-Dwelling Devas (*bhūmi-vāsin-deva*). Although they engage in sexual union, it consists merely of embracing one another with their hands;
unlike those in the human world, there is no emission of impure fluids. Those below these are called the Space-Dwelling Devas (*antarīkṣa-vāsin-deva*).

If they were to dwell among humans and did not encounter objects of desire, lustful thoughts would not arise; however, when they do encounter such objects, they engage in intercourse only once for a brief moment.

Upon departing, one becomes immediately relieved and no longer pursues longing. Having attained the full flavor of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, the movement of desire-thoughts here is slight while stillness is abundant;

thus, one’s merit is double that of before. After death, one dwells in the realm of space, where the palace of the body is self-luminous, shining everywhere and reflecting one another, rendering the sun and moon unnecessary.
Day and night are marked by the opening and closing of lotus flowers, and by [the calls of] birds.
Coming and going constitutes their spring and autumn. They dwell in the third level of the Desire Realm, named Suyāma, which in this language means the Heaven of the Time-Portion (Śakradevendra).
They engage in sexual union merely by holding hands; they do not engage in physical intercourse. If they were to dwell in the human world, they would be able [to remain pure] at all times.

It is solely tranquil and without movement; though it is naturally free from desire, it merely accords with the objects of that desire. When pressed by contact, it cannot reject them and thus complies with them.
This is not yet a state entirely devoid of mind, but because stillness greatly outweighs movement, it is superior by one degree.
Therefore, after death, one ascends to a superior realm that is refined and subtle, surpassing all the devas of the lower realms.
...and so forth; they cannot be perceived. Furthermore, this heaven consists of inner and outer courtyards.

There is also a heaven of karmic retribution, which is produced by the fruits of tainted karma and serves as the heaven of collective retribution. Those who practice the ten virtuous deeds attain birth in that heaven.

The fruits [of the lower realms] belong to the outflows (*sāsrava*) and can be destroyed by the three calamities. The Inner Court, however, is the dwelling place where Bodhisattvas in their final birth (*caramabhavika*) reside.
This current Lord of Devas is named Maitreya; even when the kalpa reaches its destruction at the third dhyāna, this Inner Court is not reached by the three calamities and has never been destroyed.
This is the fourth level of the Desire Realm. Thus, the inner and outer [realms] together are collectively termed [the *kāmadhātu*].
The Tuṣita Hall is called the Heaven of Contentment because its inhabitants are able to give rise to contentment regarding the five desires.
They fulfill their desires with but a single smile, which is unlike the grasping of hands [found among humans]. If one were among humans, one would originally have no desire in one's own mind.
Sensual objects are laid out before them, yet their faculties lack autonomy. Although they must touch these objects, they find no flavor at all, like chewing wax.
Their spiritual merit is twice that of the previous realm; therefore, after death, they are born in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
They are able to transcend the lower heavens and can themselves emanate objects of pleasure. Residing in the fifth layer of the Desire Realm, it is named "Pleasure-Emanation."

The *nirmāṇarati* devas (Devas of Delight in Emanations) are so called because all the objects of their enjoyment can be spontaneously emanated by themselves. Although they dwell in the world, they have no mind for worldly affairs;
they merely maintain the branches of the precepts and cultivate the higher realms. They only temporarily conform to worldly sentiments to perform the duties of social interaction.
When it comes to the time of intimacy, they not only find it tasteless, but remain transcendent beyond the realm of the senses, with no involvement whatsoever.
Furthermore, their merit is twice that of the former. Therefore, after the end of life, they transcend the realms of the *nirmāṇarati* and *anabhraka* heavens.

"Nirmāṇa" (creation) refers to the fifth heaven; "anabhraka" (cloudless) refers to the four lower heavens. Residing in the sixth layer of the desire realm, it is named the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Creations (*paranirmitavaśavartin*).
In all cases where objects of sensual pleasure arise, they do not manifest through one's own effort but are produced by others (*paranirmita*), which one then enjoys with sovereign ease.
As for the two heavens mentioned above, sexual union is accomplished merely by looking at one another with the eyes; thus, they are increasingly superior to the lower heavens.

The conclusion of this section states: "Thus, although the forms and the ten objects of desire of these six heavens differ from those of worldly people, they are not characterized by the restless agitation [of the human realm]."

Section. Like a wild horse without a halter, it cannot be controlled; yet, because one has not yet reached the state where mind and traces are entirely absent and social ties are severed, it is collectively termed the "Desire Realm" (*kāmadhātu*).
From this point downward, all the way down to the hells, are subsumed within the Desire Realm—what is known as the "Ground of the Mixed Abodes of the Five Destinies."
Lecture Record on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Eight;
Lecture Record on the Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa Tathāgataguhyahetubhāvanā-siddhi-nītārtha-sarvabodhisattva-daśapāramitā-śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Nine.
Ming Dynasty: Chai Zi, Shi Chengshi (lecture notes).
Proofread and published by the dharma-recipient disciple from Xin’an, Wang Yiyuan. Regarding the traditional explanation:

although the six heavens of the preceding [desire realm] have emerged from worldly disturbances, they have not yet been able to sever desire; therefore, they are collectively termed the "Desire Realm" (*kāmadhātu*).

From this point upward, the eighteen heavens are clarified. Although they are free from the defilement of desire, they still possess material form; therefore, they are collectively termed the "Form Realm" (*rūpadhātu*).

They are also collectively termed the "Brahma-world," as they have already abandoned the defilement of desire. They are collectively designated as the "Four Dhyānas," as they have already abandoned mental agitation and distraction.

While the heavens of the Desire Realm are produced through the retribution of the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action, these heavens are produced by both meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and such wholesome actions.
It arises; however, it consists specifically of the sixfold practice of impure dhyāna-contemplation. As for the six practices:

one feels revulsion toward the desire realm as being suffering, coarse, and obstructive, while taking delight in the form realm as being pure, sublime, and free from attachment. This is how ordinary persons suppress their afflictions.

This refers to the path that transcends the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, it is said: "Although there were meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) in the heavens above, only this realm is designated as 'dhyāna'.
This is because the preceding section concludes: "Though the body has emerged from movement, the traces of the mind still intersect.

From this point upward, it is evident that women are entirely absent; both mind and its traces are detached, with no further intersection. Moreover, there is neither eating nor sleeping, and the three types of desire are extinguished.

Both [hunger and fatigue] were forgotten. Whenever he encountered slight hunger or weariness, he would immediately enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Upon emerging from concentration, he was full and his spirit was refined and clear;
thus, he took the joy of meditation as both food and rest, gradually departing from the coarse and heavy body and mind.
Ānanda, when all those in the world who cultivate the mind reach a state where the various outflows (āsrava) do not move, this is called the first dhyāna.
[Commentary: This clarifies the three heavens of the first dhyāna in the realm of form (rūpadhātu). "All those in the world who cultivate the mind" refers to the devas and humans of the three realms;
although they have not yet attained the supramundane mind, they nevertheless each take this as their fundamental cause for cultivation.
Each of them says to themselves, "I have already attained the true cultivation of the mind.

Regarding the phrase "without relying on dhyāna, there is no wisdom," this means they possess only tainted (*sāsrava*) meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), which suppresses the six classes of desire through the sixfold practice and restrains the habit of lust;

however, because it is not the untainted (*anāsrava*) true samādhi of the vajra-contemplation wisdom, they are only able to restrain their bodies from engaging in sexual desire and [practice] with one [woman].

At the time of death, they are devoid of both conceptual thought and recollection. Because their bodies and minds are both pure and they have no dwelling place below, at the moment of death they are reborn in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) by virtue of their mindfulness, becoming companions of the Brahma-world.

This class of beings is thus called the Brahmakāyika (Brahma-folk) Heaven. Having eliminated the habituation to desire, the mind manifests as free from desire; this refers to the aforementioned heaven.

Having already abandoned the habitual tendencies of desire, the minds of these devas are clearly manifest in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). They take delight in and find joy in the precepts associated with concentration (*dhyāna-samvara*), and thus accord with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

Therefore, at the time of death, they are reborn in the Brahma-world by virtue of their mindfulness. Because they assist the King (Brahmā) in his transformative governance, they are called the *Brahmapurohita* (Minister of Brahmā) Heaven.

Regarding such qualities as the subtle perfection of body and mind and the lack of laxity in their deportment, it is said that these pertain to the previous heaven, where the mind is developed through concentration.
Buddhila further possessed virtuous transformation; thus his body and mind were perfectly wondrous and his dignified deportment was never deficient.

This deva, having given rise to wisdom from within meditative discipline and precepts, attained an understanding superior to that of the previous heaven and was fit to serve as the Lord of Brahmā. At the time of his death, he—
He arises by virtue of his resolve as the Brahmā King, presiding over the assembly of Brahmās; therefore, he is named Mahābrahmā.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states that his majestic power and radiance cause him to dwell alone, and he possesses no vitarka (applied thought) but only vicāra (sustained thought), being induced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The two lower heavens both possess both vitarka and vicāra.
Furthermore, after the dissolution of a kalpa and before its formation, he departs and returns respectively; because externalists cannot fathom this, they falsely cling to him [as the creator].

Constantly. Furthermore, because thoughts arise, one perceives the existence of a "Heavenly Creator" (*īśvara*) and thus clings to the notion that this being alone is the cause that produces the world.
This concludes the presentation of the three heavens, which is called the First Dhyāna. Regarding the term "superior flow" (*viśeṣa-āgama*) and so forth:

it means that having already departed from the five desires and severed the ten unwholesome paths of action, one is able to transcend the various realms of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Thus, one cannot be oppressed by the eight sufferings of the Desire Realm. Although it is not...
This is the true samādhi. Because one’s precepts and mind are pure, and the habitual tendencies of desire have been subdued such that one is no longer moved by them, it is called the First Dhyāna.
It is also called the Stage of Joy and Bliss Born of Seclusion. Joy arises because one is secluded from sensual desires and evil;
bliss arises because the body and mind are tranquil and pliant.
Ānanda, next, the Brahmā Heaven governs the Brahmā people; having already subdued the coarse outflows, it is called the Second Dhyāna.
[Commentary: This clarifies the Second Dhyāna Heaven of the Form Realm. It means that by cultivating from the preceding heaven, one is fully endowed with precepts, concentration, and wisdom;
hence it is said that "the Brahma-conduct is perfected. Upon advancing to this heaven, the three consciousnesses do not arise, and concentration is attained.

The mind is one-pointed, as it takes only internal objects as its focal point. Having attained concentration through the abandonment of desire, the depth of that concentration gives rise to illumination;

the water of the mind becomes clear and still, radiating light from within. Yet, because this mental radiance is still inferior and has not reached its full extent, it is called "Limited Light" (Parīttābha).

From the previous stage of Limited Light (*Apramāṇābha*), light further increases in brilliance; thus mind and environment mutually illuminate one another, and the environment emerges following the light, reflecting throughout the ten directions so that everything becomes universally composed of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*).
Although this light is immense, it only pervades the small chiliocosm (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*) and has not yet produced sound;
therefore, it is named "Immeasurable Light" (*Apramāṇābha*). Progressing from this through cultivation, one further attains the mastery of absorbing and sustaining the perfect light.

Regarding the essence of the teaching (*śāsana*): because this deity lacks the first five consciousnesses and is devoid of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it is able to absorb and sustain immeasurable pure light.
Thus, by means of its radiant halo, it proclaims the sublime conduct (*brahmacarya*) without depending on verbal expression; it spontaneously constitutes the essence of the teaching.

It elucidates the pure principle, which manifests infinitely through transformation; therefore, it is named "Light-Sound" (Ābhāsvara). This concludes the section identifying the three heavens as collectively belonging to the Second Dhyāna.

That is to say, these three heavens are superior to the lower heavens of the First Dhyāna. Although they have attained the factor of joy (*prīti*), they have not yet produced supreme joy (*parama-prīti*).
Although they are free from suffering and affliction, they still possess the relative states of sorrow and joy. Because this [Second Dhyāna] attains supreme joy, all sorrows...

It cannot be assailed by the [hindrances] that hang above. Because one can, through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), subdue the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), it is collectively termed the Second Dhyāna.

It is also called the Stage of Joy and Bliss Born of Concentration (*samādhi-ja-prīti-sukha-bhūmi*), because the merit of this concentration arises simultaneously with a bliss that pervades the entire body.
Ānanda, when the celestial beings thus possess the perfect radiance and the accomplishment of sound (up to) the full completion of joy, it is called the Third Dhyāna.
[Commentary: This clarifies the heavens of the Third Dhyāna within the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*).

It means that although the preceding heaven uses the perfect radiance as its teaching of sound, and by opening that sound the wondrous principle is revealed, there still remains the movement of thought through a mind of joy, which continues to obstruct pure bliss.
This deva, relying upon the sublime principle, brings forth and perfects refined practice; being tranquil and serene, they penetrate the bliss of cessation.
Because this initial penetration of the bliss of stillness first manifests pure emptiness, it is called "Limited Purity" (Parīttaśubha).

This stage initially subdues the sixth consciousness, yet it is not yet great cessation. Once the sixth consciousness is subdued, pure emptiness appears before one; this is then expanded and extended.

Yet their joyful mind becomes increasingly tranquil because the pure emptiness is boundless. As both the inner mind and the outer body attain pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), tranquility and bliss are fully realized.
Because this pure emptiness is immeasurable, it is called the "Immeasurable Purity" (*Apramāṇa-śubha*). In the previous heaven, tranquility and bliss pervaded only the body and mind;
in this heaven, the physical elements of the body are empty and still, such that every point of contact becomes sublime bliss. This is due to the pure virtues within the heavens.

There is nothing that surpasses this in the formation of a realm of bliss. Therefore, one recognizes this pure bliss as the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the blissful land, entrusting one’s own body and mind to this place.
Because every point of contact becomes pure bliss, it is named "Universal Purity" (*Śubhakṛtsna*).
This concludes by indicating that the common name for these three heavens is the Third Dhyāna. In this heaven, sublime bliss is pervasive and immeasurable; there is nothing that is not...
It accords with the mind and complies with the will; therefore, it is said to be "endowed with great compliance.

In the first two dhyānas, because there is joy (*prīti*) and mental activity, the body and mind cannot attain tranquility. Now, however, both joy and mental activity are absent, and there is immeasurable supreme bliss.
They enjoy themselves with mastery. Although this is not the true samādhi, it does not prevent the mind from possessing joy and bliss even in the absence of rapture (*prīti*).
Thus, within a state of tranquility, a profound serenity is fully realized; for these reasons, they are collectively termed the Heaven of the Third Dhyāna.

It is also called the Stage of Sublime Joy Free from Rapture (*prīti-virāga-sukha-bhūmi*). This means that rapture (*prīti*) is a mental factor that agitates the mind, whereas bliss (*sukha*) is what is refined through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);
thus it is termed "joyful," because one subsequently attains sublime bliss. Within the realms, this is designated as the Third Dhyāna, the place of ultimate bliss.
Ānanda, furthermore, when gods and humans are not oppressed in body or mind—[up to] when their application is fully matured—it is called the Fourth Dhyāna.
(Commentary: This clarifies the heavens of the Fourth Dhyāna. It means that in the First Dhyāna one is free from suffering and affliction, and in the Second Dhyāna anxiety and distress are exhausted;
therefore, there is no oppression of body or mind. Desire is the cause of suffering; since all desires are cut off, the cause of suffering is already exhausted.)
In the third dhyāna, one is detached from the feeling of joy and experiences bliss. These devas understand that even this bliss is not permanent;

because bliss must inevitably perish after a long time, its destruction gives rise to suffering. Therefore, they simultaneously and suddenly relinquish both the mind of suffering and the mind of bliss.

Having departed from suffering, they no longer experience bliss, and thus the characteristic of destruction does not arise. When one transcends both suffering and destruction, the nature of pure merit arises. Thus, one is detached.

"Birth of Merit. Herein, the mind abides unmoving; concentration and equanimity arise together. The mental faculty is free from suffering and pleasure, and it is also called the "Stage of Purity of Equanimity and Mindfulness.
In the preceding stage, the mind was initially focused on equanimity but had not yet attained full integration. Here, however, there is no longer even a thought of pleasure;
therefore, it is called "integration. Within this state of equanimity, one still generates resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), maintaining it with certainty so as not to be...
Because it is transformed by diverse conditions, it is called "pure. Because the mind is perfectly integrated (*yuanrong*), pure merit is unimpeded.
Within this state of perfect integration and non-obstruction, whatever aspirations or requests are made are invariably fulfilled; thus, one acts with sovereign mastery according to the mind.

Reaching to the furthest limits of the future, one joyfully accords with this state; therefore, it is named "Merit-Love" (*fui*). According to the ancient explanation, "reaching to the furthest limits of the future" refers to the sustaining of merit.
The two paths involve receiving retribution for a vast duration, lasting through many kalpas; they are not truly permanent.
"Loved by merit" refers to the merit of the various devas, for this heaven is considered most beloved because it is not reached by the three calamities.
Alternatively, this heaven may have a distinct craving for accumulated merit, which is precisely the hope for these two paths. These heavens are called "loved by merit," and there are two [types].
The "forked paths" arise because one follows the inclinations of one's own thoughts and karmic actions. The first is the direct path leading to the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*).

The second is the circuitous and deviant path leading to the Realm of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*). This refers to the previously mentioned mind—the mind of merit, love, and sublime compliance, as well as the immeasurable pure light.

This refers to the radiance of the mind produced by the concentration associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-sahagata-samādhi*). Regarding "dwelling in the cultivation and realization of perfect and luminous merit":
within immeasurable light, one perfumes the meditative merit through the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), thereby becoming free from the defilements of the lower stages.

Having fully traversed the four levels, it is named "Vast Fruit" (*Bṛhatphala*) because it is induced by vast merit. The preceding mind is the same as before; the Vast Fruit [mind] is characterized by a distaste for both suffering and pleasure.
Furthermore, they cultivate merit and virtue. This deva grows weary of suffering and pleasure and advances toward the cultivation of the meditative absorption of equanimity (*upekṣā-samādhi*).
These two [stages] diverge from one another. "Thoroughly investigating" means searching deeply and minutely. "Continuous" means diligent and uninterrupted effort.
"Perfectly exhausting" means seeking the ultimate realization. Through these three phrases regarding body and mind, the fruit is certainly achieved. That is to say:

By means of the concentration of equanimity (*upekṣā-samādhi*), they eliminate the mind of equanimity and cause the mental faculty to become ashen and solidified. After five hundred great eons (*mahākalpa*), the sixth consciousness no longer functions;
they falsely claim this to be *nirvāṇa*, not realizing that it is precisely the subtle flow of arising and ceasing.
Such persons, having severed the cultivation of causes characterized by arising and ceasing, are unable to bring about the fruit of non-arising and non-ceasing. (First Part)

Regarding the "destruction of the kalpa": this refers to those first born in this heaven who practice meditative concentration for half a kalpa before finally attaining the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā-nirodha*).

For those born during the latter half of the kalpa, once their karmic retribution in this heaven is exhausted, they will again give rise to perception and mind after four hundred and ninety-nine and a half kalpas.
Since it is merely the non-functioning of the six consciousnesses, it is called "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*). This concludes the indication of the common name for these four heavens.
This is dhyāna. Because both suffering and pleasure have perished, the two objects cannot disturb the mind.

The fourth dhyāna is not moved by the three calamities and is thus called the "Immovable Ground" (*aniñjya-bhūmi*). The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) true Immovable Ground refers to the eighth stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).
This refers to the devas of these dhyāna heavens: their physical environment is not truly eternal, and their sentient beings undergo simultaneous birth and extinction.

Although this is not the unconditioned realm of ultimate reality, the mastery of conditioned functions has here reached full maturity. These four superior noble classes are collectively termed the "Four Dhyānas."
Ānanda, herein there are furthermore five types of non-returner devas (up to) this class known as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
[Commentary: This clarifies the five types of non-returner devas. "Herein" refers to within the fourth dhyāna. A "non-returner" (anāgāmin) is...
By completely severing the nine grades of afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) within the desire realm, one realizes the third fruit and will no longer be reborn in the desire realm.
"Habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) refer to the seeds of these afflictions of thought;

that is, the subtle afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride are divided into eighty-one grades across the nine stages of the three realms, with nine grades in each stage. Now, [one severs] the nine grades of the single stage of the desire realm.

Because the nine grades [of afflictions] of the Desire Realm have been abandoned, suffering has ceased; yet there is no longer any place to dwell within the Desire Realm. Furthermore, because the nine grades of each of the upper three stages have been severed, pleasure has ceased;
yet there is no longer any place to dwell within the lower three stages of the Form Realm, as the afflictions of the fourth stage have not yet been completely eliminated.
Only the stage of the fourth dhyāna, characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness, constitutes its homogeneous sphere (*sabhāga*), yet it possesses a specific dwelling place.

Regarding the "extinction of both suffering and pleasure": when suffering and pleasure have not yet ceased, one feels aversion toward suffering and yearns for pleasure; these two states battle within the breast.
Thus there was "affliction" (fan). Now that both have been forgotten, the mind no longer engages [with objects]; hence it is called "without affliction" (wufan). Intense heat is called "affliction";
attaining a slight coolness is called "without affliction. "Ji" means to release and move; "kuo" means to gather and restrain.

This refers to the releasing and restraining of the mind, which consists solely of the practice of equanimity and mindfulness, with no other thoughts remaining. Although previously the contending minds did not engage, one still perceived a ground of engagement.
Now, by thoroughly investigating and exhausting even the ground of contact, the mental ground becomes pure and entirely free from even the slightest affliction;

thus it is called "without heat. Having attained clarity of the mental ground, one gives rise to the supernormal power of the divine eye, whereby one perceives the realms of the ten directions everywhere.
And there is nothing that is not a wondrous object. Therefore it is said: "The wondrous vision is perfectly clear. Dusty images are the objects; sedimentary defilements are the afflictions.
This precisely reveals the dual fusion of concentration and wisdom, where both mind and objects are pure, and all that is seen is good; thus it is named "Good Vision" (Sudarśana).
Having already attained the perfect and subtle faculty of the mind’s eye, he is thus able to smelt and refine all things through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom.

Acting with sovereign mastery according to his will, his transformations and manifestations are unimpeded; therefore, he is named "Excellent Manifestation" (Sudṛśa). "Ultimate" (*jiu*) means to investigate thoroughly to the end. "Slight" (*ji*) refers to the slightest movement.

It is said that by means of a single moment of untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-citta*), one perfumes the various moments of tainted consciousness (*sāsrava-citta*) until they reach the state of a single moment;

furthermore, this is able to exhaust the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*) until it reaches the subtlest of the subtle, as it approaches the limit of the formless (*ārūpya*). Having reached this ultimate point, one investigates it thoroughly.
Thus, form has already been exhausted; therefore, it is named the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Ānanda, from this Non-returner heaven down to those various levels of the fourth dhyāna, and all below that, is called the Realm of Form (Rūpadhātu).

The traditional explanation from this point upward clarifies the four heavens of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). "Formless" means that there is no form resulting from karmic fruition (*vipākaja-rūpa*), though there is form resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhija-rūpa*);
this applies equally to both the environment and the inhabitants. Thus, one extinguishes the body and returns to the formless state, abandoning the mixed dwellings of gods and humans;
their types are not uniform, yet all lack the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). All four heavens advance through cultivation based on the pervasive void (*ākāśa*). First...

1. One becomes weary of form and relies upon emptiness. 2. One becomes weary of emptiness and relies upon consciousness. 3. One causes form, emptiness, and consciousness—all three—to be extinguished, yet relies upon the nature of consciousness. 4.
One relies upon the nature of consciousness to exhaustively investigate extinction, yet fails to attain true extinction.

These are all superior wholesome fruits of conditioned phenomena; they do not transcend saṃsāra and do not constitute the holy path. Within this context, one exhausts form and proceeds toward emptiness.
Ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are its primary inhabitants; those of fixed destiny among the *śrāvakas* reside there as guests, while followers of heterodox views dwell there intermingled.
[Commentary:
This concludes the demonstration that although these five heavens belong to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), they are exclusively the abodes of noble ones (*ārya*). All of this...

The inhabitants of the Five Heavens must have progressed toward the third fruit [of the path], attained the four dhyānas, and given rise to untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā), thereby initiating the karma of perfumed dhyāna (vāsita-dhyāna-karma).
This arises either in a single grade or up to nine grades before they are finally able to be reborn there. Ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) do not possess such karma of perfumed dhyāna.

Therefore, they cannot be born there; that is to say, these five heavens are not seen by the humans of the four dhyāna heavens alone, but even the Four Heavenly Kings merely revere their names, for they do not know their enjoyments, nor do they see their primary and secondary residences.

This is because the inhabitants of the four heavens cultivate mundane, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) concentrations, whereas those of the five heavens cultivate supramundane, non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*) noble concentrations. Thus, there is a distinction between the coarse states of the mundane and the noble.
"Subtle. This refers to the vast difference [in scale] between them. "As in the world today" below uses the example of the human realm for clarification.

"The site of the holy path" refers to places such as Mount Wutai, Mount Emei, and Mount Tiantai. Although Arhats are mentioned, this also includes Bodhisattvas. The concluding phrase "belonging to the form realm" below [indicates their status].
"Walking alone without companions" means being free from emotional desires. "Not yet exhausting the physical form" [refers to their remaining embodiment].
There is still the accumulation of material form (*rūpa*). Therefore, from the Akaniṣṭha Heaven down to the Brahmakāyika Heaven, all are called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
