Furthermore, Ānanda, from this Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down to those who are deluded, leaking, and ignorant, they enter into the cycle of rebirth.
Commentary: This intends to clarify the heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). First, it distinguishes the noble ones (*ārya*).
The "Heaven at the Culmination of Form" (*rūpāvacara-agra*) dwells at the summit of the realm of form and is adjacent to the formless; therefore, it is called the "Middle of the Limit of Form.

Because those who are *anāgāmin* (Non-returners), regardless of whether their faculties are sharp or dull, all take the mind of equanimity at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as the causal mind for practicing meditative concentration, they [attain] equanimity.
The mind divides into two paths. If one possesses sharp faculties, they investigate the nature of form to seek the vision of true emptiness, giving rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).

When the light of this wisdom becomes perfectly pervasive, they transcend the triple world horizontally and enter the Bodhisattva vehicle; such a person is called a "Great Arhat who has turned the mind.

If one possesses dull faculties, they likewise cultivate meditative concentration through the mind of renunciation, exhausting the nature of form and feeling joy for the higher realms while wearying of the lower.

Below: being born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one gradually abandons [defilements] and gradually realizes [the fruits], thereby ascending out of the three realms. This section below clarifies the formless realm.
If one abides in a state of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and achieves the abandonment of aversion, this follows upon the previous stage. One perceives the body as an obstruction, and so forth.
According to the ancient explanation: one becomes weary of the body’s material obstruction and diligently cultivates the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

By extinguishing the body and returning to non-existence—due to being weary of form and relying upon emptiness—it is called the "concentration of the sphere of infinite space" (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*); thus, one is reborn in the sphere of infinite space as a result of this retribution. There are two ways of relinquishing the mind:

if, at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one employs the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) to sever delusions and enter emptiness, one is a *sāmayikī-kāmadhātu-vītarāga-anāgāmin* (one who attains the fruit of non-returning through concentration). If, at the Fruit of Vastness (*bṛhatphala*), one employs the tainted path...
The path of outflows involves suppressing delusions to enter emptiness; this is the state of ordinary beings and non-Buddhists.

When all obstructions have dissolved and ceased to exist, one does not rely on form (*rūpa*). When even the absence of obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*) is extinguished, one does not rely on emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
To retain the entirety of the *ālayavijñāna* along with half of the *manas* is to loathe emptiness and rely upon consciousness (*vijñāna*). The *ālaya* is the eighth consciousness; the *manas*...
Regarding the seventh consciousness, *manas*: only half of it remains in a subtle state because the sixth consciousness, through its discriminative function, has already been subdued;
thus, one portion of *manas* is also subdued. However, because the sixth consciousness’s innate (*sahaja*) aspect has not yet been severed, that portion of *manas* likewise remains unsevered.

This [subtle mind] takes the boundless void as its object of aversion and contemplates emptiness; consequently, the mind becomes distracted and obstructed by this concentration. Thereupon, it abandons the contemplation of emptiness and takes consciousness as its object.

This is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*). Therefore, one is born into the sphere of consciousness as a result of maturation (*vipākaja*). Since both space and form have vanished, one follows upon the previous state where the mind of the celestial sphere of consciousness has completely ceased.
This means that by relying on the power of profound concentration (*samādhi*), one suppresses half of the *manas* so that it does not arise as active manifestation (*pravṛtti*).

It is tranquil and without any destination, and so forth; for since the object of cognition (*ālambana*) no longer exists, the subject of cognition (*ālambaka*) does not function. This is because, through aversion toward the boundlessness of consciousness, one takes consciousness itself as the object.

Consequently, the mind becomes distracted and the meditative absorption is broken; it then relinquishes the [seventh] consciousness and takes as its object the dharma of non-existence. This is called the concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).

Therefore, one is reborn in the sphere of nothingness. As for the immovability of the nature of this consciousness, it is due to the complete suppression of the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the manas.
Only the seed-nature remains, slumbering within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), profound and difficult to stir.

Phrases such as "exhausting through investigation" mean that when a practitioner reaches this stage, their will is exhausted and their strength spent; they no longer investigate the truth or sever delusions.

Thus, within the inexhaustible nature, they forcibly attempt to manifest it, claiming they have already exhausted its potential, unaware that they are merely being driven by the constraints of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Thus, although the nature of consciousness exists, it does not arise; hence it is said that "it exists as if it did not exist. To perceive the nature of consciousness as exhausted is, in reality, not its exhaustion;

hence it is said that "if exhausted, it is not exhausted. Because one becomes weary of the previous sphere of consciousness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Because one becomes weary of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Because their dwelling is fixed, their retribution is likewise born in this place. This section below generally clarifies the grounds from which the noble and the ordinary emerge or fall.
The phrase "these [beings]" refers collectively to the humans of the aforementioned four heavens. From the first heaven, one exhausts form (*rūpa*) and returns to emptiness;

up to the fourth heaven, one exhausts the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and returns to the nature of extinction. If one exhausts emptiness in such a manner, how could it be anything other than failing to realize that the nature of form is truly empty?
The principle of the true nature of form as empty of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is, in fact, the doctrine of the twofold emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*);

yet they remain ignorant of this and falsely give rise to the notion that emptiness means total annihilation. Therefore, those who have exhausted their pursuit of emptiness up to the Heaven of No-Retreat (*Anāgāmin*) and arrive at this heaven still possess roots and practices that are truly authentic.
Only when their eighty thousand kalpas are fulfilled will they sever all afflictions of thought (*kleśa*) and transcend the triple world (*tridhātu*).
They are called Arhats of dull faculties because they are unable to turn their minds toward the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) like those who do so; thus they are termed "dull.

If one proceeds from the Sphere of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva) up to the limit of emptiness and arrives at this heaven, their faculties and conduct were originally perverted, for they mistook this contaminated (sāsrava) heaven for the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
When their retribution of eighty thousand kalpas is exhausted, they have no place of refuge and [fall].
They have fallen into ruin.
Ānanda, these various devas—each of the heavenly beings (down to) the *pudgalas*—each follow their own kind.
[Commentary: The following summarizes the distinctions between the holy and the ordinary within the three realms. Regarding "these various devas":
This refers collectively to the three realms. "Heavenly beings" (tianren) refers to the subjects and citizens of each respective heaven;

it means that these heavenly beings, having cultivated only the ten wholesome paths and the eight dhyānas during their causal stage, receive retribution in the form of the six desire heavens and the four dhyāna heavens. Consequently, when their retribution is exhausted, they re-enter the cycle of saṃsāra.
"Heavenly Kings" (tiānwáng) refers to Bodhisattvas who, while occupying these positions as a provisional station for their cultivation and progress, utilize these heavens [for their practice].

This stage is the path for attaining perfect and complete enlightenment; therefore, one does not fall back into saṃsāra. The following concludes the classification of the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).

In the first two heavens, there is no physical body or sensory objects at all; hence it is said that "the body is extinguished. In the latter two heavens, the active functioning of consciousness and mind does not arise;
hence it is said that "the mind is extinguished. Because both body and mind are extinguished, the state of fixed nature (*niyāma*) manifests before one.
Furthermore, one is able to manifest transformations of both the environment (*bhājana-loka*) and its inhabitants (*sattva-loka*), enjoying them with sovereign mastery.

Upon emerging from meditative absorption, both body and mind are tranquil, and both the environment and its inhabitants are empty; thus, there is no form resulting from karma, but only form resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*).

From this realm of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, these are collectively termed the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). Including the lower realms previously mentioned, they together summarize the Three Realms. That is to say:

From the six heavens of the desire realm up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, all arise because one cannot thoroughly comprehend that one’s own fundamentally wondrous enlightened nature—the originally luminous and perfect mind—is inherently devoid of such phenomena as birth, death, karma, and its fruits. Thus, from delusion one accumulates further delusion, and through delusion the three realms are produced.
Consequently, when the retributions of the various devas are exhausted, they once again follow their deluded karma within those realms, sinking into the seven [hells].
The *gati* (destinies) never cease. A *pudgala* is called a "repeated-taker-of-destinies," which refers to the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*).
Because it repeatedly undergoes birth and clings to various destinies, it is said that each follows its own kind.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms... (up to)... there are those included in the realm of animals due to moisture.
[Commentary: This clarifies the four kinds of asuras. Asura means "non-deva.
This refers to those who possess much anger and celestial fortune, yet lack the conduct of devas. They are also called "not upright," because the males are ugly and the females are beautiful.
"Beautiful. They are named after males; they are also called "Wineless" because, due to their anger, they lack harmonious energy and cannot brew wine.

Regarding those in the realm of ghosts and so forth, it is said that their prior causes involve generating the aspiration for the Dharma from the ghost realm—protecting sutras, mantras, meditation, and precepts—and thus, by relying on the power of these virtues, they ascend to this realm.
Riding upon supernatural powers, they dwell within the empty space, or perhaps due to their mental conceptions.
Because their vital energy (*prāṇa*) is predominant, they are born from eggs and fly through the air, yet they belong to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*).

Those who are equal to the gods—meaning those whose previous bodies were in the realm of gods—may, due to the impairment of their merit or the exhaustion of their celestial fortune, both be demoted and fall into this realm;
dwelling among humans, they are certainly womb-born and thus belong to the realm of humans (*manuṣya-gati*). As for those who uphold the world and so forth...

This refers to his ability to command spirits and deities, bringing both calamity and fortune upon the human world. His majestic power penetrates to both devas and humans, such that he has nothing to fear;
yet, because he monopolizes authority that does not extend to the various heavens, they become enraged and contend with him. Such is the transformative power of his merit.

Those who are equal to the devas are certainly of miraculous birth (upapāduka) and belong to the realm of the devas. As for those who are "equal to a certain portion" and so forth, it refers to these asuras;
because their past conduct was slightly inferior, they are born from the heart of the ocean or at its watery mouth, dwelling in aquatic cavities.
They are certainly of moisture-born (saṃsvedaja) origin, and due to their inferiority, they belong to the realm of animals.
Ānanda, in this way, the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals (up to... are but a single falsehood, having no further root or continuity.

[Commentary: This summarizes the falsity of the seven destinies. That is to say, if one minutely investigates the causes for the ascent, descent, and mutual transitions within the seven destinies, they all have ignorance, delusion, and karma as their causes; because these manifest as characteristics, they evoke the seven destinies.
The characteristics of the fruits [of karma] all arise from deluded conceptualization; one receives retribution according to deluded karma.
Within the wondrous, perfect, brilliant, and pure mind of non-action—the fundamental mind—there has never been the characteristic of cause and effect within the seven realms of existence.
These deluded, heavy phenomena of conditioned existence are, within the fundamental mind, like flowers in the sky appearing in the vast void; how could they have any real attachment?
In this state, there is only a single delusion; there is no further arising from roots, foundations, or origins. Torpor is ignorance (*avidyā*);

all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are afflictions and karma, which constitute the causes. Rebirth according to one's karma is the result. Conditioned phenomena are the opposite of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
"Ānanda, these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind... (up to) "...how could they further follow the acts of killing, stealing, and lust?
*Annotation:* This clarifies that delusion has no root or origin; it arises from confusion.

It answers the question of how the seven realms of existence can exist when the wondrous mind is all-pervading and perfect. "Not recognizing" refers to confusion. "Original mind" refers to the wondrous, perfect, and luminous [nature].

This refers to the fundamental mind. It means: you have asked from where these seven realms of existence arise; they all result from being deluded regarding one's own fundamental mind, whereby one undergoes this cycle of birth and death.
Although many kalpas may pass, one fails to attain the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature, and remains forever submerged in birth and death.
This is entirely due to employing various false thoughts and following along with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. And so forth.
These form the three evils. Even if one can reverse these by committing no killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, they further give rise to the three virtues.
If the three evils exist, one sinks into the three miserable realms; if the three evils are absent, one soars upward into the celestial realms.
Because virtue and evil mutually involve presence and absence, and because they contend with and supplant one another, there is ascent and descent, giving rise to the nature of saṃsāra without end.
If one knows that both good and evil are of the nature of universal saṃsāra, one must cause the wondrous nature to be revealed.

Yet, regarding good and evil, one should not engage in any deliberation at all, but practice only the true and correct samādhi. Thus, one realizes the fundamental, wondrous, quiescent, and eternal mind-nature.
If one can reach this state, not only will the two natures of good and evil be extinguished on the spot, but even the nature of non-duality will likewise [be transcended].
It cannot be apprehended; therefore, it is said that both existence and non-existence are absent, and even this absence of duality is extinguished.

Thus, one transcends not only the cycle of birth and death within the seven destinies, but also transcends and is liberated from the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles. In this state, there is not even the three kinds of wholesome action.
How could one further fall into the three evil realms? Therefore it is said that there is not even the non-killing, non-stealing, and non-lusting;
how then could one follow the acts of killing, stealing, and lust? These acts are themselves cause and effect.
Ānanda, the three karmas are not severed; each has its own private [cause]... (up to) ...if anyone else were to speak thus, it would be the speaking of Māra. *Guànzhù* (Commentary):
This concludes the answer to the previous question and serves as an exhortation toward authentic cultivation.

The previous question asked: "Is there a fixed place? Or is it spontaneous? Each person gives rise to karma and each privately experiences its results. Therefore, the response restates this by saying: "Because..."
Because they do not cease the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, each person creates them privately.
Because each creates them privately, they exist within the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of those who share such private acts; thus, they are not without a fixed location.

To say that while the creation of karma is private, the experience of retribution occurs within a shared sphere is precisely what is meant by "distinctive karma with a common retribution" (*pratyeka-karma-sādhāraṇa-vipāka*). Yet, from where does this distinctive karma with a common retribution arise? It is entirely...
These arise from one's own deluded karma. Since karma arises falsely, it originally has no cause.

Being without cause, the place where they are produced likewise cannot be traced or investigated to its ultimate limit. Nevertheless, although no cause can be found through investigation, they do not transcend the three delusions as their fundamental root.
You must now exert yourself in cultivation and progress, for you must certainly seek to attain the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment].
Regarding Bodhi, one should take the elimination of these three delusions as the essential method. For those three types of wholesome and unwholesome karma arise rooted in delusion;
therefore, one must eradicate them by exhausting their very roots. If one does not exhaust the root of these three karmas, [enlightenment cannot be attained].
Even if one attains the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), these are all conditioned activities (*saṃskṛta-kriyā*) and not untainted pure karma (*anāsrava-śuddha-karma*).

Because they merely suppress active manifestations (*samudācāra*) without eliminating the seeds (*bīja*), one does not attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and ultimately falls into the path of Māra.

Although one wishes to eliminate delusion, one thus uses the void to rescue the void, doubling one's hypocrisy. One merely calls oneself "one who has attained the Way," while in reality, one remains subject to karmic fruition. This is truly [the case].

This is a matter for profound sorrow and compassion. Because Ānanda initially asked about the true reality of the Buddha’s essence, yet further inquired how there could still be the various realms of existence (*gati*), [the Buddha] replied:
"You have created this through your own delusion; it is not that the *bodhi* (enlightenment) is at fault.

Here, *bodhi* refers to the essence of the Buddha. Furthermore, he issued a warning: "If, in the final age, those who preach the Dharma speak as I have said here, they shall be the true [successors] of the Buddha."
To preach in praise of those who practice the three evil paths as a means of exhortation is the perverse teaching of Māra;
this clearly demonstrates that one must sever the three delusions before one can attain true samādhi. "Xù" (勗) means to encourage or exert oneself.
The preceding section has detailed the seven destinies; the following section provides a detailed analysis of the realms of Māra. There are five kinds of Māra:

the Māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), the Māra of devas (*deva-māra*), and the Māra of ghosts (*preta-māra*). These are combined into two types:
the Māra of the aggregates subsumes both the Māra of afflictions and the Māra of death, as both arise in dependence upon the five aggregates. The two types of devas and ghosts are both caused by...
Those who cultivate false concentration and delight in harming the true path are collectively termed celestial Māras.
As for these demonic realms, none but one endowed with omniscience can discern their authenticity or falsehood.

Thus, while Ānanda knew to inquire about the cultivation of concentration and the realization of its fruits, he was unable to question regarding the subtle demonic activities within that concentration. Furthermore, although he had received the World-Honored One’s...
This directly reveals the path of true cultivation, by which one is capable of proceeding toward unsurpassed bodhi. Yet, the perils along the way have not yet been personally experienced;
only the World-Honored One deeply understands the victory or defeat of the demonic armies. Indeed, this concerns the very essence of right concentration and true cultivation—its success or failure.
Furthermore, nothing surpasses this in its capacity to ruin the mind of wondrous enlightenment and destroy the Dharma-king’s house. Therefore:

As he was about to conclude his discourse from the Dharma seat, he turned his body back and remained, pointing out each point in detail so that those in the final age who cultivate right concentration may recognize demons and heterodoxies for themselves,
remaining prepared and free from peril. For this reason, out of profound compassion, he spoke of his own accord without waiting for a question.
Immediately, the Tathāgata rose from his Dharma-seat (until) they joyfully prostrated and waited in reverence for his compassionate instruction.
[Commentary: This is an unasked self-exposition (*anupṛṣṭa-svavādita*). From "The Tathāgata" onwards is the narration by the scribe of the sutra.
His rising from the Dharma-seat signifies the manifestation of his final teaching. His turning his body to return once more signifies that his profound compassion is inexhaustible. You all—
[The Buddha] spoke below. This section generally clarifies that Māra can harm what is correct; those who cultivate right concentration must inevitably recognize this.
The true method of practice is to enter the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama* through the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing. The intent is:
"I have already pointed out for you the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama* as the true cultivation and actual realization. You all should also clearly understand it."
[The preceding stages] are understood; yet you have not yet clarified that the demonic activities appearing within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are the most subtle.
If you do not know them in advance, they may suddenly manifest before you, making it difficult to distinguish the false from the true.

Should there be even the slightest attachment in your mind, these demons will exploit the opening to lure you away, causing you to fall into false views without your own awareness. The "hidden demon" (*chāyā-māra*) refers specifically to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
When pressed by the intermediate dhyāna-concentration, the original mind manifests of itself; at this stage, there are as yet no external māras.
However, when one slightly loses right view within the two skandhas of sensation and perception—the celestial māras, ghosts, spirits, and goblins—all enter therein and lead one into external māras.
When the māra actually appears and one fails to recognize it, either identifying oneself as a sage or mistaking the māra for a sage, these are all cases of "recognizing a thief."

To act as a son and yet establish oneself as a treasure of the mourning household; to practice while recognizing the mind-manifestations within the two *āyatanas* (spheres) as the two demons—know that these do not come from without, but are all the own-mind’s own perversity, the fault of being satisfied with a little attainment.

The following cites one case to illustrate the rest. As for those who have "no learning," they merely cultivate non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*), taking no pleasure in hearing the Dharma and failing to practice what is correct.
They consider their meditative absorption to be the ultimate fruit. Yet, when their retribution is exhausted and perceptions arise again, the signs of decay manifest once more.

Unaware that they never attained true saintly realization, they instead slander the Buddha, falsely claiming that Arhats do not undergo further existence. Because they have slandered the Dharma, they consequently fall into hell.
The harm reaches such an extent; it is truly to be feared. You who wish to cultivate right concentration and proceed toward the Great [Vehicle]—
"Bodhi! You should recognize this subtle and profound demonic affliction; therefore, I shall analyze it for you in detail.
Listen attentively. When Ānanda and the others heard of these demonic activities, they rose up in trepidation and listened with joy.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly... (until) "all lands shall not be shaken or torn asunder. [Commentary:
This intends to clarify the beginning of the movement of Māra, yet first deduces the arising and ceasing of the true and the false.

"Fundamental enlightenment, wondrously luminous" refers to its function; "the perfect essence of the mind-body" refers to its substance. The meaning is that this concerns the substance and function of true enlightenment.

Sentient beings and Buddhas are fundamentally identical. It is simply because sentient beings, in a single thought-moment, undergo deluded movement—turning their backs on awakening to unite with the sensory dust, losing themselves in the true to pursue the delusive—that faults and transgressions are formed. Consequently, fundamental ignorance arises, inciting karma and moistening rebirth;

in an instant, these arise together, causing the essence of awakening to become universally obscured and suddenly manifest as the nature of emptiness. Therefore, the nature of awakening becomes deluded and forms false conceptualization.
To obscure true emptiness (*bhūtakoṭi*) is to treat it as a dull void (*tūṣṇīka-śūnyatā*). Thus, delusion transforms without ceasing, giving rise to worlds;

this is what is meant by "establishing worlds based upon emptiness. Consequently, the myriad lands of the ten directions—all those conditioned realms of dust-like particles—are all formed from mistaking true emptiness for a dull void.
They are established through the deluded mind, which obscures the nature of awakening and gives rise to false conceptions (*vikalpa*). Therefore...
Know this: when emptiness arises within the Great Awakening, it is like a fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great void;
it is already a phantom and an illusion, vast and indistinct. How much more so is the world established upon that emptiness—its illusory and indistinct nature goes without saying.
It is only because all sentient beings pursue delusion with delusion and accumulate confusion upon confusion from beginningless time that they fail to perceive it. Suppose...
If even one among you were able to abide within *samādhi*, develop the true nature, and return to primordial awakening, then the emptiness of the ten directions would all be extinguished and perish;
how much more so the lands that exist within that emptiness—how could they not tremble and shatter?
This is because the empty space and the world are, in total, but a single name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*). Name...
Phenomenal marks exist solely based upon deluded conceptualization. If one transforms deluded conceptualization into true wisdom, then all marks will return to suchness.
Therefore it is said: "When one person returns to the source, the ten voids are dissolved. Thus, an ancient master remarked:
"When space arises, it is merely a provisional name that arises; when space ceases, it is merely a provisional name that ceases."
"When you practitioners cultivate dhyāna and adorn samādhi (until) the time you enter samādhi, they will all come to harass you.
[Commentary: This clarifies that Māras cause confusion out of fear. "Adorn" means to make solemn and orderly. The meaning is:
when you deeply enter right concentration and give rise to the true return to the source, your spiritual resonance naturally connects with that of the sages and worthies of the ten directions.

The mind becomes perfectly integrated; all is merged into a single realm. Without departing from its present location, it is tranquil and unmoving, profoundly pure and empty, free from mutual disturbance.

As for the remaining celestial Māras, as well as spirits, ghosts, and deities—even those of the non-Buddhist *asaṃjñika* heavens—the palaces where they dwell, whether situated in space, upon water, or on land, will all collapse.

It splits asunder. Since the great earth trembles and cleaves open, the spirits of the rivers and seas that dwell in the waters, the ghosts and monsters of the mountains and rivers that dwell on land, and the flying yakṣas and asuras—all are struck with terror and awe.

Only the ordinary beings of the lower realms, because they have not yet attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), do not perceive the shifting and destruction of the empty realm; they merely falsely report that the mountains shake and the earth trembles.

Because it moved, there was no cause for alarm or terror. Those Māras and their like have all attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), yet they have not exhausted their residual outflows (*anuśaya*).
Since they are still attached to the dust and toil of the world, and because [the Buddha] knew their disposition, he did not allow you to shatter and tear down their palaces.

However, as for the reason that the movement pervaded the entire realm of space while only the Māras could not tolerate it: it is because the places where they dwell rely entirely upon false darkness, whereas you abide in right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).

They have discerned and perceived your deviant tracks. Each of them has exerted their utmost ability, wishing to destroy your meditative concentration; therefore, they have all come together to harass and disturb you.
Yet, although those various māras may be filled with great rage, [they shall eventually] tumble and fall away, beyond all hope of rescue or aid.
Commentary: This clarifies the benefits and harms of awakening and delusion. The meaning is this:

although they certainly take it as their business to ruin you, they are performing deviant practices within the realm of worldly toil (*saṃsāra*), whereas you are cultivating the right concentration (*samādhi*) within the state of wondrous enlightenment.

Although the heterodox may be enraged by the orthodox, they cannot harm the orthodox. To attempt to harm the orthodox with the heterodox is like the wind blowing against light or a blade cutting through water;
in the end, it can neither sever nor damage the light or the water. Using the orthodox to transform the heterodox is also like boiling water dissolving hard ice:
as the warm vapor approaches, the cold congealment vanishes of its own accord. This is truly because, although they rely upon...

As for those supernatural powers, they cause alarm and panic from the outside; in the end, they are like violent raiders. Although you have not yet attained such powers, you are able to maintain firm control within;
in the end, you are the master. That the state of disorder is brought to completion does not depend on the convenience of the raiders, but entirely upon the master.
It must wait for the master of the five aggregates to lose his own right mindfulness and mistake the thief for his son; only then can the raider gain the advantage.
Taking advantage of this opportunity, they will eventually find an interval to enter and plunder the treasures of your household.

If your *ālaya-vijñāna* (the hidden master) were to abide in right concentration, looking at nothing and illuminating only the true source, then even if the demonic power were violent and arrogant, it would have no place to enter; they could do nothing to you.
However, because your latent substance gradually dissolves and your radiance gradually emerges, they will long remain among the ranks of the heterodox.
All receive this subtle, dark energy. When they draw near to the light, they naturally dissolve and perish, like darkness encountering a lamp;

how could they dare remain long in the presence of light to disturb your right concentration? If the master’s mind does not clearly awaken to those illusory phenomena, there may arise fear or attachment, or grasping and rejecting;
thus one slightly loses the illumination of reality and momentarily deviates from right concentration, being [overwhelmed by them].
Deluded by the aggregates (*skandhas*), you will fall into their class and become their retinue. This is just like Māraṅgula; he was exceedingly lowly and inferior.
Moreover, his initial intention was merely to use incantations to entice you and cause you to break the monastic discipline (*vinaya*) of the Buddha.

Therefore, among the eighty thousand practices, he only destroyed your meditative precepts (*dhyāna-śīla*). This was because he could not destroy your pure essence of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*). You—
You have not yet fallen into their abyss. These Māras are by no means a lowly or inferior class;

moreover, at their very inception, they do not merely destroy a single precept of yours, but seek to demolish your entire body of precious awakening, causing you to lose your person and life, so that you shall forever become a son of Māra, with no end in sight.
Once you have encountered their harm, it will be like being a minister of state [caught in a political purge].
Your family has suddenly been stripped of its official registration by the Heavenly King. Not only have you lost your official rank, but you shall also not escape the penal laws.
If you were indeed to ruin your entire body, it would not merely prevent the attainment of the fruits of the Way;
you would also fall into hell, wandering and wasting away until this point. Even if there were the power of compassion, it would only serve to increase your sorrow.
"Can it be saved?
Ānanda, you should know that from your sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) [until now], solid delusion has served as its foundation.

*Commentary:* This clarifies the beginning and end of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). As for "the site of enlightenment," it refers to the simultaneous cultivation of both phenomena and principle.

The "place" is the very site where enlightenment was attained. "Dissolving all thoughts," etc., means that when he first sat at the site of enlightenment, he screened out all floating, distracted, and coarse conceptions;
after a long time, deluded thoughts naturally departed. This state of being free from thought is like the bright sun in the sky:
at all times, it is luminous and never obscured. Therefore, it is called "clarity and precision through the departure of thought. Thus, then—

The realms of movement and stillness cannot shift it; the consciousnesses of recollection and forgetfulness cannot intersect with it. Thus, the three—sense organs, objects, and consciousness—merge into a single, brilliant lucidity.
If one abides in this state of singular lucidity, one enters the Vajra Samādhi of hearing-permeation and hearing-cultivation.
However, if the power of meditative concentration is not yet deep and the realm of principle has only just entered, one is still obstructed by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Obscuration: Like a person with clear vision situated in great darkness, because one has not yet attained the great wisdom of prajñā, the subtle mind of essential nature has not yet begun to radiate light;
wherever one looks, there is only darkness. This is the confinement of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).
This covers and obscures the true nature, preventing it from being expansive and fully developed; this is the sign that the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has not yet been broken through.
If one causes the power of meditative concentration to advance and the light of the mind to radiate forth, the previously dark realms will all be transformed into the light of the mind.

Although one may not yet possess the perfect mirror-like discernment of the three thousand worlds, the ten directions will open wide, and there will be no further gloom or darkness. This is the [breaking through of] the aggregate of form.

This is the characteristic of what has already been destroyed. It refers to this aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), which, through false attachment, is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Since there is the appearance of a body, there are the first five sense organs (*indriya*), which grasp at external objects and thereby plunder the true nature, muddying the wondrous luminosity.
Therefore, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) is transcended.

At this point, looking back at the origin of the aggregate of form, one finds that it fundamentally arises from solidified false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*), formed by the interweaving of internal and external factors into a congealed mass; this is its root.
"Ānanda, you should investigate this wondrous clarity with precision within [this state]... (until) if you take it as a holy realization, you will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.
*Commentary:* The ten items below clarify the objects that appear within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

"Within this" refers to within this meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). "Investigating with precision" refers precisely to the practice of applying effort and systematic analysis while in concentration.

Furthermore, "wondrous clarity" (*miaoming*) refers to the function of the true essence. The reason its essence is not explicitly mentioned is to show that while functions may be bright or dim, the essence undergoes no change or alteration.
It is like a mirror buried within dust and grime; although its radiance is obscured, its fundamental nature has never been impaired.
Therefore, when a practitioner investigates wondrous clarity with diligence, it is like polishing a mirror: one need only remove emotional attachments and conceptualizations.
Though covered by dust and defilement, the substance of the Great Perfect Mirror lacks even the slightest increase [in its nature].

Furthermore, this wondrous luminosity has always been coextensive with the Dharma-realm, never obstructed or limited; it is only because of the false recognition of the four elements, which interweave internally and externally, that it becomes solid and obstructive.
Therefore, if one now applies oneself to intensive study with superior effort, they will no longer interweave. In a brief moment, the body will be like empty space. A single hair—

This lack of obstruction arises because the force of one's application within meditative concentration has reached its limit, causing the inner mind to overflow momentarily and external objects to become empty and harmonious.
This state is attained for a brief moment and lost as quickly; it is not the same as the permanent realization of the fruits of sainthood, which leaves nothing unverified.

You all, if you remain tranquil and free from attachment, without the slightest longing or envy, then even though this state emerges through the power of concentration, it is still a wholesome condition. If you encounter this...
If one falsely claims to have realized the state of sainthood regarding these objects, one will immediately be afflicted by malevolent influences and destroy right concentration.
Ānanda, if you again take this mind and scrutinize its subtle brilliance, yet interpret it as the realization of sainthood, you will likewise be possessed by a host of demons.

Commentary: This clarifies the state of internal penetration. Refining the subtle brilliance as before, that which is called "the body being internally penetrated" means that the light of the mind suddenly transcends and penetrates within the body, allowing one to look back at the viscera and organs and directly perceive parasitic worms.
He picked it up with his hand, and his body remained without injury. This is merely the temporary illumination of the mind’s essence overflowing into the physical form;
it is simply because one's cultivation and practice were so intense that the body was temporarily unimpeded. It is not the state of true permanence realized by the sages.
If the mind has no attachments and remains thus in a state of wholesome objects, yet gradually lacks discernment while forming a holy understanding,
you will immediately succumb to various heterodoxies and ruin your right concentration.

Furthermore, one should investigate this mind with precision both internally and externally (until reaching the point where) if one forms a conception of it as being "sagehood," one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.
*Commentary*: This clarifies the state in which both the internal and external are thoroughly penetrated. "Internal and external" refers to the mind and its objects.

When it is clear and bright, the *hun* soul is predominant; when it is dark and obscured, the *po* soul is predominant. To withdraw and consolidate within is the function of the *yi* (mind/intention).
The will (*chih*) acts as the host, manifesting outwardly; this is the spirit (*shen*) acting as the host. Both of these are functions of the sixth consciousness.
Therefore, with the exception of the eighth consciousness’s appropriation (*upādāna*), the body remains unchanged.

As for the remaining *hun* and *po* spirits and so forth, they all abandon their original functions and enter into one another in succession. To say they "mutually act as guest and host" means that one serves as the host while the others serve as guests.
The other five [elements] are all merely guests. "Hearing the Dharma preached in the air" refers to what is before one's eyes.
"Hearing the secret meanings of the ten directions" refers to that which pervades the entire dharma-realm. Regarding their alternating separation and union:
at times, the *jing* (essence) leaves its primary function and unites with the *po* (soul); at times, the *po* leaves its primary function and unites with the *jing*, and so forth. This is because...
To "separate" means to abandon one's original function; to "unite," however, is to fulfill the functions of others. Regarding the "accomplishment of the seeds of goodness":

this refers to having cultivated through hearing in the past, which, when further refined through diligent study in the present, enables one to manifest and realize what has been heard. Thus, and so forth.

As before. Furthermore, when this mind is clear, manifest, and brilliantly penetrating—up to the point where, if one forms a conception of it as being the state of a sage, one immediately falls under the influence of various delusions.
[Crown Commentary: This clarifies that because the inner mind is pellucid, the external manifestation appears as the realm of the Buddha; this arises from the power of diligent cultivation.
Excellent! The wondrous mind becomes increasingly clear. That the pure dew is bright and penetrating means that coarse delusions are gradually dissolving.
That internal radiance shines forth means that the essence of wisdom is opened and lucid. This is because when wisdom arises, delusion perishes;
thus, the insentient world everywhere becomes the Golden Realm, and all sentient beings become Tathāgatas. In Sanskrit, this is called Vairocana; here it is translated as "Universal Radiance."

"Even unto the simultaneous appearance of lotus flowers" means that both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as their adornments, all manifest in accordance with the transformations of the mind.

The phrase "this is called below" definitively identifies this realm: it is because one had previously heard the Great Dharma during past lives and attained spiritual awakening, such that the seeds and habitual tendencies now, through further investigation, cause the light of the mind to suddenly shine forth, illuminating all worlds.
The realms do so only by chance and for a brief moment; they are not like the realization of the sages, which remains constant from eternity.
Furthermore, if you take this mind and investigate its wondrous luminosity [up to] "if you interpret this as the realization of a sage, you will immediately be possessed by a host of demons."
Commentary: This clarifies that when the power of intensive cultivation reaches its ultimate limit, one perceives the color of the *ākāśagarbha* jewel.
"Observation without ceasing" means that the effort of contemplative illumination is intense and uninterrupted. Regarding all deluded thoughts, one applies even greater suppression.
Regarding all sensory objects, one further subdues them; thus, the power of restraint becomes excessive.

When the desire to transcend reaches its ultimate limit of intensity, suddenly the empty space of the ten directions appears as the color of the seven treasures, or the color of a hundred treasures, simultaneously filling it all.
Yet, these various colors do not obstruct or hinder one another—whether blue, yellow, red, or white.

The five colors appear all at once, yet each color remains pure and unmixed with the others. This arises because the subtle brilliance has been intensely cultivated to its ultimate limit, radiating forth and manifesting;
thus, one perceives these various sublime realms. Nevertheless, they are gained for a moment and lost for a moment.
It is not that what was previously unmanifest becomes permanently manifest.

Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate until it is clear and transparent, if one takes this as a realization of sainthood (*ārya*), one will immediately fall under the influence of various delusions.
[Guanzhu: This clarifies that because one investigates until clarity is reached, one sees objects even in the dark. "Investigation" means to probe and examine.
It is also like clearing away [impurities] until it is transparent and pure; this is the state of ultimate stillness.

"The refined radiance is not disturbed" means that the light of the mind is concentrated and fixed, such that the two objects of brightness and darkness cannot displace it. "Suddenly, at night, [the eyes] close" means closing the eyes.

This refers to seeing while the eyes are closed during the night; it specifically demonstrates that one sees objects within a dark room, which is not seeing from the eyes. This is the category of seeing.
Regarding "various objects and the like": these are not things that originally existed within the room; rather, they are strange objects manifested within the darkness.
Yet, every single item within the room remains as it was, never having undergone any change. This concludes the explanation of clarity:

it means that because the mind is already subtle and fine, and vision is likewise dense and limpid, the refined radiance is concentrated and stabilized, such that the realm of darkness is transparently penetrated. However, it has not yet...
This thoroughly reveals the true light of this very place; it is not that the merit of one's study has surpassed [others], but merely that it has been momentarily manifested.
Regarding the character "he" (合) herein, all Tibetan woodblock editions are identical; the people of today have arbitrarily changed it to the character "ban" (半), which must not be followed.

Furthermore, with this mind, one enters perfectly into the void and fusion (until: "if one takes this as a realization of sainthood, one will immediately be possessed by various demons"). [Commentary:
This clarifies that through perfect entry into the void and fusion, the body becomes identical to grass and trees. Regarding "perfectly entering the void and fusion," etc.:
it means that when the power of investigation is at its peak, both the internal body and external objects are entirely void and open; therefore, the four limbs are all the same [as grass and trees].
Grasses and trees, when burned by fire or cut by knives, have no perception at all. Because they lack perception, the fire does not consume them and the knife does not wound them.
This is sustained by the power of meditative concentration; both thought and mind are stilled, and their efficacy reaches the ultimate limit.
When grasping and receiving cease to function, the five sensory objects are simultaneously dissolved and the four elements are cast aside;

pure awareness remains while the body is left behind, and thus there is no longer any sensation of injury or contact. This, too, is merely a temporary glimpse; it is not yet the true realization that form is itself emptiness and emptiness is itself form.
Furthermore, by means of this mind, one achieves purity (up to the point where) if one forms a holy understanding, one will immediately succumb to various heterodoxies. [Commentary:
This clarifies that the function of the pure mind has reached its ultimate limit; it is the beholding of the realms and the beholding of the Buddha. Regarding "achieving purity" and so forth:
it means to loathe the obstructive nature of defiled turbidity and to rejoice in the empty and harmonious nature of pure subtlety, while concentrating one's contemplation upon the pure mind.
Merit has reached its ultimate limit here; therefore, one suddenly perceives the great earth, mountains, and rivers transforming into a pure and wondrous land.
Furthermore, one beholds the Buddhas currently residing in that Pure Land, and additionally sees the hells and celestial palaces, moving up and down without obstruction.

This arises from having previously heard the teachings regarding the two lands—the pure and the defiled—and subsequently giving rise to thoughts of rejoicing in the pure and loathing the defiled, thereby perfuming the mind.
Through repeated practice, seeds are formed. Now, within meditative concentration, as focused contemplation deepens, it reaches its ultimate limit and transforms;
one temporarily attains such a state, yet this is not truly dwelling in a Pure Land.
Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate the profound and remote—[extending] until, if one forms a holy understanding, one immediately falls under the influence of various heterodoxies.
[Commentary: This clarifies the investigation of the profound and remote, which refers to seeing and hearing from afar. Regarding "investigating the profound and remote" and so forth:
it means that within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one investigates with a deep mind, pervading everywhere all at once, reaching the ultimate limit, and thereby causing...
The radiance of the mind, having reached its ultimate limit, flies forth; therefore, one is able to see and hear even at remote distances and through obstructions.
This, however, is merely temporary and occurs only once; it is not the actual attainment of pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, if one uses this mind to investigate until reaching the ultimate refinement and then takes this to be the realization of a sage, one will immediately fall prey to various heterodoxies.
[Commentary: This clarifies that through diligent investigation and refinement, one perceives the nature of consciousness.

That is to say, within meditative concentration, one exhausts all effort to investigate and penetrate until reaching the most refined and ultimate state; it is precisely at the moment when one’s mind perfectly merges with that of the sages and worthies.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is about to be destroyed; the palaces of Māra tremble and split apart; the hearts of the Māras are panicked and disordered.
Thus, it is at this point that the disturbances of Māra first arise. Regarding "seeing virtuous friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*) and so forth:

this means that while the practitioner is in a state of stillness, they see virtuous friends appearing before them, or perhaps transforming into various Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and the like. This is because such a realm is fundamentally the practitioner's own [projection].
It may be that some of perverse nature have harbored [impurities] within their hearts; when their efforts reach this point, they are driven to the limit and reveal them.

This is not the true vision of a sage. Or perhaps it is a demon that has entered the practitioner’s heart and belly, seizing their consciousness, thereby causing the practitioner to preach the Dharma without cause and even to penetrate subtle meanings, thus giving rise to mad wisdom. This is not the true realization of a sage. It causes...

When the practitioner reaches this point, they first become aware [of it], and the demons naturally dissipate. If, however, one instead gives rise to a "sacred understanding," the harm will not be slight.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifested states during dhyāna (up to the point where they are maintained and protected so as to achieve the Unsurpassed Way).
The ten kinds of demonic activities mentioned above are the general outlines selected by the World-Honored One to show to beginners.
It is not that within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) these specific types must necessarily exist and be unchangeable;

nor is it that there is a fixed number of them that must necessarily exist and cannot be increased or decreased. Rather, it concerns only how the practitioner applies their mind—whether it be lax or urgent.
If one acts with appropriateness, they will vanish entirely and not be seen. If one contemplates them through alternating visualizations, those that appear become increasingly numerous;
their types may differ, and their quantities may vary—these all follow the transformations of the mind and possess no fixed substance.

If one were to insist on following the scriptures and waiting for verification, how would this differ from the man who marked the boat in search of his sword? Hereafter, all cases shall be treated in this manner.
Commentary: This concludes the section on the instructions for protection against harm.

It means that these ten states manifested within this *dhyāna* are all produced because the practitioner, while within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), has not yet fully penetrated the principle and their correct concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) is not yet pure.
They arise from the mutual conflict and alternating victory and defeat between meditative observation and solid deluded thought, just as when one person is skilled...

When the objective realm appears, it means that meditative contemplation has temporarily surpassed delusive thoughts; yet after a short while, it vanishes, meaning that delusive thoughts have again surpassed meditative contemplation.
Because these states of superiority and inferiority alternate, one cannot permanently realize the sacred realm. This is why various heterodox influences take advantage of such gaps to enter.
Sentient beings are stubbornly deluded; if they do not gauge their own capacity and practice for long, they will likewise [fail].
Observe that these appear for a moment and then vanish again. Upon encountering the manifestation of such states, one immediately claims to have attained the stage of a sage;
this is to claim what has not been attained as attained, and to claim what has not been realized as realized. How could one avoid falling into hell? You all should rely upon the Tathāgata.

By means of this very principle, you must transmit it to those who cultivate right concentration in the future, so that they may have prior knowledge [of these states] and prevent the celestial Māras and their like from [obstructing them].
Having obtained this opportunity, they further acquire supernatural powers (ṛddhi), which serve to sustain, support, shield, and protect them,
preventing them from falling into delusion and enabling them to achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
"Ānanda, those good men who cultivate *samādhi* [up to the point where] they take empty clarity as their deluded thought—this constitutes the root.

**Commentary:** This clarifies the beginning and end of the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation). The passage "cultivate *samādhi*" and below refers back to the previous stage where the *rūpa-skandha* (the aggregate of form) has already been exhausted.
Seeing the minds of all Buddhas as images appearing in a mirror signifies that one's meditative observation (*dhyāna*) has reached fruition; this is precisely the stage of the *rūpa-skandha*.
It has already been broken. One perceives through and through one’s own wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind; it is not obtained from without.

As for the phrase "if there is something obtained," etc., this means that although one sees the originally existing true essence, one is as yet unable to give rise to its wondrous function and cannot act spontaneously and at ease.
This precisely reveals that the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) has not yet been broken. It is like a person suffering from a nightmare, which serves as a metaphor for the practitioner being...

Constrained by the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), the two phrases regarding "hands and feet" metaphorically represent having something attained above; the two phrases regarding "mind and contact" metaphorically represent being unable to employ it above.
The following lines directly express the core meaning: although one perceives the true essence, one does not attain its wondrous function.
This is precisely the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) that confines and limits the true nature, shrouding the wondrous clarity so that it cannot expand or unfold in greatness.

Once the *tṛṣṇā-skandha* (craving aggregate) is shattered, it is like waking from a nightmare; one is no longer burdened by faults. The true mind is vast and great, fundamentally coextensive with the Dharma-realm.
Because of beginningless delusion and attachment, one mistakes it for being within the body; thus, throughout birth and death, one is unable to leave the body behind. If...

If the true mind leaves the body and contemplates the face, moving and staying with freedom, this is the initial manifestation of its wondrous function, and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted.
This aggregate of sensation is precisely the first five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). "Seeing" refers here to experiencing or receiving.

Because the first five consciousnesses experience objects that are either adverse or favorable, they induce feelings of suffering, pleasure, and so forth, which turbidly obscure the true mind. Now, however—

The aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is shattered, and the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāluṣya*) is transcended. Reaching this point, one turns back to contemplate the origin of the aggregate of sensation:

it originally arises from deluded thoughts within empty luminosity, woven together by mutual delusion. "Empty luminosity" means that there has never been any substantial entity; it is merely an emptiness that possesses luminosity.
"Ānanda, that son of good family, while within this state (up to) losing his right concentration, shall fall into ruin.
[Commentary: The following ten items clarify the objects manifested within the *vedanā-skandha* (aggregate of sensation).

"Within this" refers to within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), as the subsequent text states: "within that concentration. "Attaining great radiance" follows upon the preceding [description].
The quarters open wide; there is no longer any obscuration or gloom, signifying that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has been exhausted.

His mind becomes luminous and penetrating, treading upon the minds of the Buddhas he previously beheld, like images appearing in a mirror. If he suppresses this internally to excess, he will recognize that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is at fault.
One cannot attain its wondrous function; one must urgently seek to break through it.

When compassion suddenly arises, one realizes that all sentient beings are confined by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and have not yet been able to manifest the luminous clarity of their own mind as one has.
Thus, seeing all sentient beings—whether large or small—one gives rise to a heart of pity and compassion, and tears flow involuntarily. Indeed, this heart of compassion is truly not...
The great compassion of all Buddhas is of one essence; however, because its application is overly forceful and suppressive, it results in excessive compassion (*atibhakti*).
If one can swiftly awaken to the original cause and return to right mindfulness, refraining from claiming saintly realization, [this affliction] will naturally dissipate over time.

If one claims for oneself that one has already realized the great compassion of all Buddhas, then the demon of compassion (*bhaktimāra*) will take advantage of the opening to enter the mind; seeing others, one then feels only pity.
He wept incessantly and consequently lost his meditative absorption (*samādhi*), falling back into the cycle of delusion.

As for "meditative absorption," it refers precisely to that state within *dhyāna* where there is neither conceptual meaning nor a foothold; reaching this point, one must be able to maintain it without any sense of liking or disliking, nor any fear or attachment.
If even a single thought arises, the realization will not remain stable and the correct concentration will be lost.
Ānanda, furthermore, those good sons within that samādhi (up to the point where they) lose their right reception and shall fall into ruin.
[Commentary: This clarifies that by setting their aspirations equal to the Buddha, they invite demonic interference. "The aggregate of sensation becomes clear and bright" means:
The covering is somewhat lightened. As for the manifestation of superior signs, it is like attaining great radiance and so forth.

Regarding "invoking a response that exceeds expectations," this means one slightly perceives the original reality; as if the mind were identical to the Buddha-mind, one thus achieves supreme joy and success.

Yet they give rise to great ferocity and courage, claiming that without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, they shall immediately become Buddhas. This arises from wisdom being deranged while concentration is weak;

they perceive the principle with negligence and, relying on their own lofty ambitions, limit their practice. Acting with rashness to seek realization, they overstep their bounds and transgress the proper rites, thus forming this interpretation.
If they awaken to this and turn back, they may yet be free of fault; but if they recklessly persist without turning back, [they will fall].
Then a mad demon will enter one's mind, giving rise to great arrogance (*māna*). With no Buddhas above and no sentient beings below, one will falsely exalt oneself;
there is no doubt that one will lose meditative concentration and fall from it. The *Dharmapada* says: "If one gives rise to a mind of diligent effort..."
This is delusion, not true diligence. If one can ensure the mind is not deluded, then diligence will be boundless.
Furthermore, those good sons within that state of concentration (up to the point where they) lose their correct absorption shall fall into ruin.
Commentary: This clarifies that through the absence of wisdom while immersed in recollection, one becomes subject to demonic interference.

"Lacking new realization" means the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) has not yet been exhausted. "Returning to lose the former abode" means the *rūpa-skandha* (form aggregate) has already been exhausted.

At this juncture, one should simply maintain both concentration and wisdom equally to eliminate the deluded thoughts of empty clarity; then, new realization will arise spontaneously. If, however, one's power of wisdom declines...

Subtle! When the illumination of reality loses its standard, one has no means to advance or retreat; thus, the center collapses and there is nothing to rely upon, leaving one in a state of profound darkness with nothing seen.

This is because the function of the illuminating wisdom is absent, causing the concentrated mind to become parched and withered; and because of the vacuity that precedes and follows, one sinks into constant recollection at every moment.

The mind dares not disperse; yet it further takes this sunken recollection as non-dispersion, regarding it as the mark of diligent *vīrya* (exertion) while desiring to achieve the merit of breaking through the *skandhas* (aggregates).
Is this not an error? This is merely one-sided concentration (*samādhi*) without wisdom (*prajñā*), whereby one loses the skillful means (*upāya*) for oneself.
If one can awaken to this, returning to a state of balanced integration, then perhaps there will be no fault. If one takes this sunken recollection and withered concentration to be... [erroneous].

Upon realizing the state of sainthood, the Mara named "Recollection" enters the mind; morning and evening he seizes the mind and suspends it in one place, causing one to lose their fundamental concentration and inevitably fall into decline.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until) they lose their right reception (*samyaksamādhi*) shall fall into ruin.
[Commentary: This clarifies that when wisdom is excessive, one becomes狂 (*mad*), thereby leading to demonic interference.

"The power of wisdom exceeds concentration and loses its sharp intensity" means that the intensity of wisdom surpasses that of concentration. "One whose mind harbors a superior nature" refers to falsely claiming that there is a self-nature (*svabhāva*).

One is originally a Buddha; there is no need to wait for realization through cultivation. Therefore, one should naturally suspect that one’s own body is itself Vairocana, and not laboriously strive for further attainment, nor be content with meager gains.
This occurs because one’s spiritual power is not yet pure, and one fails to constantly examine oneself:

"How does my own merit compare to the merit of the Buddha? How does my own virtue compare to the virtue of the Buddha? Thus, one merely clings to one's own knowledge and views as being identical [to the Buddha's].
Because this is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one must abandon [the pursuit of] cultivation and realization. If one awakens sharply to the error, one may return to the source without fault.
But if one stubbornly persists in shamatha (śamatha) while remaining deluded and failing to return, it will be as if a demon has entered the mind;

one will utter great mad ravings, claiming to have realized the Unsurpassed Way, yet lose one's own right concentration and fall away into the realm of demons. An ancient worthy said: "Do not recollect."
Non-attachment is called precept; non-thought is called concentration; and non-delusion is called wisdom. When the single mind does not arise, one possesses precept, concentration, and wisdom;
yet it is neither one nor three.
Furthermore, those good sons within that samādhi (up to) will lose their correct reception and fall into ruin. [Commentary:
This clarifies how traversing perils and experiencing much anxiety leads to demonic interference. "A new realization" is one phrase, the same as before.

"Traversing and surveying both limits through partial concentration," etc., means that having observed that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already been exhausted, they perceive that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is not real. At this point—
Regarding the two extremes, both are difficult to rely upon; fearing one might suffer decline and loss, one gives rise to hardship and peril.
When excessive anxiety does not cease, it turns into inverted views. Thus, it is like sitting upon an iron bed, even to the point of seeking someone to end one's life.
This arises from diligent and secret exertion, yet being unaware within the mind that fear has become excessive, leaving no further skillful means for self-comfort; therefore, it reaches this state.
In this regard, if one reforms their errors and forgets their worries, they will naturally restore right mindfulness.

If one takes anxiety as a sign of saintly realization and does not cease worrying, then a demonic spirit may possess them; they will go so far as to take up a blade and cut themselves, thereby losing their own right concentration and falling into the abyss with the demons.
Thus, the Sixth Patriarch said: "All things are without mind; it is the self-nature..."
Precepts; the wisdom of the self-nature that is entirely unimpeded; the original vajra-body, neither increasing nor decreasing; the samādhi of going and coming from the body.
Furthermore, within that concentration, those sons of good family (up to: having lost right reception) shall fall into ruin.
Commentary: This clarifies that through excessive joy and tranquility, one invites demonic interference.

Because form has been exhausted and there is no longer material obstruction, and because sensation is luminous and pure, one dwells in this state with ease and pleasure, thereby giving rise to great joy.
One does not realize that the Great Matter remains unclarified—this is like losing one's parents. When the Great Matter is clarified, it is as if one has lost one's parents.
Mother, even if one dwells in pure seclusion, what joy could there be? This is because one attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) through deep concentration;

yet it is only by examining with wisdom that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are truly stilled. Wherein, then, is there sublime bliss? When the mind of joy is naturally restrained, one returns once more to faultlessness.
If you claim that the noble mind delights in the Way and ought to be thus, then demons of a similar kind will take advantage of such an interval to enter.
The mind, from this point on, indulges its passions and follows its whims, claiming to have attained great non-obstruction and realized true liberation;
having lost its own right concentration, it is bound to fall into the realm of Māra.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until) they lose their correct absorption and fall into decline.
[Commentary: This clarifies that by seeing what is superior and becoming excessively conceited, they are thereby disturbed by Māra. Those who say "I am already sufficient."

Upon seeing the exhaustion of forms, they perceive this as clarity; seeking no teacher’s seal, they claim to be self-sufficient, falsely considering themselves superior and looking down upon the sages.
Great conceit (*mahāmāna*) refers to relying on oneself to insult others and treat all things with arrogance; it is the foremost of the seven types of conceit.
The seven conceits are: reckoning oneself superior when one is inferior, and reckoning oneself equal when one is equal—these constitute simple conceit (*māna*).

To consider oneself equal to those who are superior is *adhimāna* (conceit). To consider oneself superior to those who are one's equals is *mānātimāna* (excessive conceit). To consider oneself superior to those who are actually superior is *atimāna* (over-conceit).

To claim attainment when one has not attained it, or to consider oneself superior to those who are inferior, is *abhimāna* (arrogant conceit). To possess no virtues at all [yet claim otherwise] is [the basis for such pride].

To claim one possesses virtues when one does not is false pride (*mithyāmāna*). To consider oneself inferior in the presence of those who are vastly superior, remaining disrespectful and seeking nothing from them, is the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).
If these seven types of pride arise together, one might even claim to surpass all Buddhas, let alone the followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
This stems solely from perceiving one's own spirit as uniquely noble and supreme, while lacking the wisdom to provide salvation.

This is merely due to their defects. If one were to give rise to true prajñā and contemplate the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) with equanimity, one would not even perceive a single sentient being toward whom pride could be felt;
how much less so when the aggregates have not yet been shattered and one’s practice remains inferior—how could one dare to be arrogant toward the various sages and worthies?
If one persists in delusion to the end and shows no further remorse or repentance, then a corresponding māra of pride will seize the opportunity to enter the mind;
their madness will become even more extreme, leading them even to destroy images of the Buddha—whether made of gold, copper, earth, or wood—and to claim themselves to be living Buddhas.
To disparage the scriptures as mere paper, ink, and words, while claiming one’s own words to be the true sutras— speaking such great falsehoods without shame,
misleading all others, and entering the Avīci Hell— one loses one’s own right concentration and likewise falls into ruin.
Furthermore, those good sons within that samādhi (up to) will lose their right absorption and fall into ruin. [Commentary:
This clarifies that by being self-satisfied with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), they become subject to demonic interference. Regarding "within clarity and vigor" (*jīngmíng*):

this refers to the fact that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has already dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) is about to end; hence it is called "clarity and vigor. Within this state, one also perceives sensation.

The *skandha* of form (*rūpa*) does not become defiled by external objects; therefore, it is called "perfectly awakening to the subtle principle. The *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā*) is originally but empty clarity and deluded thought;
now that this has been emptied, one perceives only the vast openness and unimpeded space within the chest. When one wishes to see, one sees; therefore, it is called "attaining great accordance.
Body and mind are both freed from coarseness and heaviness, and suddenly a lightness and ease arise, leading one to claim for oneself the attainment of sagehood.
Having attained great liberation, one no longer seeks further progress. This arises from the gradual opening of the nature of wisdom, whereby one briefly attains lightness and clarity.
In a moment of expansive awakening, one loses the support of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). From this point, by reflecting back upon oneself, one may ensure that no transgression occurs.

If, however, while seated in light and clarity, one claims to have realized the state of a sage (*ārya*), then a demon will take advantage of this interval to enter the mind, causing one to become increasingly self-limiting. Much...
Having become a monk of no learning, he not only brought himself to ruin, but also misled many others.
Furthermore, through his regret and slander of the Buddha, he ultimately lost his meditative concentration and met with a great downfall.
Furthermore, those good sons within that state of concentration (up to) shall lose their correct absorption and fall into ruin.
[Commentary: This clarifies how attachment to emptiness and the destruction of precepts lead to demonic interference.
"Within clear awakening" means to perfectly awaken to the subtle principle within the essence of clarity. "Attaining the nature of empty clarity" means perceiving that empty clarity is illusory.

The essential nature of conceptualization is fundamentally not truly existent. Because one consequently sinks into emptiness and stagnates in stillness, one suddenly lapses into annihilationism, repudiating cause and effect;
all cultivation and realization thus return to voidness, and the mind enters a deviant state, giving rise to the view of annihilation.
If one realizes that this [notion of] emptiness was originally a deviant attachment and not the realization of true emptiness, there is no fault. However, if one remains...

If one clings to the emptiness of severance (*uccheda-śūnyatā*) and takes it as a holy realization, then the demon of emptiness will enter the mind. One will then claim that drinking alcohol and eating meat are entirely empty and without fault;

that acts of lust, killing, and theft are each and every one the Way. Due to the power of this demonic influence, one causes others to feel personal trust and intimacy, even consuming both the pure and the defiled, regarding them both as equally empty.
Upon seeing those who uphold the precepts, one will single-mindedly engage in slander, leading them into error and ruin.
Many people will commit endless transgressions; they will lose their own right concentration and fall into ruin without doubt.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that state of concentration (up to the point where they) lose their right reception shall likewise descend into ruin.
Commentary: This clarifies that by becoming attached to existence and indulging in lust, one invites demonic interference. Regarding the phrase "tasting its empty clarity" and so forth:
because of the essential nature of empty clarity, one develops a deep attachment to it and refuses to let go; consequently, a mind of craving arises.
The sublime bliss within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) cannot be compared to worldly pleasures; it is experienced with sovereign mastery, such that nothing is contrary to one's will.
However, if attachment becomes excessive and leads to madness, it is inverted into craving (*rāga*).

This occurs because the object of concentration enters the mind with such peaceful conformity that, lacking the support of wisdom (*prajñā*), one erroneously falls into various desires. If one employs wisdom to investigate, one will not accept anything at all.
If one returns to right reception, then no error will be committed. If, however, one is deluded and does not turn back, the demon of desire will enter one's heart and viscera;
