one will take the preaching of desire alone as the path to Bodhi, and will even convert followers until they number in the infinite.
One must wait for the demonic mind to become weary and detach from its physical form; only then, upon rebirth, will one fall into royal peril.
Upon death, they will enter hell.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states arising during dhyāna—ranging from [the first] to maintaining and protecting [the mind] so as to achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
Commentary: This concludes the section on the dangers and the entrustment for protection. It refers to the period when the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) is about to end but has not yet ended;

one must guard against the arising of these faults. "Interchange" means the same as before. For instance, attaining radiant light, up to attaining the nature of empty clarity—all these are instances where the power of contemplation overcomes deluded thoughts.
Likewise, giving rise to inexhaustible compassion, up to the birth of limitless affection—all these are [instances of] delusion.
"Perception" refers to the power of superior contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). This, too, involves two sides clashing in battle, with the sense of victory and defeat alternating between them.
"Being deluded and unable to recognize" means not knowing from what causes and conditions the luminous, empty, and bright nature arises.

To claim one has attained the state of a sage when one has not yet attained it is to falsely claim what has not been attained; thus, it is said that a great falsehood has been committed, leading to rebirth in the Avīci Hell.
"You all, go below"—this is an entrustment for protection. This concludes the section on the signs of the māras of the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate).
"Ānanda, those good sons who cultivate samādhi [up to] take the delusion of mutual fusion as their basis.

*Commentary:* This clarifies the beginning and end of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). When the first two aggregates have been exhausted, the five sense organs and their objects no longer encounter one another;

the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are already exhausted, and the discriminating grasping at a self (*parikalpita-ātma-grāha*) is also suppressed. Nevertheless, the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) remain entirely in their innate form (*sahaja*).

Because the grasping at a self has not yet been eliminated, it is said that although the outflows have not yet been exhausted, since the first two aggregates have already ceased, one does not cling to the characteristics of the body;
thus the mind can depart from its form like a bird escaping from a cage, moving without obstruction wherever it goes.

As for the sixty stages of the sages, they begin with the three gradual steps and culminate in wondrous enlightenment, thereby manifesting perfect awakening and perfect realization without passing through the [monastic] ranks.

Therefore, it is said that one proceeds from the state of an ordinary person through the stages of the sages. As for the "mind-born body" (*manomaya-kāya*), it is named after its analogy: it moves as swiftly and without obstruction as the mind.
There are three types within the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, and many more in other scriptures; these are not cited here due to the prolixity of the texts.

Nevertheless, although the preceding aggregates (*skandhas*) have already ceased and one has attained the mind-born body, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has not yet been shattered. Furthermore—
It is like one who, though not under a spell, continues to utter somnolent speech while still in a deep sleep and has not yet awakened.
Although this person speaks of their own accord, they do not know the substance of what they say;

yet the somnolent speech they utter possesses established phonetic rhythms and a logical sequence without confusion, such that those who are not asleep can all understand its meaning. This is the analogy.
For example, regarding one whose aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) has not yet been shattered:

although such a person cannot themselves see through from beginning to end, all Buddhas of the noble stages know that this individual has already progressed through the sixty noble positions in successive order without confusion;
this is the characteristic of perception being unshattered. The sixth consciousness is the source of agitation; therefore, it conditions sensory objects.
Discrimination never ceases for even a moment, like dust and grime. The fundamentally enlightened, luminous mind is like the substance of a mirror.
When the dust and grime are cleansed, the substance of the mirror becomes bright; when the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, the luminous awareness is revealed.
Thus, one can know from where the birth of all sentient beings within the three realms comes and to where their death goes. Therefore, it is called "one class."
To illuminate the beginning and end of birth and death with perfect clarity is the sign that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted.

This aggregate of perception is precisely the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*). Because the six consciousnesses take mental objects (*dharma-ālambana*) as their conditions, they give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*) that disturb the true nature.

When this aggregate of perception is exhausted, one transcends these afflictions. Reaching this point, one looks back at the origin of the aggregate of perception; it originally arises from pervasive integration.

Delusive conceptualization: it is formed through the interweaving of delusions. This so-called aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is said to be able to harmonize and permeate that which is solid and obstructive, just as when one thinks of a sour plum, water flows from the mouth; this is what is meant.
Ānanda, when that good man’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, [he may fall into delusion and fail to realize this, thereby falling into the Avīci Hell].
(Commentary: This clarifies how attachment to the perfect clarity of the mind leads to demonic harm.

“Empty and subtle” means that he has partially attained the empty, numinous, and exquisite function within the true essence; that is, by turning the gaze back upon itself apart from the body, he attains for himself—
It exists; it differs from the previous state in that its function has not yet been attained. One does not encounter perverse thoughts, nor is one disturbed by the ten kinds of *skandha-māras*.
"The perfect concentration manifests" means that once the first two *skandhas* have been destroyed, one no longer follows the discriminations arising from external objects;
it is like turbid water settling and sinking, so that clear water appears before one. The subsequent cases are all analogous to this. The mind loves the perfection.

"Clarity and so forth" refers to the following: while within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), having attained perfect concentration and manifested illumination, one gives rise to a deluded mind that becomes attached to this perfect clarity.
Desiring to manifest sublime functions, one thus exerts oneself with vigor and sharpens one's contemplation, craving its skillful efficacy.
One’s intention is to employ great expedient means (*upāya*) to widely carry out the work of transformation and instruction. Due to this single thought of greed, the celestial Māra—
They find a fissure in the practitioner's defense and then fly forth, their essence attaching to a person. They speak the sutras and the Dharma with their own mouths to delude the practitioner.
"Flying" means rapid movement; "essence" refers to the various *piśācas* and *mārīcīs* of Māra’s faction. "Attaching to a person" means that Māra does not speak directly himself.
Furthermore, as for others who have long been possessed by malevolent spirits: because such individuals have exhausted their [karmic] retributions, their perfect wisdom and clarity are fixed;
thus, neither the preaching of the sutras and dharmas can move them, nor can inferior demons and malevolent spirits delude them. Even if it were the celestial Māra himself...

Furthermore, it cannot penetrate his heart or inner organs; therefore, it dispatches a refined demon to possess another person and delude him, thereby causing the practitioner himself to ruin his right concentration.
If that person does not realize they are possessed by a māra, then they are simply the one possessed by the demon.

Because they themselves do not know they are possessed by Māra, they speak the sūtras and the Dharma with their own mouths and even claim for themselves that they have attained realization of nirvāṇa.
Thereupon, they come before those who seek out such skillful persons and act according to whatever they desire; sometimes they preach the Dharma, and sometimes they manifest transformations of form.

They employ extensive skillful means to stir the hearts of people; these seekers of craft, having been deluded into regarding themselves as Bodhisattvas, naturally incline their minds to receive transformation.
Consequently, the concentrated mind they had cultivated is entirely shaken and agitated, and the ethical discipline they maintained is completely destroyed.
This is because whenever a practitioner is once seized by Māra and the desire-mind arises, it is due to one [of these causes].
Māra is fond of desire. This is partly because his own past karmic seeds have not been eradicated;

thus, he is frequently possessed by Māra and, having violated the precepts, is unable to escape them. However, one whose pure conduct is profound and whose wisdom is powerful can exercise unfathomable skillful means.
One need only observe that when there is seduction through lust and violation of the precepts, one knows immediately that these are the words of Pāpīyān.
This was not spoken by the Buddha. How could it be so as to unsettle the mind, violate the precepts, and cause one to become a child of Māra?

As for those who take pleasure in speaking of portents, such as calamities and auspicious signs, this refers to people possessed by Māra; their speech is strange and eccentric because it differs from ordinary discourse.
They are able to incite and delude the human mind. To say "the Buddha has appeared in the world" refers to auspicious omens; to say "the kalpa-fire and the calamity of weapons" refers to disasters.

The phrase "this is called below" specifically names and indicates the harm. "Strange ghosts" are deceitful and monstrous spirits—those so-called entities that take form by attaching themselves to objects—who only upon reaching old age begin to be driven by celestial Māras to harm those in right concentration. When they become satiated, a sense of weariness arises.
"Regarding the departure from that person's body": this means that after having attached itself for a long time, the demon or ghost becomes weary and leaves the person it has possessed.

This seeks to clarify the beginning and end of the *saṃskāra-skandha* [aggregate of formations]. First, it demonstrates the signs of the manifestation of formations when delusive perceptions have been exhausted.)

Awake and asleep, it is always one. This does not mean there is no dreaming; rather, it means that the objects of the waking state and the objects of the sleeping state are entirely without discrepancy.

Because the sixth consciousness was present prior to this [realization], during the day it functions as thought (*saṃjñā*) and at night it functions as dreams, turbidly disturbing the true nature so that it cannot remain constant.

First: When the awakening of clarity is disturbed, one is unable to remain empty and still. Once the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, the various states of both waking and sleeping are always as one, never changing or shifting;
the wondrous clarity of the nature of awakening remains凝然 (nǐngrán—congealed and still) and empty-still, never again disturbed, like a clear sky that is utterly devoid of anything.
Without the three preceding aggregates, the coarse and heavy characteristics [no longer arise].
Extinction. Since the external objects have already become empty, the evolving consciousnesses are transformed into wisdom.
Thus, one contemplates the worlds, the great earth, mountains, and rivers as being like a bright mirror reflecting various forms; mind and objects do not intersect, nor do they come or go.

It simply receives through emptiness and responds through illumination. Within the mind, there is no accumulation from the past, nor any habitual tendencies of self-grasping—there is only consciousness.
The true essence of the luminous vital source stands forth in solitary existence; this is the characteristic of the exhaustion of these perceptions.

The root-source of birth and extinction is precisely the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). Because all shifting fluxes arise from this, it is called the root-source of birth and extinction.

When the three preceding aggregates (*skandhas*) have not yet been exhausted, this root-source remains obscure and difficult to perceive; now that the three aggregates have been exhausted, [it becomes manifest].
Thus, the root source of birth and death within the three realms is revealed from this.
Because it is revealed by this, one sees that the twelve classes of beings within the realms all arise from this and likewise perish from this.

Although one has not yet fully understood their respective life-destinies and lineages, this refers to the fundamental basis of the two divisions of appearance and perception, and the seeds of the two paths of good and evil.

All these are contained within the ālayavijñāna. If one perceives the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha), then the causes and effects, merits and demerits, as well as the fundamental origins of the twelve classes of sentient beings, will all be clearly understood.
Now that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha) has been exhausted, although the aggregate of consciousness has not yet been fully penetrated, [these matters are already clear].

These are the origins by which various types of life-force are sustained. Now that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been observed, the basis for the simultaneous arising of these various types has already had its initial signs revealed.
"Like a wild horse" is a metaphor for the agitation of the aggregate of formations; it is obscure, subtle, and difficult to perceive.
"Gleaming" refers to its sudden arising and sudden ceasing, like a flickering light. "Clear agitation" refers to...
In contrast to the preceding *skandha* (āyatanas), it reveals its own lightness and clarity; in contrast to the succeeding *skandha*, it reveals its own agitation.

To say that it is "the ultimate pivot and hub for the floating sense organs and their objects" means that the arising and ceasing of the organs and objects both proceed from the movement of the *saṃskāra-skandha*.
This is what is called the "sixfold revolution," which serves as the basis for defilement and purity; this is the characteristic of the *saṃskāra-skandha* when it has not yet been exhausted. Indeed:

The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is like a great wave; the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is like subtle ripples; and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is like water without waves.
Thus, this aggregate of mental formations fundamentally lacks a real nature; it takes as its nature the sudden arising and sudden ceasing of light, clarity, and agitation.
If this nature of agitation ceases and one returns to the original essence of stillness and clarity, then the seeds and habitual tendencies of the aggregate of mental formations will be exhausted.
Furthermore, one returns to the fundamental clarity of the essence of consciousness. Therefore it is said: "It is like the subsiding of waves, which transform into clear water.

This is also the transformation of consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*). This is the sign that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted. For the eighth consciousness is fundamentally the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
it is only because of the aggregate of formations that arising and ceasing do not cease, and karmic forces constantly shift, thereby resulting in [delusion].

The perceptions and views of sentient beings turbidize their true nature; therefore, one knows that when the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, even the turbidity of sentient beings can be transcended.
Turning back here to contemplate the origin of the aggregate of formations, one finds its root lies in subtle and hidden delusive thoughts.
Because these formations shift secretly and imperceptibly, there has never been any awakening to them; hence they are called "subtle and hidden."
Ānanda, you should know that this is the attainment of right knowledge (up to the point where it is said): "this person falls into the two theories of causelessness.
[Commentary: From here below, the ten kinds of false theories within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) are clarified.

"Attainment of right knowledge" means that waking and sleeping are always one and the same, such that there are no further erroneous thoughts. "Within *śamatha*" refers to the manifestation of perfect concentration.
When concentrated, one does not waver; when clear, one does not doubt; when upright, one does not harbor deviant thoughts.
Because one applies the mind in this way, the ten classes of celestial Māras cannot find an opportunity to exploit them.

For it is when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is active that the celestial Māras are able to spy upon one’s mental activities and seek out vulnerabilities to destroy one’s right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). Once the mental consciousness has ceased, then—
External demons cannot conspire against him; they cannot even spy upon him, let alone disturb or confuse him.
Thus, the ten types [of obstacles] mentioned below are all the result of one's own mind producing calamity through false interpretations, thereby giving rise to heterodox views.

Only when one thoroughly investigates and exhaustively probes the root of all living beings—meaning that conceptualization is exhausted and demons are stilled—can one apply effort and practice, investigating and probing with precision until the ultimate limit is reached.
It is the fundamental source of the twelve classes of beings; therefore, one who can reveal the root-essence of these twelve classes does so by observing with the mind.
To observe that profound, pure, and perfectly agitated source is precisely the observation of the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Because it is more profound and subtle than the preceding *skandha* of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), which was floating, shallow, heavy, and turbid, this *skandha* of formations is revealed as being deep, subtle, light, and clear.

In contrast to this, because the subsequent consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) is profoundly still and unmoving, it reveals this activity-aggregate (saṃskāra-skandha) as the source of pervasive and circular agitation.
Taken together, they are called that which pervades all phenomena and flows on without ceasing. Hereafter, all cases shall be modeled after this.
Nevertheless, although one has observed to this extent, one still does not yet know the pure and defiled aspects within the storehouse-consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna).
...and so forth. Because of these subtle seeds, they give rise to their own divergent calculations and fall into the view of causelessness.
First, such a person perceives that there is originally no cause (up to the point where they) fall into the ways of external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
Commentary: This refers to one who perceives the flux of conditioned phenomena as impermanent and thus calculates them to be subject to annihilation.

Such a person is one for whom the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has already been exhausted. "Fundamentally without cause" means that they perceive no cause in the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). "The mechanism of birth is completely destroyed" means...

This refers to the sixth sense organ, the mind-faculty (*manas*). When the mechanism for generating successive segments is completely broken, the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is revealed.

Because the mind-faculty is completely broken, the six functions no longer operate; thus, while in meditative concentration, one relies on the merit of the eye-faculty to see clearly through eighty thousand *kalpas* of the past, observing all classes of sentient beings drifting according to their karma, dying here and being born there in a continuous cycle.
It is uninterrupted; this is precisely the basis for the simultaneous arising [of all things]. Eighty thousand kalpas ago, it was dark and invisible.
One falsely calculates that this dark state, having no object of observation, is "spontaneity" or "creation," and so forth, yet one does not realize that these are merely one's own views.
They are unable to transcend this state. Yet they maintain that all sentient beings have existed spontaneously from before eighty thousand kalpas, without cause.

By such conceptualization, they fail to realize that the seeds of birth and extinction still reside within the *ālayavijñāna*, and thus they cannot transform the *ālayavijñāna* into the *ādarśajñāna*.
Therefore, it is said that they have lost right and universal knowledge (*samyak-sarvajñatā*) and sit idly guarding this [delusion]. Furthermore...
They do not advance. They recognize this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as being the path of spontaneity and so forth;
thus, they are unable to transform birth and death into nirvāṇa, nor can they transform afflictions into bodhi. Therefore, their white delusions obscure the nature of bodhi.
Second, this person perceives that the end has no cause (up to the point where) the first type of externalist establishes the doctrine of causelessness.
[Corresponding] Commentary: "Perceiving the seeking of no-cause" means observing that there is no cause for the future limit (*aparānta*).
Regarding the phrase "Why is this? and what follows: this is based on the origin to infer the end. "Having already perceived its root within birth" refers to the twelve classes of beings.

Observing eighty thousand kalpas ago, one finds that all was merely produced spontaneously without cause. Knowing that humans arise from beneath the human realm, it becomes clear through detailed examination that everything is fundamentally causeless and occurs naturally.
Thus, they are able to formulate their calculations and name themselves "Nihilists" (Prakṛtivādins).
Now, within this present form, we are precisely refuting their doctrine of ultimate causelessness. It is just as when I observe eighty thousand kalpas [and find no beginning].
Previously, from the very beginning, one did not perceive the existence of sentient beings arising from the nature of Bodhi.

How could there be a further matter of attaining Bodhi after eighty thousand kalpas? This is entirely because one perceives this common basis of birth and consequently clings to it as the root of sentient beings, remaining unaware that each life has its own distinct causal continuity. If one can exert effort...

Proceeding forward, one causes the functioning of consciousness to reach its limit and manifest; thus, one is able to discern the origins of each individual life. How could one then persistently cling to the notion of spontaneity (*svabhāva*)?
"One should know" and below clarify that fixed attachment constitutes a false view. According to the old interpretation, this refers to the term "fundamental" (*ben*).

This corresponds to the character "ma" (末), meaning that when eighty thousand kalpas have ended, all things ultimately undergo annihilation, such that cause and effect no longer exist. The remaining points should be understood according to what precedes.

Ānanda, these are the various sons of good family within the *samādhi* [who fall into the views of] the second class of non-Buddhists who establish the doctrine of pervasive permanence (*yuan-chang*).

Commentary: This refers to perceiving the incessant flux of transformation and calculating it to be pervasive and eternal. "Stable clarity," "rectifying the mind," and so forth are the same as before.
To speak of "pervasive agitation" and "pervasive eternity" is to perceive the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) as a continuous, uninterrupted succession.

Therefore, they conceive of permanence. Because they see the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) pervading all phenomena, they conceive of it as being "round" or pervasive. Combining these two views, they call it "pervasive-permanence" and "agitation.
Thus, they fall into the four theories of pervasive permanence. First, [the theory of] "below": they conceive that both the mind and its objects are permanent.
This is because they have not yet perceived the eighth consciousness and thus do not understand the dual nature of the mind and its objects; this is the eighth [consciousness].
Regarding the two aspects of consciousness—the perceived and the perceiving—one merely attains the exhaustion of conceptualization and the manifestation of mental formations.

Relying upon this insight and practicing accordingly, one eventually investigates the dual nature of mind and objects as to how they arise. However, because the scope of such vision is limited, one cannot exhaustively penetrate it to its furthest extent.
He perceives only back to twenty thousand kalpas; prior to this, there is existence without cause, and beyond twenty thousand kalpas, he sees nothing in the darkness.

Consequently, he calculates that because all sentient beings undergo an uninterrupted cycle of arising and ceasing within these twenty thousand kalpas, he does not consider the period beyond the kalpas to be a state of annihilation due to the absence of cause.
Instead, he calculates only the continuity within the kalpas as being universal and eternal. This is why he differs from the former [view].
Second, the view that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are all eternal. This, too, is a practitioner who, relying on their own views and understanding, seeks the source of transformation.

Seeing that all phenomena are formed through the combination of the four great elements, they reckon that the essential nature (*dhātu*) of these four elements has been eternally abiding from the beginning.
They fail to realize, however, that these arise as transformations of the mind of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), and thus their nature is fundamentally empty. Therefore, [they rely on this].

This practice takes [the perceived] as eternally abiding. However, because the scope of one's vision is limited, one perceives that within forty thousand kalpas, although sentient beings undergo birth and extinction, their essential nature is eternally constant. This, too, takes what is seen within a specific number of kalpas to be perfect and eternal.
Third, at the lower level, one calculates that all eight consciousnesses are eternal; "six sense organs" refers here to the first six consciousnesses.
*Manas* refers to the seventh consciousness. *Upādāna* (appropriation) refers to the eighth consciousness.

This is because the practitioner, relying on their own insight, exhaustively investigates the fundamental source of mind, thought, and consciousness; its nature is fundamentally eternal and constant. Although both the sixth and eighth are mentioned together, the emphasis is placed solely on the seventh.
This is simply because the eighth is the internal supporting faculty (*āśraya-mūla*) for the seventh, while the sixth is [the object] of the seventh.
Beyond these, there is the root-faculty (*indriya*) upon which they depend; since seven [of the aggregates] abide therein, they are mentioned together.

The two phrases "the fundamental source" and "the locus of origin" refer exclusively to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because it is able to be constant and able to be discerning, it is said that its nature is eternally constant.
By practicing in reliance upon this, one can observe that within eighty thousand kalpas, all sentient beings die here and are born there, yet their fundamental nature remains eternally abiding.
Little do they realize that this is precisely the root-source of arising and ceasing;

yet within the eighth consciousness, even the subtle, continuous flow has not been perceived, let alone the eternally abiding true nature. From "Fourth" onwards, they reckon all conceptualization to be eternal.
The "source of perception" (*saṃjñā-mūla*) is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). The "principle of arising" (*utpāda-dharma*) is the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

"There is no further flowing, ceasing, or movement" means that once the aggregate of perception has been exhausted, the aggregate of mental formations does not arise as manifest activity (*samudācāra*).

Although the seeds of the flow [of consciousness] still remain within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), the practitioner, being unaware of this, merely observes the cessation of the perceiving mind and falsely claims that birth and extinction have forever ceased.
When cessation occurs, the principle of neither-arising-nor-ceasing is naturally accomplished. How could one know that the root of arising and ceasing lies precisely within this?
It is only because it is subtle and difficult to perceive that, amidst the causes of arising and ceasing, one falsely calculates them to be the fruit of permanent abiding.
These four types all calculate subtle arising and ceasing to be the perfect, true, and eternal; they fall entirely [into error].
These are the followers of the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Furthermore, [the passage] from "Again, within *samādhi*, these good sons... up to "the third type of non-Buddhist, the partial doctrine of permanence" [is explained].
*Annotation:* This refers to the dualistic calculation of both permanence and impermanence. "Self" refers to one's own body; "others" refers to sentient beings.
Regarding the "realms": this arises because practitioners, within the basis of co-arising, investigate the causes for the arising of themselves and others;

yet, failing to realize that within right concentration all phenomena are ultimately and firmly established as such, they instead rely upon the root of birth and cessation to conceptualize permanence and impermanence, thereby forming four inverted views. First, regarding oneself... [text truncated]

In other places, they calculate [the self] as either permanent or impermanent. "Observing the wondrously luminous mind pervading the worlds of the ten directions" refers to their meditative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
However, that which is being observed is actually the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), yet they falsely claim it to be the wondrously luminous true mind.
To regard this as a serene and ultimate divine self (*ātman*) precisely clarifies the arising of such calculations. This is also due to their failure to understand the *saṃskāra-skandha*.
This serves as the root for birth and extinction. They falsely claim that the nature of the mind is profoundly still and take this to be the "divine self" (*ātman*).
As for what is called the "divine self," it is the final of the twenty-five *tattvas* (principles).

Those who calculate based on this [notion] of a self do so because they reckon that there exists a true self that pervades the ten directions, is lucid and immovable, and is without birth or extinction; therefore, it is eternal and unitary.

All sentient beings are born and die within my own mind; therefore, they are impermanent. Second, there is the reckoning of the three calamities and the places where they do not reach as being either permanent or impermanent.
This arises from failing to contemplate one's own mind and instead contemplating only the physical realm:
everything from the third dhyāna downward is reckoned as impermanent because it is a place reached by the three calamities, whereas from the fourth dhyāna upward...
The above concerns the perception of permanence regarding those places not reached by the three calamities; this is the contemplation based on the *niśraya-vipāka* (the external environment).
Below follows the contemplation based on the *sattva-vipāka* (the sentient being). Thirdly, below that, one calculates whether one’s own body and mind are permanent or impermanent.

Because the body is coarse while the mind is subtle, one contemplates the self-mind separately as being refined, subtle, and secret, circulating throughout the ten directions, yet its nature is without... [impermanence].
Because it changes, one regards it as permanent; yet because it causes the self to exist within the mind and undergoes the transformation and decay of birth and death, it is impermanent.
Fourth, below this, one contemplates the four aggregates (*skandhas*) to reckon upon permanence and impermanence.

Having observed that the first three aggregates have already ceased, one reckons them as impermanent; observing this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one sees its present flux and movement, which never ceases.
Because they perceive [the self] as being at rest, they reckon it to be permanent. From this point downward, the external treatises are concluded.

Although these four types all dualistically reckon both permanence and impermanence, they cling exclusively to permanence as being truly existent; therefore, they are called only "Theories of Partial Permanence."
Furthermore, among the various good sons within *samādhi* (up to) the fourth heterodox school who establish the theory of finitude.
[Commentary: This pair posits both finitude and infinitude. There are four stages:

namely, the stage of the three periods of time, the stage of seeing and hearing, the stage of self and other, and the stage of arising and ceasing. First, regarding the [first]... with respect to the three [periods of time].

This refers to calculating whether there is a limit or no limit. As for "the mind calculates that the source of birth flows and functions without ceasing," it means observing that the root-source of living beings currently undergoes a shifting flow without rest;
consequently, one calculates that what has passed in the past has already been extinguished.
That which comes has not yet arrived; therefore, it is considered finite. Calculating the continuity of the present, it has never been interrupted;

therefore, it is considered infinite. This is an observation of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) by dividing it into the three time periods. Second, below, it is discussed in terms of seeing and hearing.

This is based on calculating whether there is a limit or no limit. That is to say, when observing within eighty thousand kalpas, because sentient beings can be seen and heard, one calculates that there is a limit, as they are restricted by the number eighty thousand.
When observing beyond eighty thousand kalpas, because no sentient beings are seen and no sentient beings are heard, one calculates that there is no limit, as they are absent.

Regarding quantity: that which is invisible and inaudible is considered finite, while that which is visible and audible in the present is considered infinite; these two views are mutually contradictory.
This sufficiently demonstrates that the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) hold conflicting and inverted calculations, lacking any settled view. Third, below, they calculate based on "self" and "other."
There is the view that [the world] is finite or infinite. This arises because the practitioner, observing their own aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), clings to it as a true self.

Furthermore, they falsely reckon that this self is all-pervasive and capable of complete knowledge, asserting that among all phenomena, they alone have attained the nature of the infinite, and that all sentient beings manifest within the sphere of their own nature. Yet, as for myself and others—
Within one's own nature, one has never seen a separate cognitive nature belonging to those other sentient beings. Consequently, one reckons that their nature cannot exist outside of one's own nature;
thus, it is not an infinite nature, but is merely termed a finite nature. This is precisely the grasping at a self within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
How could one know that within the fundamentally equal *tathatā* (suchness), there has from the beginning been no such thing as "person" or "self"?
Is it nature? Fourth, "the lower" refers to calculating whether there is a limit or no limit based on arising and ceasing.

This person, having exhausted the emptiness of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations), calculates that there is partial arising and partial ceasing. This is because this *saṃskāra-skandha* originally lacks a fundamental nature;

previously it relied upon the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception) as its root, and subsequently it will rely upon the *vijñāna-skandha* (aggregate of consciousness) as its root. Now that the *saṃjñā-skandha* has already ceased, the *vijñāna-skandha* is about to...

Manifesting, this first half of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) has already ceased along with perception (saṃjñā), while its second half still arises together with consciousness (vijñāna).
Therefore, based on what they themselves perceive, practitioners falsely reckon that within the bodies of sentient beings it is also the same as within their own bodies:
one half belongs to arising and one half belongs to ceasing. Furthermore, seeing that the aggregate of formations pervades all things, they consequently...
They judge all phenomena in the world such that those half which arise constitute the finite, while those half which cease constitute the infinite.

From this point downward, the external doctrines are concluded. Although these [doctrines] dualistically calculate both existence and non-existence, they take only the finite as supreme because it is the Primal Nature (prakṛti);
therefore, they are simply called the proponents of the doctrine of finitude.
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi... [up to] "the immortal, evasive, and confused proliferation of empty sophistry. (Annotated:
This calculates four types of evasive confusion. The previous calculations of permanence and impermanence, or finitude and infinity, were merely dualistic reckonings and not evasive confusion.
This calculation, however, involves both arising and ceasing, as well as both existence and non-existence.)
To claim that "existence is itself non-existence" and that within non-existence there is not existence—this is a uniform perversion and confusion, and is especially inverted.
Those who harbor conceptual calculations regarding knowledge and vision do so by making inverted assessments based on what is known and seen within their meditative states.
Because of this false inversion, they develop a frantic, indecisive understanding regarding knowledge and vision.

Thus, they distort and confuse their discourse. First, regarding the "lower": by means of a single life-cycle within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), one analyzes it according to eight meanings, thereby calculating eight kinds of distortions and confusions.
The source of transformation is precisely the *saṃskāra-skandha*. One observes the place where the flow of preceding and succeeding moments is incessant and calculates this to be "change.
One observes the continuity between the preceding and succeeding [moments] as being uninterrupted.
Regarding the locus [of existence], they reckon it to be permanent. Regarding the locus presently perceived, they reckon it to be arising;
regarding the loci of the past and future which are not perceived, they reckon them to be ceasing. They take arising as the causal nature of ceasing, and ceasing as the causal nature of arising;
thus, arising and arising, ceasing and ceasing, proceed without interruption. Regarding this, they reckon it to be increasing. As for that which is currently arising...

It does not reach the place of cessation. Because that which is truly ceasing does not reach the place of birth, yet within this process of arising and ceasing, there is a point of departure which one reckons as "diminution.
One reckons that which arises in every thought-moment as "existence," and that which ceases in every thought-moment as "non-existence.
To observe through principle all of these eight meanings is to comprehensively contemplate the single aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Furthermore, regarding those who apply their minds with partial views: this refers to generating eight distinct interpretations within the single aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Because they lack a settled view of their own, whenever they encounter a question regarding a principle, they respond with evasive and confused speech, causing the interlocutor’s understanding of the doctrine to remain unclear and preventing a definitive resolution between right and wrong. Consequently, they end up discarding their former habitual teachings all at once.

[This] is a loss, for one has forfeited what they maintain. Second, there is no calculating or artificial confusion below [this level]. Contemplate the mind with clarity; this is precisely the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
Regarding "each and every one having no locus": it means that when a thought is in the process of arising, there is no characteristic of cessation;

when a thought is in the process of ceasing, there is no characteristic of arising. From this, one realizes that all things are non-existent. Thus, when encountering people who inquire about the meaning [of the Dharma],...
He answers only that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are non-existent. Third, the inferior [type] is characterized by evasive sophistry (*vibhrama*). Regarding "each has its own place":
this means that after a thought arises, there must necessarily be the characteristic of cessation; after a thought ceases, there must necessarily be the characteristic of arising.
From this, he realizes that everything exists. Thus, when encountering someone who asks about the meaning [of reality], he answers only that all phenomena exist. This is...
This means "it exists. Fourth, "below" refers to the sophistry of reckoning existence and non-existence.
"Seeing both existence and non-existence" means that one perceives both the point at which each momentary thought arises and the point at which each momentary thought ceases.
Regarding the phrase "because its object is manifold," it means that since the observed object is indeterminate, the observing mind is likewise indeterminate. Thus, there is a questioner.

He replied: "That which 'both exists' is precisely that which 'also does not exist,' because that which arises must inevitably return to extinction. That which 'also does not exist' is not 'also exists,' because that which has been extinguished cannot arise again. The old commentary states that to be stubborn and perverse is to be contrary to principle, and for the mind to lack a central focus is to be in disorder. Now, examining the words of the first and fourth [positions]: * **The First:** Claims that all things both exist and do not exist. This is a distortion of the truth; it is like a person who, having lost their way, points in the opposite direction and claims they are on the right path. * **The Fourth:** Claims that all things neither exist nor do not exist. This is a state of mental confusion; it is like a person who, having lost their way, abandons the path entirely and wanders aimlessly in the wilderness. Thus, these two views are both erroneous. They are like a person who, having lost their way, either points toward the wrong direction or abandons the path altogether. Both fail to reach the true destination. In all these cases, the confusion of the mind through dualistic "both-and" positions is predominant; yet in the end, they do not accord with principle and are also characterized by artificiality (*kauṭilya*).

Regarding the second and third types of speech, there is primarily an abundance of one-sided artificiality; yet in the end, they do not establish what is correct, as they likewise result in confusion.
Thus, in summary, all forms of artificial confusion cannot withstand exhaustive scrutiny. From this point downward, the heterodox doctrines are concluded.
"Vanity" refers to the absence of genuine virtue within, resulting in deceptive and confused speech.
"Perversion" refers to a lack of truth in one's vision of the Truths (satya), whereby one loses right concentration. "Immortality" refers to the inconsistency of one's utterances.
"Universal speculative discourse" refers to pervasive conceptualization that entirely lacks the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi).
Furthermore, among the various good sons within *samādhi* (up to) the post-mortem theories of those with inverted minds regarding signs. [Commentary:
This calculates sixteen signs regarding the future limit (*aparānta*). "Inexhaustible flow" refers to the sign of the shifting and flowing of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
This arises from perceiving that the flow-sign of the aggregate of formations is inexhaustible, and thus includes the three aggregates previously already extinguished.
All these involve calculating that there is a characteristic [of self] after death, thereby giving rise to inverted views.
These are precisely four of the sixty-two views held by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). "To cling firmly to the body" means to tenaciously grasp at the physical form (*rūpakāya*).

"The self" refers to the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, which the seventh consciousness grasps as the internal self. "Form" refers to the appearance-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, and...

The preceding seven consciousnesses grasp at external objects as real; this is entirely due to practitioners’ ignorance of the source and its development, leading them to engage in successive layers of false attachment.
First: "Form is the self. This reckons that form itself is the self. Second: "The self contains the lands; I have form.

This reckons that the self is large while form is small, and that form exists within the self. Third: [The self is contained within form. This reckons that the self is small while form is large, and that the self exists within form.

Regarding the phrase "the preceding conditions follow me, such that form belongs to me": "preceding conditions" refers to the forms and appearances currently before one's eyes. "Returning" refers to their functional application.
Since it says "belongs to me," this clearly indicates that [form] is *mama* (mine) and not *ātman* (the self). This calculation posits that the self is distinct from form.
Fourth, regarding the statement "I abide in form" within the section on the self depending on formations (*saṃskāra*): "formations" refers to the characteristic of continuity. That is to say...

This is form (*rūpa*). Herein, one conceives that the self is great and form is small, or that the self dwells within form. As it is with the aggregate of form, so it is with the other three aggregates.
Because there are signs prior to the arising of the present life, one infers that there are likewise signs after death.
From this point downward, through successive false reckonings, one thinks: "Since I know the four aggregates to be permanent, I must know all things—both defiled and pure—to be likewise."
This is the nature of all phenomena; there is nothing that is not thus. Therefore, it is reckoned that afflictions (*kleśa*) and bodhi are ultimately inexhaustible and eternally present.
"Driving side by side" means proceeding together in the world. "Each does not touch the other" means each does not obstruct the other.

The meaning is this: since the status of ordinary person and sage is already fixed, there is absolutely no principle whereby an ordinary person could be transformed into a sage, or defilement could be turned into purity.
From this point downward, the external treatises are concluded. This collectively concludes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), yet it specifically pertains to the first four persons.
Although they appear among the first four, in meaning they refer exclusively to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Furthermore, among the various good sons within *samādhi* (up to) the post-mortem discourse on the inversion of the signless mind.
[Commentary: This reckoning concerns eight kinds of signlessness regarding the future limit (*aparānta*).

This arises from observing that the preceding three aggregates (*skandha*) have already ceased and are signless, and thereby inferring that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) will ultimately return to signlessness. Its form is like a single body; its color is like...
Because there are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), we know that form (*rūpa*) exists by depending on color (*varṇa*). If color ceases, then form has nothing upon which to depend.

Perception (*saṃjñā*) is like the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the mind (*citta*) is like the mental faculty (*manas*). Therefore, we know that the mind is bound by depending on perception.

If perception ceases, then the mind has nothing upon which to be bound. Color precedes sensation (*vedanā*), and the mind follows sensation; with sensation situated in between, it links together both color and mind.
Therefore, when there is no reception [of sensation], then form and mind are no longer linked.

Since the natures of the first three aggregates have already been dissolved and dispersed, even if the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) still exists—though it is a physiological process—it will cease. Where could the preceding aggregates rely for support?
They too return to annihilation. This is how, by taking the three aggregates as a basis, one applies the principle to the aggregate of formations to decisively know its annihilation. Now, observe:
This body in the present does not even possess the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*); how then could it have such characteristics after death?

Both the present and the future are entirely without characteristics. Thus, the four aggregates together constitute eight kinds of signlessness (*animitta*). This, moreover, refers to the period before birth.

By inferring from after death, one definitively knows that there is no [self] with characteristics (*animitta*). From this point downward, furthermore, based on the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), one infers up to *nirvāṇa*;
thus, all dharmic characteristics of cause and effect ultimately revert to annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*). From this point downward, the external treatise is concluded.

According to the traditional explanation, this opposes the aforementioned calculation because its essence is diametrically opposed; it transforms existence into non-existence, which is the "above" (*ūrdhva*).

Beholding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that has not yet ceased, one sees it as inexhaustible; consequently, one reckons that the preceding three aggregates and all phenomena are likewise inexhaustible.
Beholding the three aggregates that have already ceased, one sees them as signless (*animitta*);
consequently, one reckons that the aggregate of formations and all phenomena are likewise signless.
Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi* (up to) the post-mortem discourse on the "neither-existence-nor-non-existence" of the inverted mind. [Commentary:
This calculation involves eight kinds of "neither-existences. "While the activity-aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) remains" means they perceive that the activity-aggregate has not yet been exhausted.

"Simultaneously with the cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā* and *saṃjñā*)" means they perceive that the [other] three aggregates have already been exhausted. "Dually calculating existence and non-existence" refers to...
To reckon existence regarding that which persists, and to reckon non-existence regarding that which has ceased;

as for the phrase "the intrinsic nature and characteristics are mutually sublated," this means that by using the present existence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) to sublate the prior non-existence of the [first] three aggregates, one knows that what was called "non-existent" was originally existent, and thus it is established as not being non-existent.
By using the prior non-existence of the [first] three aggregates to sublate the present existence of the aggregate of formations, one knows that what was called "existent" is...

In the end, they return to non-existence; thus, they are established as being "not-existent. From this, one falls into the inverted doctrine that after death both [existence and non-existence] are absent.

This explains how the intrinsic nature and characteristics are refuted. The meaning is this: within the three aggregates (*skandha*) that have already ceased, one contemplates the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that has not yet ceased.
Although it currently exists, it will ultimately perish along with the three aggregates and is therefore not-existent. While in a state of flux...

Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one contemplates that although the three [other] aggregates have already ceased and are thus non-existent, they once coexisted with the aggregate of formations and were therefore not non-existent.
In this way, by thoroughly investigating the four aggregates across the two realms of birth and death, one ultimately calculates eight "neither-nor" characteristics (*ubhayathā-anirodha*).

Consequently, whichever single aggregate is cited, it is all said to be "neither existent nor non-existent" after death. Furthermore, regarding the calculation of all formations and so forth, it means:

Not only are the four aggregates all "neither," but these myriad phenomena are likewise identical in their nature of constant flux. As they interact, they mutually subvert one another, such that there is nothing that is not "neither.
Therefore, it is said that the mind gives rise to universal awakening. Regarding the phrase "neither void nor substantial":
because non-existence is itself not non-existent, one cannot call it void; because existence is itself not existent, one cannot call it substantial. It is for this reason that...
Regarding "reckoning and so forth": this means that by taking the state of being alive as an analogy for what follows after death, one concludes that it is neither existent nor non-existent.
However, since the period after death extends to the end of the future, being a realm of profound obscurity difficult to fathom, one cannot say it exists, nor can one say it does not exist;
thus, it is inexpressible in either way. This is because one has not yet perceived the eight consciousnesses and has not realized the root of birth and death. Not yet...
Because they revolve the mirror-like wisdom, they do not perceive the nature of Bodhi; they merely speculate for themselves and have newly composed external treatises.

How could this be anything other than a perversion? Furthermore, [this refers to] the theory of the cessation and annihilation of the mind after death held by certain sons of good family within samādhi... [up to] ...their perverted views.

Commentary: This refers to the calculation of annihilation at seven locations. According to the ancient explanation, one perceives that within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), there is cessation from moment to moment;

this is termed "subsequent non-existence. Based on this, they falsely calculate that even if one is born into the seven locations of humans or devas, one will ultimately be annihilated in all of them.

Regarding those who calculate the extinction of the body and so forth: because these practitioners perceive only obscure and hidden delusions that are fundamentally not substantial entities, yet undergo a cycle of arising and ceasing that does not transcend the seven limits (*sapta-koṭi*).
Once one leaves these seven limits, they no longer perceive the nature of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
What they do not realize is that the subsequent aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is still the deep-seated channel of the aggregate of formations. And...
When karma is exhausted, consciousness manifests; it does not stop at merely observing these seven limits. The seven limits are:

the four continents, the six heavens of the desire realm, the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the four formless attainments. When the body perishes, this refers specifically to humans and devas within the desire realm.
The exhaustion of desire corresponds to the first dhyāna; the exhaustion of suffering corresponds to the second dhyāna; extreme bliss corresponds to the third dhyāna;

and extreme equanimity corresponds to the fourth dhyāna, as well as the four formless attainments of the emptiness realm. "Dissolving and extinguishing before one's eyes" means that once the three aggregates have ceased, the aggregate of formations likewise does so.
When these seven locations are all manifest as severed and extinguished, the principle of birth and death is forever non-existent; how could there be any future rebirth?
This concerns the matter of birth. From here downward, the external treatise is concluded. The general summary of the meaning of the five aggregates is the same as before.
Furthermore, regarding the various good sons within *samādhi* (up to) "the mind that perceives the five [aggregates] as nirvāṇa," this is the inverted theory.

Commentary: This calculates the nirvana within the five aggregates of existence (*pañca-skandha*). "Subsequent existence" refers to the locus where the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) arises moment by moment.
This is because one observes that the aggregate of formations is uninterrupted from moment to moment, such that existence is newly constituted at every instant;

therefore, one calculates this existence to be real, concluding that as a result, it will certainly not reach non-existence. The term "perhaps" (*huòrě*) is an indefinite expression. "Desire realm" (*yùjiè*) is stated generally.

The "six desires" do not refer to a single heaven. For one who is correctly effecting the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), because they perceive the common ground of birth within the desire realm, they falsely claim that all principles of life are contained therein.
Consequently, they delusively reckon this as the transformation of birth-and-death into nirvana.

As for "perceiving the perfect luminosity": this means that once the aforementioned aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted, the perfect concentration gives rise to illumination.
It is like using the divine eye to survey the celestial radiance, which is pure, brilliant, and far surpasses the filth and turbidity of the human world;
thus, one conceives a longing for it and reckons this realm to be the manifest nirvana.
Or, those in the first dhyāna reckon the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion to be the manifest nirvana. Or, those in the second dhyāna reckon the joy born of concentration [to be so].

The "Land of Joy" (Sukhāvatī) is manifested as Nirvāṇa. According to the traditional explanation, based on the preceding text, it is appropriate to order them such that the first dhyāna is not oppressed by suffering, and the second dhyāna is not oppressed by anxiety, because suffering is heavy while anxiety is light. Now, however, it is said that the first dhyāna is without anxiety and the second dhyāna is without suffering;
this is likely a mistranslation or a reversal of the terms. Alternatively, some may calculate the third dhyāna as being free from joy.
The "Land of Wondrous Joy" is manifested as *nirvāṇa*. "Utmost delight and compliance" refers to the complete perfection of joy and the possession of great accordance (*anuloma*).
Alternatively, by means of the four *dhyānas*, the stage of the purity of equanimity and mindfulness is manifested as *nirvāṇa*.
With both suffering and pleasure extinguished, one cannot be moved by worldly suffering or pleasure, and does not undergo rebirth in *saṃsāra*.

As for "extinction" (*nirodha*): it is that which is not reached by the three calamities. All of these [beings] are deluded regarding the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and take it to be the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
they mistake saṃsāra for nirvāṇa. This arises because, having somewhat departed from the unrest of the lower realms, they falsely reckon the five abodes to be secure;
and having somewhat departed from the defilement of the lower realms, they falsely reckon the five abodes to be supremely pure. To speak of them as "ultimate" [is a misconception].
This refers to the reckoning that these five locations are all states of ultimate fruition. From this point downward, the external treatise is concluded.
Regarding "the five [views of] nirvana in the present," this refers to the reckoning that these five locations are all nirvana in the present, wherein one currently experiences its bliss.
This is because it does not depend on a future life.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded understandings regarding *dhyāna* (up to) the point where one acts as a Great Awakened King and points toward purity. [Commentary:

This concludes the instruction on the harm and the entrustment for protection. According to the old commentary: what was previously called "the manifestation of realms in *dhyāna*" refers to the heavens.
Māra seizes upon such opportunities. This is what is called "mad enlightenment" (*cīna-kṣānti*)—the deep affliction arising spontaneously from the mind-demon (*citta-māra*).

Whenever one's realization of the Way is not authentic, and various divergent paths of deluded views arise, these are all instances of mad enlightenment; this is termed the mind-demon and must be guarded against with the utmost care.
When the mind functions in a conflicted manner, as previously described, this manifestation of "awakening" is precisely the arising of mad enlightenment within the mind. [The assembly...]
Regarding the phrase "born with stubborn delusion," etc.: it means that their mental nature is obstinate and ignorant, such that they cannot attain correct awakening.

Their knowledge and vision are confused, and they easily give rise to perverse interpretations. Without considering at what stage of cultivation and realization they themselves reside, they dare to decide for themselves and rashly compose this treatise.
Furthermore, by presumptuously assuming the title of a holy office, they commit a great falsehood and fall into the heavy hells.
This is appropriate. "You all, descend" is a formal injunction for protection. "To realize this meaning" means to clearly distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.
"Do not let" is a word of prohibition. "Do not give rise to deep calamities" means that external demons shall not cause disturbance.
All these are the calamities wrought by the demons of one’s own mind. "Calamity" (*nie*) refers to the sprouting of misfortune; it also carries the sense of being cut down only to grow back again.
The two phrases regarding "maintaining" mean to prevent what has not yet arisen from arising, and to cause what has already arisen to cease.
"Ultimate meaning" (*zhenyi*) refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which stands far beyond the four propositions and the hundred negations.
Regarding those who do not encounter byways on the unsurpassed path, it refers to these ten kinds [of pride].

Within the unsurpassed right path, they are like the lateral branches of a tree or the diverging tracks of a road; none of them constitute the fundamental essence. "Seeking greatness" (*qida*) refers to the false arrogance of a deviant mind.

Indeed, encountering such byways and false arrogance leads one to fall into the paths of externalists (*tīrthika*). To consider a small attainment as sufficient likewise leads to falling [into error].
Therefore, he entrusts this to the immediate recipient to serve as a guiding finger for sentient beings toward the Great Awakened King,
so that they may proceed directly to the ultimate fruit and not abandon their path midway.
"Ānanda, those good men who cultivate *samādhi* [up to] take inverted delusions as their foundation. (Commentary:
This seeks to demonstrate the beginning and end of the *vijñāna-skandha*. First, it clarifies the signs of the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* and the manifestation of the *vijñāna-skandha*.)

The nature of all worlds refers to the twelve categories of sentient beings; it is the essential nature of their migratory flow. "Commonality of birth" (*sabhāgatā*) refers to the common ground of birth.

"Ground" (*ji*) reveals the locus where beings arise; "bench" (*ji*) clarifies the beginning of movement. As for the "subtle, deep net-knot": *(Note: This is a partial translation based on the provided fragment. The full passage likely continues with further definitions regarding the subtle, deep net-knot, which in this context refers to the fundamental substrate of consciousness and the mechanism of karmic entanglement.)*
This refers to that obscure and hidden deluded thought; it is precisely the axle-pin of birth and cessation.

Because one’s prior doubt regarding clarity has been resolved through the true mind, and one's practice has reached its ultimate depth, the deep-seated and subtle root of the life-force mechanism suddenly collapses and shatters.
*Pudgala* (person) is translated as "one who repeatedly takes up existence," referring to the *antarābhava* (intermediate state body).

Once the life-force and its binding cords have been shattered and torn asunder, then the deep channels through which the various realms of the triple world repay past karma—whereby causes evoke their corresponding effects—are all suspended, severed, and cut off.
This is the mark of the exhaustion of conditioned existence (*kṣayabhāva*). Now, the nature of *nirvāṇa* is the celestial realm...
Enveloped by the five aggregates (*skandha*), one sinks and revolves within birth and death, as dark as a long night. Thus, know that the exhaustion of each aggregate is like the crowing of a cock;
this is because once birth and death have been severed, the sky of the nature of *nirvāṇa* is about to break into great illumination, like the subsequent crowing of the cock.
Beholding the sky of the nature, it is as if the eastern horizon already possesses a subtle radiance; yet there remains but one final aggregate.
It is simply that clarity has not yet been fully penetrated. However, when there is the practice of grasping at a self, the six sense-faculties run wild;

when the practice exhausts the emptiness of self, the six faculties become empty and still, no longer running wild. Moving from activity back into stillness, it becomes deeper and deeper; hence it is said, "Internally and internally, there is profound clarity.
When the internal faculties are empty and still, external objects do not enter; hence it is said, "Entering, there is nowhere to enter. [Roots and objects...]
Once it has dissolved, the pivot-socket is also broken, whereupon the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna* is revealed from this point on;

thus, the fundamental source by which the twelve classes of beings receive their life-force becomes entirely clear. How could this be like the *saṃskāra-skandha*, where the various threads of individual life-forces remain unpenetrated?
Once the pivotal hole is broken, one is able to perceive the threads of life and destiny; once the flux of change has ceased, one is likewise able to [perceive the ultimate].
One maintains the fundamental source of sentient beings; when the life-force is exhausted, one no longer summons various classes of beings to undergo rebirth.
Thereupon, the obstacle of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*) is severed, and the universally pervasive true suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*) is realized.

One directly perceives the two retributions—the environment and its inhabitants—of the ten directions as arising from the same consciousness. At this point, the Heaven of the First Perception of Nature already possesses a refined radiance, which is not the same as what preceded it.
In a state of drowsiness, one lacks discernment. Yet, that which is revealed and manifested remains the profound and secret aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Beholding the sky of its nature is like the break of dawn; it has not yet reached midday. This is the sign that the aggregate of consciousness has not yet been shattered.
Since one does not summon rebirth among the various classes of beings, yet attains identity with them throughout the ten directions—if, furthermore...
By applying diligent practice, one grinds away the seeds of the six gates, causing them to either merge or open at will until they are fully accomplished.
Thus, the six faculties become adjacent to one another, all capable of mutual penetration and interchangeability.

The world, the body, and the mind become like *vaiḍūrya* crystal, transparent both inside and out, perfectly realizing the essence of purity and luminosity that eradicates the obscure and secret nature of karma. This consciousness—
The destruction of the *skandha* (aggregate) is its characteristic sign. For the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally without birth or extinction;
yet, regarding the origins of receiving life, it is merely that the preceding seven consciousnesses perfume the *ālayavijñāna*, causing it to grasp and maintain all seeds of defilement and purity.
This muddies the true nature, whereby one is led by karma to receive life within the various realms of existence. When this *vijñāna-skandha* is exhausted, the turbidity of life ceases.
How transcendent! To reflect back upon the origin of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*), one finds that it fundamentally arises from the formless and the void.

Perverted and deluded conceptualization constitutes its root. This "formless and void" refers to that which is hazy and unreal; it is but a reflection of light and shadow within the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), not the true essence of unconditioned reality (*asaṃskṛta*).
Ānanda, you should know that these good men (up to) turn their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa and give birth to the lineage of externalists.
Saṃkarṣaṇa—here translated as the "Yellow-Headed Externalist"—concerning the *tattva* of darkness (*tamas*):

the *Śata-śāstra* says that from darkness arises intellect (*buddhi*), from intellect arises the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃkāra*), from the "I-consciousness" arise the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and from the five subtle elements arise the five [gross elements].
The "Great" (Mahat) arises from the five great elements and produces the eleven faculties. The *puruṣa* (spiritual self) is the sovereign, abiding eternally within the state of pure consciousness;

it is indestructible and imperishable, and it appropriates all phenomena. It regards the *pradhāna* (the unmanifest principle) as the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while the twenty-three intermediate principles constitute the middle category.
From the principle of primordial darkness (*pradhāna*) arises the *puruṣa* (the divine self), which is that which experiences these twenty-three principles. [Commentary:
Below this, the ten types of divergent views within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) are clarified. First: falling into the attachment to cause and what is caused.
This gives rise to the lineage of external paths. "Exhausting the emptiness of all formations" means to exhaust the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

For this aggregate of formations—its illusory marks of arising and ceasing—originally arises from the wind of objects stirring the ocean of consciousness, causing them to mutually engender one another.

Now that the formations have been clarified and extinguished, they dissolve back into the ocean of consciousness, like waves subsiding and the water becoming clear; hence it is said, "returning to the source within consciousness."
The state of profound stillness is no longer subject to the characteristic of constant disturbance; thus it is said that "birth-and-death has already been extinguished.

Yet, as long as the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) is not yet exhausted, there remains something that obscures it. Consequently, regarding the wondrous function of the essential body of quiescent, true permanence, one’s realization is still not yet complete.

However, once the six gates have been worn away through refinement and the process of integration and opening is perfected, one will be able to cause the six sense faculties of one's own body to open.

This causes all things to be understood as entirely without obstruction. When all categories are not summoned separately but have already attained their commonality, then one’s awakened nature naturally fuses with that of all categories throughout the ten directions.
This is the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), wherein the internal and external become as one.

Above, it is harmoniously integrated with Buddha-nature; below, it merges with the minds of ordinary beings. It is the very source from which sentient beings receive their life-force and the fundamental basis for the realization of the Way by all Buddhas.
All of these do not depart from within my *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness). Therefore, it is said that one is able to enter the perfect and primordial source.
The following clarifies how, from this perfect and primordial source, one gives rise to the grasping of dharmas (*dharma-grāha*) and thereby produces external seeds. Indeed, this perfection...

The original source is precisely the substance of consciousness. If one takes this consciousness as the true place of ultimate refuge and establishes it as the locus of the eternally true, supreme fruit to serve forever as a support, then one is falsely grasping at the mind that depends [on an object] and falsely establishing the objective realm upon which it depends.
Thus, one falls into the attachment to cause and what causes the cause, becoming identical to the *amūrta-tattva* (the principle of the unmanifest) to which the Sāṃkhyas resort.

They are of one kind. "Cause" means reliance. "Being deluded regarding Buddha-enlightenment" refers to failing to awaken to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, thereby abandoning the ultimate fruit that has been realized.
"Losing one's knowledge and vision" refers to failing to manifest the substance of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

Thus, there is no correct wisdom capable of realization. This is called "inferior," which concludes the formation of external seeds. Regarding "establishing the mind that is attained and accomplishing the fruit to which one returns":

this means that if the ground is not true, the resulting fruit will be circuitous. Regarding "contrary to and distant from perfect penetration": this refers to erring regarding the mind of the causal ground.
Regarding "turning one's back on the city of Nirvana": this refers to the awakening of the resultant ground.
It is lost. Because of contravening cause and effect, one gives rise to the seeds of external paths. Hereafter, all cases shall follow this pattern.
Ānanda, furthermore, a good man who exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena... [up to] ...gives rise to the seeds of the Greatly Arrogant Heaven, whose self is pervasive and perfect.

Commentary: This falls under the attachment to the "capable" and the "incapable," thereby establishing the pervasive and complete seed of the self. From the passage "exhausting all conditioned phenomena into emptiness" onwards, it follows the previous [analysis].
Regarding the phrase "the place of ultimate return," it still builds upon the preceding text. Previously, one merely reckoned the source of consciousness as the place of return;
now, furthermore, one regards the source of consciousness as the very substance of one's own nature, and claims that all sentient beings throughout the realms are [identical to] oneself.
[They claim] it flows forth from within my own substance, and thus they cling to the notion that "I" can produce them; yet in reality, this is not so.
Therefore, it is called "clinging to the capable as incapable. By forming such an interpretation, they are of the same category as Maheśvara.
For Maheśvara is the Māra-king at the summit of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), who falsely calculates that "I" can manifest the bodies of boundless sentient beings.

In truth, they are incapable. "Those who are deluded regarding Buddha-enlightenment and have lost their knowledge and vision" is the same as before. This is termed below as "forming a different species.
"That which can act as the mind" refers to the mind that takes itself as the causal agent. "That which can perform the task as the fruit" refers to...
"I am able to accomplish the work of fruition. This means that the creation of causes and the attainment of results are entirely due to me.
To be at odds with and distant from perfect penetration is to turn one's back on the city of Nirvana, as previously described. "The Greatly Arrogant Deva" refers to Maheśvara;

because he clings to the notion that "I can produce beings," he considers himself capable, and thus he is called "Greatly Arrogant. Regarding the phrase "the pervasive and perfect seed," it arises from calculating the twelve categories [of sentient beings].
Birth arises from the self, which claims, "I am able to pervade; I am able to fulfill.
This is because it is said that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only, specifically manifesting that birth and non-birth are not real but like illusions.
If one calculates that the mind and consciousness are the producer and the dharma-realm is the produced, then the two attachments to self and phenomena will become as hard as iron and stone.
"How can one attain perfect penetration and non-obstruction?
Furthermore, "Good son, [he] exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena" (up to) "turning his back on the city of Nirvāṇa and producing the seed of inverted perfection.
*Annotation:* This is the fallacy of clinging to permanence within impermanence; it produces the seed of inverted perfection. Regarding the phrase "the state of ultimate refuge":
Following the previous [discussion], the ancient masters explain that this [view] likewise takes the fundamental consciousness (*vijñānamūla*) as the locus to which one's own self returns.
Consequently, one suspects that both the body-mind and all phenomena flow forth from within it.
