Thus, one reckons that the ground from which they arise and flow forth is the true, eternal, and unarisen essence. This, however, is to falsely reckon something as eternally abiding amidst the midst of arising and ceasing. Since—
They are deluded regarding the nature of non-arising; furthermore, they are confused about presently arising and ceasing phenomena, remaining complacently immersed therein and never awakening.
Thus, they take what is impermanent to be permanent; this is called the "grasping at permanence and impermanence. Having formed such an interpretation, [they remain in error].
This is identical to the doctrine of Īśvara, who is reckoned as the creator of all things; thus it is categorized below as a different kind [of error].
"Establishing the cause based on the mind" means taking the source of consciousness (*vijñāna-mūla*) as the object of reliance.
"Forming the fruit of false conceptualization" means taking the phenomena of deluded arising and ceasing as a permanent fruit. This is the same consciousness as the aforementioned attachment.
The fundamental principle is the same, yet the calculations differ. The former calculates that consciousness itself is the self, which gives rise to all things;

the latter calculates that the self emerges from consciousness, and that the self gives rise to all things. Therefore, this is called "inverted completeness. The remaining points are the same as before.
Furthermore, the good son exhausts all conditioned phenomena to the point of emptiness (up to) turning his back on the city of Nirvāṇa and giving rise to the seeds of inverted cognition.

[Commentary: This falls into the attachment of knowing non-knowing; it gives rise to the seeds of inverted cognition. "That which is known" refers to the fundamental source of consciousness (*vijñāna*) that is being contemplated.
"Knowing is pervasive and perfect" means that one knows the fundamental source of consciousness to be pervasive throughout the nature of all dharmas. Because of this knowledge...
"Establishing divergent views" means that because one understands [the nature of] pervasiveness and completeness, divergent views arise.

This refers, in general, to seeing that this consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) inherently possesses cognition, and that all phenomena arise through the transformation of consciousness; thus, one establishes divergent views.

One falsely calculates that grasses, trees, and humans have never had different natures. Since there is no difference in nature, one then [concludes that] the sentient and the insentient must mutually...
Because of saṃsāra, it is said that "grass and trees become humans, and when humans die, they return to being grass and trees.

Thus, sentient and insentient beings are perceived as one and the same, without any distinction. If one forms such a view, then taking what has consciousness to be without consciousness, and what lacks consciousness to have consciousness, one becomes identical to the two types of non-Buddhist heretics, the Pāṭa and Śākya.
This is of one category. This is termed "below. To establish a different kind [of error]:

regarding those who calculate that the perfectly knowing mind results in a false and deluded fruit—this means that they falsely reckon this perfect knowledge as the causal mind, whereby the resulting fruit becomes false and deluded. This is "perverted knowledge."

This refers to taking ignorance to be knowledge. Indeed, although the sentient and the insentient are of one essence, one must necessarily recognize the true mind before there will be not even an inch of ground [for delusion].

Moreover, as long as the *ālayavijñāna* has not been relinquished and the *vipākavijñāna* has not been emptied, to give rise to false conceptualizations regarding this perfect source is to differ by a hair’s breadth, which consequently results in a chasm between heaven and earth.

Furthermore, the good man, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) [up to] turning his back on the city of Nirvāṇa, gives rise to the seed of perverted transformation.

(Marginal Note: This is falling into the attachment to birth within non-birth; it is the production of a perverted seed of transformation. For when consciousness is exhausted and the six sense-fields are dissolved...)

Only then can the various faculties be employed interchangeably. Although one may now achieve the dissolution of the six [sense organs], because the "one" has not yet been extinguished, one’s mutual functioning, while not yet fully perfected, already accords with it; thus, there are no supernatural transformations that do not proceed from the mind.
Consequently, within the state of perfect transformation and production, one perceives the characteristics of the four great elements and subsequently calculates all things.

The characteristics of dharmas all arise from the four great elements; therefore, they take the radiance of fire, the purity of water, the circulation of wind, and the formation of earth as the true, eternal, ultimate fruit.

Thus, they seek pleasure and cultivate contemplation, even going so far as to revere and serve them in order to realize the fruit. Furthermore, they take these elemental phenomena as the source of their arising.
It is the fundamental source of all creation; thus, it is established as the true sovereign that constantly presides over the transformation of phenomena.

Yet, through false conceptualization, one reckons it to be able to produce the fruits of sagehood, when in reality it cannot. Therefore, it is said that this is the "clinging to birth within non-birth.

To contemplate the "dust" (rajas) is to contemplate the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). "Accomplishment" refers to its ability to bring about the myriad things of the world. "Multitudes of dust" collectively refers to the four [elements].

"Great! To claim that one cultivates the causes and realizes the fruits [of enlightenment] without departing from these four great elements is precisely the same as the views held by the Brahmin Kāśyapa and other fire-worshipping non-Buddhists.
'The deluded mind follows external objects' means to turn one's back on one's own true mind and follow those delusive objects; thus, one seeks the cause through what is not the cause."
Not seeking the fruit yet hoping for the fruit, one instead takes that which is bound by deluded thoughts to be the master who can produce and transform;
this is called a perverted principle of transformation. Desiring to transcend birth and death, one instead falls back into birth and death; this too is a perverted view.

Furthermore, good sons who exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*)—[extending] up to turning their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa and giving rise to the seed of nihilism.
[Commentary: This is falling into the attachment of having no refuge where there is no refuge, thereby giving rise to the seed of nihilism.

"Perfectly luminous" means that when the preceding aggregates (*skandha*) have all been exhausted and all states of existence (*bhava*) are empty, one perceives only the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*); yet they do not realize it is still merely a phantom-like appearance.
Regarding "vain delusions of emptiness": one erroneously calculates that the empty and non-substantial essence within this perfect luminosity is the ultimate ground.

Consequently, one desires to extinguish the body and dissolve into the earth, taking eternal extinction into emptiness as one's place of reliance. Relying on this for rest, one no longer seeks further progress.
How could such a person know that this state also belongs to the realm of the illusory and is not a true place of refuge? Such is this view.

This attachment has no refuge; yet it is taken as a true refuge. Thus, one becomes of the same class as those in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception and the devas of the four formless heavens who have attained emptiness.
This is called "inferior," concluding that these constitute distinct categories. Regarding "the mind of perfect voidness and non-existence accomplishing the fruit of empty extinction":
this means taking the deluded thought of voidness and non-existence as the causal mind, and taking the cessation and extinction of emptiness as [the result].
It is the fruit of awakening. It is not [a state of] destruction. "The manifold transformations" refers to the body and the land.

Furthermore, "Good son, you exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena" (up to) "...turning one's back on the city of Nirvana and giving rise to the seeds of delusive extension."

Commentary: This is a fallacy of grasping at non-grasping. It gives rise to delusion and prolongs the seeds [of existence]. "Perfect and eternal" refers likewise to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Because one perceives that the preceding aggregates have been exhausted and extinguished, while the essence of consciousness remains brilliant and clear, profoundly still and unmoving, one consequently reckons this to be perfect and eternally abiding.
Furthermore, one perceives that this aggregate of consciousness is able to grasp and maintain the body, causing the body...
They do not destroy [the body], but instead desire to make it firm and permanently abiding, identical to the refined essence (*ching-yüan*), seeking longevity and immortality.
This is like the practitioners of the Immortal schools who cultivate both life and nature (*hsing-ming shuang-hsiu*) with the intent of making both form and spirit firm.

Because they do not understand that this body is like a floating bubble and should not be clung to, they perversely give rise to attachment, wishing to preserve it as something permanent. Such is their view.
[Commentary: This is identical in kind to Asita’s seeking of longevity. Asita is called "The Peerless" (*Anupama*); he was an ancient seer (*ṛṣi*).
The phrase "below this name" concludes the formation of a distinct category. Regarding those who cling to the source of life:

they take the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) to be the source upon which the body clings for its life. Establishing the cause of solid delusion means that they desire to solidify the body.
"Permanence" refers precisely to the fact that the seeds of karma from beginningless time have not yet been exhausted, yet one instead establishes this as the causal mind.
"Seeking the fruit of long toil" means that as long as there is a body, there will inevitably be toil; yet one seeks longevity, which is the very fruit of such toil.
This merely increases one's long-term labor and is ultimately not the ultimate fruit. "Frivolously prolonging [life]" means that they do not know the truth.
Yet, on the contrary, they rely upon this deluded body to seek its prolongation.

Furthermore, good son, from the thorough investigation of the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (up to) turning one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa and being born into the lineage of celestial Māras.
Commentary: This is the fallacy of clinging to the non-existent as real; it gives rise to the seeds of celestial and demonic states. Regarding "observing that life-force is mutually pervasive":

this means that because the preceding aggregates have all vanished, one observes the threads of each individual life-force, seeing that they are all interconnected with the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Thus, the life-force of every body is entirely rooted in the consciousness-aggregate, and all sensory objects are likewise connected to that life-force.

Originally, these were interconnected. If the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) were to be exhausted, then the life-source of self and others, as well as the internal faculties and external objects, would all likewise perish.
Who then would realize the true and eternal? What would serve as the realm of bliss? Therefore, one must preserve the defilements (*kleśa*) as the basis for body and life;
for if they were to dissolve away, then even though body and life existed, there would be no support. Thus, one proceeds until their exhaustion.
Regarding the manifestation of consciousness: through its perfect transformation, it accords with the mind and attains great mastery.

Consequently, at this juncture, it spontaneously transforms the seven precious jewels and celestial maidens, as well as all objects of sensual pleasure; therein, one indulges the mind and yields to desire, taking this to be sublime bliss.
This is the false grasping of the karmic consciousness’s life-source, regarding it as true, permanent, pure, and joyful, when in fact it is not truly pure. These [states]...
Such a view is of the same category as that of the Takkīkālas. This concludes the section below on the formation of distinct types.
Regarding "arousing the cause of perverse thought to establish the fruit of blazing dust," this refers to using perverse thoughts and the indulgence of desire as the causal mind.
Because the defilements are intensely blazing, he is the realization of the fruit. Ṭakki is the Lord of the Summit of Desire (Kāmeśvara), who can transform objects of desire and enjoy them himself.

Furthermore, the good man exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*)... [up to] turning his back on the city of Nirvāṇa and giving rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.
[Commentary: This refers to those Śrāvakas of fixed nature who are stalled; they are called "seeds of entanglement within emptiness.

Regarding the phrase "in the midst of the clarity of life," it means that at this juncture, by thoroughly investigating the source of each life, one thereby comes to know that this aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is capable of containing and storing [all things].
Because there are seeds that are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and seeds that are without-outflows (*anāsrava*), within this context, they are analyzed and determined as follows:
the former are seeds with-outflows; because they are coarse, practicing the causes based upon them results in worldly, counterfeit fruits. These [latter] are seeds without-outflows;
because they are refined, practicing the causes based upon them results in supramundane, true fruits. The coarse belongs to the cause of accumulation (*saṃudaya-hetu*); it is counterfeit.
The suffering fruit belongs to the realm of affliction; the diligent practice belongs to the cause of the Path; and the True belongs to the fruit of Cessation.
Consequently, they reckon this to be the true cultivation and actual realization, seeking only to quickly emerge from birth and death and to early realize Nirvana.

Little do they realize that they have already turned their backs on the pure causal mind and the unsurpassed, wondrous Path. This is nothing more than seeing suffering and abandoning the origin, realizing cessation and cultivating the path, [aiming] to...
One merely exits the triple world and dwells in suffering here; once nirvana is attained, one simply rests.

If one does not give rise to a fond desire for the bodhisattvas' practices of purifying the land with a pure mind, then one has not yet ascended to the Precious Abode, but is merely stalled at the City of Transformation.
Such a person is a śrāvaka of fixed nature who does not turn the mind [toward enlightenment], a dull-witted arhat. One who lacks learning is a foolish monk.
Regarding the "Dharma Śrāvaka": those who have not attained [realization] yet claim to have attained it are categorized below as a distinct type.

"The perfect essence responds to the mind to achieve the fruit of quiescent inclination" means that one fulfills the causal mind of single-minded pursuit and response, thereby achieving the fruit of a biased inclination toward solitary emptiness.
Because they are bound by emptiness, they are said to be "entangled in emptiness."
Furthermore, the good man exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) [up to] the arising of a perfected, luminous awareness, yet he does not transform it into a perfected seed.
(Commentary: This refers to a Pratyekabuddha who is stuck in a fixed nature; he is called one with a "non-transformed perfected seed. He dissolves the six sense bases into one.

The gates function interchangeably; therefore, it is called "perfectly interfused. The faculties and their objects are unstained; therefore, it is called "pure and clean. It illuminates through to the source of life; therefore, it is called "awakened clarity.
Yet this is precisely the original clarity of the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-ghana*); as it has not yet been transformed into wisdom, it is still termed "consciousness.

Regarding those who investigate its profound subtlety, there are two types: the *pratyekabuddha*, who contemplates the transformation of things, and the *pratyayabuddha* (dependent-enlightened), who contemplates...
The twelve links of dependent origination are all said to be the unfolding of a profound and wondrous state of awakening.
Taking that awakened state as the ground for resting in nirvāṇa, one no longer proceeds further; this is likewise a "transformed city" (an illusory city) and is ultimately not the "Jewel Place.
Those who are of the same class as the various conditions are the pratyekabuddhas, those of the same class as the solitary awakeners. [End of] *Yonghuang Yuanjue*.

Regarding "the mind achieves the fruit of profound clarity": this refers to these pratyekabuddhas and solitary realizers (dujue), who all share a pervasive merging with the original clarity of the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because they take this as their causal mind, they merely achieve the stagnant fruit of profound clarity; it is not the ultimate fruit of supreme bodhi, the precious, awakened, and luminous mind.
As for "giving rise to the perfect clarity of awakening, the unchanging perfect seed": [this refers to the state where the essence of consciousness is transformed].
This means that upon awakening to the place of the primal luminosity of the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*), one clings to it and fails to transform it.
Ānanda, through these ten kinds of *dhyāna* (up to the point where), by relying on this mind's opening, one attains the Unsurpassed Way.
Commentary: This concludes the section on the harms of entrusting protection. Becoming insane midway through the journey occurs frequently in the first eight stages;

failing to find satisfaction despite having attained it occurs frequently in the final two stages. Yet these ten types [of harm] are none other than taking delusion as their cause and depending upon delusion as their fruit.
All of them, as before, fall within the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate). Regarding "that which was previously practiced and loved," this means that each has its own...
Seeds of habitual tendencies from beginningless time and seeds of partial attachment now manifest individually within meditative concentration;
thus, one becomes deranged midway through the path and fails to achieve true fulfillment. One then takes this state of joyful grasping for rest as a false claim of ultimate realization.
All such instances fall under the category of great falsehood. According to the traditional explanation, the first seven are non-Buddhist paths, while the eighth is the work of demonic spirits.
Now, as for Māras and non-Buddhists, since they have summoned forth perverse blessings through perverse causes, they have never severed their afflictions;

yet they enjoy the fruits of their meditative cultivation, and when these blessings are exhausted, they will undoubtedly fall into hell. As for the latter two types [of practitioners], although they belong to the provisional vehicle’s system of cause and effect, [they differ from the former].
Having already been able to sever delusions and attain realization, there is merely no further progress, nor is there any falling back.
"You all, go below" is a formal entrustment for protection. Regarding "maintaining the mind" and so forth:

it means to maintain one's own heart of great compassion and uphold the Tathāgata’s path of the two benefits, so as to widely disseminate this dharma-gate that distinguishes the correct from the heterodox in the final age, causing it to reach everywhere.

Sentient beings all clearly distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. Generally, those who have not yet thoroughly penetrated the principle, yet engage in conceptual discrimination and attachment, are all under the influence of the demons of views and craving (*dṛṣṭi-tṛṣṇā*).

Some say that among the [eight kinds of] pride, the first seven are purely views, while the eighth consists of both views and craving, because it retains the dust of worldly toil (*rajas*) and gives rise to superior resolve (*adhimukti*).
As for the realm of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka-pratyekabuddha*), although views and craving are exhausted within their own sphere, the realm...

If attachment to external phenomena still persists, one will then weary of existence and cling to emptiness, seeking only self-benefit; all such states belong to deluded views and conceptual discrimination.
"Sui" (綏) means peace. "False conditions" (邪緣) refer to the aforementioned false conditions that give rise to counterfeit fruits. One must extinguish these conditions.
Then one spontaneously awakens to and enters the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; between these stages, there are no further divergent branches or devious paths.
The phrase "Thus" and below concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one, thereby manifesting that all Buddhas together realize this path.

This dharma-gate refers in general to the method for discerning demons and realizing the truth within the five aggregates. It is said that among the Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there has never been...
It does not follow that one who destroys the five aggregates and eliminates demonic afflictions, thereby enabling the development of right wisdom and achieving unsurpassed bodhi,
would necessarily be identical to the "all sentient beings" mentioned in the first fascicle— those whose birth and death have continued from time immemorial,
and who, throughout the stages from beginning to end, never possess any traces of crookedness. This point corresponds to that specific passage.
The text provides a correspondence [to the preceding].
If the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) is exhausted, then from "your present" up to "perfect enlightenment returns to non-attainment.

The traditional explanation states that this mutual functioning of the sense organs (*indriya*) should be understood as referring to the initial stage of entering and abiding in the path. For those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom, from—
Regarding the stage of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*): one may directly transcend and enter the mind immediately preceding equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
As for what was previously stated—that an ordinary person ascends through the sixty holy stages of a bodhisattva—in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there are only two positions:

first, those who sever the pervasive delusions of the prior stages and directly transcend from the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing-wei*) to enter the first dwelling; in this case, no further stages are taken in between.
Realization. Second, regarding the severance of subsequent delusions: from entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one transcends directly to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

In the interim, there is no further taking of realization, unlike the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), where one must necessarily pass through many kalpas, practicing and realizing gradually until the fruit is fulfilled after three great eons (*mahākalpa*) and one takes realization of Bodhi. This Dharma-gate of Perfect Suddenness is known by those of the highest faculties.
"Becoming a Buddha upon taking one's stand" (lishi chengfo). Those of the Two Vehicles who understand this also realize the state of Nirvana without remainder.
*Commentary:* This clarifies that at the very moment of first generating the Bodhicitta, one attains perfect enlightenment.

The meaning is that when reaching this point where the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, it is precisely the time for the "dissolving of the six sense bases into one. Thus, you may now, through any single faculty, [attain realization].

It performs the functions of the various sense faculties, yet within them, it gives rise to neither grasping nor rejecting; this is precisely the mind of the causal stage that is neither born nor extinguished.
From here, one transcends directly and enters the realization of the fruit stage without further deviation or branching paths. Therefore it is said:

"From within the mutual functioning, one can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine dry wisdom. Having attained this gate of contemplation, both essence and function are perfected and complete, abiding in stillness.
Illuminating non-duality, the present state of mind and object interfuses with perfect clarity; amidst all sensory phenomena, there is not the slightest defilement.
From this heart of perfect clarity, one emanates and transforms through all the stages of the sages from beginning to end, like a pure lapis lazuli gem containing a precious moon within.
In this way, one is able to transcend the forty-four minds, reaching the final mind of Equal Enlightenment.
However, the manifestation and transformation of perfect luminosity is merely the illusory samādhi.
From this vajra path of no-interval (*anantarya-mārga*), one enters the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); hence it is said: "Entering the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous adornment.

This is precisely what is meant by the Great Buddha-Crown *Śūraṅgama* King, which fully embodies the myriad practices and serves as the single gateway through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend into wondrous adornment.
This is to solemnize the path. Since one has already perfected Bodhi, it ultimately results in nothing to be attained. What is called "Bodhi" is the wisdom of perfect enlightenment;

what is called "nothing to be attained" is the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*). When wisdom accords with this principle, it is inherently and spontaneously as-it-is (*yathābhūta*); it is not obtained from without.
"This is how the past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones... [remained] undeluded and unconfused in their minds regarding Great Nirvāṇa.
(Commentary: This clarifies following the ancients to discern demons, so as to facilitate further cultivation.

Following from what was said previously—that the demonic affairs I have described above were all employed by the various Buddhas of the past while they were within the *Lengyan* Great Samādhi—this section explains that one must likewise employ them in order to advance in practice.
The wisdom of initial awakening observes with such subtle precision that it is entirely free from error. Nevertheless, harm arises from demonic influences;

yet the cause that brings about these demons is truly the defilements of the mind. If you, the masters of the five aggregates, do not give rise to a single thought, you will be able to recognize even when demonic realms manifest before you.
Regardless of how they falsely display superior states, you should maintain a pure mind and remain unattached.

Naturally, one will not fall into false views; thus, the demons of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the celestial demons (*deva-māra*), powerful spirits and ghosts, and all *chi*, *mei*, and *wangliang* specters will have their spirits shattered and their souls scattered, fleeing far away. Having no means of remaining, how could they ever arise again to cause harm?
If one does not give rise to false views at the initial stage and does not form deluded understandings along the way, then one will proceed directly to unsurpassed bodhi.

Regarding the wealth of the Dharma of merit, there is nothing not fully possessed. One should not give rise to contentment with the inferior Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), but should advance with all one's might toward Great Nirvāṇa (Mahāparinirvāṇa).
How could one ever remain stranded at the illusory city (the *pūrvanimitta* of the *śrāvaka*) and merely increase one’s confusion and distress?
*Ān* means to know or understand; *tǐ* means to lose or perish.
"If there are sentient beings of dull faculties in the final age... [until] the ultimate cultivation and progress as the final instruction.

*Annotation:* This is to cause the mantra to provide protection. If those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom, they can naturally distinguish demonic activities from the various stages of sainthood (*ārya-bhūmi*).
However, as for those of dull faculties in the final age, since they do not [attain] meditative concentration...
They are capable of clear awakening, yet they lack the wisdom derived from hearing and do not understand the Buddha-dharma; their minds, however, delight in practicing this Great Samādhi.
If you wish to prevent them from falling into false views, by what means shall you protect and sustain them?

You should cause them to single-mindedly and exclusively uphold the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-citta-mantra*. If their faculty of hearing is so inferior that they cannot even recite it, then write it down in the meditation hall.
If one wears this upon the body, then all māras will naturally be unable to disturb them.
Indeed, this mantra-heart should be recited, copied, and transcribed not only by those of dull faculties who practice it; you all as well should revere this teaching.
It is not merely what I have spoken, but that which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have ultimately cultivated and realized—this is no mere transformation.

The cessation within the city [of the body] is the final model for posterity; it is not a provisional teaching of incomplete understanding. How could one not reverently accept and look up to it with awe?
The preceding dhyāna of the five aggregates clearly expounds the Great Buddha-Topknot (Mahā-uṣṇīṣa); this also secretly expounds the Great Buddha-Topknot.
Both are the supreme, foremost, inconceivable realm of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). There is no need to ask further.
The self-exposition on the characteristics of the demon of the five aggregates was concluded.
Ānanda then rose from his seat, having heard the Buddha’s instruction (extending to) his acting as the eye for all future sentient beings.
Commentary: This represents the interlocutor’s presentation of three further questions.

"To remember and maintain without loss" means that regarding the Dharma shown by the World-Honored One, one does not dare to let even the slightest detail slip away. The first question concerns the intent behind the arising of delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*).
It is said that the World-Honored One has, in his ordinary teachings, merely stated that these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are entirely empty in their very substance;

he never previously mentioned what constitutes their fundamental basis. Now, whenever he refutes each aggregate, he causes one to contemplate its origin, always pointing to deluded thought (*vikalpa*) as the fundamental basis.
Although I have thus received this subtle and detailed instruction, I still do not yet understand why these five aggregates all fundamentally derive from [deluded thought].

Regarding "delusive thoughts" (*vikalpa*): what are they? Second, the question concerning the sudden or gradual elimination [of these thoughts]. Following the previous statement that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) collectively belong to delusive thoughts, the question now arises:
if one wishes to dismantle them, should they be exhausted all at once, or should they be eliminated sequentially and gradually?

Third, the question concerning the fivefold boundaries. This also follows from the preceding point, stating that if one wishes to sever and eliminate them, one must understand the respective limits of each aggregate.
"Regarding the depth and shallowness of these five aggregates: to what destination do they go, and what constitutes the boundary of each aggregate?
We pray that the Tathāgata, with tireless great compassion, will explain each point in detail.

Not only should this cause the hearts of the assembly present here to open and their eyes to brighten, but it should also serve to greatly awaken the minds of sentient beings in the末法 (mofa) age and extensively open their Dharma-eye."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "From the refined and true wondrous clarity... (up to) 'the fundamental causes of the five aggregates are all equally false imaginings.
*Commentary:* This passage generally clarifies that the reason for the existence of the five aggregates is that they are all fundamentally rooted in false imaginings. "Refined and true" means:
"Pure and true" refers to the entire substance. "Wondrously luminous" refers to the wondrous function of tranquil illumination.

"Primordially enlightened, perfect, and pure" means that this entire substance and its wondrous function are, from the beginning, all-pervading and pure; they do not depend upon cultivation to be realized.
This is what is called the "primordial self-nature, the true-and-heavenly Buddha. "Not subject to death and birth, etc. means that this primordially enlightened [nature] is perfect...

Within purity, not even a speck of dust can be established; not a single thing can be admitted. Thus, from the body and its faculties and the physical world, even unto empty space, none are things inherently existing within the perfectly pure mind of original enlightenment (*mūla-āśraya*). They all arise solely through deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, know that the root of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is, in total, nothing but this single deluded conceptualization. "Birth and death" refers to the body and its faculties; "dust" [refers to the external world].
"Dust" refers to the vessel-world (the physical environment). Now, considering this root-source of the true and the deluded, to summarize it:

it originally arose from the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-jñāna*), through a single thought-moment of the true essence that followed conditions and transformed into discursive thought (*vikalpa*).
Consequently, all the various vessel-worlds were produced; they are fundamentally not real, yet they are mistakenly perceived as real—just like the case of Yajñadatta.
To mistake one's own head for the reflection in a mirror and take that reflection to be one's own head—what difference is there?

Since it arises from delusion, that delusion is fundamentally without cause. You all constantly establish the nature of causes and conditions within the phenomena that arise from false conceptualization, claiming that the dharmas such as the five aggregates all arise from causes and conditions. Now, regarding this attachment to causes...
As for "conditions": even those who have not yet attained perfect enlightenment do not [claim this], let alone those deluded regarding causes and conditions who call it "spontaneous.

They say that the dharmas such as the five aggregates exist naturally and inherently; they fail to realize that even the nature of empty space, which seems indestructible, is produced by illusory falsehood and is not truly existent.
As it is said: "Emptiness arises within the Great Enlightenment, like a single wave in the ocean."
How much more so for that which arises through causes and conditions, or that which exists spontaneously?
All these are merely the conceptual constructions and discriminations of sentient beings; how could they possess any real meaning? Moreover, it does not end here.
If you were truly able to know the reason why these false phenomena arise, you might concede that false phenomena are produced from causes and conditions. But as for these false phenomena—

Since there is originally no cause for arising, those who erroneously claim that false dharmas are produced from causes and conditions do not understand that these dharmas are fundamentally not substantially real.

How much less can those who, while simultaneously ignoring causes and conditions, further depart from them to falsely speculate that all dharmas exist spontaneously be anything other than the most deluded among the deluded? Therefore, I now [speak with them].

When you clarify that the fundamental causes of the five aggregates are all equally false thoughts, it is merely to let you know that these delusions have no [independent] cause and arise based upon the True.
Your body was originally produced from the thoughts of your parents (up to) what is called the "first solid false thought."
Commentary: This reveals that the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is called "solidified delusive thought.

Although the aggregate of form encompasses both the physical body and the external environment, it is here specifically identified as a single body because it is formed through the delusive thoughts of the parents and oneself. The intention is as follows:
Although I have explained for you the fundamental cause of the five aggregates, you still do not know that the aggregate of form is called "solid deluded conception.
This very physical body of yours was first produced because both your parents conceived thoughts of passionate attachment;
subsequently, there were the two drops of red and white. Although the parents possessed these thoughts, your intermediate state (*antarābhava*) did not yet give rise to love or hatred.

The notion of [the child as] "mine" can by no means flow forth as the seed of affection; yet within the notion of [the child as] one's "parents," there is likewise no notion of "receiving" it into the womb to continue its life.
If you do not believe that the body is composed of delusive thoughts, I shall again cite the previous analogy, and you will understand it for yourself:
as I previously said, when one thinks of the taste of vinegar or a precipice, water flows from the mouth.
When you hear of vinegar, your mouth waters; when you see a precipice, your feet ache. Yet the precipice does not actually exist, and the vinegar-plum has not yet arrived.
If your physical form were not a product of unreal, deluded thoughts, then these reactions—salivation and aching feet—would be indistinguishable from the objects themselves.

Why then do they arise as empty talk? Because of the vinegar and the precipice, these false sensations emerge. By observing this, you can clearly know that your material body is indeed formed by the binding of deluded thoughts.
What is called "solidity" refers to the fact that the defiled minds of one's parents and one's own feelings of aversion and affection are firmly bound together in one place to form it.
This very point being explained— from the contemplation of heights (up to the phrase)— is named the second delusive thought, "empty clarity."
Commentary: This reveals that the name of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is "delusive thought of empty luminosity.

To follow upon the preceding aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) in order to initiate the aggregate of sensation precisely indicates that both form (*rūpa*) and sensation are governed by perception.

For form encompasses the first five sense organs, sensation encompasses the first five consciousnesses, and perception is the sixth consciousness. Regarding the phrase "the mind of thought when facing heights," it means:

Due to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), one dwells between the aggregates of form and perception (*saṃjñā*). This is because one has previously experienced objects such as precipices, and their residual impressions have settled within the mind of perception.
Furthermore, upon hearing words such as "precipice," the mental image of being at a high, empty void can cause your physical form to truly experience a sense of stinging distress.
Therefore, it is concluded and shown: "Because of the aggregate of sensation, the aggregate of perception arises. Thus, [the aggregate of perception] is the cause.
Because of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the substance of form is moved.

If you do not awaken to this, you should observe how the two objects currently confronting you—those disagreeable and those agreeable—give rise to the two types of sensation (vedanā), namely, those that cause harm and those that bring benefit. These two sensations are now able to drive both body and mind, so that they find no rest.
This is why it is called the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); it constitutes the second deluded thought of "empty clarity. There are three types of sensation:

suffering, pleasure, and equanimity. "Damage" and "benefit" refer specifically to the two sensations of suffering and pleasure. Because emptiness is able to receive [objects] and clarity is able to discern them, yet neither possesses a substantial reality, it is termed the deluded thought of "empty clarity."
"Because of your thoughts and deliberations, they cause your physical body [to function]... this is called the third delusive thought, 'interfusion' (*yōngtōng*).
**Commentary:** This clarifies that the name of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is "delusive thought of interfusion.

"Thoughts and deliberations" refers to the aggregate of perception; it is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is because the mental consciousness is the sovereign ruler of the entire body; thus, the first five sensory consciousnesses all obey it.

As for that which you employ—your own body—if it were not of the same category as the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), by what cause and condition would it be mobilized in accordance with the perceiving mind?
Right before your eyes, you grasp various forms; all of these arise because the mind first produces false perceptions (*vikalpa*), after which the sense faculties subsequently grasp them.
Thus, one knows that this body corresponds in essence with the aggregate of perception, never departing from it for even a moment.
Therefore, when awake, the physical form opens and there is perception; when asleep, the spirit communes and there is dreaming.
Thus one knows that the mind changes according to objects, and objects arise according to the mind; these are all merely the fluctuations of thought and the movement of deluded emotions.

Hence they are called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), which constitutes the third pervasive delusion. "Pervasive" means that this empty perception is able to pervade and integrate [all things].
Furthermore, as for its substance:
the principle of transformation does not abide but shifts subtly and incessantly. This is called the "profoundly hidden" fourth deluded thought.

(Commentary: This clarifies that the name of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is "profoundly hidden deluded thought. Regarding "the principle of transformation does not abide": it means...
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has transformation as its nature, yet it possesses the characteristic of constant flux.

"Moving and moving, shifting secretly" means that it changes and migrates from moment to moment, so subtly that people do not perceive it. The growth of nails and hair is the characteristic of arising;
the depletion of vital energy and the wrinkling of the face are the characteristic of cessation. It is said that this false aggregate of formations is capable of producing [these effects].
The substance of extinction truly perishes. Day and night they alternate before us, yet not a single person is able to awaken to this;

this sufficiently demonstrates the subtlety of such transition. If this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) were not your own body, how could it cause your nails to grow and your breath to diminish?
If this aggregate of formations were truly your own body, why would it undergo alternation and transition day and night? Never...
There is no awakening. For this aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) undergoes incessant transformation; right and wrong cannot be fixed.
Therefore, it constitutes the fourth subtle and hidden delusion.

Furthermore, that which you call "vitality and clarity" and "tranquil and unmoving" (up to this point) constitutes the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) formed by the five deluded thoughts.

The five aggregates of clinging are also called the five aggregates of grasping (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). Due to a single moment of delusive ignorance, one undergoes and grasps these [aggregates] to conceal and hide oneself.
Therefore, if one uses the cognitive perspective of a sentient being and clings to these five aggregates as being truly existent, then...
Worldly dharmas: if one uses the knowledge and vision of the two vehicles to grasp these five aggregates as empty and quiescent, this is a supramundane dharma.

If Buddhas and Bodhisattvas realize that form is itself emptiness and emptiness is itself form—and that this is likewise true for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—this is the supreme-supramundane dharma, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This is the inconceivable realm. Thus, apart from these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the teachings of the five vehicles would be utterly non-existent.
We know, therefore, that to be deluded regarding them is to be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), while to awaken to them is to be a sage (*ārya*). As it is said:
"All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet, due to the attachment of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), they are unable to realize it."
Attainment of the Ear.

Commentary: This reveals that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is a subtle and refined conception. "Vitality and clarity" refers to the fundamental clarity of the essence of consciousness.
"The state of being profoundly still and unmoving" means that once the first seven consciousnesses have ceased, the eighth consciousness is like water without waves.
As for what is called "permanence": this refers to the state of brilliant clarity and profound stillness. Although it is termed "permanent," in reality it is not the entirety of true permanence.
Within your own body, it has not yet transcended the six sense organs; it merely manifests mutual resonance within the nature.
If it were the truly refined, perfect essence, it would transcend the six sense organs, being impervious to defilement and incapable of receiving delusion.
It is through habituation. For what reason? Although one may have once beheld a marvelous object in years past, and after many years have elapsed, there is neither recollection nor forgetting;
yet upon beholding that same object again, it appears exactly as before.

This is because, while the initial apprehension and memory arise from the perfuming of the first six consciousnesses, the subsequent maintenance of the seeds without loss is the function of the eighth [consciousness]. Therefore, the Sūtra says:

That after the passage of many years, one may again behold former objects and find them perfectly intact without loss is entirely due to the eighth consciousness, which is profoundly lucid and unwavering, being perfumed by every thought-moment. What need is there for calculation? This is called "inconceivable perfuming."
The following analogy clarifies that this is not the ultimate reality. It says: "Even this state of brilliant clarity and profound stillness is not truly eternal.
This is like a rapid current of water which, when viewed from afar, appears tranquil and silent; yet, because the flow is so swift and subtle, its movement is not perceived.
It is not that there is actually no movement. The ocean-deep depth of the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is likewise. Indeed, as for this *ālaya-vijñāna*:
Although this Tathāgatagarbha is perfumed, it also arises due to the perfuming of the preceding four types of deluded conceptualization.

If these preceding and succeeding deluded conceptualizations did not mutually serve as the root source, how could this ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness) possibly be perfumed by those four preceding deluded conceptualizations?
Therefore, it is not at the time when your six sense organs function interchangeably, nor at the moment when the senses are separated or joined. And so forth.
If the habitual tendencies of the six delusive seeds are not exhausted, these false imaginings will have no means by which they can be extinguished.

Why is this? Because the eighth consciousness and the preceding six are mutually the roots for one another; when they are true, they are equally true, and when they are delusive, they are equally delusive.

Therefore, when the six are liberated, the one perishes; thus, all false imaginings are suddenly perfected as true awakening. Now, regarding your present six sense faculties within the eight consciousnesses:
Moment by moment, they receive perfuming; mutually interpenetrating, they give rise to seeds and habitual tendencies of arising and ceasing.

Although these are seen as being extremely subtle, one knows that within the essence, clarity, and profound stillness, they are nonetheless like a phantom image or empty nothingness—this is the fifth inversion, the subtle and refined conceptualization.
"Phantom image" and "empty nothingness" mean that true and false are blended together; it appears real yet is empty, appearing to exist yet is non-existent.
Furthermore, "inversion" refers to being deluded regarding the truth and clinging to the semblance. "Subtle" refers to the subtle consciousness of *ādāna*.
"Essential perception" means that the essence of consciousness is fundamentally luminous; when it is in the eye, it is called the "essence of seeing," and so forth. The conclusion below answers:
although these five aggregates differ in their coarseness and subtlety, they are all formed by the five kinds of false imagination and possess no reality.
As for the essence: if one can realize that delusion is itself reality, then the five aggregates are all empty, and there remains only the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
This concludes the previous answer regarding how the five aggregates are all termed false conceptualizations.

If you now wish to know the depth of the causal realms (from "the depth of the causal realms" to) "the profound entry merges with the profound, returning to the limit of consciousness," the traditional explanation states:

within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), that which possesses "entry" is called "profound entry. This then extinguishes the flow of mental formations (*saṃskāra*) and sinks back into the ocean of consciousness.
As the Sūtra says: "The nature of entry is fundamentally clear; once this clarity is established, fundamental habits are stilled, like waves and ripples ceasing and transforming into still water."

This is so. To use "entry" (*ru*) as "convergence" (*he*) with the profound stillness (*zhan*) is as the Sūtra says: "Internally and internally profoundly luminous; entering where there is nothing to enter. This is precisely it.
For the character "converge" (*he*) carries the sense of being unmoving—it is like not seeing the flow of a river because the current is so swift.

Nevertheless, although this state of convergence with the profound stillness is deep in its degree, it still remains within the realm of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and cannot escape the four most subtle [afflictions].

They are transmuted by signs. Thus one knows that although one enters the profound stillness (*zhan*), one does not yet fully merge with it; one has not yet emerged from the boundary of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
This is what is meant by "clear light shining into the eyes, yet still resembling being lost in one's home.

All the luminous *dharmakāya* remains, for now, not yet ultimate. As the Sūtra says: "It is not your six faculties that function interchangeably, nor their merging or opening. This is [the nature of] delusion.

[The faculty of] ideation (*saṃjñā*) can never attain cessation. Therefore, one knows that it must wait until the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted before attaining perfect penetration and ultimate realization.
(Commentary on the Preface) This answers the question of which of the five aggregates serves as the gateway. "Cause" refers to each respective aggregate.

These are the false causes. "Elements" (*dhātu*) refer to the boundaries of each aggregate (*skandha*). Regarding "shallow and deep," this means that among the five types of deluded thoughts, the earlier ones are increasingly shallow and the later ones are increasingly deep.
It is not that the emptiness of signlessness (*animitta-śūnyatā*) fails to manifest the form of signs (*nimitta-rūpa*);

yet, if one were to abandon form and cling to emptiness, then emptiness would be identical to form. Until one reaches the ultimate state where form is itself emptiness (*rūpam eva śūnyatā*), there is no limit; therefore—
It is said: Only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form. Receiving [sensations] is called contact (*sparśa*); relinquishing them is called detachment (*viveka*).

If one were detached from contact yet not detached from detachment itself, then detachment would be identical to contact. Until one reaches the state of detachment that is free from all characteristics, there is ultimately no limit.

Therefore it is said that only contact and its cessation constitute the limits of sensation. That which is accompanied by mindfulness is called "recollection," and that which is without mindfulness is called "forgetting.

If one extinguishes all thoughts and falls into a state of non-mindfulness, then even non-existence is the same as existence; this is a state of non-mindfulness that has not yet reached true mindfulness.
To contemplate without contemplation is ultimately boundless; therefore, it is said that "only recollection and forgetting" mark the limits of conceptualization.
Every thought-moment constitutes the arising-characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while every thought-moment returns to the cessation-characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

If one abandons arising to pursue cessation, then cessation is itself arising. Before reaching arising, there is fundamentally no arising; it is ultimately boundless. Therefore, it is said that "only cessation and..."
Birth is the limit of these formations. To flow against the current is called "entry. To be entirely one is called "union. For the essence of consciousness is originally clear and tranquil;
it becomes turbid because of the agitation caused by the preceding aggregates (*pūrvānta*). Now, as they no longer flow outwards, they are likewise all clear and tranquil.

It further merges with the substance of consciousness (*vijñāna*) to become one. Yet, there is still entry and merging; it has not yet reached the state where both "one" and "six" are forgotten, which is ultimately boundless.
Therefore it is said: "The profound entry merges with the profound, returning to the limit of consciousness."
These five aggregates originally arise in overlapping succession... (up to) knowing that there is nirvana and not longing for the three realms.
[Commentary: This answers the preceding question regarding the sudden removal and gradual severance of the five aggregates.
"Arising in overlapping succession" means arising in order from the subtle to the coarse; it is because the true mind, in a single thought-moment, follows conditions.
It transforms into the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Because of consciousness, there arise volitional formations, perception, and feeling, and subsequently form.
Now, if one were to dismantle them, one should first cease form, then cease feeling, perception, and volitional formations, and finally cease consciousness.
In birth, it proceeds from within to without, from the subtle to the coarse; in cessation, it proceeds from without to within, from the coarse to the subtle. However...
In the ultimate truth of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there are originally no five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); these five aggregates arise solely from a single moment of deluded thought.

If one can remain in a state where not even a single thought arises, the boundaries of past and future are severed. By riding upon this opening of the mind, the five layers of deluded conceptualization are simultaneously eliminated.
What sequential order could there be? It is only because, within the gateway of phenomenal appearances (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), form and mind manifest that [one speaks of stages]. When...
By investigating reality and severing delusions, they are exhausted in successive order. Regarding these Dharma gates, I have already demonstrated them to you by tying a cloth and showing the knots;
thus, the sequence of the knots being tied and untied is as clear as the analogy itself.

Therefore, you should understand this through that. Why then do you overlook that and ask again about this? You should now set it down—this concludes the exhortation to transmit and demonstrate it. Herein lies the intention.

Regarding the phrase "these [beings]," it means that they have thoroughly realized that the root-source of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is entirely illusory conceptualization and does not exist as a substantial reality;

this teaches them self-benefit. Regarding the phrase "transmitting and showing," it means causing sentient beings of the final age to all realize that the five aggregates are empty and false, whereby they will naturally come to loathe this cycle of birth and death as suffering and know that *nirvāṇa* is bliss, yet...
Furthermore, they remain attached to the three realms. This is an exhortation to benefit others. The section on the True Doctrine (Zhengzongfen) concludes here.
"Ānanda, if there were someone who filled the ten directions... [up to] ...would the merit obtained from the causes and conditions of making offerings to the Buddha be great or not?"
Commentary: This section below constitutes the *pariṇāmanā* (concluding) portion. First, the World-Honored One cites his own merits to serve as a standard for comparison.

This is because the empty space of the ten directions is fundamentally without limit; this is used to manifest that the seven treasures filling the void are likewise immeasurable. The atoms of the *dharmadhātu* are fundamentally inexhaustible;
this is used to manifest that the Buddhas, numbering as many as those atoms, are likewise inexhaustible. [The text continues: "To uphold, receive, and serve..."
"Those who" refers to those who offer the seven treasures, filling the void, as an act of veneration to all Buddhas.

"With hearts that do not allow for a single vain passing" means that toward Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, there is not one who is left out. The phrase "this person" and following serves to compare and measure their merit.
Ānanda replied: "Space is inexhaustible... how could this merit have any limit? (Commentary:
This Venerable One establishes the immeasurability [of the merit]. The two lines beginning with "Space" cite the preceding text to state that the wealth [offered] was superior.
The passage beginning with "In the past... cites an inferior case to manifest the superiority [of the present one]; it refers to the offering of seven coins to a single Buddha.)
When both the material offerings and the field of merit are inferior, one still obtains the superior retribution of a Wheel-Turning King;

how much more so when the offerings are manifest and vast as space—this describes the superiority of the material offerings—and when the Buddha-fields are all-pervasive—this describes the superiority of the field of merit—and when precious jewels are bestowed upon both—this describes the superiority of both the material gifts and the field.
As for the phrase "exhausting the kalpas," it determines that the merit obtained is such that it cannot even be conceived by the mind or discussed in words.
How much less could one seek its ultimate limit?
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas... [up to] ...directly achieve Bodhi, with no further demonic activities.
(Commentary on the Preface: This compares the merit of propagating the Dharma as superior to the merit of bestowing material wealth. Regarding the passage beginning with "The Buddha told": first,

This clarifies that the Buddha’s words are true, so as to cause others to believe them with certainty. "If there should be another person" means, hypothetically speaking, that there might be such a person.
"One who possesses the four grave offenses" means that they have committed all four—namely, sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying. These constitute the ten *pārājika* offenses.
The ten evil grave offenses are the ultimate causes of evil. "In a mere instant" means that one is on the very verge of falling [into hell].
"The Avīci hells of the ten directions" refers to the ultimate fruit of evil.

"One who can propagate this sutra with a single thought" refers to such a person on the brink of falling who merely gives rise to the aspiration for a brief moment, without it having lasted long. This Dharma-gate refers to the entire sutra.

That which is expounded here does not go beyond the Dharma-gate of the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama, the method for penetrating deeply into perfect penetration. During the final age— specifically the latter five hundred years,

a time when the sages are distant and demons are powerful— for those who are unlearned, meaning those of initial capacity who find it difficult to progress, the karmic obstacles of their transgressions—
the heavy retributions for the aforementioned four grave offenses and ten evil deeds— shall be extinguished at the mere thought [of this teaching].
This means that by a single thought of widely propagating the sutras, all [obstacles] shall be extinguished. Regarding the phrase "transforming what lies below":
it does not merely extinguish evil karma, but can also transform the causes of extreme suffering into the fruit of ultimate bliss.

Indeed, the reason why even a minute merit of a single thought can transcend hell and lead to rebirth in a Land of Bliss is precisely because all phenomena are manifested solely by the mind. One who attains...
[The Master] Fuxia said: "Furthermore, it is not merely that one leaves suffering behind to attain happiness; rather, the merit one performs surpasses that of the former person.

Even if one were to fill the void with the seven treasures and offer them to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of dust, the degree by which this merit surpasses the former would not be merely one or two times greater—it would be hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, billions of times greater, even beyond what can be calculated. If...

The fruit [of this practice] is that this sutra can reveal the secret treasury of the Tathāgata; thus, the dharma-wealth of merit is fundamentally all-pervasive, and the adornments of blessings and wisdom are everywhere abundant.
Only then does one believe that the Buddha speaks no falsehoods, for among all forms of giving, the gift of material wealth is the most inferior.
"Ānanda," and so forth below, clarifies that those who are free from transgression and can uphold this sutra and its mantras will possess immeasurable merit.
